decisions.title: Devtools presence in release builds
decisions.gist: Choose which files and routes a shipped build includes for Jet devtools.
decisions.lesson: Jet devtools are panels, event facts, route descriptions, and request handlers for inspecting programs. A native build is a compiled program, an interpreter runs source through Jet, and a web artifact is browser or server output. A stream is the event path, and a panel is the view. This choice decides whether shipped files include these pieces and whether a deployed service can be read during an incident. A release can omit everything, keep a local same-user rail, add a protected endpoint, or carry everything; CSR-only output has no endpoint.
decisions.explainer:
Devtools have four pieces: panel functions, event-stream code, route descriptions, and endpoint handlers. A removes all four. B removes panels and routes and keeps a proposed local value rail beside the ratified `jet inspect live <pid>` scheduler rail. It adds the endpoint only when `build.release.inspect: .ReadOnly` is written; deployment then needs `JET_INSPECT=1` and `JET_INSPECT_TOKEN`. C keeps all four in every server-hosted release, but deployment still needs those two settings to enable requests.

A site is the source call that publishes a fact. Before publication, a queue count stays inside the process. After `devtools.publish(..., value: waiting, field: .waiting)`, a reader may see `waiting: 12`; no `value:` means no value leaves the process. `#PII` and `#Credential` values are refused at publish time.
decisions.story: Taylor Otwell deploys an orders service built with the defaults. During a payment timeout he opens a shell inside the service's container as the service user and runs `jet inspect live <pid>`. He reads request duration and waiting-work counts with no rebuild, no restart, and no network route. His team later builds with `inspect: .ReadOnly` and sets `JET_INSPECT=1` plus `JET_INSPECT_TOKEN`, so the operator network can read the same facts remotely.
decisions.detail: Owner tradeoff pass, 2026-09-02: option B now adds a bounded local value rail to release, as a named amendment to D-OBSERVE-LIVE1. `jet inspect live <pid>` then answers an incident on the host with no rebuild, no restart, and no route, while the network endpoint stays build-gated and token-gated.

options.name: Compile out every release
options.detail: Every shipped artifact omits panel functions, event facts, route descriptions, and endpoint handlers. A native service, interpreter run, and web output all lack the route, so `curl` gets `404`; operators use ordinary logs or metrics. The gain is no production devtools code or request surface. The loss is that an incident cannot turn on inspection; Taylor must use existing telemetry or rebuild.
options.technical: Apply one compile-time stripping rule to AOT, `jet run`, the interpreter, and web artifacts. Remove panel functions, event-stream code, route descriptions, and endpoint handlers from native and web server outputs. CSR-only web bundles also pass the stripping check. No `JET_INSPECT` setting or token can restore code that is absent.

options.name: Strip by default; a local same-user rail always; a protected network endpoint only when built in
options.detail:
Choosing B ratifies a local value rail in release, as an amendment to D-OBSERVE-LIVE1. `value:` facts land in a new bounded `published` section of the same-user, mode-0600 snapshot that `jet inspect live <pid>` reads. The writer sleeps until the same user asks: `jet inspect live <pid>` sends the runtime's reserved wake signal, the process writes bounded snapshots while reads continue, and stops soon after. So Taylor reads queue facts during an incident from a shell in the service's container, with no rebuild, no restart, and no network route.

The network endpoint is unchanged. It exists only when the `build.release` profile writes `inspect: .ReadOnly`, and it answers only with `JET_INSPECT=1` and `JET_INSPECT_TOKEN`, loopback by default, GET only, published values only. `inspect: .None` strips the value rail and its writer; the ratified scheduler rail stays opt-in through `--observe` as today. CSR-only web output carries neither and passes the stripping check.
options.technical:
The `inspect` field lives inside the existing `build.release: Build{...}` profile. Values: `.Local` (proposed default: value slots, the `published` writer, and the wake handler stay; no route), `.ReadOnly` (adds the endpoint code), `.None` (strips the value rail). `jet inspect gates run.jet` lists the field; the release receipt lists carried code. Choosing B ratifies `.Local` as the default that every release carries.

Snapshot: `published` is a new section under a bumped `schema_version`; the ratified reader rejects it today and gains validation, bounds, and per-value freshness. Slots are preallocated: at most 64 values per process. Fixed-size copyable values are stored directly; text is copied into a 256-byte slot and truncated with a flag; writes go under a sequence lock, with no allocation on the publish path. The publish sink joins the taint lattice, so `#PII` and `#Credential` values are E0722 there.

Wake: the runtime reserves SIGUSR2 on Unix and a per-user named event on Windows; `core.os` refuses a user handler on it with a diagnostic. The handler only sets an atomic flag. A runtime thread then writes one bounded snapshot per 100 ms for ten seconds after the last read and exits; wakes are limited to one per second. Readers share the process's PID and mount namespaces, through `docker exec` or `kubectl exec`; a host-side helper is not part of B.

Checks: same-uid, mode-0600, freshness, and start-identity checks are the Linux ones today. On macOS, owner and start-time checks are added. On Windows, the event and file are restricted to the user's SID. A platform without an equivalent fails closed. The endpoint accepts GET only and returns only published values; passing an event does not publish its other fields. Deploy must set `JET_INSPECT=1` and secret `JET_INSPECT_TOKEN`; either missing setting refuses access, and deploy settings cannot add code absent from the artifact.

Loopback, the service host itself, is the default. Non-loopback needs a `.ReadOnly` build and the token. Without the token the response is `HTTP/2 401 Unauthorized` with {"error":"JET_INSPECT_TOKEN required"}. An address outside the deployment's allow-list gets 403; a `.Local` build answers 404 because no route exists. Apply to AOT, `jet run`, the interpreter, and SSR hosts; CSR bundles get the stripping check (I9).

options.name: Carry authenticated devtools in every release
options.detail: Every server-hosted release carries panel functions, event facts, route descriptions, and endpoint handlers. Deployment still needs `JET_INSPECT=1` and `JET_INSPECT_TOKEN` to enable requests, but the route and code remain in the artifact when disabled. Operators can inspect without a rebuild when the deployment settings are present. Attackers can discover the route and probe authentication in every release. This avoids the build-time incident gap, but every release carries more code and a standing route to protect.
options.technical: Keep endpoint code in AOT, `jet run`, the interpreter, and SSR web outputs without a build field. Apply B's GET-only authentication, publication, taint, and network checks at runtime. Deployment still needs `JET_INSPECT=1` and `JET_INSPECT_TOKEN` for a `200` response. Server output includes the generated `__jet_devtools` route. A CSR-only web artifact cannot host a server endpoint and carries no endpoint handler, so it receives the stripping check.

comparisons.note: Telescope defaults to local-only access, uses `viewTelescope` for non-local access, and prunes stored data with `telescope:prune --hours=48`. This supports B's loopback default and explicit operator gate; its dashboard storage is outside this choice.

LiveDashboard keeps development routes inside `if Mix.env() == :dev` and uses an authenticated production pipeline. This supports A and B's separate build and deploy boundaries. Its proxy requirement for WebSocket upgrades adds a deployment failure that this read-only endpoint does not need.
comparisons.code:
if Mix.env() == :dev do
  scope "/" do
    pipe_through :browser
    live_dashboard "/dashboard"
  end
end

pipeline :admins_only do
  plug :fetch_current_admin
  plug :require_authenticated_admin
end

scope "/" do
  pipe_through [:browser, :admins_only]
  live_dashboard "/dashboard"
end

comparisons.note: Actuator exposes only `health` over HTTP by default, supports include and exclude controls, and sanitizes values. Its exposure setting changes at runtime without rebuilding. B differs on purpose: its build fact controls code presence, while deploy settings only enable code already shipped.
comparisons.code:
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info
management.endpoints.web.exposure.exclude=env
management.endpoints.access.max-permitted=read-only
management.endpoint.env.show-values=when-authorized

comparisons.note: The Vite plugin removes devtools from production by default, and its docs call `removeDevtoolsOnBuild: false` not recommended. This supports A's absence and B's safe default. B adds a server-only opt-in path with two deploy checks.

recommendation.why: B keeps the normal artifact stripped of any route and still answers an incident on the host through a local value rail, with no rebuild or restart. The build fact says whether endpoint code can exist and deployment settings say whether it is enabled. Beginners write nothing and get the local rail. Experts see the gate with `jet inspect gates`, write `inspect: .ReadOnly` for remote reads, or refuse the rail with `inspect: .None`. The endpoint still needs both deploy values, defaults to loopback, and returns only explicit untainted `value:` facts.
recommendation.tradeoff: Remote reads still need the build fact, both deploy values, a protected token, and any allow-list; a local read needs a shell in the service's container as the service user. Every default release carries the value slots and a signal handler, which is the amendment the owner is choosing. The rebuild during an incident is gone.

whyNot.reason: A gives the strongest artifact isolation, but it also removes the local rail, so an incident on the host cannot be inspected without a rebuild and redeploy of a development artifact. B answers the incident on the host and keeps the network surface exactly as small as A's.

C lets a prepared deployment enable inspection without rebuilding, but every server-hosted release retains the route and code. A scanner can discover and probe that route even while `JET_INSPECT` is off, so C carries a larger standing exposure than B's default, which has no route at all.

hybrid.synthesis: Keep A's compile-time stripping of every route by default. Add a local value rail in release, as an amendment to D-OBSERVE-LIVE1, so `jet inspect live <pid>` answers on the host with no rebuild. Use the existing `build.release` profile with proposed `inspect: .ReadOnly` for the endpoint; `.None` strips the rail. Require deploy-time `JET_INSPECT=1` and secret `JET_INSPECT_TOKEN`; bind to loopback unless a token-backed allow-list is declared. Return only explicit `value:` facts, refuse `#PII` and `#Credential` at publish time, and strip CSR-only web output.

harvest.use: Strip panel, stream, route, and handler code from every tier; keep only the local rail's value slots and writer by default.
Answer on the host through `jet inspect live <pid>`; use `.ReadOnly` at build time and `JET_INSPECT=1` plus `JET_INSPECT_TOKEN` at deployment for remote reads.
Keep GET-only auth, network, publication, and taint checks wherever a server carries the endpoint; retain no CSR endpoint.

reviewPasses.base: Base draft separated compile-time stripping, manifest-gated endpoint shipping, and always-present runtime protection. Each option showed release contents, operator visibility, attacker reach, and a concrete incident.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: Boil-the-ocean pass tested `.NET Aspire` token protection, Rails loopback defaults, and Spring Actuator runtime exposure. It kept their network and auth lessons but rejected runtime-only exposure because the build fact must control code presence.
reviewPasses.hybrid: Hybrid pass combined A's absent-by-default artifact with C's GET-only authentication and deployment checks, keeping B because only the build fact controls whether endpoint code exists. The owner's tradeoff pass added a bounded local value rail in release so an incident needs no rebuild.
reviewPasses.cooperative: Cooperative pass strengthened A with cross-tier stripping and C with server-only endpoint wording, network checks, and exact refusal output. B now names its rebuild cost, site publication rule, taint refusals, and CSR stripping check.
reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: Rli5Devtools. Skill: rli5. The first pass found unclear release terms and unexplained request results; both repaired. The second found `jet inspect gates` without its entry file, a bare object where the envelope prints, and `.None` silencing a rail it does not own; all repaired in B.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Anthropic. Adversarial model family: OpenAI. The first full pass was authored by OpenAI and attacked by Anthropic, which added deploy gating, taint rules, and tier parity. The second, on the owner's revision, found the value rail called ratified, an unsafe signal protocol, an unbounded slot claim, and a namespace gap; B now names the amendment and bounds each.

decisions.title: What a running app keeps after you save code
decisions.gist: Choose what a running web page, server, game, or command-line app keeps after you save code.
decisions.lesson: Priya saves a change while her app is open. The browser may hold a draft note, scroll position, and focus; the server may hold a connection and a counter; a game may hold its world. One choice keeps each item when its live data matches the new code, one keeps browser items only, and one resets all items. A `#Persist` mark tells Jet to try to carry an item through a server or game restart. The report names each kept or reset item.
decisions.explainer: When Priya saves code while her app is open, Jet checks current information before replacing code. One choice keeps information when its shape matches, one does this only in the browser, and one starts everything again. A number can stay a number, so its value can stay. If a number changes to text, Jet uses a written conversion rule or restarts the app part that owns it, then says why. The terminal transcript shows what stayed and reset. The devtools build view will show the same report once D-DX-DEVTOOLS-UX1 ratifies.
decisions.story: Priya Nair is fixing a checkout page while a test order is open. She types `Late shipment`, scrolls to the payment form, submits once, and sees count 1. She saves the form code, submits again, and wants the browser note and scroll, the server connection and counter, and a game's world to remain. This choice also covers a command-line app waiting for input.

options.name: Keep matching state everywhere
options.detail: After each save, Jet checks each current item. A number can stay a number, so its value stays; changing that number to text uses a written conversion or restarts only its owner. One rule covers browser pages, servers, games, and command-line programs, and the terminal transcript reports each kept or reset item.
options.technical:
The reload unit is one module. A type-stable edit commits in place. Type stability compares the ordered signature tuple, including parameter order. Compatibility is a recursive live-payload check against the new type layout, not a declared-type name comparison. A changed type uses a `#Persist` conversion rule or restarts its owner with a written reason.

Already-captured function values are rebound to the new code by symbol identity in both web and native code. A capture whose function was removed forces the announced restart. In-flight requests complete on the old code, new requests use the new code, and the swap point is announced. Server functions rebind before the browser module swap resumes. Form and mount registrations change in that order.

The terminal transcript lists kept and reset values; the devtools build view does the same once D-DX-DEVTOOLS-UX1 ratifies. Kept and reset lines use the watcher's exempt dev-tool channel, not program output. The reload channel is loopback only and carries a build identity that the runtime verifies before applying code. See the proposed `jet explain --reload` report. Spell the policy with `--swap` or `--restart`. Refuse watching with `--watch=off`. These flags are optional controls, not ballot choices.
options.code:
SHARED SCENARIO: see `inWild` for the form, counter, and first submit.

// proposed: browser module swap keeps accepted state
EDIT
server_count += 1
becomes
server_count += 2

AFTER SAVE WITH A
terminal transcript: kept note, scroll, focus, connection, server_count; reset=none
browser: note=Late shipment; scroll=420; focus=note; count=1
server: connection=open; server_count=1
next submit: browser count=3; server_count=3

TYPE EDIT
server_count: Int -> String
terminal transcript: reset server_count; reason=Int -> String
only server_count restarts; other kept items remain

$ jet explain --reload
reload: why server_count reset
$ jet dev examples/apps/feedback/run.jet --restart
restart: all values reset
$ jet dev examples/apps/feedback/run.jet --swap
swap: refuse incompatible edit
$ jet dev examples/apps/feedback/run.jet --watch=off
watch: off

options.name: Keep browser state only
options.detail: A web save keeps the draft, scroll, and focus when the changed code is accepted. A server or game restarts, then restores only items marked `#Persist`; its listener, open connection, and unmarked state are lost. A web type change reloads the page, and a native type change gives a written restart reason.
options.technical:
The web boundary keeps signals, saved browser data, form drafts, scroll, and focus when the changed code is accepted.

Native servers and games close, rebuild, and restore only `#Persist` items after a recursive live-payload check against the new type layout; it does not compare declared type names. The check uses the ordered signature tuple, so changing parameter order is not treated as unchanged.

An accepted web swap rebinds stored function values by symbol identity; a removed function causes a page reload. Listeners and requests already being handled reset. The terminal transcript lists kept and reset values; the devtools build view does the same once D-DX-DEVTOOLS-UX1 ratifies. `--restart`, `--swap`, and `--watch=off` remain optional controls.
options.code:
SHARED SCENARIO: see `inWild` for the form, counter, and first submit.

// proposed: browser-only module swap
AFTER A WEB SAVE
terminal transcript: kept note, scroll, focus
browser: note=Late shipment; scroll=420; focus=note; count=1

AFTER A NATIVE SAVE
native: restart; kept #Persist server_count=1
native: reset listener and open connection

TYPE EDIT
web: page reload; note=empty; scroll=0; focus=body
native: restart with written reason
next submit after web reload: count=2
$ jet dev examples/apps/feedback/run.jet --restart
restart: native values reset

options.name: Reload everything
options.detail: Every save closes the old app and opens a new one, or reloads the page. No current item crosses that boundary, including a form draft, connection, game world, or item marked `#Persist`. The result is easy to predict, but every edit starts from empty state.
options.technical: The process and browser page always restart after a clean build. Signals, saved browser data, form drafts, scroll, focus, listeners, connections, and `#Persist` state reset. A type change has the same clean boundary as a function edit. `--restart` and `--watch=off` make the reset policy explicit.
options.code:
SHARED SCENARIO: see `inWild` for the form, counter, and first submit.

AFTER SAVE WITH C
terminal transcript: reset note, scroll, focus, connection, server_count
browser: note=empty; scroll=0; focus=body; count=0
server: connection=closed; server_count=0
next submit after clean start: count=2

TYPE EDIT
terminal transcript: clean restart; all values reset
$ jet dev examples/apps/feedback/run.jet --watch=off
watch: off; one clean run

comparisons.note: Flutter debug hot reload injects updated Dart, rebuilds the widget tree, preserves current state, and does not rerun `main` or `initState`. Hot restart reruns the app and loses state, while native edits need a full restart. The census sample `Reloaded 1 of 448 libraries in 978ms` measures one reload, not a universal speed promise. Source: https://docs.flutter.dev/tools/hot-reload.

Vite serves native ESM and sends changed modules through the dependency graph instead of rebuilding the whole app. State survives only when the module graph accepts the update; an unaccepted chain falls back to a page reload. The local census benchmark measured ten warm page reloads on 2026-08-27: Vite 54.9 ms versus Jet 561.5 ms. Source: https://vite.dev/guide/features.html.

`dotnet watch` applies supported edits with Hot Reload and restarts unsupported edits. `Ctrl+R` forces a rebuild and restart, while a rude edit prompts `y`, `n`, `a`, or `v`. The census records response compression as a case that can block script injection. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/tools/dotnet-watch.
comparisons.code:
$ dotnet watch
edit: supported -> process continues
edit: rude -> y / n / a / v
$ Ctrl+R
rebuild and restart

comparisons.note: `Ctrl+Alt+F11` invokes Live Coding while the editor, PIE session, or attached desktop game continues. Reflected objects can be reinstanced, but existing objects do not receive `.cpp` constructor defaults; `.h` defaults do apply. Structural edits can crash without reinstancing and pointer cleanup, and consoles or mobile are outside this path. Source: https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/using-live-coding-to-recompile-unreal-engine-applications-at-runtime.

Elm turns input into a `Msg`, `update` returns a `Model`, and `view` renders it. The Model is the state carried between messages. Its debugger concept pauses model history, rewinds, replays, and can swap code into paused state. Current `elm-reactor` documentation warns that the historical debugger is unavailable during redesign, so that history path is not a current guarantee. Sources: https://guide.elm-lang.org/architecture/buttons#the-elm-architecture and https://github.com/elm-lang/elm-reactor#readme.
comparisons.code:
type Msg = Increment

update msg model =
    case msg of
        Increment ->
            model + 1

view model =
    text (String.fromInt model)

// Model survives each message update

recommendation.why: A keeps Priya's note and scroll, the server connection and counter, and a game world when their live data matches the new code. It uses one announced keep-or-reset rule for browser pages, servers, games, and command-line apps. Ratifying the law now while a web mechanism is delivered is a delivery order, not a different policy.

whyNot.reason: B makes web edits pleasant, but a native restart closes the server connection and loses unmarked game state. Only a value marked `#Persist` returns after the restart. A staged choice that ratifies native preservation now and defers web swapping is a delivery order, not a fourth policy.
C is predictable, but every edit discards the form draft, scroll, focus, server connection, counter, and game world. A clean start also loses values marked `#Persist`.

recommendation.tradeoff: A changed type can force a written conversion or a restart of its owner. For example, changing a counter from a number to text resets that counter and prints the reason, while unrelated items remain.

hybrid.synthesis: Use A's common keep-or-reset rule, B's browser module boundary, and C's clean restart path. Report every decision in the terminal transcript, and add the devtools build view once D-DX-DEVTOOLS-UX1 ratifies.

harvest.use: Check live data and report every item kept or reset.
Swap accepted browser code, while native servers and games restart.
Keep full restart and watch-off as explicit exits.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one keep-or-reset rule with browser-only preservation and full reload. It used one checkout example so each choice could be read against the same save.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth pass tested Deno's file watcher and Erlang's explicit state conversion. It added failed-swap restart and state-conversion lessons to A, but not their platform-specific controls.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The combination pass kept A's one rule, B's browser boundary, and C's clean restart. It retained A because browser pages, servers, games, and command-line apps need one visible policy.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The fairness pass strengthened B with preserved browser state and explicit native reset reports, and strengthened C with clear loss reports. A still wins because it also preserves native connections and game worlds when they match the new code.
reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: Rli5Live. Skill: rli5. The beginner pass found unclear terms, incomplete state setup, and unlabeled outcomes. The ballot now explains the number-to-text rule, shows the first and second submits, and labels the terminal transcript.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: OpenAI. Adversarial model family: Anthropic. The attack found stale captured functions, request timing, client and server swap order, deep persisted data, an unnamed build surface, and an unsecured code reload path. The ballot now defines each boundary and names the ratified devtools view condition.

decisions.title: Web rendering as a compiler fact
decisions.gist: Choose how Jet selects rendering for each web route.
decisions.lesson: Rendering means creating the HTML a browser shows. A route can render in the browser (`csr`), on a server per request (`ssr`), during a build (`ssg`), in streamed pieces (`stream`), or as an interactive island (`island`). Hydration attaches browser behavior to existing HTML. An effect is work a function needs, such as `DB.Read` or `Browser`. A serializable value can cross from server to browser; a database handle cannot. An explicit escape is a route `.render(...)` override. The choice is who selects these facts and how changes stay safe.
decisions.explainer:
Today, `jet explain --web-graph` shows each route's render label, one cache setting for the app, and the effects of the work a page needs when it first appears (its mount). It does not show per-route loader or cache facts. D proposes those facts, plus effect analysis through called functions, resumable state, and reasons that the graph and Routes panel expose.

The compared frameworks rely on written rendering, cache, or boundary conventions, and none of their comparison rows shows a transitive effect proof that keeps those conventions in step with the code. When the code changes, a convention goes stale, and the result is stale output, a leaked private page, wasted JavaScript, or a runtime error. Jet already infers a checked effect set for each function; it may be empty, and known `core.db` reads contribute `DB.Read`. So the compiler holds the input those conventions stand in for.
decisions.story: Mira maintains a shop with a home page, a public product list, a product form, and private account settings. Search crawlers, programs that download pages to index them, need complete product HTML; shoppers need data in stages; and account output must never be shared between users. She wants these rules without learning four rendering systems.
decisions.detail:
Owner tradeoff pass, 2026-09-02: option D now brings each derived mode to the person through a dev note, an editor lens, and the receipt diff. It adds a hosting pin with a release-time check, so nobody has to go read the graph and no route can silently change its hosting needs.

Owner discussion pass, 2026-09-02: option D now states that a streamed route sends its pieces in page order inside one response, so a crawler needs no detection. The explainer names the failure the compared frameworks share, the cache law admits `private` on any route, the capture example stands alone, and check instructions name commands and expected output.

options.name: Explicit route modes
options.detail: The person labels each route with `.ssg()`, `.stream()`, `.island()`, or `.csr()` before registering it. Each call applies to the next route. This gives direct control over output and timing. If `/list` gains database data, an unchanged `.ssg()` label keeps the old build-time behavior until the person edits it. It does not provide compiler-derived mode changes or resumable captured state.
options.technical: Today, `App.rs` stores one render string and copies it into the next route record. Today's data and form records are zero-argument handlers. The example uses the proposed route-path form `.form("/detail", ...)` consistently. Today's runtime maps a name without `/` to `/actions/{name}` and a leading slash to the literal path. That path convention is not part of this rendering choice.

options.name: Server render and hydrate
options.detail: The person uses one server-rendered graph and hydrates interactive parts. Hydration attaches browser events and state to HTML already sent by the server. Every route receives HTML first, including list data. Static home and other noninteractive pages still receive hydration code. Cache rules stay split between server and browser settings.
options.technical: `ssr()` sets one render value before all routes, and release mode keeps server output. A `Browser` effect belongs in the hydrated client boundary; if it runs in the server page function, the compiler reports `E_WEB_SERVER_EFFECT`. The static home still downloads the hydration runtime. The example uses the same proposed route-path form for forms.

options.name: Static shell with islands
options.detail: The person writes a static shell and marks each dynamic widget as an island. Proposed boundary metadata names its owner and timing, such as server-defer, client-load, or client-visible. This keeps JavaScript small, but loader-heavy routes need special boundaries. ClientRouter navigation can run island setup again, so state and setup counts need lifecycle rules.
options.technical: `ssg()` supplies the shell. Proposed island boundaries own `/list`, `/detail`, and `/settings`, with explicit timing and serialized inputs. A private request cannot be hidden inside a shared static shell; the host must make that boundary server-rendered or private. The design carries more boundary choices than D's default.

options.name: Derived rendering with resumable islands
options.detail:
The person writes pages, loaders, and forms; a loader fetches data for one route, and a form receives submitted data. The compiler derives route output from facts. It follows the page and its helpers, unions the effects of page, layout, loader, form, and component code, and chooses how the browser receives the HTML. A loader or page with `RequestContext.Read` is never static. Output can be server HTML, streams, resumable islands, or client code, while the graph records reasons and cache safety.

For a streamed route, the server sends the page shell first, then each data section in page order inside the same response, so the browser has the whole page when sending ends. A search crawler, a program that downloads pages to index them, can wait for the end and read the complete page. Jet never has to identify crawlers or send them a separate version. If loading rows is slow, the browser shows the shell, then waits before showing those rows and anything below them.

Choosing D adds one package of proposed surfaces. `jet dev` prints the route table with mode and reason at start, and one line per route whose mode an edit changed. The editor shows the derived mode beside each `.route` line (the editor lens). The release receipt, the saved route table that `jet build --release` writes, shows a mode change in its diff. If you dislike a derived mode, add `.render("csr")` to that route; Jet accepts it only when the route's needed work allows it.

A hosting pin is a project setting that allows static hosting, server hosting, or either, and rejects a route that needs another kind. It is written in `package.jet` as `web: .{ hosting: .Static }`; `.Server` and `.Any`, the default, are the other values. A route that derives a mode outside the pin is a compile error with the reason chain.

Without a pin, a release build that changes hosting class against the last release receipt is refused until the pin is written. So a helper that starts reading the database cannot silently turn a static site into a server; a release build, in CI or anywhere, refuses the change.
options.technical:
Derivation unions transitive effects from page, layout, loader, form, and component code. The proposed `RequestContext.Read` fact covers session, cookie, auth, and per-request header reads. Any route with that fact is never static and cannot use shared immutable cache. A loader `DB.Read` gives server plus stream: HTML from the server, rows sent later in the same response. Interaction nests an island, one interactive part kept apart from the page, and a browser-only page gives client output. `jet explain --web-graph` shows `mode`, `reason`, `facts`, and `cache` for each route.

Streaming order: a streamed route flushes complete server-rendered pieces in document order inside one response. Each island's server-rendered HTML and serialized state appear at its document position before the response ends, so crawler-specific detection is unnecessary. A slow loader delays everything that follows it; D never flushes later pieces ahead of it. D keeps page pieces in top-to-bottom order; option E is the separate choice for finer component boundaries.

Caching reuses a saved response for later visitors. The proposed cache law: `immutable` never refreshes and is permitted only for static routes. `revalidate` refreshes after a freshness period and is permitted only for public server or stream routes. `private` is never shared between visitors, is allowed on any route, and is required for request-context and form routes. A proposed project policy `rendering = "explicit"` refuses derivation globally. `.render(...)` overrides one compatible route; an incompatible override emits `E_WEB_RENDER_CONFLICT`.

Resumable islands: an interactive part saves its state as transferable data once, then continues later without running its setup again. An unsupported capture reports `E_WEB_SERIALIZE_CAPTURE`. A mode change invalidates old route cache artifacts before deploy, and an incompatible cache fact emits `E_WEB_CACHE_FACT`.

Choosing D ratifies the pin field, its default `.Any`, and `E_WEB_HOSTING_PIN`. The pin is checked after derivation or an explicit `.render(...)`, which cannot bypass it; static and client modes need static hosting, while server, stream, and server-island modes need server hosting. A route-change record holds route, old mode, new mode, ordered reason chain, source span, and baseline receipt; routes are sorted and one note prints per route. Every E_WEB code is registered with What, Why, Fix, and a snapshot before use (I4).

options.name: Derived component boundaries
options.detail: The person lets the compiler derive boundaries for every interactive component, rather than one opaque island per route. A route can contain a server shell and several sibling or nested resumable islands. This can ship less JavaScript, but it adds boundary requests, ownership rules, and more lifecycle state to inspect.
options.technical: Unlike D's route-level default, E makes component boundaries the primary unit. The compiler emits one boundary for each interactive subtree and records its owner, timing, captured values, and serialized props. A `RequestContext.Read` ancestor still blocks shared static output. Many boundaries can increase requests and coordination.

comparisons.note:
The 2026-09-01 repository census praises server data, reduced client JavaScript, actions, and streamed loading. Its recorded complaints name stale cache layers, changing `_rsc` keys, and Safari streaming. This informs D's effect facts, cache law, crawler fallback, and component option.

Source: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/54075. Source: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/58723. Source: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/86538. Source: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/59167. Source: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/73537. Source: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/54514.

The 2026-09-01 repository census praises static HTML and selective hydration with local timing choices. It records script and state reinitialization after ClientRouter and freshness limits for live collections. This informs C's explicit island timing and D's resumable lifecycle.
comparisons.code:
<MyReactComponent client:load />
<MyReactComponent client:idle />
<MyReactComponent client:visible />
<SomeComponent server:defer />

comparisons.note: The 2026-09-01 repository census praises serialized listeners and state without a full hydration replay. It records unsupported class prototypes, Streams, and other serialization limits. This informs D's resume rule and registered capture diagnostic.

The 2026-09-01 repository census praises one typed router and server function graph with validation. It records the release-candidate caveat. This informs D's typed loader source and visible graph reasons. Source: https://tanstack.com/start/latest/docs/framework/react/overview.

The 2026-09-01 repository census praises visible server-only files, generated route types, and native forms with enhancement. It records generated conventions and route boundaries as teaching costs. This informs D's one graph and explicit effect facts. Sources: https://svelte.dev/docs/kit/load and https://svelte.dev/docs/kit/form-actions.

recommendation.why: D makes route data, interaction, and request-context facts compiler inputs instead of repeated labels. It produces static, server, stream, island, or client output and explains each choice. Explicit overrides, the hosting pin, and safety refusals preserve control. A streamed route sends its shell first, then the rest in order; a browser shows the shell while waiting, and a search crawler reads the complete response. Every derived choice is shown where it changes, in the dev note, the editor lens, and the receipt diff, and a hosting-class change never ships unpinned.

whyNot.reason: Manual labels give direct control, but they drift when loader or interaction facts change. Today's zero-argument data and form builders also carry no captured state for resumable islands.
B sends HTML first, then runs browser code to add clicks and state (hydration); even static pages download that extra code. Its server and browser caching rules stay separate.

Islands keep the shell small, but the person labels every island and its timing, and loader-heavy routes and private widgets need manual boundary choices. When the browser moves between C's pages, interactive code may start again, so state and setup can run twice.
Component boundaries can reduce JavaScript further, but many nested islands add requests and lifecycle coordination. E is a useful future granularity, not the simpler route-level default chosen here.

recommendation.tradeoff: The compiler, not the person, picks each route's mode. Every pick is visible at the moment it changes through the dev note, the editor lens, the receipt diff, and the hosting pin. `.render(...)` and `rendering = "explicit"` remain for people who want to choose.

hybrid.synthesis: Use D's route-level compiler derivation for normal routes, keep explicit per-route overrides, stream loader data, and resume interactive islands from serialized state. Show every derived mode where it changes: the dev note, the editor lens, the receipt diff, and the hosting pin. Keep E's component boundaries as a later opt-in extension, not the default. Record mode, reason, facts, cache policy, and serialization diagnostics in one route graph.

harvest.use: Keep `.render(...)` for experts who need a fixed compatible route mode.
Derive server output when loader data requires it, without hydrating static routes.
Derive islands for interactive subtrees and retain explicit timing when a boundary needs it.
Show mode, reason, effects, cache safety, and serialization status in the graph and Routes panel.
Keep multiple or nested islands as a later opt-in when route-level islands are too coarse.

Run `jet explain --web-graph` on the shop program and verify `/` static, `/list` server+stream, `/detail` server+island, `/settings` client, and `/account` server+island, each with its stated reason and cache fact. decisions.title: How Jet ships six web tools
decisions.gist: Choose whether Jet ships six web tools as App methods, separate packages, or one core.web suite.
decisions.lesson: Jet needs six tools. Router maps URLs. Query loads data and shows fresh, stale, fetching, or error. Forms validate and submit values. Table sorts, filters, and paginates rows. Virtual shows only viewport rows. Store keeps app state and history. Effect-tracked invalidation exists: a query refreshes when a #Transact write changes data it read. All options use it. I9 is Jet's shared-meaning rule: one Prelude definition serves browser and native. A, B, and C differ in packaging, discovery, and spelling. This changes setup, offline work, no-script forms, native rendering, and panels.
decisions.explainer:
An effect is code that reads a value. A signal is a value that notifies its readers when it changes. `app.live` records database reads. A `#Transact` groups writes and marks changed data. An intersecting query becomes stale, fetches again, and becomes fresh or error. For a carrier API, `app.subscribe` registers the source and `app.invalidate` runs after its callback changes it. The visible Queries panel says `stale → fetching → fresh` and names the changed source.

I9 is Jet's rule for shared meaning. Under A, B, or C, suite semantics live once in the Prelude; browser DOM, `TuiBackend`, and native `JetBackend` only render or marshal them. Table and Virtual use viewport-driven rows. Native virtualization is a card obligation until its browser matrix and native proof exist. Store history has a bounded dev-only ring and is removed from release builds by default.
decisions.story: Maya Chen maintains a retail order console. Router must preserve a bookmarkable filter, Query must refresh orders, Forms must accept shipping without JavaScript, Table and Virtual must handle 100,000 rows, and Store must preserve the cart during edits. This choice decides whether those tools share one model or require several bridges.

options.name: App methods for every feature
options.detail: Put Router, Query, Forms, Table, Virtual, and Store on App. Headless means these methods return typed state instead of choosing markup. The core loop is one chain, one manual bridge between features, and one page that renders the results. This preserves today's entry point, but status rules and panel registration can drift. A still uses the existing `app.live`, `#Transact`, and Prelude semantics; its difference is the App call-site shape.
options.technical: I9 applies to A: suite semantics live once in the Prelude, and browser and native hosts marshal those facts. A's methods can call the ratified `app.live` and `#Transact` footprint law, so automatic database invalidation is not unique to C. Each method still needs explicit inputs, lifecycle mapping, state links, and devtools registration. Cross-feature rules remain App-specific code rather than route-derived defaults. Virtualization is viewport-driven; native behavior and frame-budget evidence remain card obligations until proof. I6 assumes no external dependency for query, forms, tables, virtual rows, or store history.

options.name: Separate installable packages
options.detail: Install Router, Query, Forms, Table, Virtual, and Store as separate headless packages. Headless means each package returns typed state while the application chooses markup. The core loop is install needed modules, create each package's typed state manager, and write explicit bridges into App and between feature values. Every package shares core.reactive signals and Prelude semantics, but package discovery, versioning, and panel registration are separate. This gives independent module releases and strong boundaries, at the cost of setup and repeated cross-feature wiring.
options.technical: I9 applies to B: packages marshal one Prelude meaning for browser and native hosts and do not define a competing semantic engine. Query packages call ratified `app.live` for DB.Read and use `app.subscribe` and `app.invalidate` for outside sources. Packages share core.reactive signal values and map events to the common devtools protocol, while each package owns registration and release versioning. Cross-feature rules remain explicit application bridges. Virtualization is viewport-driven; native parity is a card obligation until proof. I6 assumes no external dependency for the six mechanisms.

options.name: One core.web suite on shared signals
options.detail: Ship Router, Query, Forms, Table, Virtual, and Store in core.web on one core.reactive signal model and one devtools contract per module. Headless means modules return typed state instead of choosing markup. The core loop is define routes and input structs, derive defaults, selectively import modules, and override policy with one configuration object. This gives one path from route facts to invalidation, form state, table state, store history, and panels.
options.technical:
I9 applies to C: suite semantics live once in the Prelude, so browser DOM, TuiBackend, and native JetBackend serving share meaning. Router derives path and search data from the App graph. Forms derive editable fields from a dedicated input struct, with explicit configuration for renamed, excluded, or computed fields. Query uses the existing effect-tracked `app.live` for DB.Read only, with `app.subscribe` and `app.invalidate` for outside sources. Every option has this invalidation law.

`#Transact` intersections produce fresh, stale, fetching, and error states, while offline mutations queue. Table and Virtual consume a headless `List<T>` row model with viewport-driven virtualization. Native virtualization is a card obligation until proof, not a present fact. Store records a bounded history ring in `jet dev` and strips history capture from release builds by default.

Beginners inspect defaults with `jet explain --web-graph examples/features/web/web_app.jet`. Experts spell `web.SuiteConfig{...}` or refuse defaults with `settings: { web_suite_defaults: false }` in `package.jet`. I6 assumes no external dependency for the six mechanisms.

comparisons.note: The praised shape infers params, search, context, loader data, and navigation targets from a route tree. Its route loop uses loaderDeps and router.invalidate. The census complaint is missing edit-to-see latency data and copied file conventions that create a second graph. Source: https://tanstack.com/router/latest/docs/overview.

The praised shape gives zero-configuration caching, background refresh, mutation states, suspense, and offlineFirst mode. Its recorded complaint is manual queryKey and invalidateQueries bookkeeping. Jet applies effect footprints to DB-backed queries and keeps explicit keys through app.subscribe and app.invalidate for outside sources. Source: https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework/react/overview.

The praised shape is headless: useForm, named form.Field, subscriptions, and debounced async validators leave markup to the app. The census complaint is setup for field wiring and accessibility because the app owns markup and CSS. Jet derives fields from an input struct while keeping the headless boundary. Source: https://tanstack.com/form/latest/docs/overview.

The praised shape keeps rows, columns, state, and events headless, so the app controls markup and accessibility. The census complaint is setup around stable data, accessors, row models, and manual sorting. Jet keeps typed List<T> and derives safe columns. Source: https://tanstack.com/table/v8/docs/introduction.

The praised shape needs only count, scroll element, estimate size, total size, and virtual items, so large lists stay renderer-independent. The census complaint is that the app owns measurement, scroll wiring, item markup, and accessibility. Jet pairs it with Table and a viewport panel. Source: https://tanstack.com/virtual/latest/docs/introduction.

comparisons.note: The praised shape is a small framework-agnostic store with createStore, setState, and subscriptions. The census names derived stores, batching, and cleanup as useful composition. Jet adds bounded transaction history and time travel through the shared devtools contract. Source: https://tanstack.com/store/latest/docs/overview.

The praised shape makes server data, client islands, loading UI, actions, and cache directives visible in route files. The census complaint records stale cache layers, varying _rsc keys, cache opt-out requests, and iOS hydration delay outside Suspense. Jet keeps cache identity and render reasons in its graph. recommendation.why:
Option C wins because one core.reactive primitive serves all six modules, each module has one devtools contract, and I9 keeps suite meaning once in the Prelude for browser and native serving. Beginners get defaults from the route graph and input structs, while named core.web modules remain selectively importable.

Automatic database invalidation is not C's exclusive mechanism: A and B can call ratified `app.live` with `#Transact`, and outside sources still use `app.subscribe` and `app.invalidate`. See defaults with `jet explain --web-graph examples/features/web/web_app.jet`, spell them with `web.SuiteConfig{...}`, or set `settings: { web_suite_defaults: false }` in project manifest `package.jet`.

whyNot.reason: A remains familiar and can use the same `app.live`, `#Transact`, and Prelude semantics. It loses because six App methods scatter status rules and panel wiring, so cross-feature defaults, offline queues, and explicit native proof require separate App connections.

B is a strong package design: every package shares core.reactive signals and Prelude semantics, and each can provide complete feature behavior. It loses because discovery, versioning, panel registration, and cross-feature links spread across packages instead of one route-derived suite contract.

recommendation.tradeoff: C ties six module contracts to one shared suite and an owner ratification cadence. Per-module API ballots still let modules move separately, but package boundaries cannot provide independent semantic release schedules.

hybrid.synthesis: Keep C's one core.web suite, one core.reactive signal model, and one devtools contract per module. Expose named core.web.router, core.web.query, core.web.forms, core.web.table, core.web.virtual, and core.web.store imports for selective use, while every module remains Prelude-backed. This is C's code shape, not a fourth option.

harvest.aspect: Its App call site is compact.
harvest.use: Keep route, page, action, form, and data registration methods as the small application entry layer.

harvest.aspect: Its modules have clear names and can be added by need.
harvest.use: Expose named core.web modules and selective imports without separate state models, semantic engines, or panel protocols.

harvest.aspect: It shares route facts, signals, invalidation, and panels.
harvest.use: Make this the suite contract, derive beginner defaults from types, and keep explicit configuration for experts.
