decisions.title: Named non-returning contract: may a function declare `Never` as its return type?
decisions.gist: Whether a function can say in its signature that it never returns.
decisions.lesson: Some functions never come back. They stop the program, raise a panic, or loop forever. Today Jet knows this fact only inside the compiler, and a signature cannot say it. D-NEVER1 chose that compiler-only fact and wrote that a named contract would need a later ballot. This is that ballot. The name `Never` already exists on the failure side of a result, as in `Int !Never`, an `Int` that cannot fail.
decisions.story: Sam writes a command-line tool. He has a helper `usage()` that prints the usage text and exits the process with failure code 2. He wants `n :: Int.parse(arg) ?? usage()` to compile, and he wants people who read his library to see that `usage` never returns. Today he writes `fn usage() Never` by guess, and the compiler crashes instead of answering.
decisions.detail:
Two spellings matter here. `T !E` is a result type: it holds a `T` on success or an `E` on failure. `A ?? B` is a fallback: it uses `B` when `A` fails or is empty. `Unit` is the type of a function that returns nothing useful. A value join is any place where two paths must agree on one type: an `if` used as a value, the arms of a match, or the two sides of `??`.

This choice covers the return slot only, including the return slot of a function type such as `fn() Never`. `Never` as a parameter, field, or stored value stays an error under every option. Using `Never` as a generic type argument is out of scope and would need its own ballot. This ballot does not reopen `!Never` or process exit codes. The bug card #2431 fixes the compiler-only fact first and is not blocked by this ballot.

options.name: Inferred only: finish D-NEVER1=C
options.detail: The compiler works out by itself that `usage` never returns, and every call site may use that fact. Nobody writes `Never` on the return side. Writing it gives a clear error. Gain: nothing to learn. Loss: a library cannot promise the fact in its signature. A change to a body silently changes what callers may write, and only the caller finds out.
options.technical:
Sema computes one always-diverges fact per function from its body. A function diverges when every path ends in `panic`, `return`, `break`, `next`, a Never-typed Core call, a proven bare infinite loop, or a call to an always-diverging function. Value joins and `??` fallbacks use the fact. `Never` in a success return or parameter position is a registered diagnostic.

The published API record (`ApiFreeze`) must serialize the fact next to inferred effects. Then the publish gate (E1218, E2601) can treat a lost fact as a breaking change; today the record does not carry it. `jet doc` shows the inferred fact.

options.name: Declared `Never` return, inference stays
options.detail: A function may write `Never` as its return type. The compiler then checks that every path really stops. Functions without the word keep the inferred behavior from option A, so beginners never need to write it. A public function that always stops without the word gets a gentle lint. Gain: a visible promise in the signature that the compiler enforces at the author's desk, and generated docs show it. Loss: an existing name gains a second position.
options.technical:
No new spelling: `Never` already exists as the failure-domain name (`TYPE_NEVER` in Syntax.rs); the return position gains a ratified meaning under this id. Legal forms: `fn usage() Never`, `fn serve(addr: String) Never !NetError`, and function types `fn() Never`. Illegal: `x: Never` parameters, fields, stored values, and generic arguments (`call<Never>(f)`).

Sema requires every path of a declared function to diverge. Three exits count as returning and are each diagnosed with their span: falling off the end, a bare `return`, and `return value`. A typed failure exit (`return Err(e)`) is valid, because the failure side is not the return side. A bare `loop { }` with no `break` satisfies an expected `Never`; this narrowly amends the E0073 loop-value rule for that case only.

Calls: a completed call to `fn f() Never !E` has failed, so `f() ?? x` always yields `x`, and the success side is eliminated. Function values typed `fn() Never` reject a returning function at the assignment. Trait methods declared `Never` bind implementations to the same check. Unannotated functions keep inference from option A, and `ApiFreeze` serializes both declared and inferred facts.

options.name: Declared `Never` required across package boundaries
options.detail: Inside one package this works like option B. A function from another package counts as never-returning only when its signature says `Never`. Gain: every promise that crosses a package edge is written down, and a body-only edit in a library can never change a caller's types. Loss: a library author who forgets the word takes the benefit away from every user. The language then has two rules for one fact. The rival-family review preferred this option for the cross-package reason.
options.technical: Inference is scoped to the current package. Imported functions contribute a divergence fact only from an explicit `Never` return type. A public function whose body always diverges without the word gets an advisory lint so the omission is visible to the author. `ApiFreeze` needs no new field, because only declared return types cross the edge.

comparisons.note: Rust merged `!` (its name for this type) for version 1.100 after ten years and five attempts. Before that, libraries used the empty enum `Infallible` as a stand-in, and reconciling the two took a breaking change across every edition. The audience of the mined video repeatedly asked for a searchable name instead of a symbol.
comparisons.code:
fn usage() -> ! { std::process::exit(2) }
fn serve() -> Result<!, NetError> { loop { accept()? } }

comparisons.note: TypeScript has `never`. It infers `never` for function expressions but not for function declarations, so a declared `function fail() { throw … }` is typed `void` and callers must annotate. That split is a recorded source of confusion; option B avoids it by inferring and declaring with one rule.
comparisons.code: function usage(): never { throw new Error("usage") }

comparisons.note: Swift `Never` and Kotlin `Nothing` are declared return types with the same meaning. Neither infers the fact for an unannotated function.
comparisons.code:
func usage() -> Never { exit(2) }
fun usage(): Nothing = exitProcess(2)

recommendation.why: Beginners learn nothing new, because inference stays. Library authors get a promise the compiler checks where the mistake is made, and readers see it in the signature. No new word enters the language, because `Never` already names the failure side. Jet already publishes inferred effects across package edges, so publishing the inferred fact follows the same road.

whyNot.reason: A library cannot state the fact, and the compiler cannot warn an author who breaks the promise by accident. Only callers find out.

The written promise at package edges punishes one forgotten word. Users lose the benefit, and the language carries two rules for one fact. The lint in B gives authors the same nudge without the second rule.

recommendation.tradeoff: `Never` now appears in two positions, the failure side and the return side. The docs must teach both as one idea: this side produces no value. The published API record must learn to carry the inferred fact before the publish gate can protect it.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared inference only, a declared `Never` return with inference kept, and a declared `Never` required at package edges. The parse-or-die helper is the shared program.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a `!` symbol, an effect-style marker, `Never` in parameters and generics, and empty enums as the only uninhabited types. None became an option: the symbol was declined in D-NEVER1, the marker duplicates a type fact, generics lack evidence, and empty enums are Rust's `Infallible` mistake.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review found option B is already the hybrid: inference for beginners and a checked declaration for experts. Adding C's package-edge rule added a second rule with no safety gain, so it was not merged.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened A with `jet doc` output and a publish-gate rule, and strengthened C with an advisory lint for a public function that always diverges without the word. That lint was adopted into B.
reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: NeverBeginner. Skill: rli5. The pass found `Int !Never`, `??`, `Unit`, and "value join" undefined and asked for valid and invalid positions side by side; all four were repaired and the beginner picked B.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: GPT-5.6. The rival preferred C because inferred facts do not yet cross package edges; the author repaired every attacked seam in B, recorded the dissent on C, and kept B.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Prove every case on AOT (`jet build`), the default tier (`jet run`), and the pure interpreter (`jet eval`). The parse-or-die helper works in `??`, in an `if` value branch, and in a match arm. A declared `Never` with a falling-off, bare-return, or value-return path is rejected with the registered diagnostic and its span. `return Err(e)` inside `Never !E` is accepted.

`f() ?? x` on a `Never !E` function always yields `x`. `Never` in a parameter, field, or generic argument is rejected. A returning function assigned to `fn() Never` is rejected. A trait method declared `Never` binds its implementations. A bare `loop { }` satisfies `Never`. `#Test` bodies and the web tier agree. `jet doc` shows the contract. `ApiFreeze` carries the fact, and the publish gate flags its removal.

decisions.title: Mixed-type operands: one rule for `money * 3`, `v * 2.0`, and `2.0 * v`
decisions.gist: How an operator works when its two sides have different types, for user types and for Core vectors.
decisions.lesson: Today an operator hook, the function the compiler runs for a symbol, takes a right side of the same type: `impl Money.Add` adds `Money` to `Money`. Real code multiplies money by a count and a vector by a number, in both orders. Python answers at run time: the left side may decline, and the right side gets a second try. Rust answers at compile time with a typed right side. Jet has no answer yet, and its vector types reject `Vec3 * 2.0`.
decisions.story: Priya writes a physics demo. She writes `pos = pos + vel * dt` and expects it to work. Jet rejects `vel * dt` because `dt` is a `Float`, not a `Vec3`. She tries `dt * vel` next. That fails too. She ends up with `pos = pos + vel.scale(dt)`, and the math stops reading like math.
decisions.detail:
Three words used below. A hook is the function the compiler picks for an operator, keyed by the left type, the symbol, and the right type. Core is Jet's built-in library. Lane types are Core's built-in vectors and matrices, such as `Vec3` and `Mat3`. `2.0` on its own is a `Decimal`, the exact decimal number; lane types use `Float`, the machine number.

Every option keeps the D-OPDEF1 fence: only existing symbols, no new operators, no precedence changes, and arithmetic symbols keep doing arithmetic. Equality and ordering stay same-type. The operator ABI bug card #2430 is independent of this ballot.

Options B, C, D, and E share three rules. A plain number literal such as `3` or `2.0` takes the number type the hook expects when exactly one hook fits. When two hooks fit, the compiler asks for the type. A literal never turns into a user type. Operands are always evaluated left to right, once. `price *= 3` uses the direct hook only, and its result type must equal the left type.

Owner discussion pass, 2026-09-02: the owner asked why an operation should work one way in general. Answer: for two different non-number types the orders are usually different math, and the compiler cannot prove otherwise. For a plain number, a value of type `Int`, `Float`, or `Decimal`, beside `+` or `*`, ring arithmetic makes the orders agree, so option D now mirrors that case. An explicit hook is a hand-written `impl Int.Mul<Money>` in Money's package: the expert hatch, and it beats the mirror. The earlier lint-and-fix design is now option E.

options.name: Same type only, with named methods for mixed math
options.detail: Keep today's rule and finish it. Both sides of an operator must have the same type. Mixed math uses a named method: `price.scale(3)`, `vel.scale(dt)`, or `v * Vec3.splat(2.0)`, where `splat(2.0)` builds the vector `(2.0, 2.0, 2.0)`. The diagnostics improve so the named route is one edit away. Gain: no dispatch rule to learn and nothing new to spell. Loss: the most common vector and money operations become method calls.
options.technical: No change to the synthetic traits (`fn mul(&self, rhs: &Self) -> Self`). E0907 shows the expected signature. E0109 and E2511 name the named-method and `splat` routes. Core adds `scale` on lane types.

options.name: Typed right side, left side owns the operator
options.detail: A hook names the type of its right side: `impl Money.Mul<Int>`. Writing `impl Money.Mul` alone still means `Mul<Money>`. The left side's type owns the operation, and a type may have several hooks with different right sides. `3 * price` stays an error whose fix says to swap the sides. Core gives lane types `Vec3.Mul<Float>` under the same rule, so `v * 2.0` works and `2.0 * v` does not. Gain: one static rule with no order games. Loss: math that reads only one way.
options.technical: Spelling: `impl Money.Mul<Int> { fn mul(self, rhs: Int) Money -> … }`. The lookup key is (left type, symbol, right type); the result type is the hook's declared return type. Generic bounds may name the pair: `T: Mul<Float>`. User code may not declare a hook on a built-in left type. `+=` and friends fall out of the typed hook under the shared compound rule. Core lane types declare `Vec3.Mul<Float>`, `Vec3.Div<Float>`, and the matrix-vector pair.

options.name: Typed right side plus declared symmetry
options.detail:
Option B, plus a hook may declare that swapping the sides gives the same answer: `#Commutative impl Money.Mul<Int>`. The compiler then accepts `3 * price` by rewriting it to `price * 3`. Only `+` and `*` may be declared symmetric. Core declares the scalar hooks symmetric, so `2.0 * v` works. Gain: math reads both ways with one hook.

Loss: the compiler cannot check that the math really is symmetric. A hook marked symmetric by mistake gives a silently wrong answer, which is the class of defect Jet refuses. The rewrite also cannot express a symmetric operation whose result is a third type, such as speed times time giving distance. Both beginner readers liked this option; the rival-family review found the holes above.
options.technical:
Symmetry is opt-in because `Mat3 * Vec3` is not `Vec3 * Mat3`. Resolution: look up (left, symbol, right). If absent and (right, symbol, left) is a symmetric hook, call that hook with the sides swapped after evaluating operands left to right. Two symmetric hooks that could both match are a compile error.

Inside a generic body, `2.0 * x` needs a bound that promises symmetry; `T: Mul<Float>` alone allows only `x * 2.0`. The marker is allowed only on `Add` and `Mul` hooks whose result type is the left type. I7: `#Commutative` is a new marker spelling and needs a Syntax.rs entry. `-` and `/` never accept the marker.

options.name: Typed right side, a plain number on the left of `+` or `*` mirrors the user hook, explicit hook for the rest
options.detail:
Option B, plus one rule for a plain number, a value of type `Int`, `Float`, or `Decimal`, as the left operand of the written expression. If the symbol is `+` or `*` and the right type declares that hook for the number, the compiler swaps the sides and calls it. In ring arithmetic a number commutes with everything, so one definition serves both orders. Nothing mirrors for `-` or `/`, and nothing mirrors when neither side is a plain number, so `m * v` and `pose * delta` stay one-way.

The package that defines `Money` may also write an explicit hook on the number type, such as `impl Int.Sub<Money>`, with its own body. That hook is the expert hatch: it gives `-` and `/` a reverse body, and when both `Int.Mul<Money>` and `Money.Mul<Int>` exist, `3 * price` calls the explicit hook, never the mirror. Only that package may write it, so `3 * price` always has one owner, the same place a reader looks for `price * 3`.

The mirror trusts ring arithmetic. The known exception is transfinite ordinal arithmetic, where `1 + ω` is `ω` but `ω + 1` is not. Such a package writes the explicit number-side hooks; until it does, `1 + ω` gives the mirrored answer, and its first test of that famous case shows the need. Core declares `Vec3.Mul<Float>` and `Vec3.Div<Float>` and writes `Float.Div<Vec3>`; `2.0 * v` comes from the mirror.

`jet inspect types`, the command that lists a program's types and their hooks, shows the mirror under `Money`, so nobody hunts for a hook on `Int`. A generic body under `T: Mul<Float>` may write `x * 2.0` or `2.0 * x`. Gain: one definition serves both orders with no claim, no lint, and no fix, and a library works both ways for every user. Loss: one resolution rule to learn, and an ordinal-like type that forgets its explicit hooks gets a wrong answer until its first test.
options.technical:
Coherence, the rule for which package may write a hook: today an operator hook is legal only on a local left type (E0902, Traits.rs). D widens that rule for one case. A hook whose left type is built-in is legal when its concrete right type is local to the declaring package. A generic or foreign right type stays E0902, whose What, Why, and Fix text gains this case.

Resolution order. Built-in numeric widening (D-NUMWIDEN-CROSS1) resolves a pair of plain number types first, so `Int + Float` never reaches hook lookup. Then look up (left, symbol, right); an explicit hook wins. If absent, and left is `Int`, `Float`, or `Decimal`, and the symbol is `+` or `*`, look up (right, symbol, left) and call it with the sides swapped. Operands are evaluated left to right, once. The literal rule applies to the mirrored key, so `2.0 * v` fits `Vec3.Mul<Float>`; two fitting hooks ask for the type. `-` and `/` never mirror.

The mirror returns the forward hook's declared result type. Compound assignment never mirrors: `n *= price` with `n: Int` needs a direct `Int.Mul<Money>` hook returning `Int`, so it stays rejected. Chains follow precedence: `2 * price * 3` is `(2 * price) * 3`, a mirror then a direct call.

Generic bodies: a bound `T: Mul<Float>` admits only types whose hook returns `T`, which keeps today's `Self` result inside generic bodies. So `x * 2.0` and `2.0 * x` both have type `T`. A hook with a third result type is used through its concrete type; a bound spelling for third-type results is a separate ballot. `jet inspect types` lists `Int * Money -> Money  mirror of Money.Mul<Int>` under `Money`.

Spelling: the typed hook `Mul<Int>` is the one new spelling, shared by B, C, D, and E. It amends D-OPDEF1's same-operand clause and gets its Syntax.rs entry under this decision id. The mirror is a resolution rule in sema, not a spelling, and adds no marker; every tier sees the same resolved call (I9). Diagnostics in the sample illustrate guidance; the card registers exact copy and snapshots (I4).

options.name: Typed right side plus an explicit reverse hook on the number type, offered by a lint and written by the compiler's fix; no mirror
options.detail:
Option B, plus the package that defines `Money` may also write the reverse hook on the built-in left type: `impl Int.Mul<Money>`. Only that package may do so, so `3 * price` always has exactly one owner, the same place a reader looks for `price * 3`. Every direction is a real function with its own body, so nothing is swapped behind the reader's back.

Nobody has to remember the second hook. When a package declares an `Add` or `Mul` hook whose right side is a built-in number and writes no reverse hook, a lint fires at that declaration. Its fix writes the one-line delegating reverse hook with the forward hook's own result type. Plain `jet fix` reports the edit as skipped because it changes the package's surface; `jet fix --all` or the editor applies it. `Sub` and `Div` get no fix, because their reverse needs its own body, as `2.0 / v` shows.

Core writes both scalar hooks for lane types, so `2.0 * v` and `2.0 / v` work without the beginner knowing why. `jet inspect types` lists both directions under the `Money` row, so a hook on `Int` is never hunted for. Gain: every order and every asymmetric case is expressible, with no trusted claim and no boilerplate. Loss: one visible line per reversed hook lives in the package, and a generic body can write only `x * 2.0`.

E is the loud fallback: forgetting the reverse hook is a compile error at the use site, never a wrong answer. It is the design option D carried before the owner's discussion pass replaced it with the mirror.
options.technical:
Coherence: today an operator hook is legal only on a local left type (E0902, Traits.rs). D widens that rule for one case. A hook whose left type is built-in is legal when its concrete right type is local to the declaring package. A generic or foreign right type stays E0902, whose What, Why, and Fix text gains this case. The lookup key stays (left, symbol, right) with no order fallback.

The result type may be any type, so `Rate * Duration` giving `Distance` is expressible. A lint flags a built-in-side hook whose result type is neither operand type. Generic bodies use the forward direction only: `T: Mul<Float>` allows `x * 2.0`. Writing `2.0 * x` would need a bound on `Float`, which S45 cannot spell, so generic code writes `x * 2.0`.

Lint `one_way_scalar_operator` is registered by the card with code, What, Why, Fix, and snapshot. It fires on an `Add` or `Mul` hook with a right type of `Int`, `Float`, or `Decimal` when the same package declares no reverse hook. Its `fix_edits` entry carries the `api-changing` class (D-REPORT-FIXGRADE1).

The fix copies the forward hook's declared result type and access conventions into `impl Int.Mul<Money> { fn mul(self, rhs: Money) <Result> -> rhs * self }`. It is withheld when no type-correct delegation exists. The ratified lint policy turns it off per package or per hook for an intentionally one-way operation.

Spelling: the typed hook `Mul<Int>` is the one new spelling, shared by B, C, D, and E. It amends D-OPDEF1's same-operand clause and gets its Syntax.rs entry under this decision id. The lint and its fix add no spelling.

comparisons.note: The mined video's subject. `__mul__` (the method behind `*`) returns the `NotImplemented` marker to decline; the interpreter then tries `__rmul__` on the right side, and finally raises `TypeError`. The audience recorded three faults: order-dependent answers, accidental recursion between mutual fallbacks, and `__eq__` silently falling back to identity. Every option here is static and keeps none of them.

`Mul<Rhs>` takes the right-side type, so `Vec2 * f32` and `f32 * Vec2` are two separate hooks. The orphan rule lets Vec2's crate write the `f32` side, which is D's explicit hook and E's generated hook. Rust has no mirror, so scalar hooks are written twice throughout the ecosystem, usually as the one-line delegation that D's mirror performs by rule.
comparisons.code:
impl Mul<f32> for Vec2 { type Output = Vec2; fn mul(self, s: f32) -> Vec2 { … } }
impl Mul<Vec2> for f32 { type Output = Vec2; fn mul(self, v: Vec2) -> Vec2 { v * self } }

comparisons.note: Operators are static functions with any parameter types, so both orders are separate declarations. Swift's built-in vector types ship both scalar orders in the standard library; under option D, Core writes one and the mirror supplies the other.
comparisons.code:
static func * (v: SIMD3<Float>, s: Float) -> SIMD3<Float>
static func * (s: Float, v: SIMD3<Float>) -> SIMD3<Float>

recommendation.why: One definition serves both orders in the case beginners hit, a plain number beside `+` or `*`, because ring arithmetic makes those orders agree. No per-type claim is trusted; the one assumption is ring arithmetic, named in the tradeoff. The mirror is a fixed language rule that never touches `-`, `/`, or a pair of non-number types, so `m * v` and `2.0 / v` stay one-way with their own bodies. A library works both ways for every user without its author accepting a fix. No lint, no fix, no second hook.

whyNot.reason: The most common vector and money operations become method calls, which is the readability loss D-OPDEF1 already refused.
`v * 2.0` works and `2.0 * v` fails. Every physics beginner hits that wall, and the fix is to reorder math.

A hook marked symmetric by mistake gives a silently wrong answer, and the compiler cannot check the claim. D needs no per-type claim: it mirrors only a plain number beside `+` or `*`, where ring arithmetic fixes the answer. Speed times time giving distance stays a plain hook under D.

One accepted `jet fix --all` per type, and a library whose author ignores the lint leaves `3 * price` broken for every user. Forgetting is loud, which is E's real strength; E is the safe fallback if the owner weighs the ordinal exception above that ceremony.

recommendation.tradeoff: One resolution rule to learn: a plain number on the left of `+` or `*` mirrors the user hook. The mirror assumes ring arithmetic; transfinite ordinals are the known exception, and their package must write the explicit number-side hooks or get a wrong answer until its first test. No spelling refuses `3 * price` while `price * 3` exists; a different meaning is written as the explicit hook, which `jet inspect types` shows in place of the mirror row.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared same-type only, a typed right side with left ownership, declared symmetry, and a second hook on the built-in side. The Money and Vec3 program is the shared example.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested implicit scalar conversion, free operator functions, static reflected hooks, and implicit symmetry for every `*`. None became an option: conversion changes meaning, free functions were refused by D-OPDEF1, reflected hooks are D without ownership, and implicit symmetry for every `*` breaks matrix math.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested combining the symmetry marker with the second hook and kept the options separate, since two ways to make `3 * price` work would be two mechanisms. The owner's discussion pass made D one ordered resolver, direct hook then number mirror, with the explicit hook as precedence rather than a second mechanism, and moved the lint-and-fix design to E.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review gave A better diagnostics and a Core `scale` method, and gave B a swap hint. It restricted C's marker to `+` and `*` with a tie-break rule and gave D the same-package rule; D's lints and delegation fix now live in option E.
reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: Rli5Opmix. Skill: rli5. The first pass repaired undefined terms with a glossary and comments. The third, on the mirror revision, found the literal rule, the `-` fix text, the left-operand wording, precedence, and `jet inspect types` unexplained; D now defines each and shows both.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Anthropic. Adversarial model family: OpenAI. The first rival pass moved the recommendation from C to D by showing declared symmetry can be silently wrong. The third, on the mirror revision, found transfinite ordinals break the mirror and generic bounds left the result open; D names the exception, fixes bound results to `T`, and keeps E.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Prove every case on AOT (`jet build`), the default tier (`jet run`), and the pure interpreter (`jet eval`); a tier is one of Jet's ways to run a program. The Money and Vec3 program works in every accepted order and prints the stated values. Each rejected order uses its registered diagnostic and snapshot; the sample comments illustrate guidance, not exact copy. `price *= 3` works, and `n *= price` with `n: Int` is rejected.

`2 * price * 3` gives 1500 cents. With an explicit `impl Int.Mul<Money>` present, `3 * price` calls it, and `jet inspect types` lists it in place of the mirror row. `Int + Float` widens under D-NUMWIDEN-CROSS1 and never mirrors. A generic body under `T: Mul<Float>` resolves both `x * 2.0` and `2.0 * x` with type `T`. A type whose hook returns a third type is rejected at that bound.

The literal rule covers `v * 2.0` and `2.0 * v`, and two fitting hooks give the ambiguity error. `3 - price` and `2.0 * price` are rejected. Matrix times vector stays one-way. A hook on a built-in left type in the wrong package gives E0902. Syntax.rs carries the typed hook spelling with this decision id.

decisions.title: Where the persistent test loop lives
decisions.gist: Should the persistent test loop live under jet test or jet dev?
decisions.lesson: Jet already runs filtered tests and watches programs. It lacks one focused loop for rerunning failures, choosing captured output, bypassing only result caches, selecting checked docs, and filtering by dependency facts. Both options keep quiet passing output and preserve build artifacts.
decisions.story: Maya fixes one parser failure while a large workspace keeps changing. She needs the failed test, its output, and its dependency selection to survive each edit.
decisions.inWild:
// https://vitest.dev/guide/features.html#watch-mode
$ vitest
FAIL parser.test.ts
press r to rerun, a to run all
$ vitest run

options.name: jet test owns the loop
options.detail: Add --watch to jet test. The command keeps the failure cursor, capture policy, result freshness, doc selection, and structural predicate together. A plain jet test remains one finite quiet run.
options.technical: --fresh bypasses only cached test results. --docs selects checked documentation examples. --where selects recorded package, dependency, path, tag, or status facts. The watcher reuses the existing build graph and last-good artifact.
options.code:
$ jet test --watch --where 'package=app and dep=core.db'
FAIL parser.recovers
r  rerun failed
a  run all
o  output failed|all|none
$ jet test --fresh --docs

options.name: jet dev owns the loop
options.detail: Add a test mode to jet dev. Test selection and rerun state share the general development session, while jet test stays finite. Users must switch commands for the same suite.
options.technical: jet dev --tests owns watching and the failure cursor. Finite controls remain on jet test, so both commands must share selection, capture, and result-cache semantics.
options.code:
$ jet dev --tests --where 'package=app and dep=core.db'
FAIL parser.recovers
r  rerun failed
a  run all
$ jet test --fresh --docs

comparisons.note: Vitest starts watch mode during development and finite run mode in CI. It reruns tests selected through the module graph. Source: https://vitest.dev/guide/features.html#watch-mode.
comparisons.code:
$ vitest
$ vitest run

comparisons.note: Nextest provides one explicit run command, filters, recorded-run reruns, and output controls, but no built-in watch loop. Source: https://nexte.st/docs/running/.
comparisons.code:
$ cargo nextest run -E 'package(jet)'
$ cargo nextest run --rerun previous

recommendation.why: A keeps every test-loop control under the command users already run. Finite and watched runs differ by one explicit flag, not by ownership.
gains: One command owns test state.
Plain jet test stays finite.
Watch mode reuses the build graph.

losses.loss: Watch mode keeps one process alive.
losses.mitigation: Instant reruns require a process to observe edits and retain the dependency graph.

whyNot.reason: B splits one suite between test and dev commands, duplicating help and completion paths.

recommendation.tradeoff: The explicit watcher consumes resources until the user exits it.

decisions.title: Where job dependencies and freshness live
decisions.gist: Should job graphs live on #Job declarations or in package configuration?
decisions.lesson: Jet already discovers and runs typed jobs. It does not yet record job dependencies, declared inputs and outputs, freshness, or bounded parallelism. Both options use the existing build graph and keep jobs explicit.
decisions.story: Maya runs schema generation before client generation. She needs Jet to skip fresh work, reject cycles, and show why each job ran.
decisions.inWild:
# https://mise.jdx.dev/tasks/
[tasks.client]
depends = ["schema"]
sources = ["schema/**"]
outputs = ["src/generated/**"]

options.name: #Job owns graph metadata
options.detail: Put dependencies and freshness facts beside each typed job. Gains: One source defines behavior and scheduling.; Cycles fail during checking.; jet jobs explains freshness.. Losses: Graph changes require source edits..
options.technical: Job identity remains the declared function. The scheduler reads checked metadata, hashes declared inputs and outputs, reuses the existing graph, and limits independent jobs without running hidden work.
options.code:
#Job(
  after: [Schema],
  inputs: ["schema/**"],
  outputs: ["src/generated/**"],
  parallel: 2
)
fn Client() { generate_client() }
$ jet jobs Client --explain

options.name: package configuration owns the graph
options.detail: Keep #Job functions simple and declare scheduling in package.jet. Gains: Automation is visible in one file.. Losses: Names can drift from source.; A second graph must be checked..
options.code:
#Job fn Client() { generate_client() }

# package.jet
jobs.Client.after: [Schema]
jobs.Client.inputs: ["schema/**"]
jobs.Client.outputs: ["src/generated/**"]

comparisons.note: mise tasks declare depends, sources, outputs, and parallel controls in project configuration. Source: https://mise.jdx.dev/tasks/.
comparisons.code:
[tasks.client]
depends = ["schema"]
sources = ["schema/**"]
outputs = ["src/generated/**"]

recommendation.why: A extends the typed job declaration Jet already checks. Dependencies, freshness, help, and execution share one source identity.
gains: One checked graph.
Source-local job ownership.
Freshness remains explainable.

losses.loss: Graph changes require source edits.
losses.mitigation: Keeping scheduling beside the typed job means changing that schedule changes its source declaration.

whyNot.reason: B creates a second declaration graph whose job names and source locations can drift.

recommendation.tradeoff: Project automation changes are reviewed as source changes.

decisions.title: How explicit source generation is declared
decisions.gist: Should source generators reuse #Job metadata or use a package generator table?
decisions.lesson: Jet can emit artifacts, but it has no explicit source-generation loop. Generation must never run during build or test. It must preview writes, check authority, commit atomically, and record inputs, outputs, toolchain, and source identity.
decisions.story: Maya regenerates typed protocol records from a checked schema. She needs identical output, a reviewable preview, and no hidden build side effect.

options.name: Reuse #Job for generators
options.detail: Add checked input and output metadata to #Job, then run jet generate explicitly. Gains: No second executable mechanism.; Preview and apply share one plan.; Receipts bind source and outputs.. Losses: Generated source creates review churn..
options.technical: The command resolves one checked #Job, validates package authority, stages every output, and commits all writes together. Build and test never invoke it. An unchanged plan produces an identical receipt.
options.code:
#Job(
  generates: ["src/gen/Pill.jet"],
  inputs: ["schema/pill.json"]
)
fn PillSource() { emit_pill() }
$ jet generate PillSource
Preview: write src/gen/Pill.jet
$ jet generate PillSource --apply

options.name: Declare generators in package.jet
options.detail: Map generator names, entry functions, inputs, and outputs in project configuration. Gains: All generated paths are centrally listed.. Losses: Configuration duplicates function identity.; Source and generator declarations can drift..
options.code:
#Job fn PillSource() { emit_pill() }

# package.jet
generators.Pill.entry: PillSource
generators.Pill.inputs: ["schema/pill.json"]
generators.Pill.outputs: ["src/gen/Pill.jet"]
$ jet generate Pill --apply

comparisons.note: go generate runs explicit source comments in source order and is never part of go build or go test. Source: https://go.dev/blog/generate.
comparisons.code:
//go:generate stringer -type=Pill
$ go generate ./...

recommendation.why: A reuses the typed job mechanism and adds one explicit mutating command. Preview, authority, atomic writes, and receipts stay attached to checked source.
gains: No hidden build work.
No second executable registry.
Every write has a receipt.

losses.loss: Generated source creates review churn.
losses.mitigation: Producing checked-in source necessarily changes files that reviewers must inspect.

whyNot.reason: B duplicates the checked function identity in configuration and creates a second executable registry.

recommendation.tradeoff: Generated files remain visible repository changes rather than hidden artifacts.

decisions.title: How mobile development enters the loop
decisions.gist: Should mobile reuse jet dev or have a separate mobile command family?
decisions.lesson: A live development host owns loading, state preservation, reconnect, and restart. Jet has already chosen one such host for apps and previews. This ballot chooses the mobile commands, not another runtime. All commands and example output below are proposed; #480 remains deferred.
decisions.story: Maya checks Android prerequisites, selects one saved device, runs the app, preserves cart state through a UI edit, and inspects a slow node after reconnecting.

$ flutter devices
$ flutter run -d DEVICE
r  hot reload
R  hot restart
decisions.detail:
Neither option promotes #480 or changes D-VERDICT-480-1. Both use the ratified NativeDevHost lifecycle: an app host on the device, controlled from the workstation. Existing UI, debugger, and inspection records remain the only fact graph.

--target selects ios or android; --device selects a trust-qualified device identity. Transport comes from that record. Omission selects only one already-trusted local simulator or emulator. Zero or several candidates refuse with stable IDs. Physical or network devices always require an explicit qualified ID. Discovery grants no upload, debug, or inspect authority.

First pairing shows both host and device identities and requires approve or deny. Denial transfers no code or inspection facts. Reconnect reuses trust only for the same qualified identities and grants. Session, source revision, and artifact must match; stale actions reject and cursor gaps remain visible.

Inventory records platform, class, model, OS, transport, readiness/reason, toolchain, and authority. IDs are stable within the existing trust scope; raw hardware IDs and secrets are not printed. Platform is ios/android; class is simulator/emulator/physical; transport is local/usb/network. Existing typed JSON envelopes carry these fields.

r requests checked reload, R controlled restart, and i the existing inspector. Headless sessions use the typed action channel. Only #Persist bindings and approved #PublishedSchema migration preserve state. Ordinary local and widget state may reset. Every swap reports kept/reset state; rejection keeps last-good; incompatible/native edits announce restart/rebuild and discarded state before activation.

Pixel selection resolves JetUiNode and its source span. Temporary inspector edits never become source truth. Existing redaction, bounded logs, and removable authority-scoped subscriptions apply. Production excludes swap, code upload, debugger, overlay, and extension channels: compiled out or inaccessible, never an enabled no-op. A separately ratified read-only production endpoint is outside this choice.

decisions.title: Where mobile build and signing facts live
decisions.gist: Should mobile use the normal package and build graph or a separate mobile manifest?
decisions.lesson: A mobile build needs a target, build profile, signing identity, and store destination. Jet has already chosen one App and first-party native targets. This ballot chooses where those build facts live. Keys stay outside the project; configuration records credential references, not key material.
decisions.story: Maya scaffolds one app, builds signed Android internal and iOS TestFlight artifacts, audits every generated file and key reference, and never prints a secret.
decisions.detail:
Neither option promotes #480 or changes D-VERDICT-480-1. Preserve D-NATIVEUI3 and D-APP-UNIFY1: one App, one route graph, native targets, and one provenance chain.

A: package.jet profiles exclusively own mobile target, backend, signing-reference, and destination facts. B: mobile.jet exclusively owns them; package.jet owns generic facts. Duplicate ownership rejects. CLI arguments select declared profiles, targets, and destinations; they cannot override or invent configuration. One checked loader produces the graph.

A signing reference is a stable credential ID resolved by the existing external credential authority, not a path, environment variable, or secret value. Keys never enter project/generated files, diagnostics, logs, cache keys, or receipts. Both options require real Android tools and an admitted macOS/Apple SDK for iOS. Neither supplies a hosted builder.

Proposed jet new app NAME --target=ios,android refuses an existing destination. Generated paths record their owner and content hash. Regeneration rewrites only unchanged owned paths; an edited or unowned collision stops all writes and names a remedy. Routes and deep links retain the one App source identity.

Build validates toolchain, profile, entitlements, credential authority, and destination before publication. Ship is preview-only without --apply --receipt ID. The receipt binds artifact hash, profile, signer/account/application, destination/track, backend/toolchain, intended writes, and remote preconditions. Apply consumes exactly that preview; any changed binding rejects without submission.

Submission records the provider-issued immutable operation/build identity and status. Upload acceptance is pending, not completed. Resume reconciles that operation; it does not blindly upload again. Completion requires a terminal successful provider state and bounded receipt. Missing SDKs, credentials, account grants, targets, or execution evidence remain non-passing; there is no implicit native-only exception.

options.name: Use package and build profiles
options.detail: Keep mobile targets, generated ownership, signing references, and destinations in Jet’s existing graph.
options.technical: package.jet profiles are the sole mobile configuration authority. CLI values are selectors only. Reuse the shared owner/hash, exact-preview, credential-authority, and provider-completion contracts above.
options.code:
# Proposed: selectors name declared project facts
jet new app checkout --target=ios,android
jet build --target=android --profile=release
jet ship android --track=internal
# Preview emits receipt ANDROID_PREVIEW.
jet ship android --track=internal --apply --receipt ANDROID_PREVIEW
jet build --target=ios --profile=release
jet ship ios --destination=testflight
# Preview emits receipt IOS_PREVIEW.
jet ship ios --destination=testflight --apply --receipt IOS_PREVIEW
# Upload acceptance is pending; only provider success is completed.

options.name: Add a mobile manifest
options.detail: Use a dedicated mobile configuration file with the same graph and commands.
options.technical: mobile.jet exclusively owns mobile configuration; package.jet owns generic facts. Duplicate ownership rejects. The same checked graph and commands consume the shared owner/hash, preview, credential, and provider-completion contracts.
options.code:

# The same build/preview/apply sequence follows.
# Proposed: selectors name declared project facts

jet build --target=android --profile=release

# Preview emits receipt ANDROID_PREVIEW.
jet ship android --track=internal --apply --receipt ANDROID_PREVIEW
jet build --target=ios --profile=release
jet ship ios --destination=testflight
# Preview emits receipt IOS_PREVIEW.
jet ship ios --destination=testflight --apply --receipt IOS_PREVIEW
# Upload acceptance is pending; only provider success is completed.

comparisons.note: EAS keeps build profiles and distribution choices in project configuration and produces remote build and submission records.

recommendation.why: A extends the normal project and build graph with mobile facts. One App, one route identity, one artifact provenance chain, and explicit external secret references remain authoritative.
gains: One project graph.
No secret output.
Build and ship receipts compose.

losses.loss: iOS builds require Apple-licensed SDK access.
losses.mitigation: Apple restricts the UIKit SDK needed to link and sign native iOS applications.

whyNot.reason: B can preserve single ownership, but adds another file where ordinary project profiles already provide grouping.

recommendation.tradeoff: One project graph cannot remove real SDK, account, entitlement, and signing prerequisites. Missing prerequisites stop before publication.

decisions.title: How notebook cells react to edits
decisions.gist: Should notebook cells rerun by checked dependencies or preserve manual execution order?
decisions.lesson: Jet already computes cell dependencies, stale identities, rich outputs, and trust status. The missing contract decides reruns, deleted bindings, effect confirmation, and browser reconnection. Source remains canonical under either option.
decisions.story: Maya changes a data-loading cell and expects only its totals and chart cells to update. Deleting the loader must remove every stale value.

options.name: Checked reactive cells
options.detail: Rerun pure descendants automatically and mark effectful work for confirmation. Gains: Only affected cells rerun.; Deleted bindings are scrubbed.; Stale output is always labeled.. Losses: A live kernel keeps bounded state..
options.technical: The existing closure graph owns dependencies. Pure descendants rerun in order. Effectful cells require confirmation or remain visibly stale. Deletion removes owned bindings before any descendant runs. Reconnect requires matching source, build, and authority identity.
options.code:
$ jet notebook report.jetnb
edit sales
rerun: sales -> totals -> chart
effectful publish: confirm | skip
delete sales
removed: sales totals chart
status: chart stale

options.name: Manual execution order
options.detail: Keep notebook cells imperative and rerun only when the user requests them. Gains: No automatic computation.. Losses: Execution order changes meaning.; Stale bindings can survive edits.; Users must discover dependents..
options.code:
$ jet notebook report.jetnb
edit sales
run cell sales
run cell chart
# totals still contains the old sales value
delete sales
# dependent bindings remain

comparisons.note: marimo builds a dependency graph from variables and reruns affected cells when definitions change.

recommendation.why: A exposes the dependency graph Jet already computes. Pure reruns become predictable, effectful work stays explicit, and deleted source cannot leave current-looking values.
gains: Dependency order is visible.
Effects require confirmation.
Deletion removes owned bindings.

losses.loss: A live kernel keeps bounded state.
losses.mitigation: Reconnection and incremental reruns require the kernel to retain cell identities and current values.

whyNot.reason: B makes hidden execution order part of the program and permits old bindings to outlive deleted source.

recommendation.tradeoff: The notebook kernel consumes bounded memory until the session closes.

decisions.title: Where typed data loaders live
decisions.gist: Should complex data loaders live in core or in typed provider packages?
decisions.lesson: Jet already has typed tables, streams, limits, and structured data errors. Loaders must add deterministic snapshots, source identities, invalidation, archive members, credentials, and cleanup. Existing bridge law keeps one core data model.
decisions.story: Maya loads local CSV and Parquet sales files, then reruns only queries whose source snapshot changed. Credentials must never enter cache bytes.
decisions.inWild:
# https://docs.pola.rs/api/python/stable/reference/api/polars.scan_parquet.html
orders = pl.scan_parquet("orders/*.parquet")
result = orders.filter(pl.col("total") > 100).collect()

options.name: Small core plus provider packages
options.detail: Core owns local text loaders and snapshots; packages add complex formats and remote systems. Gains: Core stays dependency-free.; Every provider returns typed data.; Credentials stay provider-scoped.. Losses: Complex formats require an added package..
options.technical: Core defines Loader, SourceIdentity, SnapshotIdentity, status, limits, and invalidation. First-party CSV and JSON remain dependency-free. Provider packages implement codecs or remote authority without changing DataTable, DataStream, or error meaning.
options.code:
use core.data as data
use data.parquet as parquet

csv :: data.load("orders.csv")
parts :: parquet.load("orders/*.parquet")
snap :: parts.snapshot()
print(snap.status)
# fresh | stale | error

options.name: All loaders in core
options.detail: Bundle local, archive, columnar, and remote loaders into core.data. Gains: No package choice for common formats.. Losses: Core gains provider dependencies.; Credentials and releases share one boundary.; Compiler seams risk dependency growth..
options.code:
use core.data as data

csv :: data.load("orders.csv")
parts :: data.load("orders/*.parquet")
remote :: data.load("warehouse://sales")
snap :: parts.snapshot()
print(snap.status)

decisions.title: How local SQL enters the CLI
decisions.gist: Should local SQL use jet db or run as a notebook mode?
decisions.lesson: Jet already has typed SQL values and a small query kernel. It lacks a multiline console for files, tables, scripts, plans, timing, limits, and machine output. Local access stays bounded; remote systems require explicit providers and authority.
decisions.story: Maya queries a Parquet snapshot from the terminal, pipes a script in CI, then opens the same authorized result in a browser inspector.

options.name: Add jet db
options.detail: Give local typed SQL one dedicated command with optional browser projection. Gains: Interactive and CI use one command.; Plans and limits are first-class.; Remote access stays explicit.. Losses: Remote engines need provider capabilities..
options.technical: The command calls the existing typed query kernel and loader contract. It publishes schema, plan, timing, size, source, and trust facts. --browser projects the same session. Remote providers require package authority and never become the default.
options.code:
$ jet db orders.parquet
jet> select region, sum(total) from orders group by 1;
rows: 5  time: 12ms
jet> .plan
scan orders.parquet -> group region
$ jet db --json < report.sql

options.name: Add notebook SQL mode
options.detail: Run the console through jet notebook with SQL cells and stdin controls. Gains: Browser hosting already exists.. Losses: Terminal SQL inherits notebook ceremony.; CI scripts depend on notebook lifecycle..
options.code:
$ jet notebook --sql orders.parquet
cell sql> select region, sum(total)
          from orders group by 1;
rows: 5  time: 12ms
$ jet notebook --sql --headless < report.sql

comparisons.note: DuckDB offers an interactive SQL shell, stdin scripts, file readers, output modes, and EXPLAIN from one process.

recommendation.why: A gives typed SQL a direct local command while reusing loaders, query plans, limits, errors, and optional browser projection. It does not add another data model.
gains: One command serves terminal and CI.
Browser view shares the query session.
Machine output stays typed.

losses.loss: Remote engines need provider capabilities.
losses.mitigation: A remote query must authenticate and cross a network boundary owned by that provider.

whyNot.reason: B makes a focused terminal and CI tool depend on notebook cell and browser lifecycle.

recommendation.tradeoff: Remote databases require an explicit provider package and authority grant.

decisions.title: How database migrations enter the CLI
decisions.gist: Should migrations use jet db subcommands or run as ordinary jobs?
decisions.lesson: Jet already checks schema facts and provides typed database migration machinery. It lacks commands to create, preview, inspect, apply, and roll back versioned changes. Every write must name its target and lock policy.
decisions.story: Maya adds an index, reviews the exact SQL, checks production status, applies one version, and rolls it back after a failed deployment.
decisions.inWild:
# https://guides.rubyonrails.org/active_record_migrations.html
$ bin/rails generate migration AddIndex
$ bin/rails db:migrate:status
$ bin/rails db:migrate
$ bin/rails db:rollback

options.name: jet db owns migrations
options.detail: Add a migration command family beside the local SQL console. Gains: Database work has one command family.; Preview stays separate from apply.; Targets and locks are explicit.. Losses: Applying may hold a database lock..
options.technical: Versioned checked migration files are canonical. Preview never writes. Apply stages a receipt, acquires the selected lock, commits schema and receipt atomically, and records target identity without secrets. Rollback names a version or step count.
options.code:
$ jet db migrate new AddIndex
created migrations/004_add_index.jet
$ jet db migrate preview --target prod
SQL: create index ...
risk: table lock
$ jet db migrate apply --target prod
receipt: migration-004.json

options.name: Migrations are #Job functions
options.detail: Run create, apply, and rollback through project job declarations. Gains: No database command family.. Losses: Migration history becomes job-specific.; Preview and write intent are less visible.; Tooling must infer database targets..

comparisons.note: Rails exposes generation, status, apply, and rollback as explicit migration operations with versioned files.
comparisons.code:
# https://guides.rubyonrails.org/active_record_migrations.html
$ bin/rails generate migration AddIndex
$ bin/rails db:migrate:status
$ bin/rails db:migrate
$ bin/rails db:rollback

recommendation.why: A groups SQL inspection and migration lifecycle under jet db while keeping preview and writes distinct. Version, target, lock, risk, and receipt stay visible.
gains: One database command family.
Version history stays deterministic.
Preview performs no writes.

losses.loss: Applying may hold a database lock.
losses.mitigation: A schema change needs database coordination so concurrent writers cannot observe a partial migration.

whyNot.reason: B hides version, risk, target, and rollback meaning behind arbitrary job bodies.

recommendation.tradeoff: Apply and rollback can pause conflicting database writes while their lock is held.

decisions.title: Migration runtime process boundary
decisions.gist: Should migration commands call the database runtime directly or through an isolated worker?
decisions.lesson: Migration SQL and its completion record must commit together in the selected database. Both options use one shared implementation. This choice only sets the process boundary.
decisions.story: Maya applies a checked migration to her development database. Her terminal closes just after commit. The next invocation must recover the database record without applying the migration again.
decisions.inWild:
// https://docs.diesel.rs/2.2.x/diesel_migrations/trait.MigrationHarness.html
connection.run_pending_migrations(migrations)?;

options.name: Direct private runtime call
options.detail: Pass the checked plan directly to the shared database implementation.
options.code:
jet db migrate apply --target dev
# CLI passes a typed plan to the database runtime.
# SQL and completion record commit in one transaction.
options.technical: Place typed migration request and outcome records below jet-driver. The root command calls an existing native runtime adapter. Shared Prelude code owns lock acquisition, transition identity, drift checks, SQL execution, and receipt construction. Remove generated Jet transport and filesystem receipts as authority. Preserve existing db.migrate semantics through the same database ledger.

options.name: Isolated private worker
options.detail: Send the checked plan to a separate worker running the same database implementation.
options.code:
jet db migrate apply --target dev
# CLI sends a typed request to an internal worker.
# Worker commits SQL and the same database completion record.
options.technical: Use a private, typed request protocol with the same executable as worker. The worker invokes the identical Prelude database implementation. Do not generate Jet source or add a public migration API. Worker exit is not commit evidence; query the deterministic database transition before deciding whether a retry is needed.

comparisons.note: MigrationHarness applies typed migrations through a database connection.
comparisons.code:
// https://docs.diesel.rs/2.2.x/diesel_migrations/trait.MigrationHarness.html
connection.run_pending_migrations(migrations)?;

recommendation.why: The CLI is already a short-lived process. Direct calls preserve checked types without another protocol; database transactions protect committed state in either design.
gains: Existing commands stay unchanged.
Database state decides retries and recovery.

losses.loss: Runtime failures share the CLI process.
losses.mitigation: Separate crash containment requires the worker boundary in option B.

whyNot.reason: Separate crash containment adds process startup and message handling without strengthening the database transaction.

recommendation.tradeoff: Accept one CLI failure boundary; keep schema changes and completion records atomic in the database.

decisions.title: Which durable queue is the default
decisions.gist: Should jobs start with bundled SQLite durability or require an application database?
decisions.lesson: Jet already has typed jobs, service delivery receipts, retries, and bundled SQLite. The queue must support delayed and bulk enqueue, bounded retries, status, restarts, payload privacy, and an explicit delivery guarantee.
decisions.story: Maya enqueues invoice jobs locally, then runs several production workers. A crash must not silently lose accepted work or expose invoice payloads.
decisions.inWild:
# https://hexdocs.pm/oban/Oban.html
Oban.insert(MyApp.Worker.new(%{id: 41}))
# job persists in PostgreSQL

options.name: SQLite default with provider override
options.detail: Use bundled SQLite locally and one typed durable-store contract everywhere. Gains: Zero-setup local durability.; Production stores stay explicit.; One job lifecycle feeds panels.. Losses: At-least-once delivery can repeat work..
options.technical: The Prelude owns enqueue, lease, acknowledge, retry, dead-letter, wait, and status semantics. SQLite is the dependency-free default. A configured database provider implements the same typed store. Payload publication stays opt-in and bounded.
options.code:
queue :: jobs.queue()
# local default: .jet/state/jobs.db
queue.enqueue(Invoice, 41, key: "invoice-41")
queue.delay(Invoice, 42, for: 5.minutes)
$ jet jobs status
Invoice queued=2 running=0

options.name: Require the application database
options.detail: Refuse durable jobs until the project configures a database provider. Gains: Production and application data share one service.. Losses: Local jobs need database setup.; Queue availability follows app migrations.; Provider failures block first use..
options.code:
queue :: jobs.queue(store: app.database)
queue.enqueue(Invoice, 41, key: "invoice-41")

$ jet jobs status
error: configure database provider

comparisons.note: Oban stores jobs in PostgreSQL and uses transactional persistence, queues, retries, scheduling, and uniqueness controls.
comparisons.code:
# https://hexdocs.pm/oban/Oban.html
Oban.insert(MyApp.Worker.new(%{id: 41}))
# job persists in PostgreSQL

recommendation.why: A makes accepted jobs durable with no service setup, then preserves the same lifecycle when production chooses another database provider.
gains: Local durability works immediately.
One queue contract serves every store.
Provider choice stays explicit.

losses.loss: At-least-once delivery can repeat work.
losses.mitigation: A crash can occur after an external side effect but before its durable acknowledgement.

whyNot.reason: B makes the first durable local job depend on external database setup and credentials.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jobs with external effects need idempotency keys or idempotent handlers.

decisions.title: How backend scaffolds are invoked
decisions.gist: Should backend scaffolds extend jet new or use named source generators?
decisions.lesson: Jet has generic project and game scaffolds plus an explicit source-generation decision. Backend scaffolds create conventional service, route, job, migration, and test slices. They must preview changes, avoid overwrites, and reverse only recorded outputs.
decisions.story: Maya creates an Orders service, adds a Ship route and Invoice job, then removes the route without touching her edits elsewhere.

options.name: Extend jet new
options.detail: Use one scaffold engine for projects and additive backend slices. Gains: One discoverable scaffold command.; Templates use selected APIs.; Inverse operations use receipts.. Losses: Generated files still need review..
options.technical: The existing scaffold engine stages deterministic files. Backend templates consume D-DX-MIGRATE1 and D-DX-QUEUE1. Conflict handling is explicit. Removal uses the original receipt and refuses modified files unless the user resolves them.

route /orders  model Order
job Invoice  migration 004
$ jet new service Orders --apply
receipt: scaffold-orders.json

options.name: Use jet generate templates
options.detail: Publish backend templates as named generators through the source-generation command. Gains: One general generator command.. Losses: Project scaffolds mix with source emitters.; Template discovery needs another registry.; Inverse operations become generator-specific..

$ jet generate backend.service Orders --apply
$ jet generate backend.route Ship --remove

comparisons.note: Phoenix generators create contexts, schemas, migrations, controllers, and tests from explicit commands.
comparisons.code:

$ mix ecto.migrate

Generated slices use canonical APIs.

losses.mitigation: Scaffolding creates source that becomes part of the application and must be inspected like any other change.

whyNot.reason: B mixes project scaffolding with source-declared generators and needs a second template registry.

recommendation.tradeoff: Scaffold output is visible source, not hidden framework state.

decisions.title: How the backend console runs safely
decisions.gist: Should the backend console extend jet repl or live inside jet dev?
decisions.lesson: Jet already has a typed REPL, project confinement, authority checks, HTTP dispatch, and database transactions. The console must load one project, start read-only, construct in-process requests, roll back sandboxed writes, and stay unavailable in release.
decisions.story: Maya reproduces one failing request against local code, inspects rows, and tries a repair without committing data or opening a production shell.
decisions.inWild:
# https://guides.rubyonrails.org/command_line.html#bin-rails-console
$ bin/rails console --sandbox
Loading development environment in sandbox
Any modifications you make will be rolled back

options.name: Extend jet repl
options.detail: Load a project into the existing evaluator with read-only and sandbox modes. Gains: No second evaluator.; Writes require explicit authority.; Requests feed normal devtools facts.. Losses: Write access needs deliberate setup..
options.technical: Read-only is the default. --sandbox data opens one reversible transaction after authority approval. In-process requests call the existing HTTP mux. Every request and write emits redacted audit facts. Release builds omit the console entry.
options.code:
$ jet repl --project . --sandbox data
authority: DB.Write until exit
> app.request("GET", "/orders/41")

decisions.title: Project console resource initialization timing
decisions.gist: Should the project console initialize application resources before the prompt or on first use?
decisions.lesson: Real requests need live application callbacks and database handles. Both options run the existing checked entry with console authority, without starting a public server. Read-only remains the default.

options.name: Initialize before the prompt
options.detail: Check authority, initialize real resources, then open the console.
options.code:

# Check console authority.
# Initialize the application without listening.
# Open the prompt with real resource adapters.
options.technical: Resolve the project and console authority before running initialization. Reuse the checked entry and resident engine with a typed session-owned runtime lease. Capture live App callbacks before the active runtime context clears. Attach adapters to the existing ConsoleSession before accepting commands. An initialization failure closes acquired resources and prevents the prompt.

options.name: Initialize on first resource use
options.detail: Open the evaluator first; initialize the application when a command needs its resources.
options.code:
jet repl
# Open the prompt with project definitions.
# On the first permitted request or database command:
# Initialize the same application and attach real adapters.
options.technical: Load project definitions into the existing ConsoleSession first. A permitted operation needing application resources initializes the same checked entry once, then retains the same typed runtime lease. Report initialization failure on that operation. Never install an empty adapter as a successful result or infer a database path.

comparisons.note: Rails loads the application environment into its console and offers rollback-on-exit database sandboxing.

# Inside the console:

recommendation.why: Fail before the prompt if the project cannot initialize under the selected authority. Keep one explicit resource lifetime instead of deferred startup state.
gains: No extra source hook.
No second evaluator.
Resource failures are reported at startup.

losses.mitigation: The callbacks and handles do not exist until their ordinary initializer runs; avoiding this wait requires option B.

whyNot.reason: B delays authority and initialization failures until a resource command and needs a deferred resource state.

recommendation.tradeoff: Pay initialization cost before interactive work instead of during the first resource command.

decisions.title: Where reverse debugging lives
decisions.gist: Should reverse execution extend jet debug or use a separate replay debugger?
decisions.lesson: Jet debug already steps forward through Jet frames. Recorded sessions can provide reverse steps, watchpoints, and fix-and-continue. The contract must bound history, preserve source identity, and explain unavailable history or incompatible edits.
decisions.story: Maya stops after a corrupted balance, watches the field backward to its last write, repairs the function, and continues from a valid checkpoint.
decisions.inWild:
# https://rr-project.org/
$ rr record ./app
$ rr replay
(rr) reverse-continue
(rr) reverse-step

options.name: Extend jet debug
options.detail: Use one prompt for forward, reverse, watchpoint, and repair commands. Gains: One frame and breakpoint model.; Recorded history stays session-bound.; Fixes reuse source authority.. Losses: Recording consumes bounded storage and time..
options.technical: RecordedAct history gains indexed writes and checkpoints. Reverse commands never fabricate unavailable state. Fix-and-continue checks source, type, layout, and authority compatibility before rebinding code. Incompatible edits name the restart reason.
options.code:
$ jet debug --record app.jet
(jet) watch account.balance
(jet) back
write: app.jet:38  10 -> -4
(jet) fix
checkpoint compatible
(jet) continue

options.name: Add a replay debugger
options.detail: Keep live debugging forward-only and open recordings through another command. Gains: Live sessions avoid reverse controls.. Losses: Breakpoints and watches span two prompts.; Fix-and-continue cannot share live state.; Help and DAP paths duplicate..
options.code:
$ jet debug app.jet
(jet) record save trace.jettrace
$ jet replay debug trace.jettrace
(replay) watch account.balance
(replay) reverse-step

comparisons.note: rr records execution once, then supports reverse-continue and reverse stepping through a GDB-compatible replay.
comparisons.code:
# https://rr-project.org/
$ rr record ./app
$ rr replay
(rr) reverse-continue
(rr) reverse-step

recommendation.why: A keeps frames, breakpoints, watches, source maps, authority, and DAP in one debugger. Recording is an explicit capability, not another product.
gains: One debugger prompt.
Unavailable history is explicit.
Repairs share live checkpoints.

losses.loss: Recording consumes bounded storage and time.
losses.mitigation: Reverse execution needs prior state or deterministic events that forward-only debugging does not retain.

whyNot.reason: B duplicates debugger commands and separates source repair from the live session that must continue.

recommendation.tradeoff: Reverse-capable sessions pay a bounded recording overhead selected before execution.

decisions.lesson: Jet already tracks database reads through app.live and supports explicit invalidation for outside sources. Queries need typed states, freshness, cancellation, mutations, optimistic rollback, offline behavior, and devtools facts without a second cache model.

useMutation({ mutationFn: shipOrder })
queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ["orders"] })

options.name: Footprints with explicit escape
options.detail: Record database reads automatically and keep explicit keys for outside sources. Gains: Database invalidation stays targeted.; External sources remain expressible.; One lifecycle feeds panels.. Losses: Optimistic rollback retains prior values..

decisions.title: How web forms get fields
decisions.gist: Should forms derive from typed input structs or require manual field builders?
decisions.lesson: Jet has typed request values and App actions. Forms need fields, defaults, sync and async validation, pending states, errors, accessibility, and script-free submission. Persisted records must not become editable by accident.
decisions.story: Maya builds a shipping form from a dedicated input type, validates the carrier on blur, and submits through the same action without JavaScript.

options.name: Derive from input structs
options.detail: Build fields and decoding from a dedicated action input type. Gains: Parsing has one typed source.; Accessible defaults are automatic.; Explicit config handles exceptions.. Losses: Async validation creates pending states..
options.technical: Only dedicated input structs are editable. Defaults derive labels, controls, required state, parsing, and accessible names. Config can rename, exclude, group, or replace fields. The same decoder serves progressive POST actions.
options.code:
struct ShipForm {
  id: Int
  carrier: String
}

ship_form :: web.form(ShipForm, action: ship)
  .validate(.carrier, on: .Blur, with: check_carrier)

ship_form.render()

options.name: Manual field builders
options.detail: Declare every field, parser, validator, label, and action mapping. Gains: Every presentation choice is written.. Losses: Types and parsers can drift.; Accessibility repeats per form.; Progressive decoding needs duplicate glue..
options.code:
ship_form :: web.form()
  .field("id", parse: Int.parse)
  .field("carrier", parse: String.parse,
    label: "Carrier", validate: check_carrier)
  .submit((values) -> ship(ShipForm{
    id: values.id, carrier: values.carrier
  }))

comparisons.note: TanStack Form provides headless typed fields, subscriptions, and sync or async validators while applications own markup.

recommendation.why: A makes the action input type the form contract and keeps expert overrides explicit. Browser and script-free submissions use one parser and validation path.
gains: One typed decoder.
Progressive submission is automatic.
Fields stay headless and configurable.

losses.loss: Async validation creates pending states.
losses.mitigation: A validator that waits on external work cannot return its answer immediately.

whyNot.reason: B repeats names, parsers, accessibility, and mapping already expressed by the input type.

recommendation.tradeoff: Forms expose pending validation and prevent conflicting submission until it settles.

decisions.title: How tables and virtualization share state
decisions.gist: Should tables stay headless typed values or become renderer-owned widgets?
decisions.lesson: Jet needs sorting, filtering, pagination, selection, stable row identity, and viewport virtualization over typed tables. Browser, terminal, and native renderers must consume the same table state and visible-row plan.
decisions.story: Maya sorts and filters 100,000 orders, scrolls the viewport, inserts one row, and keeps selection on the same order.

options.name: One headless typed model
options.detail: Derive safe columns and feed every renderer one table and viewport plan. Gains: Rows and columns remain typed.; Stable keys survive reordering.; Renderers share table semantics.. Losses: Variable row heights require measurement..
options.technical: TableState owns sorting, filtering, pagination, selection, and row keys. VirtualPlan owns viewport, measured sizes, overscan, and visible indices. Renderers only draw the returned UiNode rows and report measurements.
options.code:
table :: web.table(orders, key: .id)
  .columns([.customer, .total, .status])
  .sort(.total, .Descending)
  .filter(.status, .Pending)

visible :: table.virtual(viewport, overscan: 8)
ui.mount(backend, visible.view())

options.name: Renderer-owned table widgets
options.detail: Let browser, TUI, and native backends manage tables and scrolling separately. Gains: Each backend can use native controls.. Losses: Selection semantics can diverge.; Headless tests need backend emulation.; Sorting and pagination repeat..
options.code:
dom.table(orders, sort: "total")
tui.table(orders, sort: .Total)
gtk.table(orders, column: 2)

# each backend owns selection and viewport state

comparisons.note: TanStack keeps table state headless and pairs it with a separate viewport virtualizer.

recommendation.why: A keeps data and viewport behavior headless, typed, and renderer-independent. Native controls may optimize drawing without owning sorting, selection, or row identity.
gains: One table state model.
Stable typed row identity.
Viewport work stays bounded.

losses.loss: Variable row heights require measurement.
losses.mitigation: A viewport cannot place rows of unknown height without measuring or receiving their sizes.

whyNot.reason: B duplicates table state and makes identical source behave differently across renderers.

recommendation.tradeoff: Variable-height tables exchange bounded size measurements with the active renderer.

decisions.title: How web store history works
decisions.gist: Should store state extend core.reactive or use a separate store runtime?
decisions.lesson: Jet already has signals, transactions, and development reload state. A store adds named state, atomic updates, subscriptions, optimistic patches, and bounded history. Release builds must not retain development history by default.
decisions.story: Maya updates a cart atomically, inspects one transaction, travels backward during development, and keeps current state through a compatible reload.

options.name: Stores are reactive transactions
options.detail: Build named stores and history on core.reactive signals and transactions. Gains: One reactive primitive.; Atomic updates feed one event stream.; Compatible reload preserves state.. Losses: Development history uses bounded memory..
options.technical: A Store groups rooted signals. Transactions publish one diff and one devtools event. Development history is a bounded ring with explicit retention. Release builds strip capture unless the existing inspected-release policy enables it.
options.code:
cart :: web.store("Cart", Cart{})

cart.transact("add item", () -> {
  cart.items.push(Item{ id: 41 })
  cart.total.set(120)
})

cart.history.back()
print(cart.total.get())

options.name: Separate store runtime
options.detail: Create independent store values, subscriptions, transactions, and history. Gains: Store APIs remain isolated.. Losses: Signals need bridge subscriptions.; Reload has two state owners.; Devtools joins two event models..
options.code:
cart :: Store.new(Cart{})
cart.update("add item", (state) -> { ... })
cart.subscribe(render_cart)
reactive.bridge(cart)
cart.history.back()

comparisons.note: Redux Toolkit provides named state slices, reducers, immutable updates, middleware, and DevTools time travel.

recommendation.why: A makes a store a named group of existing signals and transactions. It adds history and inspection without another reactive scheduler or reload owner.
gains: One reactive scheduler.
Atomic diffs stay typed.
History is development-only.

losses.loss: Development history uses bounded memory.
losses.mitigation: Time travel requires retaining prior values or inverse patches until history entries expire.

whyNot.reason: B duplicates subscriptions, transaction scheduling, reload ownership, and devtools events already provided by core.reactive.

recommendation.tradeoff: Development sessions retain a configured number of transaction diffs.
