decisions.title: How typed server calls are exposed
decisions.gist: Should server functions derive from App actions or use explicit RPC declarations?
decisions.lesson: Jet needs typed browser-to-server calls, serializability checks, auth, CSRF protection, structured errors, cancellation, retries, and progressive form submission. The server remains authoritative; clients never receive hidden capabilities.
decisions.story: Maya ships an order from a button or a script-free form. Both paths must call the same checked handler and return the same error.

options.name: Derive calls from App actions
options.detail: Generate typed clients and progressive POST handling from one registered action. Gains: One handler serves both paths.; Serialization is checked early.; CSRF defaults follow the App.. Losses: Network calls can fail after dispatch..
options.technical: Sema verifies input, output, and error serializability. App registration derives a stable endpoint and typed client. Same-origin mutation calls require CSRF protection. Auth and capabilities enter through checked request context.
options.code:
fn ship(input: ShipForm) Result<Order, ShipError> { ... }

app :: web.app().action("ship", ship)
client :: app.client(.ship)
result :: await client(ShipForm{ id: 41, carrier: "UPS" })

# no script: POST /actions/ship uses the same handler

options.name: Explicit RPC declarations
options.detail: Declare transport names, request types, response types, and client stubs separately. Gains: Every wire endpoint is written.. Losses: Handlers and stubs can drift.; Progressive forms need another adapter.; Transport details enter application code..
options.code:
rpc ShipOrder {
  path: "/rpc/ship"
  input: ShipForm
  output: Order
  error: ShipError
  handler: ship
}
result :: await ShipOrder.client(input)

comparisons.note: TanStack Start server functions define validated server handlers callable from clients while keeping server execution separate.

recommendation.why: A derives the transport boundary from the App action already serving progressive requests. Types, errors, auth, CSRF, and source identity have one owner.
gains: One server handler.
Progressive and scripted paths agree.
No second RPC route graph.

losses.loss: Network calls can fail after dispatch.
losses.mitigation: A client and server communicate across a connection that can close after either side starts work.

whyNot.reason: B repeats types and handler identity and creates a second route registry for progressive forms.

recommendation.tradeoff: Callers handle typed timeout, cancellation, and uncertain-completion errors.

decisions.title: Where the live game loop lives
decisions.gist: Should live game controls extend jet dev or use a separate game editor command?
decisions.lesson: Jet already has deterministic headless scenes, a resident development session, Canvas controls, and one devtools event stream. It lacks rendered Run, Simulate, Pause, Frame, Eject, Keep, and Discard transitions. Both options keep authored source authoritative and development controls out of releases.
decisions.story: Maya pauses a collision, advances one frame, edits a live entity, and decides whether that experiment should change source.
decisions.inWild:
# https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/scripting/debug/overview_of_debugging_tools.html
F6  run scene
F9  pause
F10 frame advance
Remote Scene -> inspect

options.name: Extend jet dev
options.detail: Add game state and controls to the existing resident development session. Gains: One session owns source and runtime.; Canvas routes stay authoritative.; Headless and rendered runs share events.. Losses: A rendered session consumes host resources..
options.technical: CmdDevTools supervises the process. Prelude game state emits typed transitions through jet.devtools.v1. Canvas commands remain revision-bound and authority-checked. Keep writes a normal source transaction; Discard removes transient changes.
options.code:

GAME running  frame=418
p  pause
f  advance one frame
e  eject
k  keep selected changes
d  discard runtime changes
state: paused source=rev-42

options.name: Add jet game edit
options.detail: Run a separate game-editor process with its own command family. Gains: Game controls get a dedicated surface.. Losses: A second session must mirror source state.; Controls split from normal dev workflows..
options.code:

GAME running  frame=418
p  pause
f  advance one frame
e  eject
k  keep selected changes

losses.loss: A rendered session consumes host resources.

decisions.lesson: Jet already has checked build targets, profiles, package plans, receipts, and a --kind game flag. Games add Cook, Stage, Export, Deploy, and Run phases. Every phase must expose invalidation, authority, and development stripping without creating another project database.

decisions.gist: Should browser tests extend jet test or use a separate browser command?
decisions.lesson: Jet already has native browser automation and one test runner. Browser tests add contexts, navigation, semantic UI actions, screenshots, traces, retries, reports, code generation, and an optional visual mode. Failures must preserve source and browser identity.

options.detail: Inject typed Browser fixtures into ordinary tests and add browser controls. Gains: One filter and verdict model.; Traces attach to normal failures.; CLI and UI mode share tests.. Losses: Browsers consume processes and memory..
options.technical: The runner creates isolated browser contexts, starts the selected local fixture, and records source-bound semantic actions. Retries create new contexts. Traces, DOM snapshots, screenshots, console, and network facts attach only to failed or requested runs.

  page.role(.Button, name: "Pay").click()

$ jet test --browser-ui --filter checkout

# two suite verdicts

decisions.title: The jet tool tree: one inspect per plane, task tools kept
decisions.gist: Whether the ledger views under jet inspect become one view per plane with four scopes, and which commands fold.
decisions.lesson: jet has 58 top-level commands and 32 inspect actions. Some inspect actions are views of the compiler ledger (facts, gates, unsafe, authority, guarantees, structure). Others are tasks (schema squash, codemod, sbom, bind, logs). Two authorities know every flag: a hand parser in main.rs and the registry in CLI.rs. This choice decides the shape of the ledger views; generating the parser from the registry is common to every option.
decisions.story: Nia wants to know why her program may not use the network. She tries jet inspect authority, then jet inspect gates, then jet report. Each shows part of the answer.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet inspect authority app.jet
$ jet inspect gates app.jet
$ jet inspect facts
$ jet report app.jet
$ jet dossier app.jet

options.name: One view per plane, four scopes; task tools stay
options.detail: jet inspect types, rights, claims, shapes, structure, build, gates. Each takes a file or package, or --live PID for a running process, or --replay ARTIFACT for a record. Ledger views fold into these; task actions (schema, codemod, sbom, bind, logs, info, outdated, digest, env, expand, output, provenance, semindex, impact, graph, query, explain-build, compiler, audit, live) keep their spelling. report and dossier fold into inspect build, jet explain stays.
options.technical: Fold table: facts→types, authority→rights, unsafe→gates, guarantees→rights, structure→structure (kept name), gates→gates (kept name), report→build, dossier→build, live <pid>→--live PID on every plane. Retired names: facts, authority, unsafe, guarantees, report, dossier (six). Scope grammar: jet inspect <plane> [TARGET] [--live PID | --replay ARTIFACT]; TARGET defaults to the current package; --live and --replay are exclusive. Amends D-DX4 and D-SHAPE-CLI-COMPLETE1. jet help prints the old name and its new home for one edition.
options.code:
$ jet inspect rights app.jet
load  -[FS.Read]>  declared; package holds FS
$ jet inspect claims --live 4242
$ jet inspect build --replay .jet/replays/r.jetproof-replay
$ jet inspect authority app.jet
Error [E2101]: `inspect authority` moved to `inspect rights`

options.name: Keep the tree; add one umbrella
options.detail: jet inspect ledger shows every plane; the 32 actions stay.
options.technical: One new action.
options.code: $ jet inspect ledger app.jet

options.name: A new top-level word
options.detail: jet ledger <plane> beside inspect.
options.technical: New command; inspect keeps its 32 actions.
options.code: $ jet ledger rights app.jet

comparisons.note: A small fixed tree; inspection lives in a few verbs with flags.
comparisons.code:
$ cargo tree
$ cargo metadata

comparisons.note: One verb per question.
comparisons.code: $ go list -deps ./...

recommendation.why: One word per ledger question, the same view on a file, a package, a live process, and a record, and every task tool keeps its name.

whyNot.reason: Thirty-three actions.
A second word for the same views.

recommendation.tradeoff: Six inspect names retire. The old name prints its new home for one edition.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one view per plane, an umbrella action, and a new top-level word.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested folding explain into inspect and rejected it.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review kept task actions by name and made parser generation common to every option after the rival review.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review gave B its case: nothing a user typed yesterday stops working.
reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: Rli5D. Skill: rli5. The beginner pass asked which names retire and what a scope is. The technical note lists the fold table, the retired names, and the scope grammar.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Anthropic. Adversarial model family: OpenAI. The rival-family review found the fold incomplete, task actions treated as ledger views, parser generation misattributed, and the scope grammar undefined. All are repaired in A.

decisions.title: A package may require a minimum claim evidence
decisions.gist: Whether and how a package says every contract must reach at least a named evidence rung.
decisions.lesson: Once every claim has evidence, a team can require a floor. A claim below the floor is an error with a fix. Lowering the floor is a visible edit in the package file. This choice picks the spelling, or rejects the idea in favor of a CI threshold.
decisions.story: A payments team wants every contract in the ledger package to pass at least 1,000 generated inputs before merge. Today nothing in the package can say that; a reviewer reads each test by hand.

options.name: A typed field in the ratified policy block
options.detail: policy.claims.min names the floor with its count. It tightens only, like every policy field. A claim below the floor is a diagnostic whose fix names the command that can raise it when a generator exists, or the property test to write when one does not.
options.technical: Amends the D-PACKAGE-POLICY-SCOPE1 field set with claims: .{ min: <rung> }. Rungs per D-GRADE1 option D; a count is part of the rung, no max field, obeys tighten-only.

options.name: A top-level claims block
options.detail: A new block beside authority.
options.technical: claims: .{ require: proved } at the top level of package.jet.
options.code: claims: .{ require: proved }

options.name: No package field; report plus a CI threshold
options.detail: Reports show evidence; a CI script fails the build when a threshold is not met.
options.technical: No manifest change; the threshold lives in CI configuration.
options.code: $ jet test --json ledger/ | check-claims --min generated:1000   # outside jet

comparisons.note: Lint levels live in one policy table in the manifest.
comparisons.code:
[lints.rust]
unsafe_code = "forbid"

comparisons.note: Coverage thresholds live in CI scripts, not the module file.
comparisons.code: go test -cover ./...

recommendation.why: It lives where every other tightening rule lives, carries its count, and one diff shows a floor going down.

whyNot.reason: A second top-level block for one number.
The rule then lives outside the package and cannot be read by jet or by a dependent.

recommendation.tradeoff: A new policy field is a new word in the manifest. It follows the ratified typed field shape, so no new grammar is learned.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a policy field, a top-level block, and no field.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a per-function floor marker and folded it into A because a marker is a fact the same policy can read later.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review dropped the max field and bound the floor to a count after the rival review.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review rebuilt C as report plus CI threshold, its honest form.
reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: Rli5B. Skill: rli5. The beginner pass could not see the package and source together or find the function the error named. The in-wild block shows both files and the error names a claim that exists.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Anthropic. Adversarial model family: OpenAI. The rival-family review found the policy spelling was not the ratified typed form, max had no semantics, a bare rung had no count, and the fix could fail. All four are repaired and C is now the CI-threshold alternative.

decisions.title: How claim evidence is named in reports
decisions.gist: The words a report uses for the evidence behind a claim, and whether they form an order.
decisions.lesson: Each claim can carry more than one kind of evidence: the solver proved it, generated inputs passed, written examples passed, or only the runtime check exists. Reports, jet inspect, and any package floor need words for these. This choice picks the words and decides whether they form a fixed order for policy.
decisions.story: A reviewer reads a claims report on her phone and must see which claims are proved, which passed generated inputs and how many, and which only have a runtime check.
decisions.inWild:
claims  4 rows   proved 1   generated 1   examples 1   checked 1   failing 0
  add_fee.Post   proved
  parse.Post     generated(4000)
  greet          examples(1)
  save.Post      checked          runtime check only; effectful, not generated

options.name: Six words in one order, including static and assumed
options.detail: static, proved, fuzzed, tested, asserted, assumed as one total order.
options.technical: Rejected by the rival review: static is compiler provenance, not claim evidence; assumed hides which gate was used; generated and example evidence are not totally ordered.
options.code:
add_fee.Post   proved
raw_copy       assumed   // which gate? #Unsafe, #Impure, a grant?

options.name: Nouns
options.detail: checked, proven, generated, example, runtime, trusted.
options.technical: Same shape as A with the same defects.
options.code:
add_fee.Post   proven
greet          example(1)

options.name: Numbered levels
options.detail: G4 down to G0 with a legend printed at the top of every report.
options.technical: Legend: G4 proved, G3 generated(n), G2 examples(n), G1 checked, G0 unchecked.
options.code:
legend: G4 proved  G3 generated(n)  G2 examples(n)  G1 checked  G0 unchecked
add_fee.Post   G4
parse.Post     G3(4000)

options.name: Producer plus outcome, kept in parallel; one acceptance order for policy
options.detail: Every evidence record is stored as producer, outcome, and count: solver proved, generated passed 4000, examples passed 1, runtime check present. A claim keeps all its records; nothing is overwritten. The report shows the strongest rung by one acceptance order used only for package floors: proved above generated(n) above examples(n) above checked above unchecked. Gates such as #Unsafe are not claim evidence and are reported by their own kind in the rights plane.
options.technical: Evidence record = { producer, outcome, count, record_id }. Summary word = strongest rung reached. Counts are part of the word: generated(4000). No static rung: compiler facts are not claims. No assumed rung: gates keep their kind.
options.code:
claims  4 rows
  add_fee.Post   proved             also: generated(1000), examples(1)
  parse.Post     generated(4000)    also: examples(2)
  greet          examples(1)
  save.Post      checked            not generated: save reaches FS.Write
$ jet inspect claims --all app.jet     # every record, not only the strongest

comparisons.note: Test results say ok or FAILED; no evidence word.
comparisons.code: test t ... ok

comparisons.note: Evidence categories are named by what was done: branch coverage, MC/DC, fuzz.
comparisons.code: 100% MC/DC

recommendation.why: It keeps every record, names each by what happened, and gives policy one narrow order without claiming that one generated run beats every written example.

whyNot.reason: It mixes compiler facts and gates into a claim order and hides the gate kind.
The same defects with vaguer words.
Numbers need the legend on every page and still imply a single order.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two-word rows are longer than one word. The summary line stays short; the detail is behind --all.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared verbs, nouns, and numbered levels.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the producer-plus-outcome option after the rival review showed the six-word order was unsound.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review kept a narrow acceptance order inside D for package floors only.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review gave C its case: numbers sort with no reading, and it now carries its legend.
reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: Rli5B. Skill: rli5. The beginner pass found the six words undefined and option C without its legend. Every option now defines its words and C prints its legend.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Anthropic. Adversarial model family: OpenAI. The rival-family review showed the six words were not a total order and that static and assumed are not claim evidence. Option D stores producer, outcome, and count with one narrow acceptance order, and the recommendation moved from A to D.

decisions.title: One ledger: one typed query over facts, instances, and evidence
decisions.gist: Whether every tool reads program facts, per-program fact instances, and per-run evidence through one typed ledger contract.
decisions.lesson: A fact is one statement Jet records about a program: a value's range, a scope's rights, a claim on a function, a type's wire shape. Jet has one law for facts and one static registry of fact kinds, but no one contract for reading them. Rights, claims, shapes, tiers, and records each keep a private table and report. This choice decides whether they are read through one typed ledger with three stores: the schema of fact kinds, the fact instances of one program, and the evidence records of one run.
decisions.story: Mara writes a parser with a postcondition, a test, and a package that forbids the network. Today three tools tell her three unrelated things. With one ledger, jet prove says her claim is generated-tested on 4,000 inputs, jet inspect rights says why the network is refused. Both answers come from the same stores through the same query.
decisions.inWild:
#Post(result.is_sorted(), "sorted")
fn sort_ids(ids: [Int]) [Int] -> { return ids.sorted() }

$ jet prove app.jet
  sort_ids.Post   generated(4000)   inputs from the Pre domain
$ jet inspect rights app.jet
  sort_ids   -[]>   inferred: no effects reached

options.name: One table with grade and time columns
options.detail: The static registry gains two columns, grade and time, and every tool reads that one table.
options.technical: Rejected by the rival review: registry rows are process-static (Registry.rs:150-182) and cannot hold per-run values such as generated(4000). Kept as an option for honesty.
options.code:
// one static table cannot store a per-run count
sort_ids.Post   generated(4000)   // where does 4000 live?

options.name: Keep the current law; six separate proposals
options.detail: Rights, claims, shapes, tiers, records, and tables are each fixed alone. No shared query, no shared vocabulary. Each may keep a private table.
options.technical: No amendment. Each slate defines its own words.

options.name: Planes and time, no evidence
options.detail: Rights, shapes, and tiers are read through the ledger. Claims keep their own reports because evidence records are judged too new.
options.technical: Amends D-FACT-LAW1 with the time clause only.
options.code:
$ jet inspect rights run.jet    # from the ledger
$ jet test run.jet              # still its own report

options.name: One typed ledger over three stores
options.detail: Three stores by lifetime: the static schema of fact kinds (the registry, unchanged), the fact instances of one checked program, and the evidence records of one run. One typed query contract reads all three. Every projection (check, test, prove, inspect, dev, receipts) uses it. Evidence grade lives on claims only; rights keep their gate kind and provenance and never receive a grade. Time is a value on the query, not a column on the schema.
options.technical: Amends D-FACT-LAW1=B by adding the evidence clause for claims and the shared-query clause for tools. Does not fold FactRegistry (Facts.rs:337-494) into Registry.rs; both stay behind the contract. Registration rows stay &'static. A parity test proves that every existing tool answer can be reproduced through the contract before any tool switches.
options.code:
// three stores, one query
ledger.kinds()                       // static: what a Type.Interval row is
ledger.facts(program).rights(sort_ids)   // instance: -[]> inferred
ledger.evidence(run).claim(sort_ids.Post)  // record: generated(4000)
$ jet inspect claims run.jet
sort_ids.Post   generated(4000)   record 2026-09-01T21-14-25

comparisons.note: One type system, then separate ecosystems for tests, fuzzing, proofs, and serde, no shared query.
comparisons.code:
#[test] fn t() {}
// cargo fuzz, kani, serde: four tools, four reports

comparisons.note: Every claim has one status in one report because the verifier and the compiler share one program model.
comparisons.code:
method Sort(a: seq<int>) returns (r: seq<int>)
  ensures sorted(r)

recommendation.why: It gives every tool one contract without pretending that a static schema and a run's evidence are one table, which the rival review showed they are not.

whyNot.reason: A static row cannot hold a per-run count.
Six private tables is what the audit measured; keeping them keeps the drift.
Without evidence records a contract, a test, and a proof stay three things.

recommendation.tradeoff: A parity test over every existing tool answer must pass before any tool switches to the contract, that is internal work with no surface change.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared one table with two columns, the current law, and planes without evidence.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a separate evidence registry beside the fact registry and folded it into the three-store design.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review produced option D from A's shared vocabulary and the rival finding that storage lifetimes differ.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review gave B and C their honest cases: least change, and evidence as a later step.
reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: Rli5A. Skill: rli5. The beginner pass found fact, registry, plane, and column undefined. The lesson now defines each word and option D shows the three stores in one transcript.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Anthropic. Adversarial model family: OpenAI. The rival-family review showed a static row cannot hold per-run evidence, the two registries are not proven duplicates, and grants are not evidence. Option D separates the stores, keeps grade on claims only, and the recommendation moved from A to D.

decisions.title: What happens to pinned state when its type changes
decisions.gist: Whether a pinned value whose type changed shape is migrated, restarted, or reset.
decisions.lesson: #Persist pins a module value across a swap. When the value's type changes shape, D-HOTSWAP1 says the program restarts with an announcement. A migration block already exists for #PublishedSchema types and walks old wire shapes to the new one. This choice decides whether that block also migrates pinned live values, and what happens when there is no migration.
decisions.story: Sam's pinned world holds a list of enemies. He adds a health field to Enemy and saves. Today the game restarts and the level is lost.

options.name: Migrate #PublishedSchema values with their migration block; announced restart otherwise
options.detail: When the changed type is #PublishedSchema and a migration covers the change, the pinned value migrates in place through the same step function that decode uses, and the save line says so. When the type is not published or no migration covers the change, the ratified announced restart happens and the line prints the migration block to write. A rename of the pinned binding resets its state, and the line says so.
options.technical: Extends D-MIGRATE4's step functions to resident values. D-HOTSWAP1 restart stays the fallback. Identity stays module path plus binding name (D-PERSIST-DEVSTATE1), no new marker.

options.name: Keep today: announced restart on any layout change
options.detail: No migration of live values.
options.technical: D-HOTSWAP1 unchanged.
options.code: saved game.jet  layout changed: Enemy gained health  restarting

options.name: Migrate any Codable pinned value
options.detail: Migration blocks are accepted on any Codable type for live values, not only #PublishedSchema.
options.technical: Would need a new migration eligibility rule (amends D-MIGRATE1); not recommended until the wire rule and the live rule are one rule.
options.code: migration Enemy { add health: Int = 100 }   // on a type that is not #PublishedSchema

comparisons.note: Added fields take their initializers on reload; removed state is dropped.
comparisons.code: // new fields get their initializers

comparisons.note: State survives only through an explicit migration callback.
comparisons.code: code_change/3

recommendation.why: It reuses the ratified migration block for the one case it already describes, and keeps the ratified restart for every other case, so no state is ever guessed.

whyNot.reason: The level is lost on every shape change even when the migration is one line.
Two eligibility rules for one block.

recommendation.tradeoff: A type must be marked #PublishedSchema to migrate live, that is one marker, and it is the same marker wire data needs.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a shape rule, the opt-in pin, and identity for everything.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a per-binding reset marker and folded it into the rename rule and the restart fallback.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review rebuilt A around #PublishedSchema eligibility and the D-HOTSWAP1 fallback after the rival review.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review gave B its case: nothing is ever stale.
reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: Rli5C. Skill: rli5. The beginner pass found shape undefined and option C self-contradictory. The lesson defines the pin and the layout rule, and every option shows its save line for the same edit.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Anthropic. Adversarial model family: OpenAI. The rival-family review showed #Persist is the ratified pin and mutation gate, migration is ratified only for #PublishedSchema, and renames drop state. A migrates only published types, keeps restart as the fallback, and reports renames.

decisions.title: jet dev swaps on save by default
decisions.gist: Whether jet dev replaces changed code in the running program by default, and what it reports on every save.
decisions.lesson: jet dev watches files and can either rerun the program or swap changed functions into the resident process; today swap is chosen by --swap or by auto-detection. Pinned state is #Persist: it is the one module binding a function may write, and it survives a swap. A layout change to a pinned type triggers an announced restart (D-HOTSWAP1). This choice decides whether swap is the default and what the dev log reports.
decisions.story: Sam tunes an enemy's chase logic in a game. Every save restarts the game and loses the level. With swap by default, the changed function runs on the next frame and the pinned world stays.

options.name: Swap by default; pinned state kept; restart on layout change stays
options.detail: Saving a file swaps the changed functions into the running program. #Persist values survive as ratified. A layout change to a pinned type still triggers the ratified announced restart, unless D-LIVE-PERSIST1 selects migration for #PublishedSchema types. Every save prints one line naming swapped functions, kept values, and any restart. jet dev --restart refuses swap for the session; dev: .{ swap: false } refuses it for the package.
options.technical: Amends D-DEV4 and D-DEVMODE1 defaults (swap first, rerun only when swap is impossible). D-HOTSWAP1 layout rule unchanged. Module mutation law unchanged: #Persist remains the one writable module binding (D-PERSIST-DEVSTATE1=A). Precondition carded before the flip: a long-lived edit test on the JIT and interpreter engines with callers mid-execution, proving swap keeps program meaning (I9).
options.code:
$ jet dev game.jet
live  game.jet  watching 1 file
saved game.jet  swapped chase  kept world
saved game.jet  layout changed: Enemy gained health  restarting (announced)

options.name: Swap by default; no pinned state
options.detail: Code swaps on save; every value including #Persist resets.
options.technical: Would amend D-PERSIST-DEVSTATE1 away; not recommended.
options.code: saved game.jet  swapped chase  reset world

options.name: Keep today
options.detail: Auto-detect with --swap and --restart overrides; no per-save receipt line.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: $ jet dev --swap game.jet

comparisons.note: Hot reload keeps state by contract and reports what it reloaded.
comparisons.code: Reloaded 1 of 512 libraries in 214ms.

comparisons.note: Old and new module versions coexist; a callback migrates state.
comparisons.code: code_change(OldVsn, State, Extra) -> {ok, NewState}.

recommendation.why: Keeping the world across a save is what the pin was ratified for; making swap the default is the missing half, and the per-save line makes every kept or restarted value visible.

whyNot.reason: It throws away the ratified pin.
The pieces exist and are off by default.

recommendation.tradeoff: A precondition proof must land before the default flips. Until then the flag stays.

decisions.title: Challenge to D-MARK-STACK1: free marker stacking
decisions.gist: Whether to amend the ratified marker-stacking rule so bare markers may stack, or keep it.
decisions.lesson: D-MARK-STACK1=A (2026-07-23) says one attached rule is written #Rule, two or more distinct rules share one #[A, B] list. A one-item list or an adjacent bare stack is E0999 with the canonical rewrite. Repeated rules such as two #Post markers are allowed. Field and variant sites take only the bracket form. This ballot is a challenge to that law; the default expectation is that the law stands.
decisions.story: Kai adds a #Post to a function that already has a #Pre and must rewrite the line into the bracket form.

#Pre(cents > 0, "positive") fn add_fee(cents: Int) Int -> { return cents + 5 }       // one rule: bare, today
#[Pre(cents > 0, "positive"), Post(result > cents, "grows")] fn add_fee(cents: Int) Int -> { return cents + 5 }   // two rules: one list, today

options.name: Amend: bare markers stack; brackets become optional grouping
options.detail: Distinct bare markers may stack on separate lines. The bracket list stays as optional grouping. Field and variant sites also accept bare markers. jet fmt writes stacked lines for functions and types and the bracket form for fields.
options.technical: Amends D-MARK-STACK1=A and S82; keeps the rule that scoped block rules do not stack. Two accepted layouts with a formatter-owned canonical form per site.

options.name: Keep D-MARK-STACK1 as ratified
options.detail: One bare rule, one list for several, E0999 with the rewrite otherwise. The audit found no new evidence that meets the bar for reopening card #761.
options.technical: No change.

#[Pre(cents > 0, "positive")] fn f(cents: Int) Int -> cents     // E0999: one-item list; fix: #Pre(...)

Attributes stack freely.

decisions.title: Generate compiler tables from their declared twins
decisions.gist: Which hand-written compiler tables become generated views of Jet declarations, and which keep a Rust home under a guard.
decisions.lesson: A compiler table is a lookup list written in Rust: effect roots, marker sites, encoding formats, taint sinks, transaction irreversibility, the Core call dispatcher. Some of these have a twin declared in Jet already, such as effect FS.Read in the Prelude. Some have no Jet twin, such as the lexer keyword map. Two twins already disagree: the dispatcher knows core.services, the inventory knows core.service. This choice decides which tables are generated and which are the one home themselves.
decisions.story: A contributor renames core.services to core.service in the inventory. The dispatcher still says core.services. Nothing fails until a user calls it.

options.name: Generate every table
options.detail: Every table listed in the proposal is generated from a Jet declaration.
options.technical: Rejected by the rival review: the lexer keyword map, the CLI inventory, and the report enums have no declared twin; a compiler needs those to parse the declarations that would generate them.
options.code: // the keyword map would generate the lexer that reads the file that holds the keyword map

options.name: Generate the dispatcher and the effect enum only
options.detail: The two largest tables are generated; the small vocabularies stay hand-written.
options.technical: Two generators, no guard on the rest.
options.code: // core_call.rs generated; sinks.rs still by hand

options.name: Fix core.services by hand
options.detail: No generator.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: // edit the row

options.name: Generate every table that has a declared twin; guard the rest as their own home
options.detail:
Tables with a Jet twin are generated from it with a drift guard that fails the build on a hand row: effect roots and leaves, marker sites. Fact reads, encoding formats, taint sinks, transaction irreversibility, the Core dispatcher, ambient routes, and the export classifier. Tables with no twin keep their Rust home as the one home, under a guard that fails when a second copy appears: the lexer keyword map. The CLI inventory, the report enums, the tier list.

Irreversibility is declared on FS.Write, Net, Exec, and FFI. Precondition: a derivability census of the 622 dispatcher rows lists every row the generator cannot derive; each becomes a declared fact or a card before the dispatcher switches.
options.technical: Generation is a workspace build step over committed declarations, checked in like the embedded Prelude, so no bootstrap cycle: the lexer that parses the declarations is not generated from them. Amends D-META-ONE1 scope note (Prelude-only markers unchanged; the Rust twin retires) and D-META-REG1 (registry as generator input). D-ONCE-LAW1 requires one home and a guard, not a Jet home; D respects that.

comparisons.note: Lang items and builtin attributes are one generated registry; the lexer is not.
comparisons.code: #[lang = "add"]

comparisons.note: Builtins are one list the compiler reads; the tokenizer is hand-written.
comparisons.code: @import

recommendation.why: It enforces the corpus law where a twin exists and states the one home where none does, with a guard either way.

whyNot.reason: It cannot generate the lexer from a file the lexer must read first.
The small tables decide user-facing behavior and are the least tested.
The drift is a symptom of the mechanism.

recommendation.tradeoff: The derivability census must finish before the dispatcher switches. Every undeclared row is work, and the count is the honest measure of hidden facts.

decisions.title: A raw string literal for ordinary text
decisions.gist: Whether an ordinary String literal can be written with no escapes, and how it is spelled.
decisions.lesson: An ordinary String in Jet interprets backslash escapes and braces for interpolation. Typed text heads such as Regex{"\d+"} and Path{"C:\\Users"} already pass their text to a domain grammar, so a regex or a path does not need doubled backslashes. A plain String still does, for example a Windows path stored as text or a template with literal braces. This choice decides whether a raw ordinary String exists and how it is spelled.
decisions.explainer: Scope: this ballot spells a literal whose value is an ordinary String. How a String crosses into C (NUL-terminated, S59, E3211) is a boundary rule, answered on the owner's question q2yn2rnn and not changed here.
decisions.story: Kai stores a template with literal braces and backslashes in a plain String for a tool that is not a regex or a path, and doubles every backslash and brace.
decisions.inWild:
template :: "C:\\tools\\{{name}}\\bin"     // plain String today: doubled backslashes and braces
pattern :: Regex{"\d+\.\d+"}                // typed head today: no doubling needed
decisions.detail:
Owner tradeoff pass, 2026-09-02: option A adopts the Markdown fence rule, so a raw string may contain backticks and the old limit is gone.

Owner discussion pass, 2026-09-02: the owner asked why not `Raw{}`. Option C now shows what the head law keeps, so a reader can see that a `Raw{}` head is not raw where raw matters most. A JavaScript row names the one habit backtick readers must unlearn, option A defines each rule in plain words, and check instructions are added.

options.name: Backtick raw String with the Markdown fence rule
options.detail:
Jet currently gives backticks no meaning; this option assigns them to raw `String` literals. Inside, backslashes, quotes, braces, line endings, and indentation stay exactly as typed; no escape is processed and `{name}` is not evaluated. A group of one or more adjacent backticks opens the literal, and the next group with the same count closes it; groups with other counts stay text. This is the Markdown code-span rule. When the text starts and ends with a space, Jet removes one space from each end, unless the text is only spaces.

That space rule lets a value begin or end with a backtick: type one space just inside each backtick group. To keep an edge space, type one extra space at each end. The empty `String` keeps its ordinary spelling `""`, because adjacent backticks merge into one opening group. A typed Windows line ending stays carriage return plus line feed.

The result is the same ordinary `String` as `""`, with every String operation, including joining with a normal string. The lexer, the part of the compiler that splits source into tokens, only looks for the closing backtick group; a backslash never starts an escape.
options.technical:
New token in Lexer/Tokens.rs; Syntax.rs entry with this decision ID (I7). Amends S8 (interpolation off inside) and S20 (escapes off inside); S70's multi-line trimming does not apply inside a fence.

Fence rule: the opening fence is the maximal contiguous run of N backticks at the token start. The literal ends at the next maximal contiguous run whose length is exactly N; runs of any other length are content. Padding rule: when the content begins and ends with an ASCII space and is not all spaces, one space is stripped from each end.

Jet borrows only these two rules from CommonMark; its line-ending normalization does not apply, and the String keeps every byte, so CRLF stays CRLF. A fence inside an ordinary string hole is one nested expression, and braces inside it do not close the hole. The formatter invariant is identical decoded bytes after reparse. An unterminated fence is reported with its opening line.
options.code:
// `name :: value` binds value to name; text after // is a comment.
template :: `C:\tools\{name}\bin`
query :: `
  select *
  from orders
`                                     // value: "\n  select *\n  from orders\n", every byte kept
shell :: ``run `date` now``          // two-backtick fence: the single backticks inside are text
pair  :: ```a `` b```                // three-backtick fence: the two-backtick run inside is text
tick  :: `` ` ``                      // padding spaces stripped: the text is one backtick
edge  :: `  a  `                      // one space removed from each end: the text is " a "
empty :: ""                           // the empty raw String is the ordinary empty literal
print(template)     // C:\tools\{name}\bin
print(shell)        // run `date` now
print(pair)         // a `` b
print(template + " ok")   // C:\tools\{name}\bin ok: an ordinary String, joined like any other

options.name: r-prefixed String, with hash delimiters for embedded quotes
options.detail: As Rust spells it: r"…" and r#"…"# when the text contains a quote.
options.technical: A prefix on a string literal; today r"…" lexes as an identifier then a string and fails E0003. Same S8 and S20 amendments.
options.code:
template :: r"C:\tools\{name}\bin"
quoted :: r#"say "hi""#

options.name: A checked-text head
options.detail:
`Raw{"…"}` would be a typed head: `Type{"…"}` is Jet's form for text checked by a named type, such as `Regex{"…"}` or `Path{"…"}`. It would create a named `Raw` value, not an ordinary `String`, so String functions would need `template.text()`, the conversion back to `String`. Its content check could accept anything, but its spelling would still give quotes and braces special meanings.

Under the ratified head law (D-BOUND-RAW1=A) only the backslash turns literal inside a head; the quote, brace, and interpolation rules stay. So a quote is written `\"` and the head receives both characters, a literal brace is still doubled as `{{`, and `{name}` is still a hole, the slot that interpolation fills. Making one head ignore those rules is a carve-out of the head law for one type.
options.technical: Ratified typed heads are Type{"…"} backed by CheckedText (D-TEXTHEAD-TYPE1); Raw would be a nominal type with an empty validation grammar. Its value is Raw, not String, and needs `.text()` to use as text. Regex is a compiler-owned exception that rejects holes after lexing; doubled braces still decode to one brace, and a backslash before a quote is preserved for the regex grammar (Lexer/Strings.rs).
options.code:
template :: Raw{"C:\tools\{{name}}\bin"}   // braces still doubled: {name} would be a hole
quoted   :: Raw{"say \"hi\""}               // the head receives say \"hi\" with both backslashes kept
print(template.text())                      // .text() converts the Raw value to a String

options.name: No raw string
options.detail: Escapes stay for plain Strings; typed heads cover regexes and paths.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: template :: "C:\\tools\\{{name}}\\bin"

comparisons.note: A code span opens and closes with the same number of backticks; any other run length is content, and one padding space allows a leading or trailing backtick. Option A borrows this rule, so the one thing Go's backtick string cannot hold is covered without Rust's hash form.
comparisons.code: `` a `quoted` word ``

comparisons.note: Backtick raw strings, multi-line, no escapes; a backtick can never appear inside, which is the limit option A removes.
comparisons.code: s := `C:\path`

comparisons.note: Template literals use backticks with `${}` holes and process backslash escapes, so they are the opposite of raw. `String.raw` preserves backslashes from the source, but `${...}` still evaluates. In Jet, backticks preserve backslashes and braces as characters, with no interpolation; that is the one habit a JavaScript reader must unlearn.
comparisons.code:
const s = `C:\tools`;            // \t is a tab: escapes apply
const r = String.raw`C:\tools`;  // C:\tools, but ${} still evaluates

comparisons.note: r prefix with optional hashes for embedded quotes.
comparisons.code: let s = r#"a "quoted" word"#;

recommendation.why: The glyph is free in Jet, the rule is the one Markdown already taught everyone, and multi-line comes with it. The value is a plain String, so nothing downstream changes, and the lexer only looks for the closing backtick group.

whyNot.reason: A prefix on a string is a second literal grammar, and the hash form solves a problem the fence already solves.

`Raw{"…"}` would be a separate type, not another spelling for `String`, so String functions would need `.text()`. Its quotes and braces would keep their syntax meaning, so it would not preserve the characters this ballot targets.
Plain Strings with backslashes and braces stay painful.

recommendation.tradeoff: A text that starts or ends with a backtick needs one padding space, and the empty raw String is written `""`; both are the small rules Markdown users already know.

reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review rewrote C in the ratified Type{"…"} form and gave it its honest cost: the value is not a String. The discussion pass added that the head law keeps its quote and brace rules.

The third, on the discussion revision, found fence, run, hole, and head undefined and C's sample contradicting its prose; A and C define each term, and C's sample matches.

The third, on the discussion revision, found a false Regex precedent, a padding contradiction, and untested hole nesting and CRLF round-trip; C cites the lexer, and the checks state each rule.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Run each valid option A example with `jet build`, `jet run`, and `jet eval`, which compile, run, and interpret the source, and on the web target where it applies. Compare each result with the exact `String` value shown in its comment. Count the opening backticks as N; only a closing group with exactly N backticks ends the literal. If the content starts and ends with spaces and holds another character, one space is removed at each end; content made only of spaces keeps every space.

Backslashes, braces, and typed line endings, including CRLF, remain characters, and `{name}` is not evaluated inside a fence. Inside an ordinary string hole, a fenced literal is one nested expression, and braces inside that fence do not close the outer hole. If no matching closing group appears, the error names the opening line. After formatting and reparsing, each fenced literal decodes to identical String bytes, including original LF or CRLF line endings. In Jet's syntax registry (`Syntax.rs`), record the backtick token under this decision id.

decisions.title: Keeping a replay as a regression claim
decisions.gist: Whether a captured replay can be saved as a claim that runs with every jet prove, how that is spelled, and how it survives edits.
decisions.lesson: Ratified law consumes a replay with `jet prove TARGET --replay ARTIFACT`, and says no option creates `jet replay` or changes `jet run`. D-RUN-RECORD1 later added `--record=NAME` on run, dev, and test, and `jet debug --replay=NAME` as the debugger's consumer. Replay identity is bound to the exact sources and build, so a plain replay fails after any edit. This choice decides whether a saved replay can stand as a regression claim, how that is spelled, and how it survives edits.
decisions.story: Ana has the replay of the crash. She wants to make sure it never comes back without writing a test by hand, and she will keep editing the program every day.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet prove app.jet --replay .jet/replays/c10aee50.jetproof-replay
replayed 14 events  fault reproduced at app.jet:31
decisions.detail: Owner tradeoff pass, 2026-09-02: `--keep` became `--save` and `kept/` became `saved/` on the owner's question. Saved claims now re-bind by a per-function anchor, so an edit elsewhere no longer makes them stale, and the saved-claim comparator is defined.

options.name: New file name and verbs under jet test
options.detail: .jetrec files, jet test --replay, jet test --keep.
options.technical: Rejected by the rival review: it amends D-PROVE-REPLAY1 consumption and the closed extension family without naming either.
options.code: $ jet test --replay r.jetrec

options.name: Add a jet replay command
options.detail: A new command replays; files unchanged.
options.technical: D-JREPLAY1 says no option creates jet replay.
options.code: $ jet replay .jet/replays/r.jetproof-replay

options.name: Replay under jet run
options.detail: jet run --replay ARTIFACT.
options.technical: D-JREPLAY1 says no option changes jet run.
options.code: $ jet run --replay r.jetproof-replay

options.name: Keep the ratified consumer; add --save with a lifecycle that survives edits
options.detail:
`jet prove TARGET --replay ARTIFACT` stays the proof consumer and `jet debug --replay=NAME` the debugger's. `jet prove TARGET --save ARTIFACT` copies the replay under `.jet/records/saved/<artifact_id>` and lists it in the index as a claim named `replay <artifact_id>`. Every `jet prove` of that target replays saved claims first. Two saves of one artifact are one claim; `--unsave <id>` removes it.

A saved claim guards a path, not a build. Each record is matched by an anchor that survives edits elsewhere: the function that made the request, the record kind, and its order within that function. An edit that does not touch that function keeps the claim alive. Operation, arguments, and request fields are still compared, as ratified.

Verdicts: passed when every record is consumed and the expectation holds. Failed when the fault returns or the output differs. Diverged (E3623) when an anchor is missing or ambiguous, or a record does not match. Vacuous when the fault's function no longer exists. Every verdict except passed names `--unsave` or a fresh capture, and only passed lets `jet prove` exit clean.
options.technical:
Adds `--save` and `--unsave` to jet prove; no new command, no new file kind, no change to jet run. Saved claims carry producer replay in the evidence report (D-CLAIM1 option C) and run before doctests, which amends D-PROVE-SEM1 producer ordering.

Amends the D-JREPLAY1 identity and outcome law for the saved-claim consumer only; plain `--replay` keeps exact identity and E3621. Anchor = (function stable id, record kind, ordinal of that kind within the function), stored in the index at save time beside the immutable artifact. Re-binding needs a unique anchor-to-site mapping; absence or ambiguity is E3623. Renaming or removing the request's function breaks its anchor: the claim reports diverged, or vacuous when it was the fault's function.

Expectation is fixed at save time from the recorded outcome. `no-fault` (recorded runtime_stop): passed when the outcome kind is exit with any status; failed on any runtime_stop, naming the code. `same-output` (recorded exit): passed when kind, status, stdout and stderr lengths, and hashes all match; failed on the first differing field. Sensitive-form records match by their ratified request digests. The index row stores the recorded identity, the identity last passed under, the fault anchor, and the expectation.
options.code:
$ jet prove app.jet --save .jet/replays/app-c10aee50b2a7.jetproof-replay
saved claim `replay c10aee50`   expects: no-fault (R0802 in fn parse, app.jet:31)
$ jet prove app.jet
  replay c10aee50   passed    14 events consumed, fault absent
// after an unrelated edit elsewhere in app.jet:
$ jet prove app.jet
  replay c10aee50   passed    14 events consumed, fault absent   (re-bound to build 7f1e…)
// the bug comes back:
  replay c10aee50   failed    R0802 reproduced in fn parse, app.jet:31   (exit 1)
    fix: repair the fault, or `jet prove app.jet --unsave c10aee50` if the change is intended

  replay c10aee50   diverged  E3623: replay diverged at record 9; no unique site in fn parse for TimeWall #3
    fix: `jet prove app.jet --capture` to re-record, or `jet prove app.jet --unsave c10aee50`

  replay c10aee50   vacuous   fault site fn parse no longer exists; the claim guards nothing
    fix: `jet prove app.jet --capture` to re-record, or `jet prove app.jet --unsave c10aee50`
$ jet prove app.jet --unsave c10aee50
removed claim `replay c10aee50`

The replay law forbids changing jet run.

decisions.title: One record index; safe capture by default in dev
decisions.gist: Whether every build, run, test, proof, and replay artifact is listed in one index with one identity, and whether jet dev captures a safe replay by default.
decisions.lesson: Jet writes receipts, proofs, and replay captures as separate files with separate formats. Replay capture has a ratified privacy law: the safe form records only the clock and refuses programs that reach randomness, raw input, or the network. The sensitive form records those only after a typed consent phrase. This choice decides whether the artifacts share one index and identity, and whether dev runs capture the safe form without being asked.
decisions.story: Ana hits a crash in jet dev after ten minutes of clicking. She cannot reproduce it. There was no capture because she did not run jet prove --capture.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet prove app.jet --capture             → .jet/replays/<id>.jetproof-replay   (Time only, ratified safe form)
$ jet check --receipt=hello app.jet       → .jet/receipts/objects/<sha>          (jet-receipt-v2)
$ jet prove app.jet                       → .jetproof                            (canonical JSON envelope)
decisions.detail: Owner tradeoff pass, 2026-09-02: option B now asks for the ratified consent phrase once per dev session, so programs that reach randomness, input, or the network are captured too. It names the two clauses that amendment touches.

options.name: One container format for every artifact
options.detail: One versioned file format embeds the ratified proof JSON and the ratified replay frames as payloads.
options.technical: Requires a new container, migration of every reader, and a new artifact kind under the closed extension family (D-ARTIFACT-EXT1). Kept as an option; not recommended before the index proves its worth.
options.code: .jet/records/<id>.jetrec   // embeds proofReport and replay frames

options.name: One index and identity over the ratified formats; dev captures the safe form by default and the sensitive form after one consent per session
options.detail:
Every artifact keeps its ratified bytes. One index under .jet/records lists them with one identity key (target inputSha256, tool, engine) and cross-links a proof to the replay it consumed and the receipt it produced. Jet dev captures the ratified safe replay (clock only) on every run, within a project retention budget. Release never captures without the ratified flag. jet build --verify rebuilds from the receipt inputs and reports identical bytes or the first differing input.

When a target reaches randomness, input, or the network, `jet dev` shows the ratified preflight once per session and asks for the phrase `capture sensitive`. Consent holds for that session while the target, the reachable authorities, hosts and streams, byte limit, disclosures, and destination stay the same; any change asks again. Each reload is one run with at most one artifact, mode 0600, under the budget. A session without a terminal runs unrecorded for such a target and says so; explicit `--record` and `--capture-sensitive` keep their E3627 refusal.
options.technical:
No format change to .jetproof (D-JPROOF1) or .jetproof-replay (D-JREPLAY1). Index: .jet/records/index.jsonl, one line per artifact, keyed by target.inputSha256 and report_id or artifact_id. Example row: `{target: 9f3a…, tool: prove, engine: dev-tir-v1, kind: replay, id: c10aee50}`; a different engine is a second row, and one changed source byte changes target. Retention: 256 MB and 200 records per project by default, oldest evicted, settable in package.jet under dev: .{ records: .{ budget: … } }. `jet build --verify` follows the one contract shared with D-BUILD-NOCHANGE1.

Choosing B amends two clauses for `jet dev` only: D-JREPLAY1's invocation unit and D-RUN-RECORD1's unchanged-preflight clause. One `jet dev` invocation is one consent scope over many runs, and the dev tier captures the safe form by default. Consent is a digest over target identity, capture mode, authorities, hosts and streams, byte limit, residual disclosures, and destination; any inequality re-prompts. Non-TTY dev prints `capture: skipped (Net at net_app.jet:9); no terminal to consent` and continues; `jet prove --capture`, `--record`, and `--capture-sensitive` keep E3627 before any effect.
options.code:
$ jet dev app.jet
… Runtime fault [R0802]: use of storage after its lifetime ended
  replay: .jet/replays/app-c10aee50b2a7.jetproof-replay   (safe form: 14 clock events; no Rand, IO, or Net reached)

$ jet dev net_app.jet
capture preflight: sensitive; Net localhost:3000 inbound, stdin; mode 0600; budget 256 MB
type `capture sensitive` to record this session, or press Enter to skip: capture sensitive
live  net_app.jet   capture: sensitive (session consent 12:03)
… ten minutes later …
… Runtime fault [R0802]: use of storage after its lifetime ended
  replay: .jet/replays/net_app-3b9c1a7e4d02.jetproof-replay   (sensitive form: 212 events)

$ jet dev net_app.jet </dev/null       # no terminal, for example CI
live  net_app.jet   capture: skipped (Net at net_app.jet:9); no terminal to consent

$ jet build --verify app.jet
built app (3.1 MB)   receipt 9f3a…
verified: identical bytes
// or: differs at input crates/jet-runtime-core (toolchain build id changed)

options.name: Keep the files as they are; add cross-references
options.detail: Each artifact gains a link to the others. Nothing captures by default.
options.technical: No index; links inside existing formats would change their bytes and identity.
options.code: // .jetproof references a replay by hash

comparisons.note: Recording is the default way to run under the tool; the trace directory is the index.
comparisons.code:
$ rr record ./app
$ rr ls

comparisons.note: A build is content-addressed over declared inputs; identical inputs give identical outputs.
comparisons.code: /nix/store/<hash>-app

recommendation.why: A crash leaves a replay whenever the program is safe to record, and after one typed consent per session when it is not. Every artifact is found from one place, and no ratified byte or privacy rule changes.

whyNot.reason: A new container reopens two ratified codecs and the closed extension family for no gain the index does not give.
Links inside the files change their identity, and nothing is captured when it matters.

recommendation.tradeoff: A program that reaches randomness, input, or the network is captured only after the session's typed consent, which is the ratified boundary spelled once per session rather than once per run.

The second, on the owner's revision, found the session consent unnamed as an amendment and no-terminal behavior unstated; B now names the amendment, keys consent by a digest, and shows the skip.

decisions.title: How to grant or deny rights on the command line
decisions.gist: The spelling for allowing and denying effects when you run a program from the command line.
decisions.lesson: An effect is a power a program uses: FS for files, Net for the network, Time for the clock. A leaf narrows a root: FS.Read is part of FS. Today jet has ten pairs of flags such as --allow-net and --deny-net. A pair per root cannot name a leaf. The package file already spells the same grant with the words allow and deny. This choice picks one command-line spelling and its precedence rule.
decisions.story: Dana runs a build script from CI. It may read files and the clock and must never write files or touch the network. She finds twenty flags and cannot say allow FS.Read but deny FS.Write.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet run --allow-fs --allow-time --deny-net build.jet
# cannot say: allow FS.Read but deny FS.Write

options.name: One flag with signs
options.detail: One flag carries the whole set with plus and minus prefixes.
options.technical: --rights=+FS.Read,+Time,-Net. Same precedence law as B.
options.code: $ jet run --rights=+FS.Read,+Time,-Net build.jet

options.name: Two flags with the manifest's words
options.detail: allow and deny take comma-separated effect names, roots or leaves. The words match authority.holds in package.jet. Precedence: names expand to their leaves first, then deny wins; naming the same effect in both flags is a usage error. Jet reads these two flags before the program's own flags; a program passes literal --allow to itself after --. The old twenty flags stop with a message that prints the exact replacement.
options.technical: --allow=FS.Read,Time --deny=Net. Amends the D-CLI-GLOBAL1 flag set; reserves the two names against #CLI structs with a diagnostic. No all sentinel: the pure preset stays jet eval --pure, which lowers to the empty row under D-RIGHTS1. Scripts outside the repository are migrated by hand; jet fix does not edit shell files.
options.code:
$ jet run --allow=FS.Read,Time --deny=Net build.jet
$ jet run --allow=FS --deny=FS.Write build.jet     # FS expands to its leaves, then FS.Write is removed
$ jet run --allow=Net --deny=Net build.jet
Error [E2102]: `Net` is both allowed and denied
$ jet run --allow-net build.jet
Error [E2102]: `--allow-net` was replaced by `--allow=Net`

options.name: Keep the twenty flags
options.detail: Nothing changes. Leaves cannot be named.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: $ jet run --allow-fs --deny-net build.jet

options.name: Repeatable flags
options.detail: One name per flag, repeated. No comma parsing; composes well in argument arrays.
options.technical: --allow FS.Read --allow Time --deny Net. Same precedence law as B.
options.code: $ jet run --allow FS.Read --allow Time --deny Net build.jet

comparisons.note: Paired allow and deny flags per capability, with values for narrowing.
comparisons.code: deno run --allow-read=/data --deny-net app.ts

comparisons.note: The manifest already spells the same grant with allow and deny.
comparisons.code: authority: { holds: { allow: [FS, Time] } }

recommendation.why: One vocabulary in the manifest and on the command line, leaves can be named, and the precedence rule is written down.

whyNot.reason: Sign prefixes are a second grammar for words that already exist.
Twenty flags cannot express a leaf.
It is B with a different separator; the comma form reads as one set, which is what a cap is.

recommendation.tradeoff: Scripts that use the old flags must change by hand. The replacement message names the exact new flag.

reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added the repeatable form as option D and tested a policy-file-only route, which C already covers.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review kept B and added its precedence, reservation, and migration rules from the rival findings.

decisions.title: One report frame for every rights denial
decisions.gist: Whether rights denials share one report frame with the call chain, and whether their ten codes stay.
decisions.lesson: When code uses a right its scope does not hold, Jet reports one of ten codes depending on where the code sits and which rule refused it. Some repairs are the same (grant the right, or remove the call); some are not (a transaction wants an undo, a pure block wants an injected clock). This choice decides whether the reports share one frame with the chain from the call to the refusing scope, and whether the codes stay distinct.
decisions.story: Priya moves an http.get from a function into a block. She gets E0740, then E0712. Each docs page explains a different mechanism. The repair was the same both times: grant Net at the package or remove the call.

options.name: One code for every denial
options.detail: Every denial uses E0740 and one shape, nine codes retire.
options.technical: Rejected by the rival review: consumers lose the machine discriminator between purity, replay, transaction, memory, and package denials, and E0750 (an undeclared effect name) is not a denial at all.
options.code:
Error [E0740]: `run` reaches `Net`, which this scope may not use.
// same code whether the cause is a row, a block, a package, purity, or a transaction

options.name: One frame and chain; the codes stay
options.detail:
Every rights report uses one frame: the call, the chain of callables it reaches the right through, the scope chain, the nearest scope that could grant it. The repairs with their safety class. The code stays distinct so a tool can tell a package denial from a transaction rule. A package grant is never an automatic edit: rights only widen by a written word, so that repair is graded needs-review; removing the call or tightening a row can be behavior-preserving.

E0750 keeps its own frame because its repair is to fix the effect name.
options.technical: Adds a denial_kind field and the chain to the jet.report/v1 objects of E0740, E0712, E1803, E3521, E3401, E3403, E0725, E0746. E0921 (amends their I4 snapshots and D-REPORT-MACHINE1 detail fields, no code retires). fix_edits use the five ratified safety classes (D-REPORT-FIXGRADE1=D).
options.code:
Error [E0712]: this `#FX` region uses the effect `Net`, which it has no authority for
  run.jet:8:15   fetch("https://x")   reaches Net through fetch → core.http.get
  scope chain:   #FX(FS) at run.jet:8 → run → package orders (holds [FS, Time])
  nearest scope that could grant Net: package orders (package.jet:2)
  fix (needs-review):        add Net to authority.holds.allow in package.jet
  fix (behavior-preserving): move the call out of the #FX(FS) block
$ jet check --json run.jet
{"schema":"jet.report/v1","code":"E0712","denial_kind":"block","chain":["run","fetch","core.http.get"],"fix_edits":[{"file":"package.jet","span":"2:31-2:31","new_text":", Net","safety":"needs-review"}]}

options.name: Keep the reports as they are
options.detail: No change.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: Error [E1803]: `Net` is not in package holds

comparisons.note: Borrow errors keep distinct codes and share one frame that shows every conflicting use.
comparisons.code:
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `v` as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable
  --> src/main.rs:4:5

comparisons.note: One code per kind of conflict; the message names both sides.
comparisons.code: error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.

recommendation.why: One frame teaches the chain and the repairs; distinct codes keep the machine meaning that tools and ratified rules depend on.

whyNot.reason: One code hides which rule refused, and it would route a misspelled effect name through a grant repair.
Two frames for one move is the measured defect.

recommendation.tradeoff: Nine snapshots change shape. No external link breaks because every code stays.

reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a per-plane code family and found it is what keeping the codes already gives.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review moved the recommendation from A to B after the rival review showed the discriminator is load-bearing and that a grant cannot be a safe edit.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review gave C its case: nothing changes for anyone.
reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: Rli5A. Skill: rli5. The beginner pass asked for the source beside the diagnostic. The in-wild block now shows both files and option B names the source line the chain refers to.

The rival-family review showed repairs differ by denial kind, a grant cannot be a safe edit, one code loses the discriminator, and E0750 is a vocabulary error. The recommendation moved from A to B with denial_kind and ratified safety classes.

decisions.title: One rights checker for every scope
decisions.gist: Whether one checker reads rights rows at every scope, and which private checkers it replaces.
decisions.lesson: A rights row says what code may do, such as -[FS.Read]> on a function. A scope is a region: a function, a block, a package, a compile-time block, or one command-line run. One walker checks the row, and a purity walker, a replayable walker, a comptime branch, and the --pure flag check the same question again. A separate transaction checker asks a different question: whether an irreversible effect inside #Transact has an undo. This choice decides which of these become one checker.
decisions.story: Ravi marks a game step #Replayable so replays are exact. He adds a log line that reads the clock and gets E0725 from the replayable walker. His pure helper got E3401 from the purity walker for the same clock read last week. Two checkers, two words, one rule.

options.name: One walker for everything, including transactions
options.detail: Purity, replayable, comptime, and invocation checks become rows read by the one walker. The transaction rule also becomes a row that excludes effects carrying an irreversible fact.
options.technical: Rejected by the rival review: #Transact admits an irreversible effect when on_commit defers it or #Undo names an inverse (syntax-decisions.md:2603-2616). A row by effect name cannot express that.
options.code: #Transact(order) { fs.write(path, text) }   // a row would refuse this even with an inverse

options.name: Keep every walker; unify only the words
options.detail: Each checker stays. The messages share one sentence shape. Behavior may still drift, as jet eval --pure already drifts (it prints).
options.technical: No deletion. Rows re-worded under I4.
options.code:
$ jet eval --pure 'print("x")'
x
()        // today: the CLI purity copy is weaker than the source one

options.name: One walker for rights rows; transactions keep their obligation checker
options.detail: Purity is the empty row. #Replayable lowers to the row that excludes Time, Rand, Net, and IO. A compile-time block holds the row that allows only Mem. Every spelling stays and one walker checks them. The transaction rule stays its own checker because it is a duty: an irreversible effect owes an undo. Which effects count as irreversible becomes a declared fact that checker reads. The command-line spelling is decided in D-RIGHTS-CLI1, not here.
options.technical: Deletes Sema/Purity.rs:77-99 and the replayable walker at Sema/Effects.rs:1480-1565. The comptime purity stage split and its impure_builtin leaf table (crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/Purity.rs:78-123) become one row read by the shared walk. Amends D-REPLAY1 and D-SHAPE8 as lowerings. D-TXN1-4 and D-BOUND-UNDO1 unchanged. Precondition: a differential matrix runs purity, replayable, comptime, and invocation cases through both the old walkers and the row walker and shows identical verdicts before the old walkers are deleted.

comparisons.note: One effect row mechanism carries inference and handlers; there is no second permission checker.
comparisons.code: fun step(s : state) : <ndet> state

comparisons.note: Purity is not checked at all; const fn is a separate, narrower checker.
comparisons.code: const fn f() -> i32 { 1 }

recommendation.why: It deletes the copies that answer the rights question and leaves the one checker that answers a different question. The rival review showed A is wrong on transactions.

whyNot.reason: A row by effect name cannot see an on_commit deferral or a #Undo inverse.
Matching words on five checkers does not stop them from disagreeing, and one already does.

recommendation.tradeoff: The differential matrix must be built before the old walkers go. A preset that is not exactly a row fails that matrix loudly.

decisions.title: Enforcing S6: the explicit semicolon
decisions.gist: How the ratified no-semicolon law is enforced when a user types one.
decisions.lesson: S6 says statements end at line end and the retired semicolon spelling is E0373. The lexer accepts an explicit semicolon today, so the law is written and not enforced. This choice decides how to enforce it: as the ratified error, as a lint that policy can promote, or by formatter only. The fix is contextual: a semicolon followed by code on the same line becomes a line break; a semicolon at line end is removed.
decisions.story: Kai comes from JavaScript and types a semicolon out of habit, it compiles. Six months later the codebase has both spellings.
decisions.inWild: a :: 1; b :: 2      // accepted today; S6 says E0373

options.name: Enforce E0373 as ratified, with the contextual fix
options.detail: An explicit semicolon is the ratified E0373 with a behavior-preserving edit: a line break when code follows on the same line, removal at line end. The parser keeps a boundary at the same position so one file reports once and parsing resumes at the next statement. Precondition: a census of the corpus for deliberate semicolons before the error lands.
options.technical: Explicit and inserted terminators share TokKind::Semi; the diagnostic dispatches on a non-empty source span. E0373 row gains fix_edits, corpus census carded.
options.code:
a :: 1; b :: 2
Error [E0373]: `;` is not a statement terminator in Jet
  fix (behavior-preserving): break the line
a :: 1
b :: 2

options.name: Accept with a lint; policy may promote it
options.detail: The semicolon compiles; a lint carries the same contextual edit; policy.lints.deny promotes it to an error per package.
options.technical: New L-code with fix_edits; E0373 retired or reserved.
options.code:
Warning [L0xxx]: `;` is not needed
  fix (behavior-preserving): break the line

options.name: Accept; the formatter rewrites it
options.detail: No diagnostic; jet fmt applies the contextual edit.
options.technical: Formatter rule only; unformatted files keep both spellings.
options.code: a :: 1; b :: 2   // fmt → two lines

comparisons.note: Semicolons are inserted by the lexer; typing them is legal and gofmt removes them.
Legal but discouraged; linters flag it.

recommendation.why: The law is ratified and the fix is one keystroke; enforcing it removes a second spelling that a reader or an agent would otherwise have to expect.

whyNot.reason: It retires a ratified code to add a lint that says the same thing.
A file that was never formatted keeps two spellings.

recommendation.tradeoff: A habit from another language meets an error on day one. The error carries the fix.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft treated the error as new; the rival review showed S6 already ratifies E0373, so the ballot is now about enforcement.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review added accept-with-lint as its own option.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review made the fix contextual after the rival review showed same-line removal is unsafe.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review gave C its case: nobody sees an error for a habit.
reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: Rli5E. Skill: rli5. The beginner pass asked what the fix does on one line. Option A shows the two-line result.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Anthropic. Adversarial model family: OpenAI. The rival-family review found the fix unsafe on one line, the census missing, the recovery boundary unstated, and E0373 already ratified. All are repaired and the ballot is now about enforcement.

decisions.title: One shape fact; text formats, env, and args are projections
decisions.gist: Whether a type's wire shape is one fact that JSON, CBOR, CSV, TOML, YAML, XML, env, and args all read, and whether database rows and FFI join later.
decisions.lesson: A shape is the named fields, their types, and their defaults that a value shows at a boundary. Jet structs are already Codable by default, env/json/toml/csv already share one codec, and a migration block already walks old wire shapes for #PublishedSchema types. Around that core a second JSON model, a five-entry format enum, and a separate command-line parser keep their own copy of the shape. This choice decides how far one shape fact reaches.
decisions.explainer: Terms: a projection is one boundary form of a value. A codec encodes and decodes it. A `Row` is the map a database driver returns. DDL is a statement that changes a table. FFI crosses a language boundary.
decisions.story: Ola writes a Config struct and reads it from a JSON file. Then she needs the same struct from environment variables on the server and from flags on the laptop, with the same defaults and renames.
decisions.detail: Owner tradeoff pass, 2026-09-02: option C now takes database rows through the same codec builder and keeps columns on the field name. It fixes the migration vocabulary, so only automatic table migration and FFI wait.

options.name: All projections, including database rows and FFI layout

Every text format, env, and args read one shape fact: default, rename, skip, short flag, doc, discriminant, version. A rename is shared by default and may be given per format when a legacy name differs. Migration stays on #PublishedSchema types as ratified. The second JSON model is deleted and formats become declared rows.

Database rows join now for reading and writing through a new `db.decode<T>(row)` and `db.encode(value)` on the same codec builder. That amends the ratified row surface, where D-DBDRIVER1 keeps `Row` maps and `db.row_*` reads. A column is named by the field name, or by `db:` when the column differs; the shared wire rename never renames a column, because the table's schema is not the program's.

A keyword-only #[Rename(json: "k", env: "K")] names formats with no shared name. args projection per D-SHAPE-PROJECT1. Migration eligibility unchanged (D-MIGRATE1, #PublishedSchema).

Declared rename slots: json, cbor, csv, toml, yaml, xml, env, args, db. Row codec: a missing column with no default, NULL into a non-optional field, an unconvertible value, or a duplicate column is a `FieldError`; extra columns are ignored; `?T` accepts NULL. The DDL card is minted on ratification and carries ballot D-SHAPE-DDL1. It is blocked on a fixture with a named table, one renamed column, typed reads before and after a migration, and rollback after a failed DDL statement. The acceptance terms forbid a second vocabulary.
