decisions.title: Command-line arguments as a decode format
decisions.gist: Whether args.decode<T>() joins the shipped env.decode<T>(), and how the two combine.
decisions.lesson: env.decode<T>() already exists: it fills a struct from environment variables with a prefix, an optional file, and an allow list. fn run(args: T) already fills a struct from command-line flags through the core.args builder, and D-CLI-GLOBAL1 already ratifies its precedence: command input, then #Env, then the field default. What does not exist is a way to decode arguments anywhere except the entry function, or that same precedence applied outside it. This choice decides that.
decisions.story: Ola wants one Config filled from flags when present, from the environment otherwise, and from the field defaults last, with an invalid value reported rather than skipped.

options.name: Add args.decode<T>() through the same builder; the ratified precedence applies anywhere
options.detail: args.decode<T>() decodes a struct from the process arguments anywhere in a program. It lowers through the same core.args builder that fn run(args: T) uses, so help and diagnostics are byte-identical. env.decode<T>() and its parameters are unchanged. A new combinator applies the ratified precedence outside the entry function: an explicit flag wins, then an environment value, then the field default (D-CLI-GLOBAL1). A present but invalid value is a FieldError, never treated as absent.
options.technical: core.args gains decode<T>() with the same signature family as env.decode. Binds to the D-CLI builder floor (syntax-decisions.md:183-196); no second parser. Precedence combinator: Config.merge(args, settings) returns T ![FieldError] with the stated order.

options.name: Keep fn run(args: T) only
options.detail: Arguments are decoded only at the entry function, where the ratified precedence already applies; env.decode stays. Elsewhere programs combine by hand.
options.technical: No change.

options.name: Constructors on the type
options.detail: Config.from_args() and Config.from_env() generated on every Codable type.
options.technical: A second verb family beside decode.
options.code: cfg :: Config.from_args()

comparisons.note: Environment and flags are separate packages; precedence is written by hand.
comparisons.code:
envconfig.Process("", &cfg)
flag.Parse()

comparisons.note: One derive reads flags and can fall back to environment per field.
comparisons.code: #[arg(long, env = "PORT")] port: u16

recommendation.why: It adds the one missing projection through the existing builder and applies the ratified precedence outside the entry function.

whyNot.reason: Every program writes the precedence by hand, and gets it differently.
A second verb family beside the shipped decode verb.

recommendation.tradeoff: One new verb and one combinator. Both follow shipped shapes.

decisions.title: When to build backward stepping over a replay
decisions.gist: What gates backward stepping through a replay, and what ships before it.
decisions.lesson: D-TIMETRAVEL1=C deferred a reversible timeline until the replay harness has shipped and jet debug is mature, with compiler work gated on an Epoch 6 slot. Since then D-RUN-RECORD1 ratified `jet debug --replay=NAME`, and the DX board carries card #2461 (replay with scrub, jump, skip; ready to implement, blocked by #2429) and card #2463 (reverse step; planning). Replay capture exists in source; the records slate in this audit is unimplemented. This choice decides what gates reverse step and what ships before it.
decisions.story: Ana replays the crash and wants to step backward three lines from the fault to see where the bad value was made, ideally the week the recorder ships.
decisions.inWild:
// illustrative future transcript; nothing below exists today
$ jet dev app.jet --record=crash
$ jet debug app.jet --replay=crash
(jet) jump 11            # card #2461: re-execute from the start to event 11
event 11   app.jet:31   buffer[64] = byte          # the fault
(jet) back 3             # card #2463: three events earlier, that is jump 8
event 8    app.jet:28   buffer :: arena.alloc(64)
decisions.detail: Owner tradeoff pass, 2026-09-02: the gate moved from a shipped release into repo fixtures. Jump (card #2461) is named as the primitive that ships first, so reverse step no longer waits on the field. B names the two amendments it makes.

options.name: Card it now behind the records slate
options.detail: jet debug --replay steps forward and backward over recorded clock events, re-executing deterministically between them, through the existing debug adapter.
options.technical: Amends D-TIMETRAVEL1=C and the Epoch 6 gate, depends on D-RECORD1. Needs a checkpoint and deterministic re-execution design between boundary events, which the ballot does not yet supply.
options.code:
$ jet debug app.jet --replay r.jetproof-replay
(jet) back 1

options.name: Jump ships with the recorder; reverse step unblocks on two fixture facts proved in the repo
options.detail:
Backward stepping is a jump to an earlier event over a deterministic replay. Card #2461 is scoped to build that primitive after #2429. `jet debug TARGET --replay=NAME` opens a capture and lets a person scrub, jump, and skip by re-executing from the start with the recorded values. Reverse step (`back N`, card #2463) is a thin verb over jump: `back 3` from event 11 is `jump 8`. Checkpoints for speed are part of #2463's design, decided by its ballot.

Reverse step unblocks on two facts proved in the repo, not in the field. First, every replay fixture in `tests/debug.rs` jumps to every event, and the debugger's locals snapshot at that event is byte-identical across repeated jumps and across the two adapters. Second, jet debug passes its adapter conformance suite. Until then replay stays forward-only through `jet prove --replay`, and jump arrives with #2461.
options.technical:
B amends the D-TIMETRAVEL1=C prerequisite wording and the D-RUN-RECORD1 clause that keeps reverse step deferred: reverse step now waits on the two fixture facts, not on a shipped release. The Epoch 6 slot stays for runtime checkpoint support.

The compared snapshot is the `jet debug` locals view at an event, redacted per D-OBS2, over the fixtures pinned in `tests/debug.rs` with their event counts, on `dev-tir-v1` and `aot-native-v1`. On ratification the two facts become criteria on #2461, and #2463 is blocked on them. Card #2463's own ballot D-DX-DEBUGBACK1 picks the verb surface and the checkpoint interval.

options.name: Drop time travel
options.detail: Replay stays forward-only forever.
options.technical: Retire D-TIMETRAVEL1.
options.code: $ jet prove app.jet --replay r.jetproof-replay

comparisons.note: reverse-continue and reverse-step over a recorded trace, built on a mature record layer.
comparisons.code: (rr) reverse-step

comparisons.note: Whole-trace queries built on rr's record layer years later.
comparisons.code: // dataflow view

recommendation.why: The record layer and the jump primitive are already scoped on the board (#2461), so nothing waits on a shipped release. Reverse step is one verb over jump; its gate proves determinism in the repo, which is the honest evidence and is available as soon as #2461 closes.

whyNot.reason: It cards reverse step before the jump primitive and the fixture gate exist, and it names no re-execution design; B orders the same work so each piece carries its proof.
Backward stepping is the reason to record at all.

recommendation.tradeoff: Reverse step waits only on its fixture gate and the adapter suite; jump arrives first. Until checkpoints land, a jump re-executes from the start, so a long recording steps slowly at first.

decisions.title: Trailing commas in every comma list
decisions.gist: Whether every comma-separated list accepts a comma after its last item, and what the formatter writes.
decisions.lesson: Jet is inconsistent today: list and map literals accept a trailing comma; parameter lists and call arguments reject it with two E0003 errors at the closing bracket. Every peer accepts it everywhere so that adding one item changes one line. This choice makes the rule uniform, one way or the other, and fixes the formatter's output.
decisions.story: Kai adds a parameter to a function and the diff touches two lines because the previous line gained a comma. In a list literal the same edit touched one line.
decisions.inWild:
xs :: [
    1,
    2,
]                                   // accepted today
fn f(a: Int, b: Int,) Int -> a + b   // rejected today: two E0003 at `)`

options.name: Accept everywhere; formatter keeps it only on multi-line lists
options.detail: Every comma list accepts a trailing comma: parameters, arguments, list and map literals, constructor bodies, marker groups, effect rows, import lists, type arguments, and loop headers. jet fmt writes a trailing comma when the list spans lines and removes it when the list fits on one line. A comment after the last item counts as part of the multi-line form.
options.technical: Grammar inventory with today's behavior: parameters (reject), arguments (reject), list literal (accept), map literal (accept), typed literal body (accept), marker group (reject), effect row (reject), import list (reject). Type arguments (reject), loop header (reject). Parser change per row; formatter contract as stated; tests per row.

options.name: Accept only in multi-line lists
options.detail: A trailing comma is legal when the closing bracket is on a later line than the last item; f(a,) on one line is E0003 with a fix.
options.technical: Same inventory; the parser checks line position. Comments after the last item count as part of the multi-line form.

options.name: Keep today's mixed behavior
options.detail: Collections accept, everything else rejects.
options.technical: No change.

options.name: Reject everywhere with a fix
options.detail: One spelling in source; collections lose the accepted form.
options.technical: Retires accepted collection syntax; one diagnostic with an edit.

comparisons.lang: Rust, Go, Swift, Kotlin, Python, Zig
comparisons.note: All accept a trailing comma everywhere; their formatters add it on multi-line lists.

recommendation.why: One rule for every list, one-line diffs, and the formatter decides the style.

whyNot.reason: A line-position rule is a second grammar for one comma.
Two rules today is the defect.
It keeps the two-line diff every peer removed and retires working syntax.

recommendation.tradeoff: Ten grammar rows change. The inventory above is the test list.

decisions.title: Repair coverage on every diagnostic, by ratchet
decisions.gist: How every diagnostic comes to carry a machine edit or a reviewed reason, and how pass and fail share one machine status.
decisions.lesson: Every Jet report is one jet.report/v1 JSON object per line with what, why, fix, location, and fix_edits carrying one of five safety classes. Only 83 of 762 active rows carry fix_edits. jet check --json prints a different status object on pass and on fail, and jet fix --json prints prose. This choice decides how coverage is enforced and how status is unified, without changing the ratified report line.
decisions.story: An agent runs jet check --json, gets an error with no edit, guesses a fix, and re-runs three times. A human reads the same error and searches the docs.

options.name: Global guard now
options.detail: Every row must carry fix_edits or a reason before the registry builds.
options.technical: Rejected by the rival review: 679 rows block the registry at once, and bulk reasons would satisfy the guard without helping anyone.
options.code: // registry build fails until all 679 rows are classified

options.name: One status object; coverage as ongoing work
options.detail: Status is unified; repairs are filled when someone gets to them.
options.technical: Amends D-DX1 status only.
options.code: // same status object; rows may still carry nothing

options.name: Guard errors only
options.detail: Error rows need an edit or reason; lints are exempt forever.
options.technical: As A for severity error.
options.code: // L-codes may stay describe-only

options.name: Per-plane ratchet with a reviewed reason field; one status object
options.detail: Every row keeps the ratified report line. A new typed no_fix_reason field, mutually exclusive with fix_edits, holds a reviewed reason and the next action. A coverage baseline per plane never decreases: a new row without fix_edits or a reason fails the registry today; existing rows are classified plane by plane. Each plane closes when its rows are all covered. Structured-edit coverage is reported separately from reason coverage. Machine status is one stable object on pass and fail; human progress lines stay plain as ratified.
options.technical: Amends D-REPORT-MACHINE1 additively: one optional typed field, no_fix_reason, joins the report object under a schema version bump to jet.report/v2. The one-object-per-line law is unchanged. Its envelope clause is unchanged: envelopes are status data holding these objects. Five safety classes unchanged (D-REPORT-FIXGRADE1=D). no_fix_reason = { kind: behavior | design | ambiguous, next: <text or link> }. Status object: { schema: "jet.status/v1", action, ok, reports: [...] } for every command in --json mode, including infrastructure failures. Amends D-DX1 (status envelope) and the I4 registry guard (baseline rule).

comparisons.note: Most lints carry machine-applicable suggestions; cargo fix applies them; coverage grew lint by lint.
comparisons.code: $ cargo fix --allow-dirty

comparisons.note: One language service is the authority; code fixes are rows in it.
comparisons.code: ts.getCodeFixesAtPosition(...)

recommendation.why: It stops the hole from growing today, closes it plane by plane, keeps every ratified schema, and keeps reason rows from counting as repairs.

whyNot.reason: It blocks the registry on 679 rows at once and invites bulk reasons.
83 of 762 is what ongoing produced.
Lints are the rows agents apply blind, so they need edits most.

recommendation.tradeoff: Coverage is reported as two numbers, not one, that is the honest shape.

decisions.title: Claims share one report; jet test and jet prove keep their jobs
decisions.gist: Whether contracts, tests, and proofs report through one evidence report, and which command produces which evidence.
decisions.lesson: A claim is a statement about code that a tool can check. The kinds are a contract (#Pre or #Post), an example test (#Test with a body), a property test (#Test fn with parameters), a doctest, and a proof obligation. Today jet test runs tests, jet fuzz generates inputs, and jet prove runs the ratified evidence set and the solver. Their reports are separate, and a contract cannot gain stronger evidence without a rewrite. This choice decides which commands produce which evidence and whether they share one report.
decisions.story: Leo writes #Post(result > cents) on a fee function and wants to know whether it holds beyond his one example. Today he must learn jet fuzz and jet prove and read three outputs.

options.name: One command; jet prove and jet fuzz retire
options.detail: jet test runs every claim up to a grade ceiling and the solver by flag; jet prove and jet fuzz are deleted.
options.technical: Rejected by the rival review: it silently retires the ratified proof slate (D-PROVE-REPLAY1, D-JPROOF1, D-JREPLAY1, D-PROVE-SOLVER1) that gives jet prove its target resolution, artifacts, replay, JSON, and exit law.
options.code: $ jet test --grade=proved app.jet    // would have to absorb every jet prove contract

options.name: Keep the commands; add an evidence word to each report
options.detail: jet test, jet fuzz, and jet prove stay. Each report prints its evidence, nothing is shared.
options.technical: Report wording only.
options.code:
$ jet test app.jet    # examples(1)
$ jet fuzz app.jet    # generated(4000)
$ jet prove app.jet   # proved

options.name: One evidence report; jet test up to generated, jet prove adds proved
options.detail:
jet test runs examples, doctests, property tests, and, new, the contracts of effect-free functions with inputs generated from their #Pre, within a bounded budget. jet prove stays the ratified umbrella; with --lens solver (the only producer-enabling lens, D-PROVE-LENS1) it adds solver evidence: it proves the implication precondition implies postcondition, never the precondition alone. Both commands write the same evidence report. jet fuzz folds into jet test --grade=generated --iterations=N. Lenses stay presentation views.

A contract that cannot be generated (an effectful function, a precondition that names another function, a type without a generator) is reported as not generated, with the reason.
options.technical: Amends D-JPROOF1 additively: ProofReport gains an evidence summary per claim (producer, outcome, count) under a version bump; D-PROVE-LENS1 unchanged; the jet fuzz surface folds into jet test. Eligibility: default generation only for callables whose inferred row is -[]>; effectful contracts need a #Test fn with fixtures. Default budget: 1,000 generated inputs per contract, settable per package.
options.code:
$ jet test app.jet
claims  3 rows   generated 2   examples 1   not generated 0   failing 0
  add_fee.Pre    generation domain   cents > 0 selects inputs; it is a caller obligation, not a claim about all inputs
  add_fee.Post   generated(1000)     inputs from Pre
  fee on 100     examples(1)
$ jet prove app.jet --lens solver
  add_fee.Post   proved      solver: cents > 0 implies cents + 5 > cents; runtime check erased

comparisons.note: Generation, shrinking, and replay of the smallest failing input happen in one test run.
comparisons.code:
@given(st.integers(min_value=1))
def test_fee(c): assert add_fee(c) > c

comparisons.note: ensures clauses are verified as implications from requires clauses, in one build step.
comparisons.code:
requires cents > 0
ensures r > cents

recommendation.why: The same #Post gains generated evidence for free and solver evidence on request, both commands keep their ratified jobs, and one report shows the ladder.

whyNot.reason: It deletes a ratified command and its whole artifact and replay law without naming them.
Three separate reports cannot show one claim rising.

recommendation.tradeoff: jet test does more work by default for pure functions with contracts. The budget is bounded and --grade=examples turns generation off.

decisions.title: One machine-wide artifact store and its size limit
decisions.gist: Whether Jet keeps one shared folder of built results on the machine, and how large it may grow before it prunes itself.
decisions.lesson: Jet has eleven reuse mechanisms today. The store replaces those eight. The remaining choice is the default size rule and how the store behaves when the disk is nearly full.
decisions.explainer:
An artifact is one built result, such as a compiled unit or a final binary. A store is one folder where every artifact is saved under the fingerprint of its contents. Any project on the machine can reuse it. An entry is one saved result. Pruning removes entries, least recently used first.

Eight of them keep files. They are the final-binary cache, the runtime-library cache, the warm JIT module cache, and whole-invocation receipts. They also include the declared-action content store and its records, package receipts, the Rust FFI bridge cache, and the C bindings cache. Each has its own folder, key, integrity rule, and failure behavior. Only the runtime cache has a size limit. The in-memory sema cache becomes store records. The replay codec and the timing JSON are deleted.
decisions.story: User's build folder once reached 619 GB without anyone noticing. He also has a laptop with a 256 GB disk that is often nearly full. He wants builds to reuse everything they can. He never wants to discover a cache by running out of disk. He wants a CI runner with a small quota to be able to say so once.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet cache status
store      ~/.cache/jet/store
limit      20 GiB   (rule: min(20 GiB, 10% of the 512 GiB filesystem holding the store) = 20 GiB)
reserve    keep 2 GiB free on that filesystem
used       4.2 GiB · 1,204 blobs · 388 records · 3 ThinLTO caches
tiers      local · team off · public off
last prune 2026-09-01 09:14 · freed 1.1 GiB · 0 live entries touched

# on the 256 GiB laptop the same rule gives min(20 GiB, 25.6 GiB) = 20 GiB, and the 2 GiB reserve still holds

options.name: Adaptive limit: the smaller of 20 GiB and 10% of the filesystem
options.detail: The store keeps at most 20 GiB, or 10% of the filesystem holding the store when that is smaller. When full, it removes the least recently used entries after a command finishes. A small laptop disk gets a small store; a workstation gets 20 GiB. It does not look at how much space is actually free. A store under its limit can still fill a nearly full disk.
options.technical: Bound = min(20 GiB, 10% of total capacity). LRU from a last-use journal. Pruning is post-command work (D-JPK-NODAEMON1). Entries used by the current process are not evicted.
options.code:
$ jet cache status
limit 20 GiB · used 19.8 GiB · prune after this command

# disk has 1.1 GiB free, store has 3 GiB of room left:
$ jet build
Error [L21xx]: no space left on device while publishing shop/net   # the limit did not protect the disk

options.name: Fixed 10 GiB
options.detail: One number on every machine. Simple to explain and predictable, which matters on CI runners and containers. A large workspace with several targets and profiles will evict and rebuild more often. A tiny disk still gives up 10 GiB.
options.technical: Bound = 10 GiB; LRU; same journal and prune mechanics.
options.code:
$ jet cache status
limit 10 GiB · used 9.7 GiB
# laptop (256 GiB) and workstation (2 TiB): same 10 GiB; the workstation with three targets evicts every few days

options.name: Fixed 50 GiB
options.detail: Almost never evicts on a workstation. On a laptop it can quietly take a fifth of the disk. That repeats the build-folder story at a smaller scale.
options.technical: Bound = 50 GiB; LRU; same mechanics.
options.code:
$ jet cache status
limit 50 GiB · used 38.2 GiB
# laptop (256 GiB): the store may hold 50 GiB, one fifth of the disk

options.name: No limit; prune only when the disk runs low
options.detail: Never rebuilds anything for space reasons. The store grows until the filesystem is nearly full, then prunes. You find out about the store when something else on the machine fails for lack of space.
options.technical: Prune when free space < 5%; LRU; same mechanics otherwise.
options.code:
$ jet cache status
used 212 GiB · no limit · prune when free space < 5%

$ jet build
note: filesystem below 5% free; pruned 40 GiB from the store   # after another program already failed

options.name: Adaptive limit with a free-space reserve, admission control, live leases, and host override
options.detail:
Same default rule as A: at most 20 GiB, or 10% of the filesystem when smaller. Three additions. First, a reserve: the store never leaves the filesystem with less than 2 GiB free, whatever the limit says. It checks that before every write, not after. Second, live leases: an entry that any running build is using cannot be pruned, even by another Jet process.

Third, a host override. A machine or organization can set a stricter limit once, outside any repository. jet cache status shows where the effective limit came from. jet cache prune [--to <size>] prunes now.
options.technical:
Bound = min(20 GiB, 10% of total capacity) unless a stricter host policy applies. Admission: free space after the write must stay at or above the reserve (2 GiB default, host-settable). Free space is read from statvfs available blocks, or the Windows volume API, and includes room for temp-plus-rename. The store evicts before it admits. An entry that cannot fit safely is refused with a tool error naming the path.

Cross-process leases with crash recovery pin entries a live build reads. The journal has checksummed frames, counts toward the cap, uses a single-writer lock, compacts by fsync plus rename, and is rebuilt from the cas on corruption. Pruning is post-command work.
options.code:
$ jet cache status
limit      20 GiB   (min(20 GiB, 10% of 512 GiB); host policy: none)
reserve    2 GiB free
used       4.2 GiB · 1 live lease (this build)

# disk has 1.1 GiB free:
$ jet build
note: store pruned 3.4 GiB before compiling to keep 2 GiB free
✓ shop built in 4.1s ...

# CI runner, once, outside the repo:
$ jet cache limit --host 4G
$ jet cache status
limit      4 GiB    (host policy)

comparisons.note: Cargo does not bound a project's target directory. Since 1.88 it garbage-collects its global download and registry cache automatically. The unbounded target directory is how 619 GB happens.
comparisons.code:
$ du -sh target/
619G    target/

comparisons.note: A fixed default limit of 10 GiB with least-recently-used eviction, set by SCCACHE_CACHE_SIZE. Praised for being predictable; the number is the same on every disk size.
comparisons.code:
$ sccache --show-stats
Max cache size        10 GiB

comparisons.note: The store has no automatic limit. Users run nix-collect-garbage or set min-free/max-free thresholds so the daemon collects when free space drops. Option E takes the free-space floor idea and adds a default cap.
comparisons.code:
$ nix-collect-garbage -d
freeing 41.2 GiB

recommendation.why: Option E keeps the owner's adaptive default and closes the two ways a capped store can still hurt. It checks free space before every write instead of after. It never prunes an entry another running build depends on. The host override answers quota-limited CI and containers without any repository setting.

whyNot.reason: A cap on total capacity ignores how full the disk already is, so a store under its limit can still cause a no-space failure mid-build.
Ten gigabytes evicts too often on a workstation with several targets and profiles. Predictability is provided in E by the host override instead.
Fifty gigabytes can silently take a fifth of a laptop disk.
The store is discovered only when the disk is nearly full, which is the failure this ballot exists to prevent.

recommendation.tradeoff: Pre-write admission and leases add a small amount of bookkeeping to every publish. A machine with many large projects will evict and rebuild some artifacts under the 20 GiB ceiling. jet cache status makes both visible.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared an adaptive limit, two fixed limits, and no limit, and recommended the adaptive limit.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a per-project quota, a time-based expiry, and an adaptive cap with a free-space reserve and host override. A per-project quota defeats sharing across projects; time-based expiry evicts hot dependencies on a quiet week; the reserve-aware cap is a genuine alternative and became option E.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review combined option A's default rule with option D's free-space awareness and option B's predictability, as a host override, into option E. It added the rule that a live build's entries are never pruned by any process.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review gave each fixed limit its predictability argument, option D its zero-rebuild argument, and option A its simplicity. Predictability survives inside E's host override; the others lose to the small-disk and disk-full cases.
reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: BallotBeginner. Skill: rli5. The beginner pass found undefined terms (store, artifact, entry, LRU), an unclear '10% of which disk', options differing only by a number, and no protection for in-use entries. The lesson defines the terms; the example states the filesystem and laptop case; B and C use the same machines; E shows a live lease.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: anthropic. Adversarial model family: openai. Rival review found wrong mechanism count, cap ignoring available space and quotas, post-command pruning after disk-full failure, no cross-process protection for in-use entries, unbounded journal, and imprecise Cargo claim. Recommendation changed to new option E with a free-space reserve, pre-write admission, live leases, journal integrity, and a host override.

decisions.title: Hidden compile units inside one package
decisions.gist: Whether the compiler may split one package into several hidden Rust crates so an edit recompiles only the touched part.
decisions.lesson: Today one package becomes one crate. Any edit recompiles the whole crate, and an optimized build re-runs the optimizer over all of it. A hidden unit is a group of modules the compiler puts in its own crate without you naming it. Units never change what a package declares: authority, policy, visibility, outputs, and dependencies stay exactly as written. The open question is how units refer to each other in the generated Rust, because that decides how much a body edit recompiles.
decisions.explainer: Terms: a package is one project part you declare. A module is one source file inside it. A crate is one box of code that rustc compiles in one go. Linking joins compiled boxes into a program. The optimizer is the slow step that makes release code fast.
decisions.story: Priya maintains a package with 40 source files, so 40 modules. She changes one line inside one function body and runs jet build. Today she waits for the whole package to compile and optimize. She wants to wait only for the file she touched, and she does not want to split her package into smaller packages to get that.
decisions.inWild:
# shop/package.jet            (one package: shop; two dependency packages: httpkit, json)
name: "shop"
version: "1.4.0"
deps: { httpkit: httpkit#2.1.0, json: json#1.4.0 }

# shop/src/net/client.jet     (40 modules in shop; the compiler groups them into 21 hidden units)
fn fetch_all(urls: [String]) [Response] {
  ...
  retries = 3   # was 2: a body edit, no signature change
}

$ jet build
# today: check 40 modules, rustc the whole package as one crate, optimize everything, link
# with hidden units: check 1 module, rustc 1 unit, optimize 1 unit, link

options.name: Two-crate units with compiler-declared symbols
options.detail:
Each unit becomes two hidden crates. The interface crate holds the unit's types, traits, method tables, generic bodies, and one declaration per plain function. The body crate holds the plain function bodies. Other units depend only on the interface crate, so a body edit recompiles one body crate and relinks. Nothing you write changes.

What can go wrong: a declaration and a body could disagree. The compiler writes both from the same proved signature. It puts a fingerprint of the signature into the symbol name. Any disagreement stops the build at link time instead of running wrong code.
options.technical:
iface crate: types (pub fields), traits, every inherent impl and trait impl for the unit's types. Rust requires inherent impls in the type's crate. It also contains generic fns and methods with bodies. Non-generic method and impl bodies are forwarders to body-crate symbols. `unsafe extern "Rust" { pub safe fn f(...) -> T; }` is emitted per plain function. body crate: `#[export_name = "_JET_<pkg>_<module>_<item>_<abihash>"]` definitions. It depends on its own iface and imported ifaces. Nothing depends on a body crate.

`<abihash>` covers the signature plus the ABI record. The ABI record contains exact rustc build, target triple and features, panic strategy, and layout-affecting flags. Every unit in a program is compiled by the same rustc, and the ABI record is in every Compile key. `safe fn` inside `unsafe extern` is stable since Rust 1.82 (RFC 3484). Under I1 the compiler's own declarations for symbols it emitted are classified as vetted internals.

Per-target contract: ELF and Mach-O keep exported symbols through `#[used]`-free export names and `--gc-sections`. COFF/MSVC uses the same export names with the MSVC linker's `/OPT:REF`. wasm units use the same symbol scheme with `wasm-ld`. If a target cannot honor the contract, that target falls back to option B for its units and `jet explain-build` says so. Cross-unit inlining returns at link time through ThinLTO in the release profile.

Adoption gate: A ships only if measured body-edit savings on the corpus exceed its extra rustc processes and metadata loading, and the iface/body differential passes on every supported target.
options.code:
# illustrative timings; nothing here is measured yet
$ jet build
✓ shop built in 1.9s · 1 of 21 units compiled, 20 reused · release · ./build/shop
$ ./build/shop --check
ok

$ jet explain-build shop
why
  shop/net       compiled   src/net/client.jet changed (fetch_all body)
  link shop      relinked   1 unit changed
  20 units       reused     store · local

# a forced declaration/body mismatch (test only) never links:
internal compiler error: unit shop/net: symbol _JET_shop_net_fetch_all_9f3a... not found at link

options.name: Single-crate units
options.detail: Each unit becomes one hidden crate. Units still compile in parallel and the optimizer still works per unit. But Rust marks a crate as changed whenever any body in it changes, so every unit that uses the edited unit recompiles too, and every unit that uses those, and so on. A body edit in a widely used module recompiles most of the package, in parallel. The compiler writes no symbol declarations of its own, so there is no ABI boundary to keep honest and half as many crates.
options.technical: One rlib per unit; dependents take the unit rlib as `--extern`. rustc's crate hash covers all bodies, so dependents miss on any body edit. Generated code contains no `extern` blocks. Parallel unit front ends remain; the ThinLTO cache still limits optimizer work to changed modules. This is also option A's fallback on targets that cannot honor its symbol contract.
options.code:
# illustrative timings
$ jet build
✓ shop built in 3.4s · 9 of 21 units compiled, 12 reused · release · ./build/shop

$ jet explain-build shop
why
  shop/net       compiled   src/net/client.jet changed (fetch_all body)
  shop/render    compiled   depends on shop/net (crate hash changed)
  shop/cli       compiled   depends on shop/render (crate hash changed)
  shop/api, shop/jobs, shop/auth, shop/db, shop/report, shop/main   compiled   same chain
  12 units       reused     store · local

options.name: No units; one crate per package
options.detail: Keep one Rust crate per package. Reuse comes only from dependency packages and from the optimizer cache. Any edit in a package recompiles that whole package, as today. Large packages get no fine-grained reuse unless you split them into smaller packages.
options.technical: Status quo emission (`emit_bundle_dbg_inner` one crate per package after sealed objects land). Sealed package objects and the ThinLTO cache still apply across packages.
options.code:
# illustrative timings
$ jet build
✓ shop built in 6.8s · 1 of 3 packages compiled (shop, all 40 modules in one crate), 2 reused · release · ./build/shop

options.name: One interface crate per package, one body crate per unit
options.detail: All of a package's types, traits, method tables, and declarations live in one interface crate; each unit still gets its own body crate. A body edit costs one body crate and a relink, like option A. A signature change anywhere in the package recompiles the one interface crate. It then recompiles every body crate. That interface crate is one serial rustc run on the critical path of every build.
options.technical: iface: one crate per package. body: one crate per unit, depending on the package iface and dependency ifaces. Fewer rustc processes (N+1 instead of 2N) and one metadata load per unit; broader invalidation after interface edits; the package iface is a serial bottleneck for large packages.
options.code:
# illustrative timings
$ jet build                     # body edit
✓ shop built in 1.9s · 1 of 21 units compiled, 20 reused · release · ./build/shop
$ jet build                     # one signature edit in shop/net
✓ shop built in 5.1s · 21 of 21 units compiled (package interface changed) · release · ./build/shop

comparisons.note: The crate is the unit of compilation and of caching. cargo build --release turns incremental compilation off, so any edit re-runs the whole optimizer for that crate. Users split crates by hand to get smaller rebuilds.
comparisons.code:
$ touch src/net/client.rs && cargo build --release
   Compiling shop v1.4.0   # whole crate, full optimizer

comparisons.note: Interface files (.mli) separate a module's signature from its body. A body edit does not recompile users of the module. This is the model option A gives the compiler internally, with no user-written interface files.
comparisons.code:
$ dune build   # client.ml changed, client.mli unchanged
# only client.ml recompiles; dependents keep their objects

comparisons.note: The Swift driver tracks fine-grained dependencies between declarations and recompiles a dependent file only when a declaration it uses changed. Whole-module rebuilds when the type checker gives up are its recorded complaint; Jet's D-TYPECHECK-BOUND1 already covers that half.
comparisons.code: // body edit inside a Swift file: dependents keep their objects when no used declaration changed

recommendation.why: Option A is the only option where a body edit costs one unit and one link and a signature edit stays local to the units that import it. It keeps the package boundary exactly as written and needs no new syntax. Its unsafe surface is a compiler-generated declaration for a symbol the same compiler emitted. The declaration is checked against a proved signature and guarded by a fingerprint in the symbol name.

whyNot.reason: Rust's crate hash makes every dependent recompile on any body edit. A change in a widely used module still rebuilds most of the package. Its lower process count is bought with the most common edit being expensive.
Large packages get no fine-grained reuse at all, which is the case the hard rule exists to protect.
One package-wide interface crate is a serial rustc run on every build's critical path and recompiles every unit after any signature change anywhere in the package.

recommendation.tradeoff: Generated Rust gains compiler-written unsafe extern declarations, which I1 must classify as vetted internals. Each unit costs two rustc runs instead of one, and the interface crate of a unit changes when a type, trait, signature, or generic body changes. A wins only if measured edit savings exceed those fixed costs; the units card carries that gate.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared two-crate units, single-crate units, and no units, and recommended two-crate units.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested item-level units, size-based coalescing, a patched rustc that skips borrow checking, and one package-wide interface crate. Item-level units churn on every new call edge; size-based grouping breaks cross-machine identity; a rustc fork fails I2; the package-wide interface crate is a genuine alternative and became option D.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review combined option A's interface crates with option B's single rustc run by putting generic bodies and forwarders in the interface crate only. It made option B the per-target fallback when a linker cannot honor A's symbol contract.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened option B with its lower process count and absent ABI boundary, option C with sealed dependency objects, and option D with its N+1 process count. Each still pays whole-package or whole-dependents recompiles on the most common edit.
reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: BallotBeginner. Skill: rli5. The beginner pass found undefined terms (package, module, unit, crate, optimizer, link), mismatched counts between story and example, and a hidden safety tradeoff. The lesson now defines each term, every count is labeled, option A states what can go wrong and how the fingerprint stops it, and timings are marked illustrative.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: anthropic. Adversarial model family: openai. The rival review found inherent impls must live in the type's crate, the ABI record must be part of the symbol fingerprint, a wrong Swift claim, and a missing package-wide-interface option. It also found unmeasured timings presented as results; all were repaired and option D was added.

decisions.title: Prebuilt runtime objects and who may publish to the public store tier
decisions.gist: Whether Jet's runtime ships as prebuilt objects a fresh machine downloads, which CPU level shared objects target, and whose signatures the public tier trusts.
decisions.lesson: Every first build on a machine compiles the runtime with rustc, which took 17 to 21 seconds on the reference workstation. Rust users never pay this because Rust ships its standard library prebuilt. Ratified law already allows ordered mirrors with signed provenance and verify-on-read. This ballot decides whether the project publishes prebuilt runtime objects, what CPU level shared objects use, and whether the project's own signing key may also vouch for other people's packages.
decisions.explainer: Terms: the runtime and Core are the shared support code every Jet program links. An object is compiled code ready to link. A mirror is a server that hands out saved artifacts. The public tier is the last mirror in the ordered list every machine may read. The baseline CPU level is the smallest set of processor features an object needs, so a baseline object runs on every machine of that family.
decisions.story: Aisha installs Jet on a new laptop and runs jet build on a ten-line program. She waits twenty seconds while the runtime compiles and wonders whether Jet is slow. Her second build takes under a second because the objects are now in her store. Her Rust colleague's first hello world links in under a second because std came with the toolchain.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet build hello.jet     # fresh machine, today
note: compiling the Jet runtime for rustc 1.97.1 once (about 20s); later builds reuse it
✓ hello built in 21.4s
$ jet build hello.jet     # same machine, second time
✓ hello up to date · 38 ms

$ jet build hello.jet     # fresh machine, with a public tier
  fetch    runtime 1.4.2 · x86-64 baseline · 38 MiB · signed by jet-release · verified
✓ hello built in 0.7s

$ jet build hello.jet     # fresh machine, mirror unreachable
note: public store unreachable; compiling the Jet runtime once (about 20s)
✓ hello built in 21.4s
decisions.detail: Owner tradeoff pass, 2026-09-02: option D now tunes the fetched runtime natively on the first optimized host build, in the foreground with no background process. It names the release matrix jobs publishing needs and the registry's own builder as the first authorized builder.

options.name: Jet signs everything on the public tier: runtime, Core, and third-party packages
options.detail: Runtime, Core, and compiled objects of third-party packages are all published under the project's release key. Fastest possible clean builds for everyone. But signing a compiled third-party object means the project vouches for that package's build, its build scripts, its tools, and its produced bytes, which is a different promise from hosting its source.
options.technical: One writer root (jet-release) for every object kind on the public mirror. Identity and ISA rules as in option D.
options.code:
$ jet build
  fetch    runtime 1.4.2 · signed by jet-release
  fetch    httpkit 2.1.0, json 1.4.0 · signed by jet-release   # the project vouches for third-party builds
✓ shop built in 0.9s

options.name: Prebuilt objects for runtime and Core only
options.detail: The project publishes and signs only code it wrote: the runtime and Core. They are split into fixed per-module objects, built for the baseline CPU level, with an identity that names the compiler, rustc, target, platform, and profile. Third-party packages compile locally or come from a team mirror. This is the simplest trust story. The multi-package clean build still pays for dependencies.
options.technical: Public mirror allowlist contains only the jet-release writer and only runtime/Core object kinds. Identity and ISA rules as in option D.
options.code:
$ jet build
  fetch    runtime 1.4.2 · x86-64 baseline · signed by jet-release · verified
  compile  httpkit 2.1.0, json 1.4.0   # third-party packages compile here
✓ shop built in 9.8s

options.name: Local and team tiers only
options.detail: No project-operated public tier. Every machine compiles the runtime once; teams share through their own mirror. A fresh machine keeps paying about twenty seconds that Rust users do not, so the smallest cold cell of the benchmark stays a loss by design.
options.technical: Status quo plus the store; runtime objects keyed and stored locally; team mirrors per D-JPK-REMOTE1.
options.code:
$ jet build hello.jet     # every fresh machine
note: compiling the Jet runtime for rustc 1.97.1 once (about 20s); later builds reuse it
✓ hello built in 21.4s
$ jet build hello.jet
✓ hello up to date · 38 ms

options.name: Federated tier: Jet signs runtime and Core; registry-authorized builders sign third-party objects under their own roots
options.detail:
Two kinds of signature live on the public tier. The project's release key signs only the runtime and Core. Third-party package objects may be published by builders the package registry has authorized, each under its own signing root, only when the build is reproducible. A machine accepts them only when its policy opts in.

Every download is verified against the digest and the signature of its own root. A bad signature or a mismatched digest means the object is refused and the package compiles locally. Shared objects target the baseline CPU level of their family, with optional higher levels chosen after CPU detection.

Baseline objects are the first-run accelerator, not the last word. The first optimized host build, `jet build --release` on the host triple or `jet test --measure`, tunes the runtime natively once, in the foreground, and says so. A `jet dev --serve` session may do it early, because it is the resident parent D-JPK-NODAEMON1 allows; no other background process exists. Dev-tier builds link the fetched object and never wait. Distributable builds keep the target's ISA level, which is exactly the public object, so they stay reproducible.

Publishing needs new matrix jobs in the release workflow: fixed Core units per target, ISA level, and profile, a signed manifest, and a reproducibility check; card #2525 builds the units. Their compute and storage are a project cost, listed in the tradeoff. The registry's own reproducible builder is the first authorized builder, so third-party objects arrive with the registry rather than after a separate program. Third-party acceptance stays off until the host policy opts in.
options.technical:
Namespaces and writer roots per D-JPK-CACHEAUTH1: jet-release for runtime/Core. Registry-authorized builders sign third-party objects with signed provenance, revocation metadata, and expiry or transparency checkpoints. Consumers re-verify on every hit. Divergent bytes are quarantined (D-JPK-REPROCACHE1). The toolchain pins the expected runtime identity, so a stale signed runtime cannot be substituted.

Object identity = compiler, rustc -vV, target triple, ISA level, and platform ABI (OS SDK/deployment target or glibc/musl baseline or MSVC toolset/CRT). It also includes linker and LTO version, panic/unwind settings, target features, profile flags, and dependency identities. Any difference is a miss.

ISA policy: x86-64 (psABI v1) baseline with optional v2/v3 variants. aarch64 base with optional feature levels. macOS uses per-architecture objects. wasm has no CPU tuning. Core is split into fixed per-module units, so pay-for-what-you-call moves to link time. Third-party acceptance is off by default and enabled per host policy, never by a repository setting.

Host builds prefer a `native` runtime object when present, else the highest fetched ISA level chosen after CPU detection. `--release` on the host triple and `jet test --measure` build the native object once per runtime identity in the foreground; `jet dev --serve` may build it early. Distributable builds use the target's ISA level and never `native`. Receipts name the linked runtime identity.

The native write passes D-BUILD-STORE1 admission first; a refused admission is a recorded skip with a note. Writer root `registry-build` signs objects the registry built from published sources under D-JPK-REPROCACHE1.
options.code:
$ jet build hello.jet     # fresh machine; host detected x86-64-v3
  fetch    runtime 1.4.2 · x86-64-v3 · signed by jet-release · verified
✓ hello built in 0.7s
$ jet build --release hello.jet     # first optimized host build: tunes once, in the foreground
  tune     runtime 1.4.2 → native (this machine) · 19.6s · once per runtime identity
✓ hello built in 21.1s · runtime native
$ jet build --release hello.jet     # next time
✓ hello built in 0.6s · runtime native

$ jet build                # default host policy: third-party objects not accepted
  fetch    runtime 1.4.2 · x86-64 baseline · signed by jet-release · verified
  compile  httpkit 2.1.0, json 1.4.0    # compiled here
✓ shop built in 6.1s
$ jet cache bind public --accept-builder registry-build     # host policy opts in (spelling per D-JPK-CACHECONFIG1)
$ jet build
  fetch    httpkit 2.1.0 · signed by builder registry-build · verified
  compile  json 1.4.0                     # no trusted object available; built locally
✓ shop built in 2.3s

$ jet build      # a download whose signature does not verify
note: public object for httpkit 2.1.0 failed verification; quarantined; compiling locally
✓ shop built in 6.1s

$ jet build --release --target x86_64-linux   # distributable: the target's ISA level, never native
✓ shop built · runtime 1.4.2 x86-64 baseline (public, reproducible)

comparisons.note: rustup installs a prebuilt std for the target; no user compiles it. Cargo compiles every third-party dependency from source per project. Option D matches the first and improves on the second without the project signing third-party builds.
comparisons.code:
$ cargo build   # std prebuilt; deps compile locally
   Compiling serde v1.0.219 ...

comparisons.note: cache.nixos.org serves signed build outputs; a machine downloads instead of building. Nix trusts a path by signature from a configured key; reproducibility is not required for publication. Jet's tier is stricter: third-party objects must be reproducible before they are published.
comparisons.code:
$ nix build nixpkgs#hello
copying path '/nix/store/...-hello-2.12.1' from 'https://cache.nixos.org'

comparisons.note: Go compiles its standard library on demand into a machine-wide build cache shared by every module, and its module cache is shared too. Go's fast clean builds are credited to that sharing, not to prebuilt archives.
comparisons.code: $ go build ./...   # std and modules land in the shared build cache

recommendation.why: Option D removes the one cost Rust users never see and keeps the structural clean-build win for multi-package programs. It draws the trust line where responsibility is: the project signs what it built, authorized builders sign what they built, and every machine verifies both before use. Host builds get native tuning on their first optimized build, and public objects stay reproducible.

whyNot.reason: It makes the project's release key vouch for builds it did not perform, and a user cannot tell runtime trust from third-party-builder trust.
It gives up the clean-build win for multi-package programs, which is where Cargo's recompile-every-dependency tax is largest, when separate signing roots make that win safe.
Every fresh machine keeps paying twenty seconds that Rust users do not, and the smallest cold cell of the benchmark stays lost by design.

recommendation.tradeoff: The project pays for matrix builds, signing, and a mirror for runtime objects. Native tuning costs one foreground optimized build per machine, and public objects stay baseline so distributable builds are reproducible.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a full public tier under one key, a runtime-only public tier, and local-plus-team tiers, and recommended the full tier.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested shipping runtime objects inside the installer and a federated tier with separate signing roots. The installer is the same object kind by a different transport and is the first-run fallback; the federated tier is a genuine alternative and became option D.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review combined option A's coverage with option B's trust boundary into option D and added the CPU-level rule for shared tiers and the root package. The owner's tradeoff pass added foreground native tuning for host builds and the registry builder as the first authorized root.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review gave option A its speed argument, option B its narrow-trust argument, and option C its no-operations argument. Speed survives in D; narrow trust survives in D's separate roots; no operations leaves the cold cell lost.
reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: Rli5Build. Skill: rli5. The first pass found runtime, object, mirror, and tier undefined; the lesson defines them. The second found no way to refuse a background rebuild and a third-party fetch without opt-in; D now has no background job and shows the opt-in.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Anthropic. Adversarial model family: OpenAI. The first rival pass found x86-64-v3 called a baseline and one key vouching for third-party builds, and moved the recommendation to D. The second, on the owner's revision, found a background job forbidden by D-JPK-NODAEMON1, an unsupported no-new-build claim, and no store admission; D now tunes in the foreground and admits writes first.

decisions.title: What jet build shows while it works
decisions.gist: The look of the build progress in a terminal, the one-line result, and whether a saved HTML report of the build ships.
decisions.lesson: Today jet build prints five fixed stage lines and a final 'Built ... in 4.1s'. With one build graph, Jet knows exactly how many modules it checked and how many units it compiled or reused. It knows which chain is the critical path and, when it has history, roughly how long is left. This ballot decides how much of that a person sees while waiting, what the one-line result says, and whether jet explain-build can write a self-contained HTML page.
decisions.explainer:
Terms: a live board is a small block of lines in the terminal that redraws in place while work runs. Piped output is what you get when the command's output goes to a file or another program instead of a terminal, as in CI logs. The critical path is the longest chain of work that decides when the build finishes. An event stream is one line of structured data per thing that happens, for tools to read. The HTML report is a saved web page you open later.

Command names are already law: jet graph, jet query build, jet explain-build. Mockups for the look are in docs/proposals/automatic-build-optimization/mockups.
decisions.story: Lena runs jet build on a program with 40 modules that the compiler groups into 21 units. She wants to know at a glance that it is working, roughly how long is left, and afterwards why it took 4 seconds instead of 1. In CI the same command must print plain lines that read well in a log.
