decisions.detail: Owner tradeoff pass, 2026-09-02: option A now renders the board, the piped lines, and the page from one model through three pure renderers over one fixture corpus in one harness. Pseudo-terminal and browser tests cover the two places a real terminal or browser is in the loop.

options.name: Live board in a terminal, one-line receipt, HTML report, standard trace export
options.detail:
In a terminal, a small board redraws in place. It has one row per stage with a bar and counts. It shows how many CPU slots are busy and with what. It shows the critical path with an estimate of the time left, shown only when Jet has enough history to estimate. It collapses to one receipt line when done. Warnings and notes print above it in the normal format.

It uses the Jet palette: red for work done and for the `jet` mark, gray for work reused, green for the `✓`.

When output is piped, each stage prints one plain line as it finishes. NO_COLOR removes color and nothing else. A non-UTF-8 terminal or --ascii gets ASCII bars. `jet explain-build --html` writes a self-contained dark page with a timeline, the graph, a why-table, and the store panel. `--trace` writes the same data in the standard Chrome trace format for existing viewers.

The board, the piped lines, and the HTML page are three renderings of one model. One pure projection turns the event record into a build report model; three pure renderers draw it for a terminal, a pipe, and the page. A small versioned fixture corpus, one file per distinct build history, drives every renderer through one table-driven golden harness crossed with width, pipe, color, and capability.

Behavior that needs a real terminal, resize, stop and continue, broken pipes, and child output, is tested in a pseudo-terminal; the page's interactions are tested in a browser. The old five-line renderer is deleted.
options.technical:
≤ 8 lines, ≤ 10 fps, cursor-up redraw. Widths ≥ 100 are full. Widths 80–99 use shortened counts. Widths < 80 drop cpu and path rows. It never wraps.

Bars cover the whole population, so red cells are the work done and faint cells are reused work. Theme::ACCENT_SGR moves from 1;96 to red so every CLI surface matches. One renderer owns stderr. It handles resize and SIGTSTP/SIGCONT, restores cursor state on every exit path, and rate-limits by terminal capability. It falls back to plain lines when cursor control is unsafe (TERM=dumb, consoles without VT support, slow links).

Estimate is shown only with recorded durations for remaining nodes and is labeled 'est.'. --json emits NDJSON stage/node/receipt events under a versioned schema. The HTML page renders from that same record embedded as escaped JSON (never HTML concatenation). It ships a restrictive CSP meta tag, redacts secrets, and is tested against hostile names containing </script>, URIs, bidi, and control characters.

Projection: `fn model(events) -> BuildReportModel`, pure. Renderers: `tty(model, width, caps) -> Lines`, `pipe(model) -> Lines`, `html(model) -> Page`, all pure. Fixtures: NDJSON files under the versioned schema for no-change, fetch, failure, absent-estimate, hostile-name, and unknown-version histories. PTY tests inject resize and SIGTSTP/SIGCONT, terminate on each exit path, and assert cursor restoration and plain-line fallback. The page embeds the record with its schema version and refuses an unknown version. `--json` wins over the board; a non-terminal gets piped lines.

Snapshot matrix: archetype × width × tty/pipe × color × terminal height, Unicode cell width, CI log folding, multiplexers, concurrent child output. Accessibility: the receipt and piped lines are screen-reader friendly. The board is decoration over the same events. Mockups: mockups/terminal.html and mockups/report.html.
options.code:
$ jet build            # terminal: board above (two-tone bars: faint = reused, red = compiled), then
✓ shop built in 4.1s · 3 of 21 units compiled, 18 reused · release · ./build/shop
  why: jet explain-build shop
$ jet build | cat      # piped
jet build shop (release, x86_64-linux)
check    42 modules, 3 rechecked                  0.18s
emit     3 units emitted, 18 reused               0.02s
compile  3 units compiled, 18 reused               2.2s
link     shop                                      1.7s
built shop in 4.1s -> ./build/shop (3 of 21 units compiled, 18 reused)
$ jet explain-build shop --html --open
wrote build/shop.explain.html   # header strip · timeline with critical path · package/unit graph · why-table (/ j k Enter) · store panel · works offline
$ jet explain-build shop --trace > shop.trace.json   # opens in Perfetto or chrome://tracing

options.name: Live board and receipt, text and JSON only
options.detail: The same terminal experience, but the deep view stays in the terminal. `jet explain-build` prints the why-table, critical path, and store summary as text and --json. `--trace` exports the standard trace format for existing viewers. This is one fewer renderer to maintain and no local web page to secure. There is no clickable graph or store panel of Jet's own.
options.technical: Identical board, receipt, events, and --trace; no HTML template.
options.code:
$ jet build            # identical board and receipt to option A
✓ shop built in 4.1s · 3 of 21 units compiled, 18 reused · release · ./build/shop

$ jet explain-build shop
why
  shop/net       compiled    2.2s   src/net/client.jet changed (fetch_all body)
  18 units       reused         –   store · local
critical path  4.1s   check 0.18 → emit 0.02 → rustc shop/net 2.2 → link 1.7
$ jet explain-build shop --trace > shop.trace.json

options.name: Cargo-like lines
options.detail: One line per unit as it compiles, a progress bar, and a summary line. Familiar to Rust users and low effort. Shows activity but not what is reused or what is on the critical path, and on a big program it scrolls.
options.technical: Sequential lines in all modes; progress bar in a terminal only.
options.code:
$ jet build
   Compiling shop/net
   Compiling shop/render
   Compiling shop/cli
    Building [=================>          ] 3 compiled + 15 reused of 21 units
    Finished release in 4.1s

options.name: Quiet
options.detail: One receipt line and nothing else; everything lives behind jet explain-build. Minimal and calm. A four-second build shows no sign of life until it ends, and a forty-second one feels hung.
options.technical: Receipt line only; explain-build text, JSON, and --trace.
options.code:
$ jet build            # 40-second cold build: the terminal shows nothing for 40 seconds, then
✓ shop built in 40.2s · 21 of 21 units compiled · release · ./build/shop
$ jet explain-build shop
critical path  38.1s   runtime objects 19.7 → rustc shop/core 9.2 → link 4.1

comparisons.note: One 'Compiling' line per crate plus a progress bar; the most familiar shape and the one option C copies. Frequent complaints: nothing says what was reused or why a build was slow, so people reach for --timings after the fact.
comparisons.code:
Compiling shop v1.4.0
    Finished `release` profile [optimized] target(s) in 4.12s

comparisons.note: Its 'superconsole' redraws a compact live board with running actions and a summary, then collapses to plain lines in CI. Widely praised for making large builds legible; this is the shape of options A and B.
comparisons.code:
Jobs completed: 2400. Time elapsed: 4.1s.
Remaining 3 actions, 2 running  ...

comparisons.note: A live console with running actions and progress, plus --profile which writes a JSON trace users open in chrome://tracing or Perfetto; analyze-profile is a command-line summary. Options A and B export that same trace format; option A additionally ships its own self-contained page with the why-table and store panel that no generic trace viewer has.
comparisons.code:
[2,400 / 2,403] 2 actions running
    Compiling shop/net; 2s

recommendation.why: Option A shows what is happening, what is reused, and roughly how long is left while it runs. It then gets out of the way with one line. It gives experts a standard trace for existing viewers and a self-contained page that answers 'why did this rebuild' with the store and unit context no generic viewer knows about. Every view renders from one model built from one record, so the views cannot disagree.

whyNot.reason: A generic trace viewer shows timing but not the why-table, the unit map, or the store panel. The page makes a slow build explainable without another tool, and it renders from the same model and fixtures as the board, so it cannot drift.
It shows activity but hides reuse and the critical path, and it scrolls on large programs.
Long builds show no sign of life.

recommendation.tradeoff: The owner's look at the rendered page is the one cost that stays, because it is taste. Everything else is one model, one fixture corpus, and one harness, plus the two tests where a terminal or a browser is genuinely in the loop.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared a live board with an HTML report, a board without it, Cargo-like lines, and a quiet receipt, and recommended the board with the report.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a browser-based live view served during the build, a desktop notification on completion, and a standard trace export instead of a custom page. The live browser view is a resident surface the session ballot owns; notifications are a shell concern; the trace export is real and was added to options A, B, and D.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review kept option A and added the width rules, the piped-mode line format, the honest estimate rule, and the standard trace export. The owner's tradeoff pass made every view a rendering of one model with one shared fixture corpus.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review gave option B its one-fewer-renderer and no-injection-surface arguments, option C its familiarity argument, and option D its calm-terminal argument. B's arguments now bound A's page (same record, escaped JSON, CSP, hostile tests); familiarity does not explain a slow build; calm hides a hung one.
reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: Rli5Build. Skill: rli5. The first pass found live board, TTY, and pipe undefined; the lesson defines them. The second derived the CI view correctly and found the one-function claim contradicted by the technical note; A now says one model, three renderers.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Anthropic. Adversarial model family: OpenAI. The first rival pass found an impossible cpu row and an unescaped page; both repaired. The second, on the owner's revision, found one function claimed for an interactive page and one fixture for a matrix; A now has one model, three renderers, and behavioral tests.

decisions.comment: The live board should have the visual features like the @docs/proposals/automatic-build-optimization/terminal.html with a progess bar for each step, similar to cargo build. the overall compile bar is fine but I want the cargo style scroll for each individual compiler unit included.

decisions.title: An opt-in resident build session
decisions.gist: Whether a running jet dev may also serve jet build and jet run from its already-loaded state, and how that is spelled.
decisions.lesson: Every jet command is a fresh process. It reads the store, rebuilds changes, and exits. A resident session keeps the checked program and build graph in memory while it runs. The next build starts warm and can compile what the last edit touched before anyone asks. D-JPK-NODAEMON1 (ratified) forbids a resident background process and says the jet dev session is the process allowed to parent work. This ballot decides whether builds may attach, under which name, and with which safety rules. Results must match either way.
decisions.explainer: Terms: a process is one running program. Warm means the work of reading and checking the program is already loaded in memory. Attaching means sending a command to a process that is already running instead of starting a new one. A daemon is a background process that keeps running after you close your terminal.
decisions.story: Marco keeps jet dev open all day while editing a service. Every few minutes he runs jet build in a second terminal to produce the release binary his tests need. Each build pays process start and store reads that the dev session already did. He wants the second terminal to reuse the first one's work, and he does not want a background process he did not start. When he closes the dev terminal, nothing should keep running.
decisions.inWild:
# terminal 1
$ jet dev --serve src/main.jet
  dev  watching 40 modules · serving builds for this workspace (session 7c1e)

# terminal 2, a minute later
$ jet build
✓ shop built in 0.9s · 1 of 21 units compiled, 20 reused · release · ./build/shop · session 7c1e

# terminal 1 closed → nothing keeps running
$ jet build
✓ shop built in 1.8s · 1 of 21 units compiled, 20 reused · release · ./build/shop   # fresh process

options.name: Attach to a running jet dev with --serve
options.detail:
jet dev gains a --serve flag. While that foreground process runs, jet build, jet run, and jet test started in the same workspace attach to it. They get the same output and exit status they would produce alone, faster.

A policy flag --session=auto|off|required controls attachment; off forces a fresh process. Closing the dev terminal ends the session. No new verb, no background process, nothing runs as root. If no valid session owns the workspace, or the session is a different Jet version, the command runs as a fresh process and says why only with --verbose.
options.technical:
Endpoint: Unix-domain socket in a user-owned 0700 directory ($XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/jet/ when set, else a private per-user directory with a warning per the XDG spec). Windows named pipe. Symlinks rejected. Peer OS identity checked. Protocol versioned. A random session nonce in the workspace's .jet/session file must be presented by the client. One owner per workspace by lock. A second --serve refuses with a diagnostic.

Request envelope carries every invocation input (argv, cwd, env allowlist, terminal mode). The session resets all request-scoped state, binds the request to one source snapshot, and re-verifies leaf digests. It schedules deterministically, holds output-path locks, propagates Ctrl-C as cancellation, bounds its queue, and never inherits secrets absent from the envelope. Speculative pre-compilation of units touched by the last edit is allowed and never blocks a request.

Amends D-JPK-NODAEMON1 only by letting the existing dev session accept build requests. Adoption gate: ship only if measured fresh-process overhead after memoized checks exceeds 100 ms or 20% of the median edit build on the corpus. Session memory must stay under a stated ceiling.
options.code:
$ jet dev --serve src/main.jet
  dev  watching 40 modules · serving builds for this workspace (session 7c1e)

$ jet build            # other terminal, attaches
✓ shop built in 0.9s · 1 of 21 units compiled, 20 reused · release · ./build/shop · session 7c1e

$ jet build --session=off
✓ shop built in 1.8s · 1 of 21 units compiled, 20 reused · release · ./build/shop
$ sha256sum build/shop   # identical for both runs (this is a permanent test)

$ jet build            # after the dev terminal closed
✓ shop built in 1.8s ...   # fresh process, no socket left behind

options.name: A background jet daemon
options.detail: A separate background process, started on demand or by jet daemon start, keeps state warm for every workspace and survives closing terminals. Fastest possible incremental latency and builds on save, at the cost of a process you must notice, stop, and trust. This contradicts D-JPK-NODAEMON1 directly.
options.technical: Bazel-style server with idle timeout; lifecycle verbs start/stop/status; per-user socket; must never hold root.
options.code:
$ jet build        # starts the daemon if absent
  starting build daemon (idle exit after 30 min)
✓ shop built in 0.9s ...
$ jet daemon status
  running · pid 41822 · 2 workspaces · 1.1 GiB · idle exit in 24 min
$ jet daemon stop
  stopped
$ jet build
✓ shop built in 1.8s ...   # fresh process

options.name: No resident session
options.detail: Every command stays a fresh process. Persisted memoized checks and the store already make an unchanged build take tens of milliseconds and an edit build proportional to the edit. Nothing to learn, nothing running. Process start plus store reads stay on every build, and explain-build shows what they cost.
options.technical: Status quo process model with the new store; explain-build reports startup and store-load time per invocation so the cost of not having a session is always visible.
options.code:
$ jet build
✓ shop built in 1.8s · 1 of 21 units compiled, 20 reused · release · ./build/shop
$ jet explain-build shop
  startup 0.06s · store load 0.11s · check 0.02s · compile 1.2s · link 0.4s

comparisons.note: Cargo has no resident process. Every build re-reads fingerprints and restarts rustc. This is one reason large Rust workspaces feel slow on no-change builds.
comparisons.code:
$ cargo build
    Finished `dev` profile in 0.41s   # 300-crate workspace, nothing changed

comparisons.note: Both keep a server alive with an idle timeout. Praised for warm builds, criticized for memory use and for surprising users with a process they did not start. Option B copies this; option A keeps the warm state without the surprise.
comparisons.code:
$ bazel build //shop
INFO: Analyzed target (0 packages loaded)   # server already warm

comparisons.note: The Gradle daemon is a background process with an idle timeout that later builds attach to; it is the most used build server and its complaints are stale state and memory. Option A takes the attach idea but ties the lifetime to a foreground process the user started.
comparisons.code: $ gradle build   # attaches to a running daemon or starts one

recommendation.why: Option A gives warm builds only when you already run a dev session, which is when you want them, and keeps the ratified rule that nothing resident runs unasked. Identical results are a tested property of a serialized request envelope and a reset per request, not an assumption.

whyNot.reason: It is exactly the resident background process D-JPK-NODAEMON1 forbids, and it adds lifecycle verbs the beginner surface does not need.

It leaves process start and store reads on every build for people who already keep a dev session open. It stays the default whenever no session is running and is the outcome if the adoption gate fails.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two execution paths must stay identical, which needs a permanent differential test across success, warning, error, cancellation, and concurrent-edit cases, plus an authenticated local protocol. The session only helps while jet dev is running.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared attaching to a running dev session, a background daemon, and no session, and recommended attaching.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested an editor-hosted session (the LSP server as the warm host), a systemd user service, and a three-state attach policy. The LSP host is option A with a different parent, noted there; the user service is option B in different clothes; the policy flag became option A as --session=auto|off|required.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review kept option A and gave it option C's explain-build cost line, so the saving a session provides is always visible. It made fresh execution the automatic fallback whenever no valid session exists.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review gave option B its idle timeout and lifecycle verbs, and option C its visible-cost argument and its role as the default when no session runs. Option B still contradicts ratified law; option C still pays on every build.
reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: BallotBeginner. Skill: rli5. The beginner pass found undefined terms (resident, warm, attach, daemon, socket), no visible rule for a missing or stale session, and identity only asserted. The lesson defines the terms, option A shows the fresh-process fallback and the digest comparison, and option B shows stop and idle exit.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: anthropic. Adversarial model family: openai. The rival review found byte identity unproven, a non-portable socket path, no authentication or symlink defense, undefined concurrency and cancellation, a misleading --detached name, a wrong Vite comparison, and no adoption threshold. Option A now specifies the envelope, endpoint rules, single ownership, request isolation, --session=off, a Gradle comparison, and a measured gate.

decisions.title: How Jet's build speed is measured against Cargo
decisions.gist: Which Cargo setups Jet must beat, on which programs, by which clock, and with what statistical rule, for the public build-speed claim.
decisions.lesson: The competitive gate in AGENTS.md allows Rust parity within 5% for runtime cells; the owner asked for a strict win on build cells. Because build times are noisy, a rule also has to say how many runs and how close is too close to call.
decisions.explainer:
Terms: a peer is the tool Jet is compared with. A cell is one measured case: one program, one profile, one state. A gate is the pass rule. A strict win means Jet's time is below the peer's, with no allowed tie. A ratio is Jet's wall time divided by the peer's; 1.00 means equal and below 1.00 means faster. A 95% confidence interval is the range the ratio is expected to sit in; only its upper end below 1.00 wins.

Ordinary Cargo is plain cargo build on a stock stable toolchain. Expert Cargo is what a Rust expert sets up: a faster linker, a warm compile cache, and native CPU flags. For debug builds it uses a nightly compiler with the parallel front end and the Cranelift backend.
decisions.story: Sam reads 'Jet builds faster than Rust' and tries it on his own project with mold and sccache already configured. If Jet only beat plain Cargo, Sam's first experience contradicts the claim. The claim has to survive Sam's machine, and it has to survive being re-run by someone who does not want it to be true.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet perf build-matrix --peer cargo --peer cargo-tuned
# columns: jet = Jet wall time · cargo = ordinary Cargo · tuned = expert Cargo · ratio = Jet/peer with its 95% upper bound
program      profile  state        jet     cargo   tuned   ratio(cargo)   ratio(tuned)   verdict
nbody        release  cold         0.41s   0.62s   0.58s   0.66 [≤0.71]   0.71 [≤0.77]   win
nbody        release  edit-body    0.19s   0.55s   0.31s   0.35 [≤0.38]   0.61 [≤0.67]   win
nbody        debug    cold         0.22s   0.55s   0.29s   0.40 [≤0.44]   0.76 [≤0.83]   win
shop(3 pkgs) release  clean-warm   1.90s   6.80s   2.10s   0.28 [≤0.30]   0.90 [≤0.97]   win
hello        release  cold         0.31s   0.30s   0.28s   1.03 [≤1.09]   1.11 [≤1.18]   LOSS  ← gate stays open
# illustrative values; nothing above is measured yet
decisions.detail: Owner tradeoff pass, 2026-09-02: option E gained a declared sequential extension above the ratified twenty pairs, a per-cell dashboard, and two labelled cold cells. The strict gate now spends extra runs only where the answer is close.

options.name: Strict win against ordinary and expert Cargo, wall clock, median rule
options.detail: Every cell must show Jet's median wall-clock time below both Cargo columns. Cells are the profile (debug versus dev, release versus release) times the state (cold machine, clean project with a warm machine, no change, and seven kinds of edit). Real programs decide pass or fail; synthetic twin programs at 10k, 50k, and 200k lines are published as scaling curves only. A median that is 0.1% lower counts as a win even though twenty noisy runs cannot tell 0.999 from 1.001.
options.technical: One warmup, twenty samples, median gate (D-PERFBUDGET-COMPILE1). Peers: stable rustc 1.97.1 for both columns' release rows; the tuned dev row uses a nightly of the same date, recorded as its own toolchain identity. No confidence interval.
options.code:
$ jet perf build-matrix --check
64 cells · 62 win · 2 loss (hello/release/cold, hello/release/no-change)
gate: OPEN — losses listed in tools/perf/build-matrix/2026-09-01.md
# illustrative

options.name: Strict win against ordinary Cargo; 5% band against expert Cargo
options.detail: Plain Cargo must be beaten outright; expert Cargo may be matched within the existing 5% Rust band. Easier to close, and honest about the fact that expert Cargo already has a fast linker and a warm compile cache. A Rust expert's machine can still tie Jet, and the claim survives only in its weaker form.
options.technical: Same cells and clock; comparator 1.00 for ordinary, 1.05 for expert.
options.code:
$ jet perf build-matrix --check
64 cells · 60 win · 4 parity (tuned within 5%) · 0 loss
gate: CLOSED
# illustrative

options.name: Existing 5% Rust band for every build cell
options.detail: Treat build time like the other Rust cells: parity within 5% passes. The weakest claim; 'as fast as Cargo' rather than 'faster than Cargo'.
options.technical: Comparator 1.05 for both columns.
options.code:
$ jet perf build-matrix --check
64 cells · 57 win · 7 parity · 0 loss
gate: CLOSED
# illustrative

options.name: Processor seconds instead of wall clock
options.detail: Gate on total processor time (user plus system) rather than elapsed time. It is less sensitive to a busy machine and catches a design that wins only by burning far more cores. But users feel elapsed time, and Jet's parallel unit front ends are a real advantage this metric would count against it.
options.technical: Gate metric cpu_ns = user+sys; wall_ns recorded only. Note: today's dashboard field named latency_ns already stores CPU time, which is a naming defect this ballot corrects by defining wall_ns and cpu_ns separately.
options.code:
$ jet perf build-matrix --check --metric cpu
64 cells · 49 win · 15 loss   # parallel front ends count against Jet
# illustrative; one parallel build: wall 1.9s, cpu 9.4s

options.name: Strict wall-clock win with a confidence bound and a declared sequential extension, plus independent resource ceilings
options.detail:
Wall clock stays the gate and both Cargo columns must be beaten. A cell counts as a win only when the statistics say so: runs are paired and their order randomized. The upper end of a 95% confidence interval on Jet divided by the peer must be below 1.00. A cell whose interval touches 1.00 is 'too close to call' and keeps the gate open rather than passing.

Processor seconds, peak memory, binary size, and the produced binary's own speed are recorded for every cell. Each has its own ceiling: a build-speed win that doubles memory or slows the binary fails. Real programs gate; synthetic twins are curves. The expert column is defined per profile and target as the fastest valid published Cargo configuration. A claim is made only for the host and target classes actually measured.

Sampling starts at the ratified twenty measured pairs (D-PERFBUDGET-COMPILE1) and never fewer; one pair is one Jet run beside one run of each peer. A cell whose intervals are clear at twenty is decided there. A cell that straddles the line continues in batches of ten to sixty pairs under a boundary declared before the run, so looking twice cannot manufacture a win. Each cell has two comparisons, ordinary and expert Cargo; it wins only when both pass and loses when either fails.

The dashboard shows each cell's state as it closes; the public claim waits for the whole matrix. Two cold cells are reported and labelled. Toolchain-installed cold, where the installer has already placed the host runtime objects as Rust places std, is the gating cell. Fresh-machine first use, which includes the download and verification, is published beside it. The produced binary's own speed is measured by the gauntlet runtime cells, which must stay within their ratified bands.
options.technical:
Paired randomized interleaving of the three commands within each pair. Estimator: bootstrap percentile interval on the paired wall-clock ratio, the pair as the resampling unit, 10,000 resamples, recorded seed. Looks at 20, 40, and 60 pairs under an O'Brien-Fleming alpha-spending boundary declared in the report. Win iff both peer comparisons pass at the current boundary, loss iff either fails, else continue; at sixty, inconclusive keeps the gate open. This amends D-PERFBUDGET-COMPILE1 only by allowing more than twenty pairs.

Sequential rule: minimum 5 paired samples per side. Stop early when upper95 < 0.90 (win) or lower95 > 1.10 (loss). Otherwise continue in batches of 5 to 40 per side; then win iff upper95 < 1.00, loss iff lower95 ≥ 1.00, else inconclusive. Early stops sit far from the gate line, so optional stopping cannot manufacture a win at the line; the report records the rule and the sample count per cell.

Secondary gates: cpu_ns ≤ 1.10 × peer for the same cell class (parallelism may cost some CPU but not unboundedly). Peak RSS ≤ 1.25 × peer. Binary size stays within 2% of the previous Jet baseline. Gauntlet runtime cells stay unchanged within noise.

Peers: ordinary = stable rustc 1.97.1, default profile and linker, no .cargo/config.toml. Expert = per profile and target the fastest valid pre-registered configuration (mold, warm sccache where the state permits, RUSTFLAGS=-C target-cpu=native, nightly-of-the-day with -Zthreads=8 and -Zcodegen-backend=cranelift for dev). Each toolchain is recorded as its own exact identity and rejected if it fails output or runtime parity.

Profile mapping: jet build --profile=debug vs cargo build. jet build --release vs cargo build --release. Default jet build also reported against cargo build --release. Toolchain-level objects (Rust std, Jet runtime units) count as present in the cold cell on both sides.

Matched pairs record LOC, module/package graph, dependency closure, features, output identity, and the exact edit patch, reviewed before entering the corpus. Missing peer row, mismatched identity, or failed parity = unavailable = gate fails; no averaging; claims per measured host/target class.
options.code:
$ jet perf build-matrix --check
64 cells · 61 win · 1 inconclusive (hello/release/no-change, ratio 0.97 [≤1.02] at 60 pairs) · 2 loss
pairs: 49 cells decided at 20; 12 continued to 40; 3 ran to 60
gate: OPEN — report: tools/perf/build-matrix/2026-09-01.md (one row per cell: values, both intervals, peer config, pairs, boundary, verdict)
# illustrative

comparisons.note: Go's published compile-speed claims are wall-clock on real repositories with a stated machine; that is why they are believed. Go's own perf dashboard records both wall and CPU.
comparisons.code:
$ time go build ./...
real 0m1.9s  user 0m9.4s

comparisons.note: cargo build --timings reports wall-clock per unit and in total. rustc-perf gates the compiler's own performance on instructions retired because it is far less noisy than wall time. It publishes wall time alongside, and both are per-benchmark, never averaged. Option E takes the lesson: gate on what users feel, but demand a noise-aware rule and keep work metrics as guards.
comparisons.code:
$ cargo build --release --timings
  Finished `release` profile in 1.05s

comparisons.note: Bazel publishes cold, warm, and incremental wall-clock numbers separately and states the cache state of every run. Mixing them is the classic benchmark sin every option here forbids.
comparisons.code: $ bazel build //... --profile=prof.json   # cache state recorded per action

comparisons.note: Kalibera and Jones, 'Rigorous Benchmarking in Reasonable Time' (ICSE 2013), show that repeated runs need confidence intervals and randomization before a small difference can be called a win. Option E applies that rule.
comparisons.code: win ⇔ upper95(jet/peer) < 1.00

recommendation.why: Option E keeps the owner's strict wall-clock win against both columns and makes it defensible. A win is a statistical fact, not a lucky median, and a build-speed win cannot be bought with memory, processor time, or a slower binary. Real programs gate because synthetic twins can be shaped, knowingly or not, toward the tool that generated them. Extra runs are spent only where the answer is close, under a boundary declared in advance.

whyNot.reason: A median that is barely below 1.00 on twenty noisy runs is not evidence; a critic can re-run it and get the opposite answer.
A tie on an expert's machine contradicts the public claim on exactly the machines experts use.
It turns 'faster than Cargo' into 'about as fast', which is not the claim.
Users feel elapsed time; processor time hides the parallelism that is part of the design, though it survives in E as a ceiling.

recommendation.tradeoff: The gate stays strict and every cell must win. The only cost that remains is run budget on near cells, bounded at sixty pairs.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared strict-both, strict-plus-band, band-only, and a processor-time metric, and recommended strict-both on wall clock with real programs gating.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested gating on the geometric mean across programs, on a percentile of edits, and on a confidence-bounded ratio with resource ceilings. Averages hide a loss, which the competitive gate forbids; the confidence-bounded rule is a genuine alternative and became option E.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review combined option A's strict wall-clock rule with option D's processor-time guard and a statistical win rule into option E. The owner's tradeoff pass added a declared sequential extension above twenty pairs.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review gave option B its honesty argument about expert Cargo, option C its consistency with the runtime band, and option D its noise-resistance argument. Noise resistance survives in E's interval and ceilings; none of the others changes what users feel.
reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: Rli5Build. Skill: rli5. The first pass found peer, cell, gate, and strict win undefined; the lesson defines them. The second found the early-stop count ambiguous with two peers and ratio undefined; E now counts pairs, defines ratio and interval, and needs both comparisons.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Anthropic. Adversarial model family: OpenAI. The first rival pass found median ambiguity and unmatched workload shapes, and moved the recommendation to E. The second, on the owner's revision, found a five-sample minimum against the ratified twenty, undeclared optional stopping, and a hidden first-use fetch; all three are repaired in E.

decisions.comment: If we consistently fail to BEAT cargo/rust, then we should ensure it is noted in gauntlet and proceed. It may not physically be possible to beat cargo/rust when we are transpiling to use cargo/rust. In that event, let's not waste time trying to chase the impossible, but we should try creative solutions to beat stock cargo/rust if possible

decisions.title: How much work should a ballot take to create?
decisions.gist: Decide which parts of a ballot are required and which review passes stay.
decisions.lesson: A full ballot today is a long record plus six review summaries. Four of the six (base, boil the ocean, hybrid, cooperative) are written by the drafter about its own draft; only the beginner pass and the adversarial pass are independent readers. This epoch's 42 ballots each took a drafter, two reviewers, and a fixer: four agent runs and 30 to 45 minutes of wall time per ballot. The reading surface is now mandatory and validated by Tower. This ballot decides what else stays required.
decisions.story: User asks for a slate of 40 decisions on Friday night. Fable must write them, review them, fix them, and sync them before morning. Every required field and pass is multiplied by 40. Each one must earn its place by changing what User decides.
decisions.inWild:
# Architecture Decision Record, Michael Nygard's template (https://cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions)
# Title
# Context
# Decision
# Status
# Consequences
#
# Python PEP process: one author, one sponsor, one PEP-Delegate decides after a discussion thread.
# https://peps.python.org/pep-0001/
# Rust RFC process: author drafts, public review, final comment period with the owning team.
# https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs#the-rfc-life-cycle
# None of the three requires the author to grade its own draft under six headings.

options.name: Keep the full process, add the surface
options.detail: Everything stays as it is today, with the reading surface on top. Gains: Nothing changes for agents already trained on the process. Every existing gate keeps running. Losses: A ballot costs more than before, not less. Four of six review summaries stay self-graded.

options.name: Surface first, two independent passes
options.detail: The surface is the ballot. Long form keeps only what grounds it: story, in the wild, option code and technical notes, comparisons. The explainer, Q&A detail, and hybrid harvest are removed. Review passes drop to the two independent ones: a fresh beginner reader and a rival-family adversary. Gains: Ballot cost drops by about half; every remaining pass is a real second reader. Nothing the owner reads is lost. Losses: The breadth pass (missing options) is no longer a named step; the adversary must cover it.

options.name: B, plus a profile by stakes and a scaffold command
options.detail:
Same record and two passes as B. The short profile (surface plus grounding, no passes) becomes the default for a ballot inside one mechanism with at most three options. The full profile with both passes is required for new syntax, any invariant carve-out, and any card the owner tags full.

A scaffold command runs the card's probe to fill the current pane and copies the cited in-the-wild snippet from the card's evidence file; the author writes the words.

Gains: Most ballots cost one agent run. The adversary still guards every syntax or invariant decision. The scaffold makes the current pane real output, never prose. Losses: Simple ballots ship with no second reader unless the owner asks. The scaffold is new Tower code to build and test.
options.code:
$ tower decision scaffold '#2612' --id D-M-NOTEBOOK1
  probe: jet run probes/notebook_cell.jet  -> surface.trio.current.code
  wild:  cards/_mechanisms/M-NOTEBOOK.json evidence[0] -> surface.trio.wild
  wrote .tower/drafts/D-M-NOTEBOOK1.json (profile: short, options: A B C)

$ tower decision add --file D-M-NOTEBOOK1.json        # short: surface + story + code
$ tower card update '#2612' --tags full                # forces beginner + adversarial passes

recommendation.why: C removes the four self-graded summaries, keeps the two real readers where the stakes are, and makes the current pane real program output. That cuts most ballots to one agent run.

whyNot.reason: A adds the surface on top of everything, so each ballot costs more than before.
B halves the cost but still spends two extra agents on every simple ballot.

recommendation.tradeoff: Simple ballots lose their second reader by default; the owner can tag any card full to get both passes back.

decisions.title: Real-time boundary: fixed-rate callbacks with exact waits and overrun receipts
decisions.gist: How does a Jet library run audio, control loops, and interrupt handlers on a deadline without allocating?
decisions.lesson: Audio and control code runs on a fixed clock: a callback gets a buffer every few milliseconds and must finish before the next one. Jet can already forbid allocation in a function. It has no callback boundary, its sleeps round to milliseconds, and its shared cells can block. A library author fakes the clock with a timer and cannot prove a missed deadline.
decisions.story: Mia writes a synthesizer in Jet. Her render function must fill 256 samples every 5.3 ms. She wants the runtime to call it on time, refuse any allocation or lock inside it, and tell her how many buffers she missed. Today she loops with a sleep that rounds to a millisecond and counts misses by hand.
decisions.inWild: Every audio engine (CoreAudio, JUCE, cpal) drives a callback from the device thread, forbids allocation and locks inside it, and reports an underrun as an "xrun" count. Real-time control (ROS 2, RTIC) binds handlers to a clock or an interrupt and measures jitter.

options.name: Callback boundary with exact waits and lock-free cells
options.detail: The runtime drives a fixed-rate callback. Its effect row forbids allocation and blocking through a new Time.Wait leaf that blocking calls carry. Scalar shared cells become lock-free reads and writes. Sleeps keep nanoseconds and an absolute wait exists. Every overrun lands in the receipt.
options.code:
level :: shared 0.8
stream :: rt.callback(rate: 48_000, frames: 256,
    -[Mem.Alloc, Time.Wait]> fn(out: &[Float]) { render(out, level) })
time.sleep_until(stream.next_deadline())
print(stream.receipt().missed)

options.name: Library only: keep the timer fake, add nanosecond sleep
options.detail: Only time.sleep changes. Authors keep spinning on a timer and count misses by hand.

options.name: Hard real-time scheduler with priorities and static WCET proof
options.detail: A priority scheduler and a compiler-proved worst-case execution time for every handler.
options.code:
#RealTime(priority: 90, wcet: 200us)
fn render(out: &[Float]) { ... }

comparisons.note: The device drives the callback; a miss is reported as an xrun.

recommendation.why: A is small: it reuses effect rows, shared cells, and receipts, and matches how every audio engine works.

whyNot.reason: B leaves misses unproven and blocking calls undetected; every library repeats the same loop.
C is years of compiler work, platform-specific, and beginners never need it.

recommendation.tradeoff: Unavoidable: overruns are counted, not prevented, because safe code cannot be interrupted mid-function. Unavoidable: exact waits need a high-resolution timer the OS must grant.

decisions.shortAuthorizedBy: Owner, 2026-09-02: "Remember we need to spend effort up front figuring out how to eliminate the losses so we dont pay for them later and get the best of all worlds."

decisions.title: Opaque C handles and native link closure in generated bindings
decisions.gist: How does a library bind a C library that hands out opaque handles, without hand-written adapters?
decisions.lesson: Most C libraries (zlib, HarfBuzz, SQLite, FFmpeg) return an opaque pointer and expect it back later, then freed. Jet's binder refuses those headers, so an author writes a C adapter per library and frees by hand. Jet already has the ownership words: ^ transfers, & lends for one call, #Close closes once. The binder only needs to use them.
decisions.story: Omar wants gzip reading in Jet. zlib's API is gzopen, gzgets, gzclose over an opaque gzFile. The binder says no bindable prototypes. He writes zr_open, zr_gets, zr_close in C over an integer table, then links zlib by hand after an undefined-symbol error.
decisions.inWild: Swift imports C opaque pointers as OpaquePointer and authors wrap them in a class whose deinit frees them. Rust bindgen emits the pointer type and authors implement Drop. Both leave ownership to the author; neither refuses the header.

options.name: Generated handle types with #Close, one link declaration
options.detail: An opaque pointer typedef becomes a handle type. The function that frees it becomes its close, found by name or named in the overlay. Returning constructors transfer with ^, borrowing calls lend with &. The binding declares its transitive libraries once.

options.name: Generated C shim with integer handles
options.detail: The binder writes the adapter C for you: a table of pointers indexed by Int.
options.code:
h :: zlib.zr_open(path)
zlib.zr_close(h)   // unchecked Int; double free reachable

options.name: Raw pointers under #Unsafe for every opaque API
options.detail: The binder emits the raw pointer type; every use sits in a reasoned #Unsafe block.

comparisons.note: Opaque pointers import as OpaquePointer; a class frees in deinit.

recommendation.why: A binds the libraries every domain needs with the ownership words Jet already ratified, and no user code is unsafe.

whyNot.reason: B hides the pointer behind an unchecked Int: leaks stay silent and a double free is one typo away.
C makes every library author write unsafe blocks and every audit repeat per library.

recommendation.tradeoff: Unavoidable: C carries no ownership data, so when no free function is recognizable the author names it in the overlay. Unavoidable: a handle crosses tasks only when the overlay says the library is thread-safe.

decisions.shortAuthorizedBy: Owner, 2026-09-02: "Remember we need to spend effort up front figuring out how to eliminate the losses so we dont pay for them later and get the best of all worlds."

decisions.title: Capability-scoped host imports for sandbox guests
decisions.gist: How does a host give a plugin exactly the file and network rights it needs, and nothing more?
decisions.lesson: A sandbox package runs in WebAssembly with no effects at all. It may not read a file or open a socket. It may only export functions over plain numbers and text. Real plugins need bounded access: read this folder, call this host. Jet already has one rights tree with path-scoped leaves. The sandbox boundary does not use it yet.
decisions.story: Priya ships a search plugin. It must index files under one folder the host chooses and nothing else. Today the guest cannot read at all, so she moves all reading into the host and streams text across the boundary by hand.
decisions.inWild: The WebAssembly Component Model lets a guest declare imports in WIT; WASI pre-opens one directory as the guest's whole filesystem. Deno grants permissions per path and host. Both give bounded rights, not all-or-nothing.

options.name: Guest declares needs; host lends a tightened Authority
options.detail: The guest names the rights it needs. The host lends an Authority value tightened to a folder or host. Guest file and network calls go through host imports checked against it. Records cross through generated typed interfaces.

options.name: Keep sandboxes effect-free; pass data through the host
options.detail: No change. The host does all reading and networking and passes scalars across.
options.code:
text :: files.read("/data/in/a.txt")
n :: plugin.count(text)     // Text in, Int out

options.name: Grant effects by ambient package rights
options.detail: A sandbox package inherits the host's authority like a native dependency does.
options.code: plugin :: plugin.load("index.wasm")   // gets the host's rights

comparisons.note: The guest declares imports; the host binds them per capability.

decisions.title: How restricted code receives file authority
decisions.gist: Should restricted code bind file authority once or pass it to every file operation?
decisions.lesson: Ordinary trusted scripts keep the direct fs.read path with no policy ceremony. Explicit authority appears only when a host deliberately lends narrower file access to untrusted or isolated code.
decisions.story: Maya runs a one-line trusted file script, then loads an untrusted document indexer that may read one Documents subtree but cannot open her SSH keys.

decisions.title: Signals and request deadlines as cancellation
decisions.gist: How does a service stop cleanly on SIGTERM and cancel a slow request with the cancellation Jet already has?
decisions.lesson: Jet cancels work at wait points and keeps cleanup running. The outside world cannot trigger that cancellation. Only Ctrl-C has a handler and there is no SIGTERM. A server cannot put a deadline on one request. A child's stdin cannot be closed to say "no more". The backend and CLI probes stopped their servers by hand and waited on a child forever.
decisions.story: Dev deploys a Jet API under systemd. On deploy, systemd sends SIGTERM and waits ten seconds. His server must finish the requests in flight, refuse new ones, and exit. Today nothing in Jet hears the signal.
decisions.inWild: Go turns a signal into a cancelled context and wraps handlers with a timeout; Node ends a child's stdin with end(). Every production runtime maps signals and per-request deadlines onto the same cancellation it uses everywhere else.

options.name: Signals cancel the root task; server deadlines are contexts; stdin closes
options.detail: SIGTERM cancels the program's root task at its next wait point; serve drains under that cancellation; a route deadline is a per-request #Context; ProcessStdin gains close.
options.code:
fn run() -[Net, Process.Signal]> {
    process.on_signal(.Term)
    server :: http.serve(mux, deadline: 5s)
    server.wait()
}
child.stdin.write_all(rows)
child.stdin.close()

options.name: Library only: poll a shared flag set by a handler
options.detail: A signal handler flips a shared Bool; every loop polls it; deadlines stay on the client side.
options.code:
stop :: shared false
loop !stop { serve_one() }

options.name: A separate lifecycle object apart from tasks
options.detail: A new Lifecycle value with its own stop and deadline methods, independent of task cancellation.
options.code:
life :: Lifecycle.new()
life.on_stop(fn() { server.close() })

comparisons.note: A signal becomes a cancelled context; a handler gets a deadline.
comparisons.code:
ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), syscall.SIGTERM)
srv := &http.Server{Handler: http.TimeoutHandler(mux, 5*time.Second, "slow")}
<-ctx.Done()
srv.Shutdown(context.Background())

recommendation.why: A adds three names and no new mechanism: signals and deadlines become the cancellation every wait point already honors.

whyNot.reason: B makes every service copy the same polling loop and leaves deadlines on the client.
C is a second way to stop work next to task cancellation; two mechanisms for one meaning.

recommendation.tradeoff: Unavoidable: SIGKILL ends the process without cleanup. Unavoidable: a CPU-bound handler notices its deadline at its next wait point, by the cancellation law.

decisions.title: Operators between different types
decisions.gist: May a library define Vector * Float and Money * Rate, or must every mixed operation be a named method?
decisions.lesson: Today an operator implementation must keep the same type on both sides and as the result. A geometry package writes v.scale(2.0) and a money package writes price.times(rate); every user pays that at every call. Units already get mixed arithmetic through #UnitFamily. Other libraries do not.
decisions.story: Lena writes a 2-D game math package. Scaling a vector by a number is the most common line in her users' code, and it must read v * 2.0. Jet refuses her impl because the right side is a Float.
decisions.inWild: Rust names the right side and the output in the trait (impl Mul<f64> for Vector { type Output = Vector }); Swift declares static func * (lhs: Vector, rhs: Double) -> Vector. Both keep symbols and precedence fixed; only the types vary.

options.name: Typed right side and result on the existing hooks

options.name: Full operator overloading with overload sets and new symbols
options.detail: Any number of implementations per symbol and user-defined symbols.
options.code: operator <*> (a: Vector, b: Vector) Float -> dot(a, b)

whyNot.reason: B keeps call-site ceremony everywhere and lets each library invent a name for multiplication.
C brings overload ambiguity and unreadable symbols, the reasons D-OPDEF1 exists.

recommendation.tradeoff: Designed away: the mirror order is derived by #Commutative, so no pair is written twice. No remaining loss was found.

decisions.gist: May a library type accept a plain literal, so accept(1) builds a Rational and 0.10 a Decimal?
decisions.lesson: A literal takes its type from context in Jet, but only for built-in carriers. A package's Rational or scaled Decimal needs Rational{numerator: 1, denominator: 1} at every call, and a suffix like 1rat is refused. Swift solves this with a protocol a type adopts; Jet can do the same with no new syntax.
decisions.story: Sam builds an exact money package. His users write total = price * 3 and tax = 0.10 in every program. Today each of those literals needs a constructor call, and the money code reads worse than the Python it replaces.
decisions.inWild: Swift types adopt ExpressibleByIntegerLiteral and ExpressibleByFloatLiteral; the compiler calls the initializer where context asks for the type. Rust has no literal hook and users write Decimal::from_str("0.10") everywhere, a known pain.

options.name: Literal capability on the existing context rule
options.detail: A type adopts a literal capability with a compile-time constructor. The float form receives the digits as text so exact types stay exact. Context already picks the target type; nothing new to type.

options.detail: A package declares suffixes the way unit families do.

decisions.title: Zero-copy views over text, bytes, and mapped files
decisions.gist: Can a scanner walk 100 MB of text or bytes without copying every piece into a new String?
decisions.lesson: Jet's View<T> already lends part of a value without copying, with checked provenance. But the text API returns fresh Strings for every grapheme, word, and line, and files have no memory mapping. The text probe measured a 100 MB scan at 6.9 s in Jet against 33 ms in Rust: allocation, not logic. Views over text, bytes, and mapped files close that gap in one mechanism.
decisions.story: Ana writes a log tool. It scans gigabytes of lines and keeps a few. Each line becomes a new String today, so her tool is two hundred times slower than ripgrep and she cannot map the file at all.
decisions.inWild: Rust slices borrow the buffer (&str, &[u8]) and memmap2 lends the file itself; Go strings and []byte share backing storage; Java has CharSequence views and MappedByteBuffer. None copies per token.

options.name: Views everywhere: text spans, byte windows, mapped files
options.detail: Text and byte APIs return views. Storing a view copies by the existing law, so old code keeps working. files.map lends a private read-only mapping whose windows are byte views.

options.name: Return offsets, not views
options.detail: APIs return Int spans and callers slice by hand.

options.name: Copy, but faster
options.detail: Keep returning Strings but allocate them in an arena.
options.code:
arena :: mem.arena()
loop word in text.words_in(arena, chunk) { ... }

comparisons.note: Slices borrow the buffer; mmap lends the file itself.

recommendation.why: A uses the view law Jet already ratified, keeps every caller working through the copy-on-store rule, and reaches the incumbents' speed.

whyNot.reason: B pushes slicing and Unicode boundaries onto every caller; off-by-one bugs return.
C still copies every token and leaks arenas into every API.

recommendation.tradeoff: Unavoidable: a view cannot cross a task or channel, by the memory law. Unavoidable: a mapping holds a lock on the file so its bytes cannot change under a view.

decisions.title: Typed sections on the one receipt
decisions.gist: May a library attach its own typed evidence to Jet's receipt and query or diff it with the same tools?
decisions.lesson: Jet has one receipt for check, build, test, prove, and benchmarks, and one status view over it. A data pipeline, a training run, or a firmware build wants to say more: r-squared, loss curve, flash checksum. Today that evidence lives in printed JSON that jet status and jet perf compare never see. The receipt's fixed fields must not change.
decisions.story: Noor trains a model nightly. She wants jet status to show last night's loss, and a diff between two runs to show what moved. Today she greps stdout.
decisions.inWild: MLflow runs carry typed metrics and params beside artifacts and the UI diffs two runs by field. Bazel's build event protocol and GitHub check runs attach typed outputs to one canonical record. Nobody keeps a second ledger.

options.name: Typed receipt sections declared by the program
options.detail: A #Receipt record is written under the program's receipt as a named typed section. Status, compare, and diff read it like built-in fields. Identity and the fixed fields never change.

options.name: Library JSON files next to the receipt
options.detail: Programs write sidecar files; tools ignore them.
options.code: files.write("evidence.json", json.to_string(fit))

options.name: Free-form key/value tags on the receipt
options.detail: Untyped string tags on the receipt.
options.code: receipt.tag("r2", "0.998")

comparisons.note: A run carries typed metrics beside the artifact; the UI diffs runs by field.
comparisons.code:
with mlflow.start_run():
    mlflow.log_param("model", "ols")
    mlflow.log_metric("r2", 0.998)
    mlflow.log_artifact("fit.json")

recommendation.why: A keeps one receipt and one status truth while letting every domain's evidence ride the same tools, typed and diffable.

whyNot.reason: B creates a second truth that status and compare never read, and no identity check covers it.
C is untyped: no schema, string diffs, and silent typos in keys.

recommendation.tradeoff: Designed away: sections are capped by the store's existing size rule with a clear error, so the store cannot bloat. No remaining loss was found.

decisions.title: Platform services in core.ui
decisions.gist: How does a desktop app open a file dialog, paste, take IME input, and name its controls for a screen reader?
decisions.lesson: core.ui draws trees, routes clicks, and mounts on three hosts. A real editor also needs the host's services: clipboard, selection, input-method composition, drag and drop, file dialogs, shortcuts, and accessible names. None exist, and a library cannot reach them safely because they live in the operating system. Text shaping (fonts, Arabic, emoji) is the same kind of service.
decisions.story: Kai builds a notes app. Paste, Ctrl+S, "Open file", a screen-reader label on the save button, and Japanese input through an IME are all missing. None can be added from a package without unsafe OS calls.
decisions.inWild: SwiftUI attaches services as modifiers: .keyboardShortcut, .accessibilityLabel, .fileImporter; UIPasteboard and UITextInput handle clipboard and IME. Flutter has Clipboard, Semantics, file_selector, and TextInput with composition. Both make services typed values on the same tree.

options.name: One ui.host service set, typed and capability-gated
options.detail: Services live under ui.host as typed values. Each carries its own capability, so a package must ask for the clipboard or file dialogs. Labels and shortcuts are node arguments. font.shape returns glyph runs.
options.code:
button("Save", shortcut: .cmd("s"), label: "Save the note") { save() }
path :: ui.host.open_file(filters: [.text]) ?? return
text :: ui.host.clipboard.read_text()
editor :: text_input(state, ime: .native, on_drop: fn(items) { ... })

options.name: Leave services to packages over FFI
options.detail: Each GUI package binds GTK, Cocoa, or Win32 itself.
options.code:
use c.gtk
#Unsafe("gtk clipboard") { gtk.gtk_clipboard_get(...) }

options.name: Bind one toolkit (GTK) as the service layer
options.detail: core.ui exposes GTK's services directly on every platform.
options.code: ui.gtk.file_chooser_dialog(...)

comparisons.note: Services are typed modifiers on the same tree.

recommendation.why: A gives every host the same typed services, gated by the rights tree. A notes app is then safe on desktop, headless in tests, and honest about its needs.

whyNot.reason: B makes every GUI package bind the OS itself, unsafe, with no headless test host.
C ships one toolkit's look everywhere, has no mobile path, and adds a second UI model.

recommendation.tradeoff: Unavoidable: headless hosts stub services (a dialog returns cancelled) because there is no OS behind them. Unavoidable: each native host implements the set separately.

decisions.title: Interrupts, DMA, and register blocks from the target profile
decisions.gist: How does firmware bind an interrupt, own a DMA buffer, and name registers without hand-written unsafe blocks?
decisions.lesson: Jet's target profiles already know a board's memory regions, linker layout, and allocator. Firmware needs three more things the profile could give it. A vector entry that runs a bounded handler. A buffer that a DMA engine owns until completion. Typed register blocks with widths and access modes. Today each is a hand-written unsafe block, and interrupts have no surface at all.
decisions.story: Tomas writes a sensor node. The UART interrupt must push bytes into a ring and a DMA channel must own the sample buffer while it fills. Registers must be typed so a 16-bit write cannot hit a 32-bit register. Today all three are raw addresses inside unsafe blocks.
decisions.inWild: Rust's svd2rust generates typed register blocks from the chip's SVD file, RTIC binds an interrupt to a task with declared shared resources, and embedded-dma transfers buffer ownership until completion. Zig and Ada SPARK have the same three ideas.

options.name: Profile-generated registers, bound handlers, owned DMA transfers
options.detail: The board profile carries the SVD; the compiler generates typed register blocks. A handler is bound to a vector with an effect row that forbids allocation and waiting. DMA takes the buffer by ^ and returns it on completion.
options.code:
use board.sensor_v1 as board
board.usart1.cr1.rxneie.set()
#Interrupt(board.USART1, -[Mem.Alloc, Time.Wait]>)
fn on_uart() { ring.push(board.usart1.dr.read()) }
transfer :: dma.start(board.dma1.ch4, ^buffer)
buffer :: transfer.wait()

options.name: Library packages over #Unsafe per board
options.detail: No compiler change; each board package hand-writes registers and handlers in unsafe blocks.

options.name: Bind Rust PAC and HAL crates through the Rust bridge
options.detail: Use svd2rust output and embedded-hal from Jet via extern rust.
options.code:
extern rust "stm32f4xx-hal@0.21"
dp :: hal.pac.Peripherals.take()

comparisons.note: Typed registers from the SVD; an interrupt bound to a task with declared resources.

recommendation.why: A extends the typed profile Jet already has, so registers, handlers, and DMA are checked by the compiler and no driver needs unsafe.

whyNot.reason: B repeats unsafe per board, checks no widths or modes, and makes every driver an audit.
C leaks Rust types into Jet APIs, shows rustc to users, and has no interpreter or JIT parity.

recommendation.tradeoff: Unavoidable: vendor SVD files must be vetted per board because they are vendor data. Unavoidable: a handler sees only shared cells and may not wait or allocate, so it stays bounded.

decisions.title: Core API additions surfaced by the probes
decisions.gist: Which of these eleven core additions, each surfaced by a probe, should land as ordinary work?
decisions.lesson: Each item adds a name to a shipped core module without a new mechanism. Examples: closing a child's stdin, an ignore-aware file walk, a frame budget for game replay, a bounded database pool. Also: OpenAPI export from routes, event-time stream operators, a leap-second label, a desktop bundler, a device flasher, a typed build-graph query. The full list with evidence is on the card.
decisions.story: Each of the eight area probes hit two or three of these on its way to a working program and wrote a workaround. None needed a new idea, only a name that was not there.
decisions.inWild: Node ends a child's stdin with end() and pools connections with pg.Pool. ripgrep walks with .gitignore rules and Godot runs headless for N frames. Flink keys and windows streams by event time. cargo-bundle packages desktop apps and probe-rs flashes boards with a report.

decisions.title: Body-first loops: add a `do` keyword or teach one shape
decisions.gist: Whether Jet adds a keyword for loops that test after the body.
decisions.lesson: Jet spells every loop with `loop` and accepts only a `Bool` test in the header. A loop that must run once before testing is written with a `break` at the bottom. C, Java, and Swift have a keyword for it; Rust, Go, Python, Zig, and Kotlin ship without one. The question is whether one more spelling earns its place.
decisions.story: Mara ports a chat bot from Python. Her loop reads a line, answers, and stops on an empty line. She types `do {` from Java habit and Jet rejects it. She wants to know the Jet way in one glance.

options.name: No new keyword; teach the shape
options.detail: Keep `loop` as the only loop word. The body-first loop is `loop { … if <stop> { break } }`. The E0003 error for `do`, `repeat`, and `until` shows that rewrite. Lints flag unreachable code after a loop and a constant-true header. Gain: nothing new to learn, one spelling per meaning. Loss: the exit test lives inside the block.
options.technical: No Syntax.rs change. E0003 fix text for the foreign words gains the rewrite; lints per card #2884. Evidence on demand: Rust, Go, Python, Zig, and Kotlin have no do-while in their official grammars; C, C++, Java, JavaScript, C#, and Swift do. The mined video's 14 comments are too few to measure demand and are not used as evidence.

options.name: `break if test`
options.detail: Add a statement form `break if test` (also `next if test`) using existing words. Gain: a one-line exit and `loop` stays the only opener. Loss: it is a second spelling of `if test { break }`, and a new statement form the parser, formatter, and every run mode must treat as the same TIR as the block form.
options.technical: No new keyword; parser rule `break [label] if expr`. Lowers to the same TIR as `if expr { break }`. Ruby and Perl have this form; Rust rejected it (RFC discussions) to keep one conditional form.

options.name: `do { … } while test`
options.detail: Adopt the C-family spelling. Gain: familiar to most programmers and the test is visible after the block. Loss: two new keywords, a second loop opener, and `while` returns as a word Jet retired in favor of `loop test`.
options.technical: New keywords `do` and `while` in Syntax.rs; the parser needs a statement that begins with a block and ends with a header. Lowers to the same TIR as A. The E0003 teaching path for `while` today points users to `loop test`; C would make `while` legal only after `}`.

comparisons.note: Canonical body-first spelling.
comparisons.code: do { … } while (test);

comparisons.note: Same shape, different words.
comparisons.code: repeat { … } while test

comparisons.note: No do-while; the idiom is a bottom break, the same as option A.
comparisons.code: loop { … if done { break; } }

comparisons.note: Statement modifier form, option B.
comparisons.code: break if line.empty?

recommendation.why: The shape has one clear spelling today and the compiler can teach it at the error site. A second spelling or two keywords shortens a line without adding a meaning.

whyNot.reason: A second spelling of a conditional break breaks the one-spelling rule.
Two keywords and a second loop opener for one shape; `while` would return.

recommendation.tradeoff: The exit test lives inside the block. Only a new spelling could move it, and both candidate spellings cost more than they return.

decisions.title: Layout facts, type alignment, and lock-free counters without #Unsafe
decisions.gist: Whether Jet reuses its ratified layout facts, adds alignment inside #Layout, and ships a safe Atomic<T>.
decisions.lesson: Jet already has one ratified layout fact: `T.@layout` reports size, alignment, and field offsets for `#Layout(c)` and `#Layout(columnar)` types (D-LAYOUT-FACTS1=B). It does not need `size_of`. `#Layout(align(64))` is a reserved spelling today (E1105), so alignment belongs inside `#Layout`, not a new `#Align`. No lock-free shared value exists; `Shared<T>` locks every access. `Atomic<T>` would be the lock-free scalar member of that family. Lock-free means a stalled thread never blocks the others.
decisions.story: Nora maintains a market-data buffer. She needs 1024 `Int` slots on a 64-byte boundary, two counters that two threads update without a lock, and the byte size of the record for a C consumer. She wants ordinary code outside `#Unsafe`, and she does not want to learn memory-order names to get it right.
decisions.detail: The card asked three questions: layout fact names, an alignment spelling, and whether atomics are safe Core or `#Unsafe`. Probing found the first is already answered: `T.@layout.size` and `.alignment` are ratified and print on `jet run`. Two defects block it today, filed as #2920 (ICE on `jet build`) and #2921 (plain `@` binding fails E0956). The ballot therefore reuses that fact instead of adding `size_of`.

options.name: Reuse `T.@layout`, add `align(N)` to `#Layout`, ship safe `Atomic<T>`
options.detail: Layout facts stay `T.@layout.size` and `T.@layout.alignment`, the ratified spelling. Alignment uses the reserved `#Layout(c, align(64))`. `Atomic<T>` is a Core type for a closed scalar set: `Bool`, `I32`, `U32`, `Int`, `U64`. Its methods are `load`, `store`, `add`, and `compare_exchange`, all sequentially consistent. Two intent-named methods, `publish` and `observe`, are the release and acquire pair. No method takes an order argument. No relaxed order exists in this version.
options.technical:
Order safety: every method is correct in every combination. The `store` and `load` methods are sequentially consistent. The `publish` and `observe` methods are release and acquire. A sequentially consistent operation is stronger than either, so mixing is safe. A user who mixes them cannot create a race; only speed changes. That is why the order-knowledge loss is eliminated rather than mitigated. Relaxed is the one order that can create a bug, so it is not offered.

Target totality. Rust exposes 64-bit and 32-bit atomics on x86_64, aarch64, and wasm32, the ratified targets, so the closed set is total. A future target without a width rejects the type at its declaration with a registered diagnostic. A lock fallback is refused: it would make `Atomic` lie about progress and would differ by tier. Floats, 128-bit values, and structs are outside the set.

One lowering. `Atomic<T>` is one Core declaration; each run mode realizes the finite operation set (D-TIER-ONEIR1). Cranelift has atomic operations; the interpreter uses the same Rust atomics as the printed release code.

Family rule. `Atomic<T>` may not be read or written inside `#Transact` (new diagnostic): a commit over two lock-free values needs a lock, which is what `Shared<T>` is for. E0041 names both `Shared<T>` and `Atomic<T>` when a user reaches for a mutex.

Layout facts. `T.@layout` is computed by one target-aware engine (spec syntax-decisions.md:2773-2783); default layout has no byte fact and reports E0959. Fixed-width fields make the numbers identical across every 64-bit target. Alignment follows the E1105 reserved spelling inside the one `#Layout` family (I8).
gains: Zero new layout spellings; the ratified fact is reused
No user ever writes a memory-order name
Lock-free counters reach every run mode with one contract
cost: Two shipped defects (#2920, #2921) must be fixed before the fact is usable outside a derive body
Rust-printed release code gains one `std::sync::atomic` import per program that uses `Atomic`

losses.loss: A second shared-mutation type stands beside `Shared<T>`
losses.attempt1: Make scalar `shared` values lock-free by law, no new type. Failed: `#Transact` over two scalars cannot be lock-free, compare-and-exchange has no statement spelling, and existing `Shared<Int>` code would change meaning.
losses.attempt2: Lower a `#Transact` over one scalar to a compare-and-exchange loop. Failed: the same block would mean lock or lock-free depending on how many values it touches, a hidden cliff the owner forbids.
losses.mitigation: One documented family: `Shared<T>` for structs and multi-value commits, `Atomic<T>` for scalars. E0041 names both. `Atomic` inside `#Transact` is a compile error.

options.name: Layout facts and alignment only; concurrency stays channels and `Shared`
options.detail: Reuse `T.@layout` and add `#Layout(c, align(64))`. Add no atomic type. Counters shared between threads use `Shared<Int>`, which takes a lock per access, or a channel.
options.technical: The channel ring in probe R1 moved one million items correctly on every tier (AOT 0.20 s, `jet run` 3.43 s, interpreter 18.65 s). It is a queue, not a user-defined structure. Hazard pointers, lock-free stacks, and sequence locks cannot be written without a compare-and-exchange primitive.
gains: No new type in Core
Channels and `Shared` stay the only concurrency words
cost: Same two defects to fix as A

losses.loss: User-defined lock-free structures remain impossible
losses.attempt1: Make scalar `shared` lock-free by law. Failed for the reasons in A: transactions and compare-and-exchange.
losses.attempt2: Cover the need with channels. Failed: a channel is one queue shape; a ring with a consumer-owned head, a hazard pointer, or a sequence lock cannot be built from it.
losses.mitigation: Channels cover the single-producer single-consumer case today, as probe R1 shows.

losses.loss: A hot-path counter pays a lock on every increment
losses.attempt1: Batch increments locally and flush. Failed: it changes when other threads see the count, which is a semantic change, not an optimization.
losses.attempt2: Let the compiler replace an uncontended `Shared<Int>` lock with an atomic. Failed: contention is a run-time fact, so the choice would be invisible and unstable.
losses.mitigation: `Shared<Int>` remains correct; the cost is one uncontended lock per access.

options.name: Gate alignment and atomics behind `#Unsafe`
options.detail: Reuse `T.@layout` for facts. Put `#Layout(c, align(64))` and every `Atomic<T>` use inside an `#Unsafe("reason")` block.
options.technical: Neither alignment nor a sequentially consistent atomic can violate memory safety: alignment changes padding, and the atomic operations are total. The audit block would therefore mark code that has no hazard, diluting what `#Unsafe` means everywhere else.
gains: The safe Core surface stays smaller
Each use carries a written reason

losses.loss: `#Unsafe` marks code with no memory hazard
losses.attempt1: Exempt alignment and keep only atomics gated. Failed: a sequentially consistent atomic has no hazard either, so the gate still marks safe code.
losses.attempt2: Gate only `publish`/`observe`. Failed: those are also always correct in any mix (see A), so the gate marks nothing dangerous.
losses.mitigation: The reason string at least documents the sharing pattern.

losses.loss: Every caller carries the audit burden
losses.attempt1: Gate once at the type declaration instead of each use. Failed: `#Unsafe` is a block marker by law; a type-level gate would be a second unsafe mechanism.
losses.attempt2: Auto-insert the block from the compiler. Failed: an audit marker the user did not write audits nothing.
losses.mitigation: The burden is one block per hot path, not per line.

comparisons.note: Rust documents `size_of`, `align_of`, aligned representations, and ordered atomics. Atomic availability and lock-free support depend on the target.
Zig documents `@sizeOf(T)`, `@alignOf(T)`, explicit `align(64)`, and atomic builtins with order arguments. Here `align(64)` aligns the variable, not the type.
C++ uses `alignas`, `alignof`, and `std::atomic`; each atomic operation receives a memory order.

recommendation.why: A answers all three card questions with the least new surface. It adds zero layout functions, keeps alignment inside the one `#Layout` family, and adds a lock-free scalar type whose six operations cannot be combined into a race. It reaches every run mode through one Core declaration.

whyNot.reason: B cannot express a compare-and-exchange, so the C++ replacement bar in the source video (lock-free hot paths) stays out of reach.
C puts an audit block around operations that have no memory hazard, which weakens what `#Unsafe` means elsewhere.

recommendation.tradeoff: One mitigated loss remains: a second shared-mutation type beside `Shared<T>`. Two attempts to fold it into `Shared` failed on `#Transact` and compare-and-exchange. The accepted cost is fixing #2920 and #2921 so the ratified fact is reachable, then a new diagnostic for `Atomic` inside `#Transact`.
