decisions.title: Exact atomic integers without a hidden lock
decisions.gist: Can exact Atomic<Int> keep one simple interface without a special memory ceiling or hidden lock?
decisions.lesson: Atomic means each update takes effect as one indivisible change. Int keeps the exact mathematical value, including beyond machine-integer widths. The redesigned A keeps ordinary dynamically growing number storage and a direct path for small and fixed-width values. It removes the earlier fixed reserve instead of asking users to size an Atomic memory pool.
decisions.explainer: A keeps exact Atomic<Int>, direct fixed-width operations, and one family. Growable canonical numeric storage replaces the fixed reserve; a local cache miss is not an allocation failure. There is no Atomic-specific capacity setup or permanent-pinning fallback. Whole-operation nonblocking progress, safe ownership/reclamation, target-provider premises, and matched performance remain mandatory implementation proof, not a claim that the design already ships.
decisions.story: Nora increments a shared exact counter past a machine-integer boundary. She wants the exact result without locks or another cell type, and checked failure if ordinary Int allocation is refused.
decisions.detail:
Owner-requested redesign: remove avoidable downsides rather than relabel them. A now uses growable canonical numeric storage; the earlier fixed admitted pool, artificial pool-exhaustion failure, and immortal-on-saturation rule are removed. The author does not claim that finite hardware has unlimited memory or that an unimplemented design is proven.

The proposal preserves D-PLACE1’s exact atomic interface and whole-operation progress requirement. Its memory policy must not be more restrictive than ordinary Int under the same admitted application policy. B explicitly permits blocking exact atomics; C adds a second exact-cell family. A accepts neither compromise.

Primary precedents establish that dynamic lock-free allocation and hazard-based reclamation are design possibilities, not that Jet already implements them. The complete Jet allocator, ownership, target-provider, and tier paths still require implementation-bound proof. The source currently retains global numeric interning and an add comment that excludes allocation from its lock-free claim; those are the root changes, not accepted final behavior.

References: https://research.ibm.com/publications/scalable-lock-free-dynamic-memory-allocation and https://research.ibm.com/publications/hazard-pointers-safe-memory-reclamation-for-lock-free-objects .

options.name: Exact, growable, one Atomic family
options.detail: Keep exact Int and direct fixed-width atomics, backed by one growable nonblocking numeric store. No Atomic-specific pool, extra family, hidden lock, or user capacity setup.
options.technical:
A supersedes the fixed-reserve recommendation. Keep one Atomic<T> family for Bool, I32, U32, I64, U64, and exact Int. A explicitly adds I64 admission and the stated try_new/try_add forms to D-PLACE1/D-ALLOCFAIL1. Preserve the one-word cell layout, existing wrapping law for fixed widths, exact nonwrapping Int, Bool’s lack of add, sequential consistency for ordinary operations, release publish/acquire observe, and the #Transact restriction. No relaxed operation or second exact-cell family is added.

Keep the existing inline Int range and direct hardware lowering for fixed-width values. Exact Int and I64 must have distinct checked internal arithmetic routes even if both use an i64 machine carrier. When both operands and the exact result are inline, do not allocate, register a hazard, or enter a limb store. Existing fixed-width users pay no numeric-store machinery.

Large values use immutable normalized sign/limb storage in the one canonical numeric module. Share unchanged storage where the existing ownership model allows it; avoid copying an entire value merely to transfer ownership. Numeric compare_exchange compares mathematical values, not storage identities. Protect the observed value, compute the replacement privately, and revalidate before the one-word publication CAS. Preserve add’s old-value return and compare_exchange’s Bool result.

Replace the fixed admitted pool with growable, reusable numeric allocation under the same process allocator policy used by ordinary Int. An empty local cache is not out of memory: consult shared reusable blocks, reclaim eligible blocks, and request additional backing extents through the canonical memory provider. There is no Atomic-only quota, up-front capacity knob, permanently fixed participant count, or second memory configuration language. Optional application-wide memory limits remain the existing expert control.

Use nonblocking allocation/free bookkeeping with recoverable publication of shared reservations. A stopped owner may retain its own live work, but cannot exclusively own the only allocation or reclamation path. Extent growth cannot require waiting for one background refill thread. Do not call a locking user-space malloc behind the lock-free claim. The exact target memory-provider progress assumptions must be stated and checked; a provider that violates the admitted model blocks that implementation instead of silently weakening the promise.

Protect only objects a reader may still use. A paused reader cannot pin an epoch, whole arena, unrelated blocks, or a history of later values. Other eligible objects remain reusable, and fully unused extents return through the ordinary allocator. Large allocations must not strand unrelated reusable capacity in one reserved Atomic pool. Live old values remain valid exactly as ordinary owned immutable values do.

Use the existing thread/worker/foreign-entry lifecycle to provide private hazard records, growing participation with actual execution contexts rather than a special Atomic limit. No lazy registration may acquire a hidden lock during an atomic operation. Registration, teardown, reclamation, return-value ownership, and error handling belong to the whole-path progress proof.

Remove the earlier immortal-on-refcount-saturation policy. Ownership counts must be proven sufficient for every representable recorded live owner, including containers, closures, foreign transfers, and temporary roots. Every count increment must correspond to a real tracked owner, and dropping or abandoning that owner releases it. Untracked repeated credits, wrapping counts, permanent pinning, or an undisclosed failure in load/store are forbidden. If the actual carrier/foreign protocol cannot establish this bound, that implementation is incomplete, not permission for a pinning fallback.

Keep D-ALLOCFAIL1’s existing ordinary-memory outcomes. try_new(value) returns Atomic<T> !AllocError; try_add(delta) returns the previous Int !AllocError. Actual allocator refusal leaves the cell unchanged; plain allocation failure follows the existing hosted policy. A local cache miss or exhausted old fixed reserve cannot synthesize AllocError while the admitted ordinary allocator can satisfy the request. Error construction/return must use the existing allocation-free error carrier semantics, including its allocator identity and requested size.

Linearizability and nonblocking progress are required for the complete operation, not just the final CAS instruction. A losing CAS must correspond to another publication; no stalled Jet participant owns a lock needed by the others. As with hardware atomics, OS scheduling/page service and real resource availability are explicit environment premises, not a wall-clock or wait-free promise. Do not describe unsupported provider assumptions as proved progress.

Cut over all ordinary exact-number storage and every AOT/JIT/interpreter/web adapter to the same semantics. Remove global mutex interning, append-only arenas, the bounded-i64 interpreter path, and independent numeric policies. Preserve retained values, exact comparison, transfer/drop safety, and target admission under D-PLACE1. No new dependency, unsafe user escape, or I9 exception is authorized.

Acceptance must prove growth past the old reserve while ordinary memory is available. Pause readers, writers, and an extent-growth participant. Reuse unrelated blocks, return unused storage, preserve old values, and reject real exhaustion without mutation. Verify ownership-count bounds rather than simulating a saturating immortal state. Exercise inline/fixed-width/multi-limb correctness and all required matched performance metrics.

No additional user-facing restriction is accepted for A. It must preserve exactness, the one interface, direct fixed-width performance, and ordinary growable memory without shifting the old pool restriction into another label. The cost of representing live exact values, contended updates, and finite physical resources is shared reality, not evidence that a special Atomic ceiling is necessary. The design is a proposal; these are required proof obligations, not completed implementation claims.
gains: Exact growth without an Atomic-specific ceiling.
Direct small/fixed-width path.
One family and ordinary memory policy.

options.name: Exact Atomic<Int> may wait
options.detail: Keep exact counters in Atomic but allow their number storage to block. Exact counters keep the same API. Atomic<Int> loses the lock-free promise.
options.technical: B explicitly amends D-PLACE1 for the entire Atomic<Int> type. Atomicity and exact arithmetic remain; progress may block even when the current value is small. Keep one canonical exact-number kernel across all execution modes, not the current inconsistent bounded interpreter. Improving or sharding locks may reduce contention but does not establish lock-free progress. Plain and fallible allocation retain D-ALLOCFAIL1 rules; this option grants no safety or execution-mode exception.

options.name: Separate exact atomic family

options.technical: C adds AtomicExact<Int> with the existing exact-counter operations and explicitly potentially blocking progress. Atomic admits only fixed-width scalar types. Both call the same canonical arithmetic kernel and preserve exact-value compare_exchange semantics. Shared<Int> remains a locked compound-value container with guards and revision operations, not an API-equivalent replacement for fetch-add and direct compare_exchange.
gains: Type names distinguish the two progress contracts.

losses.loss: Users must choose between two atomic families.

decisions.title: Portable alignment with explicit target-specific control
decisions.gist: Should portable alignment stay simple while experts can request any alignment their selected target supports?
decisions.lesson: Alignment sets the minimum byte boundary where a value may start. Portable declarations have one accepted range across supported targets. A target-specific declaration can request more, but only where the compiler can implement that exact layout. Neither form changes a requested alignment silently. Larger alignment does not by itself request huge pages, device memory, or physical placement.
decisions.explainer:
This ballot chooses which numeric values are legal in `#Layout(c, align(N))`. `c` requests C-compatible field order, and `align(N)` applies to the struct type. A target is the machine and platform selected for compilation. A shared bound gives the same source validity on every target. A target rule gives more range but can vary by target.

A menu is easy to audit but rejects values outside its list. The 1 MiB bound is a chosen policy, not an ABI fact; its cost is rejecting larger requests even when a target supports them.
decisions.story: Nora normally aligns a queue to 64 bytes. A device integration needs a 2 MiB type boundary. She wants that requirement written beside the type, without changing every ordinary layout declaration in a cross-build.
decisions.detail:
The owner asked for a portable default plus an expert version with no separate arbitrary Jet ceiling; hardware limits still apply. Both paths are explicit inside the existing layout mechanism.

Current sema imposes the 1 MiB limit. TargetMachine and TargetLayout do not yet publish the complete alignment capability required by this proposal. The plan must add and prove that fact rather than treating today's numeric constant as cross-target evidence.

The proposed portable contract is exact and voteable: positive powers from 1 through 1048576 bytes. The implementation owes that guarantee on every supported profile. A concrete contradiction cannot be averaged away, hidden behind an AOT-only label, or repaired by changing the number without another owner decision.

The expert form uses the selected profile and checked facts in sema. Source spelling alone chooses portable versus target-dependent validation. Passing --target selects a machine, not a weaker policy.

Rust documents explicit representation alignment; C++ defines fundamental and implementation-defined extended alignments; Zig imposes its own representability rules. None establishes an unavoidable 1 MiB maximum. Their allocation-layout helpers are not evidence that type alignment, page placement, and device addressing are the same operation.

options.name: Portable default, explicit target alignment
options.detail: Keep portable align(N); add align(target, N) for exact target-supported requests without a separate Jet ceiling. Beginners keep the ordinary form. Experts can express larger supported layouts. The declaration shows its portability requirement. Target-specific code may not compile on another target.
options.technical:
A keeps the ratified #Layout(c, align(N)) spelling. Its portable type-layout contract is positive powers of two from 1 through 1048576 bytes, inclusive. This is a proposed guaranteed language baseline, not a claim that current implementations were already tested across all profiles. Every supported target profile must implement that accepted range before this contract is marked delivered. If evidence contradicts the baseline, report the exact profile and return the numeric policy to the owner; do not silently narrow it.

Add only the source-local mode #Layout(c, align(target, N)). The contextual target argument opts that declaration into the selected target profile. It removes the separate 1 MiB Jet ceiling. N must still be a positive power of two. It is an exact, unclamped minimum, not a demand to weaken natural alignment. Declaration validity covers type-layout representability: effective alignment, padded size, field offsets, and array stride. Storage availability is checked separately at each use. No finite computer supports literally infinite alignment.

An explicit --target flag or package target selects the machine profile but does not change portable declarations into expert declarations. Ordinary align(2097152) therefore remains a semantic error even in a cross-build. align(target, 2097152) succeeds only when the profile supports the resulting effective type layout. This makes the loss of portability visible at the declaration rather than hidden in a build command.

The target may be native, cross-compiled, or a board profile. Target layout facts are checked compile inputs, not host guesses. Their identity participates in compiler caches and generated artifact provenance. Package composition and the CLI resolve one target fact before sema. Contradictory targets reject before code generation. Omitted target selection uses the normal native profile, but the expert marker remains written.

Sema owns all acceptance. Evaluate the literal without truncation, check positivity and powers of two, and perform checked size, padding, and address arithmetic. Read one canonical alignment-support fact; do not probe rustc to discover support. Codegen lowers the checked layout fact. A backend rejection of an admitted layout remains an internal compiler error, never the user-facing target check.

Requested alignment is a minimum for the whole type. The effective alignment is the maximum of natural field alignment and the requested boundary. It never weakens a field requirement or packs a struct. C field order and internal field padding stay unchanged; stronger whole-type alignment may add trailing padding and increase the type size. Report requested and effective alignment when they differ. Every materialized value must respect the same effective fact.

The canonical fact has separate type-representation, stack-placement, global/linker-placement, heap-allocator, and foreign-by-value-ABI support sets and size/address bounds. Bind it to target profile, backend/execution-mode set, linker/toolchain, allocator-provider digest, and fact version. Missing required facts reject in sema, never after code generation. All identities and the complete fact participate in semantic and artifact cache keys.

Declaration validity uses the intersection of type-representation support across the target profile's applicable execution modes, not whichever backend happens to run today. Portable declarations additionally satisfy the fixed 1 MiB language baseline. Expert declarations omit that extra baseline ceiling but still satisfy the profile intersection. This does not create an execution-mode exception.

Use sites check storage separately. Check array length times padded stride without overflow. Reject statically impossible stack or global placement before emission. Heap allocation requests the effective alignment through the normal allocator; an unavailable allocator or exhausted budget follows the existing allocation contract. A valid type does not promise that an instance fits in a particular board's RAM. Dynamic stack exhaustion retains the existing safe runtime behavior.

By-value foreign passing is admitted only when the selected foreign ABI and toolchain explicitly support the effective layout and calling convention. Bind that evidence to header, binding, library, target, and toolchain provenance. Otherwise sema rejects by-value crossing. Pointer or reference crossing requires a live, suitably aligned pointee and the existing ownership contract. Matching size and alignment alone never proves the calling convention.

Both forms reject zero, negative values, and non-powers. Portable excess and unsupported target requests have distinct reasons under the registered alignment diagnostic. Name the selected profile, requested value, and supported requirement when known. Never suggest clamping an ABI requirement. For a larger valid request, teach the explicit expert form; if the target cannot support it, ask for a compatible target or a correct declaration.

Use I32 slots for the C-compatible comparison, matching the Rust and C++ examples. Int is exact and its internal carrier must not be mistaken for a C int. The user-facing facts remain T.@layout.size and T.@layout.alignment. No size_of, align_of, #Align, new layout family, or per-engine numeric policy is introduced.

D-PLACE1 remains authority for layout fact names and the shared mechanism. This ballot approves the new contextual target argument and the portable range policy. Register that spelling in Syntax.rs and migrate parser, formatter, grammars, diagnostics, examples, and docs together. The new form is not claimed to parse today.

Design-away work preserves the simple portable range and removes the arbitrary expert ceiling through an explicit mode in the same rule. It rejects the tempting global --target toggle because routine cross-compilation must not silently remove a declaration's portability contract. The remaining target dependence is real: another target may lack the requested representation or resources.
gains: Beginners keep the ordinary form.
Experts can express larger supported layouts.
The declaration shows its portability requirement.

losses.loss: Target-specific code may not compile on another target.

options.name: Every request follows the selected target
options.detail: Let ordinary align(N) accept any alignment supported by the selected target. One spelling covers every supported alignment. Declarations do not distinguish portable and target-specific requirements.
options.technical: B uses the same canonical target facts, checked arithmetic, and sema rejection as A. It adds no contextual target argument. Every alignment declaration depends on the selected profile, including requests within today's common range. The language provides no source-local portable contract. This is a viable target-oriented policy, but the owner cannot identify exceptional placement requirements by reading the declaration alone. It does not allow late backend failure, implicit clamping, or host-based cross-compilation checks.
gains: One spelling covers every supported alignment.

losses.loss: Declarations do not distinguish portable and target-specific requirements.

options.name: Portable range only
options.detail: Accept portable powers through 1 MiB and provide no target-specific escape. Every declaration follows one portable range. Larger target-supported layouts remain unavailable.
options.technical: C replaces the old handpicked 13-value menu with the same explicit portable baseline as A. A separate finite list provides no benefit over the general power rule. The portable baseline still requires proof across supported profiles. C deliberately omits expert requests above it. It may suit a portability-only language but does not meet this owner's requirement for exact target-specific placement.
gains: Every declaration follows one portable range.

losses.loss: Larger target-supported layouts remain unavailable.

comparisons.note: Rust's repr alignment raises type alignment subject to representation restrictions. Layout::from_size_align also checks size and address bounds; it is not a portable-language cap.
C++ extended alignment support is implementation-defined. An unsupported request is ill-formed, not silently rounded to another ABI.

Zig can align a variable's storage and exposes target facts directly. This example does not change Ring's type layout. Its documented representability constraints still apply; explicit control is not unlimited hardware support.

recommendation.why: A removes the arbitrary expert ceiling without making ordinary declarations target-dependent. One layout rule serves both paths, with the exceptional requirement written at its declaration.
gains: No separate alignment family.
No silent loss of portability.

losses.loss: Expert declarations depend on target support.
losses.mitigation: A target cannot implement an alignment outside its address, representation, or allocation capabilities.

whyNot.reason: B makes every declaration target-dependent, even when the author wanted a portable guarantee.
C keeps rejecting larger layouts that a selected target can support.

recommendation.tradeoff: A guarantees the portable range. Expert requests go further only where the selected target can implement their exact meaning.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: AlignmentBeginner. Skill: rli5. The pass distinguished the portable and target-specific choices but found ambiguous padding and a mismatched Zig example; the revision states trailing-size growth and identifies variable alignment separately from type layout.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: OpenAI GPT. Adversarial model family: OpenAI GPT. Fresh agent: AlignmentAdversarial. The pass found ambiguity in minimum versus effective alignment, allocation availability, tier-indexed capabilities, and foreign calling conventions. The revision separates those rules, binds the complete capability identity, and requires all 21 portable powers plus physical placement wherever observable.

decisions.title: One lowering for every run mode
decisions.gist: Whether native build, fast run, interpreter, and web share one lowering.
decisions.lesson: Jet checks a program once and produces TIR, the checked tree. Today four back ends each translate TIR into something runnable: a Rust printer for release, Cranelift for the fast run, a tree-walking interpreter, and a web emitter. Each one decides what the language means again, and each has its own table of Core functions. This ballot decides whether to lower TIR once into MIR, a shared form that every back end only translates.
decisions.story: Teo tries `jet run` on a leaderboard that calls `sort_by`. The interpreter refuses it, and `jet build` dies with an internal error. He did nothing wrong; the four translations disagree. Under A the program is lowered once, so every mode gives the same answer.

options.name: One lowering; every mode reads it
options.detail:
Create MIR after TIR. Lowering resolves generic calls, layouts, closures, ownership, cleanup, checks, diagnostics, and source spans once. Every run mode reads MIR without deciding meaning again. Core declarations feed one generated table. The readers are Cranelift, the interpreter, the Rust printer, and the web emitter. Modes differ only in speed: the interpreter starts at once, Cranelift is the middle, release is fastest to run.

If the checker accepts a program, every mode runs it the same. If a target cannot run it (the web has no stdin), the checker says so once, before any mode runs. No back end can refuse a program on its own.
cost: Large migration keeps old and new paths together during cutover
options.technical:
Use E1 to declare each Core function and its semantics once. Generated rows contain only symbols and marshalling data; they cannot add defaults, validation, or errors. A row is one backend entry; a table groups rows. A missing or unequal row set fails the compiler build. During migration, one route stays authoritative; the old route runs only as a shadow until its removal gate.

Use E2 to define the finite MIR operation set and generate coverage for each operation, operand and type class, and applicable target. A MIR operation is one checked executable action. Every backend consumes every operation; wildcard and refusal arms are forbidden.

E3 stores each source program's expected result once. It runs every applicable command and target, then compares stdout, stderr, exit status, diagnostics, effects, traps, and observable cleanup. Any mismatch blocks merge. New examples enter automatically. E2 proves operation coverage; E3 proves full observable parity. E3 is generated, not hand-maintained.

E4 first reports coverage deoptimization, which means fallback because a back end lacks a construct. It then turns that fallback into a compiler-build failure. This makes the failure visible before a user program runs.

Cranelift is the dev-time compiler. `jet run` compiles MIR lazily. `jet build --profile=debug` compiles MIR eagerly for development. `jet build --release` prints MIR as Rust. rustc borrow-checks generated Rust; LLVM optimizes it. MIR keeps ownership facts per D-TIER-FORM1=A, so rustc remains the independent safety witness: its borrow-check result tests generated Rust against Jet's ownership model. Ordinary Jet ownership emits safe Rust only; generated `unsafe`, raw pointers, and erased lifetimes require an audited region. Compile-fail mutation witnesses must make rustc reject broken ownership.

Printed-Rust quality is a hard gate. Structured MIR keeps loops, blocks, typed Core calls, and cleanup explicit, so LLVM sees today's shapes. Golden Rust checks stable blocks, safe references, cleanup, calls, and no accidental state machines. Compare MIR-generated Rust with today's emitter on each corpus cell.

Keep the old printer until runtime, binary size, compile time, and target coverage meet their gates. The interpreter walks compact typed MIR blocks without per-step cloning. Each named benchmark must match today's tree-walker median, allocation count, and p95; no aggregate hides a losing cell.

Measure cold empty, cold hello, warm unchanged, and changed-source `jet run` p50 and p95. Include process start, lowering, compile, load, and first output. Store primary spans, secondary origins, and synthetic or inlined provenance on MIR locations. Snapshot diagnostics and traces for Rust, Cranelift, interpreter, and web, including generated web maps.

One finite MIR operation set is the support contract. The checker issues a closed applicability token. After it accepts a program for a route, the backend interface has no `Unsupported` result. A missing arm fails the compiler build, not the user run. Target realization is mechanical; deviations fail E2 or E3 rather than become a design loss.

An LLVM backend is a separate later choice. Self-hosting changes the compiler's implementation language, not its emitted target. A future LLVM reader need not wait for self-hosting. Keep the release Rust printer until these measured gates pass. The migration effort belongs in cost, not losses.

Canonical route matrix: current `jet build` uses native Rust, current `jet run` uses Cranelift, current `jet run --interpret` uses the TIR evaluator, and the current web target uses Web.rs. Proposed `jet run` uses lazy Cranelift, and `jet build --profile=debug` uses eager Cranelift. Proposed `jet run --interpret` uses the MIR interpreter, and `jet build --release` uses MIR -> Rust -> rustc/LLVM. The web target uses MIR -> Web.rs. Each row records command, reader, artifact, and applicability.

The differential gate is an automatically generated compiler gate, not manual upkeep. Backend realization has one MIR contract, one Core semantic declaration, and total mechanical readers. E3 remains required proof, but it is not an accepted design loss.

// Verified Jet source: examples/features/operators/spaceship.jet
leaderboard.sort_by((left: Player, right: Player) -> left.compare(right))

// Proposed architecture, not Jet source syntax

TIR --one semantic lowering--> MIR
MIR: slots, calls, control, checks, cleanup, spans
jet run -> Cranelift (lazy dev-time painter)
jet build --profile=debug -> Cranelift (eager dev-time painter)
jet run --interpret -> interpreter(MIR)
jet build --release -> MIR -> Rust -> rustc/LLVM
web -> Web.rs(MIR)

options.name: Share the two dev modes; native untouched
options.detail: Let Cranelift and the interpreter consume one shared form. Keep the native Rust emitter semantic and keep the Web.rs reader. Three semantic paths remain: shared dev, native, and web. Gain: a smaller first migration and one shared dev path. The separate native and web paths can disagree with dev.

losses.loss: Three semantic paths remain: shared dev, native, and web
losses.attempt1: Mechanical Rust printer failed as a distinct B: native reads the shared form, so B collapses into A.
losses.attempt2: Shared semantic helpers failed to remove the loss: native and dev dispatch still own separate meaning.
losses.mitigation: E1 and E2 generate Core and variant coverage. E3 blocks behavior mismatch. The separate web reader stays covered.

losses.loss: Native can still disagree with dev modes
losses.attempt1: Mechanical Rust printer failed as a distinct B: native reads the shared form, so B becomes A.
losses.attempt2: A generated native-vs-dev corpus failed to remove the possibility: it blocks mismatch after the readers disagree.
losses.mitigation: E3 compares stdout, stderr, exit status, diagnostics, effects, traps, and observable cleanup across the full route matrix. E4 makes coverage fallback visible.

options.technical:
Attempt 1 — Mechanical Rust printer. Make native read the dev form and print Rust mechanically. The two-translation loss disappears only because B becomes A; that is not a distinct B design. Attempt 2 — Shared helper library. Reuse semantic helpers from both readers. This reduces code, but both readers still own dispatch and can diverge.

For native disagreement, attempt 1 again is the mechanical printer, which collapses B into A. Attempt 2 is a generated native-vs-dev corpus. It blocks merge on different output or exit status, but it cannot stop the native reader from disagreeing before the gate rejects it. Mitigated means the mismatch remains possible but is detected before merge.

Mitigation: keep E1, E2, and E3. E1 keeps one Core semantic declaration and generated marshalling-only rows. E2 covers each MIR operation, operand/type class, and target. E3 compares stdout, stderr, exit, diagnostics, effects, traps, and cleanup across the full route matrix. E4 makes coverage fallback visible and build-failing. Web remains a separately covered reader.

options.detail: Keep native Rust, Cranelift, interpreter, and Web.rs readers. These are four semantic readers, so each semantic operation still needs four independently correct realizations. Generate Core rows and one minimal program for every TIR variant. Missing routes fail the compiler build. Gain: no semantic migration before the checks. The refusal loss is eliminated, but repeated reader meaning is only mitigated.

losses.attempt1: Generated Core and variant tables failed to remove the loss: E1 and E2 remove hand-written lists, but four readers remain.
losses.attempt2: Shared lowering helpers failed to remove the loss: each reader still chooses target behavior and can drift.
losses.mitigation: E1, E2, and E3 make missing rows and mismatches fail early. Only A removes the four readers.

options.technical:
For the four-reader loss, attempt 1 generates Core and variant tables with E1 and E2. It removes hand-written gate upkeep, but four semantic readers remain. Attempt 2 shares lowering helpers across all readers. It reduces duplicate code, but each reader still chooses target behavior and can drift. A complete shared-form reader would turn C into A.

For refused rows, attempt 1 makes every refusal fail E3 before merge. This removes the false pass, but not the refusal implementation. Attempt 2 bans wildcard matches and makes an unconsumed TIR variant fail the compiler build under E2. The old refusal-as-pass loss is eliminated. The checker issues a closed applicability token, and backend interfaces cannot return `Unsupported` after acceptance. Target limits use explicit typed boundaries. This entry stays in designAway because C originally counted a refusal as a pass.

The refusal entry is separate from the four-reader entry: E2/E3 eliminate false passes, while no gate removes the four semantic readers.

decisions.title: CI witness for Rust printed from every MIR program
decisions.gist: Should CI check every program's MIR-generated Rust with rustc before merge?
decisions.lesson: Jet's fast `jet run` uses Cranelift, and `jet run --interpret` uses the built-in interpreter. Neither calls rustc. A release build prints Rust and calls rustc, whose borrow checker gives Jet a second memory-safety witness. MIR means the one checked program form that every tier will execute. The proposed check covers every `examples/` program, every positive `tests/ui` case, and every Core row. Today's rough count is 1,621 tracked files under `examples/` and 2,476 under `tests/ui`; snapshots make that an upper bound.
decisions.story: Nora changes a Core function after the one-MIR change. `jet run` and `jet run --interpret` pass, but a bad Rust print can wait for release. She wants CI to catch that defect before it reaches the branch.

options.name: Check every printed Rust program
options.detail: CI prints Rust from each program's shared MIR and runs `rustc --emit=metadata` without linking. A failure blocks the merge. The corpus includes every `examples/` program, every positive `tests/ui` case, and every Core row. The MIR hash reuses a prior result for unchanged programs. This puts the second witness before merge. It adds CI work for up to 4,097 tracked files before cache hits; `tests/ui` also has snapshots, so this count is an upper bound.
options.technical: Current routing is explicit in `Source/CmdCompile.rs:1627-1667`: `--interpret` selects `Interpreter`, and fast `jet run` selects `Jit`. `Source/CmdCompile.rs:1796-1815` calls those adapters. Native builds write generated Rust and invoke rustc in `Source/CmdCompile.rs:8568-8628`. Ratified `D-AOT-CRANELIFT1=B` keeps Cranelift for debug AOT, while `docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:4761-4769` keeps rustc for release. `D-TIER-ONEIR1=A` makes the Rust emitter a mechanical MIR printer. The job uses `--emit=metadata`, no link, and invalidates the MIR-hash result when the rustc identity changes.

options.name: Run it nightly
options.detail: Each night, CI prints Rust from the same MIR corpus and runs `rustc --emit=metadata`. The job publishes failures but does not block merge. Pull requests avoid this extra check. The report still shows printer failures. A failure can land and remain in the branch until the nightly job runs, so the merge path has no witness.
options.technical: B uses the same check and cache as A, but its result is advisory. It catches failures only when the nightly job sees them. A changed MIR can merge first, even when its printed Rust would fail rustc. This leaves the merge path without the second witness for part of each day.
options.code:
// Proposed nightly report
corpus MIR -> generated Rust
generated Rust -> rustc --emit=metadata
publish failures; keep merge green

options.name: Trust Jet's checker
options.detail: CI does not print and check generated Rust. Jet's ownership and effect checks remain the only Jet-side check before release, and `jet build --release` still invokes rustc. This adds no merge-time work. The first Rust witness is release, so a bad MIR-to-Rust print can merge from dev CI and fail later.
options.technical: C does not change `jet run` or `--interpret`; `Source/CmdCompile.rs:1627-1667` selects `Interpreter` or `Jit`, while `Source/CmdCompile.rs:8568-8628` invokes rustc on native builds. The checker proves Jet ownership and effects, not that every MIR instruction prints valid Rust. This keeps the existing release witness but omits a pre-merge witness.

comparisons.note: Cargo documents `cargo check` as a check that skips final code generation and reuses metadata. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-check.html
comparisons.code:
$ cargo check --workspace
# check without final code generation

recommendation.why: Only A makes the Rust witness part of the merge decision while keeping the ratified release path. Its cache limits repeat work, and its corpus scope matches the programs that dev tiers execute.

whyNot.reason: B detects a broken print after merge, so an unchecked failure can stay in the branch until nightly CI.
C removes the pre-merge witness from dev CI, so release is the first check of printed Rust.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds CI work for each changed MIR hash because each generated Rust output needs a rustc check. That cost is the witness, not a separate release backend. The rough upper bound is 4,097 tracked files, since `tests/ui` also stores snapshots.

decisions.title: Which executable form should every back end consume?
decisions.gist: What single executable form should every Jet back end consume?
decisions.lesson: Jet shares its parser and checker, but four back ends read TIR differently: Rust emission, Cranelift lowering, interpretation, and web emission. D-TIER-ONEIR1 ratified exactly one semantic lowering. This ballot chooses the form produced by that lowering, not another semantic pass. TIR means Jet's typed intermediate representation. Core means the built-in library and its callable symbols. The chosen form must keep ownership, calls, control, checks, and source spans explicit. Rust and web printers must not rebuild meaning.
decisions.story: User wants one source of truth for Jet execution. D-TIER-ONEIR1 settled the number of semantic lowerings but left the concrete form open. This ballot chooses that form without reopening the ratified ruling.
decisions.inWild:
// Captured audit row D3: examples/features/operators/spaceship.jet
leaderboard.sort_by((left: Player, right: Player) -> left.compare(right))

// Observed today
jet build                  -> exit 101 (internal compiler error)
jet run                    -> E0956 "isn't supported" after two lines
jet run --interpret        -> E2201 after the same two lines

// Source-derived expected output when execution succeeds
int less: true
string less: true
Ada:10
Cal:20
Bea:30

// Prediction matrix; any refusal or mismatch fails the parity oracle
A: build, run, --interpret, and an applicable web target use one form and produce the five lines above
B: dev readers may agree, but native and dev readers can still diverge
C: every consumer must preserve the five lines while recovering Jet facts from CLIF

// Proposed, non-normative boundary
TIR -> [one chosen form] -> interpreter | Cranelift | Rust -> rustc/LLVM | Web.rs

options.name: New Jet-owned MIR
options.detail: Create a new Jet MIR after TIR. The ratified semantic lowering produces this form; this ballot does not add a second semantic lowering. It stores typed slots with stable IDs, resolved operations, explicit control blocks, logical layouts, instantiated generics, lowered closure environments, ownership facts, cleanup edges, traps, and source spans. Every back end translates that form. Gain: one target-independent meaning. Loss: another Jet-owned data model must stay complete.
options.technical:
Jet MIR is a compiler-owned data structure, not user syntax. Each slot has a stable ID, resolved type, storage and access facts, ownership state, and source span; no back end looks up a source name to recover meaning. Generic calls are instantiated, closure environments are explicit, and logical layouts are fixed before target adapters choose physical ABI or marshalling.

Calls point to typed Core symbols. Core policy, defaults, validation, and error meaning remain in Prelude and CoreLib; MIR carries the resolved operation and arguments, not a second copy of that policy. Control records branches, loops, exits, cleanup and unwind edges, bounds and overflow checks, traps, diagnostics, and source maps. Target applicability is explicit, so Web.rs can emit its Wasm Rust and JavaScript paths without pretending every operation applies everywhere.

The existing Cranelift dependency stays behind `jet-jit`; Jet MIR adds no shared external dependency. The Rust back end prints MIR mechanically and keeps release `rustc`/LLVM as both optimizer and independent safe-Rust witness. Its generated output must pass an output-equivalence and performance gate before the old emitter is removed. E1-E4 enforce one Core table, total variant coverage, differential behavior, and visible then forbidden coverage deoptimization.
options.code:
// proposed, non-normative compiler schema
parse -> check -> TIR
TIR --one semantic lowering--> JetMIR
JetMIR: slots(ids, types, access, ownership)
JetMIR: calls(Core symbols), control(blocks, loops, exits)
JetMIR -> interpreter | Cranelift | Rust printer | Web.rs
Rust printer -> rustc/LLVM

options.name: Canonicalize TIR in place
options.detail: Run a complete canonicalization pass in TIR. Give every local a stable ID, resolve calls, instantiate generics, lower closures, attach explicit checks, and make control complete. Keep TExprKind and TStmt as the shared representation. Every back end still reads those nodes. Gain: one stored form for analysis and execution. Loss: those uses remain coupled, and each new fact remains visible to every reader.
options.technical:
B is the strongest version of canonicalized TIR, not a claim that source names alone cause drift. It can carry stable slot IDs, resolved Core calls, ownership and cleanup facts, explicit checks, source spans, target applicability, and structured control. If it carries all of A's facts, it can be behaviorally complete.

The architectural difference is the boundary. `TExprKind` and `TStmt` remain the analytical and executable interface, so `Codegen/TIR/emit`, `jet-jit/src/jit/lower_ctx.rs`, `Codegen/TIR/eval`, and `Codegen/Web.rs` still match shared nodes. Each new node or annotation must be understood by those readers. E2 and E3 can constrain that design; if canonical TIR stops being source-shaped and becomes a total executable contract, it has become A's explicit boundary under another name.

B therefore has a real chance, but it keeps analysis and execution coupled and leaves less room to delete semantic readers independently. The ballot does not claim current D1-D5 failures prove a new data type is necessary; they prove that the present four readers drift.

options.name: Use Cranelift IR (CLIF)
options.detail: Use Cranelift's low-level CLIF as the only shared form. CLIF has typed SSA values, blocks, calls, and traps, so an interpreter can execute it directly. Gain: an existing code generator and block model. Loss: CLIF does not define Jet ownership, Core policy, cleanup, target applicability, or diagnostic meaning; side data would recreate a Jet-owned form.
options.technical:
The shared boundary would expose Cranelift `Function`, `Block`, `Value`, and instruction data. CLIF is a valid low-level execution form, not an empty one. Its blocks and memory operations do not define Jet ownership transfer, drop order, effects, Core defaults, cleanup and unwind rules, source diagnostics, or target applicability. Rust and web consumers would need target-specific reconstruction, or side tables that recreate A's contract.

The approved Cranelift dependencies are in `crates/jet-jit/Cargo.toml`. Exposing those types from shared compiler code has no valid layout under current I6 and crate-direction rules unless the owner approves a named dependency change. The existing JIT use remains valid. CLIF also places low-level memory and ABI choices at the shared boundary, which can weaken the independent safe-Rust witness if the Rust printer must recover ownership.

CLIF remains a useful target behind the Cranelift back end. Web.rs currently has Wasm Rust and JavaScript consumers, and both need Jet facts plus target applicability. A pure CLIF boundary is therefore a target-specific contract, not a suitable Jet-owned source for every consumer.

comparisons.note: A class file is verified at link time. HotSpot's interpreter and compiled tiers consume bytecode, then build their own internal forms.
Ignition is V8's register-based interpreter. Later tiers can build their own forms, so shared input does not mean one backend representation.
WebAssembly makes block, loop, and if structured instructions. That is a target constraint, not proof that Jet's source form must copy it.
comparisons.code:
;; https://webassembly.github.io/spec/core/syntax/instructions.html
(block $exit
  (loop $body
    local.get 0
    br_if $exit
    br $body))

comparisons.note: Rust MIR carries typed locals, places, basic blocks, and source information. Its control-flow graph is a comparison, not a requirement that Jet copy Rust's form.

recommendation.why: A gives the one semantic lowering an explicit Jet-owned contract. It carries ownership, Core calls, exits, cleanup, checks, diagnostics, and spans once; adapters choose only physical representation.

whyNot.reason: B can work only if canonical TIR becomes a total execution contract. A states that boundary directly instead of leaving it implicit in one analytical tree.
CLIF can be a Cranelift target, but it lacks Jet ownership and diagnostic contracts and needs a new shared dependency ruling.

recommendation.tradeoff: Unavoidable: a second form adds mapping, source-map, and compiler-resource work. Unavoidable: each target adapter can misread a valid form, so differential checks remain.

decisions.title: Fixed-width pairwise Float reduction: one defined order every run mode
decisions.gist: What fixed summation order should Jet define for Float reductions?
decisions.lesson: Floating-point addition rounds after each step, so grouping can change the last bits. Jet's current Float sum uses a left-to-right fold, and a 20M-element sum took 0.43 seconds versus 0.03 seconds for Int. This choice sets the order for `sum`, `fold` with `+`, and the vectorizer's accumulator.
decisions.story: Maya is reducing 20 million sensor readings for a daily report. She needs the report to match in the interpreter, fast run, and release build, but she also needs AOT to use the packed adds discussed at 19:45 in the SIMD video.

options.name: Fixed-width pairwise order
options.detail: Define one eight-way pairwise order. Each lane adds its source-order values, then a fixed tree combines the lanes. The interpreter, fast run, and AOT use that rule. Gain: AOT can use packed adds without changing the answer between modes. Loss: sums can change in their last bits from today's left-to-right fold.
options.technical:
Use K=8 independent Float accumulators. For input index i, accumulator i mod 8 reads its assigned values in source order. Combine the eight partials as (0+1), (2+3), (4+5), (6+7), then combine those results in the same fixed tree.

Initialize lane zero with `init` for `fold`; initialize all lanes with `0.0` for `sum`. Apply the same rule to `sum`, `fold` whose step is `+`, and the vectorizer accumulator on every run mode. For `para_fold` with Float addition, keep stable chunks and use this tree for each partial and final merge. Empty input returns the supplied fold seed.

Refine D-SIMD3's reduction sentence; keep automatic vectorization and `#Scalar` unchanged. Evidence: the report's Video 3 item 13 records the 19:45 autovectorization point. Item 15 records reductions outside `CheckerKernel.rs:52-320` and assigns the wider proof to #2895.

options.name: Strict left-to-right
options.detail: Keep the current left-to-right order for every Float sum and `+` fold. This preserves today's bits and is easy to explain. The loop-carried dependency blocks packed reduction. Gain: strict reproducibility. Loss: the 20M-element Float sum keeps its measured 0.43-second cost.
options.technical: Compute `(((init + x0) + x1) + ...)` in source order. Every run mode follows the same scalar fold. The current AOT emission uses this shape. It gives exact current behavior, but it cannot use independent packed accumulators for the reduction.

options.name: Unspecified grouping
options.detail: Let each implementation pick its grouping and lane width. This leaves the most freedom for local speed. It also lets rounding change between modes, so one program can print different Float bits. Gain: each backend may choose its fastest reduction. Loss: the result is not one defined Jet answer.
options.technical: Leave `sum`, Float `+` folds, and vectorizer accumulators without a language order. A backend may reassociate additions or choose another tree. C++17 `std::reduce` documents this model and warns that floating addition can be non-deterministic. C conflicts with D-DEVMODE1 and D-ONCE-TIER1.

comparisons.note: The report records the video's 19:45 autovectorization point. It says reductions are outside `CheckerKernel.rs:52-320` and assigns the wider proof to #2895.
comparisons.code:
// docs/audits/video-mine-cpp-loops-simd-build-2026-09-03.md:44-47
// crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerKernel.rs:52-320

comparisons.note: The standard permits grouping and warns that floating addition can produce a non-deterministic result.
The sequential algorithm applies the operation from the first element onward. It gives the strict order that option B keeps.
comparisons.code:
// https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/algorithm/accumulate
double total = std::accumulate(values.begin(), values.end(), 0.0);

recommendation.why: A is the only option that keeps one defined answer and lets AOT use independent packed accumulators. Its fixed tree makes the change explicit.

whyNot.reason: B preserves bits but keeps the loop-carried dependency, so the AOT reduction cannot use SIMD.
C can be fast but lets grouping change with the backend, breaking bit-for-bit output and the same-program rule.

recommendation.tradeoff: Designed away: the only remaining loss is changed last-bit rounding versus today's fold. That change is required for independent packed accumulators; keeping today's bits is option B, which gives up the speed path.

surface.gist: What fixed order should Jet define for Float reductions?
surface.lesson: Floating-point addition rounds after each step, so grouping can change the last bits. Jet now folds Float sums from left to right, which blocks safe packed addition. This choice sets one order for `sum`, `fold` with `+`, and the vectorizer's accumulator. Every run mode must return the same bits.

current.note: Today uses a left-to-right fold. A 20M-element Float sum took 0.43 seconds; the matching Int sum took 0.03 seconds.

wild.note: C++17 permits grouping and warns that floating addition can produce a non-deterministic result.

gains: AOT can use packed adds

losses: Last bits may change from today's sequential fold

options.name: Strict left-to-right
options.gist: Keep the current fold order and forbid vectorizing the reduction.
gains: Bit-exact with today's results
The order is easy to explain
losses: AOT cannot pack the reduction

options.name: Unspecified grouping

recommendation.why: A keeps one defined answer and lets AOT use independent packed accumulators. Every other mode follows the same fixed tree.

losses: Last bits may change from today's sequential fold

whyNot.reason: B preserves today's bits, but its loop-carried dependency blocks the packed reduction the video discusses.

recommendation.tradeoff: Unavoidable: A changes some last bits because its fixed tree differs from today's sequential fold. Keeping today's bits is B, which gives up packed reduction.

decisions.title: Should Jet accelerate proven kernels automatically behind a measured run-time gate?
decisions.gist: Whether release builds may add a bounded column copy and pooled threads to proven kernels, decided at run time from a measurement.
decisions.lesson: A proven kernel is a loop the checker shows to be independent across iterations. AoS is a list of records; SoA is one column per field. Today the user chooses `#Layout(columnar)` and `para_map` by hand. Probe S5 shows the release build already vectorizes the AoS loop (0.0127 s, packed `vmulpd`); the columnar list is 14x slower (bug #2889). Probe S7 shows `para_map` 2.3x slower than serial on four million cheap items (bug #2922). A fixed threshold is not enough; the decision must measure.
decisions.story: Mara writes a particle update over a list of structs. She wants the compiler to use spare cores and the hardware-friendly layout when they pay, and to do nothing when they do not. She wants the answer visible and an off switch she already knows.
decisions.detail: The two candidate transforms are a transient column copy and pooled parallel chunks. Both are optimizations inside the one MIR lowering (D-TIER-ONEIR1): output, exit status, panics, and effects stay identical on every run mode; only speed differs, and only in release builds. The question is when to apply them. The probes show that a per-target constant cannot decide: `para_map` already has one and still loses 2.3x on a bandwidth-bound kernel. A measured run-time gate can.

options.name: Both transforms, measured run-time gate, visible in `jet inspect accel`
options.detail:
The release optimizer may do two things to a proven kernel. It may copy touched columns into cache-block-sized buffers when a nested loop re-reads them. It may run the kernel's chunks on the existing bounded worker pool.

Below a static floor (1024 items) nothing happens and no clock is read. Above it, the first chunk runs serially and is timed; the kernel goes parallel only when the projected gain is at least 2x over the once-per-process measured spawn cost and memory-bandwidth floor. `#Scalar` pins scalar code and the existing `#Local` pins one thread; no new marker. `jet inspect accel` prints every decision with its numbers.
options.technical:
Behavior. Both transforms are unobservable by law. The copy is a private buffer; the parallel form is a reordering of independent iterations. A panic inside a chunk (division by zero, overflow) is collected per chunk. The lowest failing index is reported, so the message and exit match the serial run exactly. The generated cross-mode parity gate from D-TIER-ONEIR1 covers every accelerated program with the transform on and off.

Memory. The copy is per cache block (64 KiB default), not per list, so extra resident memory is a fixed constant, not N times the touched fields. A single-pass kernel never copies: probe S5 shows LLVM already vectorizes AoS, and a copy would double memory traffic. The copy applies only when a nested loop re-reads the copied columns, the O(N squared) gravity shape in #2889.

Threads. Chunks run on the bounded engine `para_map` already uses; no program gains a new thread population. The gate is measured, not constant: first chunk serial, per-item time against spawn cost and bandwidth floor, 2x margin. Card #2922 gives the explicit `para_*` family the same gate, so it is built once.

Determinism. Builds stay reproducible: the gate is generated code that runs inside the program; nothing is measured at build time. Reductions are excluded until D-FRED1 defines one order.

Visibility. `jet inspect accel` is a lens beside `layout` and `effects` (spec.md:4150). It prints one line per loop with the transform and the condition that held. When a profile exists it adds the measured numbers from the last run.
gains: Never slower than the plain loop by more than one clock read above the floor
Extra memory is a fixed block, threads come from the existing pool
Every decision and its numbers are inspectable
cost: Build the sampled gate once, shared with #2922
The `accel` lens and its golden tests
Ships behind #2889 (columnar fix) and the #2894 crossover measurement

losses.loss: A kernel just above the gate can still run a little slower on a host the sample misjudges
losses.attempt1: Static cost model with a compile-time trip count. Failed: most trip counts are dynamic, so the model covers fixed arrays only.
losses.attempt2: Run-time guard against a per-target constant, as `para_map` does today. Failed: probe S7 shows that guard letting a 2.3x loss through on a bandwidth-bound kernel.
losses.attempt3: Sampled decision: time the first chunk, compare against measured spawn cost and bandwidth floor, require 2x. Bounds the miss but cannot remove it: the rest of the data can run faster or slower than the sample.
losses.mitigation: Static floor below which nothing is measured; 2x margin; `#Local` and `#Scalar` opt-outs; `jet inspect accel` shows the numbers; the perf-budget corpus fails on regression.

options.name: Column copy only; threads stay explicit
options.detail: The optimizer may make the bounded column copy under the same reuse condition and gate. Parallel work stays `para_map` and friends, which get the measured gate from #2922 regardless.
options.technical: B keeps the second half of the owner ask manual. The checker already proves the independence that parallel chunks need, so B computes the proof and then discards it for threads.
gains: Smaller first step
Thread use stays visible in source
cost: Same gate machinery as A for the copy

losses.loss: Proven-independent loops stay single-threaded unless rewritten
losses.attempt1: A lint that suggests `para_map` when the proof holds. Failed to remove the loss: the rewrite is still manual and changes the loop into a call.
losses.attempt2: Turn the lint's suggestion on by default. Failed as a distinct B: that is A.
losses.mitigation: The lint at least names the rewrite; #2922 makes the manual rewrite never slower than serial.

options.name: Keep both choices explicit
options.detail: No automatic transform. Users pick `#Layout(columnar)` and `para_map` by hand, with #2889 and #2922 fixing their measured losses.
options.technical: C is the status quo after two bug fixes. The independence proof exists and feeds only vectorization. The 14x columnar number is a bug (#2889), not a property of C, so it is not listed as a C loss.
gains: Every transform is visible in source
No new optimizer pass

losses.attempt2: One combined marker that requests both. Failed: still manual, and a new marker for what the proof already knows.

losses.attempt1: Expose the proof result in `jet inspect` so users see which loops qualify. Failed to remove the loss: knowing is not doing.
losses.attempt2: Auto-apply for loops above a huge fixed N only. Failed as a distinct C: that is A with a bad gate.
losses.mitigation: The proof still drives vectorization, which S8 shows working.

comparisons.note: Rayon makes parallel iteration explicit with `par_iter`; the caller still owns layout and pays no compiler-created copy.
OpenMP makes threads explicit with `parallel for`; vectorization and data layout remain separate choices.

recommendation.why: A is the only option that uses the proof the checker already has for both transforms, and its measured gate is the only design the probes do not refute. Behavior is identical on every run mode by law, extra memory is a fixed block, threads are pooled, and every decision is inspectable.

whyNot.reason: B discards the independence proof for threads and leaves the second half of the owner ask manual.
C keeps two manual rewrites for facts the compiler already knows.

recommendation.tradeoff: One mitigated loss remains: a kernel just above the gate can run a little slower on a host the sample misjudges. Three attempts (static model, constant guard, sampled decision) each narrowed it; none can remove it, because no compiler knows the speed of the rest of the data before running it. Accepted cost: build the gate once with #2922, add the `accel` lens, and ship after #2889 and #2894.

decisions.title: Read until a sentinel without changing state-loop meaning
decisions.gist: Whether read-until-sentinel input uses the iterator loop with a plain break, a rerun header, or a new adapter.
decisions.lesson: Jet has two loop forms. `loop name := first, test` reads `first` once; the body changes `name`. `loop name in source` pulls one new item each turn. `io.stdin().lines()` is a source of lines. A sentinel is a value that means stop, such as a blank line. D-DO1 ratified the exit shape `if test { break }`. The interpreter and the fast runner still differ from the native build; cards #2881 and #2923 track those bugs.
decisions.story: Nia copies Python's `while (line := input()) != "":` and tries `loop line := io.readline(), line != ""`. The header ran once, so `a` prints forever. She wants one form that reads a fresh line every turn, stops at the blank line, and works the same in every run mode.

options.name: Iterator loop with a plain break
options.detail: Teach one idiom: `loop line in io.stdin().lines()` pulls one line per turn; `if line == "" { break }` stops at the sentinel. This is the D-DO1 exit shape, so there is nothing new to learn. No adapter and no closure are needed. Fix #2881 and #2923 so every run mode pulls one line per turn. Add a proposed lint for a state header whose name the body never changes when another turn is reachable.
options.technical:
The source loop is shipped grammar (`docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:442`). `.lines()` is a lazy line reader restricted to direct loop use by E2502 (`docs/spec/diagnostics.md:1390`). Card #2881 records this exact program printing `a b c` on `jet build` and `jet run`. Native pulls with `BufRead::lines` (`crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/emit/statements.rs:4350-4382`). The JIT drains stdin first (`crates/jet-jit/src/IO.rs:1127-1141`, card #2923). The interpreter returns E2201 (#2881).

Proposed lint L-STATE-UNCHANGED: warn when a state header's condition reads its name, the body never assigns it, and control can reach another turn. An unconditional `break` or `return` suppresses it. Text: `header state never changes; use loop line in io.stdin().lines() for repeated reads`. `take_while` stays available for value-position chains (`docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:1170-1178`).

options.name: Reread the header initializer
options.detail: Re-evaluate the header value before every test, not once. Then `loop line := io.readline(), line != ""` reads a fresh line each turn. But `loop i := 0, i < 3` resets `i` to 0 before each test, so a counter can never advance. Every existing two-slot state loop changes meaning with no change in spelling.
losses: A counter header resets its own state
Old state loops change meaning silently
Header side effects repeat on every test
options.technical: `docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:445-455` defines `loop i := 0, i < n` as mutable state advanced in the body. Rerunning `0` before each test makes the shipped counter form loop forever. The parser branch is `crates/jet-parser/src/Parser/Statements/control.rs:1482-1518`. Two failed repairs: rerun only effectful initializers makes meaning depend on hidden effect facts; rerun only when the body never assigns the name makes adding one assignment silently change evaluation order.

options.name: Add a proposed `until(value)` adapter
options.detail: Add a proposed Core adapter `until(value)` on any `Iter<T>` where `T` supports equality. It yields items before the first item equal to `value`, then stops. It is not a new source, so it hides no handle and inherits the iterator's end-of-input and error rules. The stop rule reads as one word. It adds a second spelling for a stop that `take_while` and `if ... { break }` already express.
losses: Three spellings for one stop rule
options.technical: Proposed: `Iter<T>.until(value: T) -> Iter<T>` for `T: Eq`, lazy, in the D-ITER1 adapter family (`docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:1170-1178`). Equivalent to `take_while((x: T) -> x != value)`. Two repairs for the overlap failed. Retiring `take_while` for equality tests breaks the ratified adapter list. Letting `take_while` accept a value adds overloading and still leaves the `break` form. Mitigation: a lint suggests `until(v)` when `take_while` tests only `!= v`. Needs the same #2881 and #2923 fixes as A.

comparisons.note: Python's official documentation shows assignment expressions in while tests when the value is needed for termination and the body. Its example reads fixed-size file blocks; `input()` returns a blank string for a blank line but raises EOFError at end of input. Source: https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.8.html#assignment-expressions
comparisons.code:
while (line := input()) != "":
    print(line)

comparisons.note: Rust's standard library documents `BufRead::lines()` as a lazy line iterator for standard input. Each item carries `Result<String>`, so read errors are explicit. The sentinel check remains explicit. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.BufRead.html#method.lines
The iterator idiom works on the native build today; the fast runner drains input first (#2923) and the interpreter refuses it (#2881).

decisions.title: Build file versions without lost locks or rewritten evidence
decisions.gist: How should Jet read older build files without losing saved facts?
decisions.lesson: Every version has a scope. In package.jet, top-level version names the package release, jet states the supported toolchain range, and format.version names the file format. Locks preserve exact dependency choices. Receipts record past runs. Only caches may be recreated without losing authoritative facts. One preservation rule governs them all.
decisions.explainer:
Two words do the work here. "Backward compatibility" means a newer Jet does something sensible with an older file. "Forward compatibility" means an older Jet does something sensible with a newer file. Direction matters more than it first appears.

A rule phrased as "if the version differs, rewrite it" lets an OLDER Jet overwrite a NEWER file with an older writer. This discards fields it never understood.

Ownership matters too. A file the user wrote by hand cannot be silently rewritten. A file that is a pure cache can always be thrown away and rebuilt. A file that is authority (the lock) or evidence (receipts, build records) can be neither rewritten nor rebuilt without losing the very thing it exists to hold. The four artifact classes in this decision are: user-authored manifest, authority, cache, and evidence.
decisions.story: Priya builds orders after upgrading Jet. Her lock still names the exact dependencies approved by her team. She wants the build to work without changing those choices. Later, an older teammate must not overwrite her newer lock or hide past receipts.
decisions.inWild:
# https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/cargo-toml-vs-cargo-lock.html
# Cargo.toml
[package]
