decisions.title: How should Jet reject a result computed from outdated shared state?
decisions.gist: How should Jet reject a result computed from outdated shared state?
decisions.lesson: A value can change while a task computes its result. Comparing only the value misses a change away and back. Jet already has shared values and transactions. Every choice needs an atomic value-and-revision check, correct ownership, and no silent retry of effects.
decisions.story: Maya starts an old search, edits the query, and receives the old result late. That result must not overwrite the current state.
decisions.detail:
This is an additive ordinary Core API choice, not new language syntax or a runtime “fact” type. D-CONC-SHARE1, D-SHARED-API1, ownership/copy law, and #Transact remain authoritative. Pool/Id retains its distinct removed-resource generation contract.

Capture value and ticket atomically. Snapshots obey existing semantic-copy eligibility; a pure projection permits copying only an eligible result from a larger value. Tickets are opaque, owner-bound, non-decodable capabilities without mutation authority. A successful replacement consumes no hidden retry and advances the committed revision. Stale returns false without mutation.

Every committed write advances revision, even equal-value writes or a change away and back. Do not wrap or recycle a live ticket’s identity. Wrong owner and exhausted generation produce typed failures. Two publications against one revision have at most one winner. Failed checks do not mutate value or revision.

A transaction publishes one revision on commit; abort restores value and revision. Transaction-local snapshots retain their local write sequence. Only snapshots of the final committed state become current; earlier intermediate snapshots remain stale, and abort invalidates transaction-local tickets. Nested rollback follows the same rule.

Reuse the shared lock and activate revision bookkeeping when snapshots are requested. Ordinary writes must not copy another value merely to maintain a stamp. All applicable modes call one semantic implementation. Negative controls cover concurrent winners, stale/ABA, wrong owner, repeated tickets, exhaustion, and transaction-local snapshots.

The new method is capture, not snapshot. Rollback.snapshot keeps its existing transaction contract and is not repurposed as a publication ticket.

options.name: Checked Shared snapshots
options.detail: Add snapshot and conditional replacement to existing Shared. Existing shared writes automatically invalidate old snapshots. Owner identity and revisions cannot be forged as ordinary data. Projection captures only the data a computation needs. An independent snapshot retains its selected data.
options.technical: Add capture() and capture(project) to Shared<T>. They return SharedSnapshot<T,U>, with an opaque owner/revision ticket and an ordinary owned semantic copy of T or projected U. Projection is pure. try_replace(snapshot, value) returns Bool !SharedRevisionError: false means stale; wrong owner and exhausted generation are typed failures. A ticket grants no mutation right. Existing Shared and transaction laws remain canonical.

options.name: Separate versioned values
options.detail: Add a distinct versioned-value API for conditional publication. The type explicitly advertises versioned publication. Existing Shared need not track revisions. Users choose between two shared-state interfaces.
options.technical: Introduce an ordinary Core Versioned<T> type with replacement-only mutation, snapshot/project, and the same owner/revision/typed-failure law. Shared retains its current interface. Composition between Versioned and Shared transactions must preserve the same atomic publication and rollback rules. No new keyword, sigil, implicit retry, or weaker ownership escape.

options.name: Explicit revision recipe
options.detail: Keep revision management in ordinary Shared transactions. No new public type or method. The protocol uses existing state and transactions. Every writer must maintain the complete revision protocol.
options.technical: Ship the complete canonical recipe and its executable controls, without new API. The full recipe captures value and revision atomically, binds owner identity, advances every committed write, rejects wrap, and composes with transaction rollback. The compact example shows only the late-publication branch. Domain authors remain responsible for applying the protocol at every writer.

comparisons.note: AtomicStampedReference reads and compares a reference and stamp atomically. The caller manages the stamp policy.

recommendation.why: Shared already owns mutation and transactions. Extending it prevents forgotten revision updates without introducing another shared-state mechanism.
gains: Existing shared writes automatically invalidate old snapshots.
Owner identity and revisions cannot be forged as ordinary data.
Projection captures only the data a computation needs.

losses.loss: An independent snapshot retains its selected data.
losses.mitigation: A delayed computation needs its observed data after the live value changes; projection avoids retaining unrelated fields.

whyNot.reason: A second state type repeats a protocol that can attach to the existing shared value.
A missed writer or owner check silently breaks the stale-result guarantee.

recommendation.tradeoff: Capture only needed fields; preserving an independent past value still requires its data.

decisions.title: Where should Jet expose reproducible comparison between two implementations?
decisions.gist: Where should Jet expose reproducible comparison between two implementations?
decisions.lesson: Running two implementations on the same cases can reveal a difference. Agreement on those cases is not a universal proof. Jet already has corpora, fixtures, and a test runner. Every choice must reject empty or inconclusive runs and preserve the declared comparison rule.
decisions.story: Maya replaces a foreign calculation with Jet. She needs reproducible cases, the first difference, and a smaller failing example before accepting the replacement.
decisions.detail:
Use D-TESTKIT1, existing test generation, D-RECORD1, and the current runner. No new language annotation, independent runner, external dependency, or generic proof claim. The API remains ordinary Core library surface under the owner’s choice.

Record case/input identity, generator seed when relevant, source/tool/target identity, relation, raw observations, first difference, and a reduced reproducer. Reduction must preserve the mismatch and declared relation. Typed failures, mutation, input consumption, ordered events, and cleanup are observed only when included in that relation.

Matched, mismatch, empty, unsupported, unavailable, timeout, cancellation, and invalid oracle are distinct outcomes. assert_equal() accepts only nonempty valid matched evidence. All-discarded inputs are empty, not matched. Both implementations must consume isolated equivalent inputs and declared environments.

Do not repeat real external effects silently. Effectful scenarios use explicit existing fixtures and reset boundaries. Numeric tolerance or allowed schedule variation requires an explicit relation and appears in the receipt. Equal sampled outputs cannot establish universal equivalence. AOT, run/dev, interpreter, and applicable web routes share the same Core behavior.

options.name: Core Testing comparison
options.detail: Add comparison to the existing Core Testing API. Ordinary tests and foreign adapters share one contract. The result retains replayable differences and explicit outcomes. Existing corpora, fixtures, and reducers remain reusable.
options.technical: Add compare(cases, reference, candidate, relation?) returning a Comparison record with assert_equal(). Default relation is existing typed equality; an explicit relation is part of recorded evidence. Reuse corpus, fixtures, reducer, and test status. Pure functions need no environment setup. Effectful comparisons require explicit isolated recorded scenarios. No implicit external-effect replay.

options.name: Test-runner comparison mode
options.detail: Expose comparison only as a project test command. Projects compare entry points without embedding an API. The existing runner owns replay and failure output. Library tests need process-entry adapters for direct function comparison.
options.technical: Add one ratified CLI mode inside jet test, not another runner. It compares declared project entry points using a case file and explicit observation contract. Preserve the same input isolation, relation, failure, and counterexample rules. Function-level users must provide runnable adapters.
options.code:
# Proposed runner-only interface for the same calculation.
jet test --compare reference.jet candidate.jet --cases cases.json
# Same outcomes, identities, and reduction contract.
# No core.testing.compare API.

options.name: Keep ordinary test loops
options.detail: Use existing corpus tools and explicit assertions only. No new command or library API. Each test states its relation directly. Authors repeat outcome, isolation, and reduction accounting.
options.technical: Keep the existing API and supply a complete canonical testing pattern using corpora, fixtures, and recorded outcomes. Every consumer must explicitly handle empty/discarded cases, unavailable sides, timeout, invalid oracle, isolation, and reduction. No pass-by-vacuity or proof language is permitted.

comparisons.note: Hypothesis supplies generated cases and reduces failures in ordinary tests.

recommendation.why: One library comparison contract serves ordinary tests, foreign replacement, and experiments while reusing the existing runner and evidence.
gains: Ordinary tests and foreign adapters share one contract.
The result retains replayable differences and explicit outcomes.
Existing corpora, fixtures, and reducers remain reusable.

whyNot.reason: It forces direct function comparisons through project-entry adapters.
Repeated accounting invites false-green empty runs and inconsistent failure replay.

decisions.title: One foreign-call contract with evidence for every guarantee
decisions.gist: Should every binding share one contract that explains which safety and effect claims the actual foreign artifact supports?
decisions.lesson: A binding translates a call between languages. Its contract says who owns each value, how long it lives, what the call may do, and how it fails. A wrapper can check callers while foreign code still breaks those promises. Proof, runtime enforcement, isolation, and trust must stay distinct.
decisions.explainer:
A binding is generated glue between languages. A facade is the callable interface that glue presents. An artifact is a compiled library or generated file. ABI means the machine-level calling and data-layout rules. Ownership decides who releases a value; lifetime decides when access is valid. Effects are operations such as file access. Isolation separates execution so foreign memory faults cannot reach protected host memory.

Native trust means relying on identified code to obey an audited promise. It is not proof. A runtime is the host machinery for executing code and managing objects. Runtime attachment prepares a foreign thread to enter that machinery. A component model is a common interface of values and resource handles shared by several languages.
decisions.story: Maya maintains a C byte-summing module in a CMake repository. Jet calls it today; C++ later calls a Jet replacement. She needs one ownership contract and honest protection claims. She cannot replace the company build system. Both options keep one canonical descriptor and both call directions; they differ in the granularity of accepted evidence.
decisions.inWild: CXX checks paired C++ and Rust declarations, but its unsafe C++ declaration still asserts implementation safety. RLBox adds isolation and requires validation of returned values. These are complementary forms of evidence. Sources: https://cxx.rs/extern-c%2B%2B.html and https://rlbox.dev/.
decisions.detail:
Preserve D-FFI-UNIFY1, D-FACT-LAW1, D-ONCE-LAW1, I1, I3, and I9. Clarify D-MEM-GUARANTEE1 using the residual foreign-pointer limit already recorded by D-HARDENED1. Claims bind to headers, source, compiler options, target, generator, loaded artifacts, and reachable native edges. Source beside a binary is not evidence that the binary implements that source. Build sandboxes are not runtime effect sandboxes. A process boundary protects memory only within its stated threat model. No dependency or execution-tier exception is approved by this choice.

The same program in both options sums three bytes and prints 60. Its C declaration is uint64_t sum_bytes(const uint8_t *bytes, size_t count). The complete supported implementation reads indices below count, retains nothing, and returns the unsigned sum. Empty input returns zero. Both options preserve that program; Option B additionally requires the rest of the module profile to pass.

Admission outcomes, PROPOSED:

**Checked proof or complete runtime enforcement**. Emit the ordinary facade for the covered operation.

**Isolation with established API equivalence**. Emit the facade with the selected isolated failure contract.

**Already vetted standard-library implementation**. Use its existing approved trust scope.

**Accepted native contract without implementation proof**. Keep the generated binding directly callable and label implementation coverage TRUSTED outside hardening. Never label that trust as proven.

**Unknown retention, validity, thread, or required authority fact**. Reject the safe projection before execution.

**Source file beside an unmatched binary**. Reject reuse of implementation evidence; matching filenames are insufficient.


The generator may keep native arity only when the remaining safety obligations already pass. It does not run an unsafe call to discover whether the contract was true.

Source-backed inspection can report: count rule proved; pointer lifetime proved; artifact matched; native placement unchanged. Binary-only inspection can report: count rule proved relative to the supplied contract; implementation retention TRUSTED; direct generated call permitted outside hardening, but not claimed as implementation-safe. A proof of translation is not a proof of the binary.

A missing-fact diagnostic says: Cannot borrow bytes for this call because the foreign implementation may retain the pointer. Supply a checked retention contract, select a valid owning transfer, or use an explicit audited native boundary. An unknown effect remains unknown foreign behavior; it never becomes pure.

Reverse direction uses the same obligation. A generated C++ sums::sum_bytes facade calls an eligible Jet export, checks native inputs before constructing Jet values, and preserves the sum. It does not make unrelated C++ host code safe. A frozen project rejects an unmatched replacement artifact before loading it.

Both choices preserve D-FFI-UNIFY1, D-FACT-LAW1, and D-ONCE-LAW1. Option B is a different evidence-admission policy on the same contract, not permission for duplicated semantic authorities.

Generated compiler-vetted bindings remain directly callable under D-FFI-UNIFY1 and D-FFI-CAP1. An asserted native contract remains visibly TRUSTED; it is not implementation proof. Raw symbols outside bindings and unsupported capability escapes still require user-written #Unsafe. Under D-MEM-GUARANTEE1 and D-HARDENED1, hardening cannot leave a dependency TRUSTED; missing required containment rejects that profile.

Preserve D-EFF4/D-EFF5 and each binder's language leaf. Every reached foreign call retains FFI.<Lang>, even when its native body is proved pure. The descriptor also includes established reachable callback and cleanup effects. Unknown native behavior remains marked as foreign and unverified; a declared row alone does not enforce native authority.

Existing guarantee labels remain the public vocabulary. A discharged static obligation is proven; a checked operation is watched; an established containment boundary is fenced. An asserted implementation obligation is TRUSTED. An operation may carry several labels for different obligations; one proven count never upgrades an unchecked native body. Unknown descriptor facts still block unsupported safe projections; an accepted explicit contract may establish a TRUSTED assumption.

decisions.title: Automatic API improvements with inspect, native shape, freeze, and refusal
decisions.gist: What evidence permits a simpler generated call, and how can a team inspect or freeze that choice?
decisions.lesson: C often passes a buffer and its length separately. A generator can supply the length, but it must know its unit, range, and meaning. A shorter call is correct only if it preserves the original operation. Tests show examples; an established adaptation rule explains why the translation preserves behavior. The same rule can lift an established resource protocol into a method; unrecognized protocols stay low-level.
decisions.explainer:
A binding is generated glue between languages. A facade is the callable interface that glue presents. An artifact is a compiled library or generated file. ABI means the machine-level calling and data-layout rules. Ownership decides who releases a value; lifetime decides when access is valid. Effects are operations such as file access. Isolation separates execution so foreign memory faults cannot reach protected host memory.

Native trust means relying on identified code to obey an audited promise. It is not proof. A runtime is the host machinery for executing code and managing objects. Runtime attachment prepares a foreign thread to enter that machinery. A component model is a common interface of values and resource handles shared by several languages.
decisions.story: Ravi imports a C function that sums bytes. He wants the length supplied automatically. A specialist needs the native argument list. Their CI must reject an unreviewed binding change. Both options keep automatic generation and the existing build system; they differ in what evidence allows shortening the call.
decisions.inWild: Swift safe C++ interop uses bounds and lifetime information to offer safer wrappers, including external annotations. Some wrapper facilities remain experimental. Such annotations describe a contract; they do not verify arbitrary C++ bodies. Source: https://www.swift.org/documentation/cxx-interop/safe-interop/.
decisions.detail:
This choice preserves D-FFI-CAP1: a borrowed buffer is exclusive for the call and cannot be retained. Raw C declarations retain D-CABI-RESULT1; only an ordinary generated Jet wrapper maps established native failures.

Inspection stays read-only. Mutating bind commands write package.jet and the existing .jet/lock system. --shape native selects one public shape. --freeze records the resolved plan. --policy frozen persists a project rule that rejects drift on ordinary builds. Changes require explicit update and review. A solver timeout cannot weaken guarantees or select another runtime.

Frozen inputs include the target and actual artifact. Initial discovery may use existing package metadata; ambiguity requires an explicit library selection.

Proposed explicit discovery: jet bind sums --header sum.h --library build/libsum.a --compile-commands build/compile_commands.json. This records a pairing, not a source-to-binary proof. The existing resolver supplies ordinary package identities. Frozen updates must be explicit and reviewable.

Evidence threshold: prove each adaptation relative to named assumptions, then require an accepted basis for those assumptions. Compiler-checked facts or complete runtime checks can discharge them. Vendor annotations can state a contract but remain trust until verified or enforced. Names, signatures, signatures on packages, and passing tests do not establish the native body. A signature on a package proves origin, not behavior.

A lying binary that retains a borrowed pointer is not stopped by count removal. Without implementation coverage or approved trust, safe borrowing is rejected. Generated compiler-vetted bindings remain directly callable under D-FFI-UNIFY1 and D-FFI-CAP1. An asserted native contract remains visibly TRUSTED; it is not implementation proof. Raw symbols outside bindings and unsupported capability escapes still require user-written #Unsafe. Under D-MEM-GUARANTEE1 and D-HARDENED1, hardening cannot leave a dependency TRUSTED; missing required containment rejects that profile.

Exact update lifecycle, all commands PROPOSED:

```sh
jet inspect bind sums --explain
jet bind sums --shape native
jet bind sums --freeze
jet bind --policy frozen
jet bind sums --update --preview
jet bind sums --update --accept <candidate-digest>
```

Preview prints a semantic diff and candidate digest, using the existing generated cache without changing project files. Accept rechecks unchanged inputs and atomically publishes the matching package.jet configuration and .jet/lock plan. Failure leaves the prior pair valid. Exit 0 means success, 1 means contract rejection or frozen drift, and 101 remains an internal compiler error.

The diff names API shape, count units, ownership, failure mapping, copies, placement, effects, cleanup, and artifact evidence. Frozen drift says: sums changed after its plan was frozen; the old bounds claim no longer applies; run jet bind sums --update --preview. No build implicitly accepts that candidate.

**Empty sum buffer**. Pass count zero; return zero, without a dereference.

**Sum buffer length exceeds native size_t**. Reject before entering C; no truncation.

**Integer might count bytes or elements**. Reject count removal; retain a safe native shape only if all safety obligations still pass.

**Native shape explicitly passes count 2 for a three-byte buffer**. Read the valid prefix and return 30.

**Explicit count exceeds the permitted view**. Reject before the call.

**Artifact changes under frozen policy**. Exit 1 without executing or rewriting the plan.


For the prefix example, the expert writes sums.sum_bytes(&bytes, 2) after selecting native shape. The default sums.sum_bytes(&bytes) means the entire supplied view, never an inferred shorter request.

Error mapping is automatic only when success states, failure states, initialized outputs, native error payloads, partial mutation, and cleanup order are established. The zlib wrapper preserves short successful reads and the distinct native error. Native shape retains original status/out parameters. A destructor cannot swallow a fallible close result. Raw C declarations still obey D-CABI-RESULT1.

The sum facade returns U64, not an extra fallible wrapper. A statically known count violation is a compile-time Jet diagnostic. A dynamic width or extent violation follows Jet's existing checked-boundary panic policy before entering C. It is a caller-contract violation, not a native library error. Production must register its diagnostic and snapshot. Valid calls preserve the U64 result; established native failures use their separately declared fallible mapping.

Protocol lifting is included in this choice. A supported operation sequence may generate an owning constructor or method when ordering, status, partial work, output initialization, and cleanup are established. An external PNG binding package may propose png.Image.open(path, format: .RGBA). This is a generated operation, not a libpng symbol. Unrecognized protocols remain lower-level operations; names and AI guesses cannot establish them.

The generated PNG operation preserves decoder initialization, explicit RGBA selection, output allocation, decode completion, native failure details, and decoder cleanup on every specified path. It returns an owning image or the corresponding typed failure. It does not silently change formats or replace libpng's algorithm. Source/body evidence remains separate from proof of the protocol translation.

The four-arrangement UX adds these proposed binding inputs: jet bind frames --source native/frame --language cpp --std c++20, and jet bind png --package c@nixpkgs:libpng. The first lets Jet build selected owned source. The second uses the existing resolver and lock without requiring source ownership. Both record the same canonical contract and inspectable plan. No implicit build takeover occurs.

Preserve D-EFF4/D-EFF5 and each binder's language leaf. Every reached foreign call retains FFI.<Lang>, even when its native body is proved pure. The descriptor also includes established reachable callback and cleanup effects. Unknown native behavior remains marked as foreign and unverified; a declared row alone does not enforce native authority.

The following package.jet fields are PROPOSED public configuration under this ballot. They extend the existing package model and D-TEAMPOLICY1; no second plan store is introduced.

```jet
bindings: .{
    sums: .{ shape: .Native, frozen: true }
}
policy: .{ bindings: .Frozen }
```

The shape field is .Automatic by default; .Native requests native arity. A binding defaults to frozen: false. The project binding policy is .Automatic by default; .Frozen requires recorded plans for every reached binding. Omitted fields use those defaults. These fields merge into the existing package records rather than replacing other policy entries.

The --shape native command writes bindings.sums.shape; --freeze writes bindings.sums.frozen and the resolved .jet/lock plan. The --policy frozen command writes policy.bindings. Manual edits and commands are equivalent and use the same validator. The lock contains resolved evidence, not another user policy.

This explicitly extends D-PACKAGE-POLICY-SCOPE1: binding-plan controls are package/artifact facts, with no lexical #Policy mirror. Single-file use keeps the same lock and needs no manifest:

```sh
jet bind script.jet --freeze
jet run script.jet --bind-policy frozen
```

Here bind records that script's reached plans in .jet/lock without creating package.jet. The run flag is invocation-only; missing plans or drift fail before execution. Project and single-file forms use the same plan and refusal law.

The png.Image.open spelling is an illustrative generated package API, not a universal reserved name. This ballot approves the established-protocol lifting rule and its guarantees, not one global image API.

decisions.title: Native host facades from one Jet export contract
decisions.gist: Should generated host APIs preserve native language types through adapters, or use one component-shaped interface everywhere?
decisions.lesson: When C++ or Python calls Jet, Jet is the guest. The host still owns its build and runtime. A generated facade translates Jet exports into familiar host types. One shared contract can drive several native facades, or every host can use a narrower common component type model.
decisions.explainer:
A binding is generated glue between languages. A facade is the callable interface that glue presents. An artifact is a compiled library or generated file. ABI means the machine-level calling and data-layout rules. Ownership decides who releases a value; lifetime decides when access is valid. Effects are operations such as file access. Isolation separates execution so foreign memory faults cannot reach protected host memory.

Native trust means relying on identified code to obey an audited promise. It is not proof. A runtime is the host machinery for executing code and managing objects. Runtime attachment prepares a foreign thread to enter that machinery. A component model is a common interface of values and resource handles shared by several languages.
decisions.story: Maya replaces a C++ document module with Jet. Native callers own bytes, keep a checked view, replace storage, detect expiration, and close. Both choices preserve those observations; they differ in native facades versus a universal component-shaped interface.
decisions.inWild: CXX preserves selected native C++ and Rust types through generated glue. WIT defines a common component interface with owned and borrowed resources. The choice concerns which model is universal, not whether components can be supported. Sources: https://cxx.rs/ and https://component-model.bytecodealliance.org/design/wit.html.
decisions.detail:
Extend D-ADOPT-GUEST1 and D-LIB-EXPORT1 without reviving retired #Extern syntax. Preserve D-FFI-CPP1, D-FFI-PY1, D-FFI-JS1, and D-FFI-GO1 runtime defaults. Rust native ABI is not assumed stable; use selected monomorphized bridge operations. Python and Node packages must root objects and preserve error distinctions. Go follows cgo pointer rules. Add real Zig discovery, target handling, packaging, and conformance. Existing #1345, #1347, and #1348 retain packaging, host-build, and mixed-repo DX ownership. A safe Jet guest does not make arbitrary in-process host code memory-safe. Browser or embedded restrictions need explicit applicability decisions.

An eligible export has a lossless mapping for the selected host, or an explicitly selected representation change. If one requested projection lacks a mapping, generation reports that projection and symbol as unsupported. A build requiring all selected outputs fails atomically. It never silently copies an identity-bearing value or publishes a partial valid-looking package.

The richer fixture owns bytes, lends a view, replaces its storage, reports expired views, and closes. Both alternatives assert the same observations: 20, an expired-view error, and 50; they print nothing. Opening or replacing can return AllocationFailure; indexed access can return BoundsFailure or ExpiredView. Close succeeds once and invalidates every view. Reusing a consumed owner is rejected or checked by the host facade.

Option A, proposed C++ facade:

The complete code appears in the corresponding option above.

Option B, proposed component-shaped resource API:

The complete code appears in the corresponding option above.

Both use an owner and invalidation identity. Option B represents the view as a resource operation protocol, not an untracked list snapshot. A component projection may preserve lifetime through handles; it is not inherently incapable of safe views. Option A can additionally integrate compatible native views directly. Neither choice earns a zero-copy claim without checking its actual bridge.

**C**. rules.h plus static/shared library. Selected C ABI; Make, CMake, or existing linker. int64_t and explicit tagged result records.

**C++**. rules.hpp plus selected shim. C-compatible shim; existing CMake/compiler. int64_t, RAII resources, checked result.

**Rust**. game_rules crate. Selected C-compatible operations; Cargo build script. i64, owned/borrowed wrappers, Result.

**Zig**. rules.zig module. Selected C ABI; existing build.zig. i64, checked resource operations, error union.

**Go**. rules Go package. cgo and permitted handles; go build. int64, values plus error.

**Python**. game_rules package, extension, and stubs. Supported CPython interface; existing wheel/build backend. Checked Python int and mapped exception classes.

**Node**. game-rules package, addon, and declarations. Node-API; existing package scripts. bigint for the I64 smoke and a lossless exact-Int facade, typed errors or explicit Promise outcomes.


These artifact names and host APIs are proposed public projections. CMake still invokes the canonical Jet build path through jet_library. Cargo's build.rs invokes that same path and declares generated output dependencies. Python's existing build backend packages the generated extension. Node scripts build the addon. Go and Zig host builds consume their generated modules and selected library. Jet does not take over those build graphs.

The CMake baseline uses three build declarations:

```cmake
find_package(Jet REQUIRED)
jet_library(rules ENTRY library.jet OUTPUT core LIBRARY rules LOADABLE)
target_link_libraries(game PRIVATE rules)
```

 The host owns its runtime, scheduler, test runner, and release. Runtime failures map through the selected facade; an unrelated native host memory fault is outside an in-process Jet guest guarantee.

The same contract supports four project arrangements. Jet applications may use owned foreign source or external packages. Foreign projects may host a Jet guest or select Jet's compiler or build driver. Build ownership is independent of whether native facades or component-shaped facades are selected.

The compiler route uses the existing jet-cc and jet-c++ driver concept with the host build unchanged. Stronger source checks and evidence are proposed additions. The driver uses the relevant native front end; it does not claim to reinterpret arbitrary C++ as Jet.

Full build import is a separate owner choice, D-FFI-BUILD1 on #2961. This ballot does not approve its commands or graph-ownership policy.


The scalar smoke export is PROPOSED #Export(c) pub fn on_tick(dt: I64) I64 -> dt + 1, with input 41 and output 42. C and C++ use int64_t; Rust and Zig use i64; Go uses int64. Python int and Node bigint are checked against I64 before entry. I64 overflow follows Jet's existing checked arithmetic and native-boundary panic policy; it never wraps or unwinds through an incompatible ABI.

Exact Jet Int is not I64. A general Int export needs a lossless owning BigInt/JetInt facade or is rejected for that projection. An explicitly selected fixed-width narrowing adapter must return a tagged/fallible result for input or result overflow. A plain fixed-width return cannot silently truncate an exact Int.

decisions.title: Captured and asynchronous callbacks with explicit registration lifetimes
decisions.gist: How should generated bindings support callbacks that retain state beyond a single native call?
decisions.lesson: A callback lets foreign code call Jet later. A closure also carries captured values. Those values must remain alive until every callback finishes. Cancellation and unregistration need a contract: stopping future callbacks does not automatically stop one already running or undo its effects.
decisions.explainer:
A binding is generated glue between languages. A facade is the callable interface that glue presents. An artifact is a compiled library or generated file. ABI means the machine-level calling and data-layout rules. Ownership decides who releases a value; lifetime decides when access is valid. Effects are operations such as file access. Isolation separates execution so foreign memory faults cannot reach protected host memory.

Native trust means relying on identified code to obey an audited promise. It is not proof. A runtime is the host machinery for executing code and managing objects. Runtime attachment prepares a foreign thread to enter that machinery. A component model is a common interface of values and resource handles shared by several languages.
decisions.story: Sam subscribes to a native byte source and prints a prefix with every event. The source retains the callback. Sam then unsubscribes and releases the captured state. The program must print each accepted event once and never call released state. The existing pure, capture-free C callback rule cannot express this directly.
decisions.inWild: Rust FFI guidance distinguishes synchronous callbacks from asynchronous ones and requires preventing calls after the target is destroyed. The generator must enforce that lifecycle, including foreign threads. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/nomicon/ffi.html.
decisions.detail:
Explicitly amend D-CABI-CALLBACK1. Pure capture-free callbacks remain the current approved subset until acceptance. Generated event, registration, and completion APIs reuse Jet ownership, effects, and tasks. No new TaskFailure variant is introduced. No new language keyword or dependency is approved.

The fixture is a byte source that can acknowledge deregistration and support producer backpressure. In Option A, emit_async completes after its one accepted callback finishes. In Option B, emit enqueues a value or returns QueueFull. Both examples print byte: 7 and then stopped. Queue projection is rejected for a native source that cannot support its declared policy.

**Active**. Call admission atomically checks this state and acquires an in-flight reference before invoking user code.

**Stopping**. No new user invocation is admitted. Previously accepted calls may finish with captures retained.

**event.stop()**. Requests Stopping without waiting; valid only within the borrowed event's invocation.

**unsubscribe(^sub)**. Consumes the owner, requests stop, and returns a task. An earlier event stop does not invalidate this final owner action.

**Stop completion**. Native acknowledgment prevents future trampoline entries and no accepted invocation remains active. Release captures and trampoline storage only then.

**Stop failure**. Report the failure and retain state needed to prevent invalid access. Do not pretend release succeeded.

**Self-dependent join**. The borrowed event exposes only nonblocking stop; it cannot reach the owning registration or its completion tasks. Sema rejects capturing or publishing those handles into that callback's reachable state. Ordinary unrelated task cycles retain existing task law.


Self-stop is shown in Option A: event.stop requests cancellation from inside its own callback. The owning subscription remains outside and is consumed exactly once by unsubscribe. No owning handle is lost on a self-stop error, because requesting stop does not consume that handle.

An accepted call has acquired its in-flight reference while Active. Draining means waiting until all such calls finish. Native deregistration acknowledgment is separate: the foreign source must promise no future trampoline entry before its storage can be freed. A wrapper cannot infer that promise from a stop function's name.

**Stop wins before admission**. No user callback runs; the emission reports Stopped.

**Admission wins before stop**. The callback may run once; its completed effects remain.

**Callback requests stop**. It returns normally; shutdown completes after that invocation exits.

**Native thread enters**. Vetted runtime attachment precedes user code; incompatible thread-affine captures are rejected.

**Native source permits concurrent calls**. Captures must satisfy Jet's concurrent access law; otherwise reject that registration.

**Callback returns a supported failure**. For a source with an established failure channel, stop admission and surface that failure through completion.

**Panic or incompatible unwind**. Never unwind across an incompatible boundary; use only the approved panic policy, not an invented recoverable exception.

**Native source cannot acknowledge stop**. Reject the safe registration contract, unless the selected protected runtime provides another established lifetime boundary.


If an accepted implementation violates its shutdown contract at runtime, report an enforcement or boundary failure according to that implementation's protection. A wrapper-only audited path cannot claim to repair arbitrary stale native calls. Returning a task does not manufacture protection.

Option B's second emit before a read returns QueueFull and preserves the first event. Reading frees capacity. Stop rejects later emissions, waits for native acknowledgment, and permits already accepted events to drain before end-of-stream. Cancellation never rolls back an event already processed. A universal queue cannot preserve synchronous return-valued callbacks; those retain a compatible explicit native contract.

Unacknowledged shutdown is not a routine successful close. The native protocol must define acknowledgment for a safe registration. If an accepted implementation violates that promise, the runtime quarantines that module: it rejects new registrations and calls, and retains only already-live wrapper state needed to prevent stale access. The consumed owner belongs to that quarantine; it is not silently freed or lost.

The stop task reports a boundary failure naming the quarantined module and retained resources. Quarantine cannot grow through new accepted registrations. Recovery is an explicit restart of the isolated worker, or termination/restart of the in-process host. No automatic restart, retry, or rollback occurs. Retrying deregistration is exposed only for a contract that establishes idempotence. An application that needs recoverable shutdown must select a boundary that can provide it.

A correlated callback failure is recorded once and appears in its emission task and the stop task after safe drain. For an external notification without an emission task, the registration records the failure and the stop task reports it. Existing unrecoverable panic policy remains separate. Neither task claims to undo effects already performed.

Preserve D-EFF4/D-EFF5 and each binder's language leaf. Every reached foreign call retains FFI.<Lang>, even when its native body is proved pure. The descriptor also includes established reachable callback and cleanup effects. Unknown native behavior remains marked as foreign and unverified; a declared row alone does not enforce native authority.

Registration is charged the retained callback's effects. For this C byte source, registration includes FFI.C and IO.Write. D-AUTHORITY-SCOPE1 and D-SCAP1 remain unchanged: Authority handles are lexical and cannot be stored, captured, or transferred into the registration.

An existing authority-holding scope must cover registration, every callback, cleanup, and stop completion. Sema rejects registration escape and requires owner consumption and drain before that scope exits. An existing application or process scope qualifies when it outlives the registration. Foreign notifications use the registration's checked effect set within that live scope, never the emitter's ambient authority. Emit and stop retain their reachable effects.

A wait deadline or quarantine does not permit that authority scope to exit while callbacks remain live. Scope completion still requires quiescence. A terminable isolated boundary can establish quiescence; otherwise forced shutdown requires host termination. No owned Authority transfer or new capability surface is proposed.

An admitted callback may never return. Default stop completion then remains pending and captures stay retained. A configured wait deadline may produce the existing TaskFailure.DeadlineBlown without freeing live state. No in-process timeout can safely reclaim executing captures. Bounded shutdown requires an explicitly selected terminable isolation boundary, or host termination.

Completion tasks return ordinary operation results. Their join keeps only the existing TaskFailure variants: Cancelled, DeadlineBlown, and Panicked. Stopped and native boundary failures belong to the operation result inside the task, not new TaskFailure variants. Both rails must be handled. No completion task or owning registration may become reachable from its own retained callback.

options.name: Managed registration with explicit completion
options.detail: Generate an owning registration and a borrowed event for each invocation. The event can request stop without waiting on itself. Unsubscribe consumes the registration and returns a task that completes after native shutdown acknowledgment and all accepted calls finish. Captures remain alive until then. Validate thread, reentrancy, effect, and failure obligations before exposing this facade.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; output byte: 7, then stopped.
prefix :: "byte"
sub :: source.on_data(event -> {
    print("{prefix}: {event.value}")
    event.stop()
})
emitted :: source.emit_async(7)
(emitted.join() ?? panic("task failed")) ?? panic("emission failed")
stopped :: source.unsubscribe(^sub)
(stopped.join() ?? panic("task failed")) ?? panic("unsubscribe failed")
print("stopped")
gains: Natural captured callbacks with checked lifetime ownership.
Native scheduling and synchronous behavior remain expressible.
Effects include callbacks and cleanup.
losses: Safe release can wait for a callback already running.

options.name: Owned messages for retained notifications
options.detail: Generate owned queued notifications for sources with an established backpressure contract. This fixture has capacity one, FIFO order, and an explicit full-queue error. It never blocks the synchronous producer or silently drops events. Stop closes admission and acknowledges native shutdown; accepted events remain drainable. Delivery placement changes, so this is an explicit API choice.
options.code:
// ALTERNATIVE queue fixture; output byte: 7, then stopped.
prefix :: "byte"
events :: source.notifications(capacity: 1)
source.emit(7) ?? panic("queue full")
value :: events.next() ?? panic("source closed")
print("{prefix}: {value}")
stopped :: source.stop(^events)
stopped.join() ?? panic("stop failed")
print("stopped")
gains: User callback state stays inside the Jet consumer.
losses: Queued delivery cannot preserve every synchronous callback contract.
Buffering needs an explicit overflow and shutdown policy.

comparisons.note: Native registration makes retained context and its stop operation explicit. The implementation must define whether stop drains active calls.

recommendation.why: Managed registration preserves native callback behavior where the lifecycle can be established. Message APIs remain explicit alternatives for suitable notification sources.
gains: Natural captured callbacks with checked lifetime ownership.
Native scheduling and synchronous behavior remain expressible.
Effects include callbacks and cleanup.

losses.loss: A callback that never returns can prevent safe in-process release indefinitely.
losses.mitigation: Live captures cannot be freed safely; a deadline does not stop native execution. Bounded reclamation needs a terminable isolation boundary or host termination.

whyNot.reason: The bounded queue is useful for suitable notification sources, but changes delivery placement and timing. It cannot cover synchronous return-valued callbacks.

recommendation.tradeoff: Safe release waits for admitted callbacks, potentially forever. A bounded shutdown requirement needs explicit isolation with termination or termination of the host.

decisions.title: Explicit activation of an imported build plan
decisions.gist: How should a project activate an imported build plan?
decisions.lesson: Jet already permits optional build import. This choice defines how a reviewed plan becomes active: through an explicit accept command or declarative package intent used by the next build. Both preserve existing host builds.
decisions.explainer:
A binding is generated glue between languages. A facade is the callable interface that glue presents. An artifact is a compiled library or generated file. ABI means the machine-level calling and data-layout rules. Ownership decides who releases a value; lifetime decides when access is valid. Effects are operations such as file access. Isolation separates execution so foreign memory faults cannot reach protected host memory.

Native trust means relying on identified code to obey an audited promise. It is not proof. A runtime is the host machinery for executing code and managing objects. Runtime attachment prepares a foreign thread to enter that machinery. A component model is a common interface of values and resource handles shared by several languages.
decisions.story: Maya has a CMake game with C++ and Jet modules. Optional graph import is already approved. She needs to inspect the proposed actions and choose exactly when Jet starts executing them. Both options rebuild the same game from the same verified plan.
decisions.inWild: CMake owns target and custom-command execution today. Its File API exposes structured project information but does not prove arbitrary custom scripts have declared every input. Source: https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/manual/cmake-file-api.7.html
decisions.detail:
Both choices preserve D-BUILDLEGACY1=A, which already approves optional graph import and lets CI ban it. This ballot chooses only the public activation surface and exact acceptance behavior. It reuses existing graph and compiler-driver mechanisms, including #1044 and #1347. Binding generation and native facades work under either choice.

Preview reads the configured CMake build and emits a candidate in Jet's existing generated cache. It shows dependencies, commands, toolchain identities, inputs, outputs, environment, working directories, custom actions, and unsupported edges. Exit 0 means a reviewable candidate was produced, not that ownership changed. Incomplete plans must say partial ownership.

Accept rechecks all candidate inputs against the supplied digest and atomically selects the plan through the existing package and .jet/lock configuration. A stale digest or changed input returns exit 1 and preserves the previous selection. Internal failures retain exit 101. Existing package configuration and its build artifact model remain the one home; this ballot does not invent a new manifest schema.

Jet may execute a fully modeled action graph. An opaque native build may remain an explicit action with declared inputs and outputs; its inner build owner remains visible. Full ownership is rejected if required actions cannot be established. No traced build run is treated as proof of an arbitrary script. Ambient environment, dynamic dependencies, generated tools, and cross-compilation belong to the model.

Both options must rebuild the same game after a header change and preserve generated-source ordering, link inputs, debug information, errors, and relevant artifact behavior. Timestamps and compiler identity are part of required observations when the project depends on them. A plan cannot claim equality from matching one executable's stdout. Cache correctness requires complete inputs and correct invalidation.

Without explicit command acceptance in A or explicit package intent in B, default behavior never imports or activates a build. The expert can inspect the full action plan and decline it. Failure does not rewrite the host build files. Selecting another compiler is explicit and requires its own supported contract. Accepted partial ownership is not advertised as full build replacement. Existing source and build files remain authoritative; repeated import compares the new candidate against the selected plan.

The native-driver path remains available in both options. A manifest-free compiler invocation does not acquire a package build owner. No automatic restart, network access, dependency upgrade, or publication is implied by build import.

Option B proposes the exact package.jet field build: .{ import: "cmake:build", plan: "<plan-digest>" }. The preview command produces the digest without changing project files. A reviewed edit to those fields expresses activation intent; the next ordinary build checks the same source, toolchain, action closure, and policy before activation.

B does not interpret an arbitrary digest as proof. The referenced checked candidate must exist and match its inputs. Failed validation preserves the previous resolved plan, reports the invalid intent, and blocks that build. Successful validation atomically publishes the resolved lock entry. A CI policy banning imports rejects either activation form.

Both choices are explicit. B combines activation with an ordinary build after a configuration edit; A keeps activation as a separate command. B retains native-driver use and full graph import. Neither option removes an already-approved build capability.

options.name: Activate through explicit preview and accept
options.detail: Preserve optional graph import and existing host builds. Review a candidate, then use a named accept command to activate its exact digest. Ordinary builds never activate new import intent.
options.code:
# PROPOSED; imports the existing CMake game build.
jet build --import cmake:build --preview
jet build --import cmake:build --accept <plan-digest>
jet build
# Existing CMake build remains available until explicit acceptance.

options.name: Activate through declarative package intent
options.detail: Keep graph import. Store the selected source and candidate digest in package.jet; the next ordinary build validates and activates that intent. Stale or incomplete intent blocks activation.
options.code:
# PROPOSED: obtain the same read-only candidate.
jet build --import cmake:build --preview
# Then edit package.jet:
# build: .{ import: "cmake:build", plan: "<plan-digest>" }
jet build
# The build checks the digest before activating the declared plan.

comparisons.note: Native target execution and structured File API metadata; the API is not a full script proof.
comparisons.code:
# https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/manual/cmake-file-api.7.html
cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build

recommendation.why: A separate accept action makes the ownership transition explicit for humans and CI, with exact input checks before activation.
gains: Existing host builds and optional import remain supported.
Activation is separate from ordinary builds.
One checked accept action pins the reviewed plan.

losses.loss: Some opaque build actions cannot be imported completely.
losses.mitigation: An arbitrary script can read undeclared inputs; observing one run cannot establish its whole behavior.

whyNot.reason: Declarative activation makes an ordinary build also perform an ownership transition. A separates that transition into one named, checked action.

recommendation.tradeoff: Incomplete action models stay explicit foreign actions or block complete import; Jet cannot silently infer missing behavior.

decisions.title: Derive endpoint contracts from typed handlers
decisions.gist: Should one typed handler define its request, response, schema, and generated client?
decisions.lesson: An endpoint exposes a function through HTTP. Jet already has typed functions, validation, and web routing. This choice decides whether their shared contract generates the request binding and client, or users maintain separate descriptions.
decisions.story: Sam exposes an order lookup. The path contains a positive order number. A browser client must send the right request and understand the response.
decisions.detail:
All proposed examples and acceptance clauses describe future behavior, not current implementation evidence.

Extend D-SHAPE-ONE1, D-SHAPE-PROJECT1, and D-WEBAPP-SERVE1. Do not create another app graph or server. Generated clients consume the checked descriptor, not documentation text. A descriptor mismatch rejects before unsafe decoding. Every in-repo manual description replaced by the new owner is removed in one cutover.

A path field is a named segment of the URL. A query field follows the question mark. A body is the separate request payload.

Worked contract, proposed: GET /orders/42 binds id=42. GetOrder requires id>=1. An Order response exposes only its declared public fields. Missing id or id=0 fails validation before lookup_order runs. The application maps a missing order to 404 and chooses authorization explicitly.

Renaming id to order_id without changing the route rejects the descriptor. The checked descriptor fingerprints request, response, and declared error mapping. Generated clients carry that identity; a mismatch requires regeneration. Adding an optional query field changes one checked input shape, not handwritten decoder and client copies.

Acceptance:
- A real generated client calls a real server with the same typed request, result, validation, and declared error mapping.
- Wrong path-field names and ambiguous binding reject as registered Jet diagnostics; invalid requests never enter the handler.
- Secret/private fields stay private; authorization and business-error status mapping remain explicit and inspectable.
- All applicable server/client targets consume the same semantic codecs; replaced metadata, examples, and callers migrate without aliases.

options.name: Generate from the handler
options.detail: Derive binding and client types from the handler, with explicit transport and policy mappings. One checked request and response contract. Renames invalidate generated clients. Transport policy still needs explicit choices.
options.code:
// Proposed; lookup_order has checked GetOrder input.
endpoint :: web.get("/orders/{id}", lookup_order)
order :: order_api.lookup_order(GetOrder{id: 42})
    ?? panic("lookup failed")
options.technical: Path placeholders match input fields. GET remainder binds query fields. Body models are explicit. Duplicate field sources reject. Validation uses the existing field-error contract. Publication is explicit. Private fields never become public automatically.

options.name: Maintain separate descriptions
options.detail: Keep manual HTTP binding, schema, and client definitions, then check their agreement. Independent transport presentation. Repeated descriptions remain.
options.technical: The ordinary function remains typed. Separate schema/client generation must still reject drift. No existing web serving or shape guarantee is removed.

options.name: Generate from a separate protocol
options.detail: Make a typed protocol the owner and bind the handler to it. Protocol can be authored before implementation. A separate protocol declaration remains.
options.code:
// Proposed protocol-first alternative:

decisions.title: One typed query with ordinary list results
decisions.gist: Should data calculations share one typed query and return ordinary lists?
decisions.lesson: A query describes a calculation before it runs. Jet currently exposes separate table, series, lazy, and stream APIs. This choice simplifies materialized results while preserving one-shot sources and the existing eager behavior of ordinary lists.
decisions.story: Mina groups ticket durations by team. Later she reads another source without rewriting the calculation or losing the key and amount types.
decisions.inWild:
# https://docs.pola.rs/user-guide/concepts/lazy-api/
q = tickets.lazy().group_by("team").agg(pl.col("minutes").mean())
groups = q.collect()
decisions.detail:
All proposed examples and acceptance clauses describe future behavior, not current implementation evidence.

Explicitly amend the public data-container design under D-DATA-SURFACE1, D-DATAFLOW1, and D-DATA-PLOT1. Keep D-SQL-SURFACE1 and D-CORE-EAGER1/2. Stable order, validation, failure order, effects, units, and numerical rules constrain optimization. A dropped column cannot hide a required source-validation error. Migrate plot adapters and every in-repo consumer; no legacy wrappers remain.

A list is already computed. Query<T> means a deferred calculation producing values of type T. collect runs it and returns a list. A stream supplies input once and can fail while reading.

Worked contract, proposed: two Core tickets of 4.0 and 8.0 minutes produce Group{key: Core, value: 6.0} for mean. The operation determines the result type; an integer sum does not become Float. Group order follows the specified first-key order unless explicitly sorted.

List input may be queried again. A consumed one-shot reader cannot reopen itself. To read again, the user opens a new reader. Opening and decoding failures remain visible even when an optimizer could omit a column. File and SQL equivalence is an acceptance target, not a reported run.

The amendment also covers affected D-DATA-STATUS1 projections and bridge/status wording. Until ratification, existing data wrappers remain law.

Exact worked sum: Region.North amounts 9007199254740993 and 2 yield Group<Region,Int> with value 9007199254740995. The key stays Region, not String. Supported unit-valued sums retain their unit; no implicit Float promotion is permitted.

Acceptance:
- The same typed query runs over lists, file sources, and checked SQL with matching values, types, errors, and specified ordering.
- Nominal keys and exact integer/unit sums do not become String or Float merely to satisfy aggregation.
- One-shot readers cannot silently reopen or be collected twice; memory/spill limits remain observable.
- Table/Series/LazyFrame and fixed DataGroup replacements cut over through callers, plots, examples, generated declarations, and all applicable modes.

decisions.title: Maintain eligible typed queries from source changes
decisions.gist: Should a watched query update its answer from edits without a second handwritten algorithm?
decisions.lesson: A changing table receives insertions, replacements, and removals. A watched query keeps an answer current. Jet already has reactive values and live-query lifecycles. This choice adds checked incremental calculation, not implicit reactive bindings.
decisions.story: A sale changes from 125 to 175 cents. Sam wants the regional total to rise by 50 without maintaining a separate update routine.
decisions.inWild:
-- https://docs.feldera.com/sql/materialized/
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW totals AS
SELECT region, SUM(cents) AS cents
FROM sales GROUP BY region;
decisions.detail:
All proposed examples and acceptance clauses describe future behavior, not current implementation evidence.

Reuse D-LIVEQUERY1 and D-SHARED-REVISION1. Required-incremental policy rejects any recomputation; ordinary watch discloses it. Budgets name retained indexes and fail rather than silently dropping rows. The standalone BigInt model passed 7056 bounded transitions and rejected two mutants. Its Float counterexample forbids an unjustified generalization; it is not Jet runtime proof.

watch subscribes to source edits and publishes a current answer. An eligible operation has a checked update rule preserving its values, failures, and order.

Worked contract, proposed: replacing North sale 1 from 125 to 175 cents increases its group total by 50. Inserting an existing key rejects. Replacing a missing key rejects. Removing the last row deletes the group rather than retaining a zero-valued ghost.

An exact integer sum may update from edits. A pure operation without an update rule recomputes its declared scope and reports that choice. Required-incremental policy refuses that query. An effectful callback is not replayed without its explicit lawful contract. Old owner/revision results cannot publish.

Model evidence only: the standalone JavaScript experiment enumerated small input states and edits. A mutant is an intentionally wrong algorithm. Its retained-empty-group mutant produced North=0 instead of no group. This does not prove Jet implementation, arbitrary histories, joins, or Float arithmetic.

Acceptance:
- Insert, replace, remove, duplicate join keys, group-key changes, empty groups, and ordering ties match batch reference observations.
- Validation, errors, effects, and numeric modes remain equivalent; the recorded Float counterexample rejects the unsafe rewrite.
- Publication is atomic and rejects old owner/revision results; cancellation and dropped subscriptions release or account for work.
- Retained-state ceilings, spill choice, incremental/recomputed operations, and explicit refusal are visible on every applicable execution path.

options.detail: Watch the ordinary query; maintain proven operations and disclose recomputation of unsupported pure scopes. One calculation serves batch and live results. Stale publication uses the adopted revision rule. Maintained counts and join indexes occupy memory between edits.

totals :: data.query(sales).group_by(s -> s.region)
    .sum(s -> s.cents).watch() ?? panic("watch failed")
sales.replace(1, changed_sale) ?? panic("missing sale")

decisions.title: Typed coordinate spaces and checked transform composition
decisions.gist: Should geometry types distinguish world, screen, camera, and device spaces?
decisions.lesson: Two positions can contain the same numbers but refer to different coordinate spaces. A transform converts between spaces. Jet already has units and shape knowledge. This choice adds space identity through ordinary types, not another unit syntax.
decisions.story: Mina converts a mouse position into a game-world position. A camera or viewport change must not make a numerically valid calculation silently use the wrong space.
decisions.detail:
All proposed examples and acceptance clauses describe future behavior, not current implementation evidence.

Do not modify protected placement or acceleration decisions. No unchecked UnknownSpace default is introduced. A space type identifies a convention, not every runtime scene instance. Stock constructors and aliases are real domain names, not compatibility shims. Conversion failures and stale frame identity need registered diagnostics or typed runtime errors.

Point2<Float,Screen> contains two floating values measured in the Screen convention. A Transform<Screen,World> converts that convention into World. These are ordinary type parameters, not a new keyword.

Worked contract, proposed: a translation by (10,20) maps screen point (240,120) to world point (250,140). Applying the same Screen-to-World transform to that World result rejects. Composing Screen-to-World with World-to-Camera is valid; composing it with Screen-to-Camera rejects.

A singular transform has no inverse and returns an error. A transform tied to an old viewport revision cannot silently serve a new viewport. Static tags should need no stored object; measuring that erasure is an implementation criterion, not current performance evidence.

ScreenPoint is the stock name for Point2<Float,Screen>. Custom spaces use the generic form; ordinary camera and input APIs return the stock types.

Acceptance:
- Wrong-space point/vector operations and invalid transform compositions reject with source-linked Jet diagnostics.
- Valid world/view/screen composition, singular inverse, perspective picking, and dynamic frame changes have the declared results or errors.
- Static tags erase without unnecessary allocation; runtime identity costs are measured and disclosed where required.
- Game/UI callers, public docs, examples, reflection, and every applicable execution mode use one geometry contract.

decisions.title: Scoped deterministic execution worlds
decisions.gist: Should tests control time and scheduling without changing production function signatures?
decisions.lesson: A background task may still be waiting when a test checks its result. A controlled world supplies virtual time and known inputs. Inside it, ordinary sleep calls register virtual timers. Production functions keep the same signatures. This choice controls existing effects and tasks, not a second execution engine.
decisions.story: Sam tests a task that completes after forty milliseconds. The test should finish quickly and reliably without a longer sleep or a global clock replacement.
decisions.detail:
All proposed examples and acceptance clauses describe future behavior, not current implementation evidence.

This is not permission to use undeclared effects. Fixed wall-clock origin and monotonic time are separate. Concurrent worlds are isolated. Ambiguous nested schedulers reject; child scopes share the parent scheduler. AOT, JIT, interpreter, and applicable web calls use the same controlled Prelude providers. No I9 exception is requested.

Inside the proposed world, ordinary time.sleep registers a virtual timer instead of blocking for real elapsed time. Production code still calls the same function.

Timeline: at virtual 0ms the task requests sleep(40ms). wait_idle runs available work until every remaining task is waiting; it does not advance time. advance(39ms) leaves the task waiting. advance(1ms) makes its timer due, runs resulting available work, and returns at virtual 40ms.

A runnable task can take a step now. A waiting task needs an event. A finished task has completed. Equal-time events use a stable recorded order. Missing effect providers fail. A task that never yields exhausts the execution budget. These are proposed provider rules, not an observed Jet run.

Acceptance:
- Timeout, cancellation, equal-time events, and negative before-deadline assertions run without real sleeps or production-signature changes.
- Uncontrolled effects, leaked tasks, invalid nesting, and exhausted execution budgets fail explicitly rather than hang or escape.
- Concurrent worlds isolate clocks, randomness, provider state, and task lifetimes.
- All applicable execution modes share the provider semantics and replay the same recorded controlled history.

options.technical: Task context carries the world. wait_idle drains currently runnable controlled work. advance processes due events in stable recorded order. Missing providers fail. Scope exit accounts for descendants. Budgets stop spinning work. No process-global override or second task engine.

options.detail: Add clock and scheduler parameters to affected functions and supply fakes in tests. Dependencies are explicit function inputs. Test plumbing spreads through production signatures.

slow :: wait_with_clock(clock, 40ms)
clock.advance(40ms)
slow.join() ?? panic("task failed")

decisions.gist: Should frame scheduling derive dependencies from the calls that read and write resources?
decisions.lesson: A renderer must wait for a resource writer before reading its result. Temporary storage can be reused only after its final real use. Jet already tracks access and ownership. This choice uses those facts instead of repeating dependency lists.
decisions.story: Mina simulates positions, draws a scene, and composites its image. The schedule must preserve those dependencies and keep images alive until device work completes.
decisions.detail:
All proposed examples and acceptance clauses describe future behavior, not current implementation evidence.

Do not reopen or write D-PLACE1 or D-ACCEL1. The new public frame API is the gated increment. Resource regions, layout, device, access, and completion identity constrain reuse. The existing explanation record shows dependencies, transfers, refused choices, and costs. A headless schedule does not qualify physical driver behavior.

Two names alias when they refer to overlapping storage. A region identifies the part accessed. Completion means the real reader or writer has finished, including device work.

Worked contract, proposed: simulate writes positions; draw reads positions and writes scene_image; composite reads scene_image and writes screen. The schedule therefore orders simulate before draw before composite. Two independent reads may overlap. Conflicting writes preserve required order.

Unknown overlap orders conservatively. An opaque operation without a complete required access contract rejects the derived schedule. An image remains owned until its final device completion, not merely until submission returns. The manual alternative must declare the same region and completion facts. Physical driver qualification remains unrun.

Acceptance:
- Read/write, write/write, region overlap, and asynchronous completion cases produce a legal schedule or a precise refusal.
- A real frame preserves the source-order reference observations and cannot reuse or release a resource before completion.
- Schedule inspection explains dependencies, transfers, reuse, and conservative choices using checked facts.
- Existing placement/acceleration controls and all applicable execution paths remain canonical; no duplicate policy or tier gap is introduced.

decisions.title: Typed ownership over the Arrow C data interface
decisions.gist: Should Jet share compatible foreign columnar buffers through one checked owner?
decisions.lesson: Columnar data stores each field together. The Arrow C interface shares those buffers and defines who releases them. This choice wraps that boundary in a typed Jet owner. It does not add a file reader or prove arbitrary foreign code safe.
decisions.story: Sam receives sales from a foreign analytics tool. He wants to query them without serializing a CSV copy or risking use after the producer releases memory.
decisions.inWild:
# https://docs.pola.rs/api/python/stable/reference/api/polars.from_arrow.html
frame = pl.from_arrow(foreign_batch, rechunk=False)
decisions.detail:
All proposed examples and acceptance clauses describe future behavior, not current implementation evidence.

The Arrow C ABI itself needs no Arrow software dependency. New external format or runtime libraries require their separate ballots. Do not treat Arrow C as Arrow IPC or Parquet support. Native, interpreter, JIT, and applicable web consumers use one semantic adapter contract. Semantic units and nominal identities require explicit metadata or conversion, not layout guessing.

A buffer is a contiguous memory region. A schema describes fields and representations. The Arrow C interface defines the fields and release callback shared by two programs. The ^ argument transfers ownership.

Worked contract, proposed: a producer supplies id:Int64 and cents:Int64 with valid lengths and no nulls. Sale requires matching fields and semantic conversions. A nullable cents column cannot silently become a required value; import returns a schema error or uses an explicitly selected checked conversion.

Ownership moves producer to ColumnBatch, then releases once after the final permitted view is gone. Moving the owner prevents the old name from releasing it again. Slices keep the base owner alive. Shared bytes are immutable. A malicious producer remains a foreign trust boundary; safe typed access does not verify arbitrary C code.

Acceptance:
- Real producers and consumers agree on supported schemas, nullability, dictionaries, slices, and values without hidden narrowing.
- Release, move, alias, producer failure, and malformed-layout cases cannot expose invalid safe views or double-release ownership.
- Measured copy behavior matches the reported shared/copied result, and no-copy refusal is explicit.
- The existing query and ownership semantics serve every applicable mode; no independent aggregation or foreign-lifetime policy is introduced.

options.name: Checked shared owner
options.detail: Import compatible buffers as ColumnBatch<Row>, using existing move and view rules. One typed lifetime across the boundary. Compatible buffers need no row-copy detour. Foreign producer contracts remain a trust boundary.
options.code:
// Proposed:

    ?? panic("incompatible data")
rows :: data.query(batch).collect() ?? panic("query failed")
options.technical: Validate supported schema, offsets, lengths, nullability, dictionaries, and limits. One owner releases the base exactly once. Children follow the producer release rule. Shared data is immutable. Copies and conversions are disclosed; explicit no-copy mode refuses incompatible inputs.

options.name: Always copy owned rows
options.detail: Require materialization into independently owned Jet rows before use. Independent ownership after decoding. Compatible data still pays conversion and copy cost.
options.technical: Preserve typed decode and limits. Direct explicit foreign bindings remain expert work under existing trust rules.

decisions.title: Use the official Arrow Rust reader behind the format boundary
decisions.gist: Should the native Parquet reader reuse Arrow Rust behind Jet’s checked data boundary?
decisions.lesson: Parquet is a storage format, not an in-memory Arrow handle. A real reader must decode its types, compression, and malformed files. Jet’s existing SQL card excluded Parquet. This choice selects a reader implementation without changing the typed query interface.
decisions.story: Mina runs the same sales query on sales.parquet. A format name that returns an unavailable-bridge error does not finish that job.
decisions.detail:
All proposed examples and acceptance clauses describe future behavior, not current implementation evidence.

This is an explicit stdlib dependency decision. The retrieved official documentation identifies parquet 59.3.0. Pin its resolved closure and license/provenance through Jetpack before implementation. No automatic future version or arbitrary codec plugin is approved. D-COLUMNAR-BOUNDARY1 is the separate Arrow C ownership choice. Card #2035 is not redefined or reopened to pretend it included this reader.

This ballot selects the Parquet decoder only. It does not select the Arrow C sharing interface or the separate Arrow IPC file format. Both options intentionally expose identical Jet code.

A runs the pinned external parquet reader behind the checked data provider. B runs a Jet-owned decoder. Both owe identical supported types, codecs, corrupt-input errors, limits, targets, and measured costs. B has no demonstrated intrinsic product disadvantage; its interoperability is not established by the proposal.

Source evidence: Prelude/Top/DataFlow.rs contains format branches returning unavailable-bridge errors. No current Parquet runtime result is claimed. Converting the same sales file to CSV is a workaround, not equivalent format support. The new acceptance case reads the original Parquet file without that conversion.

Acceptance:
- Real Parquet files from independent writers decode through the typed source/query path with supported logical and physical types.
- Malformed metadata, offsets, compression, nesting, and allocation limits produce defined Jet errors without unbounded work.
- The exact dependency closure, codecs, licenses, provenance, and target support are recorded and reproducible.
- Native AOT/run/interpreter and applicable web byte-source execution share meaning; replaced unavailable bridges and corpus callers cut over completely.

options.name: Reuse the official reader
options.detail: Approve parquet 59.3.0 and its required Arrow closure behind the existing foreign/package boundary. Real format decoding behind one typed query. Compiler crates keep path-only dependencies. The foreign decoder remains outside Jet’s own theorem.
options.technical: Approve the pinned reader closure only for the data provider, not compiler seams. Declare codec/features and target support. Bound compressed/decompressed data, nesting, rows, and allocations. Required native and web byte-source paths must be implemented before closure.

options.name: Write a Jet-owned reader
options.detail: Implement the same format contract in Jet-owned code without this external reader. Decoder can enter Jet-owned proof scope.
options.technical: The final format, corruption, codec, resource, and target obligations are identical. No reduced subset or unavailable adapter satisfies the job. Interoperability and performance need independent evidence.

comparisons.note: The official Parquet crate supplies synchronous Arrow batch reading from files or memory.

recommendation.why: A reuses the format’s existing implementation while keeping query meaning and ownership in Jet.

whyNot.reason: It establishes the same final contract without the named existing implementation. No intrinsic product loss is asserted.

recommendation.tradeoff: The foreign decoder remains outside Jet’s own theorem. Removing that assumption requires separately verifying the reused implementation and its construction, not only the Jet adapter.
