decisions.title: Models as typed, versioned packages
decisions.gist: Should model applications load a checked package instead of rebuilding model contracts around raw arrays?
decisions.lesson: A model needs more than weights. It also needs input names, shapes, preprocessing, output meaning, and a runtime. A typed model package records that contract. This is for applications that use models; Jet development never depends on an AI service.
decisions.story: Sam embeds documents for search. Replacing the model must not silently query an old index whose vectors happen to have the same length.
decisions.inWild:
# https://onnxruntime.ai/docs/api/python/api_summary.html
session = ort.InferenceSession("embedder.onnx",
    providers=["CPUExecutionProvider"])
vectors = session.run(None, {"input_ids": tokens})
decisions.detail:
All proposed examples and acceptance clauses describe future behavior, not current implementation evidence.

Reuse Jetpack, typed shapes, existing placement/acceleration controls, and the Prelude boundary. Do not write protected decisions. A model signature is not a new tensor language. Package identity changes invalidate incompatible indexes without automatic reinterpretation. The backend provider and its foreign dependency are decided separately in D-MODEL-BACKEND1.

An embedding is a model-produced numeric representation of a document. A tensor is an array with an element type and dimensions. A session owns the loaded model and its resources.

Worked identity: weights hash, tokenizer hash, preprocessing, pooling, normalization, output meaning, and distance metric. The package and index record the same complete identity. Equality requires every semantic component to match, not merely the vector length.

Two models both produce 768 values. Changing the tokenizer changes identity, so an old index rejects the new vectors with an embedding-space mismatch. Explicit rebuilding creates a new compatible index. Ordinary loading never relabels old vectors. Dynamic dimensions validate against the declared signature before inference. These are intended rules, not implemented results.

Acceptance:
- A real pinned embedding model executes and indexes documents with checked input/output signatures and full embedding-space identity.
- Same-dimension but incompatible weights, tokenizer, pooling, normalization, or metric reject index reuse.
- Dynamic shape, load failure, unsupported provider, cancellation, custom operators, resource lifetime, and buffer limits obey declared errors.
- Every applicable native/web mode uses the same package contract and numerical policy; transfers, conversion, approximation, and trust boundaries remain visible.

options.name: Checked typed packages
options.detail: Load the artifact, preprocessing, signature, and embedding identity as one pinned package. Model and index identities cannot silently drift. Tensor names, types, and shapes check at the boundary. Loading an untrusted model still requires admission and limits.
options.code:
// Proposed; Embedder is the declared package signature.
model :: models.open<Embedder>("search-embedder") ?? panic("load failed")
vectors :: model.embed(documents) ?? panic("inference failed")
index.insert(vectors) ?? panic("embedding space mismatch")
options.technical: Identity includes weights, tokenizer, preprocessing, pooling, normalization, output meaning, and distance metric. Dynamic dimensions validate once. Sessions own weights and device resources. Untrusted custom operators do not load by default. Streams expose cancellation and bounded buffering.

options.name: Keep application wrappers
options.detail: Expose raw tensor runtime calls and let each application build its model and index contract. Maximum freedom to invent model contracts. Every application must prevent contract and index drift.
options.code:
// Application-owned pipeline:
tokens :: app_tokenize(documents)
raw :: app_infer(tokens)
vectors :: app_pool_and_normalize(raw)
index.insert(app_tag_vectors(vectors))
options.technical: Existing tensors, shapes, placement, effects, and expert foreign bridges remain. No automatic correctness is claimed for raw arrays.

decisions.title: Bind a model output to its public Embedder signature
decisions.gist: Should a package export Embedder from Jet source or generate it from checked model metadata?
decisions.lesson: The output key names one checked model. Its exported signature declares documents, vectors, and errors. Both options check runtime shapes and index identity. Neither a type declaration nor metadata proves that a model understands documents.
decisions.story: Sam ships a search package. Users open its Embedder, encode documents, and query an index. Sam changes the tokenizer and expects the old index to reject, even when vector length stays unchanged.
decisions.inWild:
# https://onnxruntime.ai/docs/api/python/api_summary.html
session = ort.InferenceSession("embedder.onnx",
    providers=["CPUExecutionProvider"])
vectors = session.run(None, {"input_ids": tokens})
decisions.detail:
This is a proposed binding contract, not runtime evidence. D-MODEL-PACKAGE1 remains ratified. Every #2970 criterion remains unchanged. This ballot selects signature ownership, not model artifacts. It does not authorize fake hashes or replace the real pinned embedding workload.

A resolves the configured .Model name to exactly one exported trait. The trait references the exported batch and space carriers shown in the example. Those names are configurable, not reserved compiler spellings. The open string selects the exact package output. A missing, ambiguous or conflicting export fails before execution.

B generates the same trait and carriers from its checked signature record. Missing or conflicting signature fields fail before compile output. Neither option creates a universal core.Embedder type or a fallback alias. Renaming an output requires changing the open string. Renaming its signature requires changing the qualified type reference.

Carrier fields are private to the checked model provider boundary. Provider constructors create batches; safe consumers cannot construct or retag them. Index insertion checks the batch against the index identity. Raw arrays cannot bypass that check. Experts may export raw values, but trusted insertion still requires an explicit identity check.

The space digest represents the full canonical ModelIdentity, not a graph-only hash. Identity includes graph, weights, tokenizer, preprocessing, pooling, normalization, output meaning and metric. Changed artifact hashes or semantic identity reject index reuse even when vector dimensions match. The existing ModelPackage::check_index_compatibility remains the canonical check.

Both options preserve declared tensor names, dtypes, ranks, static dimensions and bounded dynamic dimensions. Repeated dynamic symbols must agree. Neither converts every input to f32. Native and web providers consume the same checked package contract. Load and inference failures return Err, never None.

Neither source declarations nor metadata prove that a model understands documents. The real pinned embedding/index workload remains required. Model replacement, cancellation, lifetime, bounds and numerical policy retain the original card's acceptance terms.

options.detail: The package exports a real Embedder trait with one document-to-vector method. The existing .Model name field binds it to search_encoder. The compiler checks the trait against metadata, so source and runtime cannot drift silently.
options.technical: The package uses existing `pub struct`, `pub trait`, `fn`, `use`, generic call, and method call forms. `EmbeddingBatch.space` is the owned provenance carrier; index.insert compares it with the index identity. `use search_embedder` imports the module; `search_embedder.Embedder` names its exported signature. No core.models.Embedder is added. Both open and embed return non-optional `T !Err` results.

options.name: Metadata-generated signature

decisions.title: ONNX Runtime as a pinned model-package provider
decisions.gist: Should the model package use pinned ONNX Runtime before adding another owned inference engine?
decisions.lesson: The typed model package describes meaning. A provider executes its model. This choice selects ONNX Runtime through the existing foreign/package boundary. It does not move a runtime dependency into the compiler or approve arbitrary model code.
decisions.story: Mina loads a supported ONNX model and chooses an available execution provider. Unsupported operators must report a real error, not return fabricated outputs.
decisions.inWild:

    providers=["CPUExecutionProvider"])

decisions.detail:
All proposed examples and acceptance clauses describe future behavior, not current implementation evidence.

The official release API reported ONNX Runtime v1.29.0, published 2026-08-12. Approval covers this pinned provider and required package closure, not arbitrary upgrades. Compiler seams remain path-only. CPU and device numeric behavior must match the declared exact/approximate policy. Existing D-ACCEL1 retains all provider-selection authority.

A provider runs the model operators on a selected machine. Marshalling converts arguments and results at that boundary. Both options intentionally expose identical Jet code. A uses pinned ONNX Runtime; B uses a Jet-owned engine.

Both owe the same model, operator, resource, and target contract. Native AOT, JIT, and interpreter calls use the shared package adapter. Web uses the provider’s supported web execution path. A missing operator or provider returns an unsupported-model/provider error; it never fabricates output or silently changes numerical policy.

The model declares exact operations or a specific approximate tolerance before comparing providers. No universal tolerance is guessed. Runtime and driver behavior remain named assumptions unless separately verified. B has no demonstrated intrinsic product disadvantage; owned code alone does not establish compatibility, speed, or proof.

Version source: https://github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime/releases/tag/v1.29.0 ; release metadata: https://api.github.com/repos/microsoft/onnxruntime/releases/tags/v1.29.0 . The earlier retrieved release metadata reported the pinned version and date.

Acceptance:
- The pinned runtime executes real supported models through the typed package in required native and web modes.
- Operator/provider absence, shape mismatch, load failure, and runtime errors become declared Jet results without fabricated fallbacks.
- Reproducible provenance, hashes, licenses, operator/provider closure, custom-code policy, and offline behavior are recorded.
- Same-run incumbent comparisons measure load, warm inference, transfers, peak memory, and output policy on matched work; no tier or trust boundary is hidden.

decisions.title: Let jet run request project preparation from Jetpack
decisions.gist: Should jet run prepare a declared missing environment through Jetpack before executing?
decisions.lesson: Jet executes source; Jetpack realizes dependencies. That boundary is already ratified. This amendment lets an explicit run command request preparation rather than asking the user to enter a shell first. It does not merge the tools or silently edit a lockfile.
decisions.story: Sam checks out a project and runs its main file. The declared locked environment is not realized on this machine yet.
decisions.inWild:
# https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/projects/run/
uv run main.py
decisions.detail:
All proposed examples and acceptance clauses describe future behavior, not current implementation evidence.

Explicit amendment to D-VERDICT-2188-1 and D-VERDICT-2189-1. D-ENVFLAG1 remains unchanged. The proposed --no-prepare flag is an owner-gated CLI surface; register it in the canonical command table. Never activate from merely browsing an editor folder. Locked hash mismatches, unavailable offline content, and missing trust fail before execution.

A lock records exact dependency identities. Realization puts their required artifacts on this machine. Admission is the existing trust decision allowing those artifacts.

Proposed flow: find selected environment; check lock and trust; ask Jetpack for missing admitted artifacts; execute through Jet. A valid ready environment skips preparation. A lock mismatch or missing trust stops before downloads or execution. Offline missing artifacts stop with the missing identity.

--no-prepare prohibits downloads, installation, and environment creation for this run. It does not rewrite locks, start a shell, or change normal program effects. For an unrealized environment, the diagnostic names it and prints jetpack env --prep with its existing selector when needed. Message text is illustrative until registered and snapshot-tested.

Acceptance:
- A fresh admitted locked checkout runs through Jetpack realization followed by Jet execution with visible ownership and no shell-entry ritual.
- Offline missing data, lock mismatch, untrusted inputs, and --no-prepare produce actionable failures without unauthorized downloads or lock rewrites.
- Environment selection, concurrent realization, interruptions, and target identity obey existing Jetpack behavior.
- CLI help, completion, docs, examples, and retired setup instructions migrate together; no duplicate dependency resolver or shell activation mechanism remains.

# Proposed expert refusal of preparation:

decisions.title: Generate and shrink typed operation histories
decisions.gist: Should tests generate event sequences and reduce failures to a small replayable history?
decisions.lesson: A system can handle each request correctly but fail when requests interleave. A history is the sequence of operations and decisions that led to failure. A model describes the expected simpler behavior. They must be independent enough to disagree.
decisions.story: Mina tests a booking service against a small reference model. A failure involving reserve, cancel, timeout, and retry should become a short reproducer.
decisions.detail:
All proposed examples and acceptance clauses describe future behavior, not current implementation evidence.

Do not create a second comparison schema or scheduler. The model cannot call production logic for the behavior being checked. Persist a failing schedule and artifact identity with typed operations. A seed alone is insufficient across changed artifacts. Discard rates and vacuous preconditions are reported; no silent claim of broad exploration.

A case is one generated sequence of typed operations. The seed starts repeatable choices for the same generator and artifacts. Length, value bounds, distributions, and discarded cases are recorded separately.

Conceptual failure: reserve A, inspect unrelated B, cancel A, timeout A, retry A. If retry incorrectly confirms the canceled booking, shrinking may remove inspect B. It must retain reserve A because later actions require that handle. The expected canceled state comes from the independent model.

A generated action whose precondition is false is discarded and counted, not executed. An invalid replay record rejects. Excessive discarded cases make the campaign inconclusive. A changed artifact cannot use a seed alone as identical replay; the saved operations and schedule remain a new comparison under explicit identities.

Qualifying an independent model requires a checked or reviewed dependency boundary that excludes the production behavior. Unknown opaque dependencies cannot be certified independent. Shared incidental utilities are not automatically forbidden; shared logic for the behavior under comparison is.

Acceptance:
- Generated reserve/cancel/timeout/retry histories expose an injected observable defect and shrink it to a valid independently replayable counterexample. A model calling the production behavior, including transitively, cannot qualify as an independent oracle.
- Shrinking preserves handle lifetimes, preconditions, task/event dependencies, and the same failure observation.
- Artifact identity, operations, schedule, seed, bounds, distributions, and discarded cases are recorded without leaking secrets.
- The existing comparison, controlled effects, replay, and compiler correctness distinctions remain canonical across applicable execution paths.

decisions.title: Choose the public strategy hook for typed histories
decisions.gist: Should each test choose its resource strategy, or should the command type choose it?
decisions.lesson: A strategy declares valid actions, resource lifetimes, and how often actions occur. Jet has an internal strategy interface, but no public way to supply these rules. The approved histories call remains the beginner default. Both options keep one generator, one shrinker, independent observations, and replayable failures.
decisions.story: Mina tests reserve, cancel, timeout, and retry against an independent booking model. She needs one campaign for ordinary retries and another for heavy cancellation. Both use the same Command type.
decisions.detail:
D-TEST-HISTORY1=A remains law. This choice fills its missing public strategy hook; it does not reopen histories or reduce its acceptance. No new keyword, annotation, comparison format, scheduler, or generator is proposed.

HistoryStrategy<Command> is an immutable value with generate, rebuild, valid, bounds, and distributions fields. Callbacks use the existing checked callback mechanism. The compiler supplies the lossless Command codec; users do not write a second codec.

Generate receives HistoryRng, case_index: Count, and max_steps: Count. It returns optional TypedHistoryCase<Command>. Rebuild receives HistoryCase and returns optional TypedHistoryCase<Command>. Valid receives TypedHistoryCase<Command> and returns Bool. HistoryRng exposes the existing deterministic index and bounded-integer draws.

TypedHistoryCase<Command> contains case: HistoryCase and commands: [Command]. HistoryCase contains case_id, seed, operations, and schedule. These project the existing Foundation records, not a second wire format.

Each HistoryOperation carries index, name, arguments, creates, consumes, preconditions, depends_on, task, and event. HandleId, TaskId, and EventId retain logical identity. They never persist raw host pointers. HistoryPrecondition retains HandleLive, HandleState, TaskCompleted, and EventAvailable.

HistoryBounds exposes max_steps, max_resources, max_shrink_attempts, and max_discarded_cases. The existing cases argument remains the case bound. HistoryDistribution contains operation and weight. All effective bounds and weights appear in the saved artifact.

The generator must declare handle lifetimes, domain preconditions, and task/event dependencies. Invalid generated actions count as discarded; they do not run. Rebuild failure rejects a shrink candidate. Validity and the same failure observation must survive every accepted shrink.

Unknown oracle dependencies, zero useful cases, invalid schedules, exhausted bounds, unavailable resources, cancellation, and timeout never become a pass. Source, strategy, tool, target, concrete operations, and schedule bind replay identity. Secrets use the existing redaction policy.

The source backend already derives scalar enum strategies. The public resource path is not implemented or exercised. All applicable execution modes must use Foundation TestingHistory after this choice. No runtime pass or completed booking campaign is claimed.

options.name: Choose a strategy per test
options.detail: Add an optional strategy value to the existing call. Simple tests omit it. Resource tests can vary rules without changing Command.
options.technical: Add strategy: HistoryStrategy<Command> to testing.histories. Omission uses the compiler-derived type-valid strategy. An explicit value takes precedence; it never merges silently with derived rules. All five strategy fields are required. The application can reuse an ordinary function that returns this value.
options.code:
// Proposed; callbacks declare the booking rules.
rules :: testing.HistoryStrategy<Command>(
    generate: generate_bookings, rebuild: rebuild_bookings,
    valid: valid_bookings, bounds: booking_bounds,
    distributions: booking_weights)
testing.histories<Command>(seed: 41, cases: 500,
    strategy: rules, model: reference, actual: production,
    observe: public_state)

options.detail: The Command type implements HistoryCommand and returns one strategy. Calls stay unchanged, but different campaigns need wrapper types or external configuration.
options.technical: Expose HistoryCommand with the static history_strategy() HistoryStrategy<Self> requirement. The compiler derives it only when no explicit implementation exists. An explicit implementation replaces derivation. The public histories call remains five arguments and reads the strategy from Command.

// Proposed; Command chooses one strategy.
impl testing.HistoryCommand for Command {
    fn history_strategy() testing.HistoryStrategy<Command> ->
        testing.HistoryStrategy<Command>(
            generate: generate_bookings, rebuild: rebuild_bookings,
            valid: valid_bookings, bounds: booking_bounds,
            distributions: booking_weights)
}
testing.histories<Command>(seed: 41, cases: 500,
    model: reference, actual: production,
    observe: public_state)

ReferenceStateMachine chooses transitions from current state. Its preconditions also run during shrinking. This supports explicit domain validity rather than random enum values alone. Source: https://docs.rs/proptest-state-machine/latest/proptest_state_machine/strategy/trait.ReferenceStateMachine.html

decisions.title: How much source detail should Jet profiles retain?
decisions.gist: Should profiles retain source locations as well as function totals?
decisions.lesson: A profile records what a program did during one run. Jet traces currently record elapsed samples and events. Source locations could explain repeated or costly work. Their collection method, limits, and missing evidence must remain visible.
decisions.story: User compares two search implementations. A whole-run duration does not show which source locations account for the difference.
decisions.inWild:
# https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/perf-record.1.html
perf record -e cpu-clock -F 99 -g -- \
  jet run examples/features/io/grep_scan.jet
perf report --stdio
# A short or failed run may have no useful samples.
decisions.detail:
This ballot chooses record detail only. D-PROFILE-METHOD1 chooses collection. Existing recording, source identity, privacy, and no-fake-coverage contracts remain law.

No new recorder trigger, trace family, syntax, dependency, or execution-mode exception is proposed.

options.name: Source locations and function totals
options.detail: Keep source records and derive function totals from them. Users can trace a result to its source. Function summaries do not require another collector. Source records can increase capture size.
options.technical:
Use source identity, content hash, byte range, and function identity. Derive function summaries from these records. Do not run a second profiler.

Reuse current capture, privacy, and retention policy. A limit never turns absent evidence into zero. No numeric performance win is claimed.
options.code:
# Proposed trace row for the same search workload:
{"function":"scan","range":[240,310],"method":"sample","weight":17}
# Function totals are projections of recorded source rows.
# Missing or truncated evidence remains explicit.

options.name: Function totals only
options.detail: Record counts or weights only at function boundaries. Reports stay compact. One large function can hide its costly region.
options.technical: Collect function identity and method-specific measurements. Keep source definitions for navigation, but do not claim that a definition range attributes internal cost.

options.name: Current events only
options.detail: Keep current traces and use an external source profiler. Jet adds no source-profile record. Users must combine two tools and source identities.
options.technical: Retain current trace meaning. Document the external profiler workflow and its mapping limits. Do not label current aggregate samples as source coverage.
options.code:
jet perf view scan.jettrace --json
perf record -g -- jet run examples/features/io/grep_scan.jet
perf report --stdio

comparisons.note: perf samples the same command and reports the observed call stacks. Debug information controls source detail.
comparisons.code:
# https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/perf-record.1.html
perf record -e cpu-clock -F 99 -g -- \
  jet run examples/features/io/grep_scan.jet
perf report --stdio
# A short or failed run may have no useful samples.

recommendation.why: Source detail answers the question that a function total cannot. Derived summaries keep one collector and one recorded account.
gains: Users can trace a result to its source.
Function summaries do not require another collector.

losses.loss: Source records can increase capture size.
losses.mitigation: Separate source locations need separate identity and measurement data; compact IDs reduce but cannot remove that information.

whyNot.reason: A function total cannot identify repeated work inside that function.
Separate tools require users to reconcile captures and source identities.

recommendation.tradeoff: Keep compact source identities, and accept the information needed to distinguish source locations.

decisions.title: How should Jet collect source-profile evidence?
decisions.gist: Should profiles offer sampling and explicit execution counts within one command?
decisions.lesson: Sampling periodically observes a running program. Counters record selected executions and can change timing. Counts are not time or test coverage. Jet needs to state the method and never replace missing evidence with another method silently.
decisions.story: User wants low-overhead hotspot evidence first. He also needs exact frequency evidence when a short function disappears between samples.
decisions.inWild:
# https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/perf-record.1.html
perf record -e cpu-clock -F 99 -g -- \
  jet run examples/features/io/grep_scan.jet
perf report --stdio
# A short or failed run may have no useful samples.
decisions.detail:
This is a collection control, not a second recording trigger. Existing --record behavior remains unchanged. The result stays in the current trace family.

Counter cost, sample loss, clock, instrumentation, capture window, and unavailable providers remain visible. No cross-method numeric comparison is treated as equivalent.

options.name: Sample by default; count explicitly
options.detail: Offer two named methods in the existing profiler. Normal capture avoids source counter instrumentation. Short operations can be counted explicitly. Counter instrumentation can change timing.
options.technical:
Add --profile-method=sample|count to the existing jet perf run operation. Omission means sample. Choose exactly one method for each explicit invocation.

Sampling reports sample weights and its clock. Counting reports executions within the recorded window and identifies instrumentation. Neither mode claims test coverage.

Unavailable sampling returns unavailable evidence and an explanation. Never rerun the program, switch methods, or grant host permissions automatically.
options.code:
# Proposed method option; the search program is unchanged:
jet perf run examples/features/io/grep_scan.jet --profile-method=sample
jet perf run examples/features/io/grep_scan.jet --profile-method=count
# Omitted method means sample. Each command runs once.
# Rows state method, window, clock, and completeness.

options.name: Sampling only
options.detail: Collect periodic observations without a counter mode. The profiler has one collection method. Very short work can receive no samples.
options.technical: Use one sampling method with an explicit clock and capture window. Reject unsupported providers without substituting counts. Report uncertainty for sparse or empty samples.
options.code:
jet perf run examples/features/io/grep_scan.jet
# Proposed profile method is always sample.
# No sample means missing evidence, not zero executions.

options.name: Counters only
options.detail: Instrument execution frequencies without time sampling. Short operations have direct frequency evidence. Frequency does not identify expensive operations. Instrumentation can change timing.
options.technical: Instrument selected source entries and report their counts. Do not rank these counts as CPU cost. Preserve the distinction between source execution and optimized-away code.
options.code:
jet perf run examples/features/io/grep_scan.jet
# Proposed profile method is always count.
# A row reports executions, not CPU time.

comparisons.note: perf samples the same command and reports the observed call stacks. Debug information controls source detail.
comparisons.code:
# https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/perf-record.1.html
perf record -e cpu-clock -F 99 -g -- \
  jet run examples/features/io/grep_scan.jet
perf report --stdio
# A short or failed run may have no useful samples.

recommendation.why: The methods answer different questions. Explicit selection keeps both useful without disguising counts as time or rerunning work behind the user.
gains: Normal capture avoids source counter instrumentation.
Short operations can be counted explicitly.

losses.loss: Counter instrumentation can change timing.
losses.mitigation: General execution counts require extra work; measuring its cost cannot remove that work.

whyNot.reason: Sampling can miss the short operations whose frequency the user needs.
A frequent operation can still be cheap, so counts alone cannot locate CPU cost.

recommendation.tradeoff: Use sampling for ordinary profiles. Accept counter overhead only when the user selects counts.

decisions.title: Should semantic review offer architecture advice?
decisions.gist: Should semantic review offer non-blocking advice about repeated rules and unnecessary boundaries?
decisions.lesson: A short function can still repeat a business rule incorrectly. Jet already reports semantic changes and complexity. Architecture advice would identify possible improvements, with source evidence and uncertainty. It would not prove intent or change code.
decisions.story: User reviews optimistic and persisted ordering logic. Both functions are simple, but they disagree about the next position.
decisions.inWild:
# https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mattpocock/skills/main/skills/engineering/improve-codebase-architecture/SKILL.md
/improve-codebase-architecture
# Input: duplicate-policy.jet, containing both ranking functions.
# Review the shared rule and propose a behavior-preserving boundary.
decisions.detail:
This is one extension to the existing review operation. It adds no syntax, mandatory lint, code generator, or automatic refactor.

The design pass removed automatic extraction and a global quality score. Explicit request and source evidence limit unsolicited advice. Existing architecture rules remain unchanged.

options.name: Evidence-bearing advice on request
options.detail: Add optional advice to the existing semantic review. Advice names the source facts behind each suggestion. Complexity remains separate from architecture judgment. A developer must still confirm business intent.
options.technical:
Add --architecture to jet review. Analyze the checked head program and its loaded dependencies. Retain current semantic-diff output.

Advice carries source locations, the observed relationship, uncertainty, and a suggested behavior check. It never rewrites code or changes a compilation result.

Do not invent a single architecture score. Do not infer that two similar functions must share intent. Any unsupported relationship is absent or explicitly uncertain.
options.code:
# Proposed option; compare this source with itself:
jet review duplicate-policy.jet duplicate-policy.jet --architecture --json
# Proposed evidence row, not a proof of shared intent:
{"advice":[{"kind":"agreement","intent":"unknown",
 "symbols":["optimistic_rank","persisted_rank"]}]}

options.name: Keep current review tools
options.detail: Keep semantic diffs and complexity without architecture suggestions. Compiler output stays limited to existing checked facts. Developers must locate repeated domain rules themselves.
options.technical: Retain current checked-fact review. Use ordinary human or agent review for module boundaries and shared business rules. Do not imply that a clean complexity result proves good architecture.
options.code:
jet lint duplicate-policy.jet --complexity --max=3
jet review duplicate-policy.jet duplicate-policy.jet --json
# No architecture suggestion is produced.

comparisons.note: The external skill proposes deeper modules and alternatives for the same code. A human must judge its behavior claims.
comparisons.code:
# https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mattpocock/skills/main/skills/engineering/improve-codebase-architecture/SKILL.md
/improve-codebase-architecture
# Input: duplicate-policy.jet, containing both ranking functions.
# Review the shared rule and propose a behavior-preserving boundary.

gains: Advice names the source facts behind each suggestion.
Complexity remains separate from architecture judgment.

losses.loss: A developer must still confirm business intent.
losses.mitigation: Two similar calculations can intentionally implement different policies; source shape alone cannot decide that intent.

whyNot.reason: Existing metrics and semantic diffs do not locate agreement obligations across application layers.

recommendation.tradeoff: Offer evidence and suggested checks, but leave intent and any code change to the developer.

decisions.title: Should coverage report independent condition effects?
decisions.gist: Should coverage report whether each condition can change a decision?
decisions.lesson: Branch coverage shows which outcomes ran. It does not prove that each condition can change the result. Modified condition/decision coverage, called MC/DC, checks that independence. Jet already reports branch outcomes; this choice adds distinct evidence, not a replacement.
decisions.story: User tests a permission rule with three booleans. His tests reach true and false, but they do not show which inputs control the result.
decisions.inWild:
# https://clang.llvm.org/docs/SourceBasedCodeCoverage.html
# https://www.sqlite.org/testing.html
clang -fprofile-instr-generate -fcoverage-mapping \
  -fcoverage-mcdc permission.c -o permission
# Same rule: a && (b || c).
# 010, 110, 100, 101 establish each input independently.
decisions.detail:

Preserve short-circuit evaluation and side effects. Mark optimized-away or unsupported evidence explicitly. Never infer bitmask independence from one aggregate branch.

This approval does not impose a release-wide MC/DC gate or claim coverage proves correctness. Such a gate needs its own owner choice.

decisions.title: Who should own embedded-source mappings?
decisions.gist: Should Jet own checked source regions inside host documents?
decisions.lesson: An editor may place Jet code inside another file. Current compiler entry points accept whole Jet files. A source map connects embedded positions to the host. Revisions prevent old results from overwriting new edits.
decisions.story: User edits one Jet block in a host document. He needs the same diagnostic and completion positions after text before the block changes.
decisions.detail:
This extends the existing compiler service and position code. It is not a second parser or language server.

Source checks found whole-document revisions but no external region model or cancellation token. The design pass removed host-format parsing from the compiler proposal.

options.name: Compiler-owned checked regions
options.detail: Add an explicit host-document and region contract. Diagnostics and navigation share one position map. Old results carry a revision the host can reject. Hosts must identify their embedded regions.
options.technical:
Use one SourceDocument input for whole and mapped documents. Migrate existing callers to the same check operation; do not keep parallel parsers or compatibility entry points.

Hosts supply complete generated Jet source and its unchanged source segments. They retain control of module scope and host syntax. Jet validates UTF-8 boundaries and mappings.

Every result carries the external revision. The same checked maps serve diagnostics, completion, navigation, and edits. Edits across unmapped generated text are rejected.

Generated-only locations stay labeled as generated. Cancellation never publishes a stale partial result. Editor conversion uses UTF-16 units, not byte offsets.

options.name: Host-owned mappings
options.detail: Keep whole-file checks and require each host to map positions. Jet adds no host-document API. Each integration must handle mapping and stale results.
options.technical:
Keep current compiler entry points. Publish their exact position contract. Hosts own region identity, updates, inverse mappings, cancellation, and stale-result rejection.

Do not claim that current whole-document version checks also protect host-region mappings.

comparisons.note: Volar uses explicit source mappings. Its string offsets are UTF-16 positions, unlike the proposed Jet byte ranges.

recommendation.why: One checked mapping contract prevents editor integrations from giving different answers for the same embedded program.
gains: Diagnostics and navigation share one position map.
Old results carry a revision the host can reject.

losses.loss: Hosts must identify their embedded regions.
losses.mitigation: The surrounding file format belongs to the host; Jet cannot infer every language container correctly.

whyNot.reason: Repeated mapping code can disagree on Unicode, edits, cancellation, and document revisions.

recommendation.tradeoff: Let hosts identify regions; let Jet validate and reuse their positions for every compiler result.

decisions.title: Automatic progress with expert control
decisions.gist: Should progress offer automatic helpers and full manual control through one shared task model?
decisions.lesson: Jet currently counts iterator pulls. That cannot show whether processing an item succeeded. Common helpers can own the work and its completion. Custom jobs still need editable counts and labels. Both paths can share the same facts, errors, and output policy.
decisions.explainer:
Ordinary items:

```jet
use core.term as term
term.progress_each(files, import_file, "Import")
```

Custom measurements with automatic completion:

```jet
use core.term as term
term.progress_task("Download", bar -> {
    loop chunk in chunks {
        consume(chunk)
        bar.increment(chunk.len())
    }
}, unit: "bytes", transient: true)
```

Explicit completion when the caller owns the lifecycle:

```jet
use core.term as term
bar :: term.progress_task("Download", unit: "bytes")
loop chunk in chunks {
    consume(chunk)
    bar.increment(chunk.len())
}
bar.finish()
```

The scoped callback borrows the task. The helper owns finishing it. The manual form gives that ownership to the caller. These are proposed library functions using existing Jet syntax.
decisions.story: User wants one call for an ordinary download. For resumable or callback-driven work, he wants exact custom updates and explicit completion.
decisions.inWild:
# https://tqdm.github.io/docs/tqdm/
from tqdm import tqdm
with tqdm(total=None, unit="B", leave=False) as bar:
    bar.set_description("Download")
    for chunk in chunks:
        consume(chunk)
        bar.update(len(chunk))
decisions.detail:
The owner rejected the nested result branches and mandatory finish call. The design-away pass replaces that example with a byte helper that owns the ordinary operation.

Item and byte helpers automate counting and completion. A scoped callback allows custom updates without manual finish. An owned handle keeps explicit lifecycle control. All four entry patterns use one task model.

Existing Jet named arguments and error propagation remove setter setup and panic scaffolding. No keyword, separate progress engine, or hidden work-completion heuristic is added.

options.name: Automatic helpers; expert handles
options.detail: Make ordinary progress one call; expose the same task for custom work. Common work needs no counting or finish calls. Custom work keeps all manual controls. Errors propagate without repeated panic branches.
options.technical:
Use core.term as the canonical module. Keep one ProgressTask state model and the count law chosen by D-PROGRESS-COUNTS1. Convenience functions are adapters over that model, not separate renderers or completion policies.

Keep progress(items, description) as the traversal wrapper. It measures yielded items only. It does not claim that arbitrary loop bodies processed those items successfully. Abandoning a live wrapper never produces success.

Add progress_each(items, work, description). The description defaults to Progress. Invoke work once per item. Increment by one after its successful return. Finish after successful exhaustion. Do not collect or traverse the source first to discover its size.

Add progress_bytes(chunks, work, description). Accept the existing binary-buffer and borrowed byte-view forms without copying their data. Count each buffer’s byte length only after work successfully consumes that complete buffer. This adapter supplies the byte unit automatically.

The byte helper counts fully processed buffers, not remote acknowledgements or durable storage. A callback can make partial progress before failing without exposing that amount. Partial acknowledgement workflows use the scoped reporter or owned handle with measured updates. Never count a failed buffer as fully processed.

Keep progress_task(description, callback) for scoped custom reporting. The callback borrows the same task and can update counts, estimates, labels, columns, and child tasks. The helper retains lifecycle ownership. It finishes only after successful callback return; an error fails it without a success frame.

Keep progress_task(description) for an owned manual handle. finish, fail, and cancel settle and consume lifecycle ownership. Ordinary ownership checking prevents a scoped callback from consuming or escaping its borrowed task. Destroying an unsettled owner cancels its progress, not the underlying operation.

The scoped and owned forms accept the same named settings. unit defaults to items, total is absent, and transient defaults to false. A named total supplies an estimate. The byte helper defaults to unknown total, never the number of chunks. A sized item source can supply its exact item count without a prepass.

Optional settings belong on the initial call, not in mandatory setter chains. Existing terminal width, color, Unicode, channel, and machine-output policy remain authoritative. Human output uses stderr when enabled. Non-TTY and machine modes never receive terminal escape sequences.

A shared renderer coalesces ordinary human updates to at most ten frames per second. A changed terminal transition flushes once. Facts retain every accepted update. No helper creates a per-task timer thread or materializes the source. The existing output-profile seam carries expert rendering policy.

Unknown totals show activity and counts without invented percentages or arrival times. Finished rows report actual work, even when the estimate differs. An estimate reaching zero or one hundred percent does not settle the task.

Preserve increment, set_total, set_unknown_total, set_label, set_column, set_transient, and child on the same task. Child identities are explicit and acyclic. Each child keeps its own unit and total. Unlike child units are never added into parent progress.

Preserve bounded tasks, text, columns, and frames. Release frees live-task capacity. Reused storage never gives an old handle access to a new task. Final observations remain bounded under the shared output policy.

Use one typed ProgressError. Declare its conversion to the default Err through Jet’s existing conversion mechanism. Ordinary call sites rely on existing propagation, not repeated matching or panic. Work errors remain primary if reporting cleanup also fails. A failure to initialize reporting must not execute the work callback.

Callbacks must await the work they claim to complete. Existing structured joins complete before success; detached jobs and external work require a result signal or an owned handle. Progress cancellation does not itself cancel a download. Forced process termination cannot promise a final frame.

Implement all adapters through the canonical Prelude and Core meaning. Host, default run, AOT, interpreter, and applicable web projections preserve the same counts and lifecycle. The new APIs are proposals, not claims about the current binary.

options.name: Keep iterator and text forms
options.detail: Keep manual tasks available only to Rust host applications. The existing Jet interface stays unchanged. Jet callers cannot express this byte-count workflow. Iterator pulls do not establish successful processing.
options.technical: Retain the current public Jet boundary. Keep host-only MultiProgress and the existing iterator implementation. Do not describe host capabilities as a public Jet API.

comparisons.note: tqdm’s context handles display cleanup. The caller reports each successfully consumed chunk’s byte length.

recommendation.why: Put common work behind automatic helpers, not setup code. Keep scoped reporting and owned handles for jobs whose progress cannot be observed directly.
gains: Common work needs no counting or finish calls.
Custom work keeps all manual controls.
Errors propagate without repeated panic branches.

whyNot.reason: It leaves byte counts, custom phases, and explicit completion outside the Jet application interface.

recommendation.tradeoff: No identified convenience-versus-control loss remains. Hidden external work still needs an acknowledgement; a display cannot invent one.

decisions.title: Should the UI host expose native tray entries?
decisions.gist: Should Jet expose a typed tray service with an explicit unavailable path?
decisions.lesson: A tray entry keeps actions near the desktop status area. Jet host capabilities do not include it. The GUI battery’s tray fallback is text, not a tray. Applications must keep useful controls when the desktop has no tray.
decisions.story: User compares a sync application with Open and Quit actions. It must not hide its only usable window when no tray is available.
decisions.detail:
This does not approve a second UI tree, an OS project, mobile tray support, or an external dependency. Existing host services remain canonical.

The design pass removed automatic hide-on-close and automatic background lifetime. Tray behavior must agree with the chosen application lifecycle contract.

options.name: Capability-gated tray service
options.detail: Add one owned tray entry with explicit actions and cleanup. Window and tray actions can call the same application code. Unavailable hosts keep an explicit fallback path. Some desktops cannot show a tray entry.
options.technical:
Add a Tray capability and UiTray handle to the existing host service. tray_action(label, callback) describes one action without duplicating its domain rule.

tray(title, icon_bytes, actions) validates its inputs and returns a typed service result. The handle supports set_label, set_icon, set_actions, keep_alive, and remove.

Background lifetime defaults off. keep_alive(true) requires a functioning tray and an explicit application choice. Removing the entry releases callbacks and background ownership.

Unsupported and headless hosts return Unavailable. They never report a created entry or silently hide the last usable window. Keep window actions available.

Use the same event and application state mechanisms. Callback lifetime, accessibility, and repeated removal are defined. No new external dependency is approved here.

options.name: Window actions only
options.detail: Keep application actions inside the current window. Actions work without a desktop tray protocol. The application cannot provide tray-resident controls.
options.technical: Keep the current host capability set. Treat tray absence as a product scope choice, not a simulated feature. Do not use a hidden background process as a substitute.

comparisons.note: Wails has an owned tray object, menu actions, icon updates, and destruction. Host support still matters.

recommendation.why: An explicit host capability adds desktop integration without changing application logic or pretending every desktop supports it.
gains: Window and tray actions can call the same application code.
Unavailable hosts keep an explicit fallback path.

losses.loss: Some desktops cannot show a tray entry.
losses.mitigation: An application cannot create a desktop tray protocol that its host does not provide.

whyNot.reason: Window-only actions cannot provide the tray interaction shown by the source.

recommendation.tradeoff: Expose supported tray behavior and keep window controls when the host cannot provide it.

decisions.title: Should the UI host expose document printing?
decisions.gist: Should Jet offer a native print request instead of only file export?
decisions.lesson: File export creates a document file. Printing asks a host to submit that document to a printer. Jet has file writes but no print service. A print request must distinguish user cancellation, confirmed submission, and an unknown outcome.
decisions.story: User compares printing the same invoice from an application and exporting it for an external viewer. No job may be submitted without the user’s confirmation.
decisions.detail:
This is application printing, not the JetOS network-printing service. It does not approve silent printing, printer permissions, or physical output during this audit.

The design pass separated file export, dialog closure, spool acceptance, and actual paper output. Verification requires an explicitly authorized target and a real host interaction.

options.name: Confirmed host print request
options.detail: Add a print service over an immutable document snapshot. The application can open the host’s print dialog. Results do not disguise missing submission evidence. A host may not expose a confirmed submission result.
options.technical:
Add a Print capability and print_document(title, document) to the existing host service. Snapshot the document once before the dialog.

Reuse the existing immutable UI content and layout model for printable content. Interactive or unsupported content returns a typed error, never a guessed screenshot.

The native dialog selects printer and settings and confirms submission. Silent printing is not part of this approval. Headless or unsupported hosts return Unavailable.

Return canonical cancellation, confirmed submission, failure, or unconfirmed outcome facts. A closed dialog or successful adapter call is not a printer receipt.

An uncertain outcome must not trigger automatic retry. File export remains independent. No new rendering graph or external dependency is approved here.

options.name: Export and external viewer
options.detail: Keep first-party file export without a print service. The application needs no printer access. The user must switch tools to print the document.
options.technical: Keep native printing outside the first-party application API. Preserve the file-export workflow and its real errors. Do not claim stdout or a saved file proves printing.

comparisons.note: Wails exposes window.Print(). Its current source returns nil for an absent or destroyed window, so nil is not submission proof.

recommendation.why: A host print request can keep the workflow in the application while preserving confirmation and honest outcome reporting.
gains: The application can open the host’s print dialog.
Results do not disguise missing submission evidence.

losses.loss: A host may not expose a confirmed submission result.
losses.mitigation: Some platform print APIs report only dialog closure; Jet cannot invent a receipt they never return.

whyNot.reason: Exporting the invoice does not provide an in-application print workflow.

recommendation.tradeoff: Keep confirmation in the host dialog and report uncertainty when the platform cannot attest submission.

decisions.title: Truthful progress with automatic completion
decisions.gist: Can progress keep truthful counts while ordinary work finishes automatically?
decisions.lesson: A counter records reported work; a total estimates its size. A helper can observe work ending without guessing from that estimate. Jet currently clamps host counts and fills totals on finish. Manual callers and automatic helpers must share one count rule.
decisions.explainer:
Imagine a parcel counter. It expected ten parcels but saw twelve. It should show twelve. When the courier says the delivery ended, the helper can mark it done automatically.

At parcel ten, two deliveries can look identical: one has ended; the other still has two parcels coming. A counter alone cannot distinguish them. A completed loop, successful callback, protocol result, or explicit signal supplies the missing fact.
decisions.story: User downloads twelve bytes after receiving an estimate of ten. He wants a one-call helper, not a false count or manual cleanup.
decisions.inWild:
# https://tqdm.github.io/docs/tqdm/
from tqdm import tqdm
bar = tqdm(total=10, unit="B")
bar.update(12)
bar.close()
# update records the supplied increment; total is not a count cap.
decisions.detail:
The owner rejected mandatory manual completion for common work. The design-away pass adds observed lifecycle events from automatic helpers above the expert transitions.

This removes the former option-A loss. An opaque external job still needs a completion signal, but that limitation applies to every truthful option. No new keyword, heuristic completion detector, renderer, or execution-mode exception is proposed.

options.name: Truthful counts; automatic helpers
options.detail: Keep observations intact; finish when the helper observes successful work ending. Ordinary work needs no finish call. Counts remain truthful when estimates change. Experts can report completion explicitly.
options.technical:
Counts record accepted non-negative work updates with checked arithmetic. Totals are estimates and may be absent. Changing an estimate never changes the observed count. Overflow rejects the update without altering its prior state.

Reaching an estimate, including zero, does not finish work. Finishing changes lifecycle only. A completed display reports the actual amount, not a fabricated total. Human meter width can be bounded without altering machine facts.

Automatic helpers use the same state transitions as manual handles. A work-per-item helper increments after successful callback completion. It finishes after successful source exhaustion. A byte helper uses each completed byte chunk’s length, not its item count.

The scoped callback helper finishes on successful return. Work errors produce Failed; cancellation or abandonment never produces Finished. Helpers preserve the originating error instead of replacing it with a cleanup error. Ordinary error propagation remains Jet’s existing mechanism.

A raw iterator wrapper measures yielded items, not successful processing by an unseen consumer. Exhaustion completes that traversal only. Dropping an unfinished iterator cancels its traversal. If a caller retains the iterator after break, it stays open until release or explicit cancellation.

A callback that starts detached work proves only submission when it returns. Completion requires awaiting that work, a completion event, or an owned manual handle. Existing structured joins must complete before the enclosing operation reports success.

Clean exhaustion at two bytes can complete a task whose estimate was ten. A protocol truncation error must instead produce Failed at two bytes. The protocol operation, not the progress estimate, decides whether EOF was valid.

A manual owner can explicitly finish early without filling the count. Merely destroying that owner cancels unfinished work. Forced process termination cannot guarantee cleanup or a final rendered frame.

D-TERM-PROGRESS1 owns the proposed helper spellings. These alternatives compare the same download under different count policies; they do not ratify the helper surface. Automatic completion is an event reported by a helper, not a separate completion engine.

options.name: Capped automatic completion
options.detail: Treat the total as a count cap and completion trigger. Reaching the total settles a task. Reported work can be lost or invented. Reaching an estimate can precede actual completion.
options.technical: Retain the exercised cap and finish behavior. Document completed as bounded progress units, not an observed byte count. Do not use these facts as an audit of transferred work.

options.name: Exact limits with rejected updates
options.detail: Reject overruns and incomplete finishes instead of accepting estimates. Updates enforce a fixed amount of work. Wrong estimates can reject otherwise valid work.
options.technical:
Known totals are exact contracts. Overrun, a total below the count, and early finish return typed errors without changing state.

Reaching an exact total completes the task. Unknown totals retain observed counts and require explicit finish. Numeric overflow is an error.

decisions.title: Choose a non-shipping rank-selection prototype
decisions.gist: Which rank-selection contract should a non-shipping prototype test?
decisions.lesson: An index is a position in the current list. A rank is a position in sorted order, starting at zero. Rank two means third-smallest. Rank partition places that value at index two. Existing predicate partition groups values by a true/false test instead. This choice must preserve safe bounds and existing ordering. This vote authorizes a prototype, not a public API.
decisions.story: Nora needs the third-smallest latency and then examines lower and higher samples. A full sort does work her next step does not need.
decisions.detail:
This defines a candidate method contract for a non-shipping prototype, not a public API approval. D-FLOATSORT1 and existing collection ownership rules remain binding. Predicate partition keeps its current meaning.

The source registry has no rank operation. Internal selection for scalar quantile and top_n remains covered by #3012/#3013 regardless of this vote. Neither batch quantiles nor Query.limit is included.

No speed result is claimed. The canonical candidate/plain pair and strict win are mandatory before public adoption. This research is not authorized to edit product code or the manifest.

Source-implemented now: full sort, get, copy and predicate partition. Not implemented: a public rank operation. Current checked quantile and Map.top_n fully sort; selection-based replacements are planned on #3012/#3013. The current build failure prevents new runtime proof.

Before public adoption, the canonical Gauntlet manifest must compare partition_at plus get against sort plus get on the same owned list. A preserving-input variant must include copy on both sides. Require correct results first, then candidate/plain below 1.00 on every required measured metric and workload cell. Do not average losses. The matrix records runtime, compile time and allocations separately. Every required cell must be conclusive.

Execution proof covers ahead-of-time compilation, default jet run, interpretation and applicable web output. Boundary correctness includes empty and invalid ranks. Performance inputs include random, sorted, reverse, equal, duplicate-heavy and adversarial data at several sizes. The manifest and full-run proof remain absent, so the ballot is not eligible for public adoption yet.

Decision boundary: this is a preliminary research authorization. Ratifying A or B authorizes one isolated non-shipping prototype and canonical candidate/plain registration on #3018. It does not ratify a performance surface, reserve method names, or authorize production cutover. C authorizes no public-surface prototype and leaves existing internal work unchanged. This research session performs none of those implementation steps.

The prototype must exercise the exact selected candidate contract across required modes in an isolated in-repository worktree. The canonical manifest identifies it as a non-shipping experimental build, not the production binary. After conclusive receipts, #3018 must raise a separate public-adoption ballot. That later ballot cannot be ratified unless the strict surface/plain gate passes. Failed or inconclusive evidence stays carded; it is not permission to ship a smaller feature.

Required A pairs: partition_at + get versus sort + get; partition_at_by + get versus sort_by + get. Add preserving-input A pairs with copy on both sides. Required B pairs are stated in B and never add a redundant candidate copy. Observe identical callback traces and result semantics before timing. No metric or workload loss may be averaged away.

options.name: Partition in place
options.detail: Expose rank partition; use existing get to read the selected value. Does not copy the list for plain selection. Exposes both sides for further work. Reuses existing get and explicit copy. The operation may rearrange either side.
options.technical:
Add [T].partition_at(k: Int) Bool and partition_at_by(k: Int, key) Bool. The receiver is mutable, as for sort. A valid zero-based rank returns true and puts a value of that sorted rank at k. Each earlier key is no greater; each later key is no smaller. Both sides remain unsorted. The operation preserves the multiset. It does not remove, return or clone an element; existing get/view operations supply access.

Negative k, k >= len and empty lists return false before evaluating keys or changing the list. Equal keys have no stability promise. One canonical Prelude algorithm gives identical results across execution modes for identical input and build. Output order beyond the partition law is not a stable cross-version API. Plain selection uses constant auxiliary storage and a worst-case linear comparison bound. No hidden full-list clone is allowed.

Use existing sort type admissibility and ordering. D-FLOATSORT1 applies: NaNs follow all non-NaNs; two NaNs compare equal; signed zero compares equal. Ordinary IEEE comparisons and checked data.quantile nonfinite rejection do not change. Custom types use the existing sort relation, not display strings or a new comparison protocol.

The key form follows sort_by conventions. On success, evaluate the key exactly once per original element in original order, before rearrangement. It requires worst-case O(n) key/index workspace and must report it in measurement. Existing callback failure behavior applies before receiver mutation. Inconsistent ordering cannot cause memory unsafety. No second comparator-form method or split-view carrier is added.

Before public adoption, a candidate/plain cell must exist in the canonical Gauntlet manifest and meet the strict surface/plain win. No candidate implementation, canonical pair or Jet performance proof exists in this research run. This is an evidence gate, not permission to ratify on asymptotic claims.

The key callback receives one element T and returns an orderable key K. It is not a two-argument comparator. The function contract is partition_at_by(k: Int, key: fn(T) K) Bool, with generic K inferred. Existing callback access and ownership checks prevent mutation through an alias of the selected receiver. Example: samples := [(ms: 9), (ms: 1), (ms: 5)]; samples.partition_at_by(1, sample -> sample.ms) selects the middle latency. On success, the callback runs once per original element before rearrangement.

Float order is negative infinity, finite numbers, positive infinity, then NaN. All NaNs tie. Negative and positive zero tie; either original signed zero may occupy the selected index. This operation accepts those values. The separate checked data.quantile operation still rejects NaN and infinities.

Precise callback failure law: partition_at_by(k, key: fn(T) K !E) returns Bool !E. A successful call evaluates all n keys exactly once in original order. On the first error, evaluate only the prefix through the failing element. Preserve callback side effects already performed, propagate the same error, evaluate no later keys, and leave the receiver unchanged. A non-failing callback yields plain Bool.

Keys must be owned/materialized values; receiver-borrowed keys are rejected by the existing lifetime rules. Keyed selection uses worst-case O(n) key/index workspace and worst-case O(n) key comparisons after successful key evaluation. Both forms use one canonical Prelude selection kernel across all modes. Plain partition guarantees no heap allocation and constant auxiliary storage. Callback allocation is separate from kernel allocation.

get and copy retain their existing clone/materialization requirements. Plain partition can rearrange non-cloneable sortable elements, but cannot give them a new value-copy or order-preserving copy operation. Existing legal borrowed views remain the expert access path. Cloning a large selected value can allocate; only plain partition itself has the zero-allocation guarantee.
options.code:
# Proposed; not shipped. true means the rank exists.
values := [9, 1, 5, 3, 7]
if values.partition_at(2) {
    print(values.get(2) ?? -1) # 5; read current index 2.
}
# get returns an optional; -1 is only its missing-value fallback.
# To preserve the original order instead:
original :: [9, 1, 5, 3, 7]
ranked := original.copy()
if ranked.partition_at(2) -> print(ranked.get(2) ?? -1)
print(original) # [9, 1, 5, 3, 7]

options.name: Read a rank without mutation
options.detail: Expose one rank lookup that preserves the original list. Leaves the input order unchanged. Returns the selected value directly. Selection needs a private list copy or index workspace.
options.technical:
Add [T].nth_smallest(k: Int) ?T and nth_smallest_by(k: Int, key) ?T. Invalid ranks and empty inputs return None without callbacks. A valid call preserves the receiver and returns the same value-copy semantics as get. It uses A’s ordering and key-evaluation law. Tied values have no stable original-position promise. A private copy or index workspace is required because the original list cannot be rearranged. No in-place rank method ships. The same canonical candidate/plain performance gate is required before public adoption.

The key callback maps one T to an orderable K, exactly as specified for A. Floating order and signed-zero behavior also match A. The copy semantics of get apply to the returned value; returning a large value is not advertised as allocation-free.

B also requires worst-case O(n) comparisons, not a superlinear repeated-scan workaround. Its preservation plus generic linear-comparison contract requires O(n) copy or index workspace in the worst case. The keyed form returns ?T !E for key: fn(T) K !E, with A’s success/failure-prefix law and owned keys. get-compatible value copying requires cloneable T. B does not offer a non-cloneable value-return path.

Measure nth_smallest directly against copy + sort + get. Observe the original receiver unchanged on both sides. Do not add a redundant public copy to the candidate. The keyed pair is nth_smallest_by versus copy + sort_by + get, with matching callback/error behavior.
options.code:
# Proposed; not shipped. Same third-smallest value.
values :: [9, 1, 5, 3, 7]
print(values.nth_smallest(2) ?? -1) # 5
print(values) # [9, 1, 5, 3, 7]

options.name: Keep selection private
options.detail: Optimize existing statistics without adding a public rank operation. Adds no collection API. Keeps established sorting and statistics contracts. Callers still fully sort for general rank selection.
options.technical: Keep the public registry unchanged. #3012 and #3013 may use internal selection when their existing meaning is preserved. General callers use sort then get, or copy then sort then get when input order matters. A compiler may remove unobservable work only under the existing semantic proof rules; this choice creates no promise that such optimization happens.
options.code:
# Existing workaround for the same third-smallest value:
values := [9, 1, 5, 3, 7]
values.sort()
print(values.get(2) ?? -1) # 5
# Internal quantile/top_n tuning adds no rank method.

comparisons.note: Rust partitions in place and returns borrowed access to both sides and the pivot. Invalid ranks panic.
numpy.partition returns a copy and accepts several ranks. Its ndarray method mutates in place. These are scope contrasts, not Jet speed proof.
comparisons.code:
p = numpy.partition([9, 1, 5, 3, 7], kth=2)
assert p[2] == 5
# https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.partition.html

recommendation.why: Prototype A tests no-copy rank partition and existing access paths. It does not assume a speed win or authorize a shipped API.
gains: Does not copy the list for plain selection.
Exposes both sides for further work.
Reuses existing get and explicit copy.

losses.loss: The operation may rearrange either side.
losses.mitigation: Preserving every original position requires extra storage or a different read-only selection contract, which is option B.

losses.loss: Keyed selection requires O(n) key/index workspace.
losses.mitigation: Exact-once keys and an unchanged receiver on callback failure require retaining results before rearrangement.

losses.loss: Non-cloneable values lack copy-preserving and value-copy access paths.
losses.mitigation: Duplicating such a value would violate its existing ownership contract; borrowed access remains available.

whyNot.reason: It requires workspace even when callers can safely rearrange their own list.
It leaves the general rank workload without a direct operation.

recommendation.tradeoff: Prototype the in-place contract with explicit keyed workspace and ownership limits. Public adoption still requires a later evidence-backed ballot.
