decisions.title: Complete native inline assembly through the existing function contract
decisions.gist: Where should experts declare complete assembly operands and machine effects?
decisions.lesson: Ordinary Jet arithmetic stays safe and portable. Expert assembly needs checked directions, result destinations, registers, labels, symbols, effects, unwind, and target facts. This amendment chooses where complete constraints live without adding another assembly API.
decisions.explainer: A compiler-built-in assembly body is raw machine text inside an audited `#FFI(asm)` function. Sema checks its typed descriptor; the author still audits machine behavior. A and B share one descriptor, engine law, target law, and widening-multiply result.
decisions.story: Priya uses ordinary arithmetic first. For a widening multiply, she calls an audited function and expects Product128{low: 21, high: 0} on the selected x86-64 target.
decisions.detail:
## Immutable base and scope

D-FFI-ASM1=A and D-FFI-ASMOPS1=C remain ratified. #3017 owns their existing result binding, clobber, selected-target, and matching-host execution repairs. This ballot does not reopen or duplicate #3017.

D-CODE-INSPECT2 owns the assembly viewer. D-FFI-ASM-COMPLETE1 adds operand and machine-effect expressiveness only after owner approval. The new forms remain owner-gated and prototype-gated until ratified. No example below is shipped or executed.

`#FFI(asm)` is compiler-built-in assembly. It is not `asm!`, `mem.asm`, a foreign package, or an erased-value trampoline. The complete fixture is selected for x86-64 until the independent target and CPU ballots are chosen.

## Safe baseline and shared workload

Ordinary Jet arithmetic is the safe baseline. It needs no `#Unsafe`, `use core.mem`, or `#FFI(asm)`. The compiler chooses instructions for that code, and the same result remains available when native assembly is unavailable.

`portable_wide_mul` splits each `U64` input into low and high 32-bit halves. `&` keeps the low half, and `>>` obtains the high half. Four ordinary multiplications produce the partial products. The helper combines their carries, then returns the lower and upper 64-bit halves in `Product128`.

For `a = 3` and `b = 7`, all high halves are zero. The helper returns `Product128{low: 21, high: 0}`. This result is observable through `print`, not only through an internal value.

The portable helper has no unsafe or FFI effect. A wrapper that may select assembly remains uniformly FFI-unsafe, so its call stays inside `#Unsafe`. Target composition is a separate ballot.

## One short form and one normalized descriptor

The current short form remains named placeholders and one return anchor:

```jet
#[Unsafe("scalar inputs; add writes the marked destination"), FFI(asm)] fn add_registers(a: Int, b: Int) Int -> {
    """add {a}, {b} ; -> return"""
}
```

The existing short form is not replaced by this ballot. The #3017 repair owns its actual destination binding. For this concrete target syntax, the marked destination is `a`, so the repaired normalized descriptor is:

```text
template: "add {a}, {b}"
a: inout -> return, constraint=reg
b: in, constraint=reg
result: return from a
```

This descriptor is a readable projection, not a new Jet spelling. A complete A declaration writes the same facts beside the body:

```text
; inout a -> return: reg
; in b: reg
add {a}, {b}
```

A complete B declaration writes the same facts in optional marker fields:

```text
inout: { a: { constraint: "reg", result: "return" } }
inputs: { b: { constraint: "reg" } }
```

A and B infer the same descriptor when the marker has no overrides. Neither form chooses the first parameter, guesses a destination from declaration order, or falls back to `rax`. Ambiguous or missing destinations are sema errors. Code generation consumes the descriptor and never reparses raw text.

Sema checks signature types, widths, lane shapes, directions, register aliases, destination completeness, instruction encoding, selected target and CPU features, option contradictions, ABI facts, and reachability. It records source spans for each fact. The author still audits instruction semantics, addresses, lifetimes, and machine state inside `#Unsafe("reason")`.

Checked types do not make arbitrary assembly safe. This ballot grants no I9 exemption.

## Exact body grammar

A raw body is a triple-quoted, byte-preserving template. Proposed directive lines are:

```text
; in <parameter>: <constraint>
; out <name> -> <result-path-or-_>: <constraint>
; lateout <name> -> <result-path-or-_>: <constraint>
; inout <parameter> -> <result-path-or-_>: <constraint>
; inlateout <parameter> -> <result-path-or-_>: <constraint>
; temp <name>: <Jet-type> = <constraint>
; const <name> = <Jet-comptime-expression>
; sym <name> = <Jet-symbol>
; label <name>
; clobbers <register>[, <register>...]
; clobber_abi <existing-ABI-name>
; options <option>[, <option>...]
; unwind forbid
```

An `in` operand is read by the body and initialized before entry. An `out` operand is written by the body and has no input value. `lateout` is an output whose first write is promised after all potentially aliased inputs are consumed.

An `inout` operand is both input and output. An `inlateout` operand is the same tied input/output relationship with late first-write timing. A tied operand uses one storage location for both directions, never two copied values.

A `temp` is named scratch storage supplied for the body. It is not a result and cannot escape. A temp has no usable initial value and must be fully written before it is read. A clobber is register or machine state whose old value the body may destroy without returning a Jet value.

A register is temporary CPU storage. A fixed constraint names one register, such as `rax` or `rdx`. A class constraint, such as `reg`, lets the selected target allocator choose a compatible register. `reg` is not a value and does not mean any register on every target.

A result path is `return` for a scalar or `return.<field>` for a plain-data result. Paths may descend through plain-data records. Every value-producing `out`, `lateout`, `inout`, and `inlateout` has exactly one result path. `_` explicitly discards an output.

A discarded `out _` is an early write and cannot overlap a live input. The ratified discarded-clobber lowering remains early `out("reg") _`; this ballot does not turn it into `lateout`.

A returned record field is initialized exactly once. Assembly cannot manufacture a reference, owner, or invalid plain-data value. Width, signedness, lane shape, aliases, and instruction encoding must agree. No implicit truncation or invented register is accepted.

Early `out`, `inout`, and `temp` writes cannot overlap an unrelated input used later. `lateout` and `inlateout` permit overlap only under their explicit late-write promise. Sema rejects known conflicts and records the remaining unsafe promise.

## Templates, modifiers, labels, and symbols

A placeholder is exactly `{name}` or `{name:modifier}`, where both names are identifiers. `{{` and `}}` emit literal braces. A placeholder refers to an input, output, temp, constant, symbol, or declared label in the descriptor.

The proposed modifier table is closed. x86 and x86-64 allow `:byte`, `:word`, `:dword`, and `:qword` for compatible scalar registers. AArch64 allows `:w` and `:x` for compatible scalar registers, plus `:s`, `:d`, and `:q` for compatible SIMD views.

A modifier selects the register view printed into the instruction. On x86-64, `{value}` uses the declared width and `{value:byte}` prints the low 8-bit view. On AArch64, `{value:w}` prints the 32-bit W view and `{value:x}` prints the 64-bit X view. SIMD modifiers select the declared lane view.

Modifiers are rejected for immediates, symbols, incompatible widths, and incompatible lane shapes. Unmatched braces, unknown modifiers, missing names, duplicate names, and target-inapplicable modifiers are registered sema diagnostics. They never become a late native-assembler error.

A local label names a location inside one assembly body. `; label loop` declares it, and `loop:` defines it. Branches may target only labels in that body. Expansion renames labels with the body identity. Names cannot shadow operands or reserved names.

Numeric labels, assembler-generated `.L*` names, undeclared targets, duplicate definitions, and cross-body entry or exit are rejected. A label cannot escape through a symbol or call.

A symbol names a linkable function or long-lived global. The final address comes from the linker in AOT or from JIT relocation. A relocation records that request to fill the address; it is not an address guessed by Jet.

`const` uses ordinary compile-time evaluation and checks immediate width, signedness, and relocation rules. `sym` accepts only a concrete function or global/static symbol. A generic function is accepted after monomorphization, which means choosing its concrete type arguments.

Methods resolve to their linkable function symbol. Closures, stack locals, thread-local values, non-linkable locals, and unresolved generic symbols are rejected. AOT records the mangled link symbol. JIT records a relocation to the resolved address. Jet invents no relocation suffix, PIC/GOT form, TLS form, or raw address. TLS remains rejected unless a future target contract admits it. Callable symbols retain their ABI, effects, and unwind facts.

## ABI clobbers and machine effects

`clobber_abi` names one existing ABI in the selected target registry. It expands to that ABI's caller-saved general registers, vector registers, and flags. Several declarations union without duplicates.

An explicit fixed output in the expanded set wins and removes that register from the implicit set. Its declared early or late timing still applies. A generic output or temp is rejected when allocation could choose an expanded clobber. A fixed input in the set is rejected. A generic input must use a register outside the expanded set. Diagnostics name the ABI, register, timing, and conflicting operand.

A flag is CPU condition state that later instructions can read. Default assembly may change flags. `preserves_flags` promises that surrounding observable flags remain unchanged. A false promise remains an unsafe author obligation when sema cannot prove it.

The stack is call-frame storage and stack-pointer state. Default assembly may use it. `nostack` forbids stack access and stack-pointer adjustment, but it does not forbid all memory access.

Unwind is exceptional control leaving the assembly body while runtime cleanup proceeds. The default contract is `forbid`. `; unwind forbid` or marker `unwind: "forbid"` is the only spelling in this ballot. A call to an unwind-capable symbol is rejected. Assembly cannot skip cleanup or invent a landing path.

The machine-option table is:

```text
option            permitted behavior and promise                         static law
none              memory, stack, and flag changes are allowed             author audits all effects
nomem             no memory read or write, including hidden operands      reject known memory access
readonly          reads allowed; writes, atomics, and volatile stores no   reject known writes
nostack           no stack access or stack-pointer adjustment              reject known stack use
preserves_flags   all surrounding flags stay unchanged                     reject known flag writes
pure              meaningful result plus nomem/readonly and flags promise  reject missing result or noreturn
noreturn          control does not return                                  require return type Never and no result
att_syntax        x86 template uses AT&T grammar                          reject on non-x86 targets
```

`nomem` and `readonly` are mutually exclusive. `pure` forbids `noreturn`. `att_syntax` changes only x86 template grammar. Options are optimizer promises, not effect permissions. `nomem` is not a hardware fence, `nostack` is not no-memory, and `readonly` is not pure.

Known stores, flag writes, volatile effects, missing outputs, and contradictory options are sema errors. Unknown runtime lies remain the author's unsafe obligation. Calls retain the existing FFI effect tree, transaction and determinism checks, declaration gate, call gate, authority law, and diagnostic registry.

## Concrete interpreter and native flow

The following flow is proposed support for the descriptor. Current source has `MirForeignLanguage::Assembly`, but its current native bridge validator accepts C/C++ ABIs and current assembly applicability is not complete for Cranelift or the interpreter. This ballot does not claim that current support already works.

```text
1. The interpreter validates values, declaration, Unsafe call gate, descriptor and target/CPU facts.
2. It prepares two input FfiSlots and a bounded, aligned aggregate output slot.
3. UniformFfi invokes the existing jet_ffi_* trampoline.
4. Its typed native body places a in rax and b in an allocated register.
5. mul produces rax and rdx; normalized paths map them to low and high.
6. The trampoline writes low/high to checked output offsets 0/8.
7. The interpreter validates and decodes both U64 fields, then releases call storage.
8. It returns Product128{low: 21, high: 0}; failure returns no partial record.
```

Invalid Jet values, missing bridge identity, unsupported target features, wrong ABI, output mismatch, or failed safety checks reject before native invocation. No AOT fallback or second semantic implementation is allowed. Reuse the existing UniformFfi trampoline and slots; do not add another wrapper or payload clone.

AOT compiles before launch and lowers the descriptor directly. JIT means Cranelift compiling native code while the program runs; it lowers the same descriptor. The checked interpreter uses the marshal boundary above. All three receive one descriptor and one target/CPU record.

WebAssembly, JavaScript, and incompatible hardware use an explicitly selected portable implementation or reject. They never execute host assembly. Cross-target inspection reads an identified image only. D-CODE-INSPECT2 may show the native body, wrapper, marshal boundary, spans, and target facts, but it cannot claim that bytes executed.

The descriptor retains exact body bytes, directive spans, signature, audit reason, effects, normalized operands, target, and CPU/features. Any performance claim requires a later matched candidate/plain gate. This ballot claims no speed result.

## Diagnostics and gates

Existing E3215, E3102, E3222, E3223, and E0740 remain in their current homes. New template, instruction, target, modifier, symbol, label, unwind, and option conflicts use registered sema-owned diagnostics with source spans and UI snapshots. Native tool stderr never becomes a Jet diagnostic.

Owner approval is required before either placement is implemented. A prototype must use the shared widening fixture and portable helper. Production adoption needs exact descriptor parity, safety evidence, target/CPU evidence, engine parity, and a separate performance gate. #3017 remains a separate prerequisite and card; this ballot does not edit it.

## Output names and ABI unions

Every A out or lateout declares a distinct operand identifier before its destination. For example, `out high -> return.high: reg` permits `{high}` in instructions. `out scratch_result -> _: reg` names a discarded output. Names are unique across the descriptor. Directions and destination paths retain the same checked meaning in B.

A's repeated clobber_abi directives and B's clobber_abis list name the same existing target ABI registry entries. Normalize their union without duplicates. The singular clobber_abi marker key is not proposed. Invalid names and conflicting fixed-register uses fail in sema.

## Exact raw-pointer boundary

The only pointer register carrier is the existing non-owning raw type `*T`, registered by D-TYPE-ALIAS-CANON1. No Ptr<T> type alias is added. Its machine width follows the resolved target. No implicit conversion accepts a reference, View, Pin, managed value, owner or handle as a raw operand.

A raw *T supports in, out, lateout, inout and inlateout under the existing core.mem and explicit Unsafe rules. Outputs must map to a *T result leaf or explicit discard. Scratch raw pointers must be initialized before reading. All bits are raw addresses, not proof of a live, aligned or accessible referent.

A raw address may leave the call only as that same non-owning *T value under existing unsafe-memory rules. This grants no ownership, borrow extension or dereference permission. It cannot manufacture a safe reference, View, Pin or owner. Tracked-borrow nonescape checks and pin/no-move rules remain unchanged.

The caller's audit must cover referent validity, alignment, aliasing and lifetime for every actual access, including later use of an escaped raw address. Safe code still cannot dereference it. There is no unchecked conversion from an assembly result into a safe reference or managed owner.

## Checked aggregate result through the existing bridge

Current Ffi.rs uses UniformFfi(args: *const FfiSlot, count, out: *mut FfiSlot) through a loaded jet_ffi_* trampoline. FfiSlot contains value, ptr and len. Current RetAbi has no aggregate case; mir_ret_abi rejects MirAbi::Aggregate. This proposal explicitly extends that existing boundary, not a second typed bridge.

The interpreter passes ordinary argument slots and one output slot backed by call-owned aligned storage. Reuse existing storage capacity where available. Its checked record descriptor fixes byte size, alignment, field types and offsets. The trampoline writes each result leaf to its checked offset; it never memcpy-casts a Rust record layout into Jet storage.

Result paths use declaration-order fields, recursively, and each field's checked target layout. Register allocation and directive order do not change that mapping. Product128 on the shown x86-64 target has low at byte 0 and high at byte 8, size 16 and alignment 8. Each field is native-endian U64.

Before invocation, validate descriptor identity, slot bounds/alignment, target compatibility and the engine's native-call capability. After successful return, decode each field using its declared validity rules. Failure publishes no partial record. No safe reference or owner is constructed from raw bits. Release call storage after transferring the checked result.

AOT and Cranelift still use direct typed lowering with the same result-path mapping. Only the interpreter pays its existing trampoline/slot boundary. Inspection shows that real cost; no claim of zero marshalling or zero bridge storage is made. Any performance comparison includes the complete boundary cost.

options.technical:
## A: body-adjacent directives

A keeps `#FFI(asm)`, raw body bytes, named placeholders, and the ratified return-anchor short form. Complete directives sit beside the instruction bytes. The instruction and its machine contract stay together.

The exact proposed form is:

```text
; inout a -> return.low: rax
; in b: reg
; out high -> return.high: rdx
; options nomem, nostack
; unwind forbid
mul {b}
```

For the shared input `a=3, b=7`, `a` starts in fixed `rax`. `b` starts in a compiler-selected register outside `rax` and early `rdx`. Unsigned `mul {b}` reads both inputs, writes low bits to `rax`, and writes high bits to `rdx`. The descriptor maps those writes to `return.low` and `return.high`.

The instruction may change CPU flags, so it does not promise `preserves_flags` or `pure`. It promises no memory or stack access. The call remains inside the uniform unsafe wrapper gate. The observable result is `Product128{low: 21, high: 0}` in both the native and portable implementations.

A and B infer the same descriptor for a bare `add_registers` body. B does not require repeated marker fields for that short form. A is recommended because exceptional facts remain next to the raw bytes. The target and CPU ballots remain independent owner choices.

GCC separates outputs, inputs, clobbers, and control-flow responsibilities. Jet must expose equivalent facts without opaque punctuation.

decisions.title: Choose explicit target selection for native assembly
decisions.gist: How should one Jet program select native assembly without binding it for the wrong target?
decisions.lesson: A target triple names the processor and platform selected for a build. Current Jet dispatches by operating system, but it has no shipped architecture fact. This choice selects architecture-specific assembly safely without relying on the compiler host.
decisions.explainer: The target is the requested build target, not the machine running the compiler. A target-specific assembly body must not be bound or assembled for another architecture. The common signature and safe portable code remain checked, while target-specific register and instruction checks apply only to the selected body.
decisions.story: Priya wants one widening-multiply API. x86-64 can use `mul`; another target should use the portable helper or a clear target error, never host instructions by accident.
decisions.detail:
## Scope and current law

This is an independent owner choice required by D-FFI-ASM-COMPLETE1. It chooses architecture composition only. D-FFI-ASM-CPU1 separately chooses CPU and feature defaults.

The shipped CLI `--target <triple>` selects a target triple for build, run, and dev. The shipped `#Target(...)` family includes OS and web values. The shipped `@if @build.os == { ... }` form is a function-body statement.

A source audit found no shipped `Arch.<arch>` value, `@build.target.arch` fact, or `@build.target.triple` fact. These spellings below are proposed and owner-gated. The existing OS dispatch law remains unchanged. File-scope `@if` remains invalid.

A target triple names the platform ABI and architecture requested for a build. The compiler host is the machine running Jet. The host cannot replace an explicit target.

## Exhaustive spelling inventory

The existing spellings reused by both choices are:

```text
--target <triple>
#Target(OS.Linux), #Target(OS.MacOS), #Target(OS.Windows)
#Target(Web), #Target(Wasm), #Target(JS)
@if @build.os == { .Linux -> { ... } else -> { ... } }
```

A adds exactly these proposed spellings:

```text
#Target(Arch.<canonical_arch>[, Arch.<canonical_arch>...])
@build.target.triple
@build.target.arch
@if @build.target.arch == { "<canonical_arch>" -> { ... } else -> { ... } }
```

`Arch.x86_64`, `Arch.aarch64`, and `Arch.wasm32` are proposed canonical values. The architecture fact is a build-time value, not a runtime variable. The target triple supplies both proposed facts.

B adds no Jet spelling. B uses existing source selection at the build boundary, such as `jet build wide_mul_x86.jet --target ...`. A filename is not a language construct.

Neither choice adds file-scope `@if`, a generic file or module conditional, host-over-target precedence, implicit target fallback, or automatic source discovery. A's item gate accepts architecture arguments only. It does not change the shipped OS rule that gates an `impl` block.

## Availability terms and target boundary

A declaration can be parsed and common-checked without being available to the selected target. In A, an unselected `#Target(Arch.x86_64)` item is name-known in its source but unavailable for calls on another architecture. A direct call to that unavailable item receives a registered sema unsupported-use diagnostic. It never retries a different `else` arm.

A source is absent in B when it is not passed to the build and is not imported by the selected input closure. An absent source is not parsed, checked, name-known, available, or emitted. If another source imports it, it is part of the closure and is no longer absent.

A deliberately excluded target is different. `wasm32` is a recognized web architecture, but native inline assembly is intentionally excluded there. Portable source may still be selected. A present x86 assembly source on `wasm32` receives an unsupported-target diagnostic before native generation. This is not a missing-source result.

An unknown architecture or target triple is an invalid target selection. It is neither an unavailable source nor a deliberate web exclusion.

## A lifecycle

A parses every declaration and checks shared names, signatures, unsafe reasons, effects, and portable bodies. The selected target then controls target-specific assembly binding, register and modifier validity, instruction encoding, CPU-feature validity, and native lowering.

For A, the lifecycle is:

```text
case                         parse/common checks     target checks       availability       emission
x86_64, native arm reachable yes, all declarations  x86 body runs       callable           native arm emits
x86_64, native arm dead      yes, all declarations  x86 body still runs  callable           no native arm
non-x86, x86 arm unselected  yes, shared facts      x86 body does not run unavailable      no native arm
non-x86, portable else       yes, shared facts      portable checks      callable           portable body emits
wasm32, portable else        yes, shared facts      portable checks      callable           portable body emits
```

A selected but unreachable assembly item is target-checked, because its selected target must be diagnosed deterministically. It is not emitted when reachability removes it. An unselected item receives no target-specific assembly check.

A false target predicate selects `else`. A true predicate never retries `else` after an unavailable-item or invalid-assembly error. Common checks still apply to every arm. Target-specific checks apply only to the selected assembly item.

## B lifecycle and absent source

B keeps current language syntax and chooses one source closure explicitly. Its lifecycle is:

```text
case                                      parse/check result                         availability/emission
x86 file + x86_64 target                   selected closure checks; asm target-valid  asm function available/emits
portable file + supported target           selected closure checks; portable valid    portable function available/emits
portable file + wasm32 web target         selected closure checks; portable valid    portable function available/emits
x86 file + aarch64 or wasm32 target       common checks run; asm target error         unavailable; no artifact
x86 file not passed or imported            no parse or checks                        absent; no artifact
```

B does not claim that an unselected source file was checked. It does not contain both bodies automatically. Users choose the x86 file or portable file and retain the same `wide_mul(U64, U64) -> Product128` signature and observable result.

A wrong-target body that is present is an error before native generation. An absent source produces no target diagnostic because it is outside the selected closure. A deliberately excluded web target produces an unsupported-target diagnostic when present native source is selected.

## Worked modification

The shared program calls `wide_mul(3, 7)` and prints `Product128{low: 21, high: 0}`. Its portable helper is ordinary Jet arithmetic. The wrapper stays uniformly unsafe because one target arm is assembly.

First modify only the A predicate from `"x86_64"` to `"aarch64"`, while leaving `#Target(Arch.x86_64)` unchanged:

```text
x86_64: predicate false, so the portable helper is selected.
aarch64: predicate true, but wide_mul_x86 is unavailable, so sema reports unsupported use.
wasm32: predicate false, so the portable helper is selected.
```

The AArch64 row is not an automatic `else`. A true predicate names an unavailable item, and that error is final.

Next modify both the gate and predicate to AArch64, but leave the body using x86 `mul`, `rax`, and `rdx`. The item becomes available, then target checks reject its x86 instruction or registers before generation. This is a selected-body target error, not unsupported use and not a fallback.

For B, changing the command from `wide_mul_x86.jet` to `wide_mul_portable.jet` selects the portable program. Changing only `--target` while retaining the x86 source gives a target error. Removing the x86 source from the command does not parse it and gives no error from that absent file.

## Web, host, and inspection law

A uses `wasm32` as the proposed architecture fact for web and JavaScript targets. Web takes the portable arm and never binds or executes host assembly. Direct native assembly on web is unsupported. B succeeds with the portable file and rejects the x86 file.

Cross-target inspection reads an identified image only. It does not execute the image or use the compiler host's architecture. Target triple, architecture, body identity, and source closure enter artifact and cache identity.

A keeps the target-selecting wrapper uniformly FFI-unsafe because one arm is assembly. Its call remains inside `#Unsafe` on every target. B's x86 source is unsafe, while B's portable source is ordinary Jet with no FFI effect or unsafe call gate. This difference is explicit source selection, not hidden dispatch.

A is recommended because one source-level API keeps target selection explicit before native binding. B is a valid conservative alternative. Neither choice decides CPU or feature defaults.

Architecture dispatch must cover every member of the selected closed architecture registry or contain an else arm. A recognized target with no matching arm and no else fails with a registered sema exhaustiveness diagnostic before availability or emission. The existing OS-only rule is unchanged; this is the explicit law for the new architecture subject.

The dispatch wrapper is a whole-function Unsafe region because its native arm calls an audited unsafe function. The call site remains inside its own explicit Unsafe gate, including when another target selects the portable arm.

The complete target fixture uses body-adjacent operands only to show the machine operation. Selecting marker-owned operands changes that declaration exactly as D-FFI-ASM-COMPLETE1 defines; target dispatch and availability law are unchanged.

options.name: Target-qualified items
options.detail: Proposed: extend the existing target gate for architecture items and fold one target dispatch inside the function body. Unselected assembly is not bound.

options.name: Choose a target-specific source
options.detail: Keep current Jet syntax. The build command chooses one target-specific file, and sema rejects assembly whose selected target cannot encode it.

comparisons.note: Rust target predicates select architecture-specific items. Jet must state which declarations parse, which bodies are available, and which target checks run.

recommendation.why: A keeps one API and selects target-specific assembly only after the requested target is known. B remains a conservative current-syntax alternative.
gains: One source-level API.
Wrong-target bodies are not bound or emitted.
Web has a deterministic portable outcome.

losses.loss: A adds an architecture fact and item gate.
losses.mitigation: One API needs an explicit boundary before architecture-specific binding.

whyNot.reason: B adds no syntax, but callers split sources and choose the architecture at the build boundary.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds a narrow owner-gated target surface. B avoids new syntax but gives up automatic one-program dispatch.

The reader required an exhaustive new-spelling inventory, A and B parse/check/availability/emission matrices, explicit absent-source behavior, deterministic web behavior, and separate unsupported-use versus wrong-instruction diagnostics. This repair adds those contracts and no adversarial review.

decisions.checkInstructions:
After owner ratification, use the same `wide_mul(3, 7)` program and complete portable helper in A and B.

For A, prove the spelling inventory: existing `--target`, `#Target(OS.*)`, web markers, `@build.os`, and function-body `@if`; proposed `Arch.<arch>`, `@build.target.arch`, and `@build.target.triple`; and no file-scope `@if`.

Exercise x86_64, aarch64, wasm32 web, unknown targets, selected reachable and selected unreachable assembly. Record parse, common checks, target-specific checks, availability, and emission for each row. Prove unselected assembly is unavailable and not target-checked, while shared names, signatures, unsafe gates, effects, and portable bodies remain checked.

decisions.title: Choose CPU and feature identity for native assembly
decisions.gist: How should Jet choose and record CPU features for native assembly?
decisions.lesson: A target names a platform, while CPU features name optional instructions within that target. Defaults must be explicit because native and cross builds differ. Choose host-native defaults with recorded identity or one portable baseline with explicit opt-in.
decisions.explainer: The CPU choice affects instruction validity, cache reuse, and whether a built program can launch. A canonical feature list uses `+name` and `-name` after CPU selection. The build records resolved values, not a vague `native` label. Web and JavaScript do not execute CPU-native bodies.
decisions.story: Priya builds wide_mul for her workstation, then copies it to another machine. The artifact must either record its required features and reject an incompatible launch or use a deliberate portable baseline.
decisions.inWild:
rustc -C target-cpu=native -C target-feature=+avx2,-avx512f
# https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/codegen-options/index.html#target-cpu
decisions.detail:
## Scope and current facts

This is independent of operand placement and target architecture. D-FFI-ASM-TARGET1 decides architecture composition. This ballot chooses CPU and feature identity only.

Current source shows different AOT behavior for host and cross builds. The parsed `--cpu` option does not yet provide one consuming contract, and build facts do not expose CPU or features. The flags and records below are proposed, not shipped.

## Glossary

A target triple names the operating-system, ABI, and architecture that the artifact must run under. The host is the machine running the compiler. A host build targets that host unless `--target` says otherwise. A cross build targets a different platform.

A CPU profile names a processor family and its instruction defaults. An instruction is one processor operation. A feature is an optional instruction-set capability, such as `avx2`.

A target registry lists names the selected toolchain can support. A supported feature name is present in that registry. An available feature is present on the runtime CPU or build machine. Supported and available are different facts.

An enabled feature is required or permitted by the artifact's generated code. A disabled feature is explicitly forbidden during generation. A machine may have a disabled feature; disabled does not mean physically absent.

`native` is a request to resolve the host CPU. It is never a cache identity. `baseline` is the selected target's host-independent portable CPU profile. It is not the `portable_wide_mul` source function.

An artifact is one produced image and its identity record. A cache identity decides whether that exact image can be reused. The target ABI is the binary calling and operating-system contract required at launch.

## Proposed selection and normalization law

The proposed flags are:

```text
--cpu <name>
--features <+name,-name,...>
```

CPU names and feature names come from the selected target toolchain registry. Names are lowercase canonical registry names. Feature edits apply in command order to the CPU's implied set, then become sorted unique enabled and disabled sets.

A repeated edit with the same sign is deduplicated. Opposite edits for one feature are a contradiction and fail. Unknown names, unavailable requested CPU profiles, and target-incompatible features fail before native generation. `native` is valid only when the selected target equals the host target. `baseline` is valid for the selected target and has no host-specific requirement.

The serialized resolved profile is:

```text
{ target_triple, target_abi, cpu, enabled_features, disabled_features }
```

The source closure, profile, backend, compiler, toolchain, and linker join that profile in the cache identity. Equivalent request spellings reuse one entry only when their resolved values are identical. A changed target, CPU, feature set, backend, compiler, toolchain, profile, linker, or source closure creates a different identity.

## Concrete resolution and cache example

This is an illustrative proposed resolution, not a measurement of the current workstation:

```text
request:       target=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, cpu=native,
               features=+avx2,-avx512f
host target:   x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
resolved CPU:  znver4
supported:     {avx2, avx512f, sse2}
available:     {avx2, sse2}
enabled:       {avx2, sse2}
disabled:      {avx512f}

cache identity:
source_closure=sha256:0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef
 target=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
 abi=gnu
 cpu=znver4
 enabled=[avx2,sse2]
 disabled=[avx512f]
 backend=aot
 compiler=jetc-owner-ballot
 toolchain=x86_64-target-registry
 profile=release
 linker=lld
```

The concrete CPU name, not `native`, appears in identity. Reordering `+avx2` and `-avx512f` reaches the same identity. Changing `--cpu=znver4` to `--cpu=baseline` creates a cache miss because the resolved CPU changes.

## Portable-baseline request

Option A keeps host-native defaults for a host build. To request a host-independent profile for the same x86-64 target, use the proposed reserved selector:

```text
jet build wide_mul.jet --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu --cpu=baseline
```

This asks for the selected target's portable CPU profile. It does not select the separate `portable_wide_mul` source implementation. CPU flags constrain instructions within the selected target; they never route target composition.

## Artifact compatibility

AOT launch requires matching resolved target architecture, platform and ABI, with every artifact-enabled feature available. JIT and interpreter invocation additionally require the engine’s local native-call capability. The recorded CPU name supplies code-generation defaults and cache identity. It is not an exact runtime model-name requirement.

Disabled features constrain generation but need not be absent from the machine. A newer same-target CPU may launch when it supplies every enabled feature. A weaker same-target CPU missing `avx2` rejects before execution. An artifact for another target architecture rejects even when its feature names overlap. Jet never chooses another artifact or silently falls back.

Inspection of a cross-target artifact reads the identified image and does not launch it. Web and JavaScript do not execute host CPU-native assembly. They select the explicit portable target implementation or report the target exclusion defined by D-FFI-ASM-TARGET1.

## One resolved record across engines

Resolution happens once after target selection and before backend choice. Jet serializes the resolved target, CPU, enabled set, and disabled set. AOT consumes that record before launch. JIT means Cranelift compiling native code while the program runs; it consumes the same record, not a fresh host default. The interpreter checks the same record before entering the checked native marshal boundary.

AOT and JIT lower the checked descriptor with that record. The interpreter either executes the portable implementation or enters native assembly only when the host satisfies the record. A missing engine capability is a compiler or applicability error, never an AOT fallback.

For the shared `wide_mul(3, 7)` program, every applicable engine returns `Product128{low: 21, high: 0}`. Web takes the portable target branch under the target ballot. A direct native body on web or incompatible hardware rejects before invocation.

## Option costs and honest performance boundary

Option A can use host-resolved instructions without explicit advanced flags on host builds. That may improve a workload, but this ballot claims no speed result. A creates more host-specific cache variants and may reject weaker same-target CPUs.

Option B uses one target baseline by default. It tends to improve reuse and deployment across CPUs that meet that target baseline, but may omit optional instructions until explicitly enabled. This is a portability and reproducibility property, not a measured speed claim.

Neither option makes x86-64 output runnable on another architecture. Both retain explicit CPU and feature opt-in, exact cache identity, launch rejection, and the same engine contract.

## Diagnostics and owner gates

Owner approval is required before these flags, profiles, or facts are implemented. New malformed, unknown, contradictory, unavailable, and incompatible selections use registered sema-owned diagnostics with source spans. Native tool stderr never becomes a Jet diagnostic.

A prototype must use the shared widening-multiply program and portable helper. Any performance decision requires a later matched candidate/plain gate. This ballot does not edit #3017 or decide target-selection syntax.

options.name: Resolved target profile
options.detail: Use host-native defaults for host builds, portable defaults for cross builds, and record the resolved CPU and feature set in every identity.
options.technical:
## A: resolved target profile

Proposed command, not shipped or executed:

```text
jet build wide_mul.jet --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu --cpu=native --features=+avx2,-avx512f
jet build wide_mul.jet --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu --cpu=baseline
```

On a host build, `native` resolves to a concrete CPU and feature set. On a cross build, the default is the target baseline. `baseline` is an explicit host-independent request for the same selected target. Neither request selects the separate `portable_wide_mul` source function.

The illustrative resolution for the first command is `cpu=znver4`, `enabled=[avx2,sse2]`, and `disabled=[avx512f]`. The profile record also includes the target triple and ABI. The cache identity adds source closure, backend, compiler, toolchain, profile, and linker.

AOT, host JIT/Cranelift, and the checked interpreter consume this one resolved record. A launch checks target ABI and available features. Missing enabled features reject, and no other artifact or baseline is selected. The shared program returns `Product128{low: 21, high: 0}` on every applicable engine. Web uses the portable target branch or rejects direct native use under D-FFI-ASM-TARGET1.

A is recommended because it keeps native capability while making cache and launch compatibility explicit. It may produce workload-specific improvements, but no speed result is promised.

options.name: Portable baseline by default
options.detail: Use the target baseline everywhere and require explicit CPU and feature flags for advanced native instructions.
options.technical:
## B: portable baseline by default

Proposed commands, not shipped or executed:

```text
jet build wide_mul.jet --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
jet build wide_mul.jet --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu --cpu=znver4 --features=+avx2
jet build wide_mul.jet --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu --cpu=baseline
```

With no CPU or feature flags, every build uses the selected target's portable CPU baseline, including a host build. Explicit `--cpu` and `--features` opt into advanced instructions. The resolved CPU and canonical enabled and disabled sets enter identity exactly as in A.

A target-baseline artifact launches on any same-ABI machine whose available features contain its enabled set. An explicit advanced artifact rejects when a required feature is missing. No host fallback or silent baseline substitution occurs. AOT, host JIT/Cranelift, and the checked interpreter consume the same resolved profile. The shared program returns `Product128{low: 21, high: 0}` on every applicable engine.

B is reproducible and broadly deployable within one target architecture. Native users must opt in to advanced instructions. This ballot claims no speed result; any performance choice needs a later matched candidate/plain gate.

Cross builds use a portable target profile.
Artifacts expose exact compatibility facts.

decisions.title: Keep typed JSON errors in HTTP
decisions.gist: Should HTTP JSON decoding keep the canonical field errors?
decisions.lesson: JSON decoding turns response text into a typed value. A field error names the bad field and explains the mismatch. The canonical Jet decoder has that detail, but the HTTP helper currently collapses it into InvalidFraming. A carries the field errors; B makes callers read text and decode separately. Both use the same decoder and transport.
decisions.story: Sam receives {"enabled":"yes"} while Config.enabled requires Bool. A’s one HTTP call exposes the field path and reason. B reads the body, calls the JSON decoder, and gets the same detail through a second step. A transport failure remains separate from this data error.
decisions.detail:
## Recommendation reasoning and contract notes

For Sam’s response, A keeps one convenient call while exposing the field path and reason. B retains today’s types but requires text handling before the same decoder can explain the error.

Option B: B leaves the convenient HTTP path lossy and shifts the extra read/decode steps to every caller. A preserves the canonical cause.

Contract note: A adds one distinct HTTPError case, so exhaustive consumers must handle data-validation failure separately from transport framing.

decisions.title: Release a plugin before its host stops
decisions.gist: Should a host release a plugin through Jet’s existing Close protocol?
decisions.lesson: A plugin is a separately loaded extension. A Close protocol is the existing operation for releasing an owned resource. The host can call checked exports today, but the public inventory does not show release. A releases one finished plugin; B keeps it until host shutdown. Both preserve authority checks, ownership and execution limits.
decisions.story: Mira’s editor stays open while a project extension finishes. The extension computes 6×7=42. A closes that plugin and continues editing; a later call through its handle fails as released. B leaves the finished instance allocated until the editor stops.
decisions.detail:
## Recommendation reasoning and contract notes

A lets Mira release the 42-producing extension without closing the editor. B avoids a call but retains finished resources until shutdown. Existing ownership rules make use after release invalid.

Option B: B cannot reclaim one finished extension while the host remains useful. A preserves host lifetime and makes release explicit.

Contract note: A adds an earlier lifetime boundary: the owner gains release, and any later call through that handle must fail before access.

options.name: Use the existing Close protocol
options.detail: Make Plugin participate in the existing Close protocol. The checked handle owns its live instance. Ordinary ownership rejects use after release. Existing scope cleanup may release it on earlier return or failure. The host can release a finished extension while continuing unrelated work.
options.technical:
Keep plugin.load, the frozen Component interface, canonical Authority and existing limits. Reuse the ordinary owned-resource and borrow rules, not a new ownership mechanism.

Plugin has one checked owner; the internal Copy u64 wrapper must not create independent source owners. close(^rules) consumes that owner under D-SHAPE-RESOURCE1/2; no new move syntax is introduced.

A live borrowed alias, bound export function or call prevents close until its existing loan ends. An owned task capture must be joined or otherwise settled through the existing task/lifetime law before the owner is closed; close does not secretly cancel unrelated tasks.

No new calls are admitted after closing starts. Once quiescent, release the instance exactly once.

Already-returned owned values remain valid. Borrowed views and bound functions cannot outlive the plugin owner.

Dynamic host-boundary stale handles fail with an ordinary invalid-handle error before accessing a store. No new syntax or I1-I9 exception is requested; if existing borrow rules cannot express this contract, return the ownership change to the owner rather than implementing a hidden mechanism.

options.name: Keep plugins until the host stops
options.detail: Document host lifetime as the only public release boundary. Do not expose runtime close. The host avoids a release operation but cannot reclaim a finished instance while unrelated host work continues.
options.technical: Keep the current load and checked call surface. Host termination releases all instances. This policy is unsuitable for claiming bounded repeated load/unload in a long-running host; that limitation must be public.

comparisons.note: lua_close destroys all objects in the state and closes active to-be-closed variables. C API manual is a source contract, not this campaign's runtime proof.
comparisons.code:
lua_close(state);
// https://www.lua.org/manual/5.4/manual.html#lua_close

comparisons.note: The embedding example finalizes the interpreter through Py_FinalizeEx. This is interpreter shutdown, not a claim of identical per-plugin isolation.
comparisons.code:
if (Py_FinalizeEx() < 0) return 120;
// https://docs.python.org/release/3.13.7/extending/embedding.html

whyNot.reason: B cannot reclaim one finished extension while the host remains useful. A preserves host lifetime and makes release explicit.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds an earlier lifetime boundary: the owner gains release, and any later call through that handle must fail before access.

decisions.title: Export an App HTTP contract
decisions.gist: Should web.openapi accept App directly, or require an HTTPRouter?
decisions.lesson: OpenAPI is a machine-readable description of an HTTP service. An App owns the checked action; an HTTPRouter is the existing projected route set. Today the captured function accepts HTTPRouter, not App. A accepts App directly; B asks for the router first. Both documents describe create-order: book returns order-41, empty sku returns sku_required, and internal_note stays private.
decisions.story: Maya owns one checked order action and needs a document for a client generator. She sends sku=book and expects order-41; an empty sku is rejected. A calls web.openapi(app) directly. B first obtains app.http_router(), then exports the same document. Neither adds a route or publishes the document.

options.name: Accept App directly
options.detail: Extend core.web.openapi to accept the existing checked App graph. Derive its public HTTP operation projection internally. Preserve the HTTPRouter input. The result is a document, not a new router value.

options.name: Expose the HTTP router first
options.detail: Add App.http_router() as an explicit checked projection, then use the existing core.web.openapi function. The projected router remains tied to App facts, not a copied registration store.

comparisons.note: Official Swagger introduction: https://docs.nestjs.com/openapi/introduction. Retained document APIs are real; the complete fixture is authored and NOT RUN.

recommendation.why: For Maya’s order document, A removes one conversion step while keeping book→order-41 and the sku_required rejection. B remains the route-first choice when another HTTP tool needs that router.

whyNot.reason: B adds a router value and call before the same document, without a demonstrated need for that value in this job.

recommendation.tradeoff: A chooses a direct document result. A reusable router remains a separate API question, not an implied return value.

decisions.title: Check an app's settings before it starts serving
decisions.situation: A Jet web app reads its settings, such as its port and its database address, from environment variables. Today nothing checks those settings before the app starts taking requests, so a missing value only shows up when a request needs it. On 2026-10-01 the owner chose that the framework checks a typed settings record before the app opens its port. This record writes that ruling down.
decisions.gist: Should a web app check its settings before it starts accepting requests?
decisions.lesson: A web app needs settings like a port number and a database address. If one is missing or wrong, the app should stop at startup with a clear error. The error names the setting and never prints a secret value. Option A makes the framework run this check for every app, so no author can forget it.
decisions.story: Sam deploys a web app and forgets to set the database address. The app starts, reports that it is ready, and the first sign-up request fails. Under option A the app refuses to start and prints which setting is missing.
decisions.detail:
Owner answer, 2026-10-01 chat (ask question s3086): "Framework checks before serve". The question asked, verbatim:

"#3086: Web apps read config from env vars. Should a missing/invalid config value stop the app before it starts accepting requests (with a redacted error naming the field)?"

The owner picked the first offered option, which was also the recommended one.

Today JetApp::serve (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/App.rs:1727) reads JET_APP_PORT and binds with no settings hook. env.decode already reports a bad value as E2416 with the field path and redacts secrets (Examples/features/io/app_config.jet). D-CONFIG-ENV1 stays an open spec import: this ruling does not choose a .env merge policy or a secret provider. Implementation and proof now ride on #3078, where #3086 was merged on 2026-10-04.

options.name: Framework checks before serve
options.detail: The app declares one typed settings record. JetApp.serve decodes and checks it before it binds the port. A missing or invalid value stops startup with E2416, which names the field path and hides secret values.
options.technical: Offered option text: "The app declares a typed config; JetApp.serve validates it before binding the port. Fail fast, can't forget." The hook reuses env.decode, so the field path and the redaction rule stay the ones app_config.jet already proves.

options.name: App calls env.decode itself
options.detail: A documented pattern: the app decodes its settings in run() before it calls serve. The framework adds nothing. An app that skips the step starts with missing settings.
options.technical: Offered option text: "Documented pattern: decode config in run() before serve. Less framework, easy to forget."

recommendation.why: Every app gets the check, so nobody can forget it, and the startup error looks the same in every app.

whyNot.reason: B depends on every author remembering one step, and a forgotten step only shows up in production.

losses.loss: serve gains one more parameter to learn.
losses.mitigation: Apps with no settings pass nothing and see no change.

recommendation.tradeoff: One small framework hook buys a settings check that no app can skip.

decisions.title: What a failed sandbox plugin call tells your program
decisions.situation: A Jet program can load a sandbox plugin, a separate program compiled to WebAssembly that runs walled off with only the rights and budgets the host lends it. When a call into it fails, Jet knows why: the plugin crashed, a right was refused, a budget such as running time ran out, or the host broke. Today all four causes reach your program as one line of text, so code that wants to offer "give it more time" must search that text. You are deciding whether a failed call returns a typed error with one named case per cause, or keeps the text with a fixed first word; we recommend the typed error.
decisions.gist: Should a failed plugin call tell your program the cause as a typed error, or as text?
decisions.lesson: A sandbox plugin is a separate WebAssembly program that Jet loads and calls, with only the rights and budgets the host lends it. A call can fail four ways: crash, refused right, spent budget, or host bug. A returns a PluginError value with one case per cause, plus where the plugin crashed. B keeps today's text, fixes its first word, and adds a helper to read it.
decisions.explainer:
A sandbox plugin is a separate program, compiled to WebAssembly, that a Jet program loads with plugin.load and calls like a library. It runs in its own memory and can only use the rights the host lends it, such as reading one folder.

The host also sets budgets for each call: how many instructions it may run, called fuel, how much memory it may use, and how long it may take.

A typed error is a value a function returns instead of its result when it fails. Its cases name the possible causes, and the caller matches on them, as Jet code already does for other errors.

A stack frame names one function that was running when a failure happened. A list of frames shows where inside the plugin a crash happened.
decisions.story: Lee's editor runs plugins that users install. When one plugin runs out of time, Lee wants to offer "give it more time". When another asks for a folder it was not lent, Lee wants to ask "allow access?". Today both reach Lee as the same kind of text message.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-04. The host runtime already sorts failures into four kinds: user-error, denied-authority, budget-exhausted and internal-defect (crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Prelude/Plugin.rs:66-82). It then flattens them into text: plugin_error writes E:kind:message (:227-229) and plugin_call_error adds the export name to the message (:231-236). A trap becomes guest trapped, and a fuel or interrupt trap becomes a budget failure (:1466-1505).

user-error is wider than a trap. It also covers rejected arguments and results (:1286-1361) and a component that fails to load (:1132-1147). It also covers a failed host operation the plugin asked for, such as a command it ran (:799-877). Plugin.rs captures no stack frames, and its engine keeps wasmtime's default backtrace settings (:239-244).

The decoder keeps everything after E: as one String (crates/jet-foundation/src/PluginWire.rs:88-91). The Jet checker types every export call as a Result whose error is String (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/Plugin.jet:135-143).

A failed plugin.load does not reach the program as a value today. The loaded handle has no Result type (Calls/Plugin.jet:25-27). The AOT bridge stops the program with E3001 (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/HandlesRaylib.rs:340-343). The JIT records a host fault (crates/jet-jit/src/Plugin.rs:582-588), and the interpreter route returns a diagnostic (:710-718). D-CORE-PLUGINPATH1=A and Examples/features/foundations/capabilities/run.jet:46-55 instead expect a bad component to fail on its first call.

Related law. D-PLUGIN1=A lends one Authority at load. D-CORE-PLUGINPATH1=A and D-CORE-PLUGINLIMITS1=A add typed loads and limits; D-CORE-PLUGINLIMITS1=A already says a spent budget names the limit and the export. D-SCRIPT-PLUGIN-CLOSE1=A releases plugins through Close. D-FAIL-CTX1=A records the host call site through the failure journey. D-FAIL-BREACH1=A makes every runtime stop a registered report. Under the 2026-10-01 freeze the checker change lands in the Jet compiler, and the runtime change is a runtime export.

What is the same in every option. Successful calls, rights checks and budgets behave as today. In every option a failed load is carried to the first call on every tier, as D-CORE-PLUGINPATH1=A and run.jet expect. It then follows that option's rule for its cause.

options.name: A typed PluginError, one case per cause
options.detail:
core.plugin gains #Error pub enum PluginError with four cases, one per kind the host already computes. Guest (today's user-error): the plugin trapped, or the host rejected its component, its values, or a host operation it asked for. Denied: the lent Authority refused a host import. Budget: a limit ran out, and the case names which one. Defect: the host or runtime failed.

Each case holds a PluginFault: the export that was called, the host's message, and up to 32 plugin frames, innermost first. A frame has the plugin function's name, its module and the code offset. The frame list is empty when no plugin code was running, for example a refused right, a rejected argument or a failed load; a trap always has at least one frame.

File and line from the plugin's debug information are left for a later step. They would make the runtime read and keep that information for every loaded plugin, and most plugins ship none.

Every export call returns T PluginError!. The host call site comes from the failure journey that every ? already records. A failed load reports through the first call with export "load".
options.technical:
pub struct PluginFrame { pub function: String, pub module: String, pub offset: Int }. pub struct PluginFault { pub export: String, pub message: String, pub frames: [PluginFrame] }. pub enum PluginLimit { Fuel, Memory, Table, Time, Wire }, where Wire is the 16 MiB argument and result budget. #Error pub enum PluginError { Guest(PluginFault), Denied(PluginFault), Budget(limit: PluginLimit, fault: PluginFault), Defect(PluginFault) }.

The runtime keeps its four kinds, captures wasmtime WasmBacktrace frames at the trap, and sends kind, limit and frames in the error wire. Calls/Plugin.jet:136 records Type PluginError instead of String. Display text keeps today's message, so callers that only print or use ?? are unchanged. When a plugin has no name section, function is empty and module plus offset still locate the frame. Optional file and line fields can join PluginFrame later without changing the cases.

options.name: Text with a fixed first word
options.detail:
The error stays a String. Its first word becomes a documented, stable kind: user-error, denied-authority, budget-exhausted or internal-defect. A helper, plugin.kind(text), reads that word back as a PluginKind value. Frames are appended to the text as extra lines.

No new error type is added, and code that prints the error keeps working. A program that needs the cause, the budget or a frame still parses text, now through a helper.
options.technical: Wire unchanged apart from the documented prefix and appended frame lines. pub enum PluginKind { User, Denied, Budget, Defect }; pub fn kind(text: String) -> PluginKind?. Which budget ran out stays inside the message text.

comparisons.note: A Rust host gets a typed Trap code, including OutOfFuel, and a WasmBacktrace with the guest's frames on the same error value.
Browsers throw a WebAssembly.RuntimeError for a guest trap, a separate type from host errors, with the wasm frames in its stack.

// https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/WebAssembly/JavaScript_interface/RuntimeError
try { instance.exports.check(ptr) } catch (e) { if (e instanceof WebAssembly.RuntimeError) console.log(e.stack) }

recommendation.why: The runtime already knows the cause, so A hands it over as a value instead of text. Each cause gets its own action, a crash shows which plugin function broke, and nothing needs parsing.
gains: A host can raise one budget, ask for one right, or report a crash by matching cases.
A plugin crash names the plugin function that broke.
The host call line comes from the failure journey Jet already records.

losses.loss: One new public error type, with three small records, in core.plugin.
losses.mitigation: They mirror the four kinds the runtime already computes, and code that only prints the error or passes it on with ?? needs no change.

losses.loss: Code that keeps the error as a String must convert it.
losses.mitigation: String interpolation renders today's message, and the compiler's type error points at each place that needs it.

whyNot.reason: B still makes programs read the cause and the spent budget out of text, now through a helper.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds one small public type. In return every failed plugin call says what happened and where.

decisions.title: Name the plugin frame's component field
decisions.situation: A plugin is a separate program that a Jet host calls with limited rights. Its failure report names the function and the component that contained it. The planned field name module is reserved by Jet, so ordinary code cannot use that record as written. The owner chose component rather than another identifier or changing which words may name fields.
decisions.gist: Should a plugin failure frame name its component with component, another identifier, or a reserved word?
decisions.lesson: A frame describes one function running when a plugin failed. Its component field identifies the loaded WebAssembly program; WebAssembly is the portable code format plugins use. A reserved word already has a language meaning, so Jet does not accept it as an ordinary field name.
decisions.explainer: Beginner path: read frame.component beside frame.function and frame.offset. Expert path: construct PluginFrame with function, component and offset, and use the same names when transporting failures. This changes a field name, not what information a frame carries. Shared work: update the record, all callers, examples and documentation together.
decisions.story: Lee displays a plugin crash and wants to label which component contained the failing function.
decisions.inWild:
// JavaScript illustration; not executed.
console.log(frame.component);
decisions.detail:
Owner chat on 2026-10-05 selected component for card #3115. This records an amendment to ratified D-PLUGIN-FAILURE1=A, not a new vote on typed failures. Its original technical record proposed pub module: String. The owner supplied this replacement: PluginFrame { pub function: String, pub component: String, pub offset: Int }.

Four offered spellings or policies are preserved below. To obey the three-option clarity limit, B groups the two ordinary-identifier alternatives, wasm_module and unit. They are distinct naming variants, not an instruction to expose both fields. C is the separate language-policy alternative. No runtime behavior was exercised by this ballot author.

options.name: Use component
options.detail: Name the field component. Keep the function name, component name and code offset already approved. Beginners read a plain label; experts need no special identifier rules.
options.technical: Amend only the module field spelling in D-PLUGIN-FAILURE1=A. Public shape: PluginFrame { pub function: String, pub component: String, pub offset: Int }. Remove module as a public field; add no alias. Migrate every constructor, field access, transport description, test and example.
options.code:
// Before: frame.module is a reserved-word field.
print(frame.component) // after: same component name

options.name: Use wasm_module or unit
options.detail: Both offered names avoid a language change. wasm_module explicitly names the code format; unit is shorter. Pick one, not two fields carrying the same value.
options.technical: The offered ordinary-identifier variants were wasm_module and unit. Each replaces module throughout PluginFrame's public API without changing its String value. Neither requires keyword field names. These are recorded alternatives, not compatibility names under A.

options.name: Allow reserved words as fields
options.detail: Keep module and permit reserved words in field declarations and access. The existing design wording survives, but the language must distinguish field names from keywords.
options.technical: Proposed, not current syntax: allow pub module: String in PluginFrame and frame.module at access sites. This alternative changes reserved-word handling rather than renaming the field. It was offered and rejected; A introduces no raw identifiers or keyword-field exception.
options.code:
// Before: this field access is not allowed.
print(frame.module) // after: allowed by the proposed rule

comparisons.note: JavaScript property access illustrates a named field, not a tested plugin contract.
comparisons.code: console.log(frame.component);

recommendation.why: Record the owner's choice: component names the value without changing the language.
gains: Plain field name.
No reserved-word exception.

losses.loss: The earlier record's spelling changes.
losses.mitigation: Replace it in all constructors, callers and examples in one cutover.

whyNot.reason: wasm_module ties the label to a code format; unit says less about the value.
Keeping one field name would require a broader language change.

recommendation.tradeoff: A focused rename instead of a language exception.

decisions.title: Default plugin sandbox instance cap
decisions.situation: A plugin is a separate program that runs inside a restricted host. One call can need more than one WebAssembly instance, a loaded copy of executable code. Passing text to a host function needs two, so the earlier limit of one prevents an ordinary call. The owner chose a default cap of four rather than two or eight, allowing some headroom while keeping a small bound.
decisions.gist: Should the default plugin sandbox allow four, two, or eight WebAssembly instances?
decisions.lesson: An instance is a loaded copy of WebAssembly code inside the sandbox. This cap counts instances, not plugin calls or running threads. A component can need several instances internally. The default sets the count limit; it does not reserve memory for every allowed instance.
decisions.explainer: Beginner path: use plugin calls normally; passing text must fit the default limit. Expert path: count the internal instances a component creates, not just its public exports. At the cap, another instance request is refused through the established plugin budget handling. Shared work: change the default and cover both ordinary text transfer and limit exhaustion. This vote does not change memory, time or other limits.
decisions.story: Lee's plugin sends text to a host function and needs the default sandbox to permit that ordinary call.
decisions.inWild:
// Wasmtime Rust configuration illustration; not executed.

decisions.detail:
Owner chat on 2026-10-05 selected four WebAssembly instances for card #3115. The offered alternatives were two and eight. Read-only Tower card evidence says the earlier default was one and String transfer to a host function needs two. Source inspection at crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Prelude/Plugin.rs:109-123 shows the instance-count field and earlier default of one. This ballot records the owner's default choice under D-PLUGIN-FAILURE1; it does not claim a runtime proof.

The examples reuse the same guest.check text call. Their comments describe the proposed cap, not a new Jet configuration API. No concurrency, throughput or memory-reservation guarantee follows from the chosen count.

options.name: Default to four
options.detail: Permit up to four instances in the default sandbox. Text transfer requiring two fits, with room for two more. Beginners need no special configuration; experts retain a small instance-count bound.
options.technical: Set the default plugin sandbox instance cap to 4. A request exceeding four instances must use the existing limit-failure behavior. Preserve all other budget defaults and public failure contracts. The count is not a maximum of four calls or four plugins.
options.code:
// Same call under the proposed four-instance cap:
guest.check("hello") // two-instance text transfer fits

options.name: Default to two
options.detail: Permit exactly the count needed by the known text-transfer case. This keeps the tightest offered default, but leaves no headroom for another internal instance.
options.technical: Set the default instance cap to 2 instead of 4. Requests needing a third instance fail through existing budget handling. All non-instance budgets and the same plugin call remain unchanged.
options.code:
// Same call under the proposed two-instance cap:
guest.check("hello") // fits; no extra instance headroom

options.name: Default to eight
options.detail: Permit more internal instances before reaching the cap. More components may fit unchanged, but the allowed count is twice the chosen bound.
options.technical: Set the default instance cap to 8 instead of 4. Requests needing a ninth instance fail through existing budget handling. Do not infer a measured performance gain or change other resource limits.
options.code:
// Same call under the proposed eight-instance cap:
guest.check("hello") // fits; six instances of headroom

comparisons.note: The instance-count builder illustrates the same kind of bound; this snippet was not executed.
comparisons.code: StoreLimitsBuilder::new().instances(4).build();

recommendation.why: Record the owner's choice: four permits known text transfer with modest headroom.
gains: The known two-instance call fits.
Small bounded headroom.

losses.loss: More instances are permitted than the minimum known case.
losses.mitigation: Keep the cap at four and retain independent memory, time and table limits.

whyNot.reason: Two fits the known case but leaves no instance headroom.
Eight doubles the allowed count without a stated need.

recommendation.tradeoff: A little headroom rather than the tightest or loosest offered bound.
