options.name: Stock explicit loader
options.detail: Extend the existing core.args configuration owner with a rooted, bounded JSON-layer operation. One stock operation owns include order, safe resolution, limits and origin paths. The loader reuses codec metadata and existing merge/validation ownership. Core must support a precise file-layer policy; it is not a zero-cost wrapper.
options.technical:
Home is existing core.args (whose current decode/merge rows are captured), not a new core.config tree.

Proposed load_json_layers<T>(paths:[Path], root:Path, include_key:String, limits:ConfigLimits=ConfigLimits.safe()) returns T on the ordinary fallible rail.

It retains [FieldError], EncodingError and IOError as structured causes rather than strings.

Paths are ordered JSON inputs; include_key is mandatory and designates the include member at each object.

String or ordered string-array include values load into that local object at encounter position; later fields/layers override earlier supplied fields.

Relative includes resolve against the containing file; absolute paths, root escape, symlink/reparse traversal and active-stack identity cycles fail before access beyond the root.

No hostname interpolation or raw-string path guessing: caller chooses concrete paths.

Defaults apply and required/unknown-field checks run on the final merged value through existing metadata; do not silently change CLI>environment>default precedence.

Load succeeds atomically only as a returned value, not as a filesystem snapshot.

Per-load file bytes are reused without a global cache.

Proposed ConfigLimits wraps EncodingLimits.safe(), with max_files=64, max_include_depth=32 and max_total_source_bytes=67108864.

Every source is required unless a different explicit caller operation has admitted its absence.

Error origins retain file/field/include-chain; secret field values are not diagnostic content.

Unsupported filesystem tiers reject this loader but retain pure codecs.

Do not interpret FileScope as a rooted capability without proving its existing contract.

Use native rooted open semantics or fail closed.

D-APP-ARGS1/D-CLI-FIELD-MARKERS1 stay unchanged; D-CONFIG-ENV1 is not ratified merge law.

All new namespaces, APIs and defaults here are unratified.

No new third-party dependency is approved; A is first-party implementation within Core unless explicitly stated otherwise.

Reuse current Codable, error, collection, lifetime and task mechanisms.

Source reading is not runtime proof; Main must preserve frozen/current provenance and obtain the named acceptance evidence.

decisions.gist: Should BSON preserve native typed values or accept only JSON-compatible values?
decisions.lesson: BSON carries values that JSON cannot preserve. A keeps them in format-specific typed records. B rejects them and exposes only JSON-compatible values. Neither adds a DataTree variant. Maintenance and distribution are separate votes; this vote defines both complete profiles now.

options.name: Preserve native typed values
options.detail: Keep native wire values through explicit format-specific types.
options.technical:
Common public API under the module selected by D-CORE-BSON1: decode<T>(bytes: [U8]) T ![FieldError]; encode<T>(value: T) [U8] !EncodingError; parse(bytes: [U8]) DataTree !EncodingError.

decode requires existing Decode support and encode requires existing Encode support.

Reader/writer use the existing consumed FileReader/FileWriter constructors, EncodingLimits.safe default, next/write/flush/finish, terminal-error and value-boundary law.

No second limit/error/IO model or implicit allocation queue.

Every root consumes exactly one complete value; malformed/trailing data errors before success.

Encoded output is owned; decoded variable-width values are owned and do not retain caller input.

BSON1.1 is the fixed typed codec profile.

One complete document root is required.

Typed decode<T:Decode>([U8]) returns T on the existing [FieldError] rail; encode<T:Encode>(T) returns owned [U8] !EncodingError.

Matching reader/writer and explicit-limit/caller-buffer operations reuse existing finish, value-boundary and ownership law.

BSON int32/int64 use exact Int with checked target bounds; double uses Float with explicit target checks; UTF-8 strings, Bool, Null, arrays and string-key records/maps use canonical codec metadata.

Module-local native types preserve identity through existing typed codec customization.

Binary carries subtype U8 and owned bytes; ObjectId carries exactly12 bytes.

Timestamp carries two U32 values; Regex carries pattern and options strings.

JavaScript carries inert source; JavaScriptScope<T> also carries document scope.

Decimal128 carries an exact16-byte IEEE754-2008 decimal128 payload.

DateTime maps signed64 milliseconds since epoch to Instant only if exact and in range.

MinKey/MaxKey/Undefined/DBPointer are explicit Unsupported in typed ordinary profile, never skipped as successful values.

All defined wire categories, including rejected ones, are fully bounds-validated.

Binary subtypes preserve subtype and payload; subtype-specific invalid payloads reject.

decisions.title: Keep SQLite JSONB at the database boundary
decisions.gist: Should SQLite JSONB remain an opaque database value or become a standalone Core codec?
decisions.lesson: SQLite recommends treating JSONB as an opaque database blob. Glaze exposes byte-level encoding, but that does not make an internal format a general interchange promise. The owner should decide this separately from ordinary JSON support.
decisions.story: Mira needs the specific interchange or application result shown here. She should choose its ownership once, rather than rebuild the same policy at every call.

options.name: Keep the SQLite boundary
options.detail: Do not add standalone Core JSONB; use the already selected SQLite connection for its opaque value. Core does not promise a portable internal-database wire format. Existing JSON metadata still handles the application record. A standalone JSONB producer cannot bypass SQLite conversion through Core.
options.technical:
A adds no API, parser, dependency or SQLite installation; applications already choosing SQLite use its json/jsonb functions through their existing binding.

The SQL snippet is a source-grounded worked operation, not a claim that a particular current Jet database wrapper or SQLite executable ran.

B explicitly proposes core.encoding.jsonb parse/decode/encode and shared bounded reader/writer behavior.

B uses the SQLite JSONB grammar retained in binary-profiles.md on2026-09-11.

It accepts codes0..12 and rejects reserved13..15.

It checks 1/2/3/5/9-byte headers, big-endian extended sizes, all four text encodings, byte-sized container payloads and trailing data.

No PostgreSQL compatibility or blanket future-SQLite promise.

Accept valid nonminimal headers; do not make Glaze-specific minimality prose normative.

Integers retain exact payload text until target consumption, without Glaze int64/uint64 intermediate limitation; invalid/nonfinite/unrepresentable targets error.

Format-required JSON5 numeric/text normalization must be specified from that retained grammar, not guessed from ordinary JSON defaults.

Preserve current Codable/FieldError and closed DataTree; no type-tag/data-tree fork.

Malformed input deterministically errors even though SQLite documents garbage-in/garbage-out latitude.

Cross-version SQLite interoperability and extension-reserved behavior need exact receipts before a compatibility claim.

decisions.title: Support the exact BEVE Version2 profile
decisions.gist: Should Core support BEVE Version2 through its existing encoding model?
decisions.lesson: BEVE adds compact typed arrays and explicit numeric widths to a JSON-like format. Its version, endianness, extension rules and precision boundaries must be part of the contract rather than a speed slogan.

options.name: Stock Version2 adapter
options.detail: Add core.encoding.beve with the exact Version2 wire profile and checked typed projection. A compact existing interchange format uses the same Core typed boundary. Width and layout are explicit rather than silently approximated. Core must maintain numeric-width, typed-array and extension compatibility.
options.technical:
Exact profile is official BEVE Version2 retained in binary-profiles.md on2026-09-11, corroborated by Glaze v8.3.0 header constants.

No unseen BEVE main commit is claimed.

Wire is little-endian with low-three-bit base tags, compressed counts using low-two-bit size selector and value shifted by2, headerless typed keys/elements, string UTF-8, zero reserved bits and Version2 extension IDs.

Add parse/decode/encode, reader/writer and header inspection under core.encoding.beve; keep shared EncodingLimits/Error/DataTree and module-local handles.

Ordinary encoding emits Version2 only.

Extension1 is reserved for legacy Version1 type tags and cannot be repurposed or emitted by Version2.

Legacy reads must use an explicitly identified typed Version1 operation with the required enum schema; no silent case-order reinterpretation in the default Version2 path.

Native numeric widths, typed arrays and object key kinds retain declared types.

Unrepresentable untyped projections, unsupported float widths or extensions return Unsupported.

They never lose precision, convert integer keys to strings or widen DataTree.

Supported wider typed integers use existing Int storage and exact target bounds.

Matrix/complex/aligned-array extensions require native shape/layout evidence and are tracked by CORE-F075; this ballot does not declare a parallel matrix runtime.

Header inspection returns validated kind/count/header_bytes for a supplied byte span and offset without claiming complete payload validation.

Fully decoding requires complete input/trailing checks.

All lengths, padding, multiplication and allocation are checked under the shared limits; no unchecked view is exposed by a read helper.

A adopts no Glaze/Eigen/runtime dependency.

Performance and zero-copy claims remain unmeasured.

decisions.title: Convert standalone ETF to a checked JSON view
decisions.gist: Should Core provide an explicitly one-way ETF-to-JSON conversion?
decisions.lesson: ETF contains more than JSON: atoms, lists, process identities and executable-function descriptions have distinct meanings. A useful JSON view must define losses and reject unsupported identities, not advertise a complete bidirectional codec.
decisions.story: Mira needs the specific interchange or application result shown here. She should choose its ownership once, rather than rebuild the same policy at every call.

options.name: Stock one-way view
options.detail: Add core.encoding.eetf.to_json with an exact standalone ETF profile and no Erlang dependency. Simple BEAM-produced data can use a stock checked interchange boundary. Runtime identities and distribution state are not silently serialized as ordinary values. Conversion is deliberately one-way and cannot preserve the complete ETF domain.
options.technical:
Exact profile: standalone ETF version131 as documented by OTP29.0.6/ERTS17.0.6, not node distribution or LOCAL_EXT.

to_json([U8], limits:EncodingLimits=...) -> String !EncodingError fully validates one term and trailing bytes.

Integers/bignums stay exact; finite floats use the current JSON writer.

Atoms true/false become booleans; other atoms become text.

Proper lists, NIL and tuples become arrays; STRING_EXT is the same byte-list value as LIST_EXT, so value projection is an integer array regardless of wire optimization.

Binary values become Base64 text explicitly; non-byte-aligned bitstrings are Unsupported.

Map keys may be atoms, UTF-8 binaries or proper Unicode-scalar lists converted to strings; reject other keys and collisions after conversion, even if their original ETF types differ.

Key text decoding must be strict, and invalid scalar/UTF-8 input is an error.

Process/port/reference/fun/export/native-record/local/cache-reference terms are Unsupported; do not invoke them or manufacture a parallel public Term tree.

Decode deprecated numeric/atom encodings only where the OTP profile still defines them.

Recognize compressed tag80 with bounded declared and actual decompressed size; use approved existing compression machinery, not an implicit Erlang/Glaze dependency.

Reject distribution headers by framing context, not by globally rejecting byte70, which also denotes a standalone NEW_FLOAT_EXT.

Charge input, decoded expansion and retained output to existing limits without repurposing XML-only expansion fields; bound decompressed size by max_item_bytes and count compressed wire bytes under max_total_bytes.

No writer, typed ETF round trip or all-term identity claim is part of this conversion.

Any richer native-term library, dependency or distributed-node runtime needs a separate proposal.

decisions.title: Support typed ETF values without a node runtime
decisions.gist: Should Core read and write typed ETF values, independently of its JSON view?
decisions.lesson: ETF preserves atoms, tuples and binary values that a JSON view cannot. Glaze provides typed readers and writers with separate limits and gaps. Keep native values typed and reject unsupported identities.
decisions.story: Mira exchanges typed configuration with a BEAM service. She needs ordinary records and native values without starting a node or erasing their meanings through JSON.

options.name: Stock typed ETF codec
options.detail: Add checked ETF read/write through the existing Core typed encoding model. BEAM interchange can retain types beyond a JSON view. One stock adapter owns bounds and precise failure behavior. Core must maintain native term mappings and two record layouts.
options.technical:
A independently adds a typed codec under core.encoding.eetf; D-CORE-EETF1 remains the separately decidable lossy JSON-view operation.

The wire profile is standalone ETF version131 documented by OTP29.0.6, not distribution, local terms or a BEAM node.

Proposed decode<T:Decode>(bytes:[U8], layout:Layout=Map, strings:StringEncoding=Utf8Binary, byte_arrays:ByteEncoding=Binary, limits:EncodingLimits=safe()) returns T on the existing typed FieldError rail.

Proposed encode<T:Encode> accepts the same layout/encoding controls and returns owned bytes on EncodingError.

Matching reader/writer and caller-buffer operations reuse the same adapter and current opaque-handle/error/limit contracts; no borrowed view escapes by default.

Layout is Map or Proplist and applies to records/maps.

Record keys use UTF-8 atoms from canonical known field names; reads also accept strictly decoded binary/list text keys, reject duplicate names after normalization and apply existing field metadata.

Map key types stay typed.

StringEncoding is Utf8Binary or Utf8ByteList: the latter interprets STRING_EXT/LIST_EXT as UTF-8 bytes, not a guess at Unicode codepoints.

ByteEncoding is Binary or List; this explicitly separates a byte array from an ETF byte list.

General lists, fixed tuples and exact integral values preserve their native shape; tuple arity and target bounds are checked.

Int uses exact bignum storage rather than a long/longlong intermediary.

Finite float widths must be exact for the target.

Module-local Atom is an owned validated text value with at most255 Unicode characters; it uses ordinary codec customization, never a parallel public Term/DataTree.

Atom true/false are boolean only when the target is Bool; an Atom target preserves them as atoms.

Ordinary strings never become dynamically interned atoms.

Optional/enum/variant coding must use the existing canonical metadata representation and explicit tags, never Glaze’s untagged active-alternative guessing.

All such mappings must be documented before shipping; unsupported metadata shapes fail rather than silently change tags.

Native process/port/reference/fun/export/local/cache/record-extension terms, improper lists and non-byte-aligned bitstrings are Unsupported in this data profile.

Untyped DataTree/event projection rejects native categories it cannot represent without loss.

A typed native hook must reuse the existing codec customization mechanism (CORE-F007), not add a second global event algebra.

Whole-value reads reject trailing bytes; framed readers validate each standalone version header and follow existing value-boundary semantics.

Shared limits charge all wire bytes, lengths, skipped subtrees, decoded expansion, allocation and output; bound skip recursion too.

Checked arithmetic precedes every resize, arity conversion and size multiplication.

Never inherit external ei_skip_term recursion, unchecked int casts or C-string truncation by assumption.

Embedded NULs and UTF-8 round trips are required.

Compressed input uses only approved compression machinery with declared and actual expansion bounds.

A is first-party Core code, not implicit Glaze/erl_interface/Erlang runtime adoption.

D-ENCBIN1’s existing CBOR decision is not reopened.

Exact input COUNT-ETF-131-ATOM in derived-binary-fixtures.json is analyst-derived from normative tags, not copied peer output.

Output may choose an equivalent permitted integer/atom encoding; compare typed meaning and explicit wire-policy cases, not arbitrary byte identity.

All new namespaces, APIs and defaults here are unratified.

No new third-party dependency is approved; A is first-party implementation within Core unless explicitly stated otherwise.

Reuse current Codable, error, collection, lifetime and task mechanisms.

Source reading is not runtime proof; Main must preserve frozen/current provenance and obtain the named acceptance evidence.

Readers accept deprecated atom/numeric encodings only where the retained OTP profile still defines them; writers emit UTF-8 atoms and current finite-float/integer encodings.

The new adapter has an ETF EncodingFormat identity but reuses existing EncodingErrorKind/FieldError meanings.

PublishedSchema must preserve every unknown field representable in its existing carrier; unsupported native unknown values error rather than disappear or widen that carrier.

Domain-specific external variant tags use the existing custom-codec mechanism, not automatic trial decoding.

Retained source contract metadata follows. It is provenance, not an additional choice.

The selected option above controls adoption and scope; other option contracts remain inactive.

decisions.title: Where the in-memory text and byte buffers live
decisions.gist: Should the StringBuf and BytesBuf buffers be dropped, since Bytes already does their job, so that core.io stays retired?
decisions.lesson: `core.io` was retired on 2026-08-06. A later commit brought it back to hold two buffers copied from Python's StringIO and BytesIO. The built-in `Bytes` type already covers them. It grows to a set capacity, appends with `write`, and reads back from a cursor with `seek`, `rewind`, and `read_string`. `Reader` and `Writer` already live in `core.term`. The question is whether a second pair of buffers earns a module.
decisions.story: Omar ports a Python script that collects log lines in an `io.StringIO`, prints them, and then reads the first word back. He finds `core.io.StringBuf` and `Bytes`, which do the same thing with different calls. The retirement check also fails, because `core.io` was retired.

options.name: Drop the buffers; use Bytes
options.detail:
Delete `Core/io/io.jet`, which holds StringBuf and BytesBuf. Also delete its 40 generated files under `tests/conformance/corpus/core/io/` and its Prelude `Core.jet` rows. Delete its `CoreCallRows` and `RingLayer` rows too, plus the unused `use core.io as io` line in `Jetpack/Foundation/Source/CoreImports.jet`. The `core.io` retirement row then reads zero.

Today's `Bytes` already has `Bytes.new()`, `Bytes.with_capacity(n)`, `capacity()`, `len()`, `write(bytes)`, and typed writes such as `write_u32_le`. It reads with `position()`, `seek(n)`, `rewind()`, `read_bytes(n)`, `read_string(n)`, `read_byte()`, and `eof()`. It converts with `lines()`, `to_string()`, and `to_bytes()`, and has `flush()` and `close()`.

`String` has no capacity or append call. Text is built with interpolation such as `"{log}done\n"`, or as a list of lines joined at the end. `Cursor.over(text)` reads text in pieces with `take_until` and `skip_ws`.

The spec entries D-COREIO1 and D-NETIO-CONTRACT1 still name `core.io.Reader` and `core.io.Writer`. The code already has them in `core.term`, so those entries get a note pointing there.
options.technical: Every call in the code sample ran under `jet run` on 2026-09-30 and printed `start`, `done`, and `first word: start`. `Bytes` writes in place (`&buf`). StringBuf returns a new buffer on each write, copying every byte each time. Python's `seek(offset, whence)` has no three-way origin on `Bytes`; `seek(n)` takes one position. Outside the generated conformance files, the only `core.io` use is an import line in Jetpack that no code calls.
options.code:
fn run() {
    buf := Bytes.with_capacity(64)
    &buf.write("start\n".bytes())
    &buf.write("done\n".bytes())
    print(buf.to_string())
    &buf.rewind()
    first :: &buf.read_string(5) ?? ""
    print("first word: {first}")
}

options.name: Move them to core.text and a new core.bytes
options.detail: StringBuf and its functions move into `core.text`. BytesBuf moves into a new `core.bytes` module. The 40 conformance files, registry rows, and the Jetpack import are rewritten to the new paths. The spec entries get the same note as in A.
options.technical: `core.bytes` does not exist today, so this adds a module. The prelude `Bytes` type and `BytesBuf` would both stay as byte buffers with different call styles: in-place methods on one, copy-returning functions on the other.
options.code:
use core.text as text

fn run() {
    buf := text.string_empty()
    buf = text.write_line(buf, "start") ?? return
    buf = text.write_line(buf, "done") ?? return
    print(text.getvalue(buf))
}

options.name: Bring core.io back
options.detail: Remove the `core.io` retirement row and change D-CORE-TREE1 so `core.io` is a live module again. It holds the buffers, and `Reader` and `Writer` move back from `core.term` so the old spec names become true.
options.technical: This partly reverses D-CORE-TREE1=A, ratified 2026-08-06, which sent `core.io` names to `core.term`, `core.process`, or the prelude. Code that uses `Reader` and `Writer` from `core.term` must move.
options.code:
use core.io as io

fn run() {
    buf := io.string_empty()
    buf = io.write_line(buf, "start") ?? return
    buf = io.write_line(buf, "done") ?? return
    print(io.getvalue(buf))
}

comparisons.note: Python keeps separate in-memory text and byte streams in `io`. That is the model StringBuf and BytesBuf copy. https://docs.python.org/3/library/io.html#io.StringIO
comparisons.code:

buf.write("start\n")
print(buf.getvalue())

comparisons.note: Go puts a builder in each of `strings` and `bytes`, the shape of option B. https://pkg.go.dev/bytes#Buffer
comparisons.code:
var b strings.Builder
b.WriteString("start\n")
fmt.Print(b.String())

whyNot.reason: B keeps two byte buffers and adds a module named like a type.
C reverses a ratified retirement to keep a duplicate.

recommendation.tradeoff: Python-style names are given up so there is one buffer to learn.

decisions.title: One double-ended queue: Queue or Deque
decisions.gist: Should the built-in `Queue` be the only double-ended queue, with `core.collections.Deque` removed?
decisions.lesson: On 2026-08-05 the double-ended queue was renamed from `Deque` to `Queue`. Later, `core.collections` added a new `Deque` copied from Python. It holds only text, and every push returns a copied deque. The built-in `Queue<T>` holds any type and changes in place. It pushes, pops, and peeks at both ends. Nothing outside its own generated tests uses `Deque`.
decisions.story: Lena writes a job scheduler. Urgent jobs go in at the front, normal jobs at the back. She finds both `Queue` and `core.collections.Deque` and cannot tell which one to use. The retirement check fails too, because `Deque` is a retired name.

options.name: Keep only Queue
options.detail:
Delete `Deque` from `Core/collections/collections.jet`, along with `deque`, `deque_from`, `deque_len`, `deque_is_empty`, `append`, `appendleft`, `pop`, `popleft`, `peek`, `peekleft`, `extend`, `extendleft`, `rotate`, and `deque_items`. Delete their 14 generated files under `tests/conformance/corpus/core/collections/`. Also delete the `Deque` entries in the `CoreCallRows` export row and `CoreHostSignatures`. The `Deque` retirement row then reads zero.

`Queue<T>` already has `Queue.new()`, `Queue.init(xs)`, `push_front`, `push_back`, `pop_front`, `pop_back`, `peek_front`, and `peek_back`. It also has `get`, `contains`, `len`, `capacity`, `is_empty`, `to_list`, `join`, `split`, `reverse`, `delete`, and `clear`.

`Queue` has no `rotate` or `extend`. A rotate is a `pop_back` then `push_front`, as in the sample. An extend is a loop of `push_back`. No code outside the generated tests calls either one, so no `Queue` methods are added.
options.technical: The sample ran under `jet run` on 2026-09-30 and printed `a` and `[c, b]`, the same as the current `Deque` program. `Queue` is a ring buffer with in-place `&self` methods. `Deque` copies its whole list on each `append`. Research note 3281 also lists `Counter`, `OrderedMap`, `Chain`, and `StringSet` as duplicates. They are out of scope here.
options.code:
fn run() {
    q := Queue.init(["b", "c"])
    &q.push_front("a")
    front :: &q.pop_front() ?? "-"
    print(front)
    last :: &q.pop_back() ?? "-"
    &q.push_front(last)
    print(q.to_list())
}

options.name: Keep only Deque
options.detail: Reverse D-COLLNAME1=A: the built-in `Queue<T>` is renamed back to `Deque<T>` with the same methods. The text-only `core.collections.Deque` is deleted, and every `Queue` use is rewritten.
options.technical: The retirement row flips direction, so `Queue` becomes the retired spelling. The formatter's rename edit flips too. Examples, docs, and generated tests that say `Queue` are all rewritten.
options.code:
fn run() {
    d := Deque.init(["b", "c"])
    &d.push_front("a")
    front :: &d.pop_front() ?? "-"
    print(front)
    last :: &d.pop_back() ?? "-"
    &d.push_front(last)
    print(d.to_list())
}

options.name: Keep both, with separate roles
options.detail: `Queue<T>` stays the in-place queue. `core.collections.Deque` stays as a text-only queue that returns a new copy on each change. The docs explain when to use each one.
options.technical: The `Deque` retirement row is deleted, which partly reverses D-COLLNAME1=A. A later request for a generic copy-returning `Deque<T>` would grow a second full queue API.

    &q.push_front("a")
    d :: api.appendleft(api.deque_from([String]{"b", "c"}), "a")
    print(q.to_list())
    print(api.deque_items(d))
}

decisions.title: Support an explicit INI configuration profile
decisions.gist: Should Core read and write INI configuration through its existing encoding family?
decisions.lesson: INI is still a common configuration interchange job. It needs a stated profile: section names, key normalization, duplicates, interpolation and textual scalar conversion cannot be guessed from a generic format label.
decisions.story: Mira needs the specific interchange or application result shown here. She should choose its ownership once, rather than rebuild the same policy at every call.
decisions.inWild:
import configparser
p = configparser.ConfigParser(interpolation=None)
p.optionxform = str
p.read_string("[server]\ncount=2\n")
print(p.getint("server", "count")) # Expected2; not run.
// Primary source: https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.13.2/Doc/library/configparser.rst. This matched usage is source-grounded illustration, not an executed peer receipt; the captured page supplies the actual API contract.
// The full body is an authored, unexecuted workload adaptation; the retained source ballot preserves the original excerpt.

options.name: Stock INI adapter
options.detail: Add core.encoding.ini with strict raw parsing and explicit interpolation operations. Existing INI files cross one typed, bounded codec boundary. Raw input does not silently interpolate environment or normalize keys. Core must define and maintain one INI dialect and conversion profile.
options.technical:
Home core.encoding.ini.

parse/to_string and typed decode use canonical DataTree/Codable and ordinary encoding/field errors; no IniTree.

Raw parse returns an Object of section Objects with Text values, preserving spelling/order.

Require named sections, key=value or key:value delimiters, whole-line #/; comments, no inline comments, indentation-based multiline values and no valueless options.

Reject duplicate section/option names in one input, malformed continuation and invalid UTF-8.

Names are case-sensitive by default (the matched Python example explicitly selects this); do not lowercase a public field silently.

DEFAULT is a documented reserved defaults section, inherited at lookup/typed section decode without mutating raw stored sections.

Typed decode converts text according to the declared scalar type; parse never guesses types.

Int accepts exact signed decimal values; Float accepts finite decimal values.

Bool accepts case-insensitive 1/yes/true/on and 0/no/false/off; String stays text.

Target mismatch/overflow accumulates FieldError.

Explicit decode_interpolated uses BasicInterpolation %(name)s/%%; decode_interpolated_extended uses ${section:key}/$$ and their documented same-section/default lookup.

No process environment, file discovery or custom arbitrary converter callbacks.

Existing typed user Decode handles custom types.

Interpolation cycle/missing/syntax errors preserve key path and source; max interpolation depth32 and produced bytes8388608 are explicit IniLimits fields wrapping shared EncodingLimits, not a silent reassignment of XML-only expansion budgets.

Writer emits deterministic parseable text but does not claim comment-preserving source edits.

Shared reader/writer mode remains the same format and must obey encoding ownership/finish law; ordinary file merging belongs to explicit config loader, not this pure codec.

The WinRegistry extended-value dialect and legacy unsafe RawConfigParser mutation are not adopted.

All new namespaces, APIs and defaults here are unratified.

No new third-party dependency is approved; A is first-party implementation within Core unless explicitly stated otherwise.

Reuse current Codable, error, collection, lifetime and task mechanisms.

Source reading is not runtime proof; Main must preserve frozen/current provenance and obtain the named acceptance evidence.

Retained source contract metadata follows. It is provenance, not an additional choice.

The selected option above controls adoption and scope; other option contracts remain inactive.

options.technical:
Home core.encoding.plist.

to_string is XML output; encode is binary bytes; typed decode accepts the explicit String/XML or byte-input XML/binary form.

Byte input recognizes only documented plist signatures and fully validates the selected representation; no fallback to a different parser after malformed input.

Typed support includes String, Bool, Int, Float, lists, string-key records/maps, [U8], Instant and a module-local PlistUID wrapping U64.

Binary UID range is0..2^64-1; XML output of UID is Unsupported.

Instant is an absolute UTC value, not an ambient-zone conversion.

Binary numeric-width errors are checked before output; retain exact Int until the selected format width is applied.

The format byte grammar and cross-version boundary corpus must be attached before implementation claims; the captured Python docs alone do not prove every binary width.

Untyped parse returns the existing DataTree only for representable categories.

Bytes/date/UID without a canonical DataTree category return Unsupported.

They never widen the closed algebra, tag ordinary strings or silently lose identity.

Native values remain available through typed decode/encode.

DataEvent stream projection likewise rejects nonrepresentable native categories; this does not claim a richer native event algebra.

Shared limits/ownership/errors remain under core.encoding, with plist handles local.

Reject unknown XML elements rather than copy Python silent ignoring; disable external entities/network fetch and reject malformed binary offsets, cycles, excessive counts/depth and non-string dictionary keys.

Preserve insertion order in ordinary output, with canonical ordering only through an explicit canonical operation if separately needed.

No Core-wide sorting/skipkeys default changes.

All new namespaces, APIs and defaults here are unratified.

No new third-party dependency is approved; A is first-party implementation within Core unless explicitly stated otherwise.

Reuse current Codable, error, collection, lifetime and task mechanisms.

Source reading is not runtime proof; Main must preserve frozen/current provenance and obtain the named acceptance evidence.

decisions.title: Read and write basic WAV sound files in Core
decisions.situation: A Jet game can load a sound today only through the raylib binding, so a game cannot read its own sound files without it. WAV is the simple sound file most games ship. On 2026-10-01 the owner chose a small WAV reader and writer written in Jet, kept with the Core game assets, with no audio processing. This record writes that ruling down.
decisions.gist: Should Core read and write basic WAV sound files as ordinary game assets?
decisions.lesson: A WAV file is a short header followed by raw sound samples. Reading one is plain file parsing, not audio processing. Option A puts a small, size-limited WAV reader and writer in Core next to the other game assets. The raylib binding can still load and play sounds.
decisions.story: Mia's game ships a jump.wav file. Today the game must load it through raylib, even in a headless test that only checks the file's length. Under option A the test reads the file with Core and checks the sample count.
decisions.inWild:
import wave

with wave.open("jump.wav", "rb") as clip:
    rate = clip.getframerate()
    frames = clip.readframes(1024)  # streams in chunks
# Python ships a WAV reader in its standard library.
# Source: docs.python.org/3/library/wave.html.
decisions.detail:
Owner answer, 2026-10-01 chat (ask question s3287): "Bounded WAV in Core (core.game assets)". The question asked, verbatim:

"#3287: Should Core read/write basic WAV audio files (PCM16/float32, streaming, no audio processing) as ordinary game assets, so games don't depend on raylib to load a sound? Fits your plan for a Jet-native raylib equivalent."

The owner picked the first offered option, which was also the recommended one. Earlier the same day the owner wrote that a raylib binding is "second party" and that a Jet-native first-party raylib equivalent is wanted at some point.

Today audio exists only as the raylib provider: RaylibSound and load_sound/play_sound in Core/game/raylib.jet:100-106. No WAV or RIFF parser exists under Core/. Core/encoding/binary.jet already has the little-endian byte helpers. scene.assets.sound is the ratified sound entry point (D-GAME-ASSET1=A). Implementation and proof now ride on #238 criterion 15, where #3287 was merged on 2026-10-04.

options.name: Bounded WAV in Core (core.game assets)
options.detail: A minimal WAV reader and writer written in Jet, kept with the Core game assets. It handles PCM16 and float32 samples, streams large files in chunks and enforces size limits. It does no audio processing.
options.technical: Offered option text: "Minimal reader/writer in Jet; raylib binding can still load sounds." The planned module is core.game.wav with read(bytes, limits) and write(clip). It reuses Core/encoding/binary.jet and rejects compressed or truncated files with a typed error.
options.code:
use core.files as fs
use core.game.wav as wav

fn run() {
    bytes :: fs.read_bytes("assets/jump.wav") ?? panic("read")
    clip :: wav.read(bytes) ?? panic("not a WAV file")
    print(clip.rate)
}

options.detail: Sound files load only through the raylib binding. Core never parses audio files.
options.technical: Offered option text: "Audio assets only through the raylib binding." This is today's state: load_sound in Core/game/raylib.jet.

options.detail: WAV support lives in a separate package, not in Core. Games add that package when they need it.
options.technical: Offered option text: "Not in Core."

options.name: Stock local catalog
options.detail: Add core.text.catalog with bounded GNU .mo parsing and explicit lookup/fallback objects. One stock boundary handles context/plurals/catalog errors. Languages and fallback order are explicit values, not global state. Core owns catalog parsing and plural-expression compatibility.
options.technical:
Home core.text.catalog, distinct from existing core.text.fmt.plural without replacing it.

parse([U8], limits:CatalogLimits=...) returns immutable Catalog or CatalogError; read bytes through existing files when IO is needed.

Catalog methods gettext, ngettext, pgettext and npgettext follow captured GNU lookup, context and plural semantics.

with_fallback(Catalog) returns an immutable ordered fallback chain; no process-global domain, builtins installation, environment lookup or implicit filesystem search.

Missing entries preserve source text / n==1 singular fallback, while malformed or missing required catalog input is an error.

Decode big/little-endian GNU .mo, honor its declared charset through current encoding ownership, reject unsupported charset/version rather than silently corrupt text.

Plural formulas use a bounded dedicated expression evaluator, not eval of Jet/Python/C; grammar and source corpus must be retained, and evaluation errors remain typed rather than silently using English.

Defaults: input bytes16777216, entries1000000, fallback depth32, plural expression bytes4096/nesting64/work units100000.

Arithmetic/zero division/out-of-range plural index must return a structured catalog error or fail catalog admission, never execute code.

Catalog parse owns retained bytes/index data; no mandatory global cache.

Extraction and .po/.mo compilation tools are separate tooling work, not secretly bundled dependencies.

This ballot approves no replacement CLDR/locale numeric/time subsystem or Solaris .mo dialect.

All new namespaces, APIs and defaults here are unratified.

No new third-party dependency is approved; A is first-party implementation within Core unless explicitly stated otherwise.

Reuse current Codable, error, collection, lifetime and task mechanisms.

Source reading is not runtime proof; Main must preserve frozen/current provenance and obtain the named acceptance evidence.

Retained source contract metadata follows. It is provenance, not an additional choice.

decisions.lesson: Applying a patch and finding a patch are different jobs. A generated patch must reproduce the target, but need not be the smallest possible edit list. Either choice must bound comparison work and output.
decisions.story: Sora compares two settings snapshots and sends only a meaningful edit document.

options.name: Stock coherent capability
options.detail: Put this operation under its existing Core owner. Patch generation shares canonical equality and path rules. A valid generated patch is not guaranteed to be minimal.
options.technical:
Proposed json.diff(DataTree,DataTree) -> DataTree !EncodingError returns a deterministic RFC6902 operation array.

Its contract is patch(before,diff(before,after)) equals after for supported JSON values, not minimal bytes or move detection.

Stable object traversal and array treatment are documented.

Bound visited data, comparisons, emitted bytes and allocations; limit exhaustion is an ordinary error, not a whole-document fallback disguised as an optimized diff.

Reject non-JSON/nonfinite values explicitly.

Reuse canonical equality with a JSON-appropriate numeric policy stated alongside exact values.

D-CORE-JSON-PATCH1 is a dependency; no new value model or callback protocol.

Retained source contract metadata follows. It is provenance, not an additional choice.

The selected option above controls adoption and scope; other option contracts remain inactive.

decisions.title: Generate representable Merge Patch
decisions.gist: Should Core generate Merge Patch only when it can reproduce the target?
decisions.lesson: Merge Patch uses an object member’s null value to delete that member. Some desired null assignments therefore cannot be expressed. An unchanged null can remain unchanged. Either choice must report unrepresentable updates instead of losing data.
decisions.story: Bo creates a configuration update and must not replace a desired null member with deletion.

options.detail: Put this operation under its existing Core owner. Unrepresentable updates fail instead of silently changing meaning. Some valid target documents cannot use this patch format.
options.technical:
Proposed json.merge_diff(DataTree,DataTree) -> DataTree !EncodingError.

Return a standard merge document only when applying it yields the exact supported target.

A changed/added object member desired as null may be unrepresentable; an already identical null member can be omitted, and a null root replacement remains representable.

Arrays replace whole.

Return Unsupported with the member path instead of a lossy diff; do not silently switch to JSON Patch.

Bound comparison/output/depth.

D-CORE-JSON-MERGE1 is a dependency.

No universal round-trip or minimality claim.

Retained source contract metadata follows. It is provenance, not an additional choice.

The selected option above controls adoption and scope; other option contracts remain inactive.

decisions.title: Serialize selected fields without an intermediate tree
decisions.gist: Should JSON encoding support an explicit selected-field projection?
decisions.lesson: Selective output aims to remove DTO copying and avoid serializing unused large fields. The claimed performance benefit remains unproven. It must use the existing Encode view and must not sacrifice exact numbers or turn duplicate selectors into duplicate JSON keys. A cannot be ratified before its strict candidate/plain win. No matching pair or win is recorded in gauntlet/measurement-manifest.json. Proof remains on #3298 (core-f078).
decisions.story: Mira needs the specific interchange or application result shown here. She should choose its ownership once, rather than rebuild the same policy at every call.

options.name: Stock selected output
options.detail:
Add json.to_string_selected(value, paths) using the existing typed encoder walker. A aims to skip unselected work and intermediate trees; performance remains unproven. Positive selection and wire names are explicit.

Core must define path overlap, missing fields and custom-codec behavior. A awaits its missing canonical pair and strict win: #3298 (core-f078).

A cannot be ratified before its strict candidate/plain win. No matching pair or win is recorded in gauntlet/measurement-manifest.json. Proof remains on #3298 (core-f078).
options.technical:
Add core.encoding.json.to_string_selected<T:Encode>(value:T, paths:[String], limits:EncodingLimits=...) -> String !EncodingError.

Paths use RFC6901 escaping and canonical encoded wire names, not source-private fields; share the approved pointer parser if D-CORE-JSON-POINTER1 is ratified, not its tree materialization.

Support nested object paths and whole selected arrays/values; array-element projection requires an independently specified shape-preservation rule and is not claimed by this object-field operation.

Empty list produces {}; duplicate paths collapse once; selecting an ancestor includes its whole encoded value and subsumes descendant selectors.

Root empty-string selection means the entire value explicitly.

Unknown paths and unsupported traversal error before output is returned.

Emit first-selection path order while retaining original order within a fully selected object/array.

Custom codecs use their existing Encode view; uninspectable opaque output must return Unsupported, not bypass omission/privacy metadata or silently stringify/parse.

Preserve Decimal/Int/field metadata exactly through the canonical typed writer.

No intermediate JSON text parse, parallel reflection system or output duplicate keys.

Limits and all-or-error String ownership are explicit; expert streaming projection would need the same writer finish/error contract, not an unapproved overload.

This is not automatic redaction; caller selects the allowed view and must handle future schema changes.

All new namespaces, APIs and defaults here are unratified.

No new third-party dependency is approved; A is first-party implementation within Core unless explicitly stated otherwise.

Reuse current Codable, error, collection, lifetime and task mechanisms.

Source reading is not runtime proof; Main must preserve frozen/current provenance and obtain the named acceptance evidence.

Retained source contract metadata follows. It is provenance, not an additional choice.

The selected option above controls adoption and scope; other option contracts remain inactive.

decisions.title: Choose atomic typed-record updates
decisions.gist: Should Core update existing typed records from partial wire data?
decisions.lesson: Ordinary decode constructs a value. A partial update keeps omitted fields from an existing value. These are different jobs. Either choice must preserve validation and define unsupported custom mappings, rather than silently turning decode into mutation.
decisions.story: Jin updates one configuration field while keeping the rest of an existing record unchanged.

options.name: Stock coherent capability

options.technical:
Proposed json.update<T>(existing, DataTree) -> T ![FieldError] is a nonmutating atomic result operation for supported canonical generated field mappings.

Omitted fields keep their existing values; explicit null follows target nullability; names, unknown fields, Flatten and validation keep their existing law.

Unchanged retained fields are not reconstructed through a lossy wire round-trip.

Custom mappings lacking a lawful update path return an explicit unsupported FieldError before change.

Preserve custom Decode precedence where a supported mapping exists, otherwise reject rather than bypass it.

Owned output may copy retained data; no zero-copy claim.

No new Partial<T>, marker, reflection system or changed ordinary decode semantics is approved.

decisions.title: Locale-aware number and date formatting in Core
decisions.situation: Every number and date that Jet's Core prints today uses one fixed English style, such as 1,234.56 and month names in English. A program for German or Japanese users has to build its own tables for separators and month names. On 2026-10-01 the owner chose a Core locale library where the program passes the locale on every call, with bundled data. This record writes that ruling down.
decisions.gist: Should Core format and read numbers and dates in a chosen language and region?
decisions.lesson: A locale is a language plus a region, like German in Germany. It decides details such as whether 1234.5 prints as 1,234.5 or 1.234,5. Option A adds a Core locale value that the program passes on every call. Core bundles the data, so the same call prints the same text on every machine.
decisions.story: Lena builds an invoice tool for a shop in Berlin. Core prints the total as 1,234.56, but her customers expect 1.234,56. Under option A she passes the German locale to the format call and gets the expected text.
decisions.detail:
Owner answer, 2026-10-01 chat (ask question s3307): "core.text.locale, explicit Locale". The question asked, verbatim:

"#3307: Locale-aware formatting ("1.234,56 €", localized dates, locale-correct sorting). In Core?"

The owner picked the first offered option, which was also the recommended one. The card plan called the same choice option B of a never-filed ballot named D-CORE-LOCALE1. This record replaces that draft name.

Today Core/text/fmt.jet number(n) groups with a comma and takes no locale. Core/time/calendar.jet:2-6 states that names are English and fixed. The plan on #3307 starts with numbers and dates for en-US, de-DE, fr-FR and ja-JP. Collation stays behind its own later gate. Implementation and proof now ride on #3262, where #3307 was merged on 2026-10-04.

options.name: core.text.locale, explicit Locale
options.detail: Core adds a Locale value that the program passes on every format or parse call. There is no hidden global locale. A subset of the standard CLDR locale data ships with Core as Jet tables, so results are the same on every machine.
options.technical: Offered option text: "A Locale value passed per call (no hidden global), bundled CLDR data subset as Jet tables. Deterministic, larger Core." Planned calls: format_number, format_date, parse_number and parse_date in Core/text/locale.jet. fmt.jet and time.jet stay invariant by default.

options.name: Not in Core
options.detail: Core keeps one fixed format for numbers and dates. Programs that need other languages use a package.
options.technical: Offered option text: "Core formats invariantly; locale goes to packages."

options.name: OS/ICU provider
options.detail: Core asks the operating system or the ICU library for locale data at run time. Core bundles less data, but results depend on the machine.
options.technical: Offered option text: "Ask the OS/ICU at run time; less bundled data, platform-dependent results."

recommendation.why: Programs get correct local formats, and the same call prints the same text on every machine because Core carries the data.

whyNot.reason: B leaves every program that serves other languages to rebuild the same tables.
C gives different text on different machines, which breaks tests and saved files.

losses.loss: Core grows by the bundled locale tables.
losses.mitigation: Ship a small set of locales first and add more only when a program needs them.

recommendation.tradeoff: Some bundled data buys local formats that never change between machines.

options.detail: Keep native wire values through explicit format-specific types.
options.technical:
Common public API under the module selected by D-CORE-MSGPACK1: decode<T>(bytes: [U8]) T ![FieldError]; encode<T>(value: T) [U8] !EncodingError; parse(bytes: [U8]) DataTree !EncodingError.

decode requires existing Decode support and encode requires existing Encode support.

Reader/writer use the existing consumed FileReader/FileWriter constructors, EncodingLimits.safe default, next/write/flush/finish, terminal-error and value-boundary law.

No second limit/error/IO model or implicit allocation queue.

Every root consumes exactly one complete value; malformed/trailing data errors before success.

Encoded output is owned; decoded variable-width values are owned and do not retain caller input.

MessagePack2.0 is the fixed typed codec profile.

Typed decode<T:Decode>([U8]) returns T on the existing [FieldError] rail; encode<T:Encode>(T) returns owned [U8] !EncodingError.

Matching reader/writer and explicit-limit/caller-buffer operations reuse existing finish, value-boundary and ownership law.

Nil, Bool, exact signed/unsigned64 integer wire values, finite float32/64, strict UTF-8 strings, binary, arrays and typed maps retain declared types.

Int never passes through float; narrower target bounds and nonfinite/unrepresentable floats error.

[U8] uses bin values, not an implicitly interchangeable integer list.

Module-local Extension(type I8, owned [U8]) preserves all generic ext types and lengths; type -1 is the standardized timestamp and decodes32/64/96-bit forms with checked nanoseconds0..999999999 and exact seconds.

Timestamp maps to Instant only when representable, otherwise the typed operation errors rather than truncates.

Native map key types remain typed with existing equality rules, never stringified.

Dynamic parse/events accept only losslessly representable closed DataTree values and string-key Objects; binary/ext/non-string keys return Unsupported rather than Bytes/Tags/Map variants.

Duplicate normalized record/object keys reject before overwrite.

Existing field/default/unknown/PublishedSchema and custom codec rules apply; unpreservable unknown native fields error.

Variant tags retain canonical metadata, not category guessing.

Reserved0xc1, malformed UTF-8, lengths, ext/timestamp widths, count multiplication and trailing input are checked; shared EncodingLimits bounds consumed/skipped input, nesting, retained data and output.

Writers emit valid minimal-width integral forms and explicit typed float width; no byte-identical round trip is promised across alternate legal encodings.

No external dependency or new value/event algebra.

This admission expands wire interoperability but does not reopen CBOR as the chosen first binary format.

D-CORE-MSGPACK1 separately places the admitted adapter in stock core.encoding.msgpack or release-matched first-party jet-msgpack/module msgpack; dependency adoption remains D-CORE-GLAZE-DEPENDENCY1.

Maintenance is independently gated by D-CORE-MSGPACK-ADOPT1.

The following option specifications are complete alternatives, not additive features.

The sole new format-specific value record is Extension{type:I8, bytes:[U8]}; encode/decode validate reserved type -1 separately as the standard timestamp, which maps to existing Instant.

Its byte payload is owned.

Ordinary [U8] uses binary, never array-of-integers coercion.

Other extensions preserve signed type and payload exactly through existing Encode/Decode, with no extra constructors/accessors.

Typed map keys use the declared key type and reject duplicates after checked decode.

Reader event mode uses the existing DataEvent.Bytes for binary; extension identity and non-string map keys without an existing event representation report Unsupported.

No new event or DataTree variants are added.

Retained source contract metadata follows. It is provenance, not an additional choice.

The selected option above controls adoption and scope; other option contracts remain inactive.

decisions.lesson: Copying a copyable iterator preserves its cursor position; rebuilding a source may repeat earlier work or effects. Example: Advance a over [1,2,3] once, then set b = ~a. A gives independent cursors: both next() calls return 2. B rebuilds from the source recipe, not the saved position. Expected; NOT RUN.
decisions.story: Same job: Advance iterator a over [1,2,3] once, then make b = ~a. A copies the checked cursor position so a and b advance independently; B reconstructs from the source recipe. Expected output: Both a.next() and b.next() return 2; reconstruction may rerun earlier work or effects instead of restoring state. Authored illustration; NOT RUN.
decisions.detail:
## In plain words

Checkpoint/copy reproduces cursor state at one position; reconstruction creates a new source and is not restoration.

Same job (authored illustration; NOT RUN):

Input: Advance iterator a over [1,2,3] once, then make b = ~a.

Behavior: A copies the checked cursor position so a and b advance independently; B reconstructs from the source recipe.

Expected output: Both a.next() and b.next() return 2; reconstruction may rerun earlier work or effects instead of restoring state.

Both options use this same job. Only the choice named by each option changes.

Captured facts are not execution proof. Every worked program is authored NOT RUN except a specifically linked frozen receipt.

decisions.title: Bind existing implementations before owning service packages
decisions.gist: Should existing implementations replace the current commitment to eight first-party service packages?
decisions.lesson: A binding calls existing foreign code. Eight packages cover GraphQL, gRPC, Kafka, RabbitMQ, Socket.IO, Redis jobs, Redis cache, and log export. Their answered ballots assign implementation and maintenance to Jet. A uses current bindings and defers Jet-specific service APIs. B keeps those commitments. OpenAPI remains a projection of checked application metadata, not an adapter.
decisions.story: Mina needs an application cache and later a broker-backed service. She wants a working maintained implementation, not a promise that Jet will maintain every protocol adapter. Her bounded job stores false with expiry and reads the same typed value. The policy choice is whether she binds an existing implementation or waits for the selected Jet-specific packages.
decisions.inWild:
# cache_ops.py; redis-py illustration, NOT RUN.
import json
from redis import Redis
from redis.backoff import ExponentialBackoff
from redis.retry import Retry
def roundtrip() -> bool:
    client = Redis(host="127.0.0.1", port=6380, decode_responses=True,
        retry=Retry(ExponentialBackoff(), 0),
        socket_connect_timeout=1, socket_timeout=1)
    try:
        client.set("orders:order-41", "false", ex=60)
        raw = client.get("orders:order-41")
        if raw is None: raise LookupError("cache entry absent")
        value = json.loads(raw)
        if type(value) is not bool: raise TypeError("expected bool")
        return value
    finally:
        client.close()
# Success before expiry returns False. Failures raise; no command retry.
decisions.detail:
## Exact successor scope

This is one implementation-ownership and delivery-boundary choice, not sixteen repeated votes. It amends the first-party package/API commitment in these ratified decisions:

- D-NEST-GRAPHQL1.
- D-NEST-GRPC1.
- D-NEST-KAFKA1.
- D-NEST-RABBIT1.
- D-NEST-SOCKETIO1.
- D-NEST-REMOTEQUEUE1.
- D-NEST-REMOTECACHE1.
- D-NEST-GRAPHQL-API1.
- D-NEST-GRPC-API1.
- D-NEST-KAFKA-API1.
- D-NEST-RABBIT-API1.
- D-NEST-SOCKETIO-API1.
- D-NEST-REMOTEQUEUE-API1.
- D-NEST-REMOTECACHE-API1.
- D-NEST-EXPORTER-API1.
- D-NEST-EXPORTER1.

The latest owner instruction pauses the first-party route now. B is a deliberate return to the older commitment, not permission to resume it while this ballot is open.

The predecessor records remain immutable history. Their API ballots really are answered; this preparation does not demand the same approvals again. The new question exists because the owner now wants a different maintenance boundary.

## Recommended A

Use maintained existing implementations through the current unified foreign-binding and package mechanisms. Prefer an upstream-owned or application-owned binding to another Jet-maintained service facade. Small application-specific typed helpers are allowed where an existing binding needs a bounded entrypoint. Such helpers marshal or compose calls; they do not reimplement a broker, client, queue protocol or generic service framework.

A removes the first-party delivery commitment for eight optional packages. They cover GraphQL, gRPC, Kafka, RabbitMQ, Socket.IO, Redis jobs, Redis cache and custom log export. The corresponding Jet-specific facade APIs are not the required first delivery. A binding does not become that facade by renaming imports. A later first-party facade needs its own explicit scope and complete contract.

A does not delete existing Core App, JobQueue, Cache, logging or plugin behavior. Reuse those APIs only when the bound implementation actually meets their full contracts. A low-level Redis client is not automatically a conforming JobQueue store. If a complete compatible provider is unavailable, leave that integration requirement open rather than writing an implicit first-party fallback.

The small Python helper in the surface demonstrates the ownership boundary, not every RemoteCache feature. It writes JSON false with expiry, refuses absence or a non-Boolean value, disables command retries, bounds socket operations and closes the client. Its Jet caller uses the existing py.module binding shape. No Redis server was contacted and no dependency or binder compatibility was tested. Exact installation, package pin, exception projection and target support remain prerequisites for an executable receipt.

Use the upstream API and error meaning honestly. A network exception does not prove a write or acknowledgement failed at the server. Do not silently retry an ambiguous side effect. Do not coerce missing, false, zero and empty text into the same result. Stateful handles, callbacks and async tasks retain existing ownership, close, effect, thread and cancellation obligations.

## What remains separate

D-WEB-OPENAPI-APP1=A stays approved. It projects an existing checked App HTTP contract into the existing OpenAPI renderer. That is not a network service adapter and needs no external SDK. Do not turn a visual WebRouter into an HTTP contract or copy a second schema registry.

Local JSONL logging also remains unchanged. The selected custom POST /events exporter is not OTLP. Under A, no first-party exporter package is promised. An application may compose the existing file/JSON/HTTP operations, or bind a maintained exporter whose actual protocol was separately chosen. Do not silently relabel an OTLP SDK as the selected custom sender. The deferred custom-export contract remains open evidence, not a passed feature.

A binding manifest may generate names, argument/result projections, ownership facts, documentation and glue from one checked descriptor. It cannot prove protocol compatibility, safe foreign implementation, callback shutdown, cancellation, transaction outcomes or retry policy by itself. Declared facts, verified facts, unknown obligations and executed receipts stay distinct. No universal Service<T>, new provider registry, second scheduler or new reflection authority is added.

## Candidate implementations, not adopted dependencies

GraphQL: async-graphql. gRPC: tonic with prost. Kafka: rust-rdkafka over librdkafka. RabbitMQ: lapin. Socket.IO: socketioxide. Redis value access: redis-rs or redis-py. These are candidate sources to evaluate, not approved versions or proved Jet bindings. A Redis queue integration needs a maintained queue implementation or exact store-contract evidence, not just a Redis client import.

Prefer existing supported binding routes. The current source contains a Rust bridge and a local Python-module path, but that does not establish arbitrary Rust trait, async, callback or native-handle support for these clients. Missing binder capabilities belong to the existing FFI work, not to an unadvertised service adapter. No host/runtime, automatic download, permission grant or provider dependency is authorized by this policy vote.

Each actual first-party packaged dependency still needs its normal exact-source/version/hash/license/target approval. Application dependencies remain under the existing package and permission policy. Compiler and seam crates keep path-only dependencies. Offline and missing-component behavior must be explicit.

## Alternative B

Keep the existing sixteen selected clauses. Jet delivers and maintains the eight optional packages and their exact Jet-specific APIs. The API selections call for first-party protocol binding through existing runtime IO without a linked third-party client dependency. Their lifetime, failure, privacy, acknowledgement, ordering and cancellation contracts remain mandatory. B does not mean merely wrapping an upstream client while claiming the no-dependency option was followed.

## Proof and limits

This vote changes delivery ownership, not I1-I9 or the strict performance gate. A provider import, generated stub, installed SDK, successful build or source review is not runtime, protocol, all-tier or performance proof. Required cells remain open while unavailable or failing. Do not hide a foreign runtime's startup, memory, scheduling or packaging cost.

After the owner chooses, cut over all affected plans and dependencies together. For A, prove one real binding on one named workload before expanding the supported-provider inventory. Keep lifecycle/protocol and I9 evidence on the existing work cards. A failed or incompatible provider does not authorize a first-party fallback or a reduced semantic claim.

## Source evidence

examples/interop/python/run.jet:1-5 and ops.py show the local py.module call shape. docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:3209-3213,3266-3278 and D-FFI-UNIFY1=A define existing Rust and unified binding law. D-FFI-CONTRACT1=A and existing callback/ownership laws govern the crossing; no new exemption is requested.

Primary sources read for candidates: https://github.com/async-graphql/async-graphql.
https://github.com/hyperium/tonic.
https://docs.rs/rdkafka.
https://docs.rs/lapin.
https://docs.rs/socketioxide.
https://github.com/redis-rs/redis-rs.
https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/clients/redis-py/.
https://redis.readthedocs.io/en/stable/retry.html . The Redis retry documentation states that the default can retry three times, which is why the illustration explicitly selects zero retries. Source documentation is not an exercised Jet binding.

decisions.title: Ordinary invocation of callable expressions
decisions.gist: Should every callable expression use ordinary invocation, including a returned function?
decisions.lesson: make_adder(40) returns a function that adds 40; invoking it with 2 gives 42. Int means integer. fn(Int) Int describes a function taking and returning an integer; -[]> declares no effects. Current Jet requires the special .call spelling for an immediately returned function. A allows ordinary parentheses and removes that special route; B keeps the current boundary.
decisions.story: Inez returns a small configured function. She should not need a special invocation rule merely because another function produced it.
decisions.detail:
This is a proposed grammar and public-surface amendment, not a clarification of D-CALLVALUE1. It changes no callable lifetime, capture, borrowing, effect, generic, partial-application or exception semantics. Parentheses already serve invocation; update the registered syntax/decision provenance and migrate every synthetic .call caller, diagnostic and example. Do not keep a compatibility alias. This choice is ergonomic, not a claimed performance optimization.

Source evidence:

examples/features/functions/returned_function_call.jet:1-12

crates/jet-parser/src/Parser/Expressions/postfix.rs:252-291

crates/jet-foundation/src/AST/expressions.rs:8-31,767-802,910-918

D-CALLVALUE1=B

Captured work:
Prior finding 7: remove an exposed implementation distinction when a checked ordinary call suffices.
The later syntax analysis must distinguish useful expression convenience from a second semantic mechanism.

Required evidence before implementation closure:
Returned free functions, methods returning functions, locals, grouped callable expressions, and nested invocation.
Non-callable returned values, ownership-sensitive captures, effect errors and evaluation-order side effects.
Registered diagnostics and migrated examples/goldens under every applicable execution engine.

Example status: current snippets are explicitly source-composed or captured source/test expectations. This preparation ran no Jet compiler, provider or UI scenario. Proposed alternatives are design contracts, not implemented behavior. No peer example proves Jet semantics.

Boundary trace for A: make_adder(40)(2) is accepted; a method returning a callable and a grouped callable expression are accepted through the same checked invocation. Calling a returned Int is rejected in sema. A callee-side effect and each argument effect occur once in existing order. A borrowed or moved capture is never copied or extended to make chaining work. Under B the adjacent returned-call form remains rejected; binding an intermediate callable remains available.

CallValue AST shape alone is not permission to invoke a value. Preserve compiler-private loop/autodiff provenance and constructibility limits. User-visible field/index/lambda/grouped/method-return expressions qualify only through their public checked callable type.

Migrate the existing E-CALL-VALUE boundary and infer_call_value’s .call-specific diagnostics. Keep ordinary user methods named call. Existing private-lowering fixtures must remain private and correct; this vote exposes no loop or autodiff API.

options.name: Ordinary callable invocation
options.detail: Permit postfix invocation on any expression whose checked type is callable. Parse chained calls left-to-right. Evaluate each callee expression and each argument exactly once in existing evaluation order. Preserve the existing CallBinder, receiver access conventions, effects, generic checking and callable provenance. Remove the synthetic function-value .call route in one cutover; an ordinary user-declared method named call remains an ordinary method. Non-callable results receive a registered sema diagnostic. Named and method resolution can retain distinct AST nodes. A user may still bind the intermediate callable to a local name for readability.

options.name: Explicit function-value call member
options.detail: Keep D-CALLVALUE1=B. Adjacent invocation of a returned callable remains rejected with a repair suggesting .call(...). Preserve current function-value call semantics and existing examples.

decisions.title: Share the existing Clang extractor for C and C++
decisions.gist: Should C bindings use the existing Clang extraction path instead of Jet’s focused C parser?
decisions.lesson: A C header declares functions and types; extraction turns those declarations into binding facts. Clang is an upstream C/C++ compiler that already interprets headers. Jet currently uses a focused C parser and a separate C++ Clang path. The choice changes who interprets C declarations, not the inspect command or Jet safety checks. Extraction alone does not link or safely call a function.
decisions.story: Sam binds a real vendor header. Preprocessor definitions, target layout, and declaration syntax should be interpreted by the same compiler used for the native boundary.

The official introduction demonstrates textual AST inspection. This source-composed external command is not a Jet command. It does not prove the proposed JSON extractor protocol. https://clang.llvm.org/docs/IntroductionToTheClangAST.html
decisions.detail:
Exact boundary: use the existing signed cc-toolchain descriptor and native child sandbox; do not select arbitrary host clang or add a libclang/bindgen crate. C uses C ABI calls directly, while C++ retains its necessary shim. Keep generated cache separate from the handwritten overlay and preserve compatible overlay precedence. 

Existing toolchain descriptors own immutable tool pins; this ballot does not invent an unpinned latest compiler. 

It proposes changing the standalone-C boundary recorded in the 2026-06-18 source comment. That comment is implementation/history evidence, not a ratified decision: the captured Tower D-CBIND3 record is an open spec-only import with no outcome. D-FFI-CPP1=A and D-ADOPT-CC1=B remain reference boundaries. No broad header compatibility or linked runtime success has been demonstrated by this preparation.

decisions.title: One explicit default viewport policy
decisions.gist: Should unconstrained UI mounting use the host viewport instead of hard-coded backend sizes?
decisions.lesson: A viewport is the space a host gives the root view. Browser and native hosts use their logical layout coordinates; a terminal uses cells. Current defaults differ: Rust/DOM use 80 by 24 and GTK uses 320 by 240. Explicit constraints are unchanged. The choice is whether an omitted constraint follows available host space or a fixed, documented default.
decisions.story: Robin mounts the same interface in a browser and a native window. Useful defaults should follow a clear rule, and fixed-size examples must remain reproducible.
decisions.inWild:
.screen { width: 100dvw; height: 100dvh; }
Source-composed dynamic-viewport sizing. The CSS Values 4 draft distinguishes dynamic dv* from default large-viewport v* units. This is not evidence for Jet native/terminal unit conversion: https://drafts.csswg.org/css-values-4/#viewport-relative-lengths
decisions.detail:
This explicitly amends the default policy associated with D-UI-MOUNT1=A; it preserves measure/layout/paint ordering and D-STYLEUNIT1 checked lengths. Equal explicit input constraints must retain equal logical layout meaning; physical backend conversion remains explicit. 

A does not authorize a new public viewport method or another unit family. No common physical conversion was established by the capture. A therefore selects explicit host coordinate frames for omitted constraints. It does not infer a universal pixel-to-cell factor. Observable owner acceptance: an unconstrained root fills available browser/native/terminal host space under the existing layout rules, and explicit fixed constraints remain stable during host resizing.

options.detail:
For an omitted constraint, use the attached host’s layout allocation. Browser dimensions are CSS pixels; GTK dimensions use GTK allocation coordinates; terminal dimensions are columns and rows. These are backend coordinate frames, not one physical unit.

Mount remains synchronous. Before attachment/allocation, use the declared virtual 80×24 layout. State inspection can observe that virtual layout. Do not paint a native surface using it as a guessed native allocation.

This selects a default-root policy, not a universal pixel-to-cell conversion. Do not change explicit Px/Percent/Fraction style meaning, add a public viewport method or introduce another unit family.

options.name: Result first, optional history
options.detail: Compute the actual test/build/program result independently of optional record persistence. Ordinary history is best effort and a crash may lose its latest unsaved entries. Keep mandatory authority/audit evidence and explicit saved/proof requests durable and fail closed.
options.technical:
Use FIFO across disposable run/build/test/replay histories, with a 256 MiB byte-only limit per canonical project and no record-count policy cap. Keep saved, required audit, and sensitive protected roots outside that quota. Evict reference groups consistently and never another project’s records. 

Successful saves and normal eviction are silent. A real optional persistence failure emits one nonfatal notice containing the cause and its specific corrective action. Do not auto-run destructive repair or claim a saved artifact before commit. Preserve semantic checks, claim floors, and true failures independently of persistence. Measurement mode selects measurements; it does not waive required proof artifacts. Use a minimal bounded implementation, not a mandatory daemon.

decisions.title: Warnings that prove written code will not run show on jet run
decisions.situation: When you run a program, Jet hides its advisory warnings and shows them only when you check or build. One warning is different: it says a branch you wrote can never run, because an earlier branch already handles that case. Hiding it lets a program print the wrong answer with no hint why. This vote decides whether that small kind of warning appears when you run, while every other warning stays quiet.
decisions.gist: Should warnings that prove written code never runs appear on jet run, while other warnings stay hidden?
decisions.lesson: A warning, or lint, flags suspicious code without stopping the build. An arm is one branch of a match table. An unreachable arm can never run because an earlier arm already catches its case. Today jet run hides every warning unless you pass --verbose.
decisions.explainer:
The ratified rule keeps run, dev and test quiet: advisory warnings show on jet check and jet build, or with --verbose. Errors and denied lints always apply.

Most advisories are style or speed hints, and hiding them while running is right. A few prove that code you wrote will not do what it reads as. The clearest is L0301, an unreachable dispatch arm. A copy-pasted duplicate arm silently never runs.

Under A, each lint row in the registry may carry one flag meaning it changes what runs. A lint gets the flag only if it proves written code never runs, or never runs as written. L0301 is the first member. Flagged findings print one line each on stderr before the program starts, with the jet check pointer.

Beginner path: nothing to learn; the line appears when it matters. Expert path: silence one site with #Allow(unreachable_dispatch_arm, "reason"), or deny the lint to make it an error.

Shared work: the Jet-written compiler must port L0301, which the parity ledger lists as missing, whichever option wins.
decisions.story: Lena copies an arm in a weather table and edits the wrong line. Her program keeps printing t-shirt on cold days. jet run shows nothing, so she spends an hour adding prints before running jet check.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-05.

D-LINT-VISIBILITY2=A (2026-09-15, card #3420) shows advisories on check and build. It hides them on run, dev and test unless --verbose is given. Errors, authority denials and denied lints stay enforced.

L0301 is unreachable_dispatch_arm. Its UI snapshot is tests/ui_lint/dispatch_unreachable_arm.warn. The text reads: Arm `Red` is unreachable — that case is already handled. Its fix line says to remove the arm or merge it with the one above.

The 2026-09-30 SPJ mining report (Docs/research/mine-for-jet-2026-09-30-spj-papers.md:232-234) observed this failure. A duplicated .Warm arm runs silently under jet run, while jet check reports L0301. The learning-compilers mine of 2026-10-05 raised the same case.

The parity ledger (Docs/research/rust-jet-parity-ledger-2026-09-30.md:209) lists the arm-table lints L0301, L0302, L0513, L0514 and L0517 as not yet ported to the Jet-written compiler.

Research. rustc and cargo run print warnings on every build, including unreachable_patterns, which is on by default. OCaml prints warning 11, unused match case, on every compile. dune's dev profile makes many warnings errors, and its release profile relaxes them. Elm rejects a redundant pattern outright. TypeScript's allowUnreachableCode setting chooses between an editor hint and an error.

The lesson across these tools: a proof that written code is dead is treated as a correctness signal, not a style hint. Nobody hides it while running. The tools that make it an error accept a cost: half-edited code will not run while you experiment.

Why one flag, not a list in the CLI: the registry row already carries severity and code. One flag keeps membership auditable in jet lint --list. Each new member needs the same proof test.

A lint joins only if it proves written code never runs as written; L0301 is the first. All other advisories stay hidden as ratified.
options.technical: Registry: a boolean on each lint row, read by the shared output adapter. run/dev/test filter advisories to flagged rows unless --verbose. --quiet still hides them. #Allow silences a site; deny turns the lint into an error. Membership test: the finding proves a written statement or arm is never executed, or never executed in its written position. Both compiler halves read the one registry row (I9). Port L0301 to the Jet-written compiler.
