decisions.title: Return type after the one arrow; braces on every named body
decisions.gist: Should a function's return type move to the other side of its one arrow, with braces on every named body?
decisions.lesson: A Jet function has one arrow. Today the return type sits before it: `fn double(n: Int) Int -> n * 2`; D-SIG-SHAPE1 chose that so `->` always means a body follows. This ballot moves the type after the arrow and makes braces the body: `fn double(n: Int) -> Int { n * 2 }`. On a signature `->` then reads as 'returns'; on `if`, arms, and lambdas it still means 'body follows'. That second reading is the price. The effect row keeps splitting the same arrow: `-[IO]> String`. A failure type follows the result: `-> Int !ParseError`.
decisions.story: Tomas comes from TypeScript and Rust. He reads `fn load(path: String) String -[IO]> {` and asks whether `String` is a parameter that lost its name. With the type after the arrow he reads left to right: inputs, arrow, effects, output, body. The effect-free shape then matches Rust exactly; the effect row is Jet-specific under every option.

options.name: Type after the arrow, braces on named bodies
options.detail:
`fn name(params) -> T { body }`. With effects the row splits the arrow and the type follows: `fn load(p: String) -[IO]> String !IOError { … }`. Here `!IOError` names the failure the function may return. Unit stays `fn run() { }` and `fn announce() -[IO]> { }`; a fallible unit keeps today's arrowless form, `fn save(p: String) !IOError { }` and `fn sync() -[IO]> !IOError { }`. A plain `->` with no type, and `-> Unit`, are illegal. Function types read the same way: `fn(Int) -> Int`, `fn(Int) -[IO]> Int`, `fn(String) !IOError`.

Named function and method bodies always take braces, including one-liners; `jet fmt` keeps `{ n * 2 }` on one line. `if`, `loop`, arm tables (`if n == { 0 -> "zero" }`), and lambdas keep `->` as their body arrow; lambdas write no return type (D-LAMBDA-IFACE2). After `->` a type name is only a type: `-> Point {` always opens the body, so a bare struct-literal one-liner must name it, `fn origin() -> Point { Point{x: 0, y: 0} }`. Local named functions stay lambda binds, `helper :: n -> n * 2`; there is no `fn(...) { }` expression form, so D-CALLABLE-ONE1 keeps one anonymous shape.

Cutover is one paired change: the spec entry, parser, `jet fmt` rewrite, grammars, examples, and docs land together. The old shape stays only as an error-recovery branch that prints the new spelling, removed one release after the rewrite ships.
options.technical:
Parser: after the parameter list accept `->` or `-[E]>`, then optional return facts, then `{`. Struct literals are not parsed in return-type position. Reject `-> T -> expr`, `-> T -[E]> {`, `-[E]> -> T`, `-> Unit`, and `-> {` on a unit body.

`jet fmt` rewrites the 427 typed signatures and 34 effect ceilings measured over about 1,100 shipped signatures, plus every named one-liner (counted before ratification; the figure above excludes them). Amends D-SIG-SHAPE1=B (type before the arrow) and D-CALLABLE-ONE1=A (one callable shape); D-EFFECT-ROW2=B, D-FAIL-UNIT1=A, and D-FAILURE-FOUNDATION1=A unchanged.

options.name: Keep today's shape
options.detail: `fn double(n: Int) Int -> n * 2`; braces only for multi-statement bodies. `->` keeps one meaning across `fn`, lambda, `if`, and arms: a body follows. Expression bodies and bare struct-literal bodies survive. Zero migration. Readers from Rust, TypeScript, Swift, and Kotlin meet a bare type between the parameter list and the arrow and misread it at first; Go readers parse it at once.
options.technical: Status quo D-CALLABLE-ONE1=A / D-SIG-SHAPE1=B. Grammar: `fn name ( params ) [Return facts] [-[E]>|->] body`.

options.name: Named functions become const binds
options.detail: `double :: fn(n: Int) -> Int { n * 2 }`, Jai and Odin shaped. One rhyme with `PI :: 3.14` and `@table :: make_table()` (`::` binds a name to a value). Methods and trait slots then read as constants but are not; `impl`, `migration`, and `#Test` blocks bind nothing and stay items, so two forms remain. Its real payoff, treating a function as a compile-time object you can run or specialize, is refused by the compile-time power ceiling (D-META-GATE1), leaving only the rhyme.
options.technical: Retire item-form `fn name`; `fn(...)` becomes only a callable constructor; `::` binds it. Trait requirement slots need a bodiless bind form. Largest migration of the three.

options.name: Type after the arrow, `=` for expression bodies
options.detail: `fn double(n: Int) -> Int = n * 2`, braces for multi-statement bodies: the Kotlin, Scala, F#, and C# shape. It gets the left-to-right read without the brace tax and keeps `fn origin() -> Point = {x: 0, y: 0}`. Cost: a third body opener (`=`, `->`, `{`) in a language whose owner rule is one glyph per job, and `=` already means assignment inside bodies.
options.technical: Grammar: `fn name ( params ) [-[E]>|->] [T] [!Err] ( = expr | { body } )`. Same migration count as A for typed signatures; one-liners rewrite to `= expr` mechanically.

comparisons.note: Type after the arrow, braces on every function body, arms use a different arrow.
comparisons.code: fn double(n: i64) -> i64 { n * 2 }

comparisons.note: Type after a colon; braces always; lambdas use a different arrow.
comparisons.code: function double(n: number): number { return n * 2; }

comparisons.note: Const-bind form with the type after the arrow and mandatory braces.
comparisons.code: double :: proc(n: int) -> int { return n * 2 }

comparisons.note: Bare type after the parameter list, like Jet today; braces always.
comparisons.code: func double(n int) int { return n * 2 }

comparisons.code: fun double(n: Int): Int = n * 2

decisions.title: Lambda interface under type-after-arrow: parameters and effect row only
decisions.gist: When the return type moves after the arrow, which suffixes may a lambda still write?
decisions.lesson: A lambda is a function without a name. Today it may write everything a named function writes, in today's order: `(n: Int) Int !E -[]> body`. D-SIG-AFTER1 moves the type after the arrow on named functions: `fn f(n: Int) -> Int { n * 2 }`. A lambda's `->` is its body separator, so a type after it collides with a struct value: `x -> Point{x: 1}` and `x -> Point { block }` look the same. Named functions are the canonical full interface; `::`-bound lambdas are the short form. This ballot decides what the short form keeps.
decisions.story: Lena writes `rows.map(r -> Row{id: r.id})` in a data pipeline. She expects a list of `Row` values. If a lambda could write a return type, the parser would have to read past the brace to learn whether `Row{…}` is a value or a type followed by a block. With parameters and effect row only, her line means one thing.

options.name: Parameters and effect row only
options.detail:
A lambda writes `params -> expr`, `params -> { block }`, or with a row `params -[IO]> body`. `-[IO]>` lists the effects the body may perform, `-[]>` says none, and a plain `->` adopts the expected row. It never writes a return or error type.

Those come from the expected type at the call site, or from a typed binding: `f: fn(Int) -> Int !E :: n -> …`. A written parameter type must equal the expected one; a written row must fit inside the expected row (E0747). Jet has no expression ascription, so a call-site lambda whose body under-determines the type (`fold(init, (acc, x) -> [])`) must go through a typed binding or a named `fn`.

Cost: a `::`-bound lambda that needs a failure or effect fact splits into a type and a body, repeating parameter types across the two halves. `::` lambdas at module level get their types the same way (D-LAMBDA-INFER1). Amends D-LAMBDA-IFACE1=A to parameters plus row.
options.technical: Lambda grammar: `params ( -> | -[E]> ) body`. Teaching diagnostic: after the arrow, an uppercase name followed by `!Name`, or by `{` whose contents fail to parse as a struct literal, prints the typed-binding form. `x -> Point{x}` is a struct literal with shorthand fields and gets no diagnostic. Migration: `jet fmt` rewrites `::`-bound lambdas with types into typed bindings; call-site lambdas drop the type (the parameter supplies it) or receive the diagnostic. D-LAMBDA-INFER1 untouched.

options.name: Full parity; a written type forces a braced body
options.detail:
A lambda may write `(n: Int) -> Int !E { … }`. The rule 'type present means block body' resolves the collision, but it costs the most common pipeline line. `r -> Row{id: r.id}` fails at parse (`id: r.id` reads as a truncated binding) and must be written `r -> (Row{id: r.id})`. `r -> Row{x}` parses as type `Row` plus block `{x}` and fails later with a baffling type error.

A stronger variant peeks at the first token inside the brace; `Row{x}` stays undecidable, and the grammar then depends on block contents.
options.technical: Lambda grammar: `params ( -> | -[E]> ) [Type [!Err]] body` where a type requires `{`. Parser speculatively parses a type then checks for `{`; struct-literal bodies fail in two different ways (parse vs type) depending on their contents.

options.name: Arrow lambdas as A, plus an anonymous `fn` expression
options.detail: Arrow lambdas keep A exactly. A second expression form, `fn(n: Int) -[]> Int !LambdaError { Ok(n + 1) }`, carries the full named-function interface with a mandatory block. The `fn` keyword keeps the parser in signature mode until `{`, so nothing collides. This is Kotlin's lambda plus `fun` split. Cost: two anonymous callable shapes, which D-CALLABLE-ONE1 forbids, and a typed binding already covers the same need.
options.technical: Expression grammar gains `fn ( params ) [-[E]>|->] [T] [!Err] { body }`. Amends D-CALLABLE-ONE1=A (one callable shape). No struct-literal collision because the body is always braced.

comparisons.note: Two tokens: `|` ends the parameters, a separate `->` introduces the type. Jet's `->` ends the lambda signature, so a type after it collides; option C restores a second token with `fn`.
Type before the arrow after a colon, so no return-type collision. Parentheses on object bodies are a `=> {` is-a-block rule, unrelated to types.
comparisons.code: const f = (n: number): Point => ({ x: n });

comparisons.note: Lambdas never write a return type; Kotlin pairs them with a keyword anonymous function that writes the full signature (option C).
comparisons.code:
val f: (Int) -> Int = { n -> n * 2 }
val g = fun(n: Int): Int = n * 2

recommendation.why: One lambda shape, no collision with struct-literal bodies, and the effect row still visible where it matters. The return type already has a home in the expected type, a typed binding, or a named `fn`.

whyNot.reason: Struct-literal bodies need parentheses and fail in two different ways (parse vs type) depending on their contents.
A second anonymous callable shape, which D-CALLABLE-ONE1 forbids; the typed binding and named `fn` already cover the inline-type case.

recommendation.tradeoff: A lambda stored without an expected type must get its return type from a typed binding or a named `fn` instead of writing it inline.

losses.loss: An inline return type on a lambda is no longer available.
losses.mitigation: Under the `params -> body` shape a type and a struct literal collide after the arrow; only a second token (option C) or a different placement avoids it.

losses.loss: No local return-type escape at a call site.
losses.mitigation: Jet has no expression ascription; the escape is a typed binding or a named function.

decisions.title: Compile-time IO is ordinary functions; BuildContext is the plan only
decisions.gist: Should reading files and fetching URLs at compile time go through b, or through ordinary functions?
decisions.lesson: A build entry runs at compile time. It can read files, fetch pinned URLs, and register generated code. Today the plan is to hang those reads on the BuildContext value `b`. Jet already has an effect row that says what a function may do. Putting reads on `b` would create a second permission system next to the first one.
decisions.story: Mara adds a sprite atlas to her game. She writes `pack_sprites` as a normal function and tests it with `jet test`. Her `fn build` reads the PNG paths, calls it, and registers the ids. Her package policy denies Net, so a stray `fetch` fails at compile time with the same message it would at run time.

options.name: Ordinary functions under the effect row
options.detail: `find`, `embed_file`, and `fetch(url, sha256:)` are normal functions. The build entry's effect row and the package policy allow or deny them. The lockfile records exact files and hashes. `b` keeps only the plan: `add_executable`, `generate`, `plan`, and `action` for an outside program. Unpinned reads stay behind `#Impure`.
options.technical: Remove IO methods from BuildContext in `run_build_entry_with_policy`. Check `find`/`embed_file`/`fetch` as effectful core calls inside the comptime interpreter under the entry's declared ceiling. Lock entries record path, hash, and URL.

options.name: Reads live on b as the authority path
options.detail: `b.fetch`, `b.find`, `b.embed` are the only compile-time reads. Holding `b` is the permission. A helper that needs bytes must receive `b`, so helper logic drifts into `fn build`.
options.technical: Keep BuildContext as the capability object; helpers take `b: BuildContext`. Two permission systems: effect row at run time, `b` at compile time.

comparisons.note: build.zig uses the same std library for files and fetches as run-time code. The dependency hash lives in build.zig.zon.
comparisons.code: const dep = b.dependency("gl", .{});

comparisons.note: Network is allowed only for a fetch whose output hash is known first.
comparisons.code: fetchurl { url = "..."; sha256 = "..."; }

recommendation.why: One permission system. The effect row already says what a function may do, and a package can already deny Net. The lockfile does the one job effects cannot: record exact bytes.

whyNot.reason: It duplicates the effect system and forces helper logic to take `b`, which is what the owner rejected.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet gives up a single object that visibly holds every compile-time read. The effect row and lockfile carry that audit instead.

losses.loss: No single object lists every compile-time read.
losses.mitigation: Reads become ordinary calls; the audit moves to the effect row and lockfile.

decisions.title: b.generate takes a typed template value; in-tree output is opt-in
decisions.gist: What value does a helper hand to b.generate, and may generated files live in the tree?
decisions.lesson: A generated module is a `.jet` file the compiler writes during the build and then compiles like one you typed. Today you can only make one by writing its items inline inside `b.generate("name") { … }`. The owner wants the logic in a helper such as `sqlx.client_source(sql)`, with `fn build` only registering the result. This ballot picks what the helper returns.
decisions.story: Dev keeps his SQL schema in `schema/*.sql`. He wants typed row structs and query functions without writing them by hand. His `fn build` reads the files, calls the sqlx helper, and registers the result. When a column is renamed, compiling fails at the call that used the old name. His team reviews generated code in pull requests, so the package opts into in-tree output.

options.name: Typed template value
options.detail: `generate { items with holes }` is an expression of type `Generated`. A helper returns it; `b.generate("db_client", value)` renders it under `.jet/generated` and sema checks it as ordinary items. Holes take values only, using the derive template grammar that D-META-CODE1 already ratified. The inline block stays as the same thing written in place. A package may opt into in-tree output; the file is still lock-hashed and the build fails if the committed file drifts.
options.technical: Add `Generated` as the type of a `generate { … }` expression; `b.generate(name, value)` overload alongside the block form; parse the template once at the helper's site so slips report there. Manifest key opts into materializing under the package tree instead of `.jet/generated`; drift check compares the lock hash.

options.name: A String of Jet source
options.detail: The helper builds text; the driver re-lexes it. Any string builder works. Errors point into a file nobody typed, templates cannot be checked before they run, and code-as-text is the door derive law already closed.
options.technical: `b.generate(name, source: String)`; the driver lexes and parses the string at registration time. Contradicts D-META-CODE1=A (real code with holes).

options.name: Inline block only
options.detail: No new value. Helpers may only be called from inside `b.generate("m") { … }`, so the structure of every generated module lives in `fn build`. This is the shape the owner rejected.
options.technical: Status quo: `b.generate(name) { items }` is the only form.

comparisons.note: quote! builds a typed token template with holes. Errors report in the macro crate.
comparisons.code: quote! { struct #name { #(#fields),* } }

comparisons.note: go generate writes source into the tree; a CI diff catches drift.
comparisons.code: //go:generate sqlc generate

recommendation.why: The helper owns the structure and the compiler checks the template once, at the helper's line. The build entry only registers a value. It matches D-META-CODE1, real code with holes, and keeps generated code out of text.

whyNot.reason: Errors land in text nobody wrote, and it reopens code-as-text that derive law already refused.
It keeps generated structure inside fn build, which the owner rejected.

recommendation.tradeoff: Helpers must learn the template grammar instead of gluing strings. In-tree output adds a drift check to keep the committed file honest.

losses.loss: Helpers learn a template grammar instead of string glue.
losses.mitigation: Checking a template before it runs requires structure that a string does not have.

decisions.title: b.include(pkg): a package's own build runs sandboxed inside yours
decisions.gist: How does your fn build use a package's build steps without handing over your machine?
decisions.lesson: Some packages must generate code before you can use them, for example OpenGL bindings from a pinned spec. Today a dependency's `fn build` is checked and never run, so its author must commit generated files. Running dependency code at your compile time is how Cargo build scripts leak secrets. This ballot adds one explicit, sandboxed call.
decisions.story: Kai adds the opengl package. Nothing happens on `use opengl`. In her `fn build` she writes `b.include(opengl)`. The driver runs opengl's build rooted at that package's directory, fetches only its pinned URLs, and merges the generated bindings into her plan. `grep include` shows every package whose build ran, and the lockfile records what each emitted.

options.name: Explicit sandboxed include
options.detail: `b.include(opengl)` runs the package's `fn build` with a fresh BuildContext rooted at that package. It may read only its own directory and fetch only its pinned URLs. Its effect row and lock entries are its own. The returned fragment merges into your plan. Helper functions you call from a package see only the values you pass. Nothing runs on import.
options.technical: The driver runs the dependency entry under `run_build_entry_with_policy` with FS root set to the package directory. Net is limited to lock-pinned URLs. The returned BuildPlan fragment merges into the root plan; the lock records package id, entry hash, and emitted modules. Amends the 'checked and never run' rule for explicitly included entries only.

options.name: Keep never-run; authors commit generated files
options.detail: Current law. Zero compile-time risk from dependencies. Every binding package must commit its output and re-commit on each upstream change; consumers cannot regenerate for their platform.
options.technical: No change. Import remains inert; `.jet/generated` is root-only.

options.name: Pass your b, or run on import
options.detail: `opengl.build(b)` hands your context to the dependency, or importing runs its build automatically. Least ceremony. The dependency reads your files and your network with your rights, and nothing in your build file names it.
options.technical: Dependency entry receives the root BuildContext or runs at import resolution. Reproduces the Cargo build.rs trust hole.

comparisons.note: b.dependency runs the dependency build with its own Build rooted at the dependency directory; fetch hashes live in build.zig.zon.
comparisons.code: const gl = b.dependency("opengl", .{});

comparisons.note: Every action runs in a sandbox with declared inputs only; network only through hashed fetches.
comparisons.code: http_archive(name = "gl", sha256 = "…", urls = ["…"])

comparisons.note: build.rs runs as you with full disk and network. Known supply-chain hole.
comparisons.code:
// build.rs
let home = std::env::var("HOME")?;

recommendation.why: One grep-able call names every package whose build ran. The package works inside its own directory and its pinned URLs, never your home or schema. Your build file stays the single audit point.

whyNot.reason: It forces every binding package to commit output and blocks platform-specific generation.
It hands your machine to dependency code, the exact hole Cargo build scripts are known for.

recommendation.tradeoff: Dependency code now runs at your compile time when you ask for it. The sandbox root and the lock receipt bound what it can touch and record what it did.

losses.loss: Dependency code runs at your compile time when included.
losses.mitigation: Generating bindings for your platform requires running the generator on your machine.

decisions.title: Meta.* capabilities and the compile-time power ceiling
decisions.gist: Should compile-time code generation be a named capability a package can deny, and where does compile-time power stop?
decisions.lesson: Compile-time power and world effects are different axes: denying Net does not deny code generation. Jet already enforces effects per package, per entry, and per function. This ballot names the compile-time capabilities that reuse that machinery, and states as products how far compile-time power goes.
decisions.story: Priya runs platform security at a bank. She wants every Jet package to declare that no dependency build ever runs and that generated code is visible in the lockfile. With named capabilities she writes one deny line, reads one receipt, and can point auditors at the build entry that says what it may do.

options.name: Name Generate and Include; ladder stops at const generics
options.detail:
`Meta.Generate` covers `b.generate` and derive templates. `Meta.Include` covers `b.include`. `Meta.Reflect` (reading `T.@fields`, observe) is read-only and ungated. `Meta.Const` is named with const generics. Package policy may deny; an entry may write a ceiling; the lock records receipts.

The ladder ships bake, root build generate/observe/action, helpers plus sandboxed include, named sibling derives, and const generics. Refused: splice into existing code, token or tree macros, use-site type factories, in-place rewrite, a type with no file, running the program inside the compiler. Rewrite and Tokens are never named.
options.technical: Add `Meta.Generate`, `Meta.Include` to the effect vocabulary with the same deny/ceiling enforcement as Net. Root build entries must list them (E-class when unlisted). Lock receipt lists each included package and emitted module. Amends D-METADEPTH1 with the product ladder and refusal list.

options.name: No Meta names; the call site is the gate
options.detail: Generation is reachable only through the root `fn build`, so that file is already the audit point and the lock is the receipt. Simplest. A package cannot forbid `b.include`, and an enterprise has no vocabulary for the rule it wants.
options.technical: No vocabulary change. `b.generate` and `b.include` are plain plan methods. Policy cannot name them.

options.name: Name the full tree including Rewrite and Tokens
options.detail: Every rung has a name, including the ones Jet refuses. The refusal becomes explicit in the tree, and it advertises rewrite and token macros as one flag away.
options.technical: Adds Meta.Reflect, Generate, Types, Rewrite, Tokens as vocabulary; Rewrite and Tokens permanently denied.
options.code:
effects: { deny: [Meta.Rewrite, Meta.Tokens] }   # names rungs Jet refuses anyway
fn build(b: BuildContext) -[FS, Meta.Generate, Meta.Types]> BuildPlan { ... }

comparisons.note: Capabilities are named and denied per run; a build script cannot escalate silently.
comparisons.code: deno run --deny-net --allow-read=./schema main.ts

comparisons.note: Procedural macros run with full power and no name to deny; audits rely on trust.
comparisons.code:
#[derive(Serialize)]
struct Row { id: u64 }

recommendation.why: Enterprises get one deny line and one receipt using machinery Jet already has. Naming only the rungs that ship keeps refused power refused instead of one flag away. The ladder states products, not mechanisms.

whyNot.reason: A package cannot forbid dependency builds, and auditors have no vocabulary for the rule they want.
Naming rewrite and token macros advertises rungs Jet refuses regardless of any flag.

recommendation.tradeoff: Root build entries must list two more names on their ceiling. That one line is the price of a deniable, receipted capability.

losses.loss: Root build entries list two more names on their ceiling.
losses.mitigation: A capability a package can deny must appear where the entry declares what it may do.

decisions.title: Where should Jet own String's methods and standard abilities?
decisions.gist: Where should Jet's built-in String methods and standard abilities be declared?
decisions.lesson: A Jet string is one built-in value, not a second user type. A trait is a named ability, such as printing or equality. Today String methods live in Rust lookup tables, while Unicode rules live in `Core/text/text.jet`. Choose whether one Core file owns both contracts or shows a generated guide. Keep the same public calls either way.
decisions.explainer: Option A makes a Core source file the canonical place for String's method signatures and standard trait coverage. It keeps the built-in String representation and existing calls. Option B adds a generated, read-only index while Rust tables remain authoritative.
decisions.story: Mina is changing text behavior. She can find Unicode functions in `Core/text/text.jet`, but not the source for `String.trim()` or its standard abilities. She needs one clear place to see the whole contract without learning a second String type.
decisions.inWild:
text = "  hi  "
print(text.strip())
print(len("a,b,c".split(",")))
# https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str
decisions.detail: This choice is about ownership and discoverability, not new user syntax or behavior. No option may create another String type, change public names, or split execution-tier meaning.

options.name: Core source owns String
options.detail: Keep the built-in String value and public calls. Add an internal `Core/text/string.jet` declaration file for its methods and standard abilities. Do not expose a `core.text.string` namespace. Compiler code supplies typed operations for safe storage access; no second type or dispatcher appears.
options.technical: Keep `Type::String` as the one primitive. Core source owns method signatures and trait coverage. AOT, Cranelift JIT, interpreter, and web call the same typed providers.
options.code:
// `Core/text/string.jet` owns the declarations; calls stay the same.
text := "  hi  "
print(text.trim())
print("a,b,c".split(",").len())

options.name: Generated String guide
options.detail: Keep Rust signatures and trait tables as owners. Generate a read-only reference at `Core/text/string.api.jet`; sema and codegen never read it. Users can find the list, but edits still belong in Rust.
options.technical: `Collections.rs` and `Traits.rs` stay authoritative. The generated file is only a reference; it never typechecks a program.
options.code:
// Generated reference: `Core/text/string.api.jet`.
text := "  hi  "
print(text.trim())
print("a,b,c".split(",").len())

comparisons.note: Python documents `str.strip` and `str.split` with its built-in text type: https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str.
comparisons.code:
text = "  hi  "
print(text.strip())
print(len("a,b,c".split(",")))

recommendation.why: A makes the Core source the place readers expect, while preserving one primitive, today's calls, and one implementation across execution tiers.
gains: Methods and standard abilities have one visible Core owner.
Users keep the same String value and method calls.

losses.loss: Typed compiler operations still provide safe access to String storage.
losses.mitigation: Core source cannot safely manipulate the primitive's private byte representation; narrow typed providers keep storage access safe.

whyNot.reason: A generated guide is easier to browse, but Rust remains the real owner of the method and trait behavior.

recommendation.tradeoff: Core source owns the behavior users see; Rust provides only typed storage operations.

decisions.title: Choose whether to warn on one-shot mutable selection
decisions.gist: Should Jet warn when a mutable local only selects between two values?
decisions.lesson: Jet can bind a value with `::` from an `if` expression. Some Core code instead gives a mutable name a default and immediately replaces it under a condition. Existing branch warnings do not cover this pattern. Decide whether a narrow advisory should point out the immutable form. Neither choice changes how programs run.
decisions.story: Mira reads a Core function that computes the number of right-hand-side columns. She wants to know whether later code can change that count.

options.name: Warn only for a safe one-shot selection
options.detail: A new advisory points from an adjacent literal default and one conditional replacement to the immutable `if` expression. Never warn if the name is read between those statements, reassigned later, captured, passed by mutable reference, or used in a loop. Never rewrite code automatically. A bare warning does not block building.
options.technical: Sema examines one local declaration and its immediately following Boolean `if` assignment. It proves the assigned name resolves to the same binding, checks all later uses for writes or mutable aliases, and excludes side-effectful initializers and conditions that depend on that binding. It suggests a value `if` with a full `else`. A new diagnostic must have a registered what/why/fix row, a positive UI snapshot, and negative cases. Its advice cannot make a claim about performance.

options.name: Keep this choice manual
options.detail: Keep the mutable form valid without a new advisory. Teach `if` value selection in examples when it improves clarity. Authors decide whether the mutable form suits their context.

comparisons.note: The official Rust Book binds the result of an `if` expression to an immutable local. This demonstrates the idiom, not a performance benefit or a Rust lint.
comparisons.code: let cols = if shape.len() == 2 { shape[1] } else { 1 }; // https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch03-05-control-flow.html#using-if-in-a-let-statement

recommendation.why: A narrowly scoped warning reveals a removable mutation while leaving legitimate state changes and all runtime behavior alone.

whyNot.reason: B keeps warning counts unchanged but leaves this common local pattern to manual review.

recommendation.tradeoff: Readers gain a precise suggestion at the cost of one additional advisory on an existing local pattern.

decisions.title: Keep Jet's resident compiler within its memory-address range
decisions.gist: How should Jet fix Cranelift's memory-address crash without changing jet run?
decisions.lesson: Jet runs compiled code in memory. Its current compiler puts a small jump and its target slot too far apart and crashes before the program starts. Both choices must keep ordinary jet run, live function replacement, and the same typed process result.
decisions.story: A developer sends text to a child process. Jet must report the child's exit status, but the resident compiler crashes before the child runs.

options.name: Patch the current Cranelift dependency
options.detail: Keep Jet's current compiler and its live function replacement. Vendor a corrected build of the existing version. Allocate executable jumps and writable target slots within a bounded shared region, and cover distant code relocations with tests. Exit explicitly if the region fills, rather than panic or silently switch execution modes.
options.technical: Preserve PIC and the 0.112.3 hotswap API. Keep PLT/GOT and generated-code relocations within signed rel32 range or use verified far-call veneers. Exercise both relocation directions above two gigabytes.
options.code:
process.stdin_text(process.cmd(["/bin/sh", "-c", "read input; [ \"$input\" = expected ]"]), "expected\n") ?? panic("failed")
print("stdin:accepted")

options.name: Upgrade Cranelift and port live replacement
options.detail: Adopt a newer Cranelift with distant-call support. Rebuild Jet's resident function-replacement mechanism over the new compiler API. Keep default compilation and matching process errors, without an interpreter fallback.
options.technical: The verified fixed Cranelift 0.136.0 removed the 0.112.3 hotswap and redefinition methods, so Jet must provide a new equivalent resident replacement design before cutover.
options.code:
process.stdin_text(process.cmd(["/bin/sh", "-c", "read input; [ \"$input\" = expected ]"]), "expected\n") ?? panic("failed")
print("stdin:accepted")

comparisons.note: Rust process I/O reports a child exit status without a resident compiler. See https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/process/struct.Command.html.
comparisons.code:
let status = Command::new("sh").arg("-c").arg("read input; [ \"$input\" = expected ]").status()?;
assert!(status.success());

recommendation.why: The existing resident code can keep its proven replacement behavior while the failing allocator is repaired and tested.

whyNot.reason: The newer compiler removed Jet's live replacement API; B requires a new mechanism before matching today's behavior.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet accepts maintenance of a small compiler patch to preserve its current resident behavior.

decisions.title: Make TCP streams one live handle on every execution path
decisions.gist: Should a TCP stream hide its live socket or keep public fields backed by a handle table?
decisions.lesson: A TCP stream owns a live socket, not just an address. Jet currently declares public fd, host, and port fields, while compiled network calls return a socket handle with hidden state. TLS needs to consume that same live socket. Both choices must preserve typed errors, safe ownership, and identical behavior when Jet runs or builds the program.
decisions.story: Mara connects to a server and then starts TLS on that connection. Jet checks her program but generated Rust rejects the source stream because its three public fields are not the live socket the TLS provider consumes.
decisions.detail:
D-NETSOCKET1=A requires typed socket handles shared with the task runtime. D-NETTLSSTREAM1=A requires TLS to consume the connected stream.

Core/net/net.jet currently exposes TCPStream {fd:Int,host:String,port:Int}, while Prelude/CoreLib/Top/NetHTTP.rs owns JetTCPStream {inner: std::net::TcpStream, closed, shutdown, timeout state}. The focused TLS test fails generated Rust type checking before transport (artifact://2145). Current public fields cannot reconstruct or safely authorize that live socket. No option may forge an OS descriptor, use a second socket, or turn a provider failure into success.

options.name: Opaque typed TCP stream
options.detail: Make TCPStream a source-visible nominal type whose live socket and mutable state are private and owned by the common provider. Remove public fd, host, and port construction and field access in one cutover. Use existing tcp_peer_socket_addr and tcp_local_socket_addr operations to inspect addresses; do not expose a raw descriptor. TLS consumes the same typed connection, not a reconstructed one. Invalid or closed handles produce typed errors.
options.technical: Map the checked source nominal TCPStream directly to the native socket carrier in AOT and the same logical capability in default run and interpreter. Migrate every Core caller, test, example, conformance fixture, and generated projection using the public record. Keep OS state in the provider and preserve typed error conversion; never map arbitrary source records into native sockets.

options.name: Public record plus checked handle table
options.detail: Keep TCPStream's public fd, host, and port fields. The fd is a Jet-issued handle token, not an OS descriptor. Each execution path maintains a checked table of live sockets. Every network operation validates the token and its lifetime and ignores editable host and port fields as proof of identity. A fabricated or stale token returns a typed error, and TLS consumes the matching table entry.
options.technical: Implement one provider-owned handle table with fresh non-reused tokens, safe lifetime checks, and matching ownership rules on AOT, default run, and interpreter. Test stale, fabricated, copied, and altered public records; never call from_raw_fd on user input. Preserve table state and TLS socket transfer across calls.

comparisons.note: Rust's TcpStream owns a socket through private fields and moves into the TLS stream. See https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/net/struct.TcpStream.html and https://docs.rs/rustls/latest/rustls/struct.StreamOwned.html.

recommendation.why: A gives beginners one typed connection and lets TLS consume the live socket without trusting editable fields or synchronizing handle tables.

whyNot.reason: B keeps mutable public socket fields that cannot establish identity and requires lifetime-safe handle tables on every execution path.

recommendation.tradeoff: Current programs that construct TCPStream records or read their fields must migrate to typed socket operations.

decisions.title: Choose the public shape of TCP listeners
decisions.gist: Should a TCP listener keep editable public fields or become a private live handle?
decisions.lesson: A listener owns a live socket that accepts connections. Jet currently exposes fd, host, and port as editable fields, although its native provider stores the socket privately. Both choices keep the same bind, address, and accept operations. The choice determines whether callers can construct or alter a listener without binding a socket.
decisions.story: Mara builds a local server. She binds an available port, finds its actual address, and accepts a client. Her code must never turn an edited listener record into an unchecked operating-system socket.

options.name: Private typed TCP listener
options.detail: Make TCPListener a source-visible type with private provider-owned live state, like the ratified TCPStream. Only binding returns a usable listener. Use listener_local_socket_addr to inspect the actual bound address and tcp_accept to accept. No public fd, host, or port construction or field access remains. Releasing the final owned listener closes its socket; a live shared owner keeps it usable. Update any field users in one cutover and prove bind, address, accept, and lifetime behavior on all three execution paths.
options.technical: The provider holds the listener socket. Checked source calls carry the typed listener to AOT, default run, and interpreter without reconstructing an operating-system socket from public data. Keep the existing NetError surface for failed bind, address, or accept. Do not change ratified D-NET-HANDLE-ABI1=A for TCPStream.
options.code:
use core.net as net
fn run() {
    listener :: net.tcp_listen("127.0.0.1:0") ?? panic("listen")
    address :: net.socket_to_string(net.listener_local_socket_addr(listener) ?? panic("address"))
    _client :: net.tcp_connect(address) ?? panic("connect")
    accepted :: net.tcp_accept(listener) ?? panic("accept")
    print(net.socket_host(net.tcp_peer_socket_addr(accepted) ?? panic("peer address")))
}

options.name: Public listener record with checked token
options.detail: Keep TCPListener's editable fd, host, and port fields. Interpret fd only as a Jet-issued token that must resolve to a live provider-owned listener before each use. Ignore editable host and port as proof of socket identity; the address operation returns the actual bound address. A fabricated or stale token returns a typed NetError; copies of a valid token share its listener until the final live owner releases it. Preserve bind, address, and accept calls on all three execution paths.
options.technical: A provider-owned handle table must validate identity and lifetime across AOT, default run, and interpreter, including copied tokens, edited records, and final-owner release. Never convert a public fd field directly into a native socket. Keep D-NET-HANDLE-ABI1=A for TCPStream even if listener fields remain public.

comparisons.note: Rust exposes private TcpListener fields, bind, local_addr, and accept; dropping closes it. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/net/struct.TcpListener.html.

recommendation.why: A prevents public records from claiming to own sockets and matches the already approved private TCP stream shape.
gains: Only binding creates a usable listener.

losses.loss: Callers using public listener fields would need the address operation.
losses.mitigation: Keeping editable fields would let a record claim socket identity without owning a bound socket.

whyNot.reason: Its public token still needs a checked table and lifetime rules for copied, edited, and stale records.

recommendation.tradeoff: Migrate public field access to a checked address operation in exchange for one provider-owned listener shape.

decisions.title: Choose safe Core file handle ownership across execution paths
decisions.gist: Should file handles hide live ownership or keep public fields with checked tokens?
decisions.lesson: Jet's source records expose path and fd, but the provider returns owned buffered handles. Generated Rust currently rejects this mismatch (artifact://1908). Automatic close is the only close rule. Path inspection remains required. Neither choice may forge an OS descriptor.
decisions.explainer: Choose one source handle shape: private provider ownership or public fields backed by checked Jet tokens.
decisions.story: Nora builds a file-backed cache. She creates and writes a file, opens it for reading, and inspects temporary and lock paths. Her source passes shape checks, but generated Rust sees a different provider handle.
decisions.detail:
Card #3558 chooses one file-handle representation before implementation. Core/files/files.jet:60-90 declares public path/fd records for FileReader, FileWriter, and FileLock. Its constructors are at lines 96-102, and temp/lock constructors are at lines 736-742.

The provider instead returns private buffered or cleanup-owning values: HandlesRaylib.rs:13-23, FileStream.rs:8-40, FSIoEnvOsTesting.rs:109-128, and CommonTypes.rs:686-702. The focused generated-Rust failure is captured at artifact://1908.

D-CORE-FILECLOSE1=A fixes automatic close only. D-FSOPS1 and D-IO2 fix filesystem operations, streaming, and path inspection, but no public fd shape. This ballot chooses only the source/provider handle ABI. Neither option forges an OS descriptor.

options.name: Private provider-owned handles
options.detail:
Make FileReader, FileWriter, and FileLock source-visible opaque values whose live state belongs to the provider. Keep TempDir, TempFile, and FileLock cleanup ownership with their provider values. Preserve read-only .path inspection, using a safe accessor if fields become private. Remove public fd fields and source record construction. Keep open, create, append, line methods, explicit flush, and automatic close.

A maps the checked source handle to the provider-owned native value for compiled output and the same logical value for default execution and the interpreter. Copied or fabricated source records are not handles. No operation accepts an integer as an OS descriptor.
options.technical: Canonical source: Core/files/files.jet:60-102 and :736-742. Native carrier: crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/HandlesRaylib.rs:13-23 and Top/FileStream.rs:8-40. Temporary and lock cleanup: Top/FSIoEnvOsTesting.rs:109-128 and JetStd/CommonTypes.rs:686-702, 6642-6661. Keep D-CORE-FILECLOSE1=A automatic close only, D-FSOPS1=A operation/path law, and D-IO2 streaming law. Preserve .path as a read-only inspection view. Do not call from_raw_fd or convert source integers into OS descriptors.

    writer.write_line("hello")
    writer.flush()
    reader :: files.open(path)
    loop line in reader.lines() -> print(line)
    temp :: files.temp_file("files-handle")
    lock :: files.lock("/tmp/files-handle.lock")
    print("{temp.path} {lock.path}")
}

options.name: Public fields with a checked token table
options.detail:
Keep public path/fd records for file and lock handles, while making fd a Jet-issued token rather than an OS descriptor. A provider-owned table maps live tokens to provider handles. Every operation checks the token, owner, lifetime, and record consistency. Copied, stale, fabricated, or altered records return typed IOError. Path remains readable but does not prove identity.

All execution paths must share token validation and automatic cleanup. TempDir and TempFile keep path inspection and cleanup. The provider never uses from_raw_fd or treats user integers as descriptors. This preserves existing field access, but it keeps a second identity system beside the live handle.
options.technical: Retain Core/files/files.jet public fields, but define fd as a non-OS Jet token. Each provider tier owns a checked table, validates copied/stale/fabricated/altered records before read, write, flush, or lock use, and removes entries on automatic cleanup. Editable path is display and inspection only; the table entry is identity. Never forge or reconstruct an OS descriptor from fd. This option must preserve D-CORE-FILECLOSE1=A automatic close only, D-FSOPS1=A operations/path, and D-IO2 streaming behavior.

decisions.title: When does replacing an owned resource release the old one?
decisions.gist: When does replacing an owned resource release the old one?
decisions.lesson: A resource owner keeps a file, lock, or connection alive. Reassignment gives one variable a new owner. Scope cleanup is already required, but the old owner’s release point is not specified. This choice fixes that observable point without changing safety or automatic cleanup.
decisions.explainer: Choose when a successful assignment releases the value it displaced. Both choices preserve automatic cleanup and explicit consuming close.
decisions.story: Rina replaces a temporary file while keeping its pathname for logging. She needs to know whether the old file still exists before leaving the block.
decisions.detail:
Current Jet law: docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:2377-2392 promises scope cleanup and consuming close. Memory v5 prohibits replacement while an incompatible view lives; it does not define this release point. D-FILES-HANDLE-ABI1=A assigns cleanup to private provider-owned handles, not a timing rule. The earlier compiled witness in ~/.cache/jet-test-scratch/pip-file-retired-owner-iqxa1j06/run.jet printed four true values; other resident cleanup probes disagreed or refused. Those observations do not choose the language rule. Current Core checking regressions still block a fresh complete comparison.

The beginner uses ordinary assignment in the shown program. Under A, an expert keeps distinct named owners when both must remain live. Under B, an expert uses the existing consuming close operation when release must happen before block exit. Both choices preserve error-reporting flush as separate from cleanup. A pathname alone does not own a resource. The same rule must hold in every applicable execution mode. File existence observes temporary-path removal; buffered readers and writers also need direct provider-close and rejected-reuse tests.

Executed Rust comparison: ~/.cache/jet-test-scratch/pip-rust-resource-reassign-2b8e6lis/oracle.rs; captures ~/.cache/jet-luna/pip-stabilize-flt1kvhj/resource-reassign-rust*. The comparison establishes Rust behavior only, not the chosen Jet rule.

options.name: Release on replacement
options.detail: After a replacement value is ready, release the displaced ownership before the next statement. The sample prints false, true, true, true. Existing owners or legal shared copies still control final provider cleanup.
options.technical: Applies to a successful checked overwrite of an owned resource value, including owned resource slots in aggregates. Do not change expression evaluation order. A failing right-hand side that never writes leaves the old value intact until existing exit rules apply. Reinitializing a moved-out slot drops nothing old. Existing borrow, move, explicit-close and defer checks remain binding. No new close spelling, raw descriptor access, error conversion or execution-mode exception is authorized.
options.code:
use core.files as files
fn replaced_paths() -> [String] {
    owner := files.temp_file("before") ?? panic("temp file")
    old_path :: owner.path
    owner = files.temp_file("after") ?? panic("temp file")
    print(files.exists(old_path))
    path :: owner.path
    print(files.exists(path))
    [old_path, path]
}
fn run() { paths :: replaced_paths()
    print(!files.exists(paths[0]))
    print(!files.exists(paths[1]))
}

options.name: Release at the assigning block end
options.detail: Move displaced ownership into the cleanup list of the block containing the assignment. Release it when that block exits. The sample prints true, true, true, true.
options.technical: Every successful replacement retains its displaced resource separately. Cleanup belongs to the assigning block, including an inner block, not necessarily the original declaration block. Release retained resources in reverse replacement order on every exit, including error, panic and cancellation. Moving or closing the current value does not lose its separately retained predecessors. Aggregate-slot replacement follows the same block rule. Failed right-hand sides and writes to moved-out slots retain no new predecessor. Existing borrow and move restrictions remain unchanged.

    [old_path, path]

    print(!files.exists(paths[0]))
    print(!files.exists(paths[1]))

comparisons.note: The official Rust Reference says assignment drops an initialized displaced value. This std-only file program was compiled and run on 2026-09-24: false, true, true, true; exit0; empty stderr.

recommendation.why: A releases ownership when replacement removes the old value. A saved pathname does not silently keep a file alive. Keep two named owners when both resources are needed.
gains: No hidden displaced handle remains after replacement.
All execution modes use the same observable cleanup point.

losses.loss: A saved temporary pathname may disappear at replacement.
losses.mitigation: A pathname is text, not ownership. Keeping the file alive requires keeping its owner.

whyNot.reason: B keeps resources that the variable can no longer name until its assigning block ends.

recommendation.tradeoff: A chooses immediate ownership release over keeping displaced resources alive for the rest of a block.

Preserve rejected writes while views are live and avoid duplicate close. Rebuild and compare exact outputs/provider events on AOT, default native execution and interpreter; applicable web resource values follow the same rule. No refused or skipped execution is parity. Update the durable explanation without altering historical receipts.

decisions.title: Who owns bounded raster images?
decisions.gist: Should Jet Core own checked raster decoding and resizing, or should an image package own them?
decisions.lesson: A raster image has pixel data, size, color rules, and a file format. Jet has game asset handles and a local PPM/Tensor example, but no general checked image decoder. Either choice must limit input bytes and decoded pixels, reject unsupported formats and animations, and work on every applicable execution tier.
decisions.explainer: This chooses ownership, not a faster spelling. Option A makes the small reusable image value and checked codec a Core contract. Option B keeps Core limited to bytes and tensors and requires a separately installed first-party package for the same thumbnail. Both use one immutable RGBA8 image value, explicit limits, typed failures, and a named nearest-neighbor resize.
decisions.story: Mira needs to make a four-by-four thumbnail from a supplied two-by-two PNG. She must reject huge or malformed images before allocation, and see the same pixels in a compiled program and jet run.
decisions.inWild: Go 1.25 image.DecodeConfig reads dimensions and format before decoding. image.Decode reads pixels, and image/png.Encode writes PNG. Standard image/draw has no nearest-neighbor resize call, so the example uses a loop. Official APIs: https://pkg.go.dev/image#DecodeConfig and https://pkg.go.dev/image/png#Encode. Pinned source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/golang/go/go1.25.0/src/image/format.go. PNG encoder: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/golang/go/go1.25.0/src/image/png/writer.go. This is source-backed illustration, not an executed Go receipt.
decisions.detail:
Today examples/features/foundations/arrays/arrays.jet:168-233 handles P3 PPM and calls an unchecked Tensor resize. #2812 marked that example source-only; #2919 owns runtime proof. Core/game/raylib holds atlas handles, not general pixels. Core/files/files.jet:129,144 reads and writes bytes.

A new image API requires this owner choice. This ballot authorizes no external codec dependency. A later dependency has its own gate. If A wins, implementation changes source, provider routes, examples, golden, and tier tests together. If B wins, Core cannot keep a shadow decoder. Format variants, errors, and limits below are part of this choice, not a performance claim.

options.name: Checked images in Core
options.detail: core.image owns immutable RGBA8/sRGB pixels, checked metadata, static PNG/JPEG/GIF decode, PNG/JPEG encode, and nearest-neighbor resize. A beginner passes explicit safe budgets. An expert can inspect dimensions before decoding and lower the budgets; an unsupported color profile, animated GIF, malformed input, or exceeded budget returns ImageError, never a panic or partial frame. JPEG alpha is opaque. Output dimensions and bytes are checked before allocation. No ambient filesystem or process image library is used.
options.technical:
Limits holds three positive Int budgets: max_input_bytes, max_pixels, and max_output_bytes. Exact calls:
image.inspect(&[U8], Limits) -> ImageInfo !ImageError.
image.decode(&[U8], Limits) -> Image !ImageError.
image.resize(Image, Int, Int, ResizeFilter, Limits) -> Image !ImageError.
image.encode(Image, ImageFormat, Limits) -> [U8] !ImageError.

Image is immutable RGBA8 in sRGB. ImageInfo reports dimensions, format and color. Decode supports 8-bit PNG, baseline JPEG, and single-frame GIF. Encode supports PNG and JPEG. ResizeFilter starts with .Nearest. Unsupported profiles, bit depths, animation, and formats return typed errors.

Use Core.files.read_at with max_input_bytes + 1 to bound file reads. Core.files owns read/write effects. Checked arithmetic protects dimension multiplication. Full decoding enforces byte and pixel limits even after a valid header. Jet Core owns validation and errors across all applicable tiers. Codec leaves cannot set policy or pull in an unapproved external crate. Exact tier and golden proof is needed before shipment.

options.name: Separate image package
options.detail: A first-party image package owns the same immutable RGBA8 value, explicit limits, checked codecs and resize. Core remains bytes, tensors, and game/UI handles. Every application explicitly declares a versioned image package dependency. The package may be unavailable to an offline beginner until installed; a fresh project cannot import core.image. The same malformed/bomb/color/animation safety contract is required and independently proven across applicable tiers.
options.technical:
Proposed package declaration: deps: { image: "0.1.0" } in package.jet and `use image` in source. The package exports Limits, ImageInfo, Image, ImageError, ResizeFilter, ImageFormat, inspect/decode/resize/encode with A's borrowed-byte signatures and supported static PNG/JPEG/GIF, output codecs PNG/JPEG, resource budgets, and failures.

The caller uses a bounded Core.files.read_at. No hidden Core image duplicate. Version is illustrative, not an existing published artifact. No external codec dependency is assumed; later additions require the separate dependency ballot. Tier/golden proof is a condition of shipment, not evidence already held.

comparisons.note: DecodeConfig obtains width/height before pixel allocation; image.Decode reads pixels; PNG Encode writes output. There is no stdlib nearest-neighbor scaling call, so the explicit loop matches the four-by-four job. Pinned https://raw.githubusercontent.com/golang/go/go1.25.0/src/image/format.go and src/image/png/writer.go. Illustrative, not executed.

f, _ := os.Open("photo.png")
cfg, _, _ := image.DecodeConfig(f)
if cfg.Width > 4000 || cfg.Height > 4000 { panic("image too large") }
f.Seek(0, 0)
src, _, _ := image.Decode(f)
dst := image.NewRGBA(image.Rect(0, 0, 4, 4))
for y := 0; y < 4; y++ { for x := 0; x < 4; x++ { dst.Set(x, y, src.At(x*cfg.Width/4, y*cfg.Height/4)) } }
out, _ := os.Create("small.png")
png.Encode(out, dst)

losses.loss: Core must maintain bounded PNG/JPEG/GIF parsing and shared color rules.
losses.mitigation: The beginner can only decode common images without a dependency if Core owns their checked meaning.

whyNot.reason: B preserves Core size, but common thumbnail work always needs package discovery and installation before it can run.

recommendation.tradeoff: Core owns bounded still-image data, not video, image editing frameworks or platform UI. New codec dependencies remain separately gated.

decisions.title: Bound one shared Core archive inflater for Core image
decisions.gist: Should Core archive stop decoding when a caller's output limit is reached?
decisions.lesson: Jet's archive decoder can expand a small compressed file to 64 MiB. The new image API promises smaller caller-chosen limits, but checks them only after decoding. Both choices keep one decoder and reject oversized images. One adds a public bounded archive call; the other pauses image decoding until that shared limit has an approved home.
decisions.explainer: This is a safety boundary, not a faster spelling. A gives the existing archive decoder a caller-chosen ceiling. B avoids a new public API but cannot ship bounded PNG decoding now. Neither adds a codec dependency or copies the decoder into the image module.
decisions.story: Mira reads a compressed PNG scanline under a 4096-byte output limit. A tiny input must not make her program allocate 64 MiB before it rejects the image.
decisions.inWild: Go 1.25 standard compress/zlib returns a reader. io.LimitReader caps the bytes read from that reader; reading one extra byte lets the caller detect an oversized stream. Official APIs: https://pkg.go.dev/compress/zlib#NewReader and https://pkg.go.dev/io#LimitReader. Illustration only; not an executed receipt.
decisions.detail:
Current Core/archive/archive.jet:33-34,119-200 caps inflation at 67108864 bytes. In the unmerged image branch, Core/image/image.jet:343 calls archive.decompress before checking the expected scanline length and the caller's output limit. The independent review agent://ImagePngAudit found a small-input inflation bomb against the image limit.

D-CORE-IMAGE1=A ratified explicit image byte, pixel and output limits; it did not ratify a new Core.archive API. A duplicate image-specific DEFLATE parser would break Jet's one-mechanism rule. This ballot grants no external dependency and no larger output limit. Existing archive callers must retain their current success and error behavior.

options.name: One bounded archive decoder
options.detail:
Add source-owned core.archive.decompress_bounded(data: [U8], max_output_bytes: Int) -> [U8] !ArchiveError. The positive output limit must be at most 67108864. The decoder checks the bound before every output append, including stored, fixed and dynamic DEFLATE blocks. A decoded empty stream succeeds. Zero, negative or above-cap limits and output overruns return a new ArchiveError.Limit.

Keep core.archive.decompress(data) as the beginner's 64 MiB call backed by the same decoder, preserving its old Unsupported error for oversize output. Core.image passes its checked PNG scanline length, maps ArchiveError.Limit to ImageError.Limit, and never allocates above the caller's chosen output bound. Check malformed streams and Adler-32 errors separately. No new external dependency, host policy, duplicate inflater or image-only shortcut.
options.technical:
Exact new call: core.archive.decompress_bounded(data: [U8], max_output_bytes: Int) -> [U8] !ArchiveError. Add ArchiveError.Limit. Positive max_output_bytes in 1..=67108864; check before each byte is appended, not after full inflation. Existing decompress keeps its previous 64 MiB cap and Unsupported-on-overrun behavior by delegating to the shared internal bounded decoder.

core.image.decode supplies min(its positive max_output_bytes, its checked exact PNG scanline length), never a fixed global cap. Stored, fixed and dynamic streams, checksum, empty and malformed input have one meaning on AOT, default run, interpreter and applicable web.

options.name: Defer image PNG decoding
options.detail: Leave the archive public API unchanged. Keep core.image PNG decoding unshipped until an owner-approved shared bounded decoder exists. A caller can still use core.archive.decompress with its fixed 64 MiB ceiling, but cannot truthfully claim a smaller explicit image output budget. Do not copy DEFLATE into core.image, hide another decoder in a host provider, or weaken D-CORE-IMAGE1=A's safety terms. This choice delays the PNG image example and tier proof.
options.technical: No new public Core.archive call or error variant. D-CORE-IMAGE1=A image limit remains binding. The unmerged image PNG path is blocked rather than made public with a false smaller allocation ceiling; no compatibility or I9 exception is granted.

comparisons.note: A zlib reader and io.LimitReader stop output reads at a caller's bound. Read bound + 1 to detect oversize. Official https://pkg.go.dev/compress/zlib#NewReader and https://pkg.go.dev/io#LimitReader; source-backed illustration, not run.

recommendation.why: One shared bound makes the ratified image limit real without copying a decoder or relying on a new dependency.
gains: The caller's output limit stops inflation before allocation.
Existing archive calls retain their current results.

losses.loss: Core archive gains one public call and one error case.
losses.mitigation: Image callers need a smaller bound; the current public call accepts no limit and can expand to 64 MiB.

whyNot.reason: B preserves the archive surface but blocks the approved image decoder indefinitely.

recommendation.tradeoff: Keep the old simple call and one shared decoder; an expert sets a smaller bound when input is untrusted.

surface.gist: Should Core archive stop decoding when a caller's output limit is reached?
surface.lesson: Jet's archive decoder can expand a small compressed file to 64 MiB. The new image API promises smaller caller-chosen limits, but checks them only after decoding. Both choices keep one decoder and reject oversized images. One adds a public bounded archive call; the other pauses image decoding until that shared limit has an approved home.

current.note: Today the only archive zlib call can expand up to 64 MiB before checking a 4096-byte image budget. Image code is unmerged.

wild.note: Go's zlib reader can be wrapped with a read limit. Official: https://pkg.go.dev/io#LimitReader and https://pkg.go.dev/compress/zlib#NewReader. Not run.

options.name: One bounded archive decoder
options.gist: Add a caller-chosen output cap to the shared zlib decoder.
gains: Untrusted image bytes cannot exceed their output limit.
Existing callers keep their current results.
losses: Core archive gains one call and one error case.

proposed.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
packed :: core.files.read_at("scanlines.zlib", 0, 1025) ?? panic("read")
raw :: archive.decompress_bounded(packed, 4096) ?? panic("too large or invalid")
print(raw.len())

options.name: Defer image PNG decoding
options.gist: Keep the archive API but pause the image decoder.
gains: Core archive adds no public call.
losses: Approved image PNG decoding stays unavailable.

recommendation.why: A enforces the promised limit before allocating decoded bytes.
gains: One shared decoder serves archive and images.

losses.loss: Core archive gains one call and one error case.
losses.mitigation: An image's caller-chosen limit is smaller than the archive call's fixed 64 MiB.

whyNot.reason: B leaves the ratified image decoder blocked.

recommendation.tradeoff: The simple archive call stays; experts can set a smaller cap.

decisions.title: Choose transparent RGBA input behavior for JPEG encode
decisions.gist: What should JPEG encoding do with transparent pixels in a Core image?
decisions.lesson: JPEG stores no alpha channel. Core images can contain transparent pixels whose hidden RGB bytes should not become visible by surprise. The approved image contract says JPEG output is opaque but does not choose how to handle transparent input. One option rejects it; the other blends it onto white. Opaque input works under both.
decisions.explainer: A caller can decode a transparent PNG into a safe RGBA8 image, then ask for a JPEG. JPEG cannot keep transparency. A returns a typed error so the caller keeps PNG or chooses another approved transformation. B makes the missing background choice for everyone by using white. Both retain one image value and avoid exposing invisible RGB directly.
decisions.story: Mira receives a one-pixel PNG with invisible red RGB and zero alpha. She converts it to JPEG. She must not discover that the supposedly invisible red pixel turned red after saving.
decisions.inWild: Go 1.25 image/jpeg.Encode writes the RGB bytes from an image.RGBA fast path without consulting its alpha byte. A caller can store hidden red in its public Pix buffer. Official pinned writer.go:425-447: https://github.com/golang/go/blob/6e676ab2b809d46623acb5988248d95d1eb7939c/src/image/jpeg/writer.go#L425-L447. Go's choice is evidence of a risk, not an approved Jet behavior. Source-backed illustration; not run.
decisions.detail: D-CORE-IMAGE1=A ratified immutable RGBA8/sRGB images, JPEG encoding, typed ImageError, and opaque JPEG output. It did not choose the output color when an input alpha byte is below 255. Jet's Core/image/image.jet remains unmerged and currently returns Unsupported for all JPEG encoding. In Go 1.25, image/jpeg/writer.go:425-447 can read raw RGB from image.RGBA regardless of alpha. This ballot chooses one source-owned Jet rule before JPEG encoding ships. Neither choice adds a public compositing API, a dependency, or a performance claim.

options.name: Reject transparent input
options.detail: Before JPEG output allocation, inspect every RGBA alpha byte. If any alpha is below 255, return ImageError.Unsupported. Opaque input uses the one baseline JPEG encoder. A beginner keeps PNG for transparency. An expert may use a separately approved pixel compositor if one later exists, but this decision does not add one. The check protects hidden RGB and avoids silently choosing a background. JPEG decoding still produces alpha 255.
options.technical: Exact existing call remains image.encode(Image, .JPEG, Limits) -> [U8] !ImageError. On any input alpha != 255, return Err(ImageError.Unsupported) before encoding or allocating JPEG output; all opaque pixels use their RGB bytes. Do not read or publish hidden RGB in the error. Limits and tier semantics remain those of D-CORE-IMAGE1. No new public variant, overload, quality knob, or dependency.

options.name: Blend transparency onto white
options.detail: Before JPEG output allocation, combine each RGB channel with an opaque white sRGB matte using straight alpha. A zero-alpha red pixel becomes white; a partially transparent pixel blends toward white. Then encode the opaque result as baseline JPEG. A beginner gets a JPEG without a separate conversion. An expert cannot choose another matte through this API. White is a visible policy, not a hidden fallback or a promise of exact JPEG pixel bytes. JPEG decoding still produces alpha 255.
options.technical: Exact existing call remains image.encode(Image, .JPEG, Limits) -> [U8] !ImageError. For each channel c and alpha a in 0..=255, composite sRGB byte as (c*a + 255*(255-a) + 127) /% 255 before JPEG conversion. The arithmetic fits Int and discards hidden RGB at a=0. Do not allocate above Limits; no separate public compositing call, dependency, or quality knob. This chooses an sRGB byte-space matte, not a linear-light color-managed composite.

comparisons.note: Go's RGBA fast path reads raw R, G and B bytes and does not inspect A. The caller can directly write Pix, so hidden color may become visible. Official pinned https://github.com/golang/go/blob/6e676ab2b809d46623acb5988248d95d1eb7939c/src/image/jpeg/writer.go#L425-L447; source-backed, not run.
comparisons.code:
rgba := image.NewRGBA(image.Rect(0, 0, 1, 1))
copy(rgba.Pix[:4], []byte{255, 0, 0, 0}) // invisible red bytes
var out bytes.Buffer
err := jpeg.Encode(&out, rgba, nil) // fast path reads RGB, not A
if err != nil { panic(err) }

recommendation.why: Rejecting transparent input keeps hidden RGB hidden and avoids choosing a background that the caller never requested.
gains: Opaque photos still encode as JPEG.
Transparent input fails with an explicit typed error.

losses.loss: A transparent image cannot be saved as JPEG through this API.
losses.mitigation: JPEG has no alpha, and Core has no approved background choice or image compositor.

whyNot.reason: B silently chooses white and changes partially transparent colors without the caller choosing a matte.

recommendation.tradeoff: Keep PNG for transparency. Add an explicit compositor only through a separate owner decision if needed.

surface.gist: What should JPEG encoding do with transparent pixels in a Core image?
surface.lesson: JPEG stores no alpha channel. Core images can contain transparent pixels whose hidden RGB bytes should not become visible by surprise. The approved image contract says JPEG output is opaque but does not choose how to handle transparent input. One option rejects it; the other blends it onto white. Opaque input works under both.

current.note: Core.image has not shipped. The unmerged JPEG encoder returns Unsupported, so no JPEG conversion can run in Jet today.

wild.note: Go's RGBA fast path ignores alpha. Official pinned writer.go:425-447; source evidence, not run.
wild.code:
rgba := image.NewRGBA(image.Rect(0, 0, 1, 1))
copy(rgba.Pix[:4], []byte{255, 0, 0, 0}) // hidden red
var out bytes.Buffer
_ = jpeg.Encode(&out, rgba, nil) // RGB encoded; A ignored

options.name: Reject transparent input
options.gist: A transparent pixel causes a typed error before JPEG encoding.
gains: Invisible RGB stays hidden.
No silent background choice.
losses: Transparent images cannot become JPEG without a later compositor.

options.name: Blend transparency onto white
options.gist: JPEG encoding uses a fixed white background for transparency.
gains: A transparent image can become JPEG directly.
Zero-alpha hidden RGB cannot leak.
losses: White changes partially transparent pixels without a caller choice.

proposed.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
photo :: image.decode(&png_bytes, limits) ?? panic("decode")
jpeg :: image.encode(photo, .JPEG, limits) ?? panic("encode")
print(jpeg.len() > 0) // true; composited onto white

recommendation.why: A protects hidden RGB and leaves background choice explicit.
gains: Opaque photos still encode.

losses.loss: Transparent images cannot become JPEG without a later compositor.
losses.mitigation: JPEG has no alpha, and Core has no approved background choice.

whyNot.reason: B silently changes color by choosing white.

recommendation.tradeoff: Keep PNG for alpha-bearing images until an explicit compositor is approved.

decisions.title: Rebuild an Ed25519 signing key from a stored 32-byte seed
decisions.gist: How should a program rebuild an Ed25519 signing key, and its public key, from a stored 32-byte seed?
decisions.lesson: An Ed25519 signing key is 32 random bytes called a seed, and its public verify key is computed from the seed. Tools save the seed and rebuild the key later; tests use fixed seeds for repeatable keys. Core can make a random key and derive its public key, but cannot rebuild a key from saved bytes. Whichever option wins, the rebuilt key stays secret and is never printed.
decisions.story: Priya ports the Jetpack Nix index client and its tests. The tests build a signing key from 32 bytes of the value 7, sign a fixture index, and install the matching public key. The DKIM mail signer also rebuilds its key from a stored seed. Core can only make random signing keys, so none of these can be written.
decisions.inWild:
# Go: https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/ed25519#NewKeyFromSeed
priv := ed25519.NewKeyFromSeed(seed)
# Rust ed25519-dalek: https://docs.rs/ed25519-dalek/2.2.0/ed25519_dalek/struct.SigningKey.html#method.from_bytes
let key = SigningKey::from_bytes(&seed);
# PyNaCl: https://pynacl.readthedocs.io/en/latest/signing/
key = nacl.signing.SigningKey(seed)
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3597 item 1, "Ed25519 public-key derivation from a 32-byte seed (NixIndex, ToolchainUpdate, test fixtures that build signing keys)."

Rust call sites. Test fixtures: NixIndex.rs:3453, 3619, 3802, and 3844; ToolchainUpdate.rs:2303 and 2427; Store/Tests.rs:1824. More fixtures: Store/NixCache/Tests.rs:141-1294 (thirteen fixed seeds) and Tests/tests/nix_projection.rs:268 and 578. The public test_nix_index helper at lib.rs:104-178 exposes public_key(seed) and sign(seed, bytes) to integration tests. Production: jet-pkg-model Prelude/Crypto.rs:138-147 rebuilds the DKIM key from 32 stored bytes; Prelude/SecretsCrypto.rs:805 and 3139 rebuild imported vault signing keys.

Current Jet surface. SigningKey.new_random() and key.public_key() exist (TIR method_calls.rs:5341, 2356; Collections.rs:771-773). VerifyKey.from_bytes and X25519PublicKey.from_bytes exist (method_calls.rs:5343-5345). expert.signing_key_bytes exports the seed (fixed_sigs.rs:4666-4669). There is no import of a seed as a typed key outside the vault's plan/authorize/commit import.

Prelude study (Crypto.rs rows): the signing carriers are "in-core" duplicates; moving them is implementation. The missing constructor is new surface.

Ratified law checked: D-ONCE-LAYER1=B (typed rung and expert rung), D-API-CTOR1=A (Type.from_* conversions), D-CRYPTOENV1 (secret-bearing values are move-only).

options.name: A typed constructor from bytes
options.detail: core.crypto.SigningKey gains from_bytes(seed). It returns the signing key for exactly 32 seed bytes and CryptoError.Length otherwise. The existing public_key() then derives the verify key, so Ed25519 key derivation from a seed needs no second function. The key stays a secret-bearing nominal type: move-only, zeroized on drop, never printed.
options.technical:
SigningKey.from_bytes(bytes: [U8]) -> SigningKey !CryptoError. Pure; no effects. Every 32-byte value is a valid Ed25519 seed (RFC 8032 section 5.1.5), so only the length can fail.

The TIR static table (method_calls.rs:5338-5353) gains ("SigningKey", "from_bytes") beside the existing ("VerifyKey", "from_bytes"). The Jet owner in Core/crypto/crypto.jet builds SigningKey{bytes} after the length check. public_key() uses the existing derivation (crypto.jet:1669-1680 path). One path for AOT, default jet run, and the interpreter (I9). Law 1: Type.from_*(x) is the conversion form (D-API-CTOR1=A).
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
use core.crypto as crypto
use core.files as files

seed :: files.read_bytes(key_path) ?? return
key :: crypto.SigningKey.from_bytes(seed) ?? return  // Length unless 32 bytes
print(key.public_key().bytes().len())               // 32

// Test fixture: the same key every run.
sevens :: (0..<32).map(_ -> U8{7})
fixture :: crypto.SigningKey.from_bytes(sevens) ?? return
sig :: crypto.sign(fixture, message) ?? return

options.name: An expert-only constructor
options.detail: core.crypto.expert gains signing_key_from_bytes(seed), callable only in #Unsafe, mirroring expert.signing_key_bytes for the export direction.
options.technical: expert.signing_key_from_bytes(seed: [U8]) -> SigningKey !CryptoError; checker requires an audited #Unsafe region (E0510/E0511 family).

options.name: Raw public-key derivation only
options.detail: core.crypto.expert gains ed25519_public(seed) returning 32 raw bytes, beside the existing expert.ed25519_sign(seed, message).
options.technical: expert.ed25519_public(seed: [U8]) -> [U8] !CryptoError, #Unsafe only.

comparisons.note: NewKeyFromSeed is in the ordinary crypto/ed25519 package, not a hazmat area. Docs: https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/ed25519#NewKeyFromSeed.
comparisons.code: priv := ed25519.NewKeyFromSeed(seed)

comparisons.note: SigningKey::from_bytes takes the 32-byte seed; verifying_key() derives the public key. Docs: https://docs.rs/ed25519-dalek/2.2.0/ed25519_dalek/struct.SigningKey.html.
comparisons.code: SigningKey::from_bytes(&seed).verifying_key()

comparisons.note: SigningKey(seed) rebuilds the key; verify_key derives the public key. Docs: https://pynacl.readthedocs.io/en/latest/signing/.
comparisons.code: nacl.signing.SigningKey(seed).verify_key

recommendation.why: A typed constructor matches the from_bytes doors Core already has for VerifyKey and Secret. It keeps loading a stored key out of #Unsafe, which the card asks for.
gains: Stored keys and test fixtures load without unsafe code.
The rebuilt key keeps every secret-type protection.

losses.loss: Seed bytes sit in a plain list before becoming a key.
losses.mitigation: Stored seeds arrive as file bytes; Secret.from_bytes already accepts plain bytes the same way.

whyNot.reason: It forces #Unsafe onto routine key loading, which the card asks Jetpack to avoid.
It leaves signing on raw byte calls and gives the program no typed key.

recommendation.tradeoff: A stored seed briefly lives in an ordinary byte list, as a stored Secret already does.

Whichever option wins, the rebuilt key stays secret and is never printed.
