decisions.title: One exact accept rule for crypto.verify, shared with Rust Jetpack
decisions.gist: Which Ed25519 signatures should crypto.verify accept, so Rust Jetpack and the Jet port agree exactly?
decisions.lesson: Ed25519 libraries agree on honest signatures but differ on odd ones, such as weak public keys anyone can sign for. Rust Jetpack uses the looser ed25519-dalek verify. Core's crypto.verify means two things today: its Rust path is strict, and its Jet path follows a third rule. Whichever option wins, both Core paths and Rust Jetpack use one written rule before the parity run.
decisions.story: Mei builds the parity harness for the Jetpack port. It feeds the same narinfo files, signatures, and trust keys to Rust Jetpack and to the Jet port and demands identical accept and reject results. Today the two sides use different Ed25519 rules, so adversarial test vectors would split them. She needs one rule written down and used on both sides.
decisions.inWild:
# libsodium, used by Nix (src/libutil/signature/local-keys.cc): https://doc.libsodium.org/public-key_cryptography/public-key_signatures
crypto_sign_verify_detached(sig, m, mlen, pk)
# Go: https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/ed25519#Verify (looser, like dalek verify)
ed25519.Verify(pub, msg, sig)
# ed25519-dalek: https://docs.rs/ed25519-dalek/2.2.0/ed25519_dalek/struct.VerifyingKey.html#method.verify_strict
key.verify_strict(msg, &sig)
# Survey of rules: Chalkias et al., "Taming the many EdDSAs", https://eprint.iacr.org/2020/1244
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3597 item 2. The card says Store.rs and Store/Nar.rs verify narinfo and cache signatures with ed25519-dalek verify, not verify_strict. core.crypto.verify must accept and reject exactly the same signatures, or the port needs an explicit strict or non-strict choice. The parity harness will compare. The card prefers public core.crypto.verify over expert ed25519_verify_strict, to avoid #Unsafe in Jetpack.

Rust call sites, all ed25519-dalek 2.2.0 VerifyingKey::verify with default features (crates/jetpack/Cargo.toml:32). Store.rs:2932-2958 checks the cache receipt signature. Store/Nar.rs:283-286 checks the Nix narinfo fingerprint. NixIndex.rs:2345-2390 checks index and manifest signatures. ToolchainUpdate.rs:754-798 checks toolchain manifest sidecars.

The three current rules, read from source. (1) Rust Jetpack uses dalek verify. It needs s < L (signature.rs:88-95) and accepts any decodable key, reducing a non-canonical y mod p (curve25519-dalek edwards.rs:209-220). It compares R as bytes with the recomputed point (verifying.rs:201-216) and accepts small-order keys and R.

(2) Core's Rust path, Prelude/Crypto.rs:216-219, uses dalek verify_strict, which adds small-order refusal for key and R (verifying.rs:357-378). (3) Core's Jet path, crypto.jet:445-450 and 1693-1709, refuses y >= p for key and R, checks s < L, compares points, and accepts small-order key and R.

Differences. (1) accepts non-canonical keys that (3) refuses. (3) accepts an R written with x = 0 and the sign bit set, which (1) refuses. (2) refuses small-order points that (1) and (3) accept.

The proposed rule equals Core's expert.ed25519_verify_strict (expert.jet:699-721), except that the expert call reports a non-canonical key as an error. It also equals dalek verify_strict plus a canonical-key check. Go crypto/ed25519.Verify matches (1): it accepts non-canonical keys and compares R bytes (Go source edwards25519.go:142-149, ed25519.go:315-324).

Nix calls libsodium crypto_sign_verify_detached (NixOS/nix src/libutil/signature/local-keys.cc:159). Current libsodium open.c refuses non-canonical keys, small-order keys and R, and non-canonical s. It then accepts when R - ([s]B - [k]A) has small order, a cofactored check. That differs from the proposed rule only on crafted mixed-order inputs; the exact libsodium version in the pinned Nix oracle was not checked.

Prelude study (Crypto.rs row "sign_typed/verify_typed"): the two Core paths are duplicates, and the Prelude crypto port (#3667) keeps one. Which rule that one path uses is the semantic choice balloted here.

options.name: The strict rule of Core's expert check
options.detail:
crypto.verify uses one rule on every path. It returns false when s is not below the group order L, or when the key or R is not in canonical encoding. It also returns false when the key or R has small order, or when the cofactorless equation fails.

This is exactly what core.crypto.expert.ed25519_verify_strict already checks, and what ed25519-dalek verify_strict checks plus a canonical-key test. libsodium, which Nix uses, makes the same weak-key and encoding refusals. Before the parity run, Rust Jetpack's four verify calls switch to this rule, so the harness compares like with like.
options.technical:
Signature unchanged: verify(verify_key: VerifyKey, bytes: [U8], signature: Signature) -> Bool !CryptoError. The rule is RFC 8032 section 5.1.7 plus strict checks. Decode A and R, refusing y >= p. Refuse if either point has small order. Refuse s >= L. Accept if [s]B = R + [k]A, where k = SHA-512(R || A || M) mod L.

Non-canonical or small-order input returns Ok(false), not an error. The Jet body reuses ed_small_order and the canonical checks already in expert.jet:699-721, and crypto.jet:1693-1709 gains them. The Prelude crypto port (#3667) deletes the Rust path (Prelude/Crypto.rs:216-219); until then that path adds the canonical-key check to verify_strict.

Rust Jetpack before parity: Store.rs:2951-2957, Store/Nar.rs:283-286, NixIndex.rs:2345-2390, and ToolchainUpdate.rs:754-798 call verify_strict. They also refuse a key whose compress(decompress(A)) differs from A. VerifyKey.from_bytes keeps accepting any decodable key; a weak key simply never verifies. Tiers: one Jet body on every path (I9).

options.name: The looser rule Rust Jetpack uses today
options.detail: crypto.verify follows ed25519-dalek 2.2 verify. s must be below L. The key may be any decodable encoding, including non-canonical ones. R is compared byte for byte with the recomputed point, and small-order keys and R are allowed.
options.technical: Matches VerifyingKey::verify / raw_verify (ed25519-dalek 2.2.0 verifying.rs:201-216, signature.rs:88-95 without legacy_compatibility) on curve25519-dalek 4.1.3 decompression (edwards.rs:194-235). The Jet body drops its y >= p refusal for keys and compares the encoding of [s]B - [k]A with the R bytes.

options.name: Strict by default, looser rule on request
options.detail: verify gains rule: VerifyRule with .Strict (default, as A) and .Compatible (as B).
options.technical: verify(verify_key, bytes, signature, rule: VerifyRule = .Strict) -> Bool !CryptoError; enum VerifyRule { Strict, Compatible }.
options.code:
// PROPOSED; NOT RUN.
use core.crypto as crypto
ok :: crypto.verify(trusted, fingerprint, sig) ?? false            // strict
loose :: crypto.verify(trusted, fingerprint, sig, rule: .Compatible) ?? false

decisions.title: Who owns the repository secret store and its age format once it moves into Jet
decisions.gist: Which Core door should jetpack secrets use to encrypt the repository secret store once it is written in Jet?
decisions.lesson: jetpack secrets keeps project secrets in .jet/secrets.age, encrypted in the age format to each recipient's age1 key. Core's vault.get reads the same file. Today a hidden Rust helper does the age work, and Core has no public door for writing the store. Core's own sealed box, crypto.seal, uses a different format. Whichever option wins, values stay encrypted on disk and never appear there in plain text.
decisions.story: Ravi runs jetpack secrets set stripe-dev on his team's project. The value is encrypted into .jet/secrets.age for every teammate's age1 key, and vault.get reads it at run time. The Rust command does the encryption through a hidden helper binary. When jetpack is written in Jet, that command needs a Core door that writes the same store.
decisions.inWild:
# age: https://age-encryption.org/v1 and https://github.com/FiloSottile/age
$ age-keygen -o key.txt
$ age -r age1ql3z7hjy54pw3hyww5ayyfg7zqgvc7w3j2elw8zmrj2kg5sfn9aqmcac8p secrets.env > secrets.age
# SOPS with age: https://github.com/getsops/sops#encrypting-using-age
$ sops --encrypt --age age1... secrets.yaml
decisions.detail:
Need: card #3597 item 3, "The age format keygen/encrypt/decrypt used by Secrets is missing (confirm against Trust/Secrets.rs during its slice)." There is no Trust/ folder. The file is crates/jetpack/src/Secrets.rs, confirmed here.

Rust call sites. Secrets.rs:259-285 writes the identity to ~/.jet/keys/secrets.identity with mode 0600. Secrets.rs:290-315 and 416-425 add and list recipients. Secrets.rs:441-487 decrypts and reads the store; 493-544 encrypts to every recipient and writes atomically. Secrets.rs:548-613 implements set, unset, list, import from .env, and get.

Each crypto step pipes a command to jet-secrets-helper (Secrets.rs:649-703), which calls the age crate in Prelude/SecretsCrypto.rs:25-84. The same file is the store that core.crypto.vault.get reads (SecretsCrypto.rs jet_vault_get_impl).

Current Jet surface. core.crypto.vault has get(name) and the typed-key plan, authorize, and commit calls (vault.jet:64-250). It has nothing to create an identity, manage recipients, or write a repository secret. core.crypto.seal and open use Core's own JETV format (crypto.jet:256-424).

Prelude study (SecretsCrypto.rs row): "age 0.10 stays_leaf: true", and card #3668 repeats "age stays behind a leaf". The JVLT2 store logic, about 1,725 Jet LOC of semantics, moves to Jet under #3668. That port does not add the public store calls Secrets.rs needs, so this ballot covers them and the format question.

Ratified law checked. D-CRYPTO-PUBKEY1=D keeps one public public-key mechanism in Core and sends interop formats outside Core. A keeps age private, so a public core.crypto.age is not offered; it would contradict D-CRYPTO-PUBKEY1=D. D-JPK-VAULTPROV1=D keeps the repo vault at .jet/secrets.age as the default. D-JPK-SECRETCOMPOSE1=D and D-JPK-SECRETMETA1=B read through vault.get. The spec records D-JPK-SECRETCRYPTO1=A as an age-style bridge with a native-ize obligation (syntax-decisions.md:3576-3588). D-API-STORE1 and D-ONCE-VERB1 set the keyed store verbs.

options.name: The vault owns the store and keeps age
options.detail: core.crypto.vault becomes the one owner of the repository store it already reads. It gains calls to create the local identity, add and list recipients, and add, remove, and list secret names. The age v1 file format stays. As the #3668 plan says, the age crate stays the provider for age encryption while the store rules move to Jet. There is no public age module, so Core's public sealed box stays crypto.seal. jetpack secrets becomes a thin command layer over these calls.
options.technical:
New in core.crypto.vault, all -[Secret]> and failing with the existing VaultError. One variant is added: NoRecipients, for a write with an empty recipient list.

create_identity(if_exists: CreateIfExists = .Refuse) -> Recipient !VaultError writes ~/.jet/keys/secrets.identity with mode 0600 and returns its public recipient. $JET_KEYS_DIR overrides the folder, as today. CreateIfExists is the enum from D-CORE-FILEOPEN1.

Recipient.from_text(text) -> Recipient !VaultError parses "age1..."; recipient.text() renders it. add_recipient(recipient) -> Bool returns false when the recipient is already present; recipients() -> [Recipient].

add(name, value: Secret) upserts and re-encrypts; remove(name) -> Bool; names() -> [String]. The verbs follow the keyed-store row of D-ONCE-VERB1, and get(name) is unchanged.

Format: age v1 (https://age-encryption.org/v1), with the typed-key JVLT2 payload inside the age body. The age crate stays the provider for keygen, encrypt, and decrypt (SecretsCrypto.rs:25-84), as #3668 plans. Pairs encoding, recipient files, locking, and atomic writes move to Jet under #3668. One path serves AOT, default jet run, and the interpreter (I9).

options.name: Jetpack builds the store on crypto.seal
options.detail: Jetpack keeps its store logic in Jet and encrypts with crypto.seal and crypto.open. Recipients become jetx25519 text from X25519PublicKey.text(). The identity file needs a new X25519SecretKey.text() and from_text() pair. core.crypto.vault.get reads the new format. Existing stores are re-encrypted once with the last Rust build.
options.technical: New: X25519SecretKey.from_text(text) -> X25519SecretKey !CryptoError and X25519SecretKey.text() -> String, a secret projection that D-ONCE-LAYER1 would normally keep on the expert rung. The file becomes .jet/secrets.jetc; D-JPK-SECRET1's .jet/secrets.age spelling and every recipients file change in one cutover.

use core.crypto as crypto

identity :: crypto.X25519SecretKey.from_text(files.read(identity_path)?)?
recipients :: lines.map(l -> crypto.X25519PublicKey.from_text(l)?)
sealed :: crypto.seal(recipients, encode_pairs(pairs), "jet-secrets".bytes())?
files.write_atomic(".jet/secrets.jetc", sealed.bytes())?
plain :: crypto.open(identity, sealed, "jet-secrets".bytes())?

decisions.title: Which edition goes in the Rust Cargo files
decisions.gist: Which Rust edition should Jet's Rust crates use, now that Cargo rejects "2026"?
decisions.lesson: Part of Jet's compiler is still written in Rust. Each Rust crate has a Cargo.toml with an `edition` field. That field picks the Rust language edition, not Jet's. Cargo knows only 2015, 2018, 2021, and 2024, and cargo 1.97 rejects "2026". So nothing builds. Jet's own edition 2026 already lives in Jet package manifests. Version 0.0.1 stays in every option.
decisions.story: Mia clones Jet and runs `cargo build`. Cargo stops at once because it does not know edition "2026". She meant Jet's edition, but this field only speaks for the Rust code.
decisions.inWild:
[package]
edition = "2024"

[package.metadata.docs.rs]
all-features = true
// Cargo sets the Rust edition per crate; other tools keep their settings in a metadata table Cargo ignores. Source: doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-metadata-table.

options.name: Rust 2021 now
options.detail: Every Rust Cargo.toml that says 2026 goes back to `edition = "2021"`, which the crates used before. Version stays 0.0.1. The root Cargo.toml gains `[workspace.metadata.jet]` with `edition = "2026"`, a table Cargo ignores. Jet package manifests keep `edition: "2026"`. A later card can move Rust to 2024 when the tree is quiet.
options.technical: 26 Cargo.toml files change and no Rust source changes. The six fixture and vendored crates already on 2021 stay as they are. Beginners never touch this field. Experts read the Rust edition in Cargo.toml and Jet's edition in Jet manifests or the workspace metadata.

options.name: Rust 2024 now

For example, `extern` blocks must be written `unsafe extern`, and `#[no_mangle]` becomes `#[unsafe(no_mangle)]`. `cargo fix --edition` does most of the work, but it touches crates/ and Source/ in one pass.

decisions.title: How job flags are typed after `jet jobs <name>`
decisions.gist: When you run a project job, should its flags follow the job name directly, without `--`?
decisions.lesson: A job is a named project command, like an npm script. Today `jet jobs web` runs it. Flags for the job must come after `--`, because Jet reads every earlier flag as its own. This choice decides how short a repeated job command can be. Whichever wins, `jet jobs` still lists jobs and `jet run -- <name>` keeps working.
decisions.story: User runs a web project many times a day. He declared `#Job fn web(args: WebArgs)` with a `--port` flag. He expects `jet jobs web --port 3000`, like `bun dev --port 3000`, but Jet rejects `--port` and suggests `--out`.
decisions.inWild:
$ npm run dev -- --port 3000   # docs.npmjs.com/cli/commands/npm-run-script
$ bun run dev --port 3000      # bun.sh/docs/cli/run
$ just serve 3000              # just.systems/man/en/recipe-parameters.html

options.name: Job owns everything after its name
options.detail: Amends D-DX-JOBS-UX1=E. In `jet jobs <name> …`, the first non-flag word is the job name. Every word after it goes to the job unchanged, including flags. Jet's own flags, such as `--interpret`, `--release`, `--explain`, or `-p <member>`, must appear before the name. `--` after the name is still accepted and simply forwarded. `jet run -- <name> …` is unchanged.
options.technical: The `jobs` route in `Source/main.rs` stops global flag parsing at the first positional word after `jobs` and forwards the rest as job argv. Help, completions, and the E2102 hint change with it.
options.code:
$ jet jobs web --port 3000
web host=127.0.0.1 port=3000

$ jet jobs --interpret web --port 3000
web host=127.0.0.1 port=3000

$ jet jobs --explain web

decisions.gist: How should a job set environment variables like `STAGE=prod` for the tools it runs?
decisions.lesson: An environment variable is a named setting a program reads at start, like `STAGE=prod`. npm scripts often prefix one before a command. decisions.story: User's `deploy` job runs two shell scripts that both read `STAGE`. In npm he wrote `STAGE=prod ./deploy.sh`. He wants the Jet job to set it once and not surprise a `test` job running beside it.

decisions.title: A plain value fills an optional slot
decisions.gist: Should a plain value fill a slot whose type is already `?T`, so `Val(...)` is written only where nothing expects an optional?
decisions.lesson: `?T` means a `T` or nothing. Today even a slot typed `?T` needs `Val(x)`, as in `return Val(n)`. Result-returning code already accepts a bare `return n`. This decides whether optionals work the same way.
decisions.explainer:
Reading the code: `Int` is a whole number, and `?Int` is a whole number or nothing. `Val(x)` builds an optional that holds `x`, and `None` is the empty one.

`a ?? b` uses the value inside `a` when there is one, and `b` otherwise. `x :: v` names a fixed value; `x := v` names one that `x = w` can change later.

`if find(3) == Val(v)` asks whether `find(3)` holds a value and, if so, names it `v`. Here `find(3)` holds 3, so under A both tests pass: `three` and `found 3` print.
decisions.story: Maya writes `fn find(n: Int) -> ?Int` and returns the number she found. The compiler stops her with E0108 and asks for `Val(...)`. A few lines later, `return n` in a function that can fail compiles fine, and she cannot see why the two differ.

options.name: Lift at expected optional slots
options.detail:
A plain value fills a slot when the slot's checked type is `?T` and the value's type is `T`. The slots are returns, call arguments, struct fields, list and map items, and reassignment of a `?T` variable.

Lifting never picks an overload or infers a generic. Those choices happen first, and one `Present` is added last. So `f(1)` prefers `f(x: Int)` over `f(x: ?Int)`, and `id(1)` infers `Int`.

`x == 5` is true only when `x` holds 5, and `x != 5` is its opposite. Only `x == Val(v)` names the value inside, as today. Narrowing and `??` do not change.

Nested optionals stay an error (E0309). `Val(x)` stays where no slot expects an optional, such as `limit := Val(10)`: nothing there says `?Int`, so `Val` picks the type. The formatter removes a redundant `Val(x)`.

Beginner path: return or pass a plain value or `None` where a signature says `?T`. Expert path: use `Val` where nothing expects an optional, and to name a value with `x == Val(v)`.
options.technical:
Sema inserts the existing `Present` node at the coercion site. Optional layout, wire shape, reports, and exits stay the same, so codegen needs no change.

E0108 keeps its real type-mismatch rows; only its optional-wrapping row retires, with snapshots updated. This amends S32 and E0108.

Acceptance: one example covers each slot, `None`, `x == 5`, S31 binding, and `??`. It needs golden output on AOT, `jet run`, the interpreter, and web.

The typed head `?Int{10}` would also lift, but parser defect #3686 blocks it today, so the examples use `Val`.

options.name: Lift at returns and arguments only
options.detail:
Only `return` values and call arguments lift, using A's ordering rule. Fields, list and map items, reassignment, and comparisons keep `Val(...)` and E0108.

Narrowing, S31, `??`, and nested optionals are unchanged.
options.technical: The same `Present` insertion as A, limited to returns and arguments. The acceptance example uses B's spellings.

options.name: Keep explicit wrapping
options.detail: No change. Every present optional value is written `Val(x)`, and a bare value in a `?T` slot stays E0108.
options.technical: No compiler, formatter, example, or diagnostic change. The shared program compiles and runs today.

comparisons.note: A non-null `T` is accepted wherever `T?` is expected. Source: kotlinlang.org/docs/null-safety.html.
comparisons.code: fun find(n: Int): Int? = if (n > 0) n else null

comparisons.note: Rust requires `Some(n)` explicitly; Jet's current rule matches Rust. Source: doc.rust-lang.org/std/option/.
comparisons.code: fn find(n: i64) -> Option<i64> { if n > 0 { Some(n) } else { None } }

recommendation.why: Where the type already says `?T`, the wrapper tells the compiler nothing new. One rule for every such slot is easier than a list.

whyNot.reason: B keeps E0108 for fields, list items, and reassignment.
C keeps a wrapper the compiler can infer.

recommendation.tradeoff: A present value is no longer visibly marked; its `?T` type still documents it.

decisions.title: Any #Error type flows into default-fallible code
decisions.gist: Should any `#Error` type propagate into default-fallible code with no conversion to write, keeping its type recoverable?
decisions.lesson: A function with no `!` contract, including `fn run()`, is already fallible: an unhandled error prints a report and exits 1. Library errors already pass up on their own. A program's own `#Error` type also needs a hand-written `impl MyError -> Err { ... }`, which reduces it to a message, code, and cause. This decides whether the `#Error` marker alone is enough, and whether a handler can recover the original error.
decisions.explainer:
Reading the code: `fn read_store() -> User !StoreErr` returns a `User` or fails with exactly a `StoreErr`. `#Error` marks a type as an error.

A function with no `!`, like `load_user` or `run`, can still fail. On success it returns normally; on failure it hands back the default error, `Err`.

`Err(x)` builds a failure. `Err("text")` builds a default error whose message is that text. `impl StoreErr -> Err { ... }` says how to turn a `StoreErr` into a default error.

`call() ?? { ... }` runs the block only when the call fails; inside it, `err` names that failure. For an explicit `!StoreErr` call, `err` is the `StoreErr` itself.

`err.as<StoreErr>()` returns `Val(the StoreErr)` when the failure is a `StoreErr`, and `None` otherwise. If `load_user` had failed with some other error, the test is false and nothing prints.
decisions.story: Dev's tool has its own `ConfigError`. File-read errors reach `run` on their own, but his does not: the compiler asks for an `impl ConfigError -> Err` block. Once he writes it, his handler can no longer tell which config problem happened, because only the message survives.

options.name: The `#Error` marker is enough
options.detail:
`#Error` marks a struct or enum as an error. A function with no `!` contract, including `fn run()`, accepts every `#Error` value. A plain fallible call carries it up with no declared conversion.

`Err` stays the one default carrier with its `message`, `code`, and `cause` fields. When an `#Error` value enters it, `message` comes from the value's printed form. The carrier also keeps the value and its type.

`err.as<T>()` asks the carrier for one exact `#Error` type. It returns a copy as `?T`, or `None` when the type differs. Repeated calls are fine, and causes stay in `cause`.

In `read_store() ?? { ... }` with an explicit `!StoreErr`, `err` is still the typed `StoreErr`. Only a call to a default-fallible function, such as `load_user()`, binds a carrier.

Explicit `!E` and `!(E1 | E2)` contracts stay closed and exact. Library errors use this same path; `CryptoError` and `TaskFailure` keep their current behavior.

Beginner path: mark errors `#Error`, omit contracts, and handle with `??`. Expert path: write `!E` for a closed contract, declare typed conversions, and use `err.as<T>()`.
options.technical:
The carrier stores the payload with its checked type identity. It is built only when an error enters the default contract, so success paths are unchanged.

Reports keep every field: message, code, why, fix, location, context frames, and causes. Each boundary projects the report as today, and a payload is never serialized alone.

Acceptance: the shared program with and without a handler, a cause chain, `Err("msg")`, a library error, and an explicit `!E`, on every tier, plus a failure-path cost measurement.

Amends S80, D-FAIL-MODEL1, D-FAIL-CTX1, D-FAIL-EXIT1, D-FAIL-EDGE1, D-FAIL-CONV1, and D-FAIL-CONV2. E2402 loses its default-target row, with snapshots updated.

options.name: Derive the conversion automatically
options.detail:
Every `#Error` type gets a derived conversion into `Err` that copies its printed form into `message`. It is used only when no visible user `impl T -> Err` exists.

A user conversion replaces it without a duplicate diagnostic. The original value is not recoverable, and explicit `!E` contracts are unchanged.
options.technical: Sema injects the derived conversion on the existing rail, as it already does for library errors. No new runtime carrier.

options.name: Keep declared conversions
options.detail: No change. A program error reaches the default contract only through its own `impl T -> Err`; without it, the plain call is E2402.
options.technical: No compiler, runtime, example, or diagnostic change. The shared program runs today as shown.

comparisons.note: Any type conforming to `Error` can be thrown from a `throws` function and recovered with `as?`. Source: docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/errorhandling/.
comparisons.code:
enum StoreErr: Error { case missing }
do { try readStore() } catch let e as StoreErr { print(e) }

comparisons.note: Any type with an `Error() string` method is an `error`; `errors.As` recovers the concrete type. Source: pkg.go.dev/errors#As.
comparisons.code:
var se *StoreErr
if errors.As(err, &se) { fmt.Println("missing") }

recommendation.why: Errors become ordinary types: mark one `#Error` and it propagates without subclasses or conversions, and a handler can still ask exactly which error happened.

whyNot.reason: B removes the boilerplate but discards the error, so handlers can only compare message text.
C keeps a hand-written conversion for every custom error and still reduces it to text.

recommendation.tradeoff: The default error becomes an open set checked at runtime; code that must handle every case exactly uses a typed `!E` contract.

surface.gist: Should any `#Error` type propagate into default-fallible code with no conversion to write, keeping its type recoverable?
surface.lesson: A function with no `!` contract, including `fn run()`, is already fallible: an unhandled error prints a report and exits 1. Library errors already pass up on their own. A program's own `#Error` type also needs a hand-written `impl MyError -> Err { ... }`, which reduces it to a message, code, and cause. This decides whether the `#Error` marker alone is enough, and whether a handler can recover the original error.

current.note: Today the program error needs a hand-written conversion to reach a default-fallible caller; without it the plain call in `load_user` is E2402. The handler can then read only `message`, `code`, and `cause`.

wild.note: Any type implementing `std::error::Error` converts into `anyhow::Error` with `?` and keeps its type for `downcast_ref`. Source: docs.rs/anyhow.

gains: Custom errors need one marker and nothing else.
Handlers can test the real error, not message text.
No class hierarchy: any struct or enum can be an error.
losses: The default error becomes an open set checked at runtime.

options.name: Derive the conversion automatically
options.gist: Every `#Error` type gets a compiler-derived `impl T -> Err` that copies its printed form; the original is not recoverable.
gains: Custom errors need one marker, like A.
Keeps one concrete `Err` and the single conversion rail.
losses: Handlers can only compare message text.

options.gist: No change: a program error reaches default-fallible code only through its own `impl T -> Err`.
gains: Every conversion is visible in the source.
No compiler or runtime change.
losses: Every custom error needs a boilerplate conversion.
Handlers can only read the converted fields.

losses.mitigation: Typed-to-typed conversions still need a declared mapping.

whyNot.reason: B removes the boilerplate but discards the error, so handlers can only compare message text.
C keeps a hand-written conversion for every custom error and still reduces it to text.

recommendation.tradeoff: The default error becomes an open set checked at runtime; code that must handle every case exactly uses a typed `!E` contract.

decisions.title: `?` and `!` follow the type they mark
decisions.gist: Should the optional mark and the error-contract mark follow the type they mark: `Entry?` and `SaveError!` instead of `?Entry` and `!SaveError`?
decisions.lesson: Two small marks change a signature's meaning. `?` means a value might be absent; `!` in a function's contract names the error it can fail with. Today both come first (`?Entry`, `!SaveError`). This decides whether they follow the name (`Entry?`, `SaveError!`), which is where most languages put the optional mark. It changes spelling only, not meaning.
decisions.explainer:
Reading the code: `Entry?` is an `Entry` or nothing, written `Val(e)` or `None`. `[Int?]` is a list whose items may be missing; `[Int]?` is a list that may itself be missing.

A contract names how a function can fail. `SaveError!` means the call succeeds or fails with a `SaveError`. `(DBError | TimeoutError)!` means it fails with one of those two.

A function that returns nothing writes its contract right after the parameters: `fn save(entry: Entry) SaveError!`. One that returns a value writes `-> Type` first.

`x ?? return` uses the success value, or leaves the function on failure or absence.

An effect row `-[ ... ]>` lists what a function may do, and `!` inside it forbids something. `-[!Mem.Alloc]>` means the function never allocates memory. That `!` means not, so it stays in front.
decisions.story: Sam comes from Kotlin and writes `fn find(id: Int) -> Entry?`. The parser asks for `?Entry`. In the same file, `fn save(entry: Entry) !SaveError` reads to him as "not SaveError" rather than "fails with SaveError".

options.name: Suffix both marks; denials unchanged
options.detail:
The optional mark follows ordinary types: `Entry?`, `[Int?]` for a list of optionals, and `[Int]?` for an optional list. Generic arguments work the same way: `Box<Int?>` differs from `Box<Int>?`.

Only one optional layer exists, so `T??` stays error E0309. The optional typed head becomes `Int?{...}`; parser defect #3686 blocks that one head today. List heads such as `[Int?]{...}` work now.

The error mark follows the error, and only in a function's contract: `-> Int ParseError!`, `-> Entry? (DBError | TimeoutError)!`, and unit-fallible `SaveError!`. `Err!` pins the default error.

Omitting the contract still means the default `Err`. `ParseError!` is never a field or generic-argument type.

Effect denials keep their own grammar: `-[!Mem.Alloc]>`, `-[!Mem.Alloc(above: 2048)]>`, and `-[!Panic]>`. `?(text)`, `??`, `!x`, `!=`, patterns, narrowing, and overloads are unchanged.

Beginner path: omit the contract, write `Entry?` and `None`, and let calls propagate. Expert path: write `ParseError!`, `(E1 | E2)!`, or `Err!`. Old prefix forms get a fix, not an alias.
options.technical:
In type grammar, `?` is a postfix mark that binds inside brackets and generic arguments. `??` stays one fallback token. In value grammar only `?(text)` is postfix.

A type mark is parsed before a typed-literal `{...}` head. A union contract needs parentheses: `A | B!` is rejected with a fix to `(A | B)!`.

Only parsing and formatting change. Carriers, causes, context frames, fallbacks, reports, exit codes, target delivery, Codable schemas, and layouts stay the same on every tier.

Measured on 2026-09-28 over 6,443 `.jet` files: about 3,548 optional-type lines in 346 files and 1,840 contract lines in 260 files. Syntax.rs, grammars, highlighting, docs, and snapshots move too.

This amends D-OPT1, S34, and D-FAILURE-FOUNDATION1=A, and reopens the suffix form of D-ERRSIGIL1=A and D-ERRSUFFIX1=B. Samples in #3685 and #3686 follow the ratified spelling.

options.name: Suffix optional only
options.detail:
The optional mark moves exactly as in A. Error contracts keep the prefix: `-> Int !ParseError`, `-> Entry? !(DBError | TimeoutError)`, and unit-fallible `!SaveError`.

Effect denials are unchanged.
options.technical: Only the type-grammar `?` becomes postfix, with A's binding rules. The cutover covers the optional-type lines only, and it amends D-OPT1.

options.name: Keep prefix marks
options.detail: No change: `?Entry`, `?[Int]`, `[?Int]`, `-> Int !ParseError`, `!(DBError | TimeoutError)`, and unit-fallible `!SaveError`.
options.technical: No compiler, formatter, example, or diagnostic change.

options.name: Suffix everything, including denials
options.detail: Everything in A, and effect denials also move after the effect: `-[Mem.Alloc!]>`, `-[Mem.Alloc(above: 2048)!]>`, and `-[Panic!]>`. Choosing D includes that effect-row redesign; today's parser rejects `Mem.Alloc!`.
options.technical: As A, plus a redesigned effect-row grammar for denial paths and parameters. A trailing `!` would then mean fails-with in a contract and forbids in an effect row.

comparisons.note: Nullable types suffix `?`: `User?`, `List<Int?>`. Source: kotlinlang.org/docs/null-safety.html.
comparisons.code: fun find(id: Int): User?

comparisons.note: Error unions put the error set before `!` and the payload after: `ParseError!Config`; `!Config` infers the set. Source: ziglang.org/documentation/master/#Error-Union-Type.
comparisons.code: fn load(path: []const u8) ParseError!Config

recommendation.why: It gives the owner's suffix form for both marks and matches how most programmers read optionals. Effect denials, a separate grammar, stay as they are.

whyNot.reason: B leaves `Entry? !(DBError | TimeoutError)`, with the two marks on opposite sides of one signature.
C keeps the spelling the owner wants to leave.
D makes `Mem.Alloc!` look like a failure contract and needs a separate effect-row redesign.

recommendation.tradeoff: One large cutover buys the familiar reading order for both type marks.

decisions.title: One home for live data, sync and sign-in functions
decisions.situation: Two Core libraries, app and core.web, both offer functions named live, invalidate, sync and auth. The same name behaves differently in each, so invalidate returns an error in one and a number in the other. On 2026-10-01 the owner chose one home per group: app for live data and sync, core.auth for sign-in, and core.web for routing only. This record writes that ruling down.
decisions.gist: Which Core library should own the live data, sync and sign-in functions?
decisions.lesson: When two libraries export the same function name with different behavior, a program changes meaning when it switches its import. Option A gives each group one home: app for live data and sync, core.auth for sign-in, and core.web for routes, forms and API descriptions. The duplicate copies are deleted.
decisions.story: Kai calls invalidate to refresh a cached list after a save. With one import it returns an error, and with the other it returns a number that looks like success. Under option A there is one invalidate, in app, with one meaning.
decisions.detail:
Owner answer, 2026-10-01 chat (ask question s3701): "app: live/sync; core.auth: auth; web: routing". The question asked, verbatim:

"#3701: `app` and `core.web` both export live/subscribe/invalidate/sync and auth functions with DIFFERENT behavior (e.g. invalidate returns an error in one, a hash in the other). Who owns them?"

The owner picked the first offered option, which was also the recommended one. The card plan listed the same choice as its option C.

Today Core/app/app.jet:128 invalidate returns Int AppError! and always fails with Unsupported. Core/web/web.jet:117 invalidate returns a djb2 hash of the key. Runtime routes in CoreCallRows.jet map both modules to the same host calls. Implementation and proof now ride on #3709 criterion 8, where #3701 was merged on 2026-10-04.

decisions.title: Default prompt for scripts that declare no authority
decisions.gist: When a script declares no authority, should Jet ask once with yes as the default?
decisions.lesson: Before a program runs, Jet knows every authority it will use, such as reading files or using the network. A script with no package.jet may print, read its arguments, and allocate. Anything else needs a grant, a flag, or an answer at a prompt. This choice sets that prompt and what happens without a terminal. Packages, #Abilities grants, and flags still decide when present.
decisions.story: Maya copies a 20-line script that renames photos in a folder. She types jet run rename.jet. Today she sees raw effect names and must type once. The owner wants her to see what the script will do and press Enter. Her teammate runs the same script in CI, where no one can answer.
decisions.inWild:
# Deno (https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security/)
$ deno run main.ts
⚠️  Deno requests net access to "example.com". Run again with --allow-net to bypass this prompt.
   Allow? [y/n/A] (y = yes, allow; n = no, deny; A = allow all net permissions) >

# Python and Node: no prompt; every script has full access.

options.name: Ask once, yes by default
options.detail:
The prompt appears only when package.jet, an #Abilities grant, or an --allow or --deny flag leaves some reached authority undecided. It lists each undecided authority in plain words with its call site before anything runs. Enter or y runs it once. n stops with exit code 1.

always writes the grant into the script's inline package header, or into package.jet authority.holds when one exists. The file then states what it may do. Without a terminal, the run stops with E1803, and its Fix line holds the exact --allow command.
options.technical: Source/CmdCompile.rs authority transaction keeps computing the projection before execution. The accepted set is recorded as interactive.once in the existing receipt. The always choice writes authority.holds.allow through the existing project approval path and extends it to inline package headers. The D-AUTH-AMBIENT1 floor is unchanged.
options.code:
$ jet run rename.jet
rename.jet will:
  read files    files.read(path)     rename.jet:4
  write files   files.rename(a, b)   rename.jet:9
Run it? [Y/n/always] always
Saved to rename.jet: package { authority: { holds: { allow: [FS.Read, FS.Write] } } }
renamed 12 files

$ jet run rename.jet < /dev/null
Error [E1803]: rename.jet needs FS.Read, FS.Write and nothing granted them
 Fix: jet run --allow=FS.Read,FS.Write rename.jet

options.name: Allow and report
options.detail: A script with no declared authority receives every authority it reaches. Jet prints one notice line naming them and runs, with or without a terminal. A package.jet authority block, #Abilities, or flags still decide when present, and a deny still wins. This is closest to Python or Node, plus a notice.
options.technical: The application default policy becomes allow-all for manifest-less entries when no flag is given. The notice renders from the same projection. This re-opens option C of D-AUTH-AMBIENT1, which was not chosen.
options.code:
$ jet run rename.jet < /dev/null
authority: FS.Read, FS.Write (allowed: no authority declared)
renamed 12 files

options.name: Keep the typed choice
options.detail: Keep the current behavior: the prompt waits for once, project, or deny with no default, and project still requires a package manifest. Only the wording changes to plain names and call sites. Without a terminal the run stops with E1803.
options.technical: No policy change. Rendering in Source/CmdCompile.rs switches from the JSON list to plain effect names.
options.code:

Choose once, project, or deny:
authority> project

comparisons.note: Deno is deny-by-default and prompts per permission at the first call when stdout is a terminal; flags bypass the prompt. It warns that allowing subprocesses bypasses the sandbox. Source: https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security/
comparisons.code: Allow? [y/n/A] (y = yes, allow; n = no, deny; A = allow all net permissions) >

comparisons.note: No permission system: every script can read, write, spawn, and connect. This is the convenience B copies, without the gate.
comparisons.code:

renamed 12 files

recommendation.why: It gives the owner's allow-with-confirmation flow and shows every authority before anything runs. Pressing Enter is the only extra step.

whyNot.reason: B runs a downloaded script's file and network access before anyone sees it.
C keeps a three-word ritual and still cannot remember a grant for a lone script.

recommendation.tradeoff: One keypress per new script buys a visible, complete list before any effect.

decisions.title: Waiting is something you can forbid, not something you must ask for
decisions.situation: A one-file Jet script that shares a counter between tasks refuses to run until you type a permission flag for memory sharing and for waiting. Jet's permission system is meant to guard what a program can reach outside itself, such as files, the network and other programs. Waiting for your own tasks, or keeping a shared value alive, touches nothing outside the program. This vote decides whether waiting stops needing a grant everywhere, while staying something a careful author can forbid.
decisions.gist: Should waiting on your own work need a permission grant, or only be something you can forbid?
decisions.lesson: An effect is a kind of work a function does, such as reading files. A grant is permission to do it. A denial forbids it in one place. Jet already treats memory use as deny-only: never granted, still forbiddable. Waiting is the open case.
decisions.explainer:
Today a program with no package file gets a small free set of effects: printing, reading its arguments and allocating memory. Everything else needs a grant. In a terminal Jet asks once, with yes as the default. Without a terminal, such as in CI, the run stops with E1803 and prints the exact --allow flag.

Two effects trip beginners here. Mem.Rc counts users of a shared value. Time.Wait marks a call that can block until something happens, such as a task finishing, a channel message, a lock, or input arriving.

The written rule already says memory effects are deny-only. They show up in reports and can be forbidden, but they are never granted. So the Mem.Rc prompt is a bug, and its repair is not part of this vote. This vote is about Time.Wait.

Beginner path under A: nothing to write; the script runs. Expert path: forbid waiting where it matters, for example `-[!Time.Wait]>` on an audio callback, or `deny: [Time.Wait]` in a package. A denied wait is still a compile error with the full call path.

Shared work in every option: fix the Mem.Rc prompt so Mem stays deny-only, as the spec already says. Clock reading and sleeping keep the Time root and still need a grant; this vote does not change them.
decisions.story: Priya writes her first script with two tasks adding to one shared total. It works on her laptop after she answers a prompt, then fails in CI with E1803 asking for Mem.Rc and Time.Wait. She has no idea why counting needs permission.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-05 on the dev worktree.

The free set has three effects. It is AMBIENT_BASIC_EFFECTS at crates/jet-foundation/src/Authority.rs:294-295: IO, Mem.Alloc and Exec.Args. crates/jet-pkg-model/src/EffectBudget.rs:88-97 applies it when no manifest exists. This is D-AUTH-AMBIENT1=A.

Docs/spec/spec.md:1394-1400 says Panic and Mem are deny-only rows. Mem.Alloc and Mem.Rc stay visible to diagnostics and denials. They need not be listed in a positive ceiling. Sources: D-EFFTREE1, D-PANICROOT1, D-AUTHORITY-MEM1.

Main ran the shared-value example on 2026-10-05. It still required --allow=Mem.Rc,Time.Wait. The Mem.Rc half contradicts the law above, so it is a repair, not a vote.

D-FOUND-REALTIME1=A introduced Time.Wait so real-time and interrupt rows can forbid blocking. D-FOUND-BOARD1 shows #Interrupt(board.USART1, -[Mem.Alloc, Time.Wait]>). Its purpose was denial.

Core now marks every blocking call with it. Core/term/term.jet:50 declares print as -[IO, Time.Wait]>, and :57 declares input. Core/tasks/tasks.jet:89-131 marks run, waitall, waitany, recv, get, result and wait. Core net, http, process and db calls carry it too.

The Jet-written compiler reads these Core rows. So hello-world's print carries Time.Wait, which the free set lacks. That conflicts with D-AUTH-AMBIENT1's promise that printing needs no paperwork.

Some ratified examples list Time.Wait as a grant. D-TRUST-LAUNCH1 proposes adding an uncovered Time.Wait to holds. D-LANG-IN-LIBS lists it in holds. D-SQL-AUTHORITY1's glossary says Time.Wait means waiting. Under A those entries become redundant, and a lint with jet fix removes them.

D-SCRIPT-CONFIRM1=A asks once, default yes. Without a terminal it stops with E1803, whose Fix line holds the exact --allow command.

Research. Deno's permissions cover read, write, net, env, sys, run, ffi and import. Timers and awaiting work have no flag (docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security/).

Node's permission model restricts the file system, child processes, worker threads, native addons and WASI. Timers and awaiting are not restricted (nodejs.org/api/permissions.html).

Clang 20 adds [[clang::nonblocking]] and [[clang::nonallocating]] (clang.llvm.org/docs/FunctionEffectAnalysis.html). A real-time function forbids blocking, and the compiler verifies it. Nobody requests blocking as a permission. LLVM's RealtimeSanitizer checks the same rule at run time.

The wrong way, seen in practice: prompts for harmless operations train users to approve everything. That weakens the prompts that matter. Akhawe and Felt (USENIX Security 2013) report this habituation for browser warnings.

Unchanged in every option: files, network, processes, environment, clock reading and sleeping still need a grant. Manifests still override the free set. A manifest deny still wins.

options.name: Waiting is deny-only, like memory
options.detail: Time.Wait joins Mem as a deny-only effect. Jet still infers it, shows it in hover, docs and reports, and checks every denial. No program, script or package ever needs a grant for it, so no prompt or E1803 ever names it. A grant of the Time root still covers it harmlessly. Writing Time.Wait in an allow list gets a lint whose jet fix removes it.
options.technical: Effects registry: mark Time.Wait deny-only beside Mem (spec.md:1394-1400 grows one row). Authority projection (Authority.rs, EffectBudget.rs, the Jet-compiler twin) drops deny-only leaves from required effects before computing undecided authority, exactly as Mem is meant to be dropped. Prohibitions -[!Time.Wait]> and manifest deny: [Time.Wait] keep E0921-style full-path reports. New lint for a deny-only effect named in allow/holds, with an autofix. Repair in the same cutover: Mem.Rc stops appearing in E1803 and in the prompt. Every tier shares one projection (I9).

options.name: Free for scripts only
options.detail: Add Time.Wait to the free set a program without a package file gets. Packages that write their own grant list must still list Time.Wait, as today. Forbidding it works as today.
options.technical: AMBIENT_BASIC_EFFECTS gains Time.Wait (and the Mem.Rc repair). Manifests with authority.holds replace the floor, so they keep listing Time.Wait for any blocking call, including print under Jet-written Core.

options.name: Keep asking
options.detail: Keep today's rule. A script that waits asks once in a terminal, with yes as the default, and stops with E1803 elsewhere. Only the Mem.Rc repair lands.
options.technical: No authority change. The Jet-written compiler must then add Time.Wait to the floor anyway for print, or print starts prompting.
options.code:
$ jet run count.jet < /dev/null
Error [E1803]: count.jet needs Time.Wait and nothing granted it
 Fix: jet run --allow=Time.Wait count.jet

comparisons.note: Permissions guard resources outside the process; awaiting your own work needs no flag (docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security/).
comparisons.code:
deno run --allow-net app.ts   // net needs a flag
await Promise.all(tasks)      // waiting does not

comparisons.note: Blocking is something a real-time function forbids and the compiler verifies (clang.llvm.org/docs/FunctionEffectAnalysis.html).

recommendation.why: Waiting reaches nothing outside the program, so asking teaches users to click yes. Forbidding it where timing matters keeps the real safety, exactly as memory already works.
gains: Scripts that use tasks, channels or shared values just run.
One rule for in-program effects: shown and forbiddable, never granted.
Real-time code keeps its compile-time no-blocking check.

losses.loss: A package's grant list no longer shows that it waits.
losses.mitigation: Hover, docs and jet inspect authority still list Time.Wait for every function that waits.

losses.loss: Existing grant lists that name Time.Wait become redundant.
losses.mitigation: A lint flags them and jet fix deletes the entry in one step.

whyNot.reason: Packages with grant lists still must write Time.Wait for every blocking call, including print.
It keeps a prompt that protects nothing outside the program and breaks scripts in CI.

recommendation.tradeoff: Grant lists stop recording waiting; effect reports and denials still carry it everywhere.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Drafted by BallotInventory 2026-10-05. Only the ballot validator ran; no programs ran.

In every option, stop Mem.Rc from appearing in E1803 and in the prompt. That is already law.

Under A, mark Time.Wait deny-only in the effects registry and spec. Drop deny-only effects before computing undecided authority, in both compiler halves. Add the redundant-allow lint with its autofix. Migrate ratified examples and Examples/ files that list Time.Wait.

Prove four things. A no-package script using Shared and task joins runs with stdin closed. A -[!Time.Wait]> function that calls recv is still rejected with the full call path. A manifest deny: [Time.Wait] still rejects. File access and sleep still prompt.

surface.gist: Should waiting on your own work need a permission grant, or only be something you can forbid?
surface.lesson: A grant permits outside access, such as files. A denial forbids an effect in one place. Memory is already deny-only: never granted, still forbiddable. Waiting is the open case.

decisions.title: How a library's markers are named
decisions.gist: When a library declares its own marker, how should code that imports it write that marker's name?
decisions.lesson: A marker is a # rule written before a declaration, such as #Job. Packages may declare their own markers. Today a marker declared in an imported file is written bare, #Get, and #web.Get is an error. This choice decides how library markers are named. How web routes are exposed is a separate, later ballot.
decisions.story: Priya likes FastAPI's @app.get and wants a web library whose route marker names its library. She imports routes.jet as web and writes #web.Get. Jet rejects it, accepts bare #Get, and then warns that the import is unused. The owner wants library markers in nested namespaces.

options.name: Library markers always qualified
options.detail:
A marker declared in a library module is written through the local name of its import: after use "routes.jet" as web, write #web.Get. An import alias changes the prefix. A library marker is never written bare; the bare form is reserved for language rules such as #Job, #Unsafe, and #Codable.

A library exports a marker with pub, as it does a function; an unmarked marker stays private to its module. Qualified markers work inside a #[...] group, such as #[web.Get("/a"), web.Cache(60)].
options.technical: New grammar: after # in rule position, a module path followed by a marker name. It is registered under I7. The # position rules (rule prefix, [T#N], pkg#1.2.0) are unchanged. The marker registry key becomes (declaring module, name) and the AST marker declaration gains visibility. Diagnostics with snapshots: bare use of a library marker (fix: the qualified form), unknown qualified marker, and private marker. L0103 counts marker uses as uses of their import (#3702). Placement, one-bracket stacking, and signature laws (S82, D-MARK-STACK1, D-MARKSIG1) apply unchanged.

options.name: Named like functions
options.detail: Markers follow the function naming rule. The qualified form #web.Get always works. A member import such as use "routes.jet".[Get] also allows bare #Get, and an alias such as .[Get as G] allows #G. A bare marker may therefore be a language rule or a member-imported library marker; the reader checks the imports to tell.
options.technical: Same grammar, registry key, and visibility work as A, plus member-import and alias resolution for markers, and an ambiguity diagnostic when a member import shadows a language rule name.

options.name: Keep bare names
options.detail: Imported markers stay bare, as today, and #web.Get stays an error. Two imported declarations with one name are an error at the use, and the fix is to rename one of the declarations. L0103 learns to count marker uses (#3702).
options.technical: No grammar change. Add an ambiguity diagnostic naming both declaring files.

comparisons.note: The owner's example: @app.get names the object that owns the route decorator. Source: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/path-params/
comparisons.code: @app.get("/jokes/{joke_id}")

comparisons.note: Attribute macros can be written with their crate path, such as #[tokio::main], or imported with use and written bare. Source: https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/attr.main.html
comparisons.code:
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {}

comparisons.note: Blow tags a function with a note and his metaprogram registers it as a console command with typed argument parsing (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R6rH8IGtrTI, about 6:12). This shows the value of library-owned markers.
comparisons.code:
// described in the clip, not quoted code:
// tag a function as a command -> it appears in the console with typed arguments

recommendation.why: It lets any library offer markers without clashes, and a reader always knows whether a marker is a language rule or a library's.

whyNot.reason: B gives one marker two spellings, and a bare marker could then be either kind.
C cannot hold two libraries' markers with one name and hides where a marker comes from.

recommendation.tradeoff: A few extra letters per library marker buy names that never clash and always show their source.

wild.note: A decorator is named through the object that owns it. Source: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/path-params/

gains: Same rule as calling a library function.

A bare marker may be a language rule or a library one.

gains: Shortest spelling.
No grammar change.
losses: Two libraries cannot both offer Get.
A reader cannot tell which import supplied a marker.

gains: Bare means language; qualified means library.

losses.loss: Library markers are a few letters longer.
losses.mitigation: The module name is the part that tells readers and the compiler which library the marker belongs to.

whyNot.reason: B gives one marker two spellings, and a bare marker could then be either kind.

decisions.title: How a Jet web server exposes its HTTP routes
decisions.situation: A route links a web request, such as GET /jokes/7, to the function that answers it. Today a Jet server lists its routes as mux.get calls inside run, where mux is the server's list of routes, so each path sits far from its function. The owner liked Python's FastAPI, where each function carries its route as a tag written just above it. You are deciding how Jet routes are written; we recommend tagging the methods of one struct and adding that struct to the server with one mux.mount call.
decisions.gist: Should Jet routes be tags on struct methods added with one call, a whole-program server struct, or plain calls?
decisions.lesson: A route links a request path, such as GET /jokes/7, to the function that answers it. A marker is a tag written before a declaration, such as #Job. A tags a struct's methods with #server.Get and adds them with mux.mount. B makes one #HTTP struct the whole server, the way #CLI makes a command line. C keeps mux.get calls only.
decisions.explainer:
A web server listens for requests. Each request has a method, such as GET to read or POST to send, and a path, such as /jokes/7. A route says which function answers which method and path. Jet keeps a server's routes in a mux, a value you add routes to and then serve.

A path parameter is a named slot in a path: in /jokes/:id the :id part matches 7 and passes it to the function's id parameter.

A marker is a tag written just before a declaration, such as #Job or #CLI. Library markers are written through their module, such as #server.Get. A route marker only records a fact that the compiler reads while building.

A struct is a named group of fields; its methods are functions that receive it as self. #CLI already turns a struct's methods into subcommands.

OpenAPI is a standard description of a server's routes that tools use to generate clients.
decisions.story: Sam builds a small jokes API with two routes: read a joke by number, and add a joke. He has used FastAPI, where each route sits on its function. In Jet today he writes both as mux.get and mux.post calls in run, away from the code that answers them.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-04. Routes are values today. Core/http/server.jet:15 makes a mux, and Core/http/http.jet:456 serves it. Examples/features/web/battery/run.jet:127-138 registers seven routes with mux.get and mux.post, and :135 already binds the :id path parameter to a typed (id: Int) handler.

There are two route values today. server.mux() makes an HTTPMux, the value a server serves. http.router() makes an HTTPRouter, and Core/web/web.jet:90 renders OpenAPI only from that value (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/OpenAPI.rs:1621). Both register routes through one checked operation (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/HttpRouting.jet:877-983). The mux accepts seven verbs, from get to options; the router accepts four (:878).

Markers. D-MARKER-MODULE1=A (ratified) makes library markers qualified, as in #web.Get, and exported with pub marker; card #3707 criterion 1 implements it. Today Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/MarkerRules.jet:1196 rejects an unknown marker name with E0927, and qualified names do not parse yet. #CLI already turns struct methods into subcommands (Examples/features/cli/positionals.jet:8-22). #Job collects marked functions into program commands (D-JOB-SUBCMD1=C).

Related law. D-DX-ROUTER1=A says web App page routes come from one checked App route graph, not file-name conventions; it does not cover server routes. D-ENDPOINT-SHAPE1=A derives request, response and client types from typed handlers. D-SHAPE-EXPOSE1=A requires every interface lens to keep the same callable contract. D-MARKER-LAW1=A lets package markers record facts and add items.

Card criteria every option must meet. Any route surface keeps one route record, existing route ordering, handlers returning HTTPResponse HTTPError!, OpenAPI from that one record, and the same responses on every run tier. A path parameter that names no handler parameter, or cannot parse into its type, is a compile error naming both.

What is the same in every option. OpenAPI must read the routes a program actually serves. Making web.openapi accept the served mux is shared work that no option avoids.

options.name: Tagged struct methods, added with mux.mount
options.detail:
core.http.server exports one marker per verb the mux already accepts, such as Get and Post, each taking a path. A program writes them on the methods of an ordinary struct, as #server.Get("/jokes/:id"). The struct's fields hold shared state, such as a database handle, reached through a read-only self.

mux.mount(value) reads the marked methods of that one struct type while building. It adds one route row per method, in method order, at the point of the call. Each row is exactly what mux.get or mux.post would add, so ordering, OpenAPI and handler checks are shared.

Nothing is found by scanning a package: only structs passed to mount contribute. mux.get stays for routes computed while the program runs.
options.technical:
pub marker Get(path: String, @sites: [.Method]), and Post, Put, Delete, Patch, Head and Options in the same shape, in core.http.server. They are body-less, so they record facts only. pub fn mount<T>(mux: HTTPMux, value: T) reads T's methods carrying those facts through compile-time reflection. It lowers each to the same checked registration as mux.get(path, handler) (HttpRouting.jet:983), with value captured read-only; mutable shared state uses a Cell, as the battery example does.

A marked method outside a mounted struct gets a warning naming mount. Path parameters bind to method parameters by name, checked at compile time. Duplicate method and path pairs are a compile error, whether they come from markers, mux.get or both.

options.name: A whole-program #HTTP struct
options.detail:
Jet adds #HTTP, a built-in marker on one struct, as #CLI is for command lines. Its methods carry bare #Get and #Post markers, and jet run serves that struct directly, taking the port from a flag or the PORT variable. There is no mux or serve call in the program.

This is the least code for one small server. A program gets one server, Get and Post join Jet's closed list of language markers, and a test cannot build a router value to call directly.
options.technical: #HTTP is a Prelude rule, and Get and Post become language rules, written bare. D-MARKER-MODULE1=A allows that, but it puts HTTP words into Jet's closed language vocabulary (I7). The entry fn run(api: Jokes) receives the constructed struct; the host binds and serves before run returns. One #HTTP struct per program. Tests can still call the methods directly, but not through the router.

options.name: Value routes only
options.detail:
Routes stay mux.get and mux.post calls, as today and as in Axum. Markers stay for jobs, command lines and other build-time facts, and no route markers are added.

The path-parameter compile check from the card applies to the handler lambda's parameters. Nothing new is learned, but the path sits apart from the function that answers it, as in the current battery example.
options.technical: No new surface. Criterion 3's check runs on the lambda passed to mux.get. Card #3707 criteria 2 and 3 close against value routes only.
options.code:
mux :: server.mux()
mux.get("/jokes/:id", (id: Int) HTTPResponse HTTPError! -> db.find(id))
mux.post("/jokes", (req: HTTPRequest) HTTPResponse HTTPError! -> db.add(req))
server.serve("127.0.0.1:8080", mux)

comparisons.note: Route decorators sit on functions, and an explicit include_router call adds them to the app, which is A's shape.
comparisons.code:
# https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/bigger-applications/
@router.get("/jokes/{id}")
def joke(id: int): ...
app.include_router(router)

comparisons.note: The router is a plain value built with method calls, which is C's shape and today's Jet shape.
comparisons.code:
// https://docs.rs/axum/latest/axum/routing/struct.Router.html
let app = Router::new().route("/jokes/:id", get(joke));

recommendation.why: A puts each path on the function that answers it, as the owner asked, and keeps the route list a plain value that tests can build. mux.mount turns tags into the same routes mux.get makes, so there is still one route list and one OpenAPI source.
gains: Each route path sits on the method that answers it.
Shared state, such as a database, lives in struct fields, so handlers need no globals.
The route list stays a value that tests can build and call.

losses.loss: Two ways can add a route: a tagged method or a mux.get call.
losses.mitigation: Both make the same route entry, in one order, with one OpenAPI entry. Docs teach tags, and mux.get stays for routes known only while running.

losses.loss: A tagged method in a struct that is never mounted serves nothing.
losses.mitigation: The compiler warns on it and names mux.mount as the fix.

whyNot.reason: B allows one server per program, adds web words to Jet's small fixed set of built-in markers, and leaves tests no route list to call.
C keeps every path apart from its handler and gives none of the FastAPI style the owner asked for.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds one tag per HTTP method and one mount call over today's route list. In return routes read like FastAPI and still work like plain values.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: BallotDraft0. Skill: rli5. Author-run beginner pass under Main's brief, because workers cannot start agents; it found route, mux, path parameter, marker and OpenAPI undefined, so the explainer now teaches them. A separate fresh beginner pass is still advised — Clarity rewrite 2026-10-04 by BallotClear0 per CLARITY-RULES.md.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: claude. Adversarial model family: claude. Fresh agent: BallotRev0. The review checked every cited line and the eight cited decisions, all ratified, and found that OpenAPI reads only http.router() values while servers serve server.mux() values. It made that shared gap explicit, narrowed D-DX-ROUTER1 to App pages, gave A all seven mux verbs, method sites, mount order and read-only self, and made B's test and vocabulary costs fair.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Build the jokes API with a GET and a POST route under the chosen option. Run it under jet run, jet build and the interpreter, call both routes with an HTTP client, and compare responses byte for byte. Check that web.openapi lists both routes from the value the program serves.

Write a path parameter that names no handler parameter, and one whose text cannot parse into its type, and check each is a compile error naming both. Under A, check that a marked method in a struct no mount call reaches gets the warning. Check that a duplicate method and path is an error, including one marker and one mux.get for the same pair. Check that marked and mux.get routes keep one shared order, with mounted routes in method order at the mount call.

A tags a struct's methods with #server.Get and adds them with mux.mount. B makes one #HTTP struct the whole server, like #CLI. C keeps mux.get calls only.

current.note: Routes are calls inside run, with paths apart from their handlers.

wild.note: Decorators sit on functions; include_router adds them to the app.

options.gist: Tag struct methods with #server.Get; mux.mount adds them as ordinary routes.
gains: Each path sits on its handler.
The route list stays a testable value.

options.gist: One #HTTP struct with bare #Get methods; jet run serves it.

options.name: Plain calls only
options.gist: Keep mux.get and mux.post calls; add no route tags.
gains: Nothing new to learn.
losses: Paths stay apart from their handlers.

proposed.code:

mux.get("/jokes/:id", (id: Int) HTTPResponse HTTPError! -> db.find(id))
server.serve("127.0.0.1:8080", mux)

recommendation.why: A puts each path on its handler, as the owner asked, and keeps the route list a plain value. Tags become the same routes mux.get makes, so OpenAPI has one source.
gains: Paths sit on their handlers.
Tests can build and call the route list.

losses.loss: Two ways can add a route.
losses.mitigation: Both make the same route; docs teach tags, and mux.get covers routes known only while running.

losses.mitigation: The compiler warns and names mux.mount as the fix.

decisions.title: Capitalizing the library name inside a marker
decisions.situation: Markers are the #Name labels written above code, such as #Test or #Codable, and you asked that every marker be PascalCase, with each word capitalized. Jet's own markers already are, except #allow and an unused #wire, which simply get capitals. The open part is library markers, written through the import name as in #web.Get, where web is lowercase like every module name in ordinary code. decisions.title: Let callers match the failures an unwritten contract passes up
decisions.gist: When a function writes no failure contract, may callers see and match the typed failures it passes up?
decisions.lesson: A function with no written failure contract can still fail. Since D-ERR-TRAIT1, every `#Error` value flows into the general `Err`, and `err.as<T>()` recovers it at run time. The question is whether callers also see a checked list of the failure types. Option A amends D-FAILURE-FOUNDATION1, which once rejected inferred error sets.
decisions.story: Mia writes `age_of`, which calls `find` and `parse_age`. She writes no contract and wants to print "no such person" or "bad age on file". Today it compiles, but nothing tells her which failures can arrive or whether she handled them all.

options.name: Keep the failure types
options.detail:
A function with no written failure contract fails with the union of every failure type that can reach it. That covers callee failures that pass up and each `Err(value)` it returns. A plain `Err("msg")` adds the general `Err`. An empty union means the function cannot fail.

The union is a checked view over the one `Err` carrier, so the ABI never changes when a body adds a failure. A member arm matches by type, whichever way the value arrived. A union that contains `Err` is open and needs a final `.Err(e)` or `else`. An arm for a member that can no longer arrive is a warning. A case name unique across members may be matched flat.
options.technical:
Rules from the Opus 5.5 adversarial pass 2026-09-30 (AdvErrorModel): (1) inferred set = propagated callee sets + each `Err(v)` type + `Err` for `Err("msg")` or unknown callees; empty = plain-return ABI (#3740). (2) Typing view over the D-ERR-TRAIT1 carrier (type id + boxed payload); member test = `as<T>`; a written single `E!` keeps the unboxed layout.

(3) Higher-order: argument functions' failures are attributed at the call site when propagated; stored or unknown function values count as `Err`. (4) Calls through type parameters and dynamic calls use the trait method's written bound, else `Err`. (5) SCC fixpoint with an iteration cap, then widen to `Err` with a note.

(6) E0307 names a newly arriving member and its call chain. (7) Conversions apply only against a written contract.

Measure M1-M5: success-path parity vs pinned and Rust, half-failing loop, sema time, re-check fanout, share of unions containing `Err`.

options.name: Open `Err`, checked at run time
options.detail: Today's ratified model (D-ERR-TRAIT1=A): an unwritten contract publishes the general `Err`. Typed failures ride inside it, and a handler tests them with `err.as<T>()`. Nothing checks that every failure type is handled.
options.technical: No change. A written contract remains the way to get a closed, checked set.

comparisons.note: Error tags collect through `?` with no annotation, and a match must name every tag. https://www.roc-lang.org/examples/ErrorHandlingRealWorld/README.html
Every function names its error type; `?` converts through `From`. https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch09-02-recoverable-errors-with-result.html

recommendation.why: The compiler already knows which failures can reach the function. Throwing that away forces beginners to write a contract or a conversion. A written contract still pins the type wherever stability matters.

whyNot.reason: B leaves failure handling unchecked, so a missed failure shows up only at run time.

recommendation.tradeoff: Failure types that can shift with the body buy typed failures with no ceremony.

decisions.title: A typed failure for setting fidelity out of range
decisions.gist: When `core.perf.override_fidelity` gets a number outside 0.0 to 1.0, what typed failure should callers match?
decisions.lesson: `core.perf` keeps one process-wide fidelity number between 0.0 and 1.0. `override_fidelity` rejects anything else, but today it fails with plain text (`Err!`). The owner ruled that Core must name its failures with types. No existing Core error means "number out of range". This picks the type callers match.
decisions.story: Ana's game lowers detail when frames run slow. A settings bug passes 1.5 to `override_fidelity`. She wants to match that exact case and log it, not read an error message.

options.name: New `PerfError`
options.detail: Core gains `#Error pub enum PerfError { OutOfRange(Float) }`. The case holds the rejected number. `override_fidelity` writes `PerfError!`. `reset_fidelity` writes `Never!`, because 1.0 is always in range.
options.technical: Edit Core/perf/perf.jet only. The range check already runs in Jet before the host call, so the host's text error is never reached. The private host helper names `PerfError!` too. Regenerate CoreModuleExports.rs with the Core surface ledger script.

options.name: Reuse `IOError.InvalidInput`
options.detail: `override_fidelity` fails with `IOError.InvalidInput`, with the reason in the context's `cause` text. `core.watcher.debounce` does the same for a negative interval. Callers must also cover the eight other `IOError` cases, which never happen here.
options.technical: The `IOContext` needs an `operation`, and no I/O operation describes setting a number, so it would borrow one such as `.Resolve`.

options.name: Clamp, never fail
options.detail: `override_fidelity` clamps like `perf.of`: below 0.0 becomes 0.0, above 1.0 becomes 1.0, and NaN becomes 1.0. Both setters write `Never!`.
options.technical: Reverses the module's written rule that out-of-range values are rejected. The host check becomes unreachable.

comparisons.note: Python reuses the general `ValueError` for any out-of-range argument, so callers cannot tell which check failed without reading text. https://docs.python.org/3/library/exceptions.html#ValueError
comparisons.code:
import math
math.sqrt(-1)  # ValueError: math domain error

comparisons.note: A dedicated error type for one rejected conversion. https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/time/struct.TryFromFloatSecsError.html
comparisons.code: let d = Duration::try_from_secs_f64(1.5e30); // Err(TryFromFloatSecsError)

recommendation.why: The only failure is a number out of range. A one-case type says exactly that, and callers match it without a catch-all.
gains: Exact, matchable failure for the one real mistake.
Keeps the module's rule: bad values are rejected, not changed.

losses.loss: One more small public type.
losses.mitigation: No Core error means "number out of range"; borrowing one adds cases that never happen.

whyNot.reason: B makes callers cover eight I/O cases that never happen, and a range check is not I/O.
C turns a caller's bug into a silent different setting.

recommendation.tradeoff: One tiny type buys an exact failure callers can match.

decisions.title: How a callback's failure reaches the caller of a Core function
decisions.gist: When a Core function calls a function you pass in, how should that function's failures reach you?
decisions.lesson: Some Core functions call a function you pass in, such as the key function of `table.sort`. Those parameters name no failure type today, so 13 Core functions fail with the open `Err`. The owner ruled that Core must name its failures. Either the callback's failure type flows through to the caller, or callbacks may not fail.
decisions.story: Lia sorts a price list with `table.sort`, keyed by a lookup that fails with `PriceError.Missing`. She wants to match `.Missing` after the sort. Today `sort` rejects her lookup outright.

options.name: Failure type flows through
options.detail: A Core function that calls your function takes a failure type parameter `E`. The callback is `fn(T) -> U E!`, and the Core function fails with `E`. With failures of its own it writes `(WebTableError | E)!`. The call site works out `E` from the argument. A callback that cannot fail makes `E` `Never`, so the whole call cannot fail.
options.technical:
Today a type parameter in failure position is error E2417 (checked on snapshot38). Both compilers must accept it; `E` binds to an `#Error` type, a union of them, `Err`, or `Never`. This is the written form of D-FAIL-INFER-UNION1 rule 3, which already credits argument failures to the call site.

A callback stored in a value, such as a table column's `project`, writes `Never!`, because no call site binds its `E`. That also clears today's E2404 in `table.page_state`. `testing.compare` takes two callbacks and fails with `(E1 | E2)!`.

options.name: Callbacks may not fail
options.detail: Callback parameters write `Never!`. The 13 functions then write `Never!`, or only their own typed errors. A callback that can fail is error E0112, so the caller handles its failure first, inside a wrapper.
options.technical: No language change. Checked on snapshot38: a named `Never!` function is accepted, and a `PriceError!` one is rejected with E0112. A pure lambda such as `(n: Int) -> "{n}"` is also rejected today, because its type lacks `Never!`; that checker gap must be fixed first.

options.name: Keep the open `Err`
options.detail: Keep today's `Err!`. A callback must fail with the open `Err`. On snapshot38 a typed failure cannot be put into it (E0108), so the callback fails with text. Callers can only print or compare that text.
options.technical: No change. The 13 public functions and the private `table.projected_rows` stay `Err!`, and the E2404 in `table.page_state` stays.

comparisons.note: Closures return `Result`, and the error type flows through generics to the caller. https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/result/index.html#collecting-into-result
comparisons.code:
let keys: Result<Vec<String>, PriceError> =
    names.iter().map(|n| price_key(n)).collect();

comparisons.note: `java.util.function.Function` cannot throw checked exceptions, so callers wrap or drop them. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/function/Function.html
comparisons.code: names.stream().map(n -> price(n)); // error: unreported exception PriceException

recommendation.why: A keeps the callback's exact failure type, and a callback that cannot fail makes the whole call unable to fail. Callers match `.Missing` directly, with no wrapper and no run-time test.
gains: Typed failures pass through Core unchanged.
Pure callbacks keep Core calls unable to fail.

losses.loss: New rule: a type parameter may be a failure type.
losses.mitigation: Only a parameter can carry each caller's own failure type through shared Core code.

losses.loss: Stored callbacks, like table columns, must still be `Never!`.
losses.mitigation: A stored function has no call site that could name its failure type.

whyNot.reason: B forces every fallible lookup into a wrapper that drops or hides its failure.
C keeps these 13 functions on the open `Err`, against the owner's ruling for Core.

recommendation.tradeoff: One generic rule buys exact failures through every Core callback.
