decisions.title: Honest signatures and the determinism label
decisions.gist: Should Jet name honest signatures as a principle and show whether each function is deterministic?
decisions.lesson: Logan Smith calls a function honest when it touches the outside world only through its signature, and dishonest otherwise. Dishonesty spreads to every caller. In Jet, an empty effect row is exactly honest, and an effect row names the dishonesty. This choice decides whether Jet names that principle and shows each function's full contract and determinism everywhere.
decisions.story: Sam reviews a pull request that calls load(path) inside a report function marked replayable. Hover shows fn load(path: String) String, so load looks honest. Only an inspect command reveals that it reads files. The owner wants Logan Smith's honest-versus-dishonest idea visible on every Jet signature.

options.name: Name it and show it
options.detail:
The owner adds honest signatures to philosophy.md, crediting Logan Smith's taxonomy, and vocabulary.md defines the term. Hover, jet doc, API snapshots, and diagnostics show the full inferred signature: parameters, result, failure, and effects.

Each view adds a label from the effect row. An empty row reads honest; & parameters stay honest because the caller grants that access. A row that passes the existing #Replayable check reads deterministic. Any other row names its first effect. Nothing new is written in source.
options.technical: The label comes from the D-RIGHTS1 row walker, the same one #Replayable lowers to (no Time, Rand, Net, or IO), plus the empty-row pure case. Hover reads the inferred row and failure set from the checked callable-signature facts instead of only the written row. The failure part depends on #3708, which makes sema remove the default Err route when a function cannot fail.
options.code:
fn load(path: String) -> String -[FS.Read]>
  can fail: no · dishonest: reads files

fn populate(n: Int, rng: &Rng) -> [Particle]
  can fail: no · honest

fn twice(n: Int) -> Int

decisions.title: Honest signatures: which facts each view shows
decisions.gist: Which facts should signature views show: honesty, whether it can fail, and whether results repeat?
decisions.lesson: Honest: a function reaches the outside world only through its parameters, so its effect list is empty. Can fail: it may return an error instead of its result. Deterministic: the same arguments always give the same result. Repeatable: running it again gives the same result while the files it uses are unchanged; it avoids the clock, random numbers, network, and console. In Jet, honest implies deterministic, and deterministic implies repeatable.
decisions.story: The owner asked for Smith's honest versus dishonest framing, then asked for clear definitions of honesty, failure, determinism, and repeatability. The ratified text headlines determinism instead, and its examples write `-> String -[FS.Read]>`, which is not Jet's current signature shape.
decisions.inWild:
readFile :: FilePath -> IO String   -- dishonest: does IO
twice    :: Int -> Int              -- honest
decisions.detail:
Owner question (2026-09-30): define honest, fallibility, determinism, and repeatability, and add them all. This update adds the four definitions and re-cuts the options around them. The earlier honesty-only option is now B. The earlier two-label option is replaced by C, which shows all four facts.

Honest. A function is honest when it reaches the outside world only through its parameters and result (Logan Smith, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2OMRWPOSw9s, 10:49). In Jet that is an empty effect row. Changing a `&` parameter stays honest, because the caller handed over that access. A dishonest function has an effect row, and the row names what it reaches, such as files, the network, or the clock.

Can fail. A function can fail when it may return an error instead of its result. The contract is written `T E!`, or inferred when unwritten, and `Never!` denies failure (D-FAIL-PUBSIG1=A). A missing value `T?` is not a failure; it is an ordinary value (D-OUTCOME-SHAPE1=A). A panic is not a failure either; it is a bug stop with its own report.

Deterministic. The same arguments always give the same result. D-DET1 makes an empty row reproducible: it rejects the wall clock, the system random source, files, and the network. An injected Clock or Rng is an argument, so a function given a seeded Rng stays deterministic. The only way out is an audited #Nondeterministic("reason") block.

Repeatable. Running the function again gives the same result, as long as the files and databases it uses are unchanged. It may have effects, but it may not reach the clock, random numbers, the network, or the console except through an injected provider. This is exactly the #Replayable check (D-REPLAY1, E0725; Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Effects/Checks.jet:1081-1090 forbids the Time, Rand, Net, and IO roots).

How the four relate. Honest implies deterministic. Deterministic implies repeatable. The reverse fails: a function that reads a config file is repeatable, but not deterministic and not honest. Failure is separate from all three: an honest parser can fail.

So determinism and repeatability differ. Determinism depends on the arguments alone. Repeatability also allows stored state, such as files and databases, that a test can hold still.

What A shows. Honest functions show `honest` and the failure fact, because honest already means deterministic and repeatable. Dishonest functions add `repeatable` or `not repeatable`, the one fact their effect row does not settle at a glance. The same facts appear in hover, jet doc, API snapshots, and diagnostics.

options.name: Honesty leads, then failure and repeatability
options.detail: Every view shows honest or dishonest first, then the failure fact. A dishonest function also says whether it is repeatable. Determinism is not a separate word, because honest already means it. `jet explain` prints all four facts with their reasons. Examples use the fused arrow `-[FS.Read]> String`.

decisions.title: Which unused values the compiler rejects
decisions.gist: Which values other than unit may be thrown away without a mark?
decisions.lesson: Jet already rejects dropping a result that can fail, unless you write `.drop("reason")`. Other values drop silently, and two mistakes hide there. A function without a return type throws its last value away, and the error appears later at a caller. A line that calls a pure function and ignores the result does nothing at all. Skip and Zig let only unit values drop silently.
decisions.story: Ana writes `fn average(a: Int, b: Int)` and forgets `-> Int`. The body computes the average and throws it away. The error appears at `print(average(4, 6))` and talks about `Unit`, a word she has never used.

options.name: Lost tails and pure calls
options.detail:
Two errors. First, in a named function with no written return type, a last line whose value is not unit is an error at that line. The fix suggests the return type, such as `-> Int`, or `.drop("reason")`. Second, a statement that calls a pure function and ignores a result that is not unit is an error. A call is pure when its effect row is empty and it takes nothing by `&`.

Calls with effects or `&` arguments, such as `announce("ready")`, may still drop their result. Lambdas are unaffected, because their result type is worked out from the body. Fallible and `#MustUse` results keep their existing rule.
options.technical:
The statement rule is #3717's owner-directed rule, with one clarification: a call that takes a `&` receiver or argument is not pure, even with an empty effect row, because it changes that value. The tail rule is new and fixes the p4b diagnostic (D6). Probe p15, `twice(2)`, fires once #3708 infers that `twice` cannot fail. Until then its implicit fallible result belongs to the existing must-use rule (D11). One registered code covers both sites, with a UI snapshot each.

Beginner path: follow the suggested `-> Int`. Expert path: `.drop("reason")` for a deliberate discard.

options.name: Only unit drops silently
options.detail: Any statement or last line whose value is not unit and is not used is an error. The fix names the likely intent: add the return type for a last line, or write `.drop("reason")` to discard on purpose. Methods that return `self` for chaining also need a mark or a unit-returning variant.
options.technical: One registered code over every expression statement and tail. It needs a repository-wide count and migration before landing, because every side-effect call that returns a value, like `announce("ready")`, changes. Beginner path: as A, plus `.drop("reason")` on side-effect calls. Expert path: every discard is visible.

options.name: Pure calls only
options.detail: Only #3717's planned rule: an ignored result of a pure call is an error. A value lost at the end of a function with no return type stays silent, and the error still appears at the caller.
options.technical: #3717 as planned. The p4b diagnostic stays a caller-side E0112 about `Unit`. Beginner path: decode the caller error. Expert path: unchanged.

comparisons.note: Only `void` values may be silently discarded; others are bound to `_`. https://github.com/skiplang/skip/blob/master/docs/overview/functions.md
comparisons.code: _ = twice(2);

comparisons.note: Only types or functions marked `#[must_use]` warn when unused. https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/diagnostics.html#the-must_use-attribute

recommendation.why: It catches both real mistakes where they happen: a forgotten return type and a line that does nothing. Calls made for their side effect keep working, so no existing code needs edits for them.

whyNot.reason: B also flags calls made for their side effect, like `announce("ready")`. Its cost across existing code should be counted first.
C leaves a forgotten return type silent, so the error still lands at a caller far away.

recommendation.tradeoff: Leaving impure results silent buys two precise errors with no churn.

decisions.title: A declarable name for core.reactive's effect function
decisions.gist: What should `core.reactive` call its re-running function, now that `effect` is a keyword and can't be declared?
decisions.lesson: `core.reactive` has a function that runs a block now, and again whenever a signal it read changes. It is called `effect`. But `effect` is a Jet keyword, used to declare effects, so the function cannot be written in Jet source. Today the compiler serves `reactive.effect` by name, and the module's source cannot list it. A new name lets Core declare it beside `signal` and `derived`.
decisions.story: Lina opens `Core/reactive/reactive.jet` to read how `reactive.effect` works. She finds `signal`, `derived` and `unsubscribe`, but no `effect`. The declaration was deleted because it never parsed.

options.name: `autorun`
options.detail:
`reactive.autorun(body)` runs `body` now, and again whenever a signal it read changes. It returns the same `Effect` handle, and `unsubscribe` stops it. `core.reactive` declares it as an ordinary `pub fn` beside `signal` and `derived`.

Every caller moves to the new name. `reactive.effect` becomes an unknown-member error whose fix names `autorun`. `watch` was considered and set aside, because `core.watcher` and `--watch` already use it for files. `react` would read `reactive.react`.
options.technical:
Rename the served name in the Rust checker (`core_call.rs`, the `("core.reactive", "effect")` arm), code generation, the JIT, the DOM runtime, and the Jet compiler's `ReactiveHandles.jet`. Update the E2911 and E2912 fix texts, `Examples/features/ui/reactive.jet`, `tests/ui/reactive_effect_*`, and the conformance corpus. The handle type `Effect` and the `effect_*` helpers keep their names. Behaviour is unchanged on every tier.

Beginner path: `reactive.autorun(() -> …)`. Expert path: the same, plus `unsubscribe` on the returned handle.
options.code:
use core.reactive as reactive

fn run() {
    price := reactive.signal(100)
    qty := reactive.signal(2)
    total :: reactive.derived(() -> price.get() * qty.get())
    subscription :: reactive.autorun(() -> print(total.get()))   // prints 200
    &price.set(150)                                               // prints 300
    &qty.set(3)                                                   // prints 450
}

options.name: `on_change`
options.detail: The same behaviour under `reactive.on_change(body)`. It still runs `body` once at the start, unlike Jet's other `on_*` hooks such as `on_commit` and `on_frame`, which wait for their event.
options.technical: The same rename work as A with a different name. Beginner path: `reactive.on_change(() -> …)`; docs must stress the first run. Expert path: as A.
options.code:
use core.reactive as reactive

fn run() {
    price := reactive.signal(100)
    qty := reactive.signal(2)
    total :: reactive.derived(() -> price.get() * qty.get())
    subscription :: reactive.on_change(() -> print(total.get()))  // prints 200 now
    &price.set(150)                                               // prints 300
    &qty.set(3)                                                   // prints 450
}

options.name: Keep `effect`
options.detail: No change. `effect` stays a keyword, and `reactive.effect` stays a name the compiler serves directly. `core.reactive`'s source does not declare it, because the declaration cannot parse.
options.technical: No change. Both compilers keep serving `reactive.effect` by name, and Core source keeps no declaration for it. Beginner path: as today. Expert path: as today.
options.code:
use core.reactive as reactive

fn run() {
    price := reactive.signal(100)
    qty := reactive.signal(2)
    total :: reactive.derived(() -> price.get() * qty.get())
    subscription :: reactive.effect(() -> print(total.get()))     // prints 200
    &price.set(150)                                               // prints 300
    &qty.set(3)                                                   // prints 450
}

comparisons.note: `createEffect` re-runs whenever a signal it read changes. https://docs.solidjs.com/reference/basic-reactivity/create-effect
comparisons.code: createEffect(() => console.log(total()))

comparisons.note: `watchEffect` runs now and re-runs on change; plain `watch` waits for a named source. https://vuejs.org/api/reactivity-core.html#watcheffect
comparisons.code: const stop = watchEffect(() => console.log(total.value))

recommendation.why: `autorun` names exactly what happens: the body runs now and re-runs by itself. A declarable name lets Core list it beside `signal` and `derived`, and the word no longer clashes with Jet's effects.

whyNot.reason: B reads like Jet's `on_*` hooks, which wait for an event, but this function also runs at once.
C keeps a public function that Core's own source can never declare, under a word Jet already uses for effects.

recommendation.tradeoff: One new word buys a function Core can declare and document.

fn run() {

    qty := reactive.signal(2)
    total :: reactive.derived(() -> price.get() * qty.get())
    subscription :: reactive.autorun(() -> print(total.get()))   // prints 200
    &price.set(150)                                               // prints 300
    &qty.set(3)                                                   // prints 450
}

    qty := reactive.signal(2)

proposed.code:
use core.reactive as reactive

fn run() {
    price := reactive.signal(100)
    qty := reactive.signal(2)
    total :: reactive.derived(() -> price.get() * qty.get())
    subscription :: reactive.effect(() -> print(total.get()))     // prints 200

    &qty.set(3)                                                   // prints 450

recommendation.why: `autorun` names exactly what happens: the body runs now and re-runs by itself. A declarable name lets Core list it beside `signal` and `derived`, and the word no longer clashes with Jet's effects.

losses.loss: Readers who know `effect` from web frameworks learn a new word.
losses.mitigation: `effect` is a Jet keyword, so any declarable name is a new word.

whyNot.reason: B reads like Jet's `on_*` hooks, which wait for an event, but this function also runs at once.

recommendation.tradeoff: One new word buys a function Core can declare and document.

decisions.title: Who decides between moving, sharing, and copying a stored value
decisions.gist: When a value must live in two places, how should Jet avoid wasteful copies?
decisions.lesson: Today a function that stores a parameter copies it, even when the caller is finished with it. In one measured builder, that copy cost about 20% of the run time. Every option keeps reads free. The choice is who picks between moving, sharing, and copying: the compiler or the programmer.
decisions.story: Mia writes a `build` function that puts a list into a report. Her program runs 20% slower than the same code written inline, because Jet copies the whole list into the report even though Mia never uses it again. She should not need to learn ownership symbols to avoid that.

options.name: The compiler chooses
options.detail:
A last use of a name always moves, in every position, with no mark. A function that stores, returns, or sends a parameter keeps it; Jet infers that from the body and shows it in hover and docs.

When two places need the same data, they share storage and the first write makes the copy. Text is shared and sliceable, so `.trim()` never copies. `~x` still asks for an independent copy now, and a cost denial can forbid hidden copies in hot code. Exported functions write `^T` for kept parameters; jet fmt adds it.
options.technical: Ownership conventions are sema facts. Values proven unique at compile time carry no counter and no uniqueness check. Other heap values use a counted buffer with copy-on-first-write; the counter becomes thread-safe only when the value crosses into another task (D-MEMREF-TASK1). Long-lived small slices of large text compact on store. Each automatic choice needs a paired performance cell before it ships.

options.name: The programmer chooses
options.detail: A parameter the body stores must be declared `^T`. Callers pass `^name` to move or `~name` to copy. Storing a borrowed value is an error with a fix. There is no shared storage, so there are no counters.

options.name: Keep today's copies
options.detail: The ratified copy law stays: a borrowed value entering an owning place is copied at once (D-MEM-COPYSEM1). `#Policy(copies: .Explicit)` makes those copies need `~`.

comparisons.note: Copy-on-write collections: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swift/array.
comparisons.code:
var a = [1, 2, 3]
var b = a      // shared storage
b.append(4)    // b copies here

comparisons.note: Owned parameters and last-use transfer: https://docs.modular.com/mojo/manual/values/ownership.
comparisons.code:
fn build(owned rows: List[String]) -> Report:
    return Report(rows^)

comparisons.note: Moves by value; copies need .clone(): https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-01-what-is-ownership.html.
comparisons.code:
fn build(rows: Vec<String>) -> Report { Report { lines: rows } }
let r = build(rows.clone());

recommendation.why: The compiler already knows last uses and which functions keep values. Letting it choose removes wasteful copies without putting ownership symbols in beginner code.

whyNot.reason: B removes hidden cost but puts ownership symbols into every builder.
C keeps a measured slowdown in the most common constructor code.

recommendation.tradeoff: Rare deferred copies are accepted to keep everyday code free of symbols.

decisions.title: How readers see where a failure can leave a function
decisions.gist: How should readers see which calls can pass a failure up, without extra typing?
decisions.lesson: Jet passes a failure up to the caller automatically. Today nothing in the text shows which calls can do that. Every option keeps automatic passing and the runtime report of the failure's path. The choice is whether the source text carries a mark, or tools show it.
decisions.story: Sam reviews a pull request on the web. A new line reads a file, and the function now exits early when the file is missing. Nothing in the diff shows that. Sam needs to see failure points, while beginners should not type extra marks.
decisions.detail:
Owner question (2026-09-30): how do other languages handle this, which are praised most, what friction do those have, and how can Jet fix it? The answer is below. The options keep their letters. A now adds review annotations so a web pull request shows failure points.

Four families exist. Unmarked exceptions (Python, C#, JavaScript, Kotlin) show nothing at the call or in the signature. Checked exceptions (Java) list failures in the signature, not at the call. Manual checks (Go) write an if after every call. Marked propagation (Swift `try`, Rust `?`, Zig `try`, Roc `?`, Midori `try`) passes failures up for you, but needs a short mark at each call.

Most praised. Rust's `Result` with `?` is the most cited model. Swift's `try` is praised for its written design rationale (https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/blob/main/docs/ErrorHandlingRationale.md). Zig adds error return traces, which show every place an error passed through. Joe Duffy's Midori essay is the standard argument for call-site marks. Go is praised for visible errors, yet verbosity has topped its user survey complaints for years.

Friction 1, noise. Go's own blog (June 2025) says the checks can drown out the real work. After three failed proposals, the team stopped trying to change the syntax (https://go.dev/blog/error-syntax).

Friction 2, conversion plumbing. Rust needs From conversions, and its ecosystem split into thiserror for libraries and anyhow for applications.

Friction 3, signature ripple. Adding one failure to a function forces edits in every caller: Java throws clauses, Swift try, Rust Result. Anders Hejlsberg calls this the versioning and scalability problem (https://www.artima.com/articles/the-trouble-with-checked-exceptions).

Friction 4, lost location. A Rust `?` or a Go `return err` carries no path by default, so libraries add context by hand.

Friction 5, silent escapes. Swift `try?` drops the error and `try!` crashes. Rust `unwrap` panics. Java code fills up with `throws Exception` and empty catch blocks.

Friction 6, marks that are too coarse or too faint. Swift's `try` covers a whole expression, so it does not say which call throws. Rust's one-character `?` is easy to miss in review.

How Jet answers frictions 1 to 3. (1) Failures pass up with no mark. (2) One declared rail, `impl A -> B`, converts at propagation, and the default `Err` needs no type (D-FAIL-CONV1). (3) Contracts are inferred; a written `E!` is an optional ceiling, and publish tools flag a new failure (D-FAIL-PUBSIG1=A).

How Jet answers frictions 4 to 6. (4) #3713, ready but not yet built, prints where a failure began and its path, like Zig traces; `?(text)` adds context. (5) An unhandled value is E0401, and the only discard is `.drop("reason")`. (6) The editor mark sits on each call, not on a whole expression.

What A still gives up. Swift's rationale warns that unmarked propagation hides which calls can exit, so readers must watch for half-finished changes. Jet softens this: a `#Transact` block restores changed locals when a failure passes through. The larger gap was Sam's case, plain text on a web review page. A now closes it with review annotations. Code read with no tools at all still hides failure points; teams that need marks choose `#Policy(failures: .Explicit)`.

Hejlsberg's conclusion matches A. Knowing what can fail has great value, but checking tools serve better than a hard compiler rule everywhere. The Go blog also suggests editor help for reading error paths.

options.name: Tools show it; teams may require marks
options.detail:
Failures pass up automatically. The editor draws a faint `?` at each call that can pass one up. `jet review` and `jet diff` list failure points and flag a function that newly can fail. `jet review` can also publish them as code-host annotations, so a web pull request shows a mark on each failure point. The runtime report shows the path (#3713).

A team that wants marks in the text sets `#Policy(failures: .Explicit)` at block, function, module, or package level. Then each such call needs `?` or `?(text)`, and jet fmt inserts them. This mirrors the existing `copies: .Explicit` setting.

options.name: Marks always required
options.detail: Every propagating call must carry `?` or `?(text)`. A missing mark is one grouped error per file, and jet fix or jet fmt inserts every mark. A method call directly after the mark needs parentheses.

options.name: Tools only
options.detail: Same as A without the setting. Failure points are visible only through the editor, review tools, review annotations, and reports.

comparisons.note: `try` marks each throwing expression and is praised for its written rationale: https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/errorhandling/. Friction: `try` covers a whole expression, `try?` drops the error, and errors were untyped until Swift 6 typed throws (SE-0413).
comparisons.code: let text = try String(contentsOfFile: path)

comparisons.note: `?` marks each propagation point and is the most cited model: https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch09-02-recoverable-errors-with-result.html. Friction: From conversions, the thiserror and anyhow split, no path or context by default, and a one-character mark that is easy to miss.
comparisons.code: let text = std::fs::read_to_string(path)?;

comparisons.note: `try` marks each call, and error return traces show every place an error passed through: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#Error-Return-Traces. Friction: error values carry no extra data, and traces are on by default only in debug builds.
comparisons.code: const file = try std.fs.cwd().openFile(path, .{});

comparisons.note: A manual check after each call. Verbosity has topped Go's survey complaints; after three failed proposals the team stopped pursuing new syntax in June 2025: https://go.dev/blog/error-syntax.

Checked exceptions: `throws` in the signature, nothing at the call. Hejlsberg: adding one exception breaks every caller, so teams dodge it with `throws Exception` or empty catch blocks: https://www.artima.com/articles/the-trouble-with-checked-exceptions.

Unchecked exceptions: nothing in the signature or at the call. Lowest friction, and tracebacks show the path, but readers cannot see which calls can exit: https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/errors.html.

Joe Duffy argues for call-site `try` and separates bugs, which stop the program, from recoverable errors: https://joeduffyblog.com/2016/02/07/the-error-model/. Midori was a research system, so field data is thin.
comparisons.code: int value = try Foo();

comparisons.note: Roc writes postfix `?` at every propagation point; the guest calls this Roc's strongest advantage over Rust (35:12, Roc talk https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=12yVcgQHAK0). Docs: https://github.com/roc-lang/roc/blob/main/docs/mini-tutorial-new-compiler.md.
comparisons.code:
first_str = strings.first()?
first_num = I64.from_str(first_str)?

recommendation.why: Calls that can fail are very common. Required marks add friction everywhere. Tools and review annotations give readers the same facts, and one setting serves teams that audit.

whyNot.reason: B adds a mark to one of the most common operations and collides with `?.`.
C leaves audited teams no way to require marks in the text.

recommendation.tradeoff: Default code depends on tools for failure visibility; teams can opt into marks.

decisions.title: Written failure contracts are optional ceilings
decisions.gist: Should a written failure contract be an optional ceiling, never a requirement, while tools guard public changes?
decisions.lesson: Effects work this way already: write `-[IO]>` to cap a function, or leave it out and let Jet infer. The owner rejects requiring failure contracts. This picks how an optional written contract behaves and how public changes stay safe.
decisions.story: Lee maintains a small library. He wants to write no contracts while prototyping, then cap `load` before release so a later refactor cannot quietly add a failure his users do not handle.
decisions.inWild:
func load(_ path: String) throws(IOError) -> Report
func hash(_ b: [UInt8]) throws(Never) -> UInt32

options.name: Optional ceiling, guarded publishing
options.detail: A written failure contract is both the ceiling the body must fit inside and the type callers match. An unwritten contract publishes the inferred set (D-FAIL-INFER-UNION1). `Never!` denies failure. `Err` inside a cap keeps it open for later growth. The API snapshot records each public set; infallible to fallible, or a new member in a closed set, is a major change that `jet publish` refuses without acknowledgment. `jet fix --pin-failures` writes the inferred set into source.
options.code:
pub fn load(path: String) -> Report IoError! {   // cap: body must stay inside
    fs.read(path)                                // ok: IoError
}

fn hash(b: [U8]) -[]> U32 Never! { ... }         // denial: cannot fail

pub fn fetch(id: Int) -> User? (DbError | Err)! { ... }   // open cap
options.technical: Unlike effect rows (D-EFFECT-OMIT1), callers see the written ceiling, not the narrower inferred set, because failures are values callers match. Body outside the cap: a diagnostic naming the member and its call chain. Conversions apply only against a written contract.

options.name: Required on public functions
options.detail: The earlier recommendation: a written contract on every exported function that can fail.

options.name: Always inferred, no ceiling
options.detail: No written contracts at all; `jet review` alone reports changes.

comparisons.note: Typed throws and throws(Never): SE-0413.
comparisons.code: func f() throws(Never) -> Int

comparisons.note: Inferred error sets with explicit sets optional: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#Inferred-Error-Sets.
comparisons.code:
fn load() !Report  // inferred
fn load2() IoError!Report

comparisons.note: Signatures optional; error unions inferred (talk 12yVcgQHAK0 36:18).
comparisons.code: read_str! : Path => Try(Str, ReadFileErr)

recommendation.why: It mirrors effect rows, which Jet readers already know: optional to write, a hard cap when written. Publishing checks catch silent breaking changes.

whyNot.reason: B makes contracts a requirement, which the owner rejected.
C gives authors no way to cap a function before release.

recommendation.tradeoff: Optional caps plus publish checks replace a required contract.

decisions.title: Absence and failure: one three-state outcome
decisions.gist: Should a value that may be missing or failed read as three states, and which states leave a function by themselves?
decisions.lesson: `User? DbError!` today nests two layers: a failure wrapper around an optional value. Readers match `.Ok(.Val(user))`, `.Ok(.None)`, and `.Err(e)`. Failures pass up to the caller by themselves; a missing value never does. Every option keeps `??` for local fallbacks and `.or_err("why")` to turn absence into failure.
decisions.story: Priya looks up a user. The user can exist, be missing, or the database can be down. She wants to handle three plain cases, and she wants a missing user to never skip the rest of her function by surprise.

options.name: Three states; only failure leaves by itself
options.detail: A value of type `T? E!` has exactly three states, and patterns name them directly: `.Val(x)`, `.None`, and `.Err(e)`. The nested `.Ok(.Val(x))` form stops being needed. An unhandled failure passes up automatically, as today. A missing value is ordinary data: it leaves a function only when written, with `?` on the optional, or becomes a failure with `.or_err("why")`. `??` resolves either state where it is written.
options.technical: The meaning stays one carrier (D-FAIL-CARRIER1), including partial payloads and notes on failures. The compiler may lay the three states out as one tag instead of two nested ones; that is an internal choice that needs a paired performance cell.

options.name: Three states; both leave by themselves
options.detail: Binding a `T?` value where a plain `T` is needed returns `None` from the enclosing function when the value is missing, just as a failure passes up. Functions must return `T?` for this to apply.

options.name: Keep nested layers
options.detail: Today's model stays: the combined type is a failure wrapper around an optional value.

comparisons.note: Error union around an optional; `try` and `orelse` are explicit: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#Error-Union-Type.
comparisons.code:

decisions.title: Let a function name its own error cases
decisions.gist: May a function with no written failure contract name its own error cases, without a separate `#Error enum`?
decisions.lesson: Today every typed error case lives in a declared `#Error enum` or `#Error struct`, even a one-off case. This ballot applies only if D-FAIL-INFER-UNION1 picks A, so callers can see failures the compiler works out. Then a function with no written contract could create cases where it fails. They form that function's own closed error type, which callers match like any other.
decisions.story: Leo writes `find` for a small address book. Its one failure is "no such person". Today he must declare an `#Error enum` and write a contract before he can return it.

options.name: Function-owned cases
options.detail:
In a function with no written failure contract, `Err(.Case(payload))` has no expected error type. So the case joins that function's own error type. The type is named after the function: `find` gives `FindError`, and the method `Book.find` gives `BookFindError`. The payload type comes from the `Err` argument. Using one case name with two payload types is an error.

The type is closed and joins the function's failure union like any member. When it is the only failure, callers match `.Err(.NotFound(who))`. Inside a union they name the member, as today: `.Err(.FindError(.NotFound(who)))`. To use a declared type instead, write its name: `Err(LookupError.NotFound(n))`.

Review fixes: callers match a unique case name flat (`.Err(.NotFound(w))`), so adding a second failure never rewrites their arms. A minted name that shadows a case already arriving from a callee is a lint with a fix. Cases minted inside a closure belong to the enclosing named function. A type that crosses a Codable or wire boundary needs a declared name.
options.technical:
If a declared type already uses the generated name, the function must write its contract; the error says so. Exported functions write their contract under D-FAIL-PUBSIG1 (open, recommendation A). There, `jet fix` writes out `#Error enum FindError` with the inferred cases. Because the name is unchanged, callers keep compiling. Hover, `jet doc` and `jet inspect` show the generated type and its cases. It needs no new token and works the same on every tier.

Beginner path: write `Err(.NotFound(name))` and match `.Err(.NotFound(who))`. Expert path: declare a shared `#Error enum` and pin the contract.

options.name: Declared only
options.detail: No change. Every typed error case lives in an `#Error enum` or `#Error struct`. A one-off failure without a declaration uses the general `Err("message", code: "FIND404")`, which callers can compare only as text.
options.technical: No change. Beginner path: declare the enum and write the contract, or use the general `Err`. Expert path: unchanged.

options.name: Shared tags, like Roc
options.detail: A case name is global: `.NotFound(String)` in two functions is the same case. A new type spelling lists cases directly, `[NotFound(String), BadNumber(String)]`. Payloads for one name must agree across the program.
options.technical: This adds structural tag unions beside named enums and anonymous unions (D-UNIONTYPE1), with open or closed width and new rules at host and wire edges. Roc itself bans open tag unions at its host boundary. Beginner path: write any tag. Expert path: write the tag list to pin it.

comparisons.note: The tag is the declaration, and tags from different functions merge by name. https://www.roc-lang.org/docs/main/langref/tag-unions/
Every error case lives in a declared enum. https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch09-02-recoverable-errors-with-result.html

recommendation.why: A one-off failure should cost one line, not a declaration and a contract. Keeping the type owned by one function keeps it closed and named, so nothing new enters the type system.

whyNot.reason: B keeps a declaration and a contract for every one-off failure, although the compiler already works out the rest.
C adds a second kind of sum type, and unrelated code that reuses a case name gets merged.

recommendation.tradeoff: One naming rule buys one-line error cases.

decisions.title: A debug print that works in pure code
decisions.gist: Should Jet have a debug print that works in pure and memoized code without changing the function's effects?
decisions.lesson: `print` is an effect. In a function marked pure (`-[]>`) or `#Memo`, it is an error. In other functions it silently adds `IO` to the effects the compiler works out. That changes a public function's signature. So pure code cannot be print-debugged today. `dbg(expr)` would return its value unchanged and print it for the developer. It adds no effect, because no program behaviour depends on it.
decisions.story: Sam's memoized `score` returns a wrong number. He adds a `print` to see the length and gets error E3401. His only route is the debugger, or taking off `#Memo` and adding an `IO` effect.

options.name: Debug builds only
options.detail:
`dbg(expr)` returns `expr` unchanged and writes one line to standard error: `[dbg] score.jet:3 word.len() * 3 = 9`. It adds nothing to the function's effects. It is allowed in `-[]>` functions, `#Memo` functions and comptime code. A memoized function prints only when it actually runs, not on a cache hit. Comptime code prints while compiling.

It prints in `jet run`, `jet dev`, `jet test`, `--interpret` and debug-profile builds. A release-profile build (`jet build`, or `--release` on any command) rejects any remaining `dbg` with a registered error. `jet fix` removes the wrapper and keeps the expression.
options.technical:
One builtin, `dbg`, registered in Syntax.rs with a decision ID and mirrored in the Jet compiler. One Prelude function prints the line, so every tier prints the same text. The value uses its `Debug` form. The release-build error is registered with what, why and fix, and a UI snapshot. `dbg` cannot serve as program output, because release builds reject it, so it is not a second print.

Beginner path: wrap any expression in `dbg(…)`. Expert path: `jet debug` for breakpoints; `jet build --profile=debug` keeps `dbg` in a local binary.

options.name: Everywhere, warn in release
options.detail: The same `dbg(expr)`, allowed in the same places. A release build keeps the output and prints a warning for each remaining `dbg`. This is Roc's choice; Rust keeps `dbg!` in release builds without a warning.
options.technical: The same builtin and Prelude function as A, with a registered warning instead of an error. Beginner path: as A. Expert path: must find leftovers by reading the warnings.

options.name: No debug print
options.detail: No change. Pure and memoized code is debugged with `jet debug`. To print instead, the author removes `#Memo`, changes `-[]>` to `-[IO]>`, and puts both back afterwards. In a function whose effects are left unwritten, `print` silently adds `IO`.
options.technical: No change. Beginner path: learn `jet debug` or edit the signature. Expert path: unchanged.

comparisons.note: `dbg` is allowed in pure functions because program behaviour never depends on it. Optimized builds keep it with a warning. https://www.roc-lang.org/docs/main/langref/functions/
`Debug.Trace.trace` prints from pure code and is documented as for debugging only. https://hackage.haskell.org/package/base/docs/Debug-Trace.html
comparisons.code:
score word = trace ("total = " ++ show total) (total + 1)
  where total = length word * 3

recommendation.why: Debugging pure code is common, and a trace is not behaviour the program depends on. Rejecting leftovers in release builds keeps shipped pure functions truly pure.

whyNot.reason: B lets debug output, and a hidden effect, ship inside functions marked pure.
C leaves pure and memoized code with no quick way to look inside.

recommendation.tradeoff: One removal step before release buys print-debugging everywhere.

decisions.title: Failures and the effect system
decisions.gist: Should failures join the effect row, or keep their own spelling while following the same rules as effects?
decisions.lesson: Effect rows list what a function may do and are erased before code runs. Failures are values callers match and change the return shape. The owner asked whether failures should be part of the effect system. Both options infer, cap, and deny failures the same way effects do.
decisions.story: Kim reads `fn parse(s: String) -[]> Int ParseError!`: pure, but it can fail. She needs pure and cannot-fail to stay separate facts.
decisions.inWild:
fun parse(s : string) : exn int
fun hash(b : list<int>) : total int

options.name: Same rules, own spelling
options.detail: One law, shared solver: failure sets are inferred like effects, a written set is a ceiling, and `Never!` denies failure (D-FAIL-PUBSIG1). The spelling stays where D-TYPE-SUFFIX1 put it.
options.code:
fn load(p: String) -[FS.Read]> String { fs.read(p) }   // inferred IoError!
fn parse(s: String) -[]> Int ParseError! { ... }       // pure, fallible
fn hash(b: [U8]) -[]> U32 Never! { ... }               // pure, cannot fail

options.name: Failures join the effect row
options.detail: `Fail(E)` becomes an effect row entry. Authority, `#FX`, package budgets, and E1803 would each need a `Fail` exception.

comparisons.note: Koka treats exceptions as an untyped `exn` effect and separates `total` from `pure`. See https://koka-lang.github.io/koka/doc/book.html#sec-effect-types.
comparisons.code:
fun parse(s : string) : exn int
fun hash(b : list<int>) : total int

recommendation.why: Effects are erased powers; failures are returned values. Sharing the rules gives one mental model without breaking what `-[]>` means.

whyNot.reason: B makes pure mean infallible, breaks pure parsers, and adds a special case to every effect check.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two spellings with one set of rules beat one row with special cases.

decisions.title: What happens when someone writes a type on a binding name
decisions.gist: When someone writes a type on a binding name, should Jet reject it with a fix or accept it?
decisions.lesson: Jet puts types on values, as in `limit :: U8{250}`. The form `limit: U8 :: 250` was retired by D-BIND-BARE1. Today it gets a plain parse error with no automatic fix. The choice is how Jet treats people who type the retired form.
decisions.story: Ana comes from Odin and types `limit: U8 :: 250`. Jet stops with a parse error that does not offer to fix it. She should either get a one-step fix or have the line accepted.
decisions.inWild:
limit: u8 = 250
limit2 := u8(250)

options.name: Teach and fix
options.detail: The retired form gets a registered teaching diagnostic with a safe automatic edit to `name :: Type{value}` (lists use #3739's whole-value rule). D-BIND-BARE1 stands.

options.name: Accept both; lint toward `Type{…}`
options.detail: `name: Type :: value` becomes accepted again with the same meaning as `name :: Type{value}`. A lint suggests the value form, and jet fmt rewrites it.
options.code:
limit: U8 :: 250
// Warning: prefer `limit :: U8{250}` (jet fix)

comparisons.note: Odin accepts both `x: T = v` and `x := T(v)`. See https://odin-lang.org/docs/overview/.
comparisons.code:
limit: u8 = 250
limit2 := u8(250)

recommendation.why: One spelling keeps Jet code uniform and matches the ratified rule, while the automatic fix removes the frustration for newcomers.

whyNot.reason: B brings back a retired second spelling that code in the wild would keep.

recommendation.tradeoff: Newcomers take one automatic fix instead of Jet keeping two spellings.

decisions.title: Typed failures for loading a compiled Jet module
decisions.gist: When `core.mod.load` cannot load a compiled library, what typed failure should callers match?
decisions.lesson: `core.mod.load` opens a compiled Jet library under a read grant. It fails when the grant refuses the path or the file is missing. It also fails when the file is damaged or was built for another Jet or platform. Today every case is plain text (`Err!`). The owner ruled that Core must name its failures with types. This picks the type.
decisions.story: Omar's editor loads user plugins from a folder. After a Jet upgrade, old plugins must be rebuilt, while a missing plugin should just be skipped. Today both arrive as the same text error.

options.name: New `ModError`
options.detail: Core gains `#Error pub enum ModError` with four cases, each holding a path or reason. `Denied`: the grant refuses the path, or the library needs an effect the load site does not grant. `NotFound`: nothing is at the path. `Invalid`: the file is damaged or is not a library. `Unsupported`: another Jet version, ABI or platform built it, or loading is not available here. `load` and `unload` write `ModError!`.
options.technical: Edit Core/mod/mod.jet and the host loader in crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/Mod.rs, which today returns `Result<JetMod, String>`. Each existing text error maps to one case, and the text stays as the reason. E1339 grant refusals are `Denied`; E1338 and E1341 version, ABI and target checks are `Unsupported`. `unload` returns `.Unsupported`. Regenerate CoreModuleExports.rs with the Core surface ledger script.

options.name: `IOError` for path and grant
options.detail: A refused grant is `IOError.PermissionDenied` and a missing file is `IOError.NotFound`, as in `core.files`. A smaller `ModError { Invalid, Unsupported }` covers the artifact. `load` writes `(IOError | ModError)!`. Callers need a catch-all for the other `IOError` cases, which load never returns.
options.technical: Same host mapping as A, split across two types. Grant refusals carry no operating-system code, so their `IOContext` has `os_code: None`.

options.name: `IOError` only
options.detail: Every failure is an `IOError`. Denied is `PermissionDenied`, missing is `NotFound`, damaged is `InvalidInput`. A stale build, a wrong platform and an unsupported host all become `Other`, beside every unrelated I/O failure.
options.technical: No new type. The reason text stays in the context's `cause`.

comparisons.note: Imports fail with `ImportError`, and the subclass `ModuleNotFoundError` separates a missing module from a broken one. https://docs.python.org/3/library/exceptions.html#ModuleNotFoundError
The `libloading` crate has its own error enum for library loading. https://docs.rs/libloading/latest/libloading/enum.Error.html
comparisons.code: let lib = unsafe { libloading::Library::new("score.so") }?; // libloading::Error

recommendation.why: Each failure asks the caller for a different action: fix the grant, skip, replace, or rebuild. One type with four cases says so, and callers need no catch-all.
gains: A plugin host can prompt a rebuild only when one is needed.
Load and unload share one closed failure type.

losses.loss: One more public error type.
losses.mitigation: `IOError` has no case for a stale build or a wrong platform.

whyNot.reason: B splits one call's failures across two types and adds a catch-all for I/O cases load never returns.
C hides a stale build in `Other`, next to unrelated failures, so a rebuild prompt can't be targeted.

recommendation.tradeoff: One small type buys failures a caller can act on.

gains: A plugin host can prompt a rebuild only when one is needed.

losses.mitigation: `IOError` has no case for a stale build or a wrong platform.

decisions.title: Step limit for jet run --interpret
decisions.gist: Should `jet run --interpret` stop programs after 10 million steps, when `jet run` and built binaries have no limit?
decisions.lesson: `jet run --interpret` runs a program in Jet's interpreter instead of compiling it. It stops any program after 10 million steps with error E2202, to catch loops that never end. Real work can need more. Argon2id password hashing at its smallest memory setting (8192 KiB) goes past the limit. So a program works under `jet run` and as a binary but fails in the interpreter.
decisions.story: Lee writes a sign-up handler that hashes passwords with `crypto.password_hash`. It works with `jet run`. She switches to `jet run --interpret` to chase a bug, and the same program stops with E2202.

options.name: No limit for run --interpret
options.detail: The step limit is removed from `jet run --interpret` only. A runaway loop behaves as it does under `jet run`: it keeps running until Ctrl-C. Compile-time evaluation keeps its budget, because a build must always finish. `jet dev` and the REPL keep their current budgets; this ballot does not change them.
options.technical: The run-interpret path gives the MIR evaluator no step cap. The comptime, dev, and REPL budgets stay, and E2202 stays for `jet dev`. Beginner path: nothing to learn, programs just run. Expert path: stop a runaway run with Ctrl-C, as with any binary.

options.name: A time limit
options.detail: `jet run --interpret` stops a program after 60 seconds of running, with E2202. Most real programs, including password hashing at default settings, finish in time. A slower machine or a larger input can still cross the limit.
options.technical: The step counter becomes a clock check. The exact number of seconds is part of this choice. Comptime, dev, and REPL budgets stay.

options.name: Keep 10 million steps
options.detail: No change. The 10-million-step limit and E2202 stay for `jet run --interpret`.
options.technical: No change.

comparisons.note: CPython runs without a step limit; only recursion depth is capped. https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html#sys.setrecursionlimit
comparisons.code: sys.setrecursionlimit(10000)

comparisons.note: Lua runs without a limit by default. A host can opt in to a count hook that stops after N instructions. https://www.lua.org/manual/5.4/manual.html#pdf-debug.sethook
comparisons.code: debug.sethook(function() error("too long") end, "", 10000000)

recommendation.why: `jet run` and built binaries have no step limit, and the E2202 help already says so. Removing it makes the interpreter agree with them. A time limit would make results depend on machine speed.

whyNot.reason: B still fails long real programs, and whether it fails depends on how fast the machine is.
C keeps the interpreter disagreeing with `jet run` on ordinary programs like password hashing.

recommendation.tradeoff: Losing automatic loop stops buys one behavior on every tier.

decisions.title: Let crypto failures pass up from fn run()
decisions.gist: Should a `CryptoError` pass up out of `fn run()` automatically, like `IOError` and `UUIDError` do?
decisions.lesson: In `fn run()`, a failing call passes its error up automatically when a conversion to `Err` exists. The standard library ships one for each type in its error family. `CryptoError` was left out, on the idea that crypto errors might carry secrets. So each crypto call needs local handling, or it fails with E2402. `CryptoError` has five plain cases and carries no secret data.
decisions.story: Ana decrypts a config file in `fn run()`. The compiler stops with E2402, so she adds `?? return`. Later the key is wrong, and her program ends quietly with no report.

options.name: Join the family
options.detail: `Prelude/Errors.jet` gains `impl CryptoError -> Err { return Err("{self}") }` and the same for `FileCryptoError`. A failing crypto call in `fn run()` then passes up and ends the program with exit 1 and a report naming the case, such as `CryptoError.OpenFailed`. Secret types such as `Secret` and `SigningKey` keep their print ban; only the error enums join.
options.technical: CryptoError is a payload-free enum: OpenFailed, VerifyFailed, KeyRejected, Length, Unavailable. FileCryptoError already collapses auth failures to OpenFailed. Both need the same printable registration as other members. The exclusion notes in D-FAIL-CONV2, Errors.jet, and sema Diagnostics.rs are updated. Beginner path: crypto calls just work in `fn run()`. Expert path: handle a case locally with `??`.
options.code:
use core.crypto as crypto

fn run() {
    pw :: crypto.Secret.from_text("hunter2")
    phc :: crypto.password_hash(pw)        // on failure: report, exit 1
    ok :: crypto.password_verify(pw, phc)
    print(ok)
}

options.name: Stay outside
options.detail: No change. `CryptoError` and `FileCryptoError` stay outside the family. A crypto call in `fn run()` without local handling is E2402. `UUIDError` stays in the family.
options.technical: No change. The exclusion stays in D-FAIL-CONV2 and Errors.jet.

comparisons.note: The AEAD error says only that decryption failed, and `?` passes it up like any error. https://docs.rs/aead/latest/aead/struct.Error.html
comparisons.code: let plain = cipher.decrypt(nonce, data.as_ref())?;

comparisons.note: Crypto failures are ordinary `error` values that callers return upward. https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/cipher#AEAD

recommendation.why: `CryptoError` holds no secret, so the reason for leaving it out does not apply. Passing up is not silent: the program stops with a report and exit 1. Today's workaround, `?? return`, is the silent path.

whyNot.reason: B keeps pushing authors toward `?? return`, which hides crypto failures instead of reporting them.

recommendation.tradeoff: A visible error name buys failures that are always reported.

decisions.title: One owner for time.instant()
decisions.gist: Should `time.instant()` return the compiler's time point everywhere, with a separate call for wall-clock nanoseconds?
decisions.lesson: `time.instant()` has two owners today. The Rust compiler returns a compiler-owned time point, so `t + 5min` and `b - a` work. The Jet compiler returns a plain struct, `Instant{unix_ns}`. About 33 Jetpack lines read `.unix_ns` as the wall clock. On the shipped binary that field reads 0, so those lines silently get the wrong time.
decisions.story: Core's login-token check read `time.instant().unix_ns` as the current time. On the shipped binary it was always 0, so token expiry was never enforced. Sam's own server had the same trap.

options.name: Time point everywhere
options.detail: `Instant` is the compiler-owned Time point from D-TYPE2-TIME1 on both compilers. The source `struct Instant{unix_ns}` in Core/time is deleted. A new `time.unix_ns() -[Time]> Int` returns wall-clock Unix nanoseconds, and Jetpack's `.unix_ns` reads move to it. `t + 5min` gives an Instant, `b - a` gives a Duration, and `t.elapsed()` gives a Duration. `t.unix_ns` is a compile error that points to `time.unix_ns()`.
options.technical: Rust sema already records Instant as a Point quantity in the Time family. The Jet compiler drops its source-struct row and mirrors that fact. `time.unix_ns()` reads the existing host wall-clock kernel. Beginner path: `time.unix_ns()` for a timestamp. Expert path: Instant arithmetic for deadlines and measuring.
options.code:
use core.time as time

fn run() {
    t :: time.instant()
    deadline :: t + 5min      // Instant
    took :: t.elapsed()       // Duration
    nonce :: time.unix_ns()   // Int, wall-clock Unix nanoseconds
    print(t.unix_ns)          // compile error: use time.unix_ns()
}

options.name: Plain struct everywhere
options.detail: The Rust compiler drops its time-point treatment and uses the Core/time struct. Core/time adds operator impls for `Instant + Duration`, `Instant - Duration`, and `Instant - Instant`. `t.unix_ns` becomes real wall-clock nanoseconds on every tier.
options.technical: The Point unit fact for Instant is removed from Rust sema. Duration stays a unit. Beginners and experts use the same field read.

options.name: Keep the split
options.detail: The Rust compiler keeps the time point and rejects `.unix_ns` at compile time. The Jet compiler keeps the struct. Code that compiles on one compiler can fail on the other.
options.technical: One new sema check in the Rust compiler. No shared owner.

comparisons.note: `SystemTime` is the wall clock, and `Instant` has no epoch. https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/time/struct.SystemTime.html
comparisons.code: SystemTime::now().duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH)?.as_nanos()

comparisons.note: Go uses one `Time` value that carries both a wall reading and a monotonic reading. https://pkg.go.dev/time#hdr-Monotonic_Clocks
comparisons.code:
start := time.Now()
ns := start.UnixNano()
took := time.Since(start)

recommendation.why: One type, one meaning on every compiler. The checked time point keeps `t + 5min` type-safe. Wall-clock reads become one explicit, real call instead of a field that silently reads 0.

whyNot.reason: B moves Instant out of the checked Time family and makes every operator hand-written.
C keeps two meanings for one name, which is the bug this card found.

recommendation.tradeoff: A small Jetpack migration buys one real, checked Instant.

decisions.title: Run only the tests a change can affect
decisions.gist: How should Jet run only the tests that a code change can affect?
decisions.lesson: Hack and Skip select tests by following the checked call graph from a change. Jet records only module paths today, so function-level reachability must be built first (#3851). Every option keeps full `jet test` available.
decisions.story: Dev edits one helper in a 300,000-line project. She wants the tests that can see that helper, in seconds, not the whole suite.
decisions.inWild: $ bazel test //...   # cached tests are skipped

options.name: Affected first, the rest in the background
options.detail: Selection uses function-level reachability, old plus new reverse edges, and every impl for dynamic calls. Tests whose effects touch FS, Env, Net, Clock, Random, or Process always run unless their inputs are declared. The rest of the suite then runs at idle and is cancelled by the next edit. Status never says 'all pass' while tests were skipped.
options.code:
$ jet test --watch
  change: price.jet (total)
  37 affected tests: ok
  running remaining 4,775 in background...
  full suite: ok (stale for 41s)

options.name: Explicit `--affected` flag
options.detail: Opt-in flag only.
options.code:
$ jet test --affected
  running 37 affected tests of 4,812

comparisons.note: Bazel reruns only tests whose inputs changed. See https://bazel.build/reference/test-encyclopedia. Talk: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J31LlAUtoos at 138:15.
comparisons.code: $ bazel test //...   # cached tests are skipped

recommendation.why: It gives the fast first answer Hack showed is possible, without ever claiming green on a partial run.

whyNot.reason: B hides the speedup behind a flag beginners never find.

recommendation.tradeoff: Watch mode trusts the dependency graph; full runs stay exhaustive.

decisions.title: Which peers the build-speed gate compares against
decisions.gist: Which compilers must Jet beat on build time now, given Jai is in closed beta?
decisions.lesson: The strict gate says Jet must beat every matched peer, and missing evidence counts as a failure. The owner's target is Jai- or Skip-level compile speed. Jai is not publicly available, so a required Jai cell can never pass today.
decisions.story: The compile-speed work (#3852) needs a finish line. A required cell with no obtainable peer keeps the gate open forever.
decisions.inWild: $ zig build --watch -fincremental

options.name: Public peers now, Jai when obtainable
options.detail: Build-time cells for clean, no-op, body-edit, and signature-edit builds against Rust, Go, Zig, and C now. Jai becomes a required peer the day a build is obtainable; until then its cell is recorded as pending, not passed.
options.code:
peers: rust, go, zig, c
pending: jai   # required once a licensed build exists

options.name: Require Jai now
options.detail: Jai is required now; the cell fails until evidence exists.
options.code: peers: rust, go, zig, c, jai   # jai: unavailable = fail

comparisons.note: Zig's decl-granular incremental compiler is the closest public design to beat. See https://ziglang.org/news/.
comparisons.code: $ zig build --watch -fincremental

recommendation.why: A finish line must be reachable. Zig incremental is public, fast, and closest in design, and Jai joins the moment it can be measured.

whyNot.reason: B makes the gate impossible to close for reasons outside Jet's control.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jai waits for access; public peers set the bar now.

decisions.title: Park item-level incremental compilation behind the cold-speed milestones
decisions.situation: Incremental compilation means recompiling only the parts of a program that changed, down to single functions and declarations. On 2026-10-17 the owner set a cold-compile speed target and said incremental compilation is not on that path. One ready card still plans item-level reuse, and the new compiler session design relies only on whole-package reuse. This vote confirms where that card stands. We recommend parking it until the cold-speed milestones are met, with whole-package reuse as the session's only required reuse.
decisions.gist: Should the item-level incremental compilation card wait until the cold-speed milestones are met, as the owner's 2026-10-17 direction implies?
decisions.lesson: Jet can reuse work at two sizes. Package reuse skips a whole unchanged package, using records already ratified. Item reuse goes further and rechecks only the functions and declarations an edit touches, which needs a dependency graph per item. The owner said cold speed comes first and incremental is not on that path. The card for item reuse is still marked ready to implement.
decisions.story: A lead picking the next card sees #3852, item-level reuse, marked ready. The owner's speed plan says incremental compilation is not on the path, and the session design says package records are enough. Without a ruling, an agent could spend weeks on item reuse while cold-speed work waits.
decisions.detail:
Sources: owner direction 2026-10-17 12:10 on card #5043 (500K lines per second cold; incremental is not required and not on the path). Also SPEED-500K.md line 5, which drops the incremental section of SPEED-PLAN.md. And compiler-session-protocol-2026-10-17.md section 2.2 and finding F7.

Ratified: D-INCR-UNIT1=A, amended on 2026-09-30 so the package is the unit of reuse and item reuse inside a rechecked package is optional. D-LSP1=C chose one demand-driven compiler service.

Under A, #3852 gets blockedBy #5043 with a log line naming this decision. It returns to ready when the cold-speed ladder's last milestone is met or the owner unparks it. When it resumes, it must pass the session's warm-equals-cold check (slate S1 acceptance 2): a re-check after an edit prints the same bytes as a fresh process.

Under C, D-INCR-UNIT1 and D-LSP1 would be amended to package-only reuse for good. Editor answers would then recheck a whole package per edit.

options.name: Park it behind the cold-speed milestones
options.detail: Item-level reuse waits until the cold-speed ladder is done or the owner unparks it. The compiler session ships with package reuse only. When item reuse resumes, it must produce byte-identical results to a fresh compile.
options.code:
# Tower after A
#3852 item-level reuse      blocked by #5043 (cold-speed ladder)
# session reuse today: whole unchanged packages
$ jet check   # edit in one package: that package is rechecked

options.name: Keep it ready, in parallel
options.detail: Item reuse stays ready and may be built now beside the cold-speed work. Editors get finer reuse sooner, but agents and review time split between two speed programs.
options.code:
#3852 item-level reuse      ready to implement
# runs beside the cold-speed milestones

options.name: Retire item-level reuse
options.detail: Close #3852 and make package reuse the permanent design, amending the two ratified incremental and editor-engine decisions. Simplest, but every edit then rechecks a whole package forever.
options.code:
#3852 closed: retired by vote
# D-INCR-UNIT1 and D-LSP1 amended: package is the only reuse unit

comparisons.note: Zig made fast cold builds first and added incremental compilation as an opt-in mode later.
comparisons.code: zig build -fincremental --watch

comparisons.note: Go caches whole packages and relies on fast cold compiles for the rest.
comparisons.code: go build ./...

recommendation.why: It follows the owner's 2026-10-17 direction, keeps the card's plan for later, and keeps agents on the cold-speed critical path.
recommendation.tradeoff: Editors recheck a whole package per edit until item reuse resumes; fast cold compiles make that cheap.

decisions.title: jet try runs affected tests in its overlay
decisions.gist: Should `jet try` also run the affected tests inside its overlay and return one verdict an agent can act on?
decisions.lesson: `jet try` applies proposed edits in an overlay, re-checks them, and rolls back by default. Skip's Skipper loop goes further: analysis, reachability, then the affected tests, in under a second. Every option keeps rollback as the default.
decisions.story: An AI agent proposes a fix. It needs one answer: does it compile, what did it touch, and do the reachable tests pass, before it tries again.
decisions.inWild: diff -> incremental type check -> reachability -> affected tests -> self-correct

options.name: `jet try` runs affected tests
options.detail: After a clean re-verdict, `jet try` runs the tests reachable from the change inside the overlay and reports them in the same verdict. `--no-tests` skips them. Skipped tests are reported as stale, never as passed.
options.code:
$ jet try fix.json --json
{"verdict":"tests-failed",
 "diagnostics":[],
 "impact":["pricing.total","cart.checkout"],
 "tests":{"selected":37,"failed":1,"stale":4775},
 "rolled_back":true}

options.name: Separate overlay test command
options.detail: Tests run through a second command that reuses the overlay.
options.code:
$ jet try fix.json --json
$ jet test --affected --overlay fix.json --json

comparisons.note: Talk https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J31LlAUtoos at 131:50-139:45 describes diff -> incremental check -> reachability -> affected tests.
comparisons.code: diff -> incremental type check -> reachability -> affected tests -> self-correct

recommendation.why: The agent loop needs one fast, complete answer per attempt. Folding affected tests into `jet try` gives that without a second protocol.

whyNot.reason: B splits one loop step into two commands and two schemas.

recommendation.tradeoff: Longer single calls buy a complete verdict per step.

decisions.title: Where per-function code metrics appear on the command line
decisions.gist: Which command should print per-function code metrics such as size, nesting, allocations, and call locality?
decisions.lesson: A code metric is a number about one function, such as its size or how deeply its loops nest. Jet prints one number today: a control-flow score from `jet lint --complexity`. Card #3867 adds about a dozen metrics from the checked program. A visual map will read the same numbers. This ballot picks the command that prints them.
decisions.story: Mara inherits a 40,000-line Jet service. She wants to know which functions are large, deeply nested, or allocate in hot paths before she touches anything. Today she can only see one complexity score, one file at a time.
decisions.inWild:

# https://github.com/terryyin/lizard
$ lizard src/
  NLOC    CCN   token  PARAM  length  location
     10      3     45      1      11 classify@1-11@src/probe.c
     12      4     70      1      12 collect@14-25@src/probe.c
decisions.detail: D-CLI-ONE1 made each ledger question one `jet inspect` view that accepts a file, a package, `--live PID`, or `--replay ARTIFACT`. Metrics are a new question. The mode meanings for global state and frees are decided separately in D-CODEMAP-MEANING1.

options.name: A new inspect view: jet inspect metrics
options.detail: Add one view beside types, rights, structure, and the rest. It prints one row per function and supports `--json`. `jet lint --complexity` keeps its budget check but reads the same nesting numbers.
options.technical: Grammar: `jet inspect metrics [TARGET] [--live PID | --replay ARTIFACT]`, parsed by the existing inspect parser in crates/jet-cli/src/CLI.rs. Rows come from the checked projection. `--live` and `--replay` project the source identity that the process or record already carries. The JSON is the saved snapshot that the visual map can open.

classify    21         3         2           0       0              0
collect     34         1         3           2       1              0
apply        6         0         0           0       0              1

options.name: Extend jet inspect structure
options.detail: Add a metrics section to the existing structure view. No new word is needed. Structure output then mixes architecture rules with measurements.
options.technical: `jet inspect structure [TARGET] --metrics` adds metric rows to the D-STRUCT-PLANE1 projection. Without the flag, structure output is unchanged.

  classify  size 21  branches 3  if-depth 2  allocs 0

options.name: Extend jet lint
options.detail: Add `--metrics` next to `--complexity`. It sits beside the score people already use. Lint reports warnings, and it has no live-process or record scope.
options.technical: `jet lint --metrics FILE [--json]`, parsed with other lint categories. No `--live` or `--replay` scope.

probe.jet:1 fn classify   size 21  branches 3  if-depth 2
probe.jet:14 fn collect   size 34  branches 1  if-depth 3

recommendation.why: Metrics answer a new question. Under D-CLI-ONE1, each question gets one inspect view with the same four scopes.
gains: One word per question, as D-CLI-ONE1 requires.

losses.mitigation: A new question needs its own name; hiding it inside another view makes it harder to find.

whyNot.reason: Structure checks rules. Adding measurements makes its output longer and mixes two questions.
Lint reports warnings, and it cannot read a live process or a record.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet gains one view name so each question keeps one home.

decisions.title: What the global-state and heap-free code-map modes measure in Jet
decisions.gist: Jet has no mutable globals and no manual free. What should the global-read, global-write, and heap-free modes show?
decisions.lesson: Blow's map colours functions by global reads, global writes, and heap frees. Jet has no mutable global variable and no manual free. Jet shares mutable state through `Shared<T>` cells. Memory is released automatically, sometimes through reference counts. The other modes, such as allocations and call locality, ship either way.
decisions.story: Mara hunts a race in a Jet service. In Blow's tool she would colour the map by global writes. She needs the Jet equivalent: which functions write state that other tasks can see.
decisions.inWild:
# Jonathan Blow's visualizer, hovering one procedure with Metric = Global Writes.
# https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PbVHBToltXk at 05:52
record                                   Global Writes: 2, size: 68
/sokoban/src/game/tests.jai:583
decisions.detail: This ballot covers only the three modes without a direct Jet counterpart. Polymorphic copies and macro bloat map to real Jet facts, generic instantiations and checked-versus-written size, and need no choice. D-CODEMAP-CLI1 picks the command.

options.name: Jet counterparts under Jet names
options.detail: Global Reads becomes Shared reads. Global Writes becomes Shared writes. Heap Frees becomes Reference-count updates. Each mode measures real Jet behaviour that matters for races and memory traffic.
options.technical: Shared reads and writes count field reads and writes through a `Shared<T>` handle in the function body, including compound assignment. Reference-count updates count `Mem.Rc` memory events that sema already records (crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/MemoryFacts.rs, MemoryEventKind::RetainRelease). World access through effects stays in `jet inspect rights`.

options.name: Keep the source names; show none in Jet
options.detail: The three modes appear under Blow's names. Every function shows zero, with a note that Jet has no mutable globals or manual frees. This teaches the guarantee but hides Jet's real shared-state writes.
options.technical: Rows carry `global_reads`, `global_writes`, and `heap_frees` as the constant 0 with a fixed explanation string. No new analysis.
options.code:
$ jet inspect metrics app.jet --json
{"fn":"run","global_writes":0,"note":"Jet has no mutable globals"}

options.name: Drop the three modes
options.detail: The map ships without them. It is the smallest change, but it misses the owner's request for every mode and hides shared-state writes.
options.technical: No rows or menu entries for these three modes.
options.code:
$ jet inspect metrics app.jet --json
{"fn":"run","size":40,"allocs":2}

comparisons.note: Blow counts reads and writes of global variables and explicit frees. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PbVHBToltXk at 05:23-06:33
comparisons.code: Metric: Global Reads | Global Writes | Heap Allocations | Heap Frees

recommendation.why: Shared cells are where Jet tasks can race, and reference counts are Jet's automatic release work. Measuring them keeps the purpose of Blow's modes.
gains: Shows which functions write state other tasks can see.
Shows reference-count traffic, a real memory cost.

losses.loss: Mode names differ from Blow's tool.
losses.mitigation: Jet has no global variables or frees, so those names would describe nothing.

whyNot.reason: Every value is zero, so the mode shows nothing and hides real shared writes.
It misses the owner's request and drops a useful race view.

recommendation.tradeoff: The modes use Jet names so they can measure something real.
