decisions.title: Where Jet's source formatter lives after the Rust freeze
decisions.situation: The formatter is the tool behind jet fmt: it rewrites a Jet file into one canonical layout, and editors call it when a user saves. Today it exists only in the Rust compiler, which the owner froze on 2026-10-01. New syntax now lands only in the Jet-written compiler, so the Rust formatter will reject or skip files that use any spelling added after the freeze. The Jet-hosted jet command already refuses jet fmt as not ported yet. You are deciding whether the formatter moves into Jet, and if so whether it is its own package or part of the parser. We recommend a separate JetFormatter package over the Jet parser, proven byte-identical with the Rust formatter on the whole corpus before the Rust copy is deleted.
decisions.gist: Should jet fmt be rewritten in Jet as its own package, folded into the Jet parser, or left as frozen Rust tooling?
decisions.lesson: A formatter reads source text, builds a tree of the program, and prints that tree back in one fixed layout, keeping every comment. It must understand every spelling the language accepts. A parser is the part that builds the tree. A ports the formatter to a new Jet package that reuses the Jet parser. B puts the same port inside the parser package. C keeps the frozen Rust formatter.
decisions.explainer:
Plain words first. Source code is the text a person writes. A parser reads that text and builds a tree: this is a function, this is its body, this is a call. A formatter walks the same tree and prints it again with one fixed layout, so two people never argue about spaces or line breaks.

A formatter must parse a file before it can print it. If the file uses a spelling its parser does not know, it can only refuse the file.

Jet has two compilers right now. The Rust compiler under crates/ came first. The Jet compiler under Compiler/ is written in Jet itself, which is called self-hosting. On 2026-10-01 the owner froze the Rust compiler: it gets only bootstrap fixes, deletions and runtime exports. New language features land only in Compiler/.

A package is one named folder of Jet code with its own dependency list, such as Compiler/JetParser. Byte parity means two tools give exactly the same output bytes for the same input.
decisions.story: Ada writes a script with a spelling the language gained after the freeze. It checks and runs. She saves in her editor, and the format-on-save step does nothing, because the frozen Rust formatter cannot parse that line. When she types jet fmt run.jet, the Jet-hosted jet command answers that fmt is not ported yet.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-04. The Rust formatter is 10,153 lines in crates/jet-parser/src/Formatter: mod.rs 2,683, Expressions.rs 3,393, Items.rs 2,318 and Statements.rs 1,759. Command callers are jet fmt (Source/CmdCompile.rs:9516-9566), jet fix (Source/CmdCompile.rs:5305-5307) and structural merge (Source/CmdStructuralMerge.rs:165). Editor formatting calls it from Source/LSP/Server.rs:1146 and :1454. The package-aware wrapper is crates/jet-driver/src/Formatter.rs:19-50.

jet fmt does more than print the tree. It formats package.jet and typed package sources through the Package model (CmdCompile.rs:9528-9530, :9557-9564). It rewrites retired spellings (:9446-9449, :9553-9555). With --explicit-copies it first runs the full checker and inserts copy marks (:9532-9552). It also has a stdin mode, jet fmt - (:9431-9455).

The Jet compiler has no formatter and no editor server; Compiler/ has no LSP package. Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Commands.jet:436 lists fmt, and Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Front.jet:506 answers every unported command with jet_cli_not_ported (:94), error E2104. Compiler/JetParser keeps comments as lexer tokens and skips them while parsing (Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/State.jet:126-131). A formatter can therefore reattach comments from the token list and its spans.

The parity ledger Docs/research/rust-jet-parity-ledger-2026-09-30.md:137 lists the formatter as gap P3 and asks this question at :316. Compiler policy (owner, 2026-09-30, ledger:6-8) says features that do not gate self-hosting land only in Compiler/. Existing formatter law stays: D-FMTCOLLAPSE1=B, D-BRANCH-FMT1=C, D-FMT-SIMPLIFY1=A and D-ECO12=A for non-Jet files. Codemod and fix edits are a sibling gap, card #3962.

What is the same in every option. The canonical layout does not change, and existing tests/fmt.rs, tests/fmt_project.rs and tests/fmt_round_trip_regressions.rs keep their expected output. Every jet fmt duty above keeps working.

options.name: Port to a separate JetFormatter package
options.detail:
A new package, Compiler/JetFormatter, depends on JetLexer and JetParser and prints their tree. The Jet jet fmt verb calls it and keeps the command duties above. The Rust callers, the editor server, jet fix and structural merge, keep the Rust copy until their own Jet ports land, because the freeze forbids rewiring them.

The port moves module by module: statements, items, then expressions. A gate formats every file under Examples/ and Compiler/ with both formatters and requires identical bytes. The Rust formatter is deleted with its last Rust caller.

The compiler packages do not depend on the formatter, so building the compiler never compiles it.
options.technical:
Compiler/JetFormatter/package.jet deps: jet_foundation, jet_lexer, jet_parser. Public entry: format_source(source: String, options: FormatOptions) -> String FormatError!, with FormatOptions{simplify: Bool} matching crates/jet-parser FormatOptions. Comments come from the lexer token list by span. JetCli gains the fmt verb, replacing jet_cli_not_ported; package.jet formatting, retired-spelling rewrites and --explicit-copies live in that verb, which may call the checker, so JetFormatter itself stays checker-free.

The parity gate reuses the cases in tests/fmt*.rs and adds a whole-corpus byte diff over files the Rust parser accepts. A file both formatters reject must be rejected by both. A file only the Jet parser accepts is checked for idempotence and kept comments instead.

options.name: Port into the JetParser package
options.detail:
The same port lands inside Compiler/JetParser as Source/Formatter. The tree and the printer sit side by side, so a parser change and its printing change land in one package.

The parity gate and the cutover are the same as A. The cost is that the parser package grows by about ten thousand lines. Every compiler build, and the stage-zero bootstrap, then compiles and checks the formatter too, although the compiler never calls it.
options.technical: Compiler/JetParser/Source/Formatter/{Items,Statements,Expressions}.jet; JetParser exports format_source. No new package. Compiler build time and memory grow with the parser package, which every compiler package depends on.

options.name: Keep the frozen Rust formatter
options.detail:
The Rust formatter stays as host tooling, and the Jet jet command hands jet fmt to it. Nothing is ported.

Because the Rust compiler is frozen, its parser never learns new syntax. A file that uses any later spelling cannot be formatted: jet fmt reports a parse error and editors leave the file unchanged. Each new spelling then needs a Rust exception to the freeze, or stays unformattable.
options.technical: JetCli forwards fmt argv to the Rust binary. Formatter fixes require Rust parser and formatter changes, which the 2026-10-01 freeze allows only as stage-zero blockers.

comparisons.note: gofmt is written in Go and shares the standard go/parser and go/printer packages, so new syntax reaches the formatter with the parser.

// format.Source(src) parses with go/parser and prints with go/printer.

comparisons.code:

// zig fmt main.zig   (std.zig.Ast.parse, then std/zig/render.zig)

recommendation.why: Only a Jet formatter can follow syntax that now lands only in Compiler/. A separate package keeps it out of every compiler build, and the byte-parity gate proves the port changes no layout before the Rust copy goes.
gains: jet fmt works on every spelling the Jet compiler accepts, and editor formatting and jet fix follow as they move to Jet.
The compiler and its bootstrap never compile formatter code.
The Rust formatter is deleted after a proven cutover, with its last Rust caller.

losses.loss: The port is larger than the 10,153 printer lines, because the jet fmt duties come with it. Until the editor server is ported, format-on-save still uses the frozen Rust formatter.
losses.mitigation: The port moves module by module behind the corpus byte gate. An editor can run jet fmt - as its format command, which reaches the Jet formatter before the editor server moves.

decisions.title: How a #SingleUse duty follows a value into a container
decisions.gist: When a #SingleUse value goes into a list or optional, who owes its duty?
decisions.lesson: A #SingleUse value must be used exactly once, like a lock that must be released. Today the duty vanishes when the value goes into a list or an optional. Jet needs one rule for every container. Whichever option wins, the leak closes and every tier gives the same verdict.
decisions.story: Maya keeps a pool of database leases in a list. At shutdown she forgets to release them. Jet says nothing today, so the leases stay open until the process dies. A single forgotten lease would have been E0140.
decisions.inWild:
-- Linear Haskell, POPL 2018, section 6.1
data List (p :: Multiplicity) (a :: Type p) :: Type p
  = [] | a : (List p a)
-- https://simon.peytonjones.org/linear-haskell/

options.name: The container inherits the duty
options.detail: Any value whose type contains a #SingleUse value (a list, optional, result, map, tuple, or user struct) owes the same duty. Dropping it is E0140 or E0141. Consuming it means consuming each element, for example by mapping each lease to a function that takes it with ^.
options.technical: Sema computes a type's single-use fact structurally: a type is single-use if any component type is. The existing E0140-E0143 checks then apply unchanged. Move-only follows from single-use.
options.code:
leases :: [Lease{name: "a"}, Lease{name: "b"}]
names :: leases.map(l -> release(^l))

held :: maybe_lease(1)
// E0140: `held` still owes `consume` (it may hold a Lease)

options.name: Containers may not hold #SingleUse values
options.detail: A #SingleUse value may live only in a named local, a parameter, or a field of another #SingleUse struct. Putting it in a list, optional, result, or map is a new error.
options.technical: Sema rejects instantiating any generic type argument with a single-use type, except user structs that are themselves #SingleUse.
options.code:
leases :: [Lease{name: "a"}]
// new error: a #SingleUse value can't be stored in a List

options.name: Move the duty onto parameters
options.detail: Replace type-level #SingleUse with a parameter marker that promises single use, as Linear Haskell does. Types no longer carry duties; functions do.
options.technical: Retires D-LIN1's type marker and E0140-E0143 as written; adds a linear parameter mode and multiplicity rules for generics.
options.code: fn release(l: once Lease) -> String { l.name }

comparisons.note: Section 6.1 compares linearity on arrows with linearity on types and shows that the type-based form must make containers inherit linearity. https://simon.peytonjones.org/linear-haskell/
comparisons.code: data List (p :: Multiplicity) (a :: Type p) :: Type p = [] | a : (List p a)

recommendation.why: A keeps the type-level promise that makes locks and task handles safe by default. Wrapping a lease can no longer hide it, and generic code stays unchanged.

whyNot.reason: B blocks real needs like a pool of leases or an optional handle.
C removes the default safety of #SingleUse types and rewrites the ratified D-LIN1.

recommendation.tradeoff: Containers of leases become move-only so the use-once promise survives wrapping.

surface.gist: When a #SingleUse value goes into a list or optional, who owes its duty?
surface.lesson: A #SingleUse value must be used exactly once, like a lock that must be released. Today the duty vanishes when the value goes into a list or an optional. Jet needs one rule for every container. Whichever option wins, the leak closes and every tier gives the same verdict.

current.note: A dropped list of leases runs with no error. A dropped single lease is E0140.

wild.code:
-- the paper's list for a linear-by-type system
data List (p :: Multiplicity) (a :: Type p) :: Type p
  = [] | a : (List p a)
-- the list's linearity follows its elements

options.name: The container inherits the duty
options.gist: A list, optional, or struct holding a lease owes the lease's duty.
gains: Closes the leak for every container at once.
Generic code like map keeps working unchanged.
Matches the rule the Linear Haskell paper gives.
losses: A container holding a lease becomes move-only too.

proposed.code:

held :: maybe_lease(1)
// E0140: `held` still owes `consume` (it may hold a Lease)

options.name: Containers may not hold #SingleUse values
options.gist: Storing a lease in a list or optional is an error.
gains: The rule is short to state.
No container ever becomes move-only.
losses: A pool of leases needs a hand-written holder type.

options.name: Move the duty onto parameters
options.gist: Drop #SingleUse on types; mark parameters that must use a value once.
gains: Containers never need special rules.
This is Linear Haskell's own design.
losses: A Lock type no longer carries its duty by itself.
Every #SingleUse example and D-LIN1 must be rewritten.

recommendation.why: A keeps the type-level promise that makes locks and task handles safe by default. Wrapping a lease can no longer hide it, and generic code stays unchanged.
gains: One rule covers every container and every tier.

losses.loss: A container holding a lease becomes move-only too.
losses.mitigation: Copying the container would copy the lease, and then the lease could be used twice.

whyNot.reason: B blocks real needs like a pool of leases or an optional handle.
C removes the default safety of #SingleUse types and rewrites the ratified D-LIN1.

recommendation.tradeoff: Containers of leases become move-only so the use-once promise survives wrapping.

decisions.title: Whether earlier checks count when checking a later dispatch table
decisions.gist: Should each dispatch table be a complete unit, with a hint to fuse an earlier check on the same value?
decisions.lesson: After `if t == .Warm -> return …`, a later table on `t` can never see `.Warm`. Jet must decide whether the table still names every variant. Owner guidance: tables should be complete units, and a lone earlier check should usually be fused into the table. Lint L0514 already suggests one table for three or more adjacent checks.
decisions.story: Sam handles the warm case first with an early return, then writes a table for the rest. Jet makes him add a `.Warm` arm that never runs, and never suggests the simpler single table.
decisions.detail: Revised 2026-09-30 after the owner's question: tables should be complete units; an early check on the same subject is usually fused into the table unless other logic separates them. The former recommendation (earlier checks count) is now option B. Under A, L0514 (same_subject_dispatch, card #2395) also fires on one more shape. An early single-variant check is followed by a table on the same subject. Nothing between them reads or writes that subject.

options.name: Complete tables, with a fuse hint
options.detail: Coverage stays per table: every table names every variant, whatever happened above it. L0514 gains one more shape. A single-variant early check followed directly by a table on the same subject suggests one table. The fix moves the early branch into the table as its arm.
options.technical: Extend the L0514 detector to a one-guard-plus-table shape; quiet when statements between them touch the subject or have side effects. Structured edit graded like the existing L0514 fix. UI snapshot for the new shape.

options.name: Earlier checks count
options.detail: Coverage checking starts from the cases that can still reach the table. An arm for a case already ruled out gets a new warning, and omitting it is accepted. A variant added later still errors.
options.technical: FlowFacts records enum-variant exclusions like optional narrowing; the coverage matrix starts from the remaining variants.

comparisons.note: Lower Your Guards section 4.1 flags a case made redundant by an earlier match. https://simon.peytonjones.org/lower-your-guards/
comparisons.code:
f True = 1
f x = case x of { False -> 2; True -> 3 }   -- True arm redundant

comparisons.note: Narrowing after an early return is a core, widely used feature. https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html
comparisons.code: if (t === "warm") return …; switch (t) { … }

recommendation.why: Complete tables keep every variant's handling in one place, as the owner asked. The fuse hint removes the dead arm the right way: by merging the early check into the table.

whyNot.reason: B splits one variant's handling across two places and makes tables incomplete on their own.

recommendation.tradeoff: Tables stay whole, and the lint nudges authors to merge instead of relying on facts from above.

decisions.title: Whether jet dev runs a program with type errors in code that has not run yet
decisions.gist: Should jet dev run a program whose type errors sit only in code that has not run yet?
decisions.lesson: GHC can defer type errors: the program runs, and a bad spot stops with its error only if reached. Jet refuses to run any program with a type error. `#Todo` already stops at run time with the expected type. Jet must decide whether jet dev treats type errors the same way. jet build and jet test stay strict either way.
decisions.story: Priya renames a field across a large program. Half the files are updated. She wants to run the finished half to check it, but one leftover error in an unused function stops everything.
decisions.inWild:
-- Equality proofs and deferred type errors, ICFP 2012: https://simon.peytonjones.org/equality-proofs/
$ ghci -fdefer-type-errors
ghci> fst foo
True
decisions.detail: Deferral changes which programs a command accepts, not what any feature means, so the one-meaning-across-tiers law (I9) still holds for programs that run. jet check, jet run, jet build, and jet test keep rejecting any type error under every option.

options.name: jet dev defers; everything else stays strict
options.detail: jet dev prints every diagnostic first, then starts the program. Each item with a type error is replaced by a stop that reports the original error (code and span) if execution reaches it, in the same shape as the #Todo stop E3011. jet run, build, test, and check are unchanged.
options.technical: Sema marks items with unresolved errors; lowering replaces their bodies with a shared Prelude stop carrying the diagnostic. Only the jet dev host enables it.
options.code:
$ jet dev
Error [E0113]: … `broken` returns String
Deferred: 1 type error; the program stops if it reaches it.
42

options.name: Every command stays strict
options.detail: No change: any type error prevents the program from starting.
options.technical: No change.
options.code:
$ jet dev
Error [E0113]: … `broken` returns String

options.name: Opt-in flag
options.detail: A `--defer-errors` flag on jet dev and jet run enables the same behavior as A. Without the flag, both stay strict.
options.technical: Same mechanism as A, gated by a CLI flag registered in the command table.
options.code: $ jet dev --defer-errors

comparisons.note: -fdefer-type-errors turns type errors into warnings plus run-time failures at the exact spot, with no cost for correct code. https://simon.peytonjones.org/equality-proofs/
comparisons.code: ghc -fdefer-type-errors Main.hs

recommendation.why: A helps the edit loop by default and keeps every shipped or tested build strict. The stop reuses the #Todo format, so there is nothing new to learn.

whyNot.reason: B keeps the whole program hostage to one unfinished function.
C hides the help behind a flag that beginners will not know exists.

recommendation.tradeoff: The dev loop tolerates known errors so work continues; everything that ships stays strict.

decisions.title: Where automatic inlining lives in Jet's optimizer
decisions.gist: Should Jet's shared optimizer inline small functions automatically, for every tier?
decisions.lesson: Inlining replaces a call with the called function's body. GHC calls it its most important optimization. Today Jet expands only `#Inline(Always)`; jet run uses Cranelift without optimization, and AOT relies on rustc. Jet must choose where automatic inlining lives. Any change must beat the plain program in paired performance cells.
decisions.story: Theo splits a hot loop into small helper functions to make it readable. On jet run the program slows down, so he is tempted to paste the helpers back in.
decisions.inWild:
-- Hollenbeck, Inlining in GHC (PhD thesis, 2025): https://simon.peytonjones.org/hollenbeck-inlining/
area w h = w * h   -- inlined without a pragma
decisions.detail:
Evidence: card #2892's closing notes say the shared MIR optimizer performs checked expansion only for #Inline(Always), and the JIT uses Cranelift opt_level=none; the timing proof is deferred to #2919. Sources: Hollenbeck thesis (26% mean speedup from tuned thresholds; about 10% from profile-guided hints), Compiling without Continuations (PLDI 2017) and the 2025 join-points keynote.

Compile cost (owner question 2026-09-30): checking is untouched, because inlining runs after sema on MIR. The helper is checked and lowered once. Each caller that receives a copy is optimized and turned into machine code with that copy inside. So the cost grows with copied size; it is not a link step.

Caching keys each caller's optimized result on its own body plus the bodies it copied. An unchanged program reuses everything. Editing a copied helper re-optimizes only the callers that hold its copy.

options.name: One automatic inliner for every tier
options.detail: The shared MIR optimizer inlines functions used once and functions under a size limit, before any back end. Recursive functions are never unrolled. Limits are tuned on the gauntlet corpus, not by hand, and each choice is listed by jet inspect decisions. Every change ships with paired performance cells against the plain program.
options.technical: Occurrence analysis in MIR (single-use and small-body rules, loop breakers for recursion), reusing the #Inline(Always) expansion machinery. The incremental key for a caller's optimized MIR includes the content hashes of the bodies inlined into it, so a helper edit invalidates exactly those callers. Sema facts and the #3852 check graph are unaffected. Measure join-point block duplication in MIR at the same time.

options.name: Leave it to the back ends
options.detail: Keep today's behavior. #Inline(Always) is the only inlining in the shared optimizer; AOT relies on rustc; jet run and the interpreter do not inline.
options.technical: No change.
options.code:
#Inline(Always)
fn area(w: Int, h: Int) -> Int { w * h }

options.name: Inline hot paths in the JIT only
options.detail: jet run records which call chains are hot and recompiles them with the callee inlined. AOT and the interpreter are unchanged.
options.technical: Tier-up profiling in the JIT host feeds an inlining pass on hot functions only.
options.code: $ jet run   // hot chains inlined after warm-up

comparisons.note: Automatic inlining with INLINE as an optional hint; thesis evidence on tuning: https://simon.peytonjones.org/hollenbeck-inlining/
comparisons.code: {-# INLINE area #-}   -- optional

recommendation.why: One optimizer that every tier shares keeps performance behavior consistent and measurable, and jet run is the default path most programs take.

whyNot.reason: B leaves the default jet run path paying a call for every small helper.
C helps only long JIT runs and makes the tiers optimize differently.

recommendation.tradeoff: Builds do a little more work so every tier runs small helpers without a call.

Any change must beat the plain program in paired performance cells.

current.note: On jet run, `area` stays a real call inside the loop.

wild.note: GHC inlines small and single-use functions without pragmas. A 2025 thesis measured 26% mean speedup from better inlining thresholds.
wild.code:
area :: Int -> Int -> Int
area w h = w * h       -- small: inlined at each call

total rs = sum [area w h | (w, h) <- rs]
-- no INLINE pragma needed

options.name: One automatic inliner for every tier
options.gist: The shared optimizer inlines single-use and small functions everywhere.
gains: jet run, the interpreter, and AOT all benefit.
Thresholds are tuned on the gauntlet corpus.
jet inspect decisions shows each choice.
losses: Editing a copied helper rebuilds the callers that hold its copy.

options.name: Leave it to the back ends
options.gist: Keep #Inline(Always) only; rustc inlines AOT code.
gains: No new optimizer work.
Compile time stays as it is.
losses: jet run and the interpreter never inline automatically.

options.name: Inline hot paths in the JIT only
options.gist: jet run measures hot call chains and inlines them while running.
gains: Spends effort only where time goes.
losses: Short runs and the interpreter never benefit.
AOT and jet run make different choices.

proposed.code:
$ jet run
// after warm-up, the JIT inlines area into total

recommendation.why: One optimizer that every tier shares keeps performance behavior consistent and measurable, and jet run is the default path most programs take.
gains: Small helper functions stop costing a call on every tier.

losses.loss: Editing a copied helper rebuilds the callers that hold its copy.
losses.mitigation: Each caller's machine code contains the helper's body. Only small bodies are copied, and unchanged callers come from cache.

whyNot.reason: B leaves the default jet run path paying a call for every small helper.
C helps only long JIT runs and makes the tiers optimize differently.

recommendation.tradeoff: Builds do a little more work so every tier runs small helpers without a call.

decisions.title: How Jet improves where errors point
decisions.gist: How should Jet make its first error point at the real mistake more often?
decisions.lesson: When facts disagree, a checker often blames the last place it looked. Studies found GHC pointed at the true mistake 48% to 68% of the time; a ranking that weighed every clue reached 88% to 89%. Required signatures keep Jet's errors close, but inferred failures and effects add distance. Jet must pick how to improve blame.
decisions.story: Kofi, new to Jet, leaves a parameter without a type. He gets three errors about variants and missing names, fixes the wrong one, and makes things worse.
decisions.inWild:
-- Diagnosing Type Errors with Class, PLDI 2015: https://simon.peytonjones.org/diagnosing-type-errors/
fac n = if n == 0 then 1 else n * fac (n == 1)
decisions.detail:
Revised 2026-09-30 after the owner asked for a SHErrLoc-like system inside sema without duplicates. Sema already records provenance for effect rows (RightsProvenance in crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/Effects.rs) and failure calls (FailureCallProvenance in CheckerInfer/fallible.rs). Required signatures keep most checks local, so few inference points need new provenance: local bindings, lambdas, literals, inferred failure unions and effects (#3418).

The corpus covers type, effect, failure, and authority errors. For authority and effect denials, the Fix names the single smallest allow edit (SHErrLoc's missing-assumption idea). Card #3968 is the first concrete fix.

options.name: Blame ranking built into sema
options.detail: Each fact sema derives keeps the span that produced it. When a check fails, sema gathers the conflicting facts and the facts that agree with them. It then ranks each source by how many conflicts it explains and how many agreeing facts it would break. The top source becomes the diagnostic's primary span, and the others become notes. A corpus of seeded mistakes measures first-error accuracy and gates each change.
options.technical: Provenance fields on inferred facts in sema; a ranking step invoked only on the error path, sharing sema's own facts. Budgeted per error so jet check time on failing files stays bounded. Harness over tests/blame compares the primary span with the labeled mistake. Command name illustrative.
options.code:
// Error: parameter `x` needs a type
//   likely cause: `x` (line 1)

options.name: Build a separate ranking engine
options.detail: Translate sema's facts into a separate constraint graph and rank causes there, as the SHErrLoc tool does.
options.technical: A second constraint solver beside sema; runs when a check fails.
options.code: most likely cause: `n == 1` (line 2)

options.name: Measure, then fix cases one by one
options.detail: Build the same corpus and fix the most frequent misses one at a time with hand-written rules and UI snapshots.
options.technical: Harness only; no ranking step.
options.code: first error at the seeded mistake: 81% (412/508)

comparisons.note: Holistic localization reached 88-89% accuracy versus 48-68% for GHC; median analysis time 3.3 s. https://simon.peytonjones.org/sherrloc/
comparisons.code: sherrloc program.con

recommendation.why: Building the ranking into sema gives SHErrLoc-style blame without a second checker, and it only runs when a check has already failed. The corpus proves it helps.

whyNot.reason: B keeps a second solver beside sema, and it can drift out of step.
C needs a hand-written rule for every miss and never helps unseen mistakes.

recommendation.tradeoff: Sema records a little more about each fact so that failed checks can explain themselves.

decisions.title: A pre-1.0 audit for rules that reject reasonable programs
decisions.gist: Before 1.0, should Jet audit for rules that reject reasonable programs only to avoid a rare ambiguity?
decisions.lesson: Haskell's designers named the monomorphism restriction as a lasting mistake. It rejects or changes reasonable programs to avoid a rare ambiguity, and beginners hit it without knowing why. Jet will freeze its language at 1.0. A focused audit now would find such traps while removing them is still cheap.
decisions.story: A newcomer writes a function the obvious way and is told it breaks a rule they have never heard of. The rule exists to avoid a case they will never write.
decisions.inWild:
-- A History of Haskell: Being Lazy with Class, HOPL III, section 6.2: https://simon.peytonjones.org/history-of-haskell/
plus = (+)
decisions.detail: Under A, the audit walks every error rule and asks whether it rejects a program whose meaning is clear. Each hit becomes a defect card or a ballot. The #Todo example is observed on a dirty-tree build and is already tracked by #3065; it illustrates the kind of rule, not the audit's findings.

options.name: One trap audit before the 1.0 freeze
options.detail: Before 1.0, audit each error rule for programs the user clearly meant but Jet rejects. For each hit, relax the rule or make the Fix show the working spelling.
options.technical: Audit over the diagnostics registry with a minimal program per rule; results feed defect cards and ballots.
options.code: rule -> meant program -> relax rule or improve Fix

options.name: Rely on normal defect reports
options.detail: No audit; traps are fixed when reported.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: (no change)

comparisons.note: The authors list the monomorphism restriction and seq's effect on parametricity among their real compromises. https://simon.peytonjones.org/history-of-haskell/
comparisons.code: plus = (+)

recommendation.why: Traps are cheapest to remove before the language freezes, and experts rarely report rules they have learned to dodge.

whyNot.reason: B leaves in place exactly the traps experts have learned to avoid.

recommendation.tradeoff: One audit pass now in exchange for a friendlier frozen language.

decisions.title: When a syntax ballot includes a small study with real users
decisions.gist: Should high-impact syntax ballots include a small study with real users before ratification?
decisions.lesson: Ballots today compare options by argument and by AI readers. Champagne Prototyping (2004) got real user data cheaply. It used one sharp question, a few credible users, a realistic task, and a structured review. A 2020 study measured workload with a standard questionnaire. Jet must decide when user evidence belongs in a ballot.
decisions.story: Two spellings for a common construct look equally good on paper. A one-hour session with four developers shows that one of them is misread by half of them.
decisions.inWild:
Champagne Prototyping, VL/HCC 2004: https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/~afb21/publications/VLHCC04.pdf
Elastic sheet-defined functions, JFP 2020 (20 participants, NASA-TLX): https://simon.peytonjones.org/elastic-sdfs/
decisions.detail: Under A, a study uses the ballot's own same-program options as tasks, records completion, errors, and a NASA-TLX workload score, and quotes participants anonymously. The owner still decides; the study is evidence, not a vote.

options.name: Owner marks which ballots get a study
options.detail: The owner flags a ballot for study. An agent prepares a scripted scenario from the ballot's options; the owner or a helper runs it with a few people and records results in the ballot before ratification.
options.technical: A `study` tag on the decision plus a results block in its long form; no Tower schema change is required to start.
options.code: ballot D-EXAMPLE1 [study] -> scenario study -> results in ballot -> ratify

options.name: Every syntax ballot gets a study
options.detail: Any ballot that touches Syntax.rs requires a recorded study.
options.technical: Tower refuses --ready on a syntax ballot without study results.
options.code: syntax ballot -> study -> ratify

options.name: No study step
options.detail: Keep today's process.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: (no change)

comparisons.note: Cheap early evaluation on the real product with a mocked feature. https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/~afb21/publications/VLHCC04.pdf
comparisons.code: crisp question -> few credible users -> scenario -> coded review

comparisons.note: Counterbalanced 20-person study; lower workload and roughly half the task time for the new design. https://simon.peytonjones.org/elastic-sdfs/
comparisons.code: NASA-TLX: 37.5 vs 52.3 (lower is better)

recommendation.why: A spends study effort only where the owner judges the stakes high, so evidence arrives where it matters without slowing every ballot.

whyNot.reason: B slows every small spelling choice for little gain.
C keeps the highest-stakes choices on designer opinion alone.

recommendation.tradeoff: A few important ballots take longer so that their answers rest on evidence.

decisions.title: Which dependencies may run #Unsafe code
decisions.gist: Should a package decide which of its dependencies may run #Unsafe code?
decisions.lesson: #Unsafe marks audited code the compiler cannot prove safe, such as raw memory access. A mistake there can corrupt memory. Your package.jet `policy` limits #Unsafe in your own code only. For dependencies you can fence named ones with `contain`, or all of them with `harden`. Nothing tells you when a dependency starts using #Unsafe.
decisions.story: Ana maintains a web app. Its JSON dependency adds a fast path with #Unsafe in a minor update. Nothing in the app's policy changes, and nobody notices until an audit months later.
decisions.inWild:
-- Safe Haskell, Haskell 2012: https://simon.peytonjones.org/safe-haskell/
$ ghc -fpackage-trust -trust bytestring Server.hs
-- Jet terms: the app's package.jet plays the role of the -trust list.
decisions.detail:
Today: policy.unsafe checks only root-package gates; dependency modules are skipped (crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/UnsafeObligations.rs:87-104). A defect found in review makes a path dependency inside the project folder count as root code (card #3977); A needs that fixed first. D-MEM-GUARANTEE1 already offers `contain: [deps]` and `harden: true` as run-time fences; targets without an OS get no fence.

Identity and updates: each list entry names a dependency anywhere in the resolved graph, including dependencies of dependencies. The lock already records each package's version, source, and fingerprint (crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Lock.rs:30-45). A adds a fingerprint of its #Unsafe gates. If an update changes that fingerprint, jet check fails until the update is accepted and the lock is rewritten.

Scope: "uses #Unsafe" means any #Unsafe gate in the dependency's compiled modules, not only reachable ones. A dependency without Jet source, such as a prebuilt, native, or foreign package, counts as using #Unsafe unless its metadata records its gates. When the fact is missing, the check fails closed. Gate facts do not carry package identity yet, so A adds it.

Authority: the root package's author owns the list in package.jet; an org policy can still refuse gates (D-ONCE-GATE1). A library's list never grants trust to its consumers. Listing a dependency does not let the app call its `#Unsafe fn` without an enclosing #Unsafe; D-UNSAFE2 still applies. `jet inspect gates` and `jet inspect rights` (D-CLI-ONE1) show gates and the list; the older `inspect guarantees` name is retired.

The E2960 text in option A is illustrative. The registered E2960 row (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet) gains typed holes for the dependency name and version, with a new UI snapshot.

options.name: List the dependencies trusted with #Unsafe
options.detail: A new policy field lists the dependencies allowed to use #Unsafe. If any other dependency has an #Unsafe gate, jet check and jet build fail with the dependency, version, gate, and file and line. The lock pins each approved dependency's gates, so an update that changes them needs a fresh approval.
options.technical: Adds package identity to unsafe gate facts; records per-dependency version, digest, and gate fingerprint in the lock; policy check in sema after module-to-package attribution (card #3977). Amends D-TEAMPOLICY1's field list and the policy parser.
options.code:
policy: .{
    unsafe: .Deny,
    unsafe_deps: .List(["sqlite"])
}

$ jet build
Error [E2960]: dependency `json` 2.1 uses #Unsafe (json/src/fast.jet:12)
 Fix: add "json" to policy.unsafe_deps, or keep json at 2.0

$ jet inspect gates   // lists each dependency's #Unsafe gates

options.name: Keep today's rules
options.detail: No change: `deps` allows whole dependencies, `contain` fences named ones, and `harden` fences all of them at run time.
options.technical: No change.

options.name: Fence unlisted unsafe dependencies automatically
options.detail: Listed dependencies run normally. An unlisted dependency with an #Unsafe gate still builds, but is contained as if named in `contain`. Targets without an OS cannot be fenced.
options.technical: Per-dependency harden fact driven by the list.
options.code: policy: .{ unsafe_deps: .List(["sqlite"]) }

comparisons.note: Modules are Safe, Trustworthy, or Unsafe; the builder decides which packages to trust. https://simon.peytonjones.org/safe-haskell/
comparisons.code: ghc -fpackage-trust -trust bytestring

recommendation.why: A turns an invisible trust decision into a reviewed list, and the lock catches a later update that adds #Unsafe. Fences stay available for defense in depth.

whyNot.reason: B lets a dependency update add #Unsafe without anyone noticing.
C finds problems only while running and cannot protect targets without an OS.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more policy line in exchange for knowing exactly which dependencies may use unsafe code.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: BeginnerUnsafeDeps. Skill: rli5. The beginner pass found #Unsafe harm, fencing, and list ownership unexplained, with no end-to-end output. The lesson, option A output, and ownership rules were repaired.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: AdversaryUnsafeDeps. The review found the contain fence omitted, no version pinning, missing package identity, a retired command, and a boundary defect. All were repaired, #3977 was filed, and A survives.

whyNot.reason: B lets a dependency update add #Unsafe without anyone noticing.
C finds problems only while running and cannot protect targets without an OS.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more policy line in exchange for knowing exactly which dependencies may use unsafe code.

decisions.title: When a guarded dispatch table on an enum needs else
decisions.gist: When must a dispatch table with guarded arms end with else?
decisions.lesson: A guard is a condition on an arm, like `.Rect(w, h) && w == h`. An exhaustive enum table must not end with else, so adding a variant later forces an error. A guarded arm may not match, so the table needs a rule. Whichever wins, the E0003 parse error becomes a clear coverage message.
decisions.story: Lena writes a guarded table, gets a parse error, adds else, and is told to delete it. She loops between the two messages and gives up on the guard.
decisions.detail: Owner guidance 2026-09-30: an exhaustive enum table gets no else, so a later enum change forces handling every variant. Else may be required only when other conditions make the table more than a pure enum match. Under A, a table on a non-enum subject (Int, String) still needs else as today. Under A, when only guarded arms cover a variant, else is accepted. The Fix suggests the plain variant arm first because it keeps the new-variant error.

options.name: Unguarded arms decide coverage
options.detail: Coverage is computed from unguarded arms only, as in Rust and in GHC's Lower Your Guards. If they name every variant, the table is exhaustive and L0303 rejects an else. If a variant appears only in guarded arms, E0307 names it; the Fix offers a plain arm for that variant, and else is accepted but not suggested first.
options.technical: The parser accepts guarded tables without else in value and statement position. Sema's coverage matrix drops guarded rows (it already treats them as partial). E0307 gains a 'covered only by a guard' wording.

options.name: Any guard requires else
options.detail: Any table containing a guarded arm or a non-pattern condition must end with else. L0303 never fires on such tables. A missing else is a coverage error with plain wording, not E0003.
options.technical: Sema checks for a guard and requires the else arm; the parser change only improves the error.

options.name: No guards in enum tables
options.detail: Guards are rejected on enum-subject tables. The condition moves into the arm body as an ordinary if.
options.technical: Parser or sema rejects `pattern && condition` arms on enum subjects; examples such as nested_payload_safety.jet and encoding_json_stream.jet are migrated.

comparisons.note: Match guards are not counted when checking exhaustiveness; unguarded arms must cover every variant. https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/match-expr.html#match-guards
comparisons.code: Shape::Rect(w, h) if w == h => …, Shape::Rect(w, h) => …

comparisons.note: Lower Your Guards (ICFP 2020) treats a guard as possibly failing and reports a variant that only guards cover. https://simon.peytonjones.org/lower-your-guards/
comparisons.code:
f (Rect w h) | w == h = …
f (Rect w h) = …
f (Circle r) = …

recommendation.why: A keeps the owner's rule that an exhaustive enum table has no else, so a new variant always forces an error. Guards stay a readable way to split one variant.

whyNot.reason: B puts else in guarded enum tables, so a new variant is swallowed silently.
C removes a readable spelling that Rust and Haskell both keep, and nests logic deeper.

recommendation.tradeoff: Tables that split a variant with a guard must still name that variant plainly once.

surface.gist: When must a dispatch table with guarded arms end with else?
surface.lesson: A guard is a condition on an arm, like `.Rect(w, h) && w == h`. An exhaustive enum table must not end with else, so adding a variant later forces an error. A guarded arm may not match, so the table needs a rule. Whichever wins, the E0003 parse error becomes a clear coverage message.

current.note: Without else the table does not parse. With else, L0303 says to delete it.

wild.note: A guarded arm does not count as covering its pattern. Later unguarded arms can make the match complete without `_`. The Rust Reference, match guards.

options.name: Unguarded arms decide coverage
options.gist: Guards never count; if plain arms name every variant, else is forbidden.
gains: A new variant still errors in guarded tables.
Matches Rust and GHC.
One rule for guarded and plain tables.

gains: Easy to state and to see.

losses: A new variant silently goes to else.

gains: Guarded and plain tables follow one coverage rule.

decisions.title: Let one function serve every number type through traits
decisions.gist: Should one function like `math.max` work for every number type, through a `Numeric` trait that `#Numeric` implements?
decisions.lesson: Jet allows one definition per name, so Core's `math.max` takes only `Int`. Floats, `U8`, and `#Numeric` distinct types fail. Here `#Numeric` implements a real Core `Numeric` trait, and built-in numbers implement it too. Core and user code write one generic function. Each call compiles to that type's own code, so nothing runs slower.
decisions.explainer:
Reading the code: `#[Numeric, Printable] Meters :: distinct Float` makes a new number type over `Float`. It keeps arithmetic, ordering, and printing, but never mixes with plain `Float`.

`fn sum<T: Numeric>(xs: [T]) -> T` works for any type `T` that implements `Numeric`. `T.zero()` is that type's zero. `loop x in xs -> total += x` adds each element.

`math.max(U8{3}, U8{9})` returns a `U8`, the type of its arguments. Today the same call widens both arguments to `Int` and returns an `Int`.
decisions.story: Priya writes a physics toy with `Meters` and `Seconds` as `#Numeric` distinct floats. `math.max` rejects both, so she writes `max_meters` and `max_seconds`. Then she needs a total for each and copies `sum` twice. She wants one `sum` that works for any number type.
decisions.inWild:
newtype Meters = Meters Double deriving newtype (Show, Eq, Ord, Num)
total :: Num a => [a] -> a
total = foldr (+) 0
main = print (max 3 5, max 2.5 1.5, total [Meters 1.5, Meters 2.5])
-- Haskell: `deriving newtype` lets a wrapper join `Num` and `Ord`, so `max` and `total` work for it.
-- Source: downloads.haskell.org/ghc/latest/docs/users_guide/exts/newtype_deriving.html.

options.name: Markers implement traits
options.detail:
Core declares one new trait. `Numeric` builds on `Add`, `Sub`, `Mul`, and `Comparable`, each with the same type on both sides and as the result. It adds two static members, `zero()` and `one()`. Division is left out because `7 / 2` is `3.5`, so `/` does not return the input type for every number. Unary minus is left out because `U8` has none. `abs` and `sign` are ordinary Core functions built from `zero()` and `<`.

`Int`, `Float`, `F32`, every sized integer, `Decimal`, and `Fraction` implement `Numeric` in Core. `#Numeric` on a distinct type implements it from the base, beside the `Add`, `Sub`, `Mul`, `Div`, and `Comparable` hooks it already exposes. A struct such as `Money`, or a library `Rational`, may write `impl Money.Numeric { … }` by hand. `Complex` stays outside because it has no order; it keeps an `abs` method that returns `Float`.

`math.max`, `math.min`, and `math.clamp` take `T: Comparable`, because they only compare. They therefore also accept `String`, dates, and any `#Comparable` type. `math.abs`, `math.sign`, `sum`, and `product` take `T: Numeric`. The result keeps the argument's type, so `math.max(U8{3}, U8{9})` is a `U8`, not a widened `Int`.

The general marker rule: a type marker that promises operations other code can call implements the trait of the same name. `#Comparable`, `#Equatable`, `#Printable`, `#Debug`, `#Encode`, and `#Decode` already work this way. `#Codable` and `#CodableAsBase` implement `Encode` and `Decode`. `#Numeric` joins them. Markers that only change how the compiler treats a declaration name no trait: `#Inline`, `#MustUse`, `#Redact`, `#Memo`, `#Layout`, `#Unsafe`, and `#Commutative`, which mirrors one operator hook.

Overloading via traits means one generic definition serves many types, and each type supplies its behaviour through its trait implementation. Ad-hoc overloading stays closed. Two functions named `max` in one scope are still E0105. Overloads by argument count or type, specialised copies beside the generic, implicit conversions to satisfy a bound, and multi-heads beyond variant patterns all stay out.

Performance: a bound `<T: Numeric>` is always compiled per concrete type, as S48 already rules. `math.max(3, 5)` becomes the same machine code as today's `Int` version, and the `U8` copy uses 8-bit compares. There is no boxing, no method table, and no runtime type check. A bare `Numeric` in value position, such as `fn f(x: Numeric)`, is a compile error rather than silent dynamic dispatch, because its members use `Self`.

Diagnostics: `sum` over an affine unit such as `Celsius` reports E0905, `Celsius` isn't `Numeric`, because two temperatures cannot be added. Its fix names `#Numeric` for distinct types and `impl T.Numeric` for structs. Using `/` inside a `T: Numeric` body reports E0109, and its why says division is not part of `Numeric`. A duplicate `fn max` keeps E0105, and its fix points at one generic function with a bound.

Beginners call `math.max` on any number and write `#Numeric` on a distinct type; they never meet the word trait. Intermediate users write `fn sum<T: Numeric>(xs: [T]) -> T`. Experts implement `Numeric` for their own number structs and declare their own trait bundles with the same building-on list.
options.technical:
New surface: a trait may list the traits it builds on, reusing the D-VARARGBOUND1 bound list: `pub trait Numeric: [Add, Sub, Mul, Comparable] { fn zero() -> Self; fn one() -> Self }`. A bound on such a trait admits the listed traits' operators and methods in generic bodies. The hooks are the D-OPDEF1 traits with the D-FOUND-OPMIX1 right side fixed to `Self`.

Core/math becomes plain generic Jet, and the private `CoreCallTypeConstraint` rows (`Integer`, `Numeric`, `Comparable`, `Floating`) in Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/CoreSignatures.jet are deleted. Amends D-CAP10: a generic definition is the only way one name serves many types. Amends D-CAPBUNDLE1 and D-CAPPLANE1: `#Numeric` implements a named trait. D-FOUND-OPMIX1 and S83 multi-heads (D-CHOOSE-HEADS1=A) are unchanged. `#UnitFamily` already derives `Numeric` for delta and non-affine units and `Comparable` for affine ones (Registration/Checked.jet).

Observed on the current snapshot: `Meters.from_float(Float{2.0})` passed to a `T: Comparable` function fails with E0905 although `#Numeric` exposes `<`. E0905's fix for `Int` spells `impl Int: Numeric`, which is not Jet syntax. `math.max(Float{2.5}, Float{1.5})` fails with E0112 because Core/math/math.jet declares `max(a: Int, b: Int)`.

options.name: Built-in bound only
options.detail: `Numeric` becomes a bound the compiler knows by name, like the private table Core calls use today. Built-in numbers and `#Numeric` distinct types satisfy it; nothing else can. Generic bodies may use `+`, `-`, `*`, ordering, and `T.zero()`. There is no trait declaration and no hand-written implementation. Performance, diagnostics, and the closed overloading rule match A.
options.technical: Exposes the existing `CoreCallTypeConstraint.Numeric` check to user bounds. `impl X.Numeric` is an error naming the built-in list. No new syntax. Library number types from the exact-numerics example (#2802) cannot qualify.
options.code:
use core.math as math
#[Numeric, Printable] Meters :: distinct Float

fn sum<T: Numeric>(xs: [T]) -> T {
    total := T.zero()
    loop x in xs -> total += x
    total
}

fn run() {
    m :: Meters.from_float(Float{2.0})
    print(math.max(3, 5))
    print(math.max(Float{2.5}, Float{1.5}))
    print(math.max(U8{3}, U8{9}))
    print(sum([m, math.max(m, m)]))
}

impl Rational.Numeric { … }   // error: `Numeric` is built in; only numbers qualify

options.name: Type lists
options.detail: A bound may list concrete types: `T: Int | Float | U8`. A distinct type counts when its base is listed, as Go's `~float64` does. Generic bodies may use any operation that every listed type has. User structs cannot appear in Core's lists, so a library `Rational` never works with `math.max`. Every generic number function repeats its own list.
options.technical: Reuses the D-UNIONTYPE1 union spelling in bound position, which gives `|` two meanings in types. Compiled per type like A. Precedent: Go `cmp.Ordered`, pkg.go.dev/cmp#Ordered.
options.code:
use core.math as math
#[Numeric, Printable] Meters :: distinct Float

fn sum<T: Int | Float | U8>(xs: [T]) -> T {
    total := xs[0] - xs[0]
    loop x in xs -> total += x
    total
}

fn run() {
    m :: Meters.from_float(Float{2.0})
    print(math.max(3, 5))                 // Core lists every built-in number
    print(math.max(Float{2.5}, Float{1.5}))
    print(math.max(U8{3}, U8{9}))
    print(sum([m, m]))                    // Meters counts as its base, Float
}

options.name: One name, one type
options.detail: D-CAP10 stays as written. `#Numeric` and each built-in number gain `.max`, `.min`, `.abs`, and `.clamp` methods; a method belongs to one type, so this is not overloading. `math.max` stays `Int`-only. Code that sums numbers is written once per type.
options.technical: Like Rust's inherent `f64::max` beside `Ord::max`. No generic numeric bound; `<T: Numeric>` stays E0905 for every type.
options.code:
use core.math as math
#[Numeric, Printable] Meters :: distinct Float

fn sum_meters(xs: [Meters]) -> Meters {
    total := xs[0] - xs[0]
    loop x in xs -> total += x
    total
}

fn run() {
    m :: Meters.from_float(Float{2.0})
    print(math.max(3, 5))
    print(Float{2.5}.max(Float{1.5}))   // method on Float
    print(U8{3}.max(U8{9}))             // method on U8
    print(sum_meters([m, m.max(m)]))    // #Numeric adds the method
}

comparisons.note: `max<T: Comparable>` is one generic function, and `AdditiveArithmetic` lets one `sum` serve every number. `abs` takes `T: Comparable & SignedNumeric`. Source: developer.apple.com/documentation/swift/numeric.
comparisons.code:
func sum<T: AdditiveArithmetic>(_ xs: [T]) -> T { xs.reduce(.zero, +) }
print(max(3, 5), max(2.5, 1.5), sum([1.5, 2.5]))

comparisons.note: The standard library has no numeric trait. `Ord::max` covers integers, `f64::max` is a separate method, and generic math needs the `num-traits` crate. Source: docs.rs/num-traits.
comparisons.code:
fn sum<T: num_traits::Zero + Copy>(xs: &[T]) -> T { xs.iter().fold(T::zero(), |a, &b| a + b) }
println!("{} {}", 3.max(5), 2.5f64.max(1.5));

comparisons.note: Type-set constraints list the allowed types. `~float64` admits named types over `float64`, but user structs cannot join. Source: pkg.go.dev/cmp#Ordered.
comparisons.code:
type Number interface{ ~int | ~uint8 | ~float64 }
func Sum[T Number](xs []T) T { var t T; for _, x := range xs { t += x }; return t }

recommendation.why: It turns the compiler's private number list into one trait Core and users share. Beginners just call `math.max`. Code compiles per type, so it runs as fast as hand-written code.

losses.loss: A trait may now list the traits it builds on.
losses.mitigation: `Numeric` must promise `+`, `-`, `*`, and ordering; the list reuses the existing bound spelling.

losses.loss: Complex numbers stay outside `Numeric`.
losses.mitigation: Complex numbers have no order, so `max` means nothing for them.

whyNot.reason: B locks user number types such as `Rational` and `Money` out forever.
C cannot admit user structs, and its bound reads like a union type.
D keeps generic number code impossible and repeats every method per type.

recommendation.tradeoff: One small trait spelling buys shared generic math with no runtime cost.

decisions.title: core.compiler.lang.Effect and the one effect list
decisions.gist: How should core.compiler.lang.Effect relate to the one effect list in Effects.jet?
decisions.lesson: An effect names what a function touches, such as Net or FS. Effects.jet says it is the only effect list. But core.compiler.lang.Effect is a separate enum with different names, including Crypto, Random, and Proc. Whichever option wins, Effects.jet becomes the only source of effect names.
decisions.story: Lena writes #FX(lang.Effect.Random) because the enum offers it. The compiler's effect list has no Random, so her marker names an effect nothing else knows.

options.name: Generate the enum from Effects.jet
options.detail: lang.Effect keeps its name. Its variants are generated from Effects.jet, so Rand replaces Random and Crypto and Proc disappear.
options.technical: Restores ratified D-META-ONE1=A. Deny-only roots Mem and Panic stay deny-only (D-PANICROOT1=A, D-AUTHORITY-MEM1=B). The repository has no uses of Crypto, Random, or Proc. Source: Docs/audits/elegance-audit-2026-09-30.md section 3.3.

options.name: Delete the enum
options.detail: lang.Effect is removed. Markers and reflection use the bare effect names from Effects.jet.
options.technical: tests/marker_rule_signatures.rs:108-115 uses the qualified form and would migrate. Source: Docs/audits/elegance-audit-2026-09-30.md section 3.3.

comparisons.note: Deno keeps one permission list; CLI flags and the permissions API share it. docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security
comparisons.code:
// deno run --allow-net app.ts
await Deno.permissions.query({ name: "net" })

recommendation.why: Generating the enum keeps the typed value that reflection and qualified markers use, while the effect list becomes the single source.

whyNot.reason: B also ends the drift but removes a typed value that reflection and markers use.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet keeps one typed enum, generated so it cannot drift.

decisions.title: Diagnostic code law: the letter says when, the number says where
decisions.gist: Should every diagnostic code follow one law: the letter says when, the number says the topic?
decisions.lesson: A diagnostic code is the short label on an error, such as E0501. Jet has 968 codes in six shapes, and the number rarely tells you the topic. Whichever option wins, every code keeps one registry row, What/Why/Fix text, and a UI snapshot.
decisions.story: Maya's build fails with a TLS error. The number does not tell her it is a network error, and a second TLS error lives in another group. She cannot find related codes by number.
decisions.inWild:
200 OK            # 2xx success
404 Not Found     # 4xx client error
503 Unavailable   # 5xx server error
# HTTP puts the class in the first digit, so 4xx always means the client's fault. RFC 9110 section 15.

options.name: One law, one cutover
options.detail: E means Jet stops before your program runs, L is advice, and R means the running program stopped. The first digit is one of 10 areas; the first two digits are one of 28 topics.
options.technical:
Area 0 is source: 00 text, 01 grammar. Area 1 is structure: 10 names, 11 data, 12 functions. Area 2 is types: 20 types, 21 traits, 22 values. Area 3 is flow: 30 control, 31 failure. Area 4 is memory: 40 ownership, 41 unsafe.

Area 5 is effects: 50 authority, 51 concurrency. Area 6 is compile time: 60. Area 7 is libraries: 70 data, 71 network, 72 UI, 73 FFI, 74 targets, 75 files. Area 8 is assurance: 80 tests, 81 proof, 82 performance. Area 9 is project: 90 packages, 91 build, 92 CLI, 93 registry.

Tie rule: a code lives where its fix is made. 812 of 835 codes placed cleanly. A closed-book test scored 12 of 12. This amends Docs/spec/diagnostics.md:18-21. Source: Docs/audits/elegance-audit-2026-09-30.md section 3.1.
options.code:

E7201  reactive.derived lambda
L7202  accessibility label
E8101  proof evidence missing
E7101  TLS handshake failed
E7102  HTTPS TLS handshake failed
R4101  raw memory fault at run time

options.name: Law for new codes only
options.detail: Existing codes keep their numbers. New codes take a free number in their topic range.
options.technical: Existing ranges overlap the new key, so new codes must avoid numbers already taken. Source: Docs/audits/elegance-audit-2026-09-30.md section 3.1.
options.code:
E2802  TLS handshake failed      (unchanged)
E4201  HTTPS TLS handshake failed (unchanged)
E7103  new TLS error             (follows the key)

options.name: One cutover plus an old-code lookup
options.detail: Same law as A. A generated table maps each old code to its new code for jet explain only.
options.technical: The lookup rows sit outside the active registry. AGENTS.md requires an owner-ratified exception with a removal condition. Source: Docs/audits/elegance-audit-2026-09-30.md section 3.1.
options.code:
$ jet explain E2802
E2802 is now E7101: TLS handshake failed.

comparisons.note: HTTP puts the class in the first digit, so 4xx always means the client's fault. RFC 9110 section 15.
comparisons.code:
200 OK            # 2xx success
404 Not Found     # 4xx client error
503 Unavailable   # 5xx server error

recommendation.why: One law makes every code findable by topic. Greenfield law already removes legacy readers such as an old-code table.

whyNot.reason: B keeps today's 15 mixed groups and adds a second numbering system.
C keeps a legacy lookup table, which needs a compatibility exception.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet gives up old-code lookup to get one numbering law.

decisions.title: One runtime and one Jet code generator with levels O0, O1, and O2
decisions.gist: Should Jet run programs through one shared runtime and one Jet-written code generator with three levels: O0, O1, and O2?
decisions.lesson: Jet checks a program once, then hands it to one of three engines. `jet build` prints Rust for rustc. `jet run` compiles in memory with Cranelift, which carries its own 130,000-line copy of the built-in library. An interpreter runs compile-time code. Bugs seen on one engine but not another come from these copies. Either way, today's stage-zero and parity work finishes first.
decisions.explainer:
Reading the code: lines that start with `$` are commands typed in a terminal, and the line under a command is what it prints. `fn run() { print("hi") }` is a whole Jet program that prints `hi`.

The runtime, or built-in library, is the code every program calls, such as `print` and lists. A code generator turns a checked program into machine code. A JIT does this into memory just before the program runs. LLVM is the optimizer behind Clang, Rust, and Swift.

O0, O1, and O2 are optimization levels. A higher number takes longer to build and makes a faster program. O0 writes machine code into memory; O1 and O2 write an executable file.
decisions.story: Priya fixes a bug in how Jet formats a list. Her test passes with `jet build` but fails with `jet run`, because the Cranelift engine keeps its own copy of that code. She fixes the copy too. Next month a third engine disagrees, and she starts again.

options.name: One runtime, one Jet code generator
options.detail:
One runtime. The Prelude and Core are compiled once for each Jet version, at O2, and ship with Jet. Every level calls these same compiled functions. No engine keeps its own copy.

One code generator, written in Jet. It reads one shared low-level form of the program. That form spells out memory layout, drops (where values are freed), and the calling convention (ABI). O0 serves `jet run`, `jet dev`, and compile-time code, and writes machine code into memory. That is the JIT. O1 is the `jet build` default and writes an executable file. O2 is `--release`.

O2 uses LLVM first, and Jet passes what it knows about the program to LLVM as metadata. A Jet-written O2 may come later. Benchmark O1 against O2 build times on large codebases. If O2 costs only a few seconds more, consider O2 as the `jet build` default, with a flag for O1.

No interpreter tier. Compile-time code runs through O0 in memory. A tiny evaluator is added only for a platform that forbids creating machine code at run time, and only if Jet must run there.

Order of work. First finish stage zero and parity on today's engines. Then unify the runtime. Then build the Jet backend for x86-64, then aarch64, the platforms people develop on. LLVM covers release builds and unusual or embedded targets. Then retire Cranelift and MIREval.

Beginner path: `jet run` and `jet build` just work, and no level is ever named. Expert path: the `-O0`, `-O1`, and `-O2` flags pick a level, and `--release` means O2.
options.technical:
The shared low-level form sits below Jet MIR (D-TIER-FORM1). It is lowered once, and no level decides meaning again (D-TIER-ONEIR1). O0 must keep `jet dev`'s live function replacement before Cranelift retires.

This ballot amends I9. Its tier list (AOT, Cranelift JIT, interpreter, web) becomes O0, O1, O2, and web. Its "same Prelude symbols" rule becomes the one compiled runtime.

It replaces the unsubmitted draft D-JETCLI-RUN1, which asked how `jet run` works in the Jet CLI without the Rust JIT. The answer is O0.

As each step lands, it also changes these ratified rulings. D-TIER-ONEIR1 loses Cranelift and the interpreter from its reader list. D-ONCE-TIER1's first-class interpreter tier ends. D-AOT-CRANELIFT1's Cranelift debug build becomes O1.

D-BUILD-DEFAULT1's optimized `jet build` default becomes O1, unless the benchmark makes O2 the default. D-INTERP-BUDGET1 ends with `jet run --interpret`. D-JIT-ARENA1 and D-JIT-SPEED1 govern Cranelift until it retires.

Cranelift and MIREval retire only after the Jet backend runs the whole example corpus with the same output.
options.code:
fn run() { print("hi") }

$ jet run hi.jet                # O0: compiled into memory
hi
$ jet dev hi.jet                # O0, rebuilt on save
hi
$ jet build hi.jet && ./hi      # O1: executable file
hi
$ jet build --release hi.jet && ./hi   # O2: LLVM first
hi
$ jet build -O2 hi.jet          # expert: same as --release
$ jet build -O1 hi.jet          # expert: names the default
// compile-time code also runs at O0, in memory
// every level calls the same compiled Prelude and Core

options.name: Keep Cranelift for O0 and O1
options.detail:
The Prelude and Core are compiled once and shared, as in A. Every level calls the same compiled functions.

Cranelift stays the code generator for O0 (`jet run`, `jet dev`, and compile-time code) and for O1 (`jet build`). O2 (`--release`) uses LLVM. There is no interpreter tier: compile-time code runs through Cranelift at O0.

The Cranelift engine's duplicate runtime, about 130,000 lines, is deleted. Its code generator, about 30,000 lines of Rust, stays and reads the shared low-level form.

Beginner and expert paths match A: `jet run` and `jet build` just work, and `-O0`, `-O1`, or `-O2` picks a level.
options.technical: I9 is amended as in A, and D-JETCLI-RUN1 is answered the same way. The patched Cranelift from D-JIT-ARENA1 becomes a permanent dependency. MIREval still retires. Jet facts can reach Cranelift only through what its own input form can express.

options.name: Keep today's three engines
options.detail:
No change. `jet build` prints Rust and calls rustc. `jet run` and `jet dev` use the Cranelift JIT with its own runtime copy. `jet run --interpret` uses MIREval, and compile-time code uses MIREval and JetEval.

I9 keeps its four-tier list. Every runtime change lands in the Rust Prelude and again in the Cranelift engine's copy.
options.technical: crates/jet-jit stays at about 161,000 lines. About 30,000 generate code. About 130,000 re-implement Collections, the runtime host, Data, Encoding, Crypto, DB, UI, Net, HTTP, and FFI. D-JETCLI-RUN1 still needs an answer for `jet run` in the Jet CLI.
options.code:
fn run() { print("hi") }

$ jet run hi.jet                # Cranelift JIT, own runtime copy
hi
$ jet build hi.jet && ./hi      # generated Rust, then rustc
hi
$ jet build --release hi.jet && ./hi   # rustc with link-time optimization
hi
$ jet run --interpret hi.jet    # MIREval interpreter
hi
// compile-time code: MIREval and JetEval interpreters

comparisons.note: Go's own code generator serves every build, with no LLVM step. Optimizations are on by default and turned off with a flag. Source: go.dev/doc/gdb.
comparisons.code:
$ go build hi.go                         # optimized, Go's own backend
$ go build -gcflags=all="-N -l" hi.go    # optimizations off, for debugging

comparisons.note: Rust can swap LLVM for Cranelift to build debug code faster. LLVM stays the default. Source: github.com/rust-lang/rustc_codegen_cranelift.
comparisons.code:
$ cargo build                                                   # LLVM
$ CARGO_PROFILE_DEV_CODEGEN_BACKEND=cranelift cargo +nightly build -Zcodegen-backend   # Cranelift

recommendation.why: One runtime copy removes the cause of engine-only bugs. One Jet-written generator lets Jet's own facts shape the machine code. LLVM still covers release builds and rare targets.

whyNot.reason: B keeps a Rust code generator that Jet cannot shape around its own facts.
C keeps the runtime copies that cause engine-only bugs.

recommendation.tradeoff: Default builds may trade some run speed for build speed, LLVM stays as the O2 generator, and locked-down platforms may need a small evaluator.

decisions.title: Jet's own back end builds release programs; LLVM is retired once it is beaten
decisions.situation: Every Jet program is turned into machine code by a back end. Jet is building its own back end, but the plan still hands the fastest release builds to LLVM, the large outside optimizer that Rust and Clang use. LLVM brings regressions, slow builds and a heavy dependency. The vote decides whether Jet's own back end also builds release programs, with LLVM kept only as a measured fallback until Jet beats it; we recommend yes.
decisions.gist: Should Jet's own code generator also build release programs, so Jet stops depending on LLVM?
decisions.lesson: A back end turns checked code into machine instructions. LLVM is a large outside back end used by Rust, Clang and Zig. Jet is writing its own; the current plan still uses LLVM for release builds. Whichever option wins, release speed is measured against Rust, C and Zig, and every loss stays on a card.
decisions.story: Priya's release build waits on LLVM for minutes, and a new LLVM version made one hot loop slower. Her team wants one compiler they can read and fix.
decisions.detail:
Source: owner scratch note, line 66: LLVM has regressions, is slow, buggy and not ideal; consider our own back end replacing LLVM. Line 31 asks for fewer layers between the language and the generated assembly.

Jet today. D-EXEC1 ratified one runtime and one Jet-written code generator with O0, O1 and O2, where O2 uses LLVM first and a Jet-written O2 may come later. D-EXEC2 retired the Cranelift JIT. D-TIER-FORM1 makes every back end read one Jet-owned MIR. A Jet x86-64 back end exists in Compiler/JetBackend, with instruction selection, register allocation, an encoder and an ELF linker. Shipping builds still emit Rust and call rustc, which uses LLVM. Owner directive 19 removes Rust from the toolchain.

Option A, technical. O2 becomes a Jet optimizer pass pipeline over Jet MIR plus the Jet back end. Jet facts that LLVM cannot see feed it directly: proven ranges remove bounds checks, ownership proves no aliasing, and effect rows prove purity.

The fallback. `--backend=llvm` stays as an explicit, measured fallback that lowers the same MIR through LLVM's C API. It is removed when Jet O2 strictly beats it on every required gauntlet cell and every supported target has a Jet generator. Until then the fallback is reported in the build dossier, never chosen silently.

Evidence. Go has always used its own back end and is competitive for its workloads. Zig 0.15 made its self-hosted x86-64 back end the debug default for faster builds. Cranelift exists as a Rust back end because LLVM's compile time hurts debug loops. LLVM releases have repeatedly regressed specific optimizations, which downstream compilers then work around.

Why B loses: it keeps two code generators that must agree on every program, and keeps LLVM's compile time and regressions on Jet's critical path.

Shared work for either option: finish the Jet back end for O0 and O1 (card #4013) and measure every level in the gauntlet.
