decisions.title: Retire the old run engine now; ship the Jet compiler first
decisions.situation: Today a program can work when built but fail when run, because the commands use different engines. Keeping the old run engine also consumes time needed to finish the compiler written in Jet. This vote records your choice to run every program through the working build path while the faster replacement grows. We recommend shipping the Jet compiler with every existing feature before freezing the old compiler.
decisions.gist: Should running reuse building now, while we finish and ship the compiler written in Jet?
decisions.lesson: A compiler turns source into a runnable program. A bootstrap seed is an older compiler kept only to build its replacement.
decisions.explainer: The examples are plans, not execution receipts. Lines beginning with $ are terminal commands. Each example uses the same tiny program, which prints hi. A run engine is the machinery that executes a program. A native backend makes machine code directly. O0 means unoptimized machine code, eventually created in memory without building a separate executable. Shared work: finish the Jet compiler, prove every existing feature, and complete the native backend.
decisions.story: Maya wants the same program to work whether she builds it or runs it, without waiting for a new chip port.
decisions.inWild:
$ go run hello.go       # compiles, then executes
hello
$ go build hello.go     # the same compiler builds an executable
$ ./hello
hello
decisions.detail:
Owner answers, chat of 2026-10-05, supplied in this assignment: A records all three answers together. Retire Cranelift now on x86-64; aarch64 comes later and is not a prerequisite. Until native covers every program, run and dev compile through the normal build path and execute. Small programs should start in approximately 1-5 seconds; dev restarts on change rather than hot-swapping. Keep the comptime evaluator only until native in-memory O0 lands.

Critical path, also the owner's answer: ship the Jet compiler with full 1:1 Rust-compiler feature parity. Then freeze Rust as a bootstrap seed, with no more Rust-half fixes. Remove Rust entirely once native is complete. This OPEN posting payload records the answers without claiming a Tower ratification. Only the owner/Main can post or ratify it.

Why an amendment is needed: D-EXEC1=A is ratified, but its order explicitly requires x86-64, then aarch64, before Cranelift and MIREval retirement. Its technical text also requires the whole example corpus and live function replacement before Cranelift retirement. These conditions conflict with the owner's new answers; this is not merely an implementation choice. The final one-runtime, Jet-native O0/O1 and LLVM-first O2 direction remains settled by D-EXEC1.

Attachment checked read-only: card #4134, c08xt185, is titled 'Jet backend 8: example-corpus parity against Cranelift and rustc (gate before Cranelift retires)'. It has the native golden and regression criteria, so this payload attaches there through cardId. Its old retirement gate must be amended after ratification, not silently treated as already changed.

Research: Zig's primary account, https://ziglang.org/news/goodbye-cpp/ (2022-12-07), reports deleting an 80,000-line legacy C++ compiler. Keeping two implementations meant implementing language changes twice. A small committed bootstrap artifact replaced the live second implementation. Its release build measurement fell from 10.3 GiB peak RSS to 3.2 GiB; debug fell from 11.3 to 3.8 GiB. Timings were volatile and do not predict Jet performance. The bootstrap kernel was 2.4 MiB before compression, accompanied by about 4,000 lines of portable C.

Zig also documents what went wrong and what removal can cost. Its old no-free-until-exit memory policy became impractical as comptime work and programs grew. Maintaining cleaned-up generated C would still leave two evolving compilers. Removing the old compiler's opt-out also removed access to async functions not yet implemented in the replacement. Jet must avoid that last mistake: full feature inventory and parity proofs precede shipping/freezing, not merely a hello-world self-compile.

Go provides a semantics-preserving migration example: https://go.dev/doc/go1.5#implementation and https://go.dev/doc/go1.5#build. Go 1.5 translated the compiler from C to Go, retained compatibility, removed the old C implementation from the active toolchain, and built with an existing Go compiler. https://go.dev/doc/install/source#install documents Go 1.4 as the seed for Go 1.5 through 1.19.

Go's source-install guide also warns that the old seed cannot run on every newer host, including current macOS. Cross-built or downloaded seeds address that constraint. Jet should not make support for a later CPU a gate on the present x86-64 cutover.

Rust separates seed and shipped compiler: https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/building/bootstrapping/what-bootstrapping-does.html. A downloaded beta stage0 builds current-source stage1; stage1 rebuilds stage2, which is distributed. An optional stage3 checks identical results. The guide warns that stage0 and current-library calling conventions can differ, so testing only the seed is not proof of the shipped compiler.

Jet parity tests must exercise the actual shipped Jet binary and its runtime, not just source fragments run by Rust. Rust's seed advances over time; Jet's proposed Rust seed freeze is a bounded migration step, not a claim that Rust itself freezes forever.

Proven right ways: keep a seed separate from the product, preserve semantics during the language migration, and test the real replacement. Proven wrong ways: keep two evolving compilers, retire before covering old features, or mistake a seed test for replacement proof. A combines those lessons with a build-and-execute bridge that already covers programs. It does not replace a broken JIT with a partial native path or make the later chip port block the current cutover.

Jet maintenance evidence: the owner/assignment reports jet-jit builds being OOM-killed at an 8 GB memory cap. This is reported evidence, not a new measurement, and was not rerun. No matching exact build receipt was located in proofq/done or by the JIT-retirement worker. D-EXEC1's ratified technical record describes about 30,000 lines generating code and about 130,000 lines duplicating runtime/library behavior in crates/jet-jit. Those are its historical figures, not a fresh count.

Additional measured maintenance evidence from JITRetire on 2026-10-05: its offline cargo tree inventory lists 321 packages for jet and 102 when pruning jet-jit. The difference is 219 packages. Existing receipts are $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/JITRetire/tree-all.txt and tree-nojit.txt; their line counts were read for this ballot. This demonstrates dependency surface, not an OOM cause or a measured speedup.

Read-only Tower bug evidence on 2026-10-05: #4572 records String += producing wrong or empty output under run while build is correct. #4578 records a tail Bool becoming false only inside a larger JIT program. #4581 records recursive Option.map over a large payload core-dumping or passing garbage, disrupting native-backend fixtures. #4615 records missing memo call/result wrappers in the JIT although native/AOT emitters use the memo store. These are concrete costs of keeping another execution mechanism.

#4590 records the JIT printing Float raw bits as an Int. Its newer card log identifies a shared semantic error accepting Int{float}, with different failures across engines. It is evidence of engine divergence and maintenance burden, not proof that every root cause is JIT-only. Retirement does not waive shared language bugs or their regression coverage. All five cards remain evidence/tests for the retained build path and eventual native backend, not permission to close unproven criteria.

The approximately 1-5 second startup is the owner's stated expectation/target for small programs, not a measured guarantee. No local builds or compiler tests were run for this ballot. External measurements are evidence about their own systems only.

options.name: Retire now; build to run
options.detail:
Remove the Cranelift JIT now on x86-64. Until the native backend covers every program, run and dev use the normal build path and execute its result. Every supported program keeps working through one mechanism. Small programs target approximately 1-5 seconds to start. Dev rebuilds and restarts on a saved change, rather than replacing functions in a running process.

Critical path: make the compiler written in Jet the shipped jet, with every Rust jetc feature re-homed and proven by 1:1 parity tests. Then retire the Rust compiler to a bootstrap seed and freeze it: no more Rust-half fixes or features. Complete the native backend, then remove Rust entirely. aarch64 support comes later and does not block x86-64 JIT retirement.

Keep the existing compile-time evaluator only until native in-memory O0 can execute all compile-time programs with identical meaning. Then retire it. This is not a public interpreter replacement for run or dev. All commands use the shipped Jet compiler after cutover; there is no per-feature dispatch back to the old compiler.
options.technical:
Amend D-EXEC1's order-of-work paragraph and its corpus/aarch64/live-replacement retirement prerequisites. Retire Cranelift independently of native coverage, with the working build-and-execute route carrying every run/dev program during transition. The native corpus gate still proves backend completeness; it no longer gates Cranelift retirement. Preserve D-EXEC1's final shared runtime, single lowering meaning, O0/O1/O2 levels and LLVM-first O2 design.

Re-home every feature of Rust jetc, not only its compiler entry point. Inventory all language, diagnostics, compile-time evaluation, code-emission, command, flag, package and tool behavior before cutover. Prove each applicable feature through the actual Jet-compiled shipped jet, with positive and negative parity cases. No missing feature may be hidden by a wrapper, skipped test, Rust fallback, narrower corpus or grammar-only proof.

The deliberate changes approved here are removal of Cranelift and live hot-swapping, and compile-and-execute run/dev during transition. They are explicit amendments, not accidental parity omissions. Keep source/runtime semantics and every other Rust jetc feature in the parity contract. Comptime means code evaluated while compiling; its evaluator remains temporary until native in-memory O0 covers that role.

Freeze the retained Rust compiler seed only after full shipped-compiler parity passes. Its sole role is producing the Jet compiler; fixes and new work then belong to Jet. The existing generated-Rust build backend may still invoke rustc until native is complete; that is not permission for new Rust-half compiler fixes. At native completion, remove the retained Rust compiler and Rust build/runtime dependency path entirely, using the Jet compiler for subsequent bootstrap.

Migrate all Cranelift callers and remove its crate, dependencies, duplicated runtime and obsolete engine-specific flags/tests at cutover. Preserve their behavioral regression cases on the retained execution mechanism. Run/dev reuse build preparation and execution contracts rather than adding another interpreter or an incomplete-program fallback. Preserve arguments, environment, working directory, exit status and diagnostics; dev must actually restart the child on change.

On #4134, retain every native golden/regression criterion and change only the outdated retirement prerequisite after ratification. Shared-source defects on #4590 and elsewhere must still be fixed in the live compiler and proven. No JIT-only code repair is required once the removed engine has no callers.

options.name: Wait for every native example
options.detail:
Keep the Cranelift JIT until the native backend passes every golden program, meaning each saved example's expected output. Then retire it on x86-64; aarch64 is not a retirement prerequisite. Run and dev retain their current mechanism until native covers the corpus.

Keep the full Jet-compiler parity and Rust seed/freeze/removal milestones proposed in A. Keep compile-time evaluation until native in-memory O0 covers it. The real difference is the retirement gate: pay for the old run engine while proving native output before switching run/dev to native.
options.technical: Change D-EXEC1's aarch64 sequencing, but retain a whole-corpus native-parity gate before Cranelift retirement. Keep cross-engine repairs and comparisons during that period, including the five cited cards. This avoids the build-and-restart bridge, but makes native coverage the predecessor of JIT removal. Compiler feature parity still gates shipping Jet and freezing the Rust seed; native completion gates Rust removal.

options.name: Wait for both chip backends
options.detail:
Keep the previously approved order: finish stage zero and parity on today's engines, unify the runtime, build the x86-64 backend, then build aarch64, and only then retire Cranelift and the evaluator. Keep live function replacement and whole-corpus output parity as retirement prerequisites.

This chooses the existing sequence instead of the owner's earlier x86-64 retirement. It preserves today's run/dev mechanism while both chip backends are completed. It does not adopt the new Jet-shipped-first, then frozen-Rust-seed critical path as an amendment.
options.technical: No amendment to D-EXEC1's ordering or technical retirement gates. Preserve stage-zero/parity-first, runtime unification, x86-64, aarch64, and then Cranelift/MIREval retirement. This accepts the longest continued JIT maintenance interval in exchange for both developer architectures reaching the native engine before its removal.

$ jet dev hi.jet  # keep live replacement until both backends are ready

decisions.title: Let team policy forbid any kind of gate, and let every gate say why
decisions.situation: A gate is a written spot where code steps around a Jet safety check, such as an #Unsafe block or an #allow that silences a warning. A team policy can forbid only three of the thirteen gate kinds, and an #allow cannot say why it is there. You are deciding whether every gate kind can be forbidden and can give a reason; we recommend yes, with today's behaviour as the default.
decisions.gist: Should a team policy be able to forbid every kind of gate, and should every gate be able to say why?
decisions.lesson: A gate is a written step around a Jet safety check, such as #Unsafe("why") { } or #allow(lint). A team policy is a rule in package.jet that can forbid a gate kind. Today it can forbid only three kinds, and #allow takes no reason. A lets policy forbid every kind and lets every gate give a reason. B does that for security kinds only. C keeps today's rules.
decisions.explainer:
Plain words first. Jet checks a lot for you: types, effects, units and precision. Sometimes you must step around a check on purpose. Jet calls that written step a gate.

Some gates are blocks, such as #Unsafe("reason") { } for raw memory work. #allow(lint_name) silences one warning. Others are quieter: a dependency grant in package.jet, a forced version pin, or turning an exact number into a Float.

The audit list shows every gate in a program. You read it with jet inspect gates. Thirteen gate kinds exist today, and lint switches are being added as a fourteenth.

A policy is a rule a team writes once, in package.jet or in an organization file that covers many packages. A policy key names a gate kind, such as unsafe. The value .Forbid makes that kind an error; .GateOnly allows it and lists it.

Today only three keys accept .Forbid: unsafe, impure and nondeterministic. #Unsafe must give a reason. #Impure may leave it out, but a missing reason raises a warning that a team can turn into an error. #allow has no place for a reason at all.
decisions.story: Rosa leads security for a team of forty. She can ban #Unsafe in the payments package but not silent conversions to Float. Her audit finds #allow(float_money) with no reason, and nobody remembers why.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-04. The Rust compiler names thirteen gate kinds in crates/jet-foundation/src/Authority.rs:660-676 and records them in crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/GateLedger.rs. The Jet compiler has no gate ledger yet; a search of Compiler/ finds no GateLedger or GateKind.

Policy keys in the Jet compiler are unsafe, impure, nondeterministic, gc, explicit_units, copies and sentries (Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/AST/Statements.jet:74-82). Impure and nondeterministic default to .GateOnly and unsafe to .Default (crates/jet-foundation/src/Policy.rs:876-882). All three audited keys parse the same eight values, from .Forbid to .Skip (Policy.rs:898-908). Source code cannot set these three keys; E0355 sends the writer to package.jet (Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/Declarations/Policies.jet:162-165).

The lint switch is marker allow(lint: Ident) with no reason slot (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Markers.jet:207). Card #4016 respells it #Allow; this ballot is independent of the spelling. The repository has 9 #allow sites in 9 .jet files, all test fixtures under tests/. Card #4078 adds lint switches to the ledger under every option.

Sema drops a diagnostic named by a statement #allow before package policy runs (crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerCore/statements.rs:620-645,1181-1182). So policy.lints.deny cannot refuse a lint switch today.

Reasons today: a missing #Unsafe reason is the error E3112. A missing #Impure reason is the advisory lint impure_reason, L3102 (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet:492), which policy.lints.deny can turn into an error. A .Force writer's reason is optional (GateLedger.rs:151-154). The test corpus keeps a second home for #allow reasons in manifest [exception] rows (tests/support/corpus_policy.rs:636-705).

Ratified law this builds on. D-FACT-GATE1=A puts every gate in one ledger. D-AUTHORITY-GATE1=A makes the lint bypass law the law of every gate. D-ONCE-GATE1=A gives the three audited escapes one policy ladder and the --gate <name>=allow escape, which the organization file can refuse. D-LINTPOLICY1=A says every bypass is spelled and recorded, lints never block a build by default, and walls are team policy. D-IMPURE-REASON1=B kept the #Impure reason optional but auditable and promotable to an error; A applies that same rule to #allow.

Scope of a policy: each package starts from the organization policy and adds its own (crates/jet-driver/src/Loader.rs:1911,2130). A package .Forbid covers only that package; an organization .Forbid covers every package built under it, dependencies included.

Shared work under every option: the Jet compiler must port the gate ledger (card #4078), and the 9 fixture #allow sites are updated in the same cutover. Determinism's old assume_deterministic label is a cleanup that needs no ballot.

Clarity rewrite: B now differs from A only in which kinds policy may forbid, so both give #allow the optional reason. The draft's B had no reason slot, which mixed two questions.

options.name: Every gate kind can be forbidden and explained
options.detail:
Every gate kind becomes a policy key, named exactly as jet inspect gates names it. The keys are unsafe, impure, nondeterministic, dependency_grant, build_flag, session_flag, trust_grant, force_pin, taint_scrub, duty_drop, state_transition, precision_demotion, structure and the new lint_allow. Each new key accepts .GateOnly, the default, or .Forbid. .GateOnly means a written gate is allowed and listed, which is today's behaviour; .Forbid makes it an error. unsafe, impure and nondeterministic keep the values they accept today.

The lint switch gains an optional reason: #allow(float_money, "prices are whole cents"). A switch without one raises the advisory lint allow_reason, the twin of #Impure's missing-reason lint, and the audit list marks the row. A team that wants a reason on every switch adds allow_reason to policy.lints.deny.

The outermost refusal wins. An organization .Forbid beats a package .GateOnly, and a package .Forbid beats a --gate allow on the command line.
options.technical:
PolicyKey grows to the GateKind list plus lint_allow, using the .Forbid and .GateOnly values impure already uses. Like the three audited keys, they are package.jet and organization-file keys only, and writing one in source is E0355. --gate <key>=allow accepts every key name. Policy resolution reuses the D-MARK-SCOPE1 ladder.

The refusal diagnostic names the gate kind, the site and the policy file, with a UI snapshot per kind. allow_reason is registered beside impure_reason (L3102); its fix names the reason slot, and #allow cannot name allow_reason itself. The corpus manifest's per-site #allow reason rows are deleted, because the reason now lives at the site.

options.name: Only security gate kinds can be forbidden
options.detail:
Policy keys cover the gate kinds that widen what a program may do: unsafe, impure, nondeterministic, dependency_grant, trust_grant, force_pin, taint_scrub and lint_allow. #allow gains the same optional reason as in A.

Precision demotions, state transitions, duty drops, structure gates and build or session flags stay in the audit list but cannot be forbidden. A money team therefore cannot ban silent conversions to Float.
options.technical: PolicyKey grows by five keys. GateKind keeps thirteen entries plus lint_allow, so policy names and ledger names no longer match one to one.
options.code:
policy: { lint_allow: .Forbid }          // allowed key
policy: { precision_demotion: .Forbid }  // error: not a policy key

#allow(float_money, "prices are whole cents")

options.name: Keep today's three
options.detail: Policy keys stay unsafe, impure and nondeterministic. Lint switches join the audit list through card #4078, as in every option, but cannot be forbidden and take no reason.
options.technical: No policy or marker change beyond #4078.
options.code:
policy: { unsafe: .Forbid }       // works today
policy: { lint_allow: .Forbid }   // error: not a policy key

#allow(float_money)               // listed, but cannot say why

comparisons.note: Rust lints accept a reason, and forbid at an outer level cannot be undone by an inner allow.
Go's staticcheck ignore comment must carry a reason, or the tool reports the ignore itself.
comparisons.code:
//lint:ignore SA1019 the old API is needed for Go 1.20
// https://staticcheck.dev/docs/configuration/#ignoring-problems

recommendation.why: Jet already lists every gate in one place. A finishes the rule: any kind you can see in the list, a team can forbid, and every gate can say why. Nothing changes for a team that sets no policy.
gains: One rule covers every way around a safety check.
A team can forbid any gate kind it can see in the audit list.
Lint switches can record why they exist, and a missing reason is flagged.

losses.loss: An organization-wide ban on a gate kind also stops any dependency that uses that kind.
losses.mitigation: The error names the dependency, the gate and the policy file. A package-level ban covers only that package.

losses.loss: Eleven new policy key names to document and learn.
losses.mitigation: They are the audit list's own kind names, so one table documents both, and every new key defaults to today's behaviour.

whyNot.reason: B makes readers learn which kinds can be banned, and money code cannot ban silent conversions to Float.
C leaves eleven gate kinds unbannable and lint switches unable to say why.

recommendation.tradeoff: Eleven more policy names buy one rule for every gate.

decisions.title: Run a project's own jobs as jet X
decisions.situation: A job is a named chore in a Jet project, such as deploy, written as a function marked #Job. Today you run it with jet jobs deploy; typing jet deploy is an unknown-command error, though tools like just accept just deploy. You are deciding whether jet deploy should run the job. We recommend yes: Jet's own commands win, then your jobs, and a job may not reuse a command's name.
decisions.gist: Should jet deploy run your project's deploy job directly, with job names kept apart from Jet's own commands?
decisions.lesson: A job is a function marked #Job that a project runs by name; today you type jet jobs deploy. A makes jet deploy work: Jet tries its own commands, then your jobs, then a jet-deploy program on your system. A job may not reuse a Jet command's name. B keeps jet jobs deploy. C runs jobs at the top level but lets a job share a command's name.
decisions.explainer:
Plain words first. The jet program takes a first word, the command, such as build or test. Jet has 62 command words today.

A job is a function in your project marked #Job, such as #Job fn deploy() { ... }. It is how a project names its own chores, the way a justfile recipe or a package.json script does.

Today you run a job with jet jobs deploy. Words after the job name go to the job, so jet jobs deploy --region eu hands --region eu to deploy. Jet's own flags, such as --interpret, go before the job name.

PATH is the list of folders your shell searches for programs. Like git and cargo, Jet treats an unknown word X as a request for a program named jet-X on PATH.

One more shortcut already uses the first word. When X names a file or folder, such as deploy.jet or a deploy folder, jet X means jet run X.

A name clash happens when a job and a Jet command share a word, for example a job named lint. Today that is allowed, because jobs never reach the top level.
decisions.story: Lena adds #Job fn deploy and types jet deploy. Jet says deploy is not a command, and she wonders why Jet needs the extra word jobs when just deploy worked in her old project.
decisions.inWild:
# just: recipe names are top-level words.
# https://just.systems/man/en/
deploy:
    ./ship.sh
$ just deploy

# Cargo: an alias cannot replace a built-in command.
# https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/config.html#alias
[alias]
b = "build"
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-04. Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Commands.jet registers 62 top-level command words. The Jet-written front end reports E2101 for any other word (Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Front.jet:475-479) and has no PATH fallback yet. Its main dispatch handles only finished output, check and build (Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Host.jet:184-192). The Rust jet looks up jet-<word> on PATH before E2101 (Source/main.rs:1587-1607,3154-3158). Retired and moved spellings are taught before the command check (Front.jet:378-391).

Before E2101, both front ends run jet X as jet run X when X looks like source. That means X ends in .jet, names a file or folder, or has a matching X.jet file (Front.jet:269-273,476; Source/main.rs:782,3157-3160). Job names already have a registered error, E0928, for reserved names and two jobs with one name.

Ratified law this would amend. D-DX-JOBS-UX1=E makes jet jobs both the list and the runner. D-JOB-ARGV1=A gives the job every word after its name and puts Jet's flags before it; A keeps that rule. D-JOB-NAMES1=A reserves only run, dev, build, test, help and version, and says it holds only while jobs stay under jet jobs. D-JOB-SUBCMD1=C makes a bare #Job a dev job that release builds strip, and .Internal jobs are never reachable from the command line.

Still open: the owner's comment ratifying D-JOB-ARGV1 says to use job instead of jobs. The spec records it as an open question on card #3684 (Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:6663-6665). Under A it covers only the listing command.

What stays the same in every option. jet run, jet build, jet dev and jet test keep running fn run, fn build, fn dev and fn test (D-ROLEFILE1, D-CMDOVERRIDE1). jet run -- deploy keeps working, because the built program's own job table picks the job (D-JOB-SUBCMD1=C).

Clarity rewrite: four draft losses of A were reviewed. The flag position is D-JOB-ARGV1's existing rule, not a new cost. The unknown-word lookup reads only job names, an implementation cost. The jet jobs <name> retirement is a one-time cutover with a teaching error. A job named like a folder winning over the folder shortcut is stated in A's rules below.

options.name: Jobs at the top level, names must not clash
options.detail:
jet X looks up X in one fixed order. First, Jet's own command X. Second, the current project's #Job X. Third, a retired or moved spelling, which is taught as today. Fourth, a source file or folder named X, run as today. Fifth, a program named jet-X on PATH. Otherwise E2101, whose did-you-mean searches commands and jobs.

A job named like any of the 62 Jet commands is a compile error naming the clash and a fix. When a new Jet release adds a command, a job with that name fails the same way on the next build. Retired words are not reserved.

A job beats a same-named file or folder; jet run X still runs the path, and a word ending in .jet always names a file. .Internal jobs are never found, and outside a project the job step is skipped.

Arguments follow D-JOB-ARGV1 with jet in place of jet jobs: Jet's flags before the job name, the job's words after it. jet jobs with no name lists the jobs, and its --graph, --status, --explain and --watch views stay. jet jobs <name> retires with a teaching error that names jet <name>.
options.technical: Front.jet gains a project job lookup between the command check and the PATH lookup. It reads job names from the parsed project sources, so an unknown word costs a parse, not a build. The clash check extends E0928 and reads the same command registry the help text reads. Amends D-DX-JOBS-UX1=E, D-JOB-ARGV1=A and D-JOB-NAMES1=A. Examples, help text and shell completion migrate from jet jobs deploy to jet deploy in one cutover, with no alias.
options.code:
#Job fn deploy(region: String) { ship(region) }

$ jet deploy --region eu    // runs the job
$ jet jobs                  // lists jobs
#Job fn lint() { ... }      // error: lint is a Jet command; rename the job

options.name: Keep jet jobs X
options.detail: Nothing changes. Jobs run as jet jobs X, may use any name except run, dev, build, test, help and version, and never reach the top level. The owner's open note to spell the runner job instead of jobs still needs an answer.
options.technical: D-DX-JOBS-UX1=E, D-JOB-ARGV1=A and D-JOB-NAMES1=A stay as ratified.

options.name: Top-level jobs, clashes allowed
options.detail: jet X runs the job X when Jet has no command X. A job may still be named lint; it runs only as jet jobs lint, because jet lint stays Jet's command. Both jet deploy and jet jobs deploy run the same job.
options.technical: Same lookup as A without the clash error. D-JOB-NAMES1=A stays.
options.code:
#Job fn lint() { ... }   // allowed

$ jet deploy             // runs the job
$ jet lint               // runs Jet's lint, not the job
$ jet jobs lint          // runs the job

comparisons.note: just runs recipe names as the first word.
comparisons.code:
deploy:
    ./ship.sh
$ just deploy
# https://just.systems/man/en/

comparisons.note: Cargo looks up a built-in command first, then an alias, then cargo-X on PATH. An alias may not redefine a built-in command.
comparisons.code:
$ cargo b          # alias for build
$ cargo expand     # runs cargo-expand from PATH
# https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/external-tools.html#custom-subcommands

recommendation.why: jet run and jet build already run your project's own code. A extends that to every job with one fixed lookup order, and the name rule keeps each first word meaning one thing.
gains: jet deploy just works, like just deploy.
Every first word has one meaning in a given project.
One lookup order covers commands, jobs and programs on PATH.

losses.loss: A job cannot use a Jet command name such as lint or check, now or after an upgrade.
losses.mitigation: The build error names the clash and suggests a rename. Common job names such as deploy, seed and serve stay free.

losses.loss: Scripts that type jet jobs deploy must change to jet deploy.
losses.mitigation: The old form gives an error that shows the new one, and jet jobs still lists every job.

whyNot.reason: B keeps an extra word on every job run, unlike jet run, jet build and every task runner users know.
C gives one job two spellings, and a new Jet command silently hides a job of that name.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jobs give up Jet's command names so every project chore reads as jet X.

decisions.title: Spell bit arithmetic as named methods; keep the marks for ownership and outcomes
decisions.situation: In Jet, the marks &, | and ! mostly say who may change a value or whether something failed: edit(&list) lets a function change the list. The same marks also do bit arithmetic, so flags & mask keeps shared bits and !flags flips every bit. A newcomer who just learned &list must learn a second, unrelated meaning. You are deciding whether bit arithmetic moves to named methods such as flags.bit_and(mask); we recommend yes, keeping side ^ 2 for power.
decisions.gist: Should bit arithmetic use named methods such as flags.bit_and(mask), so &, | and ! keep only their everyday meanings?
decisions.lesson: Jet's short marks mostly mean ownership and outcomes: &list lets a function change a list, ^item hands an item over, and ! marks failure. The same marks also do bit arithmetic, which treats a number as a row of ones and zeros. A moves bit arithmetic to methods such as a.bit_and(b) and keeps a ^ b as power. B also moves power to x.pow(n). C changes nothing.
decisions.explainer:
Plain words first. A sigil is a single mark that changes what the next word means. In Jet, &list passes a list so the function may change it, ^item gives the item away, and ~item passes a copy. A trailing ? or ! on a type names the success or failure side.

Bit arithmetic treats a whole number as a row of ones and zeros. Bitwise AND keeps a bit only when both numbers have it; OR keeps it when either has it; exclusive-or keeps it when exactly one has it; NOT flips every bit. Checksums, compression and encryption code use these all the time. Most other code never does.

Today Jet spells them with the same marks: a & b, a | b, a ~| b and !a on an integer. Shifts, a << 3 and a >> 3, have their own marks. Power is a ^ b, as on a calculator.

The compiler tells the meanings apart by position: &list stands before a value, a & b sits between two. A reader still has to learn both.
decisions.story: Ana has learned that &list lets a function edit her list and that ! means failure. Then she reads pack_u8(n & 255) in the encoding library and has to stop and ask what & means here.
decisions.inWild:
// Kotlin: bit operations are named infix functions, not sigils.
// https://kotlinlang.org/docs/numbers.html#bitwise-operations
val low = flags and mask
val all = a or b
val diff = a xor b
val flipped = flags.inv()
val shifted = 1 shl 3
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-04. Bit operators appear in ordinary Core code, for example n & 255 in Core/encoding/binary.jet:39 and lo | (hi << 32) at binary.jet:123. Power appears in Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Types/Types.jet:1046-1049 as (2 ^ bits) - 1.

A rough count over git-tracked .jet files finds about 570 infix & uses in 140 files and 248 ~| uses in 41 files. Core/crypto leads both, followed by Core/encoding, Core/archive and the Jetpack store and Nix hashing code. Infix ^ appears about 26 times in 7 files. These counts include comments, so they are upper bounds.

The operators already lower through the names bit_and, bit_or, bit_xor and pow (Compiler/JetCodegen/Source/Codegen/Expressions.jet:356-358; Compiler/JetEval/Source/Routes/Prelude.jet:24). Sema accepts them on integers only, with E0109 otherwise (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Expressions.jet:746-749). Core already has two named spellings beside the operators: math.pow for Float (Core/math/math.jet:121) and math.xor for Int (math.jet:358).

Ratified law this would amend. D-EXPOP1=A made infix ^ power so formulas read as in maths tools. D-XORSPELL1=A spelled exclusive-or as ~|. D-BITNOT1=A extended ! to flip integer bits. D-BITOREXPR1=A admitted a | b in value position. Option A amends the last three and keeps D-EXPOP1. Option B amends all four. One cutover migrates every caller, with no alias.

What stays the same in every option. Prefix &, ^ and ~ keep their ownership meanings (D-MEM1). The type-level | keeps union meaning, and pattern | keeps alternatives. Shifts << and >> stay. Generated machine code is identical, because the methods lower to the same operations.

A real cost example under A and B: SHA-256's choice step (e & f) ~| (!e & g) becomes e.bit_and(f).bit_xor(e.bit_not().bit_and(g)). A Core helper can name a repeated step such as this one.

Clarity rewrite: the draft listed ^ keeping two meanings as a loss of A. It is today's state and C's too, so it is no longer counted against A; B is the option that removes it.

options.name: Words for bit arithmetic, ^ stays power
options.detail:
Every integer type gains four methods: a.bit_and(b), a.bit_or(b), a.bit_xor(b) and a.bit_not(). The infix forms a & b, a | b and a ~| b retire, with their compound forms &=, |= and ~|=. Integer !a retires too, so ! works only on Bool again. Shifts << and >> stay. Power stays a ^ b, as D-EXPOP1 ratified.

Each retired spelling is an error with a teaching message and a fix that rewrites it, so h ~|= k becomes h = h.bit_xor(k).
options.technical:
The four methods are Core intrinsics on Int and every fixed-width integer type. They lower to the existing BitAnd, BitOr and BitXor binary operations and the integer Not (Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/AST/Expressions.jet:155-157,173). They keep the operators' typing rule: integers only, E0109 otherwise.

The lexer keeps ~| only to report the retirement. The parser rejects infix & and value-position | between operands with a structured fix. The fix follows the old precedence, so a rewrite never changes a result. Sema rejects ! on a non-Bool operand with a fix to bit_not.

math.xor (Core/math/math.jet:358) is deleted, because bit_xor replaces it. Core, Compiler, Jetpack, Examples and tests migrate in one cutover, and Syntax.rs and the lexical ledger update.

decisions.title: One growing home for future features and for intent written in code
decisions.situation: Jet keeps adding features, and a new built-in name could clash with a name someone already wrote. You also want people to state intent in code, such as this function must stay fast, because comments drift away from the code they describe. Jet already has markers, the #Name labels written above code, and one-line marker declarations. This vote decides where future names and your intent labels live, and what happens when they overlap. We recommend markers under an implicit Jet root: #Hot means #Jet.Hot unless you declare your own Hot, which wins with a warning.
decisions.gist: Where should future Jet features and your intent labels live, and what happens when your name overlaps a built-in?
decisions.lesson: A marker is a #Name label above code that the compiler reads. A marker declared in one line with no body is a pure intent label; adding a body later lets it check the code. An implicit root means every built-in marker also has a full name, #Jet.Name, that you only write when a clash needs it.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: a marker is a #Name label above code. The declaration marker Hot($sites: [.Function]) creates your label.

Placement metadata is $sites. Brackets hold allowed sites; .Function is the function-site enum value. The command jet inspect markers lists markers and supported sites. Prelude means Jet's automatically available built-ins; a row is one registered marker.

Under A/C every built-in has #Jet.Name. Under A, current-module source markers win over built-in bare names within that module only. Parent/sibling declarations do not enter bare lookup. Library/other-module markers need qualified prefixes under D-MARKER-MODULE1. For example, use web supplies #Web.Get. A declaration warning names both; default policy continues, deny policy stops. Root claims and missing permissions remain errors.

Two-module example: module a declares Hot and applies #Hot, meaning a's marker. Module b has no Hot declaration, so its #Hot means Jet's if available. Access to a.Hot from b must be qualified; it changes no bare lookup. This is proposed resolution, not today's checker.

Expert path: add a body to enforce a check. The call assert(target.name.starts_with("step"), "a hot function's name starts with step") tests the attached item. Here target is that item, starts_with tests its name's beginning, and assert stops on false. Function step_fast passes; walk fails with E0953. Body-less Hot checks nothing. The common effect limit -[!Mem.Alloc]> rejects allocation independently under every option.

Rename preview: jet fix proposes Hot -> UserHot, or the first unused UserHot2, UserHot3, and so on. The preview covers the declaration and all references resolved to it across the workspace, including qualified uses. It never changes #Jet.Hot or unrelated text. Missing dependent sources are named; no incomplete semantic rename is applied. Qualification reaches Jet's without renaming yours.

Permission example: after declaring Unsafe, #Unsafe("reason") attaches only your marker. It cannot authorize unsafe operations. The missing-permission error names #Jet.Unsafe("reason"). The formatter removes #Jet. only when the bare spelling resolves to the identical built-in row. It never redirects a built-in reference to yours.

Under A/C, ~ remains unassigned with an ordinary syntax error under D-S14-PAUSE. Copying stays x.copy().
decisions.story: Ravi's team writes // hot path above functions that must never allocate. Months later someone adds an allocation, and the comment stays. He wants the label to live in code, and he does not want Jet's next release to take his label's name or break his build.
decisions.detail:
Owner question q15v9vdc proposes an implicit Jet root and asks for a warning or error on overlap. A directly answers with default local precedence plus a declaration warning and an always-reachable #Jet.Name. C gives the same root with every overlap an error; B retains a separate unchecked tilde plane and does not answer the overlap problem.

Letters: A extends the former marker-home option; B stays the tilde option so D-SIGIL-FREED2's dependency holds; C is new. The former future-built-ins-only prefix is withdrawn: every built-in gets the root now.

Current evidence from the supplied 2026-10-05 probes: Numeric declarations and applications triggered both built-in E0355 site checks and local site checks; a local Unsafe still triggered built-in E3112. Thus today's rows silently combine rather than selecting one. These are recorded observations, not rerun by this review.

Resolution under A/C follows the module boundary stated in the explainer and public-by-default visibility directive 21; the root adds no privacy or re-export rule. Registration remains mandatory (D-MARK-REG1). Jet's root names built-in markers only, not core.lang types. The marker Hot used here is a hypothetical future built-in, not a current API claim.

Default marker-name overlaps under A do not break an upgrade. That is not an unconditional upgrade guarantee: deny-warning policy, newly reserved jet module/import names, missing built-in permission, and unrelated language changes may still stop a build. A package may set policy: { lints: { deny: ["marker_shadows_builtin"] } }, producing E1293. C intentionally trades upgrade resilience for no hidden built-in name; this is a valid stricter owner preference, not a claim that C is inherently unsafe.

The root is an implicit marker import. Scope and spelling do not create two semantic mechanisms: #Name is an elided qualification, and formatting must preserve resolved identity. Root reservation applies to Jet/jet marker, module and import-alias names that could claim that prefix. Other library markers remain qualified; no new unqualified library import is added.

Intent labels can still drift when body-less. Tools list them and expert checks or effect limits enforce them. Metrics and foreign-language analogies motivate the idea but do not prove Jet's behavior. A is retained because one registered marker plane, default non-blocking overlap and explicit built-in access answer the owner's suggestion without a new sigil.

options.name: Markers under an implicit Jet root
options.detail: Future features use markers or Core names; a new keyword or symbol still needs a ballot. Every built-in has #Jet.Name. Under A, a current-module source marker wins at the bare name with one declaration warning; default policy permits this ordinary overlap, and #Jet.Name still names the built-in. Root claims and missing built-in permission are errors, and teams may deny the warning. Body-less markers are searchable intent labels; bodies add checks. The tilde stays unassigned.
options.technical:
Bare lookup selects a source marker declared in the current module, otherwise a Jet Prelude row. No parent, sibling or dependency marker implicitly participates. Qualified library lookup stays D-MARKER-MODULE1/A and D-MARKER-CASE1/A. Both site validation and body execution use only the selected row; same-named rows never combine. #Jet.Name bypasses user lookup.

Each local overlap raises marker_shadows_builtin once at its declaration. Deny policy produces E1293. Rename preview and formatting preserve declaration identity as described in the explainer. Neither a local Unsafe nor any other same-named row inherits built-in permission. Jet/jet root claims error.

Registration stays D-MARK-REG1; resolution changes in both checkers. jet inspect markers lists sites, bodies and overlaps. ~ gets an ordinary syntax error, not a new teaching layer.

options.name: A tilde root for intent
options.detail: Any name after ~ is a free intent label with no declaration, such as ~hot or ~owner("ravi"). Jet keeps ~jet for its own future names. Tools list the labels, but nothing checks them, and they live beside markers as a second label system. Built-in markers keep their bare names, and today's silent clash is not addressed.
options.technical: Adds an unregistered annotation plane, which contradicts D-MARK-REG1's no-drift rule unless the plane is exempted by name. Marker resolution is unchanged.

options.name: Implicit Jet root, every overlap an error
options.detail: The same implicit root as A: built-ins are #Jet.Name, and the bare name means them. Declaring a marker with a built-in's name is an error at your declaration. Nothing is ever hidden. But a Jet release that adds a built-in with your marker's name stops your build until you rename yours, which jet fix does.
options.technical: Same root, resolution and root reservation as A. A local row with a Jet row's bare name is an error at the declaration, with a jet fix rename. Upgrades that add Prelude rows can therefore fail existing builds; release notes list new marker names.

comparisons.note: A local name wins over a prelude name, and std:: always reaches the original; #[expect] is a checked intent.
Names of the form __name__ are reserved; match and case became soft keywords.

recommendation.why: A gives features and intent one registered marker home. The root keeps Jet's marker reachable while ordinary current-module overlaps preserve user meaning under default warning policy; stricter policy and safety exceptions remain explicit.
gains: No new symbol or label plane.
Ordinary marker-name overlaps survive upgrades under default policy.
Jet's markers stay reachable as #Jet.Name.

losses.loss: A built-in now has two written forms, #Hot and #Jet.Hot.
losses.mitigation: jet fmt writes the bare form unless a clash needs the full one, so each site has one form.

losses.loss: Your marker hides a new built-in marker with the same bare name.
losses.mitigation: A warning names both, #Jet.Name reaches Jet's, and jet fix renames yours if you prefer.

whyNot.reason: B adds a second, unchecked label system beside markers and leaves the silent clash in place.

C prevents hidden built-ins and makes overlap immediately visible, but a newly added Jet marker can stop an otherwise valid existing build. A prefers a default warning while allowing teams to deny it.

recommendation.tradeoff: One warning when names meet, and a full #Jet. name you rarely write, for labels that grow without breaking code.

decisions.title: What the freed ~ and ^ mean next: no job, Odin bit operators, or a pattern pin
decisions.situation: Jet just decided that copies and moves are written as words, so the ~ and ^ symbols lose their last jobs. Your notes suggest giving ~ the bit meanings it has in Odin. An earlier draft proposed ^ to compare inside patterns, because a name inside a pattern always makes a new name today. This vote decides what the freed symbols do. We recommend giving neither a job, so no old code can silently change meaning. The pattern gap closes now with the parentheses Jet already uses to compare text patterns.
decisions.gist: Should freed ~ and ^ get jobs, Odin bits or a pattern pin, or stay free, with parentheses for pattern compares?
decisions.lesson: A sigil is a single symbol that changes what the next word means, such as & in &score. Jet's rule, ratified on 2026-10-04, is that symbols mean ownership and outcomes, while arithmetic uses words. Once copy and move are words, ~ and ^ have no meaning. A pattern is the left side of an if-table arm; a bare name there makes a new name.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A sigil is a symbol that changes the next word, as & in &score. An error release is one released version in which an old spelling is only an error. Code checked with that release is migrated before any new meaning arrives; source first compiled after it, such as an old branch, is not protected.

Bit operations work on the binary digits of a whole number. Exclusive or keeps a bit when exactly one side has it: 5 is 101, 4 is 100, and 5 exclusive-or 4 is 001, which is 1. And-not clears from the left side every bit set on the right. Today these are methods: flags.bit_xor(4), flags.bit_not().

Not flips every bit. A signed Int stores negative numbers so that flipping every bit of x gives -x - 1, so not 5 is -6. On an unsigned 8-bit U8, 5 is 00000101, and flipping gives 11111010, which is 250.

A pattern is the left side of an if-table arm, such as .Val(x). A plain name inside it binds: it makes a new name for the value found. Writing .Val(wanted) when wanted already exists is error E0118, because the arm would make a second wanted. Jet already has a fix for the same trap in text patterns: wrapping the text in parentheses compares it, as in symbol == ("{root}jet").

Under A, the same parentheses work inside any pattern. .Val((wanted)) compares the payload with wanted, and .Val(other) still makes a new name. A missing name inside the parentheses is an unknown-name error, never a new binding, so adding or removing an outer name never changes what an arm does.

The example program. codes.first() gives the first item marked as present, Val(404); an empty list gives None. Regex{"^GET "} matches lines that start with GET and a space; that ^ is regex text and this vote leaves it alone. Two of the three lines match, so hits counts to 2, and the program prints 2 wanted 1.

Timeline. The copy and move cutover ships first; under every option its errors and jet fix rewrite old ~x, ^x, ~|, a ^ b and a &~ b. Under A, ~ and ^ then stay ordinary syntax errors, and the parentheses rule ships whenever it is built. If B or C wins, it turns on one release after the cutover, so that release serves as the error release.

Beginner path under every option: you never need either symbol. Writing ~board or ^held gives an error whose fix writes board.copy() or held.move(). Under A, writing .Val(wanted) for a taken name gives E0118 with a fix that writes .Val((wanted)). Expert path under B: ~, ~= and &~ are integer bit operators with Odin's precedence. Expert path under C: ^name inside a pattern compares.
decisions.story: Ravi ports a hash function from Odin and wants short bit operators. Mia's older Jet code still writes ~board for a copy. Both need a symbol that never silently changes what their code computes.
decisions.inWild:
// Odin overview, Operators: ~ is bitwise not and exclusive or, &~ is and-not
x := flags ~ 4
y := flags &~ 4
// Elixir: ^ pins a pattern to an existing value
case code do
  ^wanted -> "wanted"
  _ -> "other"
end
decisions.detail:
Revision, 2026-10-10, by BallotPolishA. The posted A held both symbols for one release and promised a follow-up vote. Its costs were a second vote, bit methods meanwhile, and a pattern trap left open. The owner ratified D-INTENT-ROOT1=A at 2026-10-07T20:38, after this ballot was posted. That decision keeps the tilde unassigned. The new A makes this final for both symbols and drops the scheduled re-vote.

A also closes the pattern trap now, with no symbol, by extending a ratified rule. D-PATTERN-HOLE-NAME1=A (2026-10-04) makes E0118 offer parentheses to compare a text pattern with an existing value. Probe s7 shows that message today: "Wrap the pattern text in parentheses to compare with the existing value." Probe s5 shows symbol == ("{root}jet") compares and prints same. A applies the same meaning, a value in parentheses is compared, inside payload slots.

Probes on dev-595e0dca3, 2026-10-10 ($JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/BallotPolish/probesA). s1: .Val((wanted)) in an arm is E0003, "Expected a name for a pattern binding". s2: if code == Val((wanted)) is E0003, "Expected a name inside Val(...)". s3: .Val(== wanted) is E0003. s4: .Val(wanted) is E0118, "The name wanted is already taken here". s5: matched :: code == Val(wanted) prints true. s6: .Val(404) in an arm is E0003 about range patterns, the known separate defect.

So parentheses have no meaning in a payload slot today, and A's rule changes no accepted program.

Precedent for marking a compare explicitly: Elixir's ^ pin, Scala's backtick stable identifiers, and Python 3.10's dotted value patterns all keep a bare name binding. Each marks the compare with its own existing syntax, so A uses Jet's.

Irreducible parts of A. Short bit symbols cannot come without B's two costs: a partial reversal of the 2026-10-04 rule, and stale ~x copies that would compute a bit flip. So A keeps bits as methods; a helper function names a repeated step, and the machine code is the same. Doubled parentheses come from reusing the existing compare mark inside an existing payload pair. A second mark such as == wanted would avoid them only by adding another way to say compare.

B and C are independent of each other. Under A, choosing B or C instead replaces the matching half: B gives ~ a job, and C replaces the parentheses rule with a pin.

Withdrawn options, each with its reason. ~ as a text-matches test would serve 17 regex tests and needs an exception to the symbol rule; is_match already reads well. C-family bits, ~x and a ^ b, change 2 ^ 3 from 8 to 1 and reverse the 2026-10-04 bit vote for both symbols. Odin's set (B) delivers the owner's bit idea and leaves ^ untouched.

Research record from D-SIGIL-FREED1, restated in current letters; where it names the posted A, read it as the hold-and-revote draft.

Owner direction, 2026-10-06 04:15: copies and moves become words, which frees the ~ and ^ symbols. The spelling of the words is D-COPY-MOVE-SPELL1; D-COPY-WORD1=A has since chosen x.copy() for copies. The owner wants to decide what the free symbols do, so every option below gives a concrete job a worked program. It is on card #4141, whose principle D-SIGIL-ALGEBRA1=B ratified on 2026-10-04: symbols mean ownership and outcomes, and arithmetic uses words.

Inventory of every meaning today, from crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax/ and the parser, checked on the dev candidate dev-595e0dca3. ~ has three. First, prefix ~expr makes a copy (D-SHAPE-COPY1, binary_unary.rs:854). Second, infix ~| and ~|= are exclusive or (D-XORSPELL1, math_layout.rs:447). Third, ~~ is lexed only to report the retired method connector, E0325. ~ has no meaning in types (xs: ~[Int] is E0003) or patterns.

^ has five. First, prefix ^place moves a name or field, takes a receiver as in ^buf.seal(), or marks a take argument (binary_unary.rs:785, providers.rs:42). Second, name: ^T and ^self declare take parameters (functions_params.rs:1086 and 1113). Third, task ^name { } moves a name into a task (primary.rs:981). Fourth, defer close(^res) is required. Fifth, infix a ^ b and ^= are power (D-EXPOP1, math_layout.rs:444).

What is actually freed. D-SIGIL-ALGEBRA1=B retires infix ^ (power, now x.pow(n)) and ~| (now bit_xor). D-COPY-MOVE-SPELL1 retires prefix ~ and ^, the ^T parameter mark (its default is move T) and task ^name. So both symbols become free before a value, between two values and in a type. ~~ keeps its teaching error. If the owner overrides D-COPY-MOVE-SPELL1 to keep ^T in signatures, only prefix and infix ^ are free; no option here uses type position.

Probes on dev-595e0dca3, jet run, 2026-10-06 ($JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/BallotSigils/probes; reviewer probes in $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/ReadSigilsA). The ballot program in today's words prints 2 wanted 1 (p16). Today ~n on an Int is a copy and prints 5, and 2 ^ 3 is 8, because D-SIGIL-ALGEBRA1 is ratified but not yet built (p6, q6).

The pattern gap, stated exactly. A bare name as a top-level arm already compares: if n == { wanted -> ... } tests n against wanted (q13). In an ordinary expression, matched :: code == Val(wanted) also compares and prints true (q15). But inside an if condition or a payload slot, a name binds, so .Val(wanted) -> ... and if code == Val(wanted) -> ... are E0118 (p9, q16). The same text means two things depending on where it sits.

Today's workaround is a separate test first, matched :: code == Val(wanted). Jet has no arm guards: an if after a pattern is E0003 (p9). A related defect, for a card under every option: integer payload literals do not parse. .Val(404) -> is E0003 about range patterns, while .Ok(false) and a top-level 404 -> work (q7, q12).

Other ways to close the gap. A pin, ^name (option C). Arm guards, .Val(c) if c == wanted -> ..., which are unratified and would need their own exact contract: a new arm form with its scope and effect rules. Or an Erlang-style rule where a name already in scope compares. The last one is unsafe under edits: adding an outer name silently turns a binding arm into a compare, and removing it turns it back. Today E0118 catches that, which is why Elixir, which allows rebinding, made the pin explicit.

Usage evidence, from git grep on dev-595e0dca3, 2026-10-06. Regex tests: 17 sites, all in Examples (12 is_match, 5 .matches), none in Core, Compiler or Jetpack. Exclusive or: 223 ~| sites (27 Examples, 133 Core, 51 Compiler, 12 Jetpack), mostly hashing and crypto. Infix power: about 26 sites in 7 files per D-SIGIL-ALGEBRA1.

The silent-meaning hazard. Under the withdrawn C-family bits, stale source keeps compiling with new results. ~n changes from a copy (5) to bitwise not (-6), and 2 ^ 3 from power (8) to exclusive or (1). That covers other branches, Jetpack packages, docs, generated code and habit. The withdrawn text-match option and C use positions that were never valid before, so they carry no such hazard.

Odin's bits (B), added 2026-10-07. The owner's scratch note reads "~ as not, complement with ~=, &~" (Tools/tower/.tower/scratch/owner-scratch.md:44). That is Odin's bit set: prefix ~x is not, a ~ b is exclusive or, and a &~ b is and-not (odin-lang.org/docs/overview, Operators). No other option offered it, so B records it here rather than in a new ballot. The note names ~, ~= and &~ but not infix a ~ b. B takes infix ~ from Odin, where ~= is its assign form.

B's hazard is smaller than the C-family set's, because ^ gets no new meaning, so 2 ^ 3 never turns into exclusive or. Two old forms still change. ~n changes from a copy (5) to not (-6). Today flags &~ 4 reads as a bit-and with a copy of 4 and prints 4, where B prints 1 (AliasBallot probe tilde2.jet, dev-595e0dca3). Infix a ~ b is E0003 today (tilde.jet), so it is a new position.

Where B beats A. Exclusive or is the most used retired bit operator, 223 ~| sites, far more than the 17 regex tests the text-match option would serve. SHA-256's choose step under A is e.bit_and(f).bit_xor(e.bit_not().bit_and(g)). Under B it is e.bit_and(f) ~ g &~ e. A keeps the longer form for the hold because the vote of 2026-10-04 chose words for arithmetic, and because B changes what old ~n and &~ compute.

Precedence migration. Today ~| binds looser than + and shifts (binary_unary.rs:620-658), so 1 ~| 2 + 3 is 1 xor 5, which prints 4 (AliasBallot probe xorprec.jet). Under B, infix ~ sits with + as in Odin's table. Swapping the glyph alone would give (1 xor 2) + 3, which is 6. So every Safe fix keeps the old grouping with parentheses: 1 ~ (2 + 3).

D-INTENT-ROOT1, on the same card, was ratified as A on 2026-10-07: markers under an implicit Jet root, and the tilde stays unassigned. Its option B, a free ~hot intent label, lost. So ~ has no claim from that vote, and A here matches it.

Candidates considered and dropped. Text joining with ~ (the D language, Raku) and approximate equality are arithmetic or text work. A weak link ~@Node is the one ownership-shaped candidate, but Swift and Rust write weak as a word and Jet already has Shared.Weak. Release this value now (C++ ties ~T to destruction) is covered by D-COPY-MOVE-SPELL1's standalone move statement. Swift's ~Copyable duplicates Jet's Close and #MustFinish markers.

More dropped candidates. An intent root ~hot belongs to D-INTENT-ROOT1. Objective-C block literals ^{ } duplicate Jet's lambdas. Pascal's pointer p^ duplicates Jet's raw pointers and @ links. Smalltalk's ^ return duplicates return. Power ^ was retired two days ago. A regex-style anchor ^ already works inside regex strings.

Parsing, per option. The withdrawn text-match option added infix ~ at the precedence of ==, not chained. The withdrawn C-family set brought back prefix ~ for bitwise not and infix ^ for exclusive or. B adds prefix ~, infix ~ at the precedence of + and -, and infix &~ at that of * and /, as Odin's table does; ^ stays an error. C allows ^name only inside a pattern; in a value it stays an error.

options.name: Both stay free; parentheses compare inside patterns
options.detail:
Neither symbol gets a job. After the copy and move cutover, ~ and ^ are ordinary syntax errors outside string and regex literals, as your intent-root vote already set for ~. A later job needs its own ballot, like any new symbol. Bit operations stay methods, as voted on 2026-10-04.

The pattern gap closes without a symbol. Inside a pattern, a value in parentheses is compared, not bound: .Val((wanted)) compares, and .Val(other) still makes a new name. These are the parentheses Jet already uses to compare text patterns.
options.technical:
Lexing: Tilde and Caret stay tokens only to report them. The copy and move cutover owns the fixes for old ~x and ^x (D-COPY-MOVE-SPELL1=A). The retired infix forms keep D-SIGIL-ALGEBRA1=B's fixes. a ^ b becomes a.pow(b), and a ~| b becomes a.bit_xor(b) with the old grouping. a &~ b and a & ~b become a.bit_and(b).

After that, both are ordinary E0003. Syntax.rs lists them as unassigned in the lexical ledger, with no revisit point. The stale doc comment at core_surface.rs:371 (~T = copy) is deleted.

Pattern rule: in a payload slot or an if-condition pattern, a parenthesized expression is a value pattern compared with ==, so its type needs Equal. It resolves in the scope enclosing the whole pattern, before any name the pattern binds, so .Pair(x, (x)) is an error asking for an outer name. The value is read once per test of that arm, not moved or copied.

A missing name is an unknown-name error. A bare name still binds. E0118 for a taken payload name gains the Safe parenthesis edit it already offers for text holes (D-PATTERN-HOLE-NAME1=A). Exhaustiveness treats a compared arm as not covering its case.

options.name: Odin-style bits: ~x is not, a ~ b is exclusive or, a &~ b clears bits
options.detail:
The tilde gets Odin's bit meanings. Prefix ~x flips every bit, infix a ~ b is exclusive or, and a &~ b is and-not: it clears from a the bits set in b. ~= and &~= assign. ^ gets no job. The methods bit_not and bit_xor are deleted, so each operation keeps one spelling, while bit_and, bit_or and pow stay methods.

Timeline. In the copy and move cutover release, ~x, a & ~b, a &~ b and ~| are teaching errors with fixes that keep their old meaning. B turns on one release later. Two old forms then compute something new: ~5 was a copy and becomes -6, and 5 &~ 4 printed 4 and becomes 1. Code checked with the cutover release has already been migrated; source first compiled after it is not protected.

The case for it: the owner's note asks for ~, ~= and &~, and infix ~ follows Odin. Hash and crypto code gets short again: SHA-256's choose step becomes e.bit_and(f) ~ g &~ e. That is a reading gain for experts, not a speed gain. Here ^ stays free and power keeps x.pow(n), so 2 ^ 3 never changes meaning.
options.technical:
Amends D-SIGIL-ALGEBRA1=B for the tilde only. Each operator keeps the operand rules of the method it replaces: integer operands of one integer type, E0109 otherwise; Bool keeps !. Width and signedness come from the type: on a signed Int, ~x equals -x - 1, so ~5 is -6; on a U8, ~5 is 250. Prefix ~ binds like unary minus. Infix ~ takes the precedence of + and -, left to right, and &~ that of * and /, as in Odin's table. ~= and &~= follow ordinary assignment: the left side must be a mutable place, evaluated once.

Tokens and lines. &~ is one token only when written with no space. A line that starts with ~ continues the line before, as other infix operators do. To start with a not, bind it, as in x :: ~y. ~~ keeps its retired-method error.

Migration in the cutover release. Every Safe fix keeps the old meaning, not only the old grouping. 1 ~| 2 + 3 becomes 1.bit_xor(2 + 3), and x ~|= e becomes x = x.bit_xor(e). Old a &~ b and a & ~b meant bit-and with a copy of b, so their Safe fix is a.bit_and(b), which keeps 5 &~ 4 at 4.

The and-not reading is offered only as a separate, labeled suggestion that changes the result: if you meant clear bits, write a &~ b once B turns on. The same holds for a nested right side, a &~ (b + 1), and for assignment, x &~= m.

Migration when B turns on. bit_not and bit_xor are deleted, and each call gets a Safe fix to the operator with its grouping kept. So 1.bit_xor(2 + 3) becomes 1 ~ (2 + 3) and still gives 4, where 1 ~ 2 + 3 would give 6. D-INTENT-ROOT1=A kept the tilde unassigned, so B would assign it here. Source: owner-scratch.md:44; Odin overview, Operators.
options.code:
fn run() {
    flags :: 5                 // binary 101
    print(flags ~ 4)           // 1: 101 xor 100 is 001
    print(flags &~ 4)          // 1: clears the 100 bit
    print(~flags)              // -6: on a signed Int, ~x is -x - 1
    small :: U8{5}             // 00000101
    print(~small)              // 250: 11111010
    bits := 5
    bits ~= 1                  // exclusive-or assign
    print(bits)                // 4
    print(1 ~ (2 + 3))         // 4: old 1 ~| 2 + 3, regrouped by jet fix
    print(1 ~ 2 + 3)           // 6: ~ shares +'s precedence, left to right
    e :: 6
    f :: 3
    g :: 5
    print(e.bit_and(f) ~ g &~ e)   // 3: SHA-256 choose step; 2 ~ (5 &~ 6) is 2 ~ 1
}

options.name: ^ pins a pattern to a value; ~ held
options.detail:
In a payload slot or an if condition, ^name compares against the existing value of name instead of binding, as Elixir's pin does. So .Val(^wanted) -> ... and if code == Val(^wanted) -> ... both compare. Outside a pattern ^ stays an error, and ~ gets no job.

Timeline. The copy and move cutover rejects ^x under every option. C turns on one release later; no old code changes meaning, because ^ was never valid inside a pattern.

The case for it: the gap is real and surprising, since code == Val(wanted) compares in a binding but binds in an if. The pin shows at the spot that this is a compare. Adding an outer name never changes its meaning, and removing the pinned name is an unknown-name error, never a silent bind. A does the same job with parentheses Jet already uses for text patterns; C costs one character less per compare. C needs a stated exception to the symbol rule.
options.technical:
Pattern parsing accepts ^ before a name or a field path in a payload slot or an if-condition pattern. It produces a value pattern that compares with ==, so the type needs Equal; otherwise the error names the missing Equal.

Scope. Every pin resolves in the scope enclosing the whole pattern, before any name the pattern binds. A pin never sees a name bound earlier in the same pattern: .Pair(x, ^x) is an error asking for an outer name. A field path such as ^cfg.code qualifies only if its root, cfg, comes from the enclosing scope. A missing name is an unknown-name error, never a new binding.

Evaluation. The pinned value is read, not moved or copied, and == runs exactly as it would in code == wanted, once per test of that arm. A pin in an arm that is never tested is never evaluated.

One spelling. At the top level of an arm table a bare name already compares, so ^name there is an error whose Safe fix deletes the ^. Exhaustiveness treats a pinned arm as not covering its case, so the table needs an else or a binding arm, as in C's code. Prerequisite shared by every option, as a bug fix: integer payload literals such as .Val(404) parse.

comparisons.note: Perl's =~ and awk's ~ test a string against a regex and give true or false. PostgreSQL also writes text ~ pattern. That was the withdrawn text-match option.
comparisons.code:
if ($line =~ /^GET /) { $hits++ }   # Perl
$0 ~ /^GET / { hits++ }              # awk

comparisons.note: A bare name in a pattern binds, even if the name exists; ^name compares against the value already bound. That is option C.
comparisons.code:
case code do
  ^wanted -> "wanted"
  _ -> "other"
end

comparisons.note: Erlang compares a name that is already bound, which silently flips when an outer name is added or removed. Rust has no pin and writes a match guard; Jet has no guards today.
comparisons.code:
{ok, Wanted} -> wanted;                 % Erlang: Wanted already bound
Some(c) if c == wanted => "wanted",     // Rust guard

comparisons.note: ^ is exclusive or in both. C writes ~ for bitwise not, Rust writes !. That was the withdrawn C-family option.
comparisons.code:
flip = flags ^ 4;   // C, Rust
inv = ~flags;       // C

comparisons.note: A bare name in a pattern binds; backticks mark an existing value to compare. Like option A, it reuses an existing mark instead of a new symbol.
Odin writes not and exclusive or with ~ and clears bits with &~; ^ is a pointer mark there. That is option B. Source: odin-lang.org/docs/overview, Operators.
comparisons.code:
inv := ~flags      // bitwise not
flip := flags ~ 4  // exclusive or
low := flags &~ 4  // and-not: clear bit 2
flags ~= 1         // exclusive-or assign

recommendation.why: Giving neither symbol a job means no old ~x or ^x can ever silently compute something new, and bits stay the words you chose on 2026-10-04. The real gap, comparing inside a pattern, closes now with parentheses Jet already uses for the same job in text patterns.
gains: No old code can change meaning under a new symbol job.
Patterns can compare with an existing name, with no new symbol.
One meaning for parentheses in every pattern: compare this value.

losses.loss: Bit-heavy hash and crypto code keeps method names instead of Odin's short ~.
losses.mitigation: That is your 2026-10-04 choice; a helper names a repeated step, and ~ stays free for any later ballot.

losses.loss: A compared name in a payload reads with doubled parentheses: .Val((wanted)).
losses.mitigation: E0118 offers the parentheses as a one-step fix, the same fix it already gives for text patterns.

whyNot.reason: B gives hash code Odin's short bits, but mixes ~ with bit_and and bit_or methods, partly reverses the 2026-10-04 rule, and lets stale ~x copies silently compute a bit flip.
C closes the same gap with a new symbol and an exception to the symbol rule, where existing parentheses already do the job.

recommendation.tradeoff: Method-named bits and doubled parentheses, for symbols that can never silently change meaning and a pattern gap closed now.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: SuiteBeginner. Skill: rli5. The beginner pass tested the complete ballot. Repaired: not on a signed Int, first() and Val, the regex count, E0118 and the release timeline are taught, and all letters are current.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: claude-opus. Adversarial model family: gpt. Fresh agent: SuiteAdversary. The adversarial review attacked the recommendation. Repaired: A's costs and safety are stated honestly, B and C can both win, B's old-form fixes keep meaning, and C's pin has scope rules.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Drafted by BallotSuite1 from D-SIGIL-FREED1; repaired by SuiteRepair1; revised by BallotPolishA on 2026-10-10 with a new A. The reader passes above reviewed the earlier draft; run fresh beginner and adversarial passes on this revision before posting. Full profile, because it touches Syntax.rs, the lexer and pattern parsing. When posted, close D-SIGIL-FREED1 as superseded by this ballot.

Cutover acceptance, every option, each a jet check probe after the copy and move cutover. ~board gets a fix that writes board.copy(), and ^held one that writes held.move(). 2 ^ 3 gets 2.pow(3), flags ~| 4 gets flags.bit_xor(4), and 1 ~| 2 + 3 gets 1.bit_xor(2 + 3). 5 &~ 4 and 5 & ~4 get 5.bit_and(4), which prints 4. Regex{"^GET "} and "~/notes" are unchanged.

Acceptance for A. A's program prints 2 wanted 1. After the cutover, ~x and ^x outside literals are ordinary syntax errors. .Val((wanted)) and if code == Val((wanted)) compare. .Val(wanted) for a taken name is E0118 with a Safe edit to .Val((wanted)). .Val((wantd)) is an unknown-name error, .Pair(x, (x)) asks for an outer name, and a value whose type lacks Equal names Equal. Removing the .Val(other) arm reports a missing case.

Acceptance for B, one release after the cutover. B's code prints 1, 1, -6, 250, 4, 4, 6 and 3, as its comments state. 1.bit_xor(2 + 3) gets a Safe fix to 1 ~ (2 + 3) and still prints 4. ~board on a non-integer is E0109. x ~= 1 on an immutable x is the ordinary assignment error. bit_not and bit_xor no longer exist.

Acceptance for C, one release after the cutover. C's program prints 2 wanted 1. Each arm in probe-errors gives its stated error, and probe-fallback compiles; removing its .Val(other) arm reports a missing case. .Pair(x, ^x) is an error. ^wanted at the top level of an arm table gets a Safe fix deleting ^.
