decisions.title: Clean casts: keep Float{count}, or write <Float>count
decisions.situation: Generic code no longer uses angle brackets, so a lone < or > now only compares. You asked whether the brackets could write clean casts, such as <Float>count, and earlier whether they could mark compile-time code, hold bytes or swap values. Today Float{count} already converts with a check, and the other ideas would be second spellings of things Jet has. The vote decides whether conversions move into angle brackets, which parse cleanly but give < a second role; we recommend keeping Float{count}, so every typed value starts with its type.
decisions.gist: Should a conversion be written <Float>count, or stay Float{count} with angle forms reserved?
decisions.lesson: A cast converts a value to another type. Jet writes both converting and building with Type{…}. The rule: if a parameter of that type would accept the one value inside, as a Float parameter accepts an Int, the value is converted with a check. Otherwise it becomes an item: [[Int]]{xs} builds a one-item list. A reserved form gives an error naming today's spelling.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A cast converts a value to another type, such as a whole number to a Float, a number with a fractional part. A checked conversion stops with error E3010 when the value has no exact match in the new type. 300 does not fit in a U8, a byte that holds 0 to 255. 9007199254740993 is within Float's range but has no exact Float, so it stops too. A reserved form has no meaning yet and gives an error that names the right spelling.

How Type{…} decides today. When the braces hold one value, Jet first asks whether a parameter of that type would accept it. A Float parameter accepts an Int, with the check above, so Float{count} converts count. A [[Int]] parameter does not accept xs, a [Int] list, so [[Int]]{xs} builds a list holding xs, of length 1. Under A both readings stay; under B the converting reading moves to <Float>count.

Literals take the type they are written for. 2.5 inside Float{2.5} becomes a Float. Bound first, x :: 2.5 takes Jet's default, Decimal, and a Float parameter does not accept a Decimal, so Float{x} is E0108. Under both options, write the literal as Float{2.5}. A literal that cannot fit, such as U8{300}, is a compile-time error; only values known at run time stop with E3010.

Beginner path under A: write Float{count}; writing <Float>count gives an error whose fix writes Float{count}. Beginner path under B: write <Float>count; writing Float{count} gives an error whose fix writes <Float>count. Under both, named conversions such as U8.from_int(x) and Int.parse(text) report failure as a value instead of stopping. They are expert reference, the same under A and B, and not taught here.

Expert path under B: the prefix binds like unary minus, so <Float>xs.len() converts the length, and jet fix keeps grouping, as in <Float>(a + b).

Parsing. Under B, <Float> can only appear where a value starts, and a comparison < only between two values, so the parser never guesses. Rust's ::< and C++'s >> rule are not needed. The cost is for readers: < has two roles to learn. Doubled angles stay shifts and <: :> stay fences under both options.
decisions.story: Tom sees a > b and c < d in a loop condition. He is glad he never has to wonder whether one of them opens a bracket.
decisions.detail:
Suite revision by BallotSuite1, 2026-10-07, repaired by SuiteRepair1 after the suite reader passes. This ballot replaces D-ANGLE-PAIR1, which offered four options, on the same card. Every letter below is a current letter: A keeps Type{…} and reserves the angle forms, B writes casts with angle brackets. Withdrawn options are named, not lettered.

Withdrawn options. Angle tags for compile-time code are a second spelling of the compile-time word, which D-COMPTIME-WORD1 settles. Doubled angles for byte data are a second byte literal beside [U8]{…}, and they reverse the 2026-10-04 vote that kept << and >> as shifts. The bowtie >< had no proposed job; it stays reserved under both options here.

Order and allowed outcomes. Vote D-MARKUP1 before this ballot. If it picks checked literal (its A) or labeled block (its C), both options here stand. If it picks bare markup (its B), a lone < where a value starts belongs to markup, so B here is withdrawn, as TypeScript forbids <T>x in .tsx files. No new disambiguation rule is invented. A then keeps only its >< and statement-start rows.

D-SIGIL-FREED2 and D-META-HASH1 are independent votes on other symbols.

What decides between A and B. Both convert with the same check, and both parse deterministically: a cast starts a value, while a comparison < sits between two values. So this is a reading judgment, not a parsing fix. B makes a conversion visible in plain source. A keeps the rule that every typed value starts with its type, and gives < one role.

A's cost is that Float{count} and [[Int]]{xs} look alike while doing different jobs; a reader needs the acceptance rule, or hover, to tell. B's cost is a second role for <, and legality that follows a value's type: changing x from Float to Int turns Float{x} into an error.

Research record from D-ANGLE-PAIR1 follows, restated in current letters.

Owner feedback, 2026-10-05: find a use for <> since they were retired in favor of generics via prep or comptime. Ideas: marking compile-time code like <if>, inline HTML, a bowtie >< and nested <<>>.

Jet today. D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1=A (2026-10-02) removes <> from generics. The dev candidate still accepts fn larger<T: Comparable>, because the cutover is unbuilt; its target spelling is fn larger(prep T: Comparable, a: T, b: T). Shifts << and >> stay under D-SIGIL-ALGEBRA1=B. Fences use <: and :> (D-FENCE2=A). Byte literals and byte patterns already exist as [U8]{"…"} (D-BINPAT1=A, D-UNIFYLIT1=A). A probe shows a >< b is a parse error today (E0003), so the bowtie is free.

Owner note, 2026-10-07: "Type conversions generally need casts, how can we make this clean? Maybe use <>?" (Tools/tower/.tower/scratch/owner-scratch.md:48). Option B records it. Jet today bans cast punctuation (D-SHAPE-CONVERT1=A, spec.md:108-109).

The D-DOTCTOR3 amendment of 2026-09-28 decides a one-value Type{value} by the value's type (spec.md:473-482, syntax-decisions.md:1004-1017). A value of the head type, or one a parameter of that type accepts, is used whole; that branch is today's checked conversion. It includes the checked Int to Float widening, which stops with E3010 when the whole number has no exact Float. Otherwise the head's literal notation applies, so the value is an element. Spreads and inferred-head bodies always use element notation.

Cast probes on dev-595e0dca3, jet run, 2026-10-07 ($JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/AliasBallot). Float{total} / Float{count} with 10 and 4 prints 2.5, and U8{big} with big = 300 stops with E3010 (cast.jet). <Float>count is E0003, "Expected a value, found <" (cast_angle.jet), so the prefix position is free. SigilRepair reran bytes.jet and cast.jet with the installed jet on 2026-10-07, and the cast results repeat.

Boundary probes from that run: [U8]{0x89, 0x50, 0x4E, 0x47} has length 4, [[Int]]{xs} with xs = [1, 2] has length 1, and Float{2.5} prints 2.5. An unannotated 2.5 is a Decimal, so Float{x} with x :: 2.5 is E0108 ($JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/SigilRepair/prec.jet).

Use counts, 2026-10-05, outside comments and strings. Spaced < comparisons: 159 in Examples, 1,162 in Core, 1,708 in Compiler. Shifts <<: 25, 140 and 48. Hand-written swap functions: one in Examples, none in Core.

What ambiguity costs elsewhere. Rust needs ::<> because a < after a name could be a comparison. C++ needed a C++11 rule so that >> can close two template lists. TypeScript bans <T>x casts in .tsx files and needs <T,> for generic arrows. C# keeps special rules for reading F(G<A, B>(7)). Jet escapes all of this once generics leave.

A prefix <Type> where a value starts would not bring these back, because a comparison < only appears between two values. Its one real clash is with bare markup tags, and only if D-MARKUP1 picks them.

Candidates. <if> resembles template languages and would be a second spelling of the compile-time word. Erlang writes byte data as <<1, 2, 3>>, but Jet already has [U8]{…} byte literals, and << is a shift. A >< b as swap is rare: one swap in the whole corpus, and Rust, Python and C++ use a function. Icon's :=: swap operator never spread. In relational algebra the bowtie means join, which Jet's query methods name in words.

A <Float>count cast borrows the spelling of TypeScript's older type assertion, not its behavior. The TypeScript handbook says an assertion is removed by the compiler, with no runtime check and no conversion. C's (float)x converts but can silently lose range, as (unsigned char)300 gives 44. B keeps Jet's checked rule. TypeScript later added x as T, because <T>x clashes with markup tags in .tsx files.

Suite pass repairs (SuiteBeginner and SuiteAdversary, 2026-10-07). The recommendation no longer claims B makes parsing guess; it rests on a reading judgment. The lesson states the real rule, parameter acceptance, with the one-item list beside the conversion, and the explainer teaches literal typing, U8's range and exactness.

B now has a full cast contract: allowed pairs, same-type and literal casts, aliases, generic code, tokenization and probes. The markup outcomes are stated, and both options show a whole program plus a stop probe.

options.name: Comparisons only; the pairs stay reserved
options.detail:
< and > mean comparison in ordinary code, apart from the shifts << and >> and the fences <: and :>, which stay. >< and an angle tag such as <if> or <Float> are teaching errors that name the right spelling. A keeps today's conversion rule and adds only these error rows.

Its cost: a reader must know the acceptance rule to tell Float{count}, a conversion, from [[Int]]{xs}, a one-item list. The text alone does not show it; errors and hover name the job.
options.technical: Adds retired-glyph rows for >< and for a tag-like where a statement or a value starts. At a statement start the error names prep if or prep loop. Where a value starts it names the markup block D-MARKUP1 chooses, and when the word is a type name, as in count, it names Type{value}. If D-MARKUP1 picks bare markup, the value-start rows are dropped, since that position is markup's. The rows apply to ordinary code only; text inside a library-checked block, such as in markup, is untouched. Removes the generic angle productions in the D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1 cutover.

options.name: Angle brackets write casts
options.detail:
<Float>count converts count to Float, with the type first. The spelling is C's (float)x and TypeScript's older <number>x. The behavior is Jet's: the same checked conversion Float{count} performs today, stopping with E3010 when the value has no exact match. C's cast can silently lose range, and TypeScript's <T>x only tells the checker a type, with no runtime check or conversion.

B moves one branch, not everything. Type{…} keeps building values and keeps using a same-type value whole. Only the converting branch moves: one value of a different type that a parameter of the head accepts, such as Float{count} with count an Int. It becomes an error whose Safe fix writes <Float>count. Float{2.5}, a Float value inside Float{…}, [U8]{42, 0} and [[Int]]{xs} with xs a [Int] stay as they are.

Named conversions such as U8.from_int(x) and Int.parse(text) stay.

The case for it: you asked for clean casts, and a conversion then looks different from building a value, in plain source without hover. Float{count} and [[Int]]{xs} no longer share a shape while doing different jobs, and the prefix parses deterministically.

Its costs: < gains a second role for readers, and which form is legal follows the value's type. Changing x from Float to Int turns Float{x} into an error whose fix writes <Float>x. It also amends two ratified rules, the ban on cast punctuation and the 2026-09-28 conversion amendment; that is informed acceptance, not the reason it loses.
options.technical:
Adds a prefix production <Type>expr where a value starts. Type is read by the existing type parser. Types no longer use angle brackets, so the first > at bracket depth zero closes it, and the > of -> belongs to the arrow. So <Pair(Int)>x, <?Int>v and <fn(Int) -> Int>f parse.

The prefix binds like unary minus: tighter than binary operators and looser than postfix calls and fields. So <Float>total / <Float>count converts both operands, <Float>xs.len() converts xs.len(), and <Float>count < limit compares the converted count.

Which casts are allowed. <T>x is allowed exactly when x's type differs from T and a parameter of type T accepts x; that is today's conversion branch, with the same check and E3010. Types compare by identity, so an alias of T counts as T. A cast to the value's own type is an error whose fix deletes the cast.

A cast no T parameter accepts, such as <String>n or <[Int]>text, is the ordinary type error, which teaches the named conversion. A cast never builds a collection or reads domain text: <[[Int]]>xs with xs a [Int] is an error, not a one-item list.

Literals. A literal operand keeps Type{literal}, as today: <Float>2.5 is an error whose fix writes Float{2.5}, so each literal keeps one spelling. Known-out-of-range literals keep their compile-time errors, U8{300} included; only runtime values stop with E3010.

Generic code. In a body with a prep type parameter T, a cast or conversion is checked once at the definition against T's bound, as D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1 checks bounds. If the bound does not guarantee acceptance, the definition errors, so the legal form never depends on a caller's type.

Grouping in the Safe fix. jet fix keeps each old body whole and evaluates it once: Float{a + b} becomes <Float>(a + b), and a method called on Float{count} is called on (<Float>count). A bare name, literal or call needs no parentheses.

Scope of the retirement. The fix fires only when the one-value body takes the D-DOTCTOR3 whole-value branch with a type other than the head. Whole values of the head type, element notation, spreads, inferred-head bodies, map bodies and domain-text heads such as Regex{"…"} are unchanged. So are literals elaborated against the head, such as Float{2.5} and U8{250}.

It reverses the cast-punctuation clause of D-SHAPE-CONVERT1=A and narrows the D-DOTCTOR3 amendment. Option A's teaching row for <TypeName> where a value starts becomes this cast.

Markup. B is ratifiable only if D-MARKUP1 picks checked literal (its A) or labeled block (its C). If D-MARKUP1 picks bare markup (its B), a value-start < already belongs to markup, and B here is withdrawn rather than given a new disambiguation rule.

recommendation.why: Both spellings convert with the same check and parse cleanly, so this is a reading judgment. A keeps the rule that every typed value starts with its type, and gives < one role.
gains: A lone < or > has one role for readers in ordinary code.

whyNot.reason: B shows a conversion plainly in source and parses deterministically, a real reading gain. It loses on judgment: < takes a second role, typed values stop sharing one shape, and a type change can make Float{x} illegal.

recommendation.tradeoff: One shape for converting and building, in exchange for a < with one role.

decisions.title: Serialization options move onto #Codable
decisions.gist: Should the serialization markers become options on #Codable, keeping every current capability?
decisions.lesson: Serialization is controlled by seven type markers and two field markers besides #Codable. The proposal moves them onto #Codable as options. #Rename (all ten projections) and #Redact (debug output) stay separate. A silent conflict between #Discriminant and #Untagged is fixed either way (card #4153).
decisions.story: Rosa needs an enum tagged by a field. She writes #Discriminant and #Untagged by mistake, and Jet silently uses untagged.
decisions.inWild:

#[serde(deny_unknown_fields, tag = "kind")]
enum Shape { Circle, Square }
# serde gathers options in one attribute: serde.rs/container-attrs.html

options.name: Type and field options
options.detail: On a type: #Codable alone means both directions. Options: only: .Encode or .Decode; unknown: .Deny; tag: .External (default), .Field("kind"), or .None (untagged); from: .Base for distinct types; published for schema snapshots and migrations. On a field: #Codable(.Skip) or #Codable(.Flatten). #!Codable stays the refusal.
options.technical: Mapping: #Encode=only: .Encode; #Decode=only: .Decode; #DenyUnknownFields=unknown: .Deny; #Discriminant(k)=tag: .Field(k); #Untagged=tag: .None; #CodableAsBase=from: .Base; #PublishedSchema=published; #Skip/#Flatten=field forms. Combinations keep today's results: unknown: .Deny with published still rejects unknown fields; a .Flatten field still disables the top-level unknown check; tag applies to enums only. Keeps E2407-E2415, E0905, E0910. Evidence: card #4152; fact sheets FuseCodec, FuseStateOffCli, FuseCodegenFfi, FuseDerive; reader review ReadMarkerBallots (2026-10-01).

options.name: Type options only
options.detail: As A for the type options; #Skip and #Flatten unchanged.
options.technical: Same type mapping as A. Evidence: card #4152; fact sheets FuseCodec, FuseStateOffCli, FuseCodegenFfi, FuseDerive; reader review ReadMarkerBallots (2026-10-01).

options.name: Keep separate markers
options.detail: Nothing changes except the #4153 diagnostic.
options.technical: Current D-SERDE4/5/7/8 law. Evidence: card #4152; fact sheets FuseCodec, FuseStateOffCli, FuseCodegenFfi, FuseDerive; reader review ReadMarkerBallots (2026-10-01).

decisions.title: One CLI field marker: #Arg(flag_only:, short:, env:)

decisions.title: One marker shape: package markers add and reject; only Jet's markers change checking
decisions.gist: Should every marker be Jet code with one shape, with only Jet's own markers allowed to change compiler checking?
decisions.lesson: A marker such as #Codable attaches meaning to code. Jet has marker bodies that run at build time and a separate derive provider form. A checking setting is a rule the compiler enforces, such as effects or unsafe. Whichever option wins, use sites like #Equatable do not change.
decisions.story: Iris writes a marker that adds a to_row function to her structs. She wonders whether a library marker could also switch off safety checks without her noticing.

options.name: One shape, two tiers
options.detail: A marker declared in a package may read facts about its target, add ordinary items, and reject the program. It may not change compiler checking settings. Items it adds are checked like hand-written code, so a generated #Unsafe still needs its reason and is recorded. Only the built-in rows in Jet's Prelude change checking settings. A derive provider becomes a marker body that adds the same items.
options.technical: Today built-in rows come only from the embedded Prelude Markers.jet, and package markers are marker declarations in package source (Examples/features/comptime/prep_loop.jet:11). The proposal adds an explicit origin field so the checker enforces the tier. Migration: the 2 Prelude providers (Derives.jet:13,55) and 20 package derive declarations in 12 files. Unchanged: built-in derives implemented in the compiler, #!X refusals, auto-derive. Amends D-METADERIVE1 and D-ONCE-DERIVE1; extends D-META-USER1. Evidence: card #4152; fact sheets FuseCodec, FuseStateOffCli, FuseCodegenFfi, FuseDerive; reviews ReadMarkerBallots and LunaAdversarial (2026-10-01).

options.name: Two tiers, keep derive
options.detail: Package markers read, add, and reject; Prelude rows own checking settings; derive T.X { … } stays.

decisions.title: Named marker groups
decisions.gist: Should a project be able to name a fixed group of markers and apply it with one name?
decisions.lesson: Today a stack of markers is written #[A, B, C] at every use. A named group writes a fixed stack once. Gate markers, refusals such as #!Debug, and markers with varying arguments stay written at the site.
decisions.story: Theo's service has forty record types that all start with #[Codable, Equatable, Debug]. A new teammate forgets Debug on three of them.

options.name: marker Name = #[…]
options.detail: marker Model = #[Codable, Equatable, Debug] is a top-level declaration, imported and exported like any item. A group has no parameters. Members are active markers with fixed arguments. A member may not be a gate (#Unsafe, #Impure, #Nondeterministic, #allow, #Scrub, #FX), a refusal (#!X), a retired marker, or another group. #Model expands before checking, and each member is checked at the use site as if written there.
options.technical: Unknown group: today's unknown-marker diagnostic. Forbidden member: a new registered diagnostic at the declaration. Duplicates after expansion keep E0999 and D-MARK-STACK1 order. Needs a group row in the marker registry. Evidence: card #4152; fact sheets FuseCodec, FuseStateOffCli, FuseCodegenFfi, FuseDerive; reviews ReadMarkerBallots and LunaAdversarial (2026-10-01).

options.name: No groups

decisions.title: #Rename(.Camel) on a type replaces #RenameAll
decisions.gist: Should a type-wide naming style be written #Rename(.Camel) instead of #RenameAll(camel)?
decisions.lesson: #Rename("name") renames one field or variant; #RenameAll(case) sets a naming style for a whole type. Both rename, at two scopes. Whichever option wins, a field's or variant's own #Rename still beats the type's style.
decisions.story: Omar wants camelCase JSON keys for one type. He tries #Rename on the struct, it fails, and he has to learn a second marker name.

options.name: One #Rename at both scopes
options.detail: #Rename's first argument is a string or a NamingCase (.Camel, .Snake, .Pascal, .Kebab, .Screaming). A string renames one field or variant and keeps its projection arguments: json, cbor, csv, toml, yaml, xml, args, env, db, layout. A case is legal only on a type and covers exactly what #RenameAll covers today. Order: a format-specific field or variant name, then its plain name, then the type case.
options.technical: Rename gains the Type site; the parser tells the forms apart by argument type. #Rename(.Camel) is the only spelling; lowercase camel and #RenameAll leave the grammar, with E2409 teaching the new form. NamingCase is Core/compiler/lang.jet:85-92. Evidence: card #4152; fact sheets FuseCodec, FuseStateOffCli, FuseCodegenFfi, FuseDerive; reviews ReadMarkerBallots and LunaAdversarial (2026-10-01).

decisions.title: #State(A -> B) replaces #Transition(A, B)
decisions.gist: Should typestate use one marker: #State(S) to require a state and #State(A -> B) to move between states?
decisions.lesson: Typestate tracks which state a value is in. #State(S) means the method needs the value in state S. #Transition(A, B) means it needs A and produces B. The proposal writes that as A -> B, read as needs A, produces B. Whichever option wins, checks and errors stay the same.

options.name: #State with an arrow
options.detail: The argument is exactly a state name, or a state name or _ followed by -> and a state name. Nothing else parses there: no chains, no expressions, no _ on the right. #State(A -> A) means what #Transition(A, A) means. A state may be written plainly or qualified as Workflow.State.Pending, as today.
options.technical: A restricted marker-argument production, not a general expression. Malformed arrows: E0930. Unknown states: E0151. Wrong-state calls: E0150. Path warnings L0152 and L0153 unchanged. Needs parser, sema, formatter, and fixture rows for valid and malformed forms. Amends D-STATE1 spelling. decisions.lesson: These look like code-generation hints, but only #Scalar is a pure hint. #Inline(Always) is a checked promise, #Kernel is a checked safety proof, and #Static gives a constant a stable address. Whichever option wins, every check stays.

options.detail: Signature: #Codegen(inline: InlineMode = none, scalar: Bool = false) on functions and methods. Both may appear in one #Codegen; a second #Codegen on the same item is E0999. inline: .Always keeps its checked promise. Constant #Inline, #Kernel, and #Static stay.
options.technical: Keeps E0917-E0919 for inline: .Always and today's site errors for other sites. Evidence: card #4152; fact sheets FuseCodec, FuseStateOffCli, FuseCodegenFfi, FuseDerive; reviews ReadMarkerBallots and LunaAdversarial (2026-10-01).

options.name: Fuse all four
options.detail: Options keep their current sites: inline and scalar on functions and methods; kernel on functions; static and constant inline on constants. Writing an option on another site gives today's marker-site error for the original marker.

decisions.lesson: #Off removes a statement or block from every build. #DebugOnly removes it only from release builds. Release builds are the release and hardened profiles, and a custom profile named release. Both markers are type-checked in every build. Whichever option wins, behavior in each build stays the same.
decisions.story: Theo wants a statement off in release only. He finds #Off, then has to discover a second marker.

options.name: #Off with a condition
options.detail: The condition menu is closed: #Off (every build) and #Off(.Release). #Off(.Release) code runs in dev, debug, ci, and other non-release builds, and is erased in release builds. Code under either form is type-checked in every build, so a type error is reported even in a release build. Two #Off forms on one statement remain E0344, whose fix text now names #Off and #Off(.Release).
options.technical: Release builds are BuildProfile Release, Hardened, or a profile named release (Source/main.rs:595-598). Amends D-CANVASSTATE1=D spelling and the E0344 row text. Sites stay Statement and Block. Evidence: card #4152; fact sheets FuseCodec, FuseStateOffCli, FuseCodegenFfi, FuseDerive; reviews ReadMarkerBallots and LunaAdversarial (2026-10-01).

options.name: Keep separate markers
options.detail: Nothing changes.
options.technical: Current D-CANVASSTATE1=D law. Evidence: card #4152; fact sheets FuseCodec, FuseStateOffCli, FuseCodegenFfi, FuseDerive; reviews ReadMarkerBallots and LunaAdversarial (2026-10-01).

comparisons.note: Rust uses one cfg attribute with a condition. doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html
comparisons.code:
#[cfg(debug_assertions)]
println!("debug builds only");

recommendation.why: One marker with a condition reads as one idea.

whyNot.reason: B keeps two names for one family.

recommendation.tradeoff: A small migration for one presence marker.

decisions.title: #Arithmetic becomes a #Policy setting; #PubFile and #NoPrelude stay
decisions.gist: Which of #Arithmetic, #PubFile, and #NoPrelude should become #Policy settings?
decisions.lesson: #Policy holds scoped settings. Each setting has a compiler-owned rule for where it may appear and whether inner scopes tighten, override, or merge (D-MARK-SCOPE1). #Arithmetic picks overflow behavior per function or block. #PubFile and #NoPrelude change a whole file. Whichever option wins, behavior stays the same.
decisions.story: Rosa looks for overflow control in #Policy, where Jet's other scoped settings live, and does not find it.

options.name: Fold #Arithmetic only
options.detail: arithmetic becomes a #Policy setting allowed at function, method, and block scope, and refused at module and package scope, exactly like #Arithmetic today. The innermost declaration wins, and it never crosses a call: mix() keeps its own checked arithmetic. #PubFile and #NoPrelude stay, because the scope ladder has no file level.
options.technical: Adds an override row to the D-MARK-SCOPE1 applicability matrix. The key writes the same ArithmeticPolicyFact as #Arithmetic, with its source span, so lowering and operation coverage are unchanged. Keeps D-WRAP-SCOPE1, E0930, and E0355. Evidence: card #4152; fact sheets FuseCodec, FuseStateOffCli, FuseCodegenFfi, FuseDerive; reviews ReadMarkerBallots and LunaAdversarial (2026-10-01).

options.name: Fold all three
options.detail: As A, plus #Policy(visibility: .Pub) and #Policy(prelude: .Off) at a new file level. They apply to the whole file, keep #PubFile's priv exceptions and #NoPrelude's removal of print and input, and never leak into other files.
options.technical: Adds a File level to D-MARK-SCOPE1 with file-only rules and new placement diagnostics. Evidence: card #4152; fact sheets FuseCodec, FuseStateOffCli, FuseCodegenFfi, FuseDerive; reviews ReadMarkerBallots and LunaAdversarial (2026-10-01).

options.name: Keep all three separate
options.detail: Nothing changes.
options.technical: Current law. Evidence: card #4152; fact sheets FuseCodec, FuseStateOffCli, FuseCodegenFfi, FuseDerive; reviews ReadMarkerBallots and LunaAdversarial (2026-10-01).

comparisons.note: Rust keeps prelude control and visibility as separate attributes. doc.rust-lang.org/reference
comparisons.code:
#![no_implicit_prelude]
pub(crate) fn hash(x: u32) -> u32 { x.wrapping_mul(31) }

recommendation.why: Arithmetic is already a scoped, innermost-wins setting, which #Policy supports; file-wide markers would need a new file level.

whyNot.reason: B adds a ladder level and file-only rules for two settings.
C leaves a scoped setting outside #Policy.

recommendation.tradeoff: One migration puts every scoped setting in #Policy.

decisions.title: Generics the Zig way: types made by build-time functions, replacing <>
decisions.gist: Should Jet write generic types as build-time functions that return a type, as Zig does, replacing `<>`?
decisions.lesson: A generic type is a recipe that takes types, like a list of Int. Jet writes it `List<Int>`. Zig writes the recipe as an ordinary function that runs while building and returns a type: `List(i32)`. One idea then covers plain generics and picking a type by size. Unlike Zig, these options still check trait bounds once, where the recipe is written.
decisions.story: Priya writes a ring buffer for a game. Small buffers should live inline with no heap allocation; large ones should use a list. In Zig she writes one function that returns the right type. In Jet she writes two types and asks every caller to pick, and she reads generics in a second syntax, `<...>`, that ordinary functions never use.
decisions.detail:
Every spelling below for A and B is new, proposed syntax.

What changes under A and B. Every generic form moves from `<>` to build-time parameters and recipes:

- Generic type: `struct Pair<T> { first: T, second: T }` becomes `prep fn Pair(T: Type) -> Type { struct { first: T, second: T } }`. Use: `Pair(Int){first: 1, second: 2}`.

- Number parameter: `struct Inline<T, prep N: Int> { items: [T#N] }` becomes `prep fn Inline(T: Type, n: Int) -> Type { struct { items: [T#n] } }`. Value parameters are snake_case, like other values.

- Generic enum and alias: `prep fn Tree(T: Type) -> Type { enum { Leaf(T), Node([Tree(T)]) } }`; `prep fn Grid(T: Type) -> Type { [[T]] }` replaces `type Grid<T> = [[T]]`.

- Type choice: `prep fn Storage(T: Type, n: Int) -> Store(T) { if n <= 16 -> Inline(T, n) else -> Heap(T) }`.

- Generic trait: `prep fn Store(T: Type) -> Trait { trait { fn get(self, i: Int) -> T } }`.

- Generic function or method: `fn largest<T: Comparable>(items: [T]) -> T` becomes `fn largest(prep T: Comparable, items: [T]) -> T`. Build-time parameters come first, after `self` in methods. Several bounds keep the list form (D-VARARGBOUND1): `prep T: [Show, Hash]`.

- Impl blocks (new head grammar): the head declares the build-time parameters its body uses. `impl Pair(T: Type) { fn swap(self) -> Pair(T) { Pair(T){first: self.second, second: self.first} } }`. A trait impl repeats any bound: `impl Pair(T: Show).Show { ... }` implements Show for every Pair whose T implements Show. `impl Heap(T: Type).Store(T) { ... }` implements a generic trait.

- Generic modules (D-GENMOD1/2) keep their module declaration; only the parameter list and application change: `module cache(prep K: Hash, capacity: Int)` and `module cache64 :: cache(String, 64)`.

- Typed decode: `json.decode<Person>(raw)` becomes `json.decode(Person, raw)`; `tree.decode<T>()` becomes `tree.decode(T)`.

- Built-in shorthands do not change: `[T]`, `[K:V]`, `T?`, `[T#N]`, and function types.

Rules shared by A and B (all new):

- A trait in the type position of a build-time parameter or recipe result means "a type that implements this trait": `prep T: Comparable`, `-> Store(T)`. `prep T: Type` means any type. Mojo's trait-bounded parameters work this way.

- What is checked once: anything that depends only on bounds. Inside `largest`, only `Comparable`'s methods may be used on `T`, and a mistake is an error at the definition. A recipe declared `-> Store(T)` has every branch checked against `Store(T)` at the definition. This is the main difference from Zig, which checks generic bodies at each use (Zig issue #1268).

- What is checked at each use: facts that depend on argument values. Examples are the size of `[T#n]` and the chosen branch of a recipe declared `-> Type`. Unchosen branches are name-checked, as `prep if` arms are today (D-PREP-BRANCH1=A). Such errors name the use and the recipe line.

- Identity: the same recipe with the same arguments is one type, however often it is written. A branch that picks a declared type returns that type itself: `Storage(U8, 100)` is `Heap(U8)`.

- Arguments to recipes and `prep` parameters must be build-time values: types, or the D-GENMOD-VALUE1 value kinds (`Bool`, `Int`, `Char`, `String`, fieldless enums). A run-time value is an error. Types never exist at run time.

- Self-reference: when Jet starts building `Tree(Int)`, it reserves that name and identity first. Inside the struct or enum body, `Tree(Int)` then refers to the type being built; Jet does not run the recipe again. So `Node([Tree(T)])` is a normal recursive type. It is legal wherever today's recursive types are (behind a list, optional, or other indirection).

- Runaway recipes: a recipe whose arguments change on every call, such as `Deep(n) -> Deep(n + 1)`, never reaches a reserved identity. It stops at the prep step limit (D-PREP-FUEL1).

- Names: a `prep fn` whose result is a type or trait (`Type`, `Trait`, or a bound such as `Store(T)`) is PascalCase. Values stay snake_case, so `largest(Int, xs)` shows which argument is a type.

- Errors print types as written: `Pair(Int)`, `Storage(U8, 8)`.

- Function values: a generic function passed as a value needs an expected function type that fixes its build-time parameters. For example, `xs.reduce(larger)` works where the parameter type is `fn(Int, Int) -> Int`. Otherwise wrap it in a lambda.

The one difference between A and B: type arguments at calls.

- A: a call passes either all of a function's leading build-time arguments or none. Jet decides by count, never by guessing kinds. If the call has exactly as many arguments as the ordinary parameters, the build-time ones are inferred. They come from the arguments or the expected result. If the call has the full count, they are given. Any other count is an error showing both forms.

- A, defaults and variadics: a function with default or variadic ordinary parameters cannot be counted reliably. Its callers always pass the build-time arguments, and the error says so. Build-time arguments are positional, never named. This rule is new. Mojo marks infer-only parameters with `//` in a separate list, and Lean uses `{}`.

- No inference through a recipe: in `fn first(prep n: Int, s: Storage(U8, n))`, `first(buf)` cannot work out `n`, because many values of `n` give `Heap(U8)`. Callers pass it: `first(8, buf)`.

- B: as in Zig, every call passes its build-time arguments: `largest(Int, xs)`, `xs.map(String, fn(x) -> x.to_string())`, `Pair(Int).new(1, 2)`. Leaving them out is an error that shows the full call.

Laws amended by A and B. S26: build-time code may now create and select types through recipes; polymorphism stays traits-only. S33 and D-GENERIC-CALL1: no `<>` arguments. S45: the declaration spellings above. D-CONSTGEN1/D-CONSTGEN2: `<prep N: Int>` becomes a build-time parameter. D-GENMOD1/2: parameter and application spelling. D-PREP-FN1: `prep fn` gains a second role, type recipes. D-SERDE6/D-SERDE16: decode spelling.

D-META-GATE1=A refused use-site type factories. A and B amend that refusal, because a recipe is a type factory used at many sites. What stays refused: every recipe is written in a source file. Building types from reflection or editing other declarations stays behind D-META-OPTIN2=A. C amends only S26 and D-CONSTGEN1's "no type is computed".

Performance gate: the Storage case is a performance surface. Ratification needs a paired cell comparing `Storage(U8, 8)` (or `Storage<U8, 8>` under C) with a plain heap list on the ring-buffer workload.

Options removed from the earlier draft. First, "keep `<>` with no type choice". It avoided migration and kept the rule that build-time code never builds types. The owner ruled out migration as a reason and prefers the Zig model. C is the strongest form of keeping `<>`. Second, "computed shapes with no bounds". A and B can build new struct shapes in a recipe and still check bounds once. Migration of existing generic code is implementation work and does not rank the options.

Example outputs in the options are predicted from the rules above; none of these spellings can run today.

options.name: Zig-style recipes, types inferred at calls
options.detail: Generic types, traits, and aliases are `prep fn` recipes called with parentheses. Generic functions take leading `prep` parameters with trait bounds, checked at the definition. A call may leave out all of its build-time arguments when Jet can infer them. `<>` is removed.
options.technical: Recipes run in the prep evaluator and are memoized by normalized arguments. Bounds are checked once in sema. Types never reach run time, so every tier sees ordinary types.

options.name: Zig-style recipes, types always written
options.detail: Everything in A, but every call passes its build-time arguments, as in Zig.
options.technical: As A, with no inference of build-time parameters.

options.name: Keep <>, add bounded type choice
options.detail: Generics keep `<>`. A type alias may have a prep body that picks among declared types under one trait bound: `type Name<params>: Bound = prep { ... }`.
options.technical: Transparent alias; branch selection in the prep evaluator; every branch checked at the definition.

comparisons.note: Generic types are functions returning types; types are passed explicitly; bodies are checked per use (issue #1268).
Compile-time parameters with trait bounds; `//` marks parameters that are only inferred.
comparisons.code:
def averaged_poll[SensorType: DeflectionSensing, //](
    sensor: SensorType, samples: Int) -> Float64:
    ...
averaged_poll(sensor, 10)

comparisons.note: Angle-bracket generics with bounds checked at the definition; type arguments inferred.
comparisons.code: fn largest<T: PartialOrd>(list: &[T]) -> &T { ... }

recommendation.why: A gives Zig's reading model, where types come from ordinary-looking functions, while keeping definition-time bound checks and short inferred calls.

whyNot.reason: B makes every generic call name its types, even `xs.map(String, f)`, so Jet's most common calls get longer.
C keeps a second syntax, `<>`, that ordinary functions never use, and recipes can only pick a type.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet adopts Zig's recipe syntax but not its per-use checking of bounds, and adds one all-or-none rule for leaving out type arguments.

decisions.title: Narrowing authority to folders, files, hosts, and URLs
decisions.gist: How should code and manifests narrow authority to specific folders, files, hosts, and URLs?
decisions.lesson: Authority is what a program may touch: files, network, processes. A package manifest sets the ceiling, and `#FX(...)` narrows one block. Manifests can already scope a file grant, as "FS.Read:config/", but code blocks cannot, and network hosts are never checked. Every option keeps whole leaves like `FS.Read` working.
decisions.story: Sam ships a weather tool to his company. Security review asks one question: what can it touch? Today the honest answer is any file it can read and any host on the internet. Sam wants the manifest to say: the config folder and one weather host, nothing else, and for Jet to enforce it.
decisions.detail:
Conflicts and existing law: D-AUTHORITY-MODEL1=A (one rights tree) is kept. Scoped leaves are descendants in that tree, as `Authority::covers` already documents. D-AUTHORITY-MANIFEST1=A (one authority block) is extended, not replaced. The registered `#FX` signature `FX(Effect...)` changes to accept scoped leaves.

Option A reuses the rights strings that plugins and process specs already pass to `Authority.from_rights` (Docs/spec/spec.md:3989). Those strings become the printed form of the new typed values, so there is one meaning with one source spelling.

Edge cases A must handle. Path escapes through `..` or symlinks fail, because FS already uses no-follow, descriptor-relative opens. Each HTTP redirect hop is checked again. The check uses the requested host name, and IP literals must be granted explicitly. Ports and subdomains are written in the URL, as in `https://*.example.com:8443/`. Child processes inherit the narrowed set.

Rules A needs. The effective right is the manifest ceiling intersected with every enclosing `#FX` scope. A literal `#FX` scope outside the ceiling is a build error naming both. Manifest paths resolve against the package root and become pre-opened folders at start, so they do not depend on the working directory. Build-time proof covers only literal paths passed directly to Core calls; library functions declared `-[FS.Read]>` are checked at run time.

Network safety: host names are normalized (lowercase, IDNA, no trailing dot). Loopback, link-local, and private addresses are denied after resolution unless granted by an IP literal or `localhost`. The check runs on the address actually connected, on every redirect. A foreign child process cannot run Jet's checks, so inside a scoped block it runs only under the OS process policy or is refused.

Migration: the manifest string form `"FS.Read:dir/"` moves to `FS.Read("dir/")` in one cutover and stays only as display text. Unlike Java's SecurityManager, the check is lexical (block and package), not a stack walk.

Related ratified law (found 2026-10-02): D-CORE-FILEDIR1=A already ratifies a directory handle that does not follow symlinks; path-scoped rights should be enforced through that handle.

options.name: Scoped leaves everywhere
options.detail: Effect leaves gain an optional scope argument: a folder (trailing slash), a file, a host, or a URL prefix. The same typed values appear in `#FX(...)` and in `authority: { holds: { allow: [...] } }`. A literal argument outside every grant is a build error. A computed argument is checked by the shared runtime carrier before the call, and failure is a typed `AuthorityDenied` failure, never a crash.
options.technical: Scoped leaves are rights-tree descendants (`FS.Read:config/` under `FS.Read`). Sema proves literal calls; the Prelude carrier checks dynamic ones on every tier (I9). FS checks reuse descriptor-relative opens from FSRuntimeOps; Net checks run before connect and on each redirect.
options.code: #FX(FS.Read("config/"), Net.HTTP("https://api.weather.example/")) { ... }

options.name: Manifest strings plus hosts
options.detail: Keep the manifest's existing string form and add host scopes to it. Code keeps whole leaves. The runtime enforces the manifest's scopes.
options.technical: The manifest parser forwards strings to `Authority.from_rights`. No sema change.
options.code: allow: ["FS.Read:config/", "Net.HTTP:api.weather.example"]

options.name: Keep whole leaves
options.detail: No scoping inside Jet. Teams that need path or host limits run the program under an OS sandbox or a firewall.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: #FX(FS.Read, Net.HTTP) { ... }

options.name: Scoped handles
options.detail: Folder and host grants become capability handles (`Dir`, `HostClient`) opened from manifest roots, as WASI preopens do. Code passes handles; paths are relative to a handle.
options.technical: Builds on D-SCAP1 and D-AUTHORITY-SCOPE1's handle head and descriptor-relative FS.
options.code: config :: files.dir("config/")?("open")

comparisons.note: Handler-based policies with Allow, Mock, and Deny; symlinks are left to the runtime.
comparisons.code: access.read_file.allow_under(["fixtures"])

comparisons.note: Runtime permission flags per host and path; all code on a thread shares one level (docs.deno.com security).
comparisons.code: --allow-net=api.example.com --allow-read=/path

comparisons.note: Descriptor-relative filesystem; paths outside a preopened directory fail with not-permitted.
comparisons.code: preopened "config" descriptor

comparisons.note: Removed (JEP 411): permissions were global, stack-based, and hard to review. Jet keeps grants in one block per package.
comparisons.code: permission java.io.FilePermission "/config/-", "read";

recommendation.why: A gives auditors one readable list of exact folders and hosts, and stops literal mistakes before the program runs.

whyNot.reason: B leaves library code unable to narrow its own blocks, and strings escape the checker.
C keeps every Net.HTTP grant open to every host on the internet.
D is the strongest for files but threads a handle through every function.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet adds a runtime check before each scoped call, in exchange for exact, auditable grants.

surface.lesson: Authority is what a program may touch: files, network, processes. A package manifest sets the ceiling, and `#FX(...)` narrows one block. Manifests can already scope a file grant, as "FS.Read:config/", but code blocks cannot, and network hosts are never checked. Every option keeps whole leaves like `FS.Read` working.

current.note: Probe J4: manifests accept folder-scoped strings; `#FX` blocks reject them; hosts are never limited.

wild.note: Policies allow one host and one folder; everything else is denied. EYG guides/access_policies.md, commit 75f09475.

options.name: Scoped leaves everywhere
options.gist: A leaf may take a folder, file, host, or URL, in code and manifest.
gains: One spelling in `#FX` and in package.jet.
Literal mistakes fail at build time.
Hosts and redirects are checked at run time.
losses: Computed paths and URLs fail at run time, not build time.
Scoped `#FX` blocks gain a run-time check per resource call.

options.name: Manifest strings plus hosts
options.gist: Keep today's manifest strings, add hosts, and leave `#FX` whole-leaf.
gains: Smallest change: hosts join today's string form.
Reuses rights strings the runtime already parses.
losses: A library cannot narrow one of its own blocks.
Strings are not checked like code.

options.name: Keep whole leaves
options.gist: Narrow by leaf only; use OS sandboxing for paths and hosts.
gains: Nothing new to learn or build.
losses: A grant of Net.HTTP reaches every host.
Path limits need tools outside Jet.

options.name: Scoped handles
options.gist: Code opens a folder or host handle from a manifest grant and passes it.
gains: Escapes through `..` are impossible by construction.
No string-prefix matching.
losses: Every function that touches files takes a handle.

recommendation.why: A gives auditors one readable list of exact folders and hosts, and stops literal mistakes before the program runs.
gains: The manifest names exact folders and hosts.
Network access is finally limited per host.

losses.loss: Computed paths and URLs fail at run time, not build time.
losses.mitigation: A path built from user input is unknown until the program runs.

losses.loss: Scoped `#FX` blocks gain a run-time check per resource call.
losses.mitigation: Library calls carry whole leaves, so only the run time sees the actual path or host.

whyNot.reason: B leaves library code unable to narrow its own blocks, and strings escape the checker.
C keeps every Net.HTTP grant open to every host on the internet.
D is the strongest for files but threads a handle through every function.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet adds a runtime check before each scoped call, in exchange for exact, auditable grants.

decisions.title: Raising the prep step limit for intentional long build-time work
decisions.gist: When build-time code legitimately needs more than ten million steps, how does the author raise the step limit?
decisions.lesson: Prep code runs while Jet builds your program. A step limit stops an endless loop from hanging the build. Jet's limit is ten million steps per prep binding, and nobody can raise it. Zig and Clang let authors raise their limits. Whatever wins, the default limit and its error stay.
decisions.story: Wen builds a 65,536-entry lookup table at build time for a codec. The math is right, but it needs about thirty million steps. Jet stops at ten million and offers no way forward except splitting the table by hand.
decisions.detail:
Naming: the owner rejected "fuel" as theatrical. The plain name is "step limit", after Clang's `-fconstexpr-steps`. The marker is `#StepLimit(n)`, a PascalCase marker under D-CASING1. Diagnostics, docs, and the proposed manifest key use the same words. The evaluator constants FUEL_BUDGET and DEV_FUEL_BUDGET rename to match; that rename is implementation and needs no ballot. Names considered and dropped: `#PrepSteps(n)` reads like a measured count, not a ceiling; `#EvalQuota(n)` copies Zig but "quota" hides the unit; Lean's `maxHeartbeats` is as metaphorical as fuel.

Current law: FUEL_BUDGET (10,000,000) and DEV_FUEL_BUDGET (1,000,000,000) are documented as not user settings (crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/Interpreter.rs:15-30). E0952 is the registered diagnostic. Probe J1 shows E0956 instead today; card #4186 fixes that regardless of this ballot.

What a step is: one evaluated expression or statement in the prep evaluator. The count is deterministic, never wall time, so every machine stops at the same point. A new compiler version may count a little differently; the ballot does not promise identical counts across compiler versions.

Scope under A: the marker goes on a prep binding (`NAME :: prep { ... }`). Its limit covers all the work that binding causes, including every `prep fn` it calls. A `prep fn` cannot carry the marker, because a helper must not raise the limit of whoever calls it. Writing it there is an error that points to the binding.

Values under A: the value must be a positive Int literal. A value below the default tightens the limit. The limit is part of the cache key, so a tighter limit re-runs the binding and fails the same way every time. Call depth (1024) and collection length (1,000,000) limits stay fixed.

Packages: D-META-GATE1=A treats the build-time power ceiling as package policy. A package may set a maximum step limit in its authority block. A dependency's `#StepLimit` above the default needs a grant from the root package's authority block, so a library cannot silently slow every build.

Conflicts: S26 says prep work is limited but names no override. A registers one marker, so Syntax.rs and the marker registry change. Today `#StepLimit` is not a registered marker, so writing it now fails with the unknown-marker diagnostic.

options.name: Marker on the binding
options.detail: `#StepLimit(n)` may precede a prep binding. It sets the step limit for all work that binding causes. E0952's fix names the marker and the step count reached. A package may set a maximum in its authority block.
options.technical: The evaluator reads the marker's literal from the binding's checked facts. The value is part of the cache key.
options.code:
#StepLimit(50_000_000)
CRC_TABLE :: prep { crc_table() }

options.name: Package setting
options.detail: package.jet gains a new top-level key, `prep: { step_limit: n }`, applying to every prep binding in that package.
options.technical: Manifest key read by the driver and passed to the evaluator.
options.code: prep: { step_limit: 50_000_000 }

options.name: Fixed limit
options.detail: Keep the constant. Authors split work into chunks or move large tables to a build-entry generation step.
options.technical: No change beyond the rename of the internal constants.
options.code: CRC_LOW :: prep { crc_range(0, 32768) }

comparisons.note: Compiler flag for constexpr evaluation steps, outside the source. Default 1,048,576.
comparisons.code: clang++ -fconstexpr-steps=50000000 table.cpp

comparisons.note: Limit raised inside the comptime code; default 1000 backward branches.
comparisons.code: @setEvalBranchQuota(10000);

comparisons.note: Crate-wide attribute; limits recursion depth, not total work.
comparisons.code: #![recursion_limit = "256"]

recommendation.why: A keeps the safe default and puts each raised limit, with its size, right where reviewers read the code.

whyNot.reason: B raises the limit for every binding when one table needs it.
C forces awkward splitting for work that is correct but large.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet adds one audited marker, so large build-time work stays possible without weakening the default.

decisions.title: Struct-of-arrays chosen per collection with Columns<T>
decisions.gist: Should struct-of-arrays layout be chosen where a list is declared, instead of once on the struct?
decisions.lesson: Struct-of-arrays (SoA) stores each field in its own array, so a loop over one field reads memory in a straight line. Jet marks the struct itself `#Layout(columnar)`, so every list of that struct is SoA. Odin and Zig choose per list instead. Fixing the 15x slowdown in #2889 is required whatever wins.
decisions.story: Ana keeps game entities in one big list for physics, where SoA is fast, and a small list for networking, where whole structs are sent. Her `Vec3` comes from a math package, so she cannot mark it at all.
decisions.detail:
Conflicts: D-SOA1 and D-SOA2A=C ratified the type marker; D-SOA2B limits v1 to whole-struct columnar; D-SOA2D keeps JSON identical between layouts. A retires the marker and keeps D-SOA2D's serialization rule for `Columns<T>`. D-SOA-TIER1=A (how dev tiers run a columnar list) applies to `Columns<T>` unchanged.

Two defects block any option: #2889 (columnar runs 15x slower than AoS, with no vector math in the packed path) and #4187 (jet run crashes on the columnar example). The ballot decides the surface; those cards decide speed and correctness.

Under A, `ps.y` returns a column view, so `ps.y.sum()` can vectorize directly. Zig exposes the same through `items(.y)`.

`Columns<T>` is a compiler-provided Core type, like today's columnar list. It is not built from reflection, which D-META-GATE1 and D-META-OPTIN2 refuse in standard code. Performance gate: ratification waits on a paired cell comparing `Columns<T>` with an array-of-structs list on the #2889 workload, under the strict comparator.

Related ratified law (found 2026-10-02): D-ACCEL1=A lets Jet make measured automatic column copies and parallel loops behind a run-time gate. Any explicit columnar surface must beat that automatic path in its paired cell.

options.name: Columns<T> replaces the marker
options.detail: `Columns<T>` is a Core collection for any struct T. It supports the list API: literal, push, index, len, and iteration of whole structs. Each field is also a column view, `ps.field`. `#Layout(columnar)` is removed in one cutover, and its uses become `Columns<T>`.
options.technical: Compiler-provided Core type with one buffer per field; field views are ordinary slices, so auto-vectorization applies. D-SOA-TIER1's tier rules carry over.
options.code:
ps := Columns<Particle>{...}
print(ps.y.sum())

options.name: Both forms
options.detail: Keep `#Layout(columnar)` as the struct-level default and add `Columns<T>` for explicit per-list choice. Both share one storage implementation.
options.technical: `[T]` of a marked struct lowers to `Columns<T>`.
options.code: other := Columns<Vec3>{...}

options.name: Keep the type marker
options.detail: No surface change; fix #2889 and #4187.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: #Layout(columnar) struct Particle { ... }

comparisons.note: `#soa[N]T` with `v[i].x` and `v.x[i]` both valid; addresses match (probe O1).
comparisons.code: v_soa: #soa[4]Vector3

comparisons.note: Library type; fields are separate slices.
comparisons.code: var list = std.MultiArrayList(Vector3){};

comparisons.note: Layout is a compile-time value on the tensor type (max/kernels/src/layout).
comparisons.code: LayoutTensor[DType.float32, Layout.row_major(64, 64)]

recommendation.why: A puts the layout choice where the performance need is, works for any struct, and keeps one mechanism.

whyNot.reason: B gives one storage two spellings, so readers must check two places.
C forbids AoS and SoA of one struct in one program.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet migrates the columnar marker once, so layout is chosen per list for any type.

decisions.title: One call spelling per function: ending the method and free-function dialect
decisions.gist: Should each function have exactly one call spelling, either `x.f()` or `f(x)`, never both?
decisions.lesson: Odin's author warns that methods split a language into dialects: `f(x)` in one file, `x.f()` in the next. Jet lets a `#Root` function be called both ways and keeps whichever you wrote. Methods may be declared only in their type's own module. Traits and Numeric operator hooks stay whatever wins.
decisions.story: Ravi reviews a pull request where one file calls `scale(total, 4)` and the next calls `total.scale(4)`. He has to check that they are the same function. He wants each function to look the same at every call.
decisions.detail:
Ratified law and its reasons: D-CALLDUAL1=E chose `#Root` for completion after a dot, left-to-right chains, and a rule that a dot which mutates is a method, since `#Root` is read-only. A and B keep all three. A carries D-CALLDUAL1's lookup rules over to extensions. Dot lookup goes only through imports. A real method with the same name is an error, and two imported candidates are an ambiguity error. Extensions take a read-only `self`.

A amends S27/D-EXTMETH1, whose orphan rule keeps `fn Type.method` in the type's source module, and retires `#Root`. The repository has one `#Root` use (Examples/features/functions/root_calls.jet). D-UFCS1=B rejected general UFCS, which E reopens.

Under A and B, a function may still be named as a value (`xs.map(Int.twice)`). Calling a method in qualified form, `Circle.area(c)`, is rewritten by the formatter to `c.area()`.

Operators are unchanged under every option: D-OPDEF1 hook traits, D-OPMIX1 mixed pairs, and the `Numeric` capability, which the owner judged a reasonable balance against Odin's no-overloading stance.

options.name: Extensions replace #Root
options.detail: `fn Type.method(self)` may be declared in any module. Outside the type's module it is an extension: read-only `self`, visible only where imported. Calling it as `method(x)` is an error with a fix. `#Root` is retired in one cutover.
options.technical: Dot lookup checks the type's own methods, then imported extensions; conflicts are errors as in D-CALLDUAL1.
options.code: pub fn Int.twice(self) -> Int { self * 2 }

options.name: Dot-only #Root
options.detail: Keep `#Root`. Its functions are called only with a dot; the prefix form is an error that `jet fmt` fixes.
options.technical: Amends D-CALLDUAL1's formatter rule.
options.code: print(5.twice())

options.name: Keep both spellings
options.detail: D-CALLDUAL1=E as ratified.
options.technical: No change.
options.code:
print(twice(5))
print(5.twice())

options.name: No methods
options.detail: Remove method declarations. Types carry data; behavior is free functions. Traits keep their signatures and dispatch on the first argument.
options.technical: Every S27 method migrates; dot is field access only.
options.code: print(area(c))

options.name: Dot for every function
options.detail: Any function may be dot-called on its first argument without a marker.
options.technical: Reopens D-UFCS1.
options.code: print(5.twice())

comparisons.note: Extension functions: dot-only, import-scoped, cannot override members.
comparisons.code: fun Int.twice() = this * 2

comparisons.note: No methods, no operator overloading, explicit procedure groups (probe O4).
comparisons.code: to_string :: proc{bool_to_string, int_to_string}

comparisons.note: UFCS: `x.f()` and `f(x)` are interchangeable.
comparisons.code:
echo 5.twice
echo twice(5)

recommendation.why: A leaves one way to declare a dot call and one spelling per function, and keeps dot completion and readable chains.

whyNot.reason: B keeps two ways to declare a dot-called function.
C keeps two spellings for one call, the dialect itself.
D migrates every method in Jet and loses readable chains.
E reverses D-UFCS1 and makes every dot an import search.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet lets modules extend types they do not own, so `#Root` and its second spelling can go.

decisions.title: Source file extension: .jet only, or an emoji alias
decisions.gist: Should Jet source files also accept an emoji extension, as Mojo advertises with its fire emoji?
decisions.lesson: A file extension tells editors, shells, and Git what a file holds. Jet uses `.jet`. Mojo's author called its emoji extension a fun first. Probe J12 found `jet run hello.🛩` already runs one file, because direct runs ignore the extension. Module imports still look only for `.jet`.
decisions.story: Zoe saw Mojo's fire-emoji files and asked whether Jet could do the same with a plane. She also found that her misnamed `notes.txt` ran as Jet code without complaint.
decisions.inWild:
$ mojo run hello.🔥   # Mojo talk, 2024
# Many plane emoji carry an invisible variation selector (U+FE0F), so two
# files that look identical may have different names.
decisions.detail:
Current law: N2 says the extension is `.jet`. Greenfield law forbids aliases without an owner-ratified exception that names its scope and removal condition, so B needs that exception.

Practical risks for B: some plane emoji include an invisible variation selector, so names that look the same can differ. Windows consoles, some CI log viewers, and GitHub language detection do not recognize emoji extensions.

options.name: .jet only
options.detail: Direct runs and imports accept only `.jet`. Other names get one registered diagnostic with a rename fix.
options.technical: Driver checks the extension before loading.
options.code: Error: Jet source files end in `.jet`

options.name: Add an emoji alias
options.detail: `.🛩` (U+1F6E9, with and without U+FE0F) is accepted everywhere `.jet` is. Tooling and editors learn both.
options.technical: Module resolution tries both names; the formatter and LSP register both.
options.code: use "./greeting"  // greeting.jet or greeting.🛩

options.name: Keep today's split
options.detail: Leave direct runs permissive and imports strict.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: $ jet run hello.🛩

comparisons.note: Advertised `.🔥`; current repository uses `.mojo` and `.mojoc` only.
comparisons.code: hello.🔥

comparisons.note: One ASCII extension each.
comparisons.code: main.rs  main.go  main.zig

recommendation.why: A keeps one extension that every tool understands, and turns today's accidental acceptance into a clear message.

whyNot.reason: B adds a second spelling and breaks some tools for a cosmetic gain.
C leaves files that run directly but cannot be imported.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet gives up a novelty extension so every tool sees one file type.

decisions.title: Replacing a Core service inside a scope, for tests and sandboxes
decisions.gist: How should a test or sandbox replace how HTTP, files, or processes behave, without rewriting the code under test?
decisions.lesson: An effect is work beyond computing, like a network call. Jet checks effects at build time and then erases them. EYG lets a scope answer an effect with its own handler. Jet already passes deterministic clocks and random sources as explicit handles (D-REPLAY1). Nothing can replace network or file calls today. Permissions stay with D-AUTH-NARROW1.
decisions.story: Lena tests a weather service. Her tests must not depend on the internet. Today she either calls the real server or rewrites every function to take a client. In EYG she would wrap the test in a handler. She wants that, with Jet's checks intact.
decisions.detail:
Why not key replacement on effect names: effect leaves are permission names, not operations. `FS.Read` covers read, list, stat, and open, each with a different signature, and Core's `http.get` declares `-[Net, Time.Wait]>`. Effects stay erased under A and B (Docs/spec/spec.md:1325-1329). Only C reverses the "effects are not handlers" rule.

A builds on D-CTX1 (`#Context(field: value) { … }`), which already swaps ambient fields such as the allocator and deadline. A adds Core service fields (`http`, `fs`, `process`) typed by Core traits (`HTTPTransport`, `FileSystem`, `ProcessRunner`). Spawned tasks inherit the provider, as they inherit deadlines today. A closure called after the block exits sees the provider that is current at the call.

Authority stays orthogonal. A provider's own effects are checked against the enclosing `#FX` grant, so a fake HTTP transport cannot read files unless the block grants FS. Foreign code (FFI) is never intercepted. Under the ratified `expert: .Deny` policy, release profiles can refuse `#Context` providers, and the lookup then compiles out.

options.name: Service providers in #Context
options.detail: Core defines one trait per replaceable service: HTTP transport, filesystem, and process runner. Core functions call the provider in the current context; the default is the real implementation. `#Context(http: Fake{})` replaces it for the block's lexical and dynamic extent and restores it on exit, return, `?`, or panic.
options.technical: One task-local slot per service, read by the shared Prelude carrier on every tier (I9). A provider failing returns its typed failure; a panicking provider unwinds like any call.
options.code: #Context(http: FakeWeather{}) { assert_eq(temperature("Oslo") ?? 0.0, 21.0) }

options.name: Explicit service handles
options.detail: Core exposes `Client`, `FileSystem`, and `ProcessRunner` handles with real and fake constructors. Testable code takes a handle parameter, following D-REPLAY1.
options.technical: No compiler change.
options.code: fn temperature(net: Client, city: String) -[Net, Time.Wait]> Float HTTPError! { ... }

options.name: Full algebraic effects
options.detail: Users declare effects with operations; `handle` blocks answer them and may resume once, many times, or never. Built-in effects become ordinary effect declarations.
options.technical: Needs delimited continuations or a CPS transform on AOT, JIT, interpreter, and web. FFI frames cannot be captured.
options.code: handle Fetch { get(url) -> resume(body) } in { ... }

comparisons.note: Delimited continuations; host sees UnhandledEffect for unknown effects.
comparisons.code: perform Alert(greeting)

comparisons.note: Inferred effect rows; `fun` handlers resume at once and compile cheaply.
comparisons.code: with fun ask() 21

comparisons.note: Dependency injection through an explicit client, like option B.
comparisons.code: func temperature(c *http.Client, city string) (float64, error)

recommendation.why: A gives EYG's main benefit, swapping a service for a scope, through Jet's existing `#Context` with typed fakes and erased effects.

whyNot.reason: B threads a handle through every function between the test and the call.
C needs continuations on every execution tier for a job providers already do.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet adds one context slot per Core service, so tests can fake services without new syntax.

decisions.title: A dynamic object type: growable fields, checked while running, with a real type underneath
decisions.gist: Should Jet have one dynamic object type whose fields can be added while running, like a Python object?
decisions.lesson: In Python you can write `row.qty = 4` on an object and it simply grows. In Jet a struct's fields are fixed when it is declared; only maps grow. A dynamic type is one real Jet type whose contents are checked while running. Jet already has one, `DataTree`, for parsed JSON, but it is clumsy to build and read. This ballot asks how far to go.
decisions.story: Maya is a data analyst moving from Python. She loads rows from several sources, adds computed fields as she goes, and only later decides which shape to keep. In Jet she must declare a struct before she knows the shape, or build `DataTree` values by hand with a wrapper around every number.
decisions.detail:
Today (ratified): `DataTree` is Jet's one dynamic value, with cases `.Object/.Array/.Int/.Float/.Text/.Bool/.Null` (D-ENC-DYN1). JSON, TOML, YAML, and CSV parse into it. Its Object case is already a growable map from String to DataTree. D-ANY-JAI1 rejects a general `Any` type. Building one by hand looks like Examples/features/serde/tensor_codec.jet: `fields := [String:DataTree]{}` then `fields["data"] = DataTree.Array(data)`.

How far each option goes. A gives growable data objects: fields hold numbers, text, booleans, null, lists, and nested objects. B is the full Python object: fields may also hold owned functions, structs, and resource handles, read and called by name while running. C adds nothing. The owner's request covers at least A; B is the complete version of it.

Under A (new), `Dyn` takes over DataTree's role and name. It is still one real type, a tagged value, with the same seven cases, so `match` on `.Int(n)` and friends works as today. JSON, TOML, YAML, and CSV parse to `Dyn`. On top of that:

- Fields with dots: `row.price` reads a field; `row.price = 2.5` adds or replaces one, on a mutable (`:=`) binding. `row[key]` does the same with a computed String key, and `row[i]` indexes an array (D-DATATREE-PATH1). Data keys have no visibility rules; any key can be read.

- Values go in without wrappers: assigning an `Int`, `Float`, `String`, `Bool`, list, or map of these into a `Dyn` place wraps it automatically. Typed structs go in with `Dyn.from(value)` when they implement `Encode`.

- Values come out typed: `row.price.decode<Float>()` gives `Float FieldError!`, a failure you handle, never a stop. `row.decode<Row>()` builds a typed struct the same way (D-SERDE16). Under D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1=A these become `decode(Float)` and `decode(Row)`.

- Arithmetic: `+ - * /` on `Dyn` gives `Dyn`, checked while running. An `Int` mixed with a `Float` gives a `Float`, as in Python. Any other mismatch, such as Text times Int, stops with a report naming both kinds. That is the same way a bad list index stops (S39). Code that must not stop checks kinds with `match` or uses `decode` first.

- Comparisons: `==` and `!=` give `Bool` and compare contents. Int and Float stay distinct (`1 == 1.0` is false), as DataTree's `equal_unordered` already rules. This holds even though arithmetic mixes them, and it differs from Python. `< <= > >=` give `Bool`, mix Int and Float like arithmetic, and stop on other mismatched kinds.

- No truthiness: a `Dyn` is never a condition by itself. `if row.active -> ...` is an error that shows `if row.active.decode<Bool>() ?? false -> ...`, keeping D-DATATREE-ERGO1's rule.

- Missing fields: reading a missing field stops with a report, like a missing map key (S39). `row.get("discount")` gives `Dyn?` instead. JSON `null` is a value, not a missing field.

- Changing kind: assigning a Text to a field that held an Int is allowed; the object is dynamic.

- Name clashes: `Dyn` has a small fixed set of its own methods (`get`, `has`, `keys`, `remove`, `len`, `decode`, `to_text`). A field with one of those names is reached with `row["len"]`. Writing `row.len = 3` is an error that shows that fix.

- Ownership: under A, `Dyn` holds data only, so it is an ordinary Jet value, copied or moved by Jet's normal rules (D-COPY-DEFAULT1). Two names never share one mutable object, so cycles cannot form. Shared mutable objects use Jet's existing sharing tools.

- Writing as JSON: every `Dyn` under A is data, so it encodes subject to the encoder's usual rules. For example, a NaN or infinite Float gives the usual encoding error.

- What A does not hold: functions, handles, or arbitrary structs. That keeps D-ANY-JAI1 (no `Any`) and keeps effect checking exact.

- Cost: every field read is a hash lookup plus a kind check. Only `Dyn` values pay it; typed code is unchanged.

- Where it may appear: anywhere a type can, including public signatures. `pub fn load() -> Dyn` is a written contract that says "dynamic".

Under B (new), `Dyn` is everything in A, and fields may also hold owned functions, structs, and resource handles such as open files. Borrowed references and values that must be finished on purpose (`#SingleUse`, D-OWES1) cannot be stored. Storing one is a compile error, because a dynamic box cannot keep their lifetimes or duties. This amends D-ANY-JAI1 (it is a general `Any` over owned values). B must keep, at run time, what the compiler checks today:

- Reading versus keeping: an unmarked read such as `row.file`, `row["file"]`, or the payload of `row.get("file")` is a borrowed view of the field. It can be used within the statement or lent to a call. It cannot be stored or returned, and it never copies or removes the field. To keep a value, take it out with `^` (below), copy it with `.copy()`, or convert it with `decode`. Each gives a fresh owned value.

- Calling stored functions: `row.discount(10.0)` calls a stored function by name. Suppose a parameter has a declared type, such as `p: Float`, and the argument is a `Dyn`. Then the argument is converted with the same checked rule as `decode<Float>()`. A mismatch stops before the call with a report naming the parameter. So `row.discount(row.price * row.qty)` works when the product is a Float.

- Stored structs: dot access reads a stored struct's fields, and a method can be called by name, both looked up while running. Every type stored in a `Dyn` keeps its field and method table at run time.

- Visibility: dynamic lookup sees only fields and methods the calling code could reach by name in typed code (`pub` and module rules). A private or missing member stops with a report.

- Receiver marks: methods that write or consume their receiver keep D-CAP-RECEIVER1's marks. `&row.cart.add(item)` writes, and `^row.file.close()` consumes and removes the field. A missing or wrong mark stops before the call, using the stored method table.

- Taking a value out: `^row.shape.take<Point>()` gives `Point?`. On a match the field is moved out and removed. On a mismatch the result is `None` and the field stays in place, untouched.

- Effects: Jet's effect checks erase after compiling today (spec.md:1335-1339). A function or method reached through a `Dyn` keeps its effect list. The call first checks that the caller may perform those effects; if not, it stops before running.

- Ownership: under B, `Dyn` is always move-only, because the compiler cannot know whether it holds a handle. `row.copy()` gives `Dyn CopyError!`. It copies data, functions, and copyable structs, and fails, naming the field, when it meets a handle. Dropping a `Dyn` runs the cleanup of any handle inside, as any owner would.

- Writing as JSON: a `Dyn` holding a function, struct, or handle gives an encoding error naming the field. It is never turned into text silently.

Under C, nothing new: build a `[String:DataTree]` map and read it with D-DATATREE-PATH1 indexing.

Not in this ballot: the earlier question, "may a file-private function leave out its parameter types?", is a separate axis. Leaving out a type does not mean `Dyn` under any option here. That question moves to its own ballot, D-INFER-HELPER1, which keeps its earlier main alternatives.

Conflicts: A amends D-ENC-DYN1 and D-SERDE13 (the name DataTree becomes Dyn) and S39's list of indexable types. B also amends D-ANY-JAI1, the effect-erasure rule, and copy defaults for `Dyn`. C amends nothing.

options.name: Dynamic data objects
options.detail: `Dyn` replaces `DataTree` as the one dynamic type and keeps all of its features: the same cases, every codec, pointer, patch, canonical bytes, events, and typed encode and decode. Fields are read and added with dots, values go in without wrappers, and operators are checked while running. It holds data only.
options.technical: A tagged value with an insertion-ordered String map for objects. Field access lowers to a map lookup plus a kind check. No change to typed code.
options.code:
row := Dyn.object()
row.qty = 4

options.name: Full dynamic objects
options.detail: Everything in A, and fields may also hold owned functions, structs, and handles, read and called by name while running. `Dyn` becomes move-only.
options.technical: Adds boxed arbitrary values and run-time effect lists for stored functions.
options.code: row.discount = fn(p: Float) -> Float { p * 0.9 }

options.name: No new type
options.detail: Keep `DataTree`. Build growable data as a `[String:DataTree]` map and read it with indexing.
options.technical: No change beyond D-DATATREE-PATH1.
options.code: row["qty"] = DataTree.Int(4)

comparisons.note: Plain objects keep fields in a dictionary, so they grow at run time.
comparisons.code:
from types import SimpleNamespace
row = SimpleNamespace(price=2.5)
row.qty = 4
print(row.price * row.qty)  # 10.0

comparisons.note: `ExpandoObject` is a real class; `dynamic` checks member access while running.
An index signature allows any key; `unknown` values must be checked before use.
comparisons.code:
const row: { [key: string]: unknown } = {};
row.price = 2.5;

recommendation.why: A gives Python's growable objects with one real underlying type, keeps typed code untouched, and needs no `Any` or run-time effect checks.

whyNot.reason: B adds a general `Any` and moves effect checks for stored functions to run time.
C keeps a wrapper around every value, so dynamic code stays clumsy.

recommendation.tradeoff: Mistakes inside `Dyn` values surface while running; typed code keeps every check before running.
