decisions.title: Actors as a Core library over tasks and channels
decisions.gist: Should Jet's Core library ship actors, tasks that own state and process messages one at a time?
decisions.lesson: An actor is a task that owns some state and handles one message at a time, so no locks are needed. Jet has tasks, typed channels, and race-free sharing rules, but no actor type. Mojo's author wants actors mainly as a library. Swift built them into the language. Tasks and channels stay whatever wins.
decisions.story: Bea writes three services, and each one has a hand-written loop that owns state and reads a channel. Each also needs restart-on-crash. She wants one tested actor she can reuse.
decisions.detail: Conflicts: none with ratified law. Tasks, channels, and sendability (Docs/spec/spec.md:2036-2140, D-CONC-UNIT1, D-CONC-CHAN1) stay the mechanism under A; actors are library code over them. C would add a keyword (Syntax.rs) and overlap tasks.

options.name: Library actors in Core
options.detail: `core.actor` provides spawn, send, ask with typed replies, and supervision strategies, written in Jet over task and channel.
options.technical: No compiler change; state stays owned by the actor task, so sendability rules apply.
options.code: c :: actor.spawn(0, handler)

options.name: No actor type
options.detail: Document the pattern; no Core module.
options.technical: None.
options.code: fn counter(inbox: Receiver<Msg>) { ... }

options.name: Language actors
options.detail: An `actor` declaration whose methods run serially, enforced by the compiler.
options.technical: New keyword, isolation checking, and await points.
options.code: actor Counter { ... }

comparisons.note: Supervisors restart failed processes; the model Jet's library would copy.
comparisons.code: spawn_link(fun loop/1)

comparisons.note: Language actors with await at every cross-actor call.
comparisons.code: await c.add(1)

recommendation.why: A gives the actor pattern and supervision with no new syntax, on top of checks Jet already has.

whyNot.reason: B leaves every service to rebuild the same loop and restart logic.
C adds a keyword and a second concurrency model for what a library can do.

recommendation.tradeoff: Core grows one module so services share one tested actor.

decisions.title: Write bit-exact data the way binary patterns already read it
decisions.gist: How should Jet write bit fields, such as packet headers and device registers, now that binary patterns can read them?
decisions.lesson: Jet's binary patterns read bit fields from bytes: `{version:U4}` takes the next four bits, high bits first. Nothing writes bits back the same way, so code shifts and masks by hand. The marker `#Layout(packed)` is reserved for bit-exact structs, such as a device's control register, but is rejected today.
decisions.story: Kai writes firmware for a sensor. He parses incoming packets with binary patterns in one line. Building the reply and setting the sensor's control register take a page of shifts, masks, and range checks.
decisions.detail:
Current law: D-BINPAT1=A reads widths U1-U64, high bits first, with `be`/`le` byte order (Examples/features/parsing/binary_pattern.jet). D-BINPAT1 declined packed structs as a second byte-parsing mechanism (its option C). D-BYTELIT1=B makes `[U8]{"…"}` a byte value; its typed holes are pattern-only today. `#Layout(packed)` reports E1105 (Docs/spec/spec.md:638, D-REPRC1). Typed flag sets over enums are measured on #3133.

Under A, a byte value hole `{expr:Un}` writes the value at that width. A numeric hole in a byte value must name a width, so text selectors (D-FMT-INTERP3) never mix with binary bytes. A value must be proven to fit, as with range types (D-RANGETYPE1); otherwise the byte value is fallible. In `==` pattern position, a holed literal is always a pattern.

A packed struct converts only to and from its backing integer (`bits`, `from_bits`); bytes go through patterns, where a hole may name the packed type. That keeps D-BINPAT1's single parsing mechanism. Fields are Bool, range types, fieldless enums, or sized integers. The total is any multiple of 8 up to 64.

Device registers: a packed value is one scalar. Volatile access (spec.md:1573-1574) reads or writes the whole backing integer at once, and a field update is a read-modify-write, never a sub-word store. Volatile use requires 8, 16, 32, or 64 bits. Reserved bits are an ordinary named field.

Conflicts: A extends D-BYTELIT1 and defines D-REPRC1's reserved `packed`. B adds a new integer family, against I8 and the beginner surface.

Adversarial review (2026-10-02) changed the field order to high-bit-first, removed width words from field types, and replaced overflow stops with range checks.

options.name: Writes mirror reads
options.detail: Byte values accept `{expr:Un}` width holes. `#Layout(packed)` structs pack Bool, range, enum, and sized-integer fields from the high bit, convert to and from their backing integer, and appear in patterns as a hole width.
options.technical: One bit codec shared with the D-BINPAT1 matcher on every tier; packed structs lower to one backing integer with shift/mask accessors.
options.code: [U8]{"{c:Control}{tos:U8}"}

options.name: Integers of any width
options.detail: Add `U1`-`U128` and `I1`-`I128` as integer types with their own overflow and widening.
options.technical: New integer family in sema, codegen, and every tier; packed structs use them.

options.name: Patterns read; code writes
options.detail: No change; `#Layout(packed)` stays reserved.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: U8.from_int(version * 16 + ihl)

comparisons.note: Packed structs are backed by one integer, but the first field takes the lowest bits.
comparisons.code: const Control = packed struct(u8) { divider: u5, mode: u2, enable: u1 };

comparisons.note: bit_field declares field widths over a backing type.
comparisons.code: Control :: bit_field u8 { enable: u8 | 1, mode: u8 | 2, divider: u8 | 5 }

recommendation.why: A reuses the bit order and width words patterns already read, so one vocabulary reads, writes, and lays out bits. No new integer family is needed.

whyNot.reason: B adds hundreds of integer types to solve a layout problem.
C keeps every writer on error-prone shifts and masks.

recommendation.tradeoff: Width words show up in two more places; in return, bits are read, written, and stored with one vocabulary.

It made fields fill from the high bit like patterns, used Bool, range, and enum fields, and replaced overflow stops with range checks. It also added pattern-position, volatile, and D-BINPAT1 rules.

surface.gist: How should Jet write bit fields, such as packet headers and device registers, now that binary patterns can read them?
surface.lesson: Jet's binary patterns read bit fields from bytes: `{version:U4}` takes the next four bits, high bits first. Nothing writes bits back the same way, so code shifts and masks by hand. The marker `#Layout(packed)` is reserved for bit-exact structs, such as a device's control register, but is rejected today.

current.note: Reading uses a pattern (D-BINPAT1); `be` means the high byte comes first. Writing the same header uses arithmetic that places each field by hand.

wild.note: The same bit syntax both matches and builds binaries.

options.name: Writes mirror reads
options.gist: Proposed: byte values take the same width holes as patterns. Packed fields fill from the high bit; `Int(0..3)` takes the 2 bits its range needs.
gains: One bit order and one width vocabulary for reading, writing, and registers.
A field literal that does not fit is a compile error.
losses: Byte values gain width holes, so numeric holes there must name a width.

options.name: Integers of any width
options.gist: `U1` to `U128` and `I1` to `I128` become ordinary integer types usable everywhere.
gains: Most general: any width works in any position.
losses: Over two hundred integer types with their own overflow rules.
Beginners meet odd widths in errors and docs.

options.name: Patterns read; code writes
options.gist: Keep patterns for reading and write bits with shifts and masks.
gains: No change.
losses: Every writer repeats error-prone bit arithmetic.
`#Layout(packed)` stays reserved.

recommendation.why: A reuses the bit order and width words patterns already read, so one vocabulary reads, writes, and lays out bits. No new integer family is needed.
gains: Packet and register code without hand-written shifts.

losses.loss: Width words appear in byte values and packed fields too.
losses.mitigation: Writing bits needs the same width facts that reading them does.

whyNot.reason: B adds hundreds of integer types to solve a layout problem.
C keeps every writer on error-prone shifts and masks.

recommendation.tradeoff: Width words show up in two more places; in return, bits are read, written, and stored with one vocabulary.

decisions.title: Let one function promise it never reaches #Unsafe code
decisions.gist: Should a function be able to promise, checked at build time, that nothing it calls reaches an `#Unsafe` block?
decisions.lesson: Only `#Unsafe` blocks may do things Jet cannot check, such as raw pointer reads. A package already lists which dependencies may contain them (the `policy.unsafe_deps` list in the package file). An effect row, written `-[ … ]>`, lists what a function may do, and `!` forbids something for everything it calls. No row can yet say that one function never reaches `#Unsafe` code.
decisions.story: Priya's payment app allows `fastsum`, a fast checksum library with `#Unsafe` code, for its reports. Her auditor wants the build to prove that checkout code never reaches it, even after a refactor.
decisions.detail:
The owner asked for manual memory to stay possible but be tracked as an effect. Most tracking already exists. D-AUTHORITY-GATE1 records every gate in one ledger, shown by `jet inspect gates` (D-CLI-ONE1). D-TEAMPOLICY1's `policy.unsafe` places gates in your own source. D-UNSAFE-DEPS1=A (ratified 2026-09-30, card #3977) lists the dependencies allowed to hold gates and pins their gate fingerprints in the lock. D-MEM-SENTRY1, D-HARDENED1, and D-MEM-GUARANTEE1 watch or fence gates at run time.

The remaining gap is per-function reachability. Under A, `Unsafe` is a deny-only root like `Panic` and `Mem` (D-EFFTREE1). It is never granted or listed, only forbidden.

Conflicts: A adds a deny-only root to the effect tree, an owner gate under I7 and I8. It does not overlap `policy.unsafe`, which governs where gates may be written. B makes the root visible in signatures, which changes D-HONEST-SIG2's views. I1's escape hatch stays `#Unsafe` under every option.

Adversarial review (2026-10-02) found that this ballot's first draft re-asked D-UNSAFE-DEPS1; the package-level option was removed.

options.name: A deniable `Unsafe` fact
options.detail: Reaching any `#Unsafe` gate kind (raw memory, consume, CheckedText.raw, crypto expert APIs) records the deny-only `Unsafe` fact on the enclosing function and its callers. `!Unsafe` in a row, or `--deny=Unsafe`, rejects any such path. The diagnostic prints the call path and gate.
options.technical: Built on D-UNSAFE-DEPS1's package-attributed gate facts. Opaque foreign calls fail closed. Open-world dispatch needs a sealed target set or a signed summary, as for !Mem.*. Vetted Core internals are sealed.
options.code: fn verify(data: [U8]) -[!Unsafe]> Bool { … }

options.name: Shown in every signature
options.detail: `Unsafe` is a visible effect that every reaching function displays, with no grant needed.
options.technical: Same fact as A, surfaced in inferred rows and honest-signature views.
options.code: fn report(data: [U8]) -[Unsafe]> Int { … }

options.name: Package lists only (as ratified)
options.detail: No per-function rule. D-UNSAFE-DEPS1 and policy.unsafe govern which packages and paths hold gates.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: policy: .{ unsafe_deps: .List(["fastsum"]) }

comparisons.note: forbid(unsafe_code) is crate-local; a safe wrapper hides its unsafe from every caller.
comparisons.code: #![forbid(unsafe_code)]

comparisons.note: Contexts in signatures make hidden capabilities visible to callers.
comparisons.code: function f()[write_props]: void {}

whyNot.reason: B floods ordinary signatures with a fact most callers cannot act on.
C cannot separate checkout code from report code in one package.

recommendation.tradeoff: Auditors learn one deny-only name; in return, a function can prove it never reaches unchecked code.

decisions.title: Let a trait author add a hint to the error when a type does not implement it
decisions.gist: Should a trait's author be able to add advice to the error shown when a type lacks the trait?
decisions.lesson: When a type lacks a trait a function needs, Jet's error says so and suggests writing the `impl`. The library that owns the trait often knows a better fix, such as a helper that implements it for you. Today a library cannot add that advice.
decisions.story: Omar uses a web library whose routes need a `Handler`. He passes a plain function and gets E0905 telling him to write an impl. The library's docs say to call `handler_fn`, but the error never mentions it.
decisions.detail:
The hint appends to the registered E0905 diagnostic. It never replaces Jet's What, Why, or Fix, so I4 stays intact: the code, text, and snapshot are Jet's. The hint is plain text with `{Self}` as its one substitution. It is shown in terminal, LSP, and `--json` output.

Core traits may carry hints too, but Jet's own advice for Core belongs in its diagnostics table, not in markers.

Conflicts: a new marker must be registered under the marker law (D-MARK-VOCAB1; #4152 is reworking marker families). No Tower decision covers library-authored diagnostic text.

options.name: A hint on the trait
options.detail: `#Hint(text)` on a trait declaration. Every unmet-bound error for that trait adds one Hint line.
options.technical: Marker row in Prelude/Markers.jet; sema stores the text on the trait; diagnostics renderer appends it to E0905 and related bound errors.
options.code:
#Hint("…")
trait Priced { … }

options.name: A hint on each bound
options.detail: `#Hint(T, text)` on a generic function adds advice for that function's bound on `T`, like Mojo's message on a constraint.
options.technical: Marker on functions keyed by type parameter; same rendering path.
options.code:
#Hint(T, "…")
fn total<T: Priced>(…)

options.name: Compiler text only
options.detail: No change.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: trait Priced { … }

comparisons.note: on_unimplemented sets message, label, and note for a trait.
comparisons.code: #[diagnostic::on_unimplemented(note = "…")]

comparisons.note: A conformance constraint carries its own message; the explicit-destroy manual uses it to name the required cleanup call.

recommendation.why: A lets a trait's owner teach its fix once, at the exact error learners see. Jet's own Why and Fix stay unchanged.

whyNot.reason: B repeats advice at every function and lengthens signatures.
C keeps library shortcuts out of the error where learners look.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more marker to learn; in return, library authors can explain their own traits at the point of failure.

decisions.title: 16-bit and 8-bit floating-point numbers
decisions.gist: Which small floating-point formats should Jet add for machine learning, graphics, and very large numeric data?
decisions.lesson: Jet has two binary floating-point types: `F32` and `Float`, which is 64 bits. Modern chips also compute with 16-bit and 8-bit floats. They halve or quarter memory use and run much faster in machine learning. Graphics shaders also use 16-bit `half` values.
decisions.story: Ana loads a language model's bf16 weights into Jet. Converting them to F32 doubles the memory, and the model no longer fits on her laptop.
decisions.detail:
Semantics under A: each `F16` or `BF16` operation rounds to its format after every step. Where a chip lacks native support, the operation computes in F32 and rounds, which gives the same result. This keeps I9 parity across AOT, JIT, interpreter, and web.

Widening follows D-VERDICT-1304-1: `F16` and `BF16` widen on their own to `F32` and `Float`. Narrowing is an explicit conversion. Lanes (D-LANES1, pending) and tensors (D-GPU-F32-STORAGE1) gain the same element formats.

Conflicts: D-NUMTYPE1=A listed Core number types beyond whole and decimal without small floats; A adds to that list rather than changing it. Performance gate: each new type needs a paired cell against F32 on a memory-bound workload.

options.name: Two 16-bit types; 8-bit for storage
options.detail: Add `F16` (IEEE binary16) and `BF16` (bfloat16) as number types. Add `F8E4M3` and `F8E5M2` as tensor and lane storage formats only.
options.technical: Hardware instructions where present (F16C, AVX-512 FP16, AMX-BF16, SVE BF16); otherwise F32 compute with per-op rounding.
options.code: scale :: F16{1.5}

options.name: Four full types
options.detail: All four formats are number types with arithmetic.
options.technical: Same lowering; 8-bit formats need saturation rules for every operator.
options.code: scale :: F8E4M3{1.5}

options.name: Storage formats only
options.detail: Tensors and lanes store small floats; every read widens to F32.
options.technical: Conversion at load and store only.
options.code: compute.zeros([n, n], storage: .BF16)

comparisons.note: Optional extended float types with standard names.
comparisons.code: std::bfloat16_t w = 0.5bf16;

comparisons.note: f16 is a primitive float type.
comparisons.code: const h: f16 = 1.5;

recommendation.why: A covers memory-bound models, meshes, and shaders with two well-behaved types. The tricky 8-bit formats stay inside tensors.

whyNot.reason: B exposes saturating 8-bit arithmetic as everyday types.
C leaves shader and kernel math without a half-precision type.

recommendation.tradeoff: Learners see two more types they can ignore; in return, models and meshes take half the memory.

decisions.title: Cleanup that runs only when a function fails
decisions.gist: How should a function undo half-finished work only when it fails, and keep it when it succeeds?
decisions.lesson: Some work must be undone only if a function fails. A half-written file should be deleted on failure but kept on success. Jet's `scope.guard` runs on every exit. A guard that checks a flag does not work, because the guard copies the flag when it is made.
decisions.story: Sam writes a report generator. When a check fails halfway, a broken report.tmp is left on disk. His guard with a `done` flag deletes good reports too, and nothing warns him.
decisions.detail:
Current law: D-DEFER1 option B made `scope.guard` the lexical cleanup mechanism; it runs on every exit (Examples/features/io/scope_guard.jet). `defer close(^r)` consumes a resource on every exit (Examples/features/memory/defer_consume.jet).

Under A, `scope.on_fail` uses the same compiler-owned guard carrier. It fires on the same failure exits as the type-level `on_fail` proposed in D-OWES1 option A: `return Err`, propagated failure, panic unwinding, and task cancellation. A success exit drops it silently.

Related law: named `#Transact(t)` blocks already have `t.on_rollback` hooks that run only on failure (D-TXN-ROLLBACK, Docs/spec/spec.md:1150-1155). They cannot serve here, because file effects inside the block are E0746.

Conflicts: none for A. B amends D-TXN2. D-OWES1 settles failure per type; this ballot settles it per site, for work that is not a typed resource. The flag workaround's stale copy follows the capture rule (Docs/spec/spec.md:714-718); a separate card asks for a warning.

Probe (2026-10-02, jet run): option C's code and the guard-with-flag trap both compile; the trap prints the cleanup on success.

options.name: A failure-only guard
options.detail: Add `scope.on_fail(fn)` to `core.mem.scope`. It returns the same must-use guard and runs its callback only on a failure exit, in reverse registration order with other guards.
options.technical: Compiler-owned guard carrier with a failure flag set by the failure-exit lowering shared with D-OWES1 on_fail; same on AOT, JIT, and interpreter.
options.code: _undo :: scope.on_fail(() -> remove_temp())

options.name: Stretch transactions
options.detail: Allow irreversible effects inside a named `#Transact` when an `on_rollback` hook is registered, and use that hook as the failure-only cleanup.
options.technical: Amends D-TXN2's E0746 irreversible-effect rule; reuses the D-TXN-ROLLBACK hook path.
options.code: #Transact(t) { … t.on_rollback(() -> remove_temp()) … }

options.name: Clean up by hand
options.detail: No change. Handle each failure locally.
options.technical: No change.

comparisons.note: errdefer, with an optional captured error.
comparisons.code: errdefer |err| log.err("{}", .{err});

comparisons.note: Scope guards with exit, success, and failure variants.
comparisons.code: scope(failure) remove(tmp);

recommendation.why: A puts failure-only cleanup next to the work it undoes, using the guard mechanism Jet already has, without weakening transactions.

whyNot.reason: B weakens the transaction promise and snapshots locals that only needed cleanup.
C leaks whenever one failure path is missed.

recommendation.tradeoff: Learners meet one more guard function; in return, undo-on-failure is one line placed beside the work.

decisions.title: Reading nested JSON without a struct: allow tree["user"]["name"]?
decisions.gist: Should untyped JSON support `tree["user"]["name"]`, the same indexing lists and maps already use?
decisions.lesson: Most programs should decode JSON into a struct, and that path does not change here. Sometimes you read JSON with no struct. Jet then gives you a `DataTree`. Today you walk it one level at a time with `.field("user")`, or pass a JSON Pointer string like `"/user/name"`. Lists and maps already allow `xs[1]` and `m["key"]`. This ballot asks whether `DataTree` should allow the same.
decisions.story: Lena moves a data script from Python. She reads a few fields from an API reply and does not want a struct for each one. In Python she wrote `data["user"]["name"]`. In Jet she writes one line, one `&`, and one fallback per level, or learns JSON Pointer strings with their own escape rules.
decisions.detail:
What exists today. These rules are ratified, and the example files exist in the repository.

- Typed decode: `json.decode<T>(raw)` into a `#Codable` struct (Examples/features/serde/json_typed.jet). This is the main path for JSON with a known shape. No option changes it.

- Untyped walking: `DataTree` accessors `.field(name)` and `.at(i)` return `DataTree FieldError!` (D-SERDE13/14/15, respelled by D-TYPE-SUFFIX1). Scalar reads are `.text()`, `.int()`, and `.bool()`, which fail on the wrong kind. `.to_text()` gives `String?` and also turns numbers and booleans into text (D-DATATREE-ERGO1=A). See Examples/features/serde/datatree_accessors.jet.

- Paths: `json.pointer(tree, "/user/tags/1")` reads a nested value with RFC 6901 JSON Pointer syntax, including its `~0` and `~1` escapes (D-CORE-JSON-POINTER1=A; Examples/features/serde/json_pointer.jet). The earlier draft's `.path("user.name")` option was invented and duplicated this, so it is removed.

- Lists and maps: S39 says `xs[i]` and `m[k]` stop with a friendly report when the item is missing, and `.get` returns an optional (Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:1309-1310). `?.` chains optionals (S71). A method that itself returns `T?` gives one `T?`, not a nested optional (Examples/features/syntax/optional_method_chain.jet:4-6, 72).

Under A (new, proposed), `DataTree` gains the S39 forms.

- `tree["key"]` reads an object member. `tree[i]` reads an array item. Ownership of the result follows list and map indexing.

- A missing key, an index out of range, or the wrong kind stops with the S39 report. Wrong kinds are a String key on an array, an Int on an object, or any index on a scalar. The report quotes the source expression and the failing step, for example: `tree["user"]["nickname"]: no key "nickname"`. It is built from the source text, so no path is stored at run time.

- A negative index stops, as it does for lists; it does not count from the end.

- `tree.get("key")` and `tree.get(i)` return `DataTree?`. A missing key, an index out of range, or the wrong kind gives `None` instead of stopping.

- Safe chains use the existing `?.` rule: `tree.get("user")?.get("name")?.to_text()` is one `String?`. The strict `.text()` returns a failure, not an optional, so a `?.` chain that must not stop ends in `.to_text()`.

- A JSON `null` member is a value, not a miss: `tree.get("x")` on `{"x": null}` is `Val(DataTree.Null)`. This matches `json.pointer`.

- No conversion: `tree["0"]` on an array stops; it does not mean index 0.

- Writing follows maps and lists, on a mutable (`:=`) binding. The new value must be a `DataTree`. `tree["key"] = v` inserts or replaces an object member. `tree[i] = v` replaces an array item in range. An out-of-range index or a wrong kind stops. Writing never creates missing objects or arrays along the way.

- `.field`, `.at`, and `json.pointer` stay. Hand-written decoders keep `.field` because its `FieldError` carries the path for decode errors.

What A does not do: with JSON of unknown shape, a mistyped key is found only when the program runs. That is true whether it is written as `["key"]` or as a pointer path. A makes reads shorter and consistent with lists and maps; it does not move key mistakes to compile time. Typed decode is the way to get compile-time field checks.

Conflicts: none. A applies S39 to one more Core type. Probe (2026-10-02, from the earlier draft, not rerun): `tree["user"]` is E0505 today. `tree.field("user")?.field("name")` fails with E2402, because `?.` chains optionals while `.field` returns a failure.

Related: D-INFER-PRIVATE1 now asks about a dynamic object type. If the owner picks one there, it reads with the same `[ ]` rule, so the two choices fit together.

decisions.title: Text on the same line as a triple-quote delimiter
decisions.situation: A triple-quoted string is text written between a pair of three double quotes, so that it can span several lines. Today Jet silently drops any text that sits on the same line as either set of quotes, so a one-line """hello""" prints an empty line and no warning appears. The program then prints something different from what its source shows. You are deciding whether that text is kept or refused with a clear compile error; we recommend refusing it, as Swift does, with an error that shows the fix.
decisions.gist: Should text on the same line as an opening or closing """ be kept, or refused with a compile error?
decisions.lesson: A triple-quoted string starts with three double quotes and ends with three more, and may span lines. Jet removes the line breaks next to the quotes and the closing line's indentation. Today other text on those two lines silently disappears. A refuses that text with a clear error. B keeps it. C keeps it only when the whole string fits on one line.
decisions.explainer:
A string is a piece of text in a program. An ordinary string has one double quote at each end and stays on one line.

A triple-quoted string has three double quotes at each end and may span many lines. Jet trims it the way Swift does. The line break right after the opening quotes goes, and so does the line break right before the closing quotes. The spaces in front of the closing quotes are removed from every line, so the text can be indented with the code around it.

The bug: Jet also throws away any other text on the opening line after the quotes, and on the closing line before the quotes, without a word.

A raw string is Jet's backtick string, `like this`, where quotes and backslashes are plain characters.
decisions.story: Mia writes """say "hi" to Ann""" on one line, so the inner quotes need no backslashes. Her program prints an empty line. Nothing in the compiler output tells her why.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-04. The Jet lexer finds the content range in Compiler/JetLexer/Source/Lexer/Payload.jet:712-729. Line 724 moves past everything up to the first line break after the opening quotes. Line 726 ends the content at the start of the closing line. The Rust lexer does the same in crates/jet-lexer/src/Lexer/Strings.rs:441-469. So """abc""" on one line decodes to an empty string, and closing-line text before the quotes is dropped.

The same trimming runs for a checked text head such as SQL{"""…"""}, because the head modes are applied after it (Payload.jet:708-730). Neither lexer treats a carriage return specially here, so a file with CRLF line endings has a carriage return just before each line break.

The written rule is S70 in Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:1417-1419 and Docs/spec/spec.md:73-77. It says which line breaks and indentation are removed. It does not say what happens to other text on the delimiter lines.

Foreign code bodies are separate. A #FFI(c), #FFI(cpp) or #FFI(asm) body is one raw triple-quoted string, often on one line, and it keeps every byte between the quotes (D-FFI-RAWBODY1, syntax-decisions.md:3491). The Jet lexer takes that path first, at Payload.jet:700-707, so no option changes foreign bodies.

The registered lexer errors for strings are E0001, a character, escape or lone brace that means nothing, and E0002, an unterminated literal (Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/DiagnosticRows.jet:6-37). Refusing delimiter-line text is a different mistake, so A and C add one new registered lexer code rather than stretching either.

A search of Compiler/, Core/, Jetpack/, Examples/ and tests/ on 2026-10-04 found no ordinary triple-quoted string with text on a delimiter line, so no source migrates under any option. Text after the closing quotes, such as `""" }`, is outside the string and stays legal. Card #4241 asks for both lexers to change in one cutover; the Rust lexer still builds Compiler/ at stage zero, so the two must agree.

options.name: Refuse delimiter-line text with a clear error
options.detail:
After the opening quotes, only spaces or tabs may follow before the line break. Before the closing quotes, only spaces or tabs may sit on that line. Anything else is a compile error with a new registered code, reported by both lexers at the exact span of the stray text. The rule is the same for checked text heads.

The error names both fixes. Move the text to its own line, or, for one line of text, use an ordinary string or a backtick raw string. A one-line """abc""" is refused the same way. Foreign code bodies keep their own raw rule and are not checked.
options.technical:
Both lexers check the bytes between the opening quotes and the first line break, and between the closing line start and the closing quotes. A carriage return directly before the line break counts as part of the line break, so CRLF files are not refused. Any other byte except space or tab produces the new code, with the span of the first offending byte through the end of that run. When both delimiter lines hold text, both are reported.

The string still decodes with today's trimming so later errors stay useful. The registry row, both lexers, the formatter round trip and one UI fixture per case land in one change. S70's text gains one sentence naming the rule.

options.name: Keep delimiter-line text
options.detail:
Text after the opening quotes becomes the start of the first line. Text before the closing quotes becomes the end of the last line, with no line break after it. A one-line """abc""" is the string abc. A one-line string that ends in a quote needs a space before the closing quotes, and that space stays in the string.

Indentation stripping needs a new rule when the closing line holds text, because the closing quotes no longer mark a clean column. B would strip the smallest common indentation of the content lines after the first in that case, as Kotlin's trimIndent does. That gives the language two indentation rules.
options.technical: content_start becomes open_end when the opening line holds non-blank text. content_end becomes close when the closing line holds non-blank text. Indent then falls back to the minimum leading whitespace across content lines after the first; text that shares the opening line is never stripped. Both lexers, the formatter and S70's text change together.
options.code:
msg :: """Hello,
    world"""
print(msg)   // Hello,\nworld
one :: """say "hi" """
print(one)   // say "hi"  (with a trailing space)

options.name: Keep one-line strings, refuse mixed multi-line ones
options.detail:
A triple-quoted string that opens and closes on the same line keeps everything between the quotes, so """say "hi" to Ann""" is the string say "hi" to Ann. A string that spans lines follows A: text on either delimiter line is a registered error.

This keeps a quote-friendly one-liner but gives triple quotes two meanings, decided by whether a line break appears inside. As in B, a one-liner that ends in a quote needs a space before the closing quotes, and the space stays in the string.
options.technical: If no line break occurs between the opening and closing quotes, the content is the full range with no trimming. Otherwise A's checks apply. The registry row and both lexers change together.
options.code:
one :: """say "hi" """   // kept: say "hi" plus a space
msg :: """Hello,
    world
    """
// error: text after the opening """

comparisons.note: Swift refuses text after the opening delimiter and text before the closing delimiter on its line. Jet's S70 trimming already copies Swift.
comparisons.code:
// https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/stringsandcharacters/#Multiline-String-Literals
let quotation = """
    The White Rabbit put on his spectacles.
    """

comparisons.note: Java text blocks refuse text after the opening delimiter. Text before the closing delimiter is allowed and means no final line break.

recommendation.why: A turns silent text loss into a clear compile error with a fix, and keeps one shape and one indentation rule for multi-line strings. It is the rule Swift uses, whose trimming Jet already copies. One-line text with quotes already has two spellings: an escaped ordinary string or a backtick raw string.
gains: No source text is ever silently lost.
One shape and one indentation rule for every multi-line string.
Both compilers share one rule and one registered error.

losses.loss: A one-line """text""" is refused, so a quote-heavy one-liner needs another spelling.
losses.mitigation: The error suggests the backtick raw string, which keeps quotes and backslashes as plain characters, or an ordinary string with escapes.

losses.loss: Authors used to Python or Kotlin may put text on the closing line out of habit.
losses.mitigation: The error points at that text and shows the corrected layout, and the formatter keeps the corrected shape.

whyNot.reason: B needs a second indentation rule whenever the closing line holds text, so two strings that look alike can be trimmed differently. It also leaves Jet unlike Swift, whose trimming it already copies.
C gives triple quotes two meanings that depend on whether a line break appears inside, which a reader must check before trusting the trimming.

recommendation.tradeoff: A refuses a few spellings other languages accept. In return no text ever vanishes, and every multi-line string has one shape with one indentation rule.

decisions.title: How a live link behaves when its target owes a job
decisions.gist: What happens when a link points at a value that still owes a job?
decisions.lesson: Some values owe a job, like a lock that must be released. A link lets other code see a value without owning it. This choice decides who does the job once links exist.
decisions.explainer:
Two ratified rules meet in one case. D-MEMREF-LIFE1=A says that when the compiler cannot prove a link's owner outlives the link, the target moves to counted memory. It then stays alive while any link remains.

D-LIN1 says a #SingleUse value must be used exactly once. D-OWES1, still open, extends this to declared debts. If such a value sits behind a link, the last link to go would drop it with its job undone.

This ballot decides only that case. Ordinary values keep D-MEMREF-LIFE1=A under every option. Link build status is tracked on #3645.
decisions.story: Mara builds a game server. Each match holds a Lease on a shared map slot that must be released when the match ends. Spectator panels keep links to the Lease to show its name. She needs to know who releases the Lease, and what happens when a panel looks after the match ended.
decisions.detail: Option A makes a link to a debt-carrying value a checked link: it stores the target's generation and stops with a source-located report if used after the owner settles. Option B makes such a link a compile error unless the owner provably outlives it. Option C keeps D-MEMREF-LIFE1's counted fallback and requires the type to name a no-argument failure action that runs when the last link is released.

options.name: Owner settles, links check
options.detail: The owner keeps the job and must settle it, as D-LIN1 already requires. A link to the value never keeps it alive. Using the link after the owner settled stops the program with the link's source location.
options.technical: A link to a value whose type owes a duty stores the target's generation, the same check Pool Ids use (MathTaskMem.rs checked_get). Settling bumps the generation. The counted-memory fallback of D-MEMREF-LIFE1=A is not used for these targets.

options.name: Reject unproven links
options.detail: A link to a value that owes a job compiles only when the compiler proves the owner outlives the link. Otherwise it is a compile error with a fix.
options.technical: Sema rejects the link at the point where D-MEMREF-LIFE1=A would promote the target to counted memory, and names the debt-carrying type.

options.name: Last link settles
options.detail: The target moves to counted memory like any other link target. When the last link goes, Jet runs the type's declared failure action instead of dropping it.
options.technical: Requires D-OWES1's on_fail field (or an equivalent no-argument action) on every type that can sit behind a link. The action runs at the last release, on whichever task releases last.

comparisons.note: Single ownership plus generation-checked references; linear values are settled only by their owner. https://verdagon.dev/blog/generational-references
Rc<T> drops its contents when the last Rc goes, so it cannot hold a value that must be settled by a call with arguments.

recommendation.why: A keeps one owner responsible, so the job always runs at a place you can read. It reuses the stale-Id check Jet already has.

whyNot.reason: B forbids common observer and back-link designs instead of checking them.
C hides when the job runs, and its failure action cannot take the arguments a real settle needs.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet accepts a rare run-time stop so that every job is settled by one owner at a visible place.

decisions.title: Record task message and lock order so concurrent runs replay exactly
decisions.gist: Should a recorded run also record which task got each message and lock first?
decisions.lesson: Jet can record a run and replay it to reproduce a bug. Today it records time and outside input, not the order tasks take turns. A race can then vanish on replay.
decisions.explainer:
Ratified D-JREPLAY1=A and D-RUN-RECORD1=A give `jet prove --capture`, `jet run --record=NAME`, and `jet debug --replay=NAME`. Capture records Time by default, and Time, Rand, IO, and Net when sensitive.

Task order is not captured. The order in which tasks receive channel messages, take locks, or take Shared guards is lost. The core.testing world already gives exact task order inside tests.

Option A adds order records to the .jetproof-replay schema as a minor version, with no new flag. Option B adds a flag, which amends D-JREPLAY1's closed capture grammar. Option C changes nothing outside tests.
decisions.story: Theo runs a chat server. Once a week two users join the same room at the same instant and a message is lost. His recording replays the inputs, but on replay the join order differs and the bug never appears. He needs the replay to follow the order that actually happened.
decisions.detail: Under A, the capture adapters for channels, locks, Shared guards, and task joins record which waiter won each turn, and replay blocks other waiters until the recorded one proceeds. Under B the same records exist only when a new flag is given. Under C capture is unchanged and exact order exists only in core.testing world.

options.name: Always record order
options.detail: Every capture records the order in which tasks receive messages and take locks. Replay follows that order, so races replay exactly. There is no new flag.
options.technical: Each channel receive records the sender's message sequence number; each lock or Shared guard records its version on acquire. Stored as new record kinds in the .jetproof-replay schema, minor version bump. Replay wakes only the recorded waiter.
options.code:
$ jet run --record=race server.jet
capture preflight: safe Time only; task order recorded
$ jet debug --replay=race
replay: 1,284 task-order steps matched

options.name: Order only with a flag
options.detail: Task order is recorded only when the run asks for it with a new flag. Runs without the flag pay nothing and cannot replay a race.
options.technical: Same record kinds as A, gated by `--capture-order`, which amends D-JREPLAY1's closed capture grammar.
options.code:
$ jet run --record=race --capture-order server.jet
capture preflight: safe Time only; task order recorded

options.name: Tests only
options.detail: Exact task order stays a feature of the testing world. Recorded real runs keep today's capture roots.
options.technical: No schema change. Deterministic scheduling remains core.testing world only.

comparisons.note: Records channel message ids and mutex versions per OS thread; replay waits for the recorded one. https://verdagon.dev/blog/perfect-replayability-prototyped
comparisons.code:
./main --vale_record recording.bin
./main --vale_replay recording.bin

comparisons.note: Records a whole Linux process, including scheduling, but replay does not survive source changes.
comparisons.code:
rr record ./server
rr replay

recommendation.why: A makes every recorded run replay exactly, including races, with no extra step for the user.

whyNot.reason: B misses the run that matters, because bugs appear in runs nobody flagged.
C leaves real concurrent runs impossible to replay.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet pays a small per-message recording cost so that every recorded run replays exactly.

decisions.title: Keep large-input capacity with compact local indexes
decisions.gist: Should compact compiler indexes reject oversized inputs or split them into segments?
decisions.lesson: A four-byte index saves compiler memory but cannot address every possible large input. Jet currently uses wider owned counters in many places. decisions.title: Keep the environment captured before user code
decisions.gist: Should Jet keep the environment from program entry, first access, or each host read?
decisions.lesson: The environment is the inherited list of names and values, such as MODE. Jet captures it before user code starts. Foreign code may later change the host list. This choice decides which list Jet sees. Jet changes still use its own table. Safe copying and child-process behavior remain required.

decisions.gist: Should ordinary executables keep protection and diagnostics while full debug symbols ship separately?

Cleanup and required diagnostic facts never become optional.

decisions.gist: May smaller allocator bookkeeping change how many values fit in Fixed?
decisions.lesson: Fixed allocates inside a fixed byte budget and never falls back to the heap. Payload, alignment, and bookkeeping all consume that budget. decisions.title: Keep String; stop building throwaway text
decisions.gist: Should ordinary String-returning functions write directly when nobody keeps their text?
decisions.lesson: String is Jet's one text type. Today display builds text even for printing. A keeps its signature but sends pieces straight to their destination. In the examples, {x} fills a hole, += appends, loop repeats, and saved keeps a String. Exact rules and fallbacks are in A's details; output is identical in every case. All options owe caller-handled write errors.
decisions.story: Wen prints thousands of Shown records and sometimes saves their text. She wants one ordinary String function, no output among its inputs, and no throwaway String for direct printing.
decisions.detail:
This is a proposed language guarantee, not a claim about the current compiler. It keeps D-DISPLAYDBG1's String-returning public signature. It adds no syntax, public writer parameter, deferred text value, or second text type. The owner chooses between improving String's execution, exposing the destination, and always building the result.

Sources: Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:1962-1966 records Display, Debug, and redaction. tests/print_branch_tiers.rs:75-98 supplies the Shown method and shown=9 expectation. tests/agent_workloads/adapters/mcp_resource.jet:28-29 demonstrates an empty local and string += inside a loop. These sources ground existing spelling, not the proposed allocation guarantee.

The three printed lines in the workload are shown=9, outer=shown=9, and shown=9shown=9. saved holds shown=9. A uses no temporary whole-result String for these prints; saved builds one result. The loop's out remains an ordinary String in source, not a separate builder type.

No performance probe or implementation acceptance test was run for this draft. A performance decision still needs paired candidate/plain programs in the canonical matrix before ratification. Validation of the draft's fields is separate from proving the proposed compiler contract.

options.name: Fix String, not the signature
options.detail:
Keep fn display(self) -> String. Every qualifying text-building String function is compiled once as a body that sends pieces to the destination. An ordinary String-returning call is a thin wrapper around that same body, using a fresh String as destination. No duplicate formatting body is generated.

Printing, file writing, interpolation holes, and appending into another String call that body directly. This is guaranteed for the closed rule, including nested displays and separately compiled functions. Binding, storing, or returning the value further uses the ordinary wrapper and builds one result String. Ordinary function behavior remains available for every other body.

The compiler, not the programmer, supplies the destination internally. Destination failures are remembered and reported at the caller's print or file-write site, never inside display. String remains the one public text type. Built-in, derived, and handwritten Show, Display, and Debug retain their existing text and redaction rules.
options.technical:
Exact rule and fallbacks:

1. Bodies: literals, interpolation, String +, and one local initialized as out := "", only appended to with +=, then returned. Branches and loops may select or repeat pieces. The local cannot be read, measured, indexed, shared, captured, passed elsewhere, replaced, or returned early. Nested qualifying calls stream too; existing String pieces are borrowed or moved without duplicate text copies.

2. Uses: output must go straight into print, a file text write, an interpolation hole, or String append. Binding, storing, or returning the value further builds one result through the ordinary wrapper. Unlisted bodies remain valid and build their ordinary result once. These are guarantees, not optimizer guesses.

3. Effects: the declared effect row decides. A display with input/output effects never streams; it builds its ordinary String first. Its actions and output remain identical.

4. Aliasing: ownership must prove that the destination is not a borrowed input. For s += describe(s), build the result before changing s.

5. Getters: returning stored text, such as -> self.name, is not text-building. Keep the normal value return, so existing sharing and moves remain free.

6. Function values: make an adapter carrying the streaming entry and ordinary wrapper where a function becomes a value. Generate it only for functions used as values. Separate compilation and dynamic trait calls carry both entries; captures keep their ownership rules.

7. Padding: width/alignment holes such as {x:>20} render into small stack storage, pad, then write once. If the text exceeds that storage, continue the same invocation into one String, never rerun display. Only the hole needs stored text, not the surrounding display's whole result.

8. Buffering: every destination groups small writes and sends them at each operation's end. Use existing destination storage, not a second full-text copy; String append fills the destination itself. Oversized text may require earlier commits. Only that case risks earlier partial output on a crash, which already stops the program. Failed physical writes retain today's possible partial output; buffering is not rollback.

9. Errors: the destination remembers its first write failure. Report it at the caller's print/file-write site, never inside display. No output-error parameter, return, effect, or handler is added to display. Preserve flushing, capture, and error precedence.

10. Debugging: show the text emitted so far and map hidden writes to source holes and append lines. This is tooling, not another runtime text type.

Every qualifying function has one compiled writing body and a thin String-return wrapper. No duplicate body or length-measuring rerun is allowed. One result means one String value, not one allocator call during growth. Fallbacks preserve text, argument order, effects, and correctness. These repairs leave no remaining user-facing loss.

options.name: Put the writer in the inputs
options.detail:
Change display to receive a destination and return no text value. It writes directly, even if its body also performs input/output actions. Saved interpolation calls the same rule using the saved String's storage. Buffering and caller-reported failures can remove repeated write costs and error handling.

This is a real alternative, not A's hidden implementation. The writer becomes part of the programmer's signature. Existing implementations and direct display() callers must change. It delivers direct output but rejects the owner's preference that an output should not be an input.
options.technical: Proposed public API: display(self, out: &FormatWriter) -> Unit. FormatWriter is a borrowed destination, not a second owned text type. Its lifetime is limited to the call. It buffers pieces and remembers destination errors for the outer operation. A clean cutover would change every implementation, derive, adapter, exported signature, and direct caller. No compatibility overload remains.

options.name: Always build the returned String
options.detail:
Keep today's public signature and execution rule. The function builds and returns a String before its caller prints, writes, or appends it. Saving the value is naturally supported. No source migration is needed.

The worked display allocates its text even when print immediately discards it. Nested display calls and a loop's appends still build stored text. This option has no language guarantee that removes those temporary results.
options.technical: Return an ordinary materialized String on every call. A getter may reuse or move an existing String; this is not a claim that every method call creates new storage. The text-building workload, however, constructs its result before writing. Destination failures remain the caller's responsibility.

comparisons.note: Interpolated string handlers let the compiler lower interpolation into AppendLiteral and AppendFormatted calls for a destination-aware API. This is a real precedent for compiler-written appends, not a guarantee for arbitrary String-returning functions. Jet adopts the useful lowering without requiring a public handler type beside String. Official tutorial: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/advanced-topics/performance/interpolated-string-handler. The tutorial's basic handler still builds a StringBuilder result; destination-directed handlers supply the stronger mechanism.

Swift's StringInterpolationProtocol lowers holes into appendLiteral and appendInterpolation. TextOutputStream is a destination for print; String itself conforms, so the same output can be kept. These are complementary precedents, not Swift's guarantee that every String-returning function streams. Sources: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swift/stringinterpolationprotocol and https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swift/textoutputstream.
comparisons.code:
let value = 9
let text = "shown=\(value)"
var saved = ""
print(text, terminator: "", to: &saved)
// String is also a TextOutputStream destination.

comparisons.note: format_args! avoids heap allocation for the formatting arguments. Display writes through an explicit Formatter parameter, and ToString saves the result. This is B's public shape; A hides the destination behind the unchanged String API. Sources: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/macro.format_args.html and https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/trait.Display.html.

toString returns a String before output: C's shape. The shown concatenation builds text; the contract does not promise destination streaming. A method returning an already stored String need not allocate again. It would be inaccurate to claim every toString call allocates fresh storage. Official API: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Object.html#toString().

__str__ must return a str object, including when print calls it: C's shape. The shown interpolation builds text before output. Returning a stored str can reuse it, so always returning stored text is not always allocating fresh storage. Official data model: https://docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html#object.__str__.
comparisons.code:
class Shown:
    def __init__(self, value): self.value = value
    def __str__(self): return f"shown={self.value}"
x = Shown(9)
print(x)
saved = str(x)

recommendation.why: Keep the easy String API and guarantee direct output for the stated rule. Compile one body; build one result only when needed. No writer input or second text type is needed.
gains: No temporary whole-result String for qualifying direct output.
One formatting body serves direct output and saved String values.

whyNot.reason: B exposes the destination as an input and requires source changes. A gets direct output without that public shape.
C keeps the simple signature but builds throwaway text for the worked printing workload. A keeps the signature and removes that work.

recommendation.tradeoff: No remaining user-facing loss. Effects, input aliasing, padding beyond the stack buffer, and unlisted bodies keep ordinary String behavior. The guarantee never promises these cases are allocation-free.

decisions.title: Start compiler jobs only when useful work and memory permit
decisions.gist: Should compiler jobs start only when enough memory and useful work are available?
decisions.lesson: Several workers can compile independent bodies at once. Each worker also needs memory for its active work. The research proposes bounded admission, not a new universal memory ceiling. This choice sets the default. Tiny inputs stay serial; expert caps, complete checking, deterministic diagnostics, and identical artifacts remain required.
decisions.story: Theo builds hello on a many-core machine, then a large project. He wants useful parallel work without one large scratch allocation per core.
decisions.detail:
B12c. Section 5 B12c, lines 784–789; S section 6; M sections 4.5,5,7. No claim is made about currently measured worker scheduling.

These are owner-requested short drafts, not approvals or implementation receipts. Current examples are source-derived unless a cited test records output. No Jet program was run for these drafts. Proposed results are contracts, not measured improvements. Performance choices still need matched candidate/plain cells before ratification.

Required witnesses: Tiny serial input; large parallel input; oversized dependency cycles; expert caps; reserved/live bytes; identical one-worker/multiworker diagnostics and artifacts.

options.name: Bound useful work and memory
options.detail: Admit independent useful work against catalog plus live body batch, scratch, and codegen memory. Release scratch between jobs. Do not start one self-build-sized worker per detected core.
options.technical: Use correctness-preserving spill or partitioning for oversized dependency cycles where available. Otherwise diagnose an exact capacity failure; never omit work. Benchmark 24/768 MiB goals are workload targets, not a new user-wide hard cap. No new CLI option spelling is proposed.

options.name: Serial unless requested
options.detail: Use serial admission as default and existing controls for opt-in parallel execution. The parallel path must still preserve complete deterministic checking.

options.name: Every detected core
options.detail: Use every detected core as the admission basis. No memory-aware reservation bounds simultaneous active bodies; retained worker scratch counts in measurements.

comparisons.note: Go has a parallel-build cap; its default follows available CPUs. Source: https://go.dev/cmd/go/

recommendation.why: Parallelism should reduce useful build time, not duplicate scratch until memory runs out. Keep the tiny-program path serial.

whyNot.reason: Serial default leaves useful independent work waiting on large builds.
CPU count alone cannot predict how much memory simultaneous jobs need.

recommendation.tradeoff: Some cores wait so simultaneous compiler work stays within available memory.

losses.loss: Memory-heavy jobs may wait despite idle cores.
losses.mitigation: A worker needs its active data in memory. If that reservation does not fit, admitting it can exhaust memory.

decisions.title: Small Linux programs without mandatory support libraries
decisions.gist: Should a Linux program need a separate support library when it can safely run without one?
decisions.lesson: A support library supplies code a program needs beyond its own functions. The C library, called libc, is one example. Jet's measured release hello was 575 KB; gcc's was 14 KB. Linking means putting needed code together. We can include only required functions, keeping safety checks and cleanup. Some operations genuinely require host libraries. Those requirements must be preserved, not silently replaced.
decisions.story: Lena sends a hello program to a small Linux machine. She wants the ordinary build to be tiny, safe, and runnable without installing Jet there.
decisions.detail:
This is a deployment-default choice, not permission to change runtime semantics. D-EXEC1 requires one semantic runtime, compiled at O2 and shipped per version/target/ABI. Shared implementation does not mean mandatory dynamic loading. A links independently removable functions and data from that same shipped implementation, with audited OS-call adapters and lawful startup. It does not rebuild a runtime for every program, require FatLTO, invent fast_print, or select a second tiny-program language.

Source grounding: Docs/research/efficiency-architecture-2026-10-02.md:440–456 defines one separable runtime; :488–554 covers borrowed literal output, error handling, finalizers, startup, and safe images; :713–719 identifies this genuine provider choice. Docs/audits/compile-cost-hello-2026-10-02.md:28–41 records gcc 14 KB stripped, assembly 744 bytes, and Jet release 575 KB. The 744-byte assembly is a scale reference, not matched safety evidence. The synthesis also records 243/249/258-byte scratch assembly/C/Rust experiments with weaker contracts. No proposed Jet size is measured.

Current source: Compiler/JetBackend/Source/Image/Object.jet:1–9 links the compiled runtime through a hosted main. Image/ELF.jet:1–59 writes a fixed-address executable and :66–93 supplies raw startup. Image/Runtime.jet:128–157 retries positive short writes but stops on nonpositive results and exits directly on stops. That separate hand-assembled implementation is not the recommended production path.

crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/mod.rs assembles Rust support. Core/term/term.jet:50–53 supplies the existing stdout line/error handling. Docs/spec/spec.md:831–846 and syntax-decisions.md:1722–1727 require reports, exit attribution, and cleanup. D-NOSTD1, syntax-decisions.md:3270–3271, rejects a separate no_std beginner flag. D-NETDNS2=A, :4198–4200, requires host resolver behavior; such behavior can require libc even without user-written foreign calls.

Static research only. Current example output follows source and the historical audit; no Jet build, benchmark, or probe was run here. All proposed behavior is a design contract, not a claimed improvement.

Self comprehension pass: explain—include needed functions, not whole libraries. Predict—hello runs alone, while a library that requires libc keeps libc. Modify—adding a database may add its required libraries without changing the build command. Derive—libc and linking are defined in the lesson. Friction removed: eligible closure, lawful provider, and hosted dependency were replaced with concrete program behavior. No exact future size or unconditional startup-speed claim remains.

options.name: Include only needed support
options.detail: Ordinary builds include only required functions from Jet's one shipped support implementation. Programs needing only Linux calls have no separate support library or loader. Genuine host/library requirements select their correct startup and dependencies at build time. Existing explicit build declarations can request shared support for deployments that benefit from it; the default never imposes that installation requirement.
options.technical:
Calculate the complete function/data/service dependency set from checked code and declared foreign/load boundaries before layout. Include possible failure/cleanup paths, dynamically published entrypoints, TLS and foreign startup requirements; never infer a safe set from one successful run. Use independently removable archive sections and stable symbol-to-layout mappings. Direct Linux adapters implement OS transport only, not a second arithmetic/text/error runtime.

Preserve short writes, EINTR, broken-pipe handling, output ordering/flush behavior, lexical drops, atexit, typed reports and exact exit semantics. Elide absent services only with compiler proof. Keep existing image-security requirements: randomized load addresses where feasible, non-executable stack, and never simultaneously writable/executable memory. Host-required code uses lawful host startup, never libc calls from incomplete handcrafted startup.

Default and release must meet matched C size and startup requirements; declarations for explicit dynamic linkage reuse existing build/target policy. No new dependency or override syntax is approved. Measure executable bytes and full deployment separately, counting dependencies in the latter. Any repeated-runtime-code cost across different programs can be addressed by an explicit existing shared-linkage deployment, without making every standalone program pay it.

options.name: Always use libc
options.detail: Every Linux program starts through libc, even if its needed operations could use Linux directly. Only required Jet functions are included. This supplies one conventional host startup path, but every deployment keeps a libc requirement. Static libc counts inside the executable; shared libc counts as a deployment dependency.
options.technical: Preserve the same canonical Jet runtime semantics and security as A. Declare and measure static versus dynamic libc packaging. Do not claim a 14 KB dynamically linked peer contains libc's implementation. Host services retain their real semantics under every option.

options.name: Always load shared Jet support
options.detail: Every Linux program requires an installed matching Jet support library. Different programs can share that library's code pages and maintenance. Standalone deployment is lost, and even hello must load the library. Dependency sizes and startup costs remain charged.
options.technical: Use one version/ABI-verified shared canonical runtime, not another semantic implementation. Verify loader identity and permission boundaries; reject absent or mismatched support before user code. Count the full transitive deployment, including libc if required. The strength of shared pages across different executables remains available explicitly under A rather than being mandatory for every program.

comparisons.note: GCC's official linking manual documents -nostdlib, its requirement to supply omitted support routines, and -static-pie for load-address independence without a dynamic loader. https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Link-Options.html. Hosted puts is not a no-libc program; supplying a correct writer and startup is additional work. The historical 14 KB peer is dynamically linked, not a 14 KB standalone runtime.

recommendation.why: A keeps everything the program needs and removes only unnecessary support. Ordinary hello stands alone; real host requirements still work. Shared deployment remains explicit, not compulsory.

whyNot.reason: B adds a libc requirement even when no required operation needs it.
C requires a matching library installation for every program, including hello.

recommendation.tradeoff: No safety or functionality is traded for size. A requested foreign library still brings its genuine requirements.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Before ratification, record executable candidate/plain cells with the same source and approved comparator. Before implementation acceptance, verify default and release hello stdout, stderr, status, short-write/EINTR/broken-pipe behavior, diagnostics, lexical cleanup and atexit against hosted/native/Web equivalents. Exercise host DNS, libc-requiring foreign libraries, TLS, constructors, explicit shared deployments and dynamically declared exports. Verify image permissions and lawful randomized startup.

Report exact as-built, stripped, and complete-deployment bytes; no hidden runtime dependencies. Beat or meet the owner's same-program C size requirement without dropping safety; compare the strongest matched freestanding C arm, not only gcc's 14 KB hosted form. The sub-KB objective is a target, not earned evidence. Compare paired startup, compiler/runtime RAM and build time independently. Verify an installed-toolchain build and execution on a machine without Jet support installation. These checks are owed after implementation; none was exercised in this draft.

Linking means putting needed code together. We can include only required functions, keeping safety checks and cleanup. Some operations genuinely require host libraries. Those requirements must be preserved, not silently replaced.

Default release keeps local inspection; development keeps debugging support. This choice extends that same policy to all observation code. Required stop reports and cleanup stay. decisions.title: Release finished compiler phase data unless inspection needs it
decisions.gist: Should normal compilation keep full intermediate program data after its last consumer finishes?
decisions.lesson: The compiler builds intermediate forms while checking and generating code. Keeping every form alive raises memory use. Jet already clears some phase data, but other owners remain. This choice sets the normal retention promise. Required source facts, diagnostics, generic bodies, and build-time execution remain available. Requested inspection and archives must still be complete.
decisions.story: Mara compiles hello without opening compiler internals. She wants finished working data released, while an explicit inspection still returns the full requested facts.
decisions.detail:
B12b. Section 5 B12b, lines 778–783; M section 7 and 4.4. M notes Pipeline.jet:2470–2472 clearing only the flattened list.

These are owner-requested short drafts, not approvals or implementation receipts. Current examples are source-derived unless a cited test records output. No Jet program was run for these drafts. Proposed results are contracts, not measured improvements. Performance choices still need matched candidate/plain cells before ratification.

Required witnesses: Normal build retirement of every owner; exact diagnostics; requested compiler inspection; complete bootstrap archive; demanded generic/comptime closure; later-source identity.

options.name: Release finished work
options.detail: Retire phase/per-function owners after their last semantic consumer. Keep exact source, diagnostic facts, summaries, and genuinely demanded generic/comptime bodies. Stream inspection and bootstrap archives.
options.technical: IR means intermediate representation. No diagnostic or semantic check is omitted to save memory. Requested full output is an explicit consumer and gets every promised record. Later requests may rebuild from exact authorized source; they must not return incomplete cached internals.

options.name: Keep all forms
options.detail: Always retain complete AST/TIR/MIR with exact source identity until the normal compilation session ends or its result is released.

decisions.title: Decimal by default, binary by name
decisions.gist: Should byte formatting keep decimal units by default and offer binary units through a clearly named function?
decisions.lesson: Decimal units count 1000 bytes per kB and 1000000 per MB. Binary units count 1024 bytes per KiB and 1048576 per MiB. Human-size displays round numbers. Decimal is already approved, but today's call prints binary units. This choice adds explicitly named binary formatting while correcting the default to its approved decimal meaning.
decisions.story: Ana prints the same file size in a download report and a memory report. She wants decimal units for downloads and binary units for memory, without writing division and rounding herself.
decisions.inWild:
import (
    "fmt"
    humanize "github.com/dustin/go-humanize"
)
size := uint64(1500000)
fmt.Println(humanize.Bytes(size))  // 1.5 MB
fmt.Println(humanize.IBytes(size)) // 1.4 MiB
decisions.detail:
Measured with ~/.cache/jet-luna/laneS.sh and ~/.cache/jet-test-scratch/jet-release-night12/jet on 2026-10-02. Scratch: ~/.cache/jet-test-scratch/sol/BallotRev4/bytes.jet. The displayed current program exits successfully and prints 1.430511474609375 MiB followed by 1.5 MB. The first line calls fmt.bytes; the second explicitly divides by 1000000 before printing MB. Do not describe night12's byte formatter as decimal.

Core/text/fmt.jet:93-105 divides by 1024 and uses KiB through TiB. Its division produces a fractional value, not integer truncation. Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md:2534-2563 documents binary units. crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/Fmt.rs:317-333 separately divides by 1000 and rounds scaled output. That source kernel is not the behavior observed from night12's fmt.bytes call. Its decimal output for 1500000 is source-derived as 1.5 MB.

A direct fmt.decimal(Float{1.5}, 1) probe on night12 exited 139. An earlier probe using that function after division also exited 139. Neither establishes working decimal-formatting execution. The final successful probe verifies the byte count and decimal scaled output through real division and printing. Proposed formatter rounding remains grounded in the Rust source kernel and the cited peer, not claimed executed.

Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:4179-4182 records D-HUMANFMT1=A and explicitly says SI bytes. Read-only `decision show D-HUMANFMT1` confirms outcome A and the owner's comment: 'full go-style humanize support in the fmt module/lib.' The default-scale question is not reopened. This ballot adds the public fmt.bytes_binary function while bringing fmt.bytes into agreement with the approved meaning.

Peer source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dustin/go-humanize/master/bytes.go, read 2026-10-02. Bytes and IBytes call one humanateBytes implementation with fixed bases and disjoint SI/IEC suffix lists. For 1500000, the source derives 1.5 MB and 1.4 MiB. These peer outputs were not freshly executed. Separate names select the scale without a required mode argument.

A uses one signed, deterministic formatter with the scale fixed by the function. fmt.bytes uses powers of 1000 and B, kB, MB, GB, TB, PB, EB. fmt.bytes_binary uses powers of 1024 and B, KiB, MiB, GiB, TiB, PiB, EiB. Decimal and binary share the current Rust kernel's display rule.

Below the first unit, print the exact integer byte count. Below ten scaled units, keep one fractional digit and remove trailing .0. Otherwise round to whole scaled units. Choose the scale before rounding. Compute unit boundaries from the exact magnitude, including negative and wide Int values; avoid lossy threshold selection. Thus 1500000 is displayed as 1.5 MB or 1.4 MiB. This remains approximate display, not an exact byte-count codec.

Each function fixes its scale, requiring no runtime mode lookup, extra copy, or allocation beyond the requested string. Unused binary formatting adds no work to decimal calls. Update Core source, runtime routes, every execution path, reference prose, examples and goldens together. Move intentional binary-report callers to bytes_binary; keep decimal callers on bytes. Remove the obsolete binary meaning of bytes rather than keeping a contradictory alias.

Design-away pass: a named binary entry point removes the old recommendation's missing binary support without adding an argument or changing the approved default. C's mandatory choice is unnecessary when the function name fixes the scale. Correcting currently binary callers is the already-owed decimal contract repair under every option, not a new concession in A.

Self comprehension pass, BallotRev4 using RLI5: explain derives the scales from the lesson; predict sees 1.5 MB versus 1.4 MiB for the same count. Modify selects bytes_binary for a memory report; derive finds both unit sizes defined on the surface. The pass replaced the misleading ten-megabyte example, explains rounding, and separates measured current behavior from proposed behavior.

options.name: Decimal default, named binary function
options.detail: Keep fmt.bytes decimal and add fmt.bytes_binary. Both are ordinary one-argument functions. Reports can use either convention, and the printed suffix identifies the scale.
options.technical: One shared deterministic kernel, with scale and suffix family fixed at each entry point. Preserve decimal rounding, use SI kB, and give binary the same display rule. Align all implementations and migrate intentional binary callers.
options.code:
use core.text.fmt as fmt
size :: 1500000
print(fmt.bytes(size))        // 1.5 MB
print(fmt.bytes_binary(size)) // 1.4 MiB
// Same byte count; both displays round to one decimal.

options.name: Decimal only
options.detail: Correct fmt.bytes to decimal everywhere and add no binary formatter. Ana writes division and display rules herself for her memory report.
options.technical: Honor the ratified default and align current implementations, but provide no built-in binary entry point. Authors retain responsibility for binary scale selection, signs, units and rounding.
options.code:
use core.text.fmt as fmt
size :: 1500000
print(fmt.bytes(size)) // 1.5 MB
print("{size / 1048576} MiB") // 1.430511474609375 MiB
// Ana must supply the binary display's rounding herself.

options.name: Required scale argument
options.detail: Require every fmt.bytes call to choose Decimal or Binary. Both scales are built in, but every existing call must change.
options.technical: Add a required ordinary enum argument. Decimal and binary share the same signed formatter. This amends the approved one-argument call even when the author only wants decimal output.
options.code:
use core.text.fmt as fmt
size :: 1500000
print(fmt.bytes(size, .Decimal)) // 1.5 MB
print(fmt.bytes(size, .Binary))  // 1.4 MiB
// fmt.bytes(size) now fails: choose a scale.

comparisons.note: Bytes selects decimal SI units; IBytes selects binary IEC units. Both call humanateBytes with fixed scale and suffixes. Source read 2026-10-02: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dustin/go-humanize/master/bytes.go. Example outputs are source-derived, not freshly executed.
comparisons.code:
size := uint64(1500000)
fmt.Println(humanize.Bytes(size))  // 1.5 MB
fmt.Println(humanize.IBytes(size)) // 1.4 MiB

recommendation.why: A keeps the approved decimal call and makes binary reports equally easy. Names select the scale; suffixes identify it. Neither report needs extra arguments or handwritten formatting.

whyNot.reason: B makes binary-report authors recreate formatting already provided by the peer library.
C changes every existing call merely to offer a second scale.

recommendation.tradeoff: No remaining decision-specific loss. Human-size displays remain rounded; print the original number when an exact count is needed.
