decisions.title: Report invalid stored data as an IOError kind
decisions.gist: How should Jet report that data stored on disk is broken, as opposed to a bad request?
decisions.lesson: A bad argument from the caller is a different problem from a file whose contents are broken. Today both are reported as InvalidInput, so code cannot choose the right repair. Every option keeps the same error details and still refuses the broken data. They differ in where the new distinction lives.
decisions.explainer:
Words first. IOError is the value Jet returns when reading or writing fails. Its kind, such as NotFound, says what went wrong. Its IOContext says which operation failed, on which resource, the optional system error number and an optional human cause. Returning an error does not print or repair anything; the caller decides.

A symlink is a file that redirects to another path. The store requires a real file and refuses redirects, because a redirect could point anywhere. A match is an if error == { ... } table. A complete match lists every kind; a match with else catches the rest.

Option A adds IOError.InvalidData. The simple rule is: InvalidInput means fix your call, InvalidData means fix what is stored. Option B keeps InvalidInput for both, but adds a second field that says CallerInput or StoredData. Both show the same operation, resource and cause.

Which kind wins. A missing file is NotFound. A system refusal is PermissionDenied with its error number. A bad size or option from the caller is InvalidInput. A file that opened and read cleanly but holds broken contents is InvalidData. That includes text that is not UTF-8, a broken record, a record cut short at a clean end of file, and a symlink where a real file is required.

A broken frame on a live network connection stays Protocol. When a store reads saved frames back from disk and they are broken, the store reports InvalidData, because the repair is to fix the stored file. A failure while closing after a good read keeps its own close kind, never InvalidData.

Reading the code: :: names a value. .Read picks the read operation. Val(x) means a value is present and None means absent. {error} inside quotes inserts the error's message.
decisions.story: Mina's package store refuses to open its index because one row is malformed. Her recovery code must rebuild the index file, not reject the request that asked for it.
decisions.detail:
Current code. crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/JetStd/Open.rs:19-63 defines IOContext with operation, resource, os_code and cause, and IOError with no InvalidData. Core/files/files.jet:110-133 builds every refusal as InvalidInput, and lines 139-141 use it for non-UTF-8 reads.

crates/jet-foundation/src/StructuralDebug.rs:182-216 is the one display table every tier calls, ending in a generic I/O error fallback. Jetpack/Publication/Source/Registry/Trust.jet:85-96 already constructs IOError.InvalidData, waiting on this vote.

D-IOERROR-TREE1 stays the shared context contract. AlreadyExists and fsync refusals belong to the files workstream (#3593), not this ballot. Examples are proposed, not run.

options.name: Add IOError.InvalidData
options.detail:
Add one kind, IOError.InvalidData(IOContext), with the same context as every other kind. Broken stored contents and wrong on-disk object kinds report it; bad caller arguments keep InvalidInput.

Beginner: read the message, which says invalid data and names the file. Expert: match .InvalidData to rebuild or repair stored data, without reading the cause text.

Migration: jet fix rewrites every .InvalidInput(x) -> body arm as .InvalidInput(x) | .InvalidData(x) -> body. That keeps every existing match arm catching the same failures. Authors split the arm when they want the new distinction.

Some things visibly change for broken-data failures, on purpose. The message says invalid data instead of invalid input, and Debug shows InvalidData(...). A saved error records the kind name InvalidData, and an == comparison against an InvalidInput value no longer matches. An else arm that prints the error prints the new message. jet fix flags each such inspection it cannot rewrite.
options.technical:
IOError gains InvalidData(IOContext), declared right after InvalidInput. Display text is "invalid data during <operation>", then the resource and cause as today. The shared display table becomes an exhaustive mapping, so no kind can fall through to the generic I/O error text.

Every tier reads the shared table: StructuralDebug.rs, the comptime parity copy at CorePureParity.rs:1954 and the JIT at jet-jit Process.rs:256. Debug prints InvalidData(...). Saved errors use the kind name, never a position number. An error saved earlier as InvalidInput still loads as InvalidInput.

Producers: Core file text reads that hit invalid UTF-8, store record decoders and regular-file-only reads become InvalidData.

Regular-file-only opens never check a path and then reopen it. On Unix, Core opens the parent directory, then opens the last name relative to that directory handle with O_NOFOLLOW and O_NONBLOCK. Because only one name is resolved, the platform's no-follow refusal can only mean the last name is a symlink. That is ELOOP on Linux and macOS; each other Unix target lists its own code, such as EMLINK on FreeBSD.

That refusal becomes InvalidData and keeps the OS code in os_code, whether the symlink is dangling or not. After a successful open, fstat on the same handle must show a regular file; a directory, FIFO or device is InvalidData. O_NONBLOCK keeps a FIFO from blocking the open.

On Windows, CreateFileW uses FILE_FLAG_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT, so a symlink or junction is opened as itself. GetFileInformationByHandleEx then reads its attributes from that same handle. A reparse point or a non-regular file is InvalidData, and a regular file is read through the same handle.

Order, first match wins. A failure opening the parent directory keeps its OS kind and code. Then the last-name open: the no-follow symlink refusal is InvalidData, and any other open failure, such as NotFound or PermissionDenied, keeps its OS kind. Then a non-regular handle is InvalidData. Then an OS read failure keeps its kind. Then a decode failure is InvalidData. A later close or flush failure keeps its own kind.

jet fix adds | .InvalidData(x) to every .InvalidInput(x) arm across the repository, so complete matches stay complete and each arm catches the same failures. It reports, without rewriting, every == or != against an IOError.InvalidInput value and every text comparison with "invalid input" display text. It also reports every reader of saved kind names, since each may need the new case. Golden outputs that recorded the old message are updated in the same cutover.

options.name: Reason field on InvalidInput
options.detail:
Keep the kinds unchanged. InvalidInput gets a second field, IOInputReason, which is CallerInput or StoredData. Other kinds are untouched.

Beginner: the message still says invalid input, even for a broken file. Expert: match .InvalidInput(_, .StoredData) to repair stored data.
options.technical: IOError.InvalidInput(IOContext, IOInputReason). Every InvalidInput construction and pattern gains the second field; jet fix fills in CallerInput, then producers of broken stored data switch to StoredData. Display is unchanged. Precedence and no-follow rules match A.

comparisons.note: Rust distinguishes invalid caller input from invalid stored data.

recommendation.why: Name the repair directly: InvalidInput means fix the call, InvalidData means fix what is stored. jet fix keeps every existing InvalidInput match catching the same failures, and flags the other places that inspect the old kind.
gains: Code and people see at once to repair the stored data.
Existing InvalidInput matches catch the same failures after jet fix.
The Jetpack store port matches its Rust original.

losses.loss: For broken-data failures, the message, Debug text and saved kind name change, and == against an InvalidInput value stops matching.
losses.mitigation: This change is the point: the text now names the right repair. jet fix flags every comparison, text match and saved-kind reader it cannot rewrite, and the cutover updates golden outputs. Old saved errors still load unchanged.

whyNot.reason: The kind still reads "invalid input", which misleads people, and every InvalidInput use changes shape.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds one error kind and changes the message for broken data; jet fix keeps match arms working and flags every other inspection.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Run the store malformed-row and refused-symlink tests and the display text on every tier. Check missing, denied, bad-argument, non-UTF-8, truncated-record and close-after-read cases against the precedence order.

Run symlink and open cases on Linux, macOS and Windows. A symlink to a regular file, a dangling symlink and a symlink to a directory are each InvalidData, with the OS code kept on Unix. A Windows junction is InvalidData. A missing last name is NotFound, an unreadable file is PermissionDenied and a missing parent is NotFound. A directory or FIFO at the last name is InvalidData, and the FIFO open does not block.

Run jet fix over the repository and prove every rewritten InvalidInput arm catches the same failures. Prove it flags a seeded == comparison, a seeded "invalid input" text match and a saved-kind reader. An old saved InvalidInput error still loads. Prove no tier renders InvalidData as the generic I/O error text.

Every option keeps the same error details and still refuses the broken data. They differ in where the new distinction lives.

gains: The list of error kinds stays the same.

gains: Code and people see at once to repair the stored data.

losses.mitigation: That is the point: the text names the repair. jet fix flags comparisons and kind readers; old saved errors still load.

decisions.situation: When a Jet program reads or writes files, a failure comes back as an IOError, a value that names what went wrong, such as NotFound or PermissionDenied. There is no kind for "the stored file itself is broken", so a corrupt store index or an unexpected symlink is reported as InvalidInput. InvalidInput is also what a caller gets for passing a bad argument. A program, or a person reading the message, therefore cannot tell whether to fix the call or repair the file, and the Jetpack store port cannot match its Rust original. This matters to tools that keep data on disk, such as package stores and caches, and to anyone writing recovery code. You are deciding how Jet names "the stored data is bad". We recommend one new kind, IOError.InvalidData, plus a jet fix step that keeps existing InvalidInput matches catching the same failures; only broken-data messages change.

decisions.title: A plain shortest spelling for decimal numbers in data files
decisions.gist: How should Core name the shortest exact text spelling of a Float for data files?
decisions.lesson: Printing a number for people and writing it into a data file can need different spellings. Jet's normal printing writes 0.0; the reference files write 0. Normal printing stays as it is. The question is only how you ask for the file spelling: a named function, or a mode passed to one general function.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A Float is a decimal number stored in binary, so most values are close approximations. Shortest means the fewest digits that, read back in, give exactly the same stored number. Positional means plain digits and a decimal point, never e-notation like 1e20. So shortest does not mean fewest characters: 1e20 prints as 100000000000000000000.

NaN means not a number, the result of something like 0/0. Inf means infinity. A Float also has a negative zero, -0, which compares equal to 0 but keeps its sign.

The example builds one build-record field and one complex number, a value with a real part and an imaginary part i. Both options print the same text. The last line shows ordinary printing, which does not change.

Option A adds one named function, fmt.shortest. Option B adds one general fmt.float function that takes a mode, and moves the existing number formats under it.
decisions.story: Ana writes a build record and a complex number to a file. The file must match the reference tools' text exactly, including 0 for zero, without special cases in her code.
decisions.detail:
Code facts. Core/text/fmt.jet:35-61 has fmt.grouped, fmt.decimal, fmt.percent and fmt.sci, each a named Float formatter, and no shortest mode. Card #4417 records the exercised build-record mismatch: proof1.log shows 3 pass and 1 fail, because interpolation writes 0.0 where Rust Display writes 0. That observation is kept, not rerun.

Both options leave ratified interpolation unchanged. Both use one shared shortest positional writer, also used for Complex components. Neither adds per-field trimming or reuses the JSON canonical exponent rule. Proposed examples are not executed.

options.name: One named function: fmt.shortest
options.detail:
Call fmt.shortest(x) wherever a file needs the reference spelling. It never fails and never uses e-notation. It sits next to fmt.decimal and fmt.sci, which already name one Float format each.

Normal printing is untouched, so beginners notice nothing. The documentation for Float printing and for fmt.decimal points to fmt.shortest for data files.
options.technical:
Signature: fmt.shortest(value: Float) -> String Never!. For a finite value, produce the shortest decimal digit sequence that parses back to the same binary64 bits. Lay it out positionally with no exponent and no forced fraction digit. Expanding digits into place adds zeros only and never rounds again.

Authority: Rust Display for f64 as frozen by rust-reference Cargo.lock, including its tie choice. Spellings: +0 is 0, -0 is -0, 1.0 is 1, NaN is NaN, and infinities are inf and -inf. NaN payload and sign do not round-trip through text.

Non-finite values print exactly as the reference writes them, because matching it is the job. Formats that forbid them, such as JSON, already reject them in their own writers before any digits are made. Very small or large finite values can be long, as in the reference, and are never truncated.

One shared runtime writer owns the digits on every execution level, and Complex display formats each component with it. A generated corpus covers adjacent floats, ties, subnormals, extremes and signed zero.
options.code:
use core.text.fmt as fmt
// one record field and one complex number, as text
record :: "energy={fmt.shortest(0.0)}"
complex :: "{fmt.shortest(-0.0)}+{fmt.shortest(1e-7)}i"
print(record)              // energy=0
print(complex)             // -0+0.0000001i
print(fmt.shortest(1.25))  // 1.25
print(fmt.shortest(1e20))  // 100000000000000000000
print("{0.0}")             // 0.0  ordinary printing unchanged

options.name: One general function with a mode
options.detail: Call fmt.float(x, mode) with a mode such as .ShortestPositional or .Fixed(2). The existing fmt.decimal, fmt.grouped, fmt.percent and fmt.sci move under this one entry point as the modes .Fixed, .Grouped, .Percent and .Scientific. Because those modes take a number that can be out of range, every call can fail and needs ?? to handle that, even for modes that cannot fail.
options.technical:
Add enum FloatFormat { Display, ShortestPositional, Fixed(Int), Grouped(Int), Percent(Int), Scientific(Int) } and fmt.float(value: Float, mode: FloatFormat) -> String FloatFormatError!. ShortestPositional has exactly A's contract. Display uses the existing display spelling. The four precision modes validate p from 0 to 1024 and return Range otherwise; today's functions instead treat a negative p as 0.

Fixed(p) is today's fmt.decimal: round to p fraction digits. Grouped(p) is today's fmt.grouped: the Fixed(p) text with a comma before every third whole-part digit counted from the right. Sign and fraction are untouched, so 1234567.5 with p 1 is 1,234,567.5. Percent(p) is today's fmt.percent: Fixed(p) of value * 100, then a % suffix, so 0.125 with p 1 is 12.5%.

Scientific(p) is today's fmt.sci: one leading digit, p fraction digits, then e, a sign and at least two exponent digits, so 1234.5 with p 2 is 1.23e+03. Non-finite values print as interpolation does.

fmt.decimal, fmt.grouped, fmt.percent and fmt.sci migrate to fmt.float in a clean cutover with no aliases. All modes share the same digit writer, so no new algorithm is added.
options.code:
use core.text.fmt as fmt
// one record field and one complex number, as text
zero :: fmt.float(0.0, .ShortestPositional) ?? panic("format")
re :: fmt.float(-0.0, .ShortestPositional) ?? panic("format")
im :: fmt.float(1e-7, .ShortestPositional) ?? panic("format")
print("energy={zero}")      // energy=0
print("{re}+{im}i")         // -0+0.0000001i
half :: fmt.float(1.25, .ShortestPositional) ?? panic("format")

decisions.title: Where a full web-page (HTML) parser should live
decisions.gist: Should the full web-page parser be a first-party Jet package, or part of Core?
decisions.lesson: Removing tags is not parsing. A real HTML parser repairs broken markup the way browsers do and builds a tree of elements. That repair algorithm is large and changes over time. Core's small escaping helpers stay either way. Neither choice runs scripts or downloads anything from the page.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. An element is one tagged part of a page, such as

A

, a paragraph containing A. Elements nest, so a page is a tree: each element has children. Attributes are named values on an element, such as href. An entity is a coded character such as & for &. Escaping turns < into < so text is shown, not treated as markup. Parsing means reading the page text into that tree. Browsers agree on one published repair algorithm, the WHATWG HTML standard, so the same broken page gives the same tree everywhere. Tag stripping just deletes everything between < and >, which loses structure and is not safe for showing untrusted pages. Both options offer the same functions and give the same tree. html.parse reads a page. html.elements lists the elements with one tag name, in page order. html.text_content joins all the text inside one element. In the code, :: names a value, ?? panic("...") stops if the page is over the size limits, and loop runs once per paragraph. The only difference is where the parser lives. In A it is a first-party package you add once. In B it ships inside Core.
decisions.story: Sam pulls the paragraphs out of a badly written web page. Nothing from the page may run or be downloaded.
decisions.inWild:
// https://html5lib.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ import html5lib doc = html5lib.parse("

A

B", treebuilder="etree") # Two repaired paragraph nodes; no script execution.
decisions.detail:
Code facts. Core/text/html.jet:14-16 calls tag stripping a span operation, not a parser. Lines 62-81 skip text between angle brackets without building any tree, and lines 88-100 decode only a dozen named entities. Core/encoding/xml.jet:220-225 makes element objects with name, attrs and children only, and has no kind field. The HTML node layout below is therefore a new, fully declared schema.

The package name jet is reserved for first-party packages (Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md:82-84). D-WD3=B (ratified) requires the missing-dependency error to offer the one command that adds it. No package, HTMLError or HTMLLimits exists yet. Proposed examples are not executed. The historical unescape defect from #4425 is not asserted as current.

options.name: First-party package jet.html_parser
options.detail:
Create a first-party package, written in pure Jet and kept in the Jet repository, named jet.html_parser. Write use jet.html_parser as html. If the package is not added yet, the compiler error shows the exact command, jet add jet.html_parser, so getting started is one step.

Core keeps escape, unescape and strip_tags for quick text jobs, and their documentation points to the package for real parsing. Updates to the HTML standard ship as new package versions, without waiting for a new Jet release.
options.technical:
This ballot approves creating the package. It does not claim the package already exists, is installed or is signed. It uses no Rust, C or external package bridge, so no unapproved dependency is hidden. Its content hash is recorded in the ordinary package lock.

API: parse(text: String) -> DataTree HTMLError!. parse_with(text: String, limits: HTMLLimits) -> DataTree HTMLError!. elements(tree: DataTree, name: String) -> [DataTree] Never! returns matching element nodes in document order. text_content(node: DataTree) -> String Never! joins descendant text nodes in document order. No separate event or streaming API is added.

Algorithm: whatwg/html commit a5e15011a00ddefd648c29e4d27734f3e7ff821f, tokenizer and tree construction for a full document. The scripting flag is off, so noscript content is parsed as markup. Input is an already-decoded Jet String, so no byte-encoding sniffing happens. Fragment parsing is out of scope. Nothing executes and nothing is fetched.

Covered rules: implied html, head and body; optional end tags; entities; raw text and RCDATA; comments; doctype and quirks; foster parenting; adoption-agency repair; select, table and template; SVG and MathML namespaces. Spec or entity-table updates are explicit version changes.

Schema: document {kind:"document", quirks:"no-quirks"|"limited-quirks"|"quirks", children}. Element {kind:"element", name, namespace, attrs, children}, with spec-adjusted names and canonical namespace URIs. Attribute {name, namespace, value}; first occurrence kept in order, later duplicates dropped per spec.

More schema: text and comment nodes are {kind:"text"|"comment", data}. Doctype is {kind:"doctype", name, public_id: Text or Null, system_id: Text or Null}. A template element also owns template_content: {kind:"fragment", children}, never merged into its ordinary children.

HTMLLimits.safe(): max_input_bytes 1048576, max_depth 256, max_nodes 100000, max_attributes_per_element 128, max_name_bytes 1024, max_expansion_bytes 16777216. Nodes are counted after repair, including nodes the repair creates. Depth is final-tree depth. Arithmetic is checked before allocation.

Errors: HTMLError {kind: Limit or InvalidLimits, offset, line, column, reason}. A zero or negative limit is InvalidLimits. The first limit crossed returns Limit naming it, before any partial tree is published. Broken markup is never an error; it is repaired by the standard.

options.name: Parser inside Core
options.detail: Put the same parser into Core's existing core.text.html module, next to escape and strip_tags. Nothing needs adding; use core.text.html works at once. Core then carries a large algorithm that changes over time. Every update needs a new Jet release and passing tests on every target Core supports.
options.technical: Add parse, parse_with, elements and text_content to core.text.html, with the identical signatures, pinned WHATWG commit, schema, limits, errors and repair law as A. Pure Jet owns the parser, with no host browser, DOM or XML fallback. Core ships it with its normal pinned source on every execution level and target.

gains: Core stays small; its quick text helpers are unchanged.

The compiler offers the one add command when it is missing.

whyNot.reason: Core would carry a large, changing browser algorithm that most programs never use.

recommendation.tradeoff: One add command the first time; the parser is the same either way.

Test each limit at its value and one past it, including repair-created nodes. Show no script runs and nothing is fetched. Check that the missing-package error offers jet add jet.html_parser.

decisions.situation:
HTML is the markup language of web pages. Core can already escape text for HTML, decode a few entities like &, and strip tags, but it cannot read a page into a tree of elements. Real pages are often broken. For example,

A

B never closes its paragraphs, and browsers follow a long published repair algorithm that turns it into two paragraphs. Anyone scraping or checking web pages needs that same repair, or they get the wrong text. You are deciding whether this full parser lives inside Core or in a separate first-party package written in Jet. We recommend a first-party package named jet.html_parser, which the compiler offers to add with one command the moment you import it, while Core keeps its small text helpers.

decisions.title: One set of rules for Core statistics
decisions.gist: Which single set of rules should mean, sum, rank, min, max and kde_random follow everywhere?
decisions.lesson: Jet has two copies of five statistics functions, and they disagree on huge numbers, infinity, ties and random sampling. One set of rules must win on every execution level. The recommended rules avoid needless overflow, rank ties fairly, accept infinities where the math allows, and keep sampling random but repeatable.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A Float stores numbers only up to about 1.8e308; 1e308 means 1 followed by 308 zeros. Overflow means a result too large to store, which becomes inf, infinity. NaN means not a number, the result of something like inf minus inf. Val(x) means an answer x is present; None means there is no meaningful answer.

The mean is the sum divided by the count. Adding 1e308 and 1e308 overflows, but their mean, 1e308, fits. A careful mean scales the numbers down first, so it never overflows when the answer fits. A compensated sum keeps track of the tiny rounding errors, so 1e16 + 1 - 1e16 gives 1, not 0.

A rank is a value's position after sorting, starting at 1. Ties can share the average of their positions, so [1, 1, 2] ranks [1.5, 1.5, 3]. Competition ranking gives them both the lower position, [1, 1, 3]. Spearman correlation, already in Core, needs averaged ties.

Kernel density estimation (KDE) smooths a set of samples into a curve. kde_random draws new random values from that curve, so it needs Jet's Rand effect, the permission to use randomness. random.seed(7) makes the draws repeat exactly.

Option A is the recommended rule set. Option B keeps the native Rust rules. Option C keeps the current Jet rules exactly as written today. All three run the same program.
decisions.story: Ana analyses large measurements and tied scores. Her results must not change when she switches how the program runs, and her random samples must repeat when she fixes the seed.
decisions.detail:
Code facts. Core/math/stats.jet:73-84 has a scaled mean that rejects any non-finite sample. Lines 87-110 have a Neumaier compensated sum with explicit infinities. Lines 493-505 sample kde_random with Rand. Lines 528-544 reject any non-finite sample in min and max. Lines 755-768 average ties with an n squared loop.

The native copy is crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/MathLibPure.rs. Lines 143-155 use a Kahan sum. Lines 222-229 use competition rank, also n squared. Lines 265-267 compute sum divided by n. Lines 467-475 make kde_random repeat density values without randomness, and lines 477-483 use f64 min and max, which skip NaN.

The arithmetic results shown are worked out from these rules and have not been run. Functions outside these five keep their current rules.

options.name: Careful rules, overflow-safe sum, infinities where the math allows
options.detail:
One rule covers all five functions. If the input contains NaN, there is no answer: None, an empty list, or NaN for sum. Infinities count as very large values in mean, sum, rank, min and max wherever the math still has an answer. The mean of +inf and -inf has none, so it gives None. kde_random is the exception: it needs finite samples, so an infinite sample gives an empty list.

mean scales before adding, so a mean that fits never overflows. sum keeps rounding errors, so 1e16 + 1 - 1e16 is 1. If its running total overflows, it starts over at a smaller scale, so 1e308 + 1e308 - 1e308 is 1e308; only a total that is truly too large gives infinity. rank shares positions between ties and sorts once, so it stays fast on long lists. min and max skip nothing silently. kde_random draws real random samples, and random.seed makes them repeat exactly.
options.technical:
One Jet implementation serves every execution level; the native Rust copies are deleted. Every level evaluates the same operations in the same order, with no fused multiply-add and no reordering. Acceptance therefore compares exact bits, and for kde_random exact bits under a fixed seed.

mean(xs) -> Float? Never!: empty or any NaN gives None. Infinities of one sign give that infinity. Infinities of both signs give None. Otherwise it scales by the largest magnitude, sums, divides and rescales, as stats.jet:73-84 does. [1e308, 1e308] gives Val(1e308).

sum(xs) -> Float Never!: a corrected Neumaier compensated sum. Empty gives +0.0. Any NaN gives NaN. Infinities of one sign give that infinity, and of both signs give NaN. Otherwise pass one is a plain Neumaier sum, as today. Today's stats.jet:87-110 fails when the running total overflows. For [1e308, 1e308] the correction becomes -inf, so the result is inf - inf, NaN. For [1e308, 1e308, -1e308] line 98 skips the cancelling value, so the result is NaN again.

The fix is pass two, which runs only if a partial total becomes infinite. Values of magnitude at least 2^-894 are multiplied by 2^-128, which is exact, and Neumaier-summed into a big total. Smaller values are Neumaier-summed unscaled into a small total. The result is big * 2^128 + small. Scaled totals stay below n * 2^896, so only the final multiply can overflow, and then the true sum is too large: the signed infinity. [1e308, 1e308] gives inf; [1e308, 1e308, -1e308] gives 1e308.

rank(xs) -> [Float] Never!: one-based positions in input order, ties sharing their average position. It is computed by one stable sort plus a tie-group pass, in n log n time, with the same answers as stats.jet:755-768 on finite input. Any NaN gives an empty list. Infinities rank as the largest or smallest values; today they give an empty list.

min and max -> Float? Never!: empty or any NaN gives None. Infinities are ordinary ordered values, so min([-inf, 1]) is Val(-inf); today that is None. Among equal values such as 0.0 and -0.0, the first one in the list wins. range keeps its own rule: a non-finite spread gives None.

kde_random(xs, bandwidth, n) -[Rand]> [Float] Never!: keeps stats.jet:493-505 unchanged. Each draw picks a sample with random.int, then adds random.normal noise. An empty list comes back for empty samples, any infinite or NaN sample, a bandwidth that is not positive and finite, or n of 0 or less. If a draw overflows to infinity, the whole call returns an empty list, as line 501 does today. Callers that want repeatable output call random.seed first. Fixed densities come from stats.kde.
options.code:
use core.math as math
use core.math.random as random
use core.math.stats as stats
inf :: math.infinity()
print(stats.mean([Float]{1e308, 1e308}))     // Val(1e308)
print(stats.mean([Float]{inf, 1.0}))         // Val(inf)
print(stats.sum([Float]{1e16, 1.0, -1e16}))  // 1
print(stats.sum([Float]{1e308, 1e308, -1e308})) // 1e308
print(stats.sum([Float]{inf, 1.0}))          // inf
print(stats.rank([Float]{1.0, 1.0, 2.0}))    // [1.5, 1.5, 3]
print(stats.min([Float]{math.nan(), 1.0}))   // None
print(stats.min([Float]{-inf, 1.0}))         // Val(-inf)
random.seed(7)
print(stats.kde_random([Float]{1.0, 2.0}, 0.5, 3)) // 3 draws near 1 or 2; same with seed 7

options.name: Native Rust rules
options.detail: Every execution level copies today's native results. mean adds first, so two huge numbers average to infinity. sum can lose a 1 next to 1e16. Ties share the lower position. min and max silently skip NaN. kde_random repeats the density values in a cycle and is not random at all, despite its name.
options.technical: Adopt MathLibPure.rs for all five. mean is sum divided by n, letting infinities and NaN flow through. sum is the Kahan fsum. rank is one plus the count of smaller values, n squared. min and max reduce with f64 min and max, which skip NaN. kde_random cycles the kde density array and drops the Rand effect. All Jet-side tests and docs migrate to these results.

print(stats.min([Float]{-inf, 1.0}))         // Val(-inf)

print(stats.kde_random([Float]{1.0, 2.0}, 0.5, 3)) // [d1, d2, d1]: densities, not random

options.name: Current Jet rules, unchanged
options.detail: Every execution level copies today's Jet results exactly. mean is careful, ties share their average position, and kde_random is truly random. But sum turns a running total that briefly overflows into NaN, even when the true total fits. Any infinity makes mean, min, max and rank give up, even when the math has a clear answer. Ranking a long list stays slow.
options.technical: Adopt Core/math/stats.jet as written. mean, min, max and rank reject any non-finite sample, returning None or an empty list. sum handles input infinities explicitly, but an overflowing running total gives NaN: the correction becomes -inf, and later values are skipped (lines 98 and 110). rank keeps its n squared loop. kde_random samples with Rand. The native copies are deleted.

print(stats.kde_random([Float]{1.0, 2.0}, 0.5, 3)) // 3 draws near 1 or 2; same with seed 7

comparisons.note: Python's statistics module avoids needless overflow in mean, and SciPy ranks ties by their average position by default.

recommendation.why: Every execution level gives the same, most useful answer. Huge values do not overflow needlessly, a sum survives a brief overflow, infinities work where each function has an answer, ties rank fairly and fast, and sampling stays random yet repeatable.
gains: Identical results, bit for bit, on every execution level.
Infinities get an answer wherever the function has one; the only None or empty results are NaN input, mixed-sign infinities in mean, and kde_random's finite-input rule.
Fast fair tie ranking and repeatable real random sampling.

losses.loss: Jet code that treated None or an empty list from mean, min, max or rank as an alarm for infinite input now gets a value.
losses.mitigation: the release note lists each changed case, and a one-line math.is_inf check on the input or result restores the alarm.

whyNot.reason: Native rules overflow needlessly, hide NaN, and make kde_random not random.

recommendation.tradeoff: Native-only results change to the documented answers. Jet results change only where Jet was wrong or refused: sums whose running total overflows, infinite input to mean, min, max and rank, and rank speed with the same answers.

print(stats.rank([Float]{1.0, 1.0, 2.0}))    // [1, 1, 3]
print(stats.min([Float]{math.nan(), 1.0}))   // Val(1)
print(stats.min([Float]{-inf, 1.0}))         // Val(-inf)
random.seed(7)
print(stats.kde_random([Float]{1.0, 2.0}, 0.5, 3)) // [d1, d2, d1]: densities, not random

options.name: Current Jet rules, unchanged
options.gist: Copy today's Jet results exactly, including refusing every infinity.
gains: Today's Jet results stay exactly the same.
losses: A sum whose running total briefly overflows becomes NaN.
Any infinity makes mean, min, max and rank give up.
Ranking a long list stays slow.

proposed.code:
use core.math as math
use core.math.random as random
use core.math.stats as stats
inf :: math.infinity()
print(stats.mean([Float]{1e308, 1e308}))     // Val(1e308)
print(stats.mean([Float]{inf, 1.0}))         // None
print(stats.sum([Float]{1e16, 1.0, -1e16}))  // 1
print(stats.sum([Float]{1e308, 1e308, -1e308})) // NaN
print(stats.sum([Float]{inf, 1.0}))          // inf
print(stats.rank([Float]{1.0, 1.0, 2.0}))    // [1.5, 1.5, 3]
print(stats.min([Float]{math.nan(), 1.0}))   // None
print(stats.min([Float]{-inf, 1.0}))         // None
random.seed(7)
print(stats.kde_random([Float]{1.0, 2.0}, 0.5, 3)) // 3 draws near 1 or 2; same with seed 7

recommendation.why: Every execution level gives the same, most useful answer. Huge values avoid needless overflow, and sums survive a brief overflow. Infinities work where the math allows. Ties rank fairly and fast, and sampling stays random yet repeatable.
gains: Identical results, bit for bit, on every execution level.
Infinities answered where the math allows; NaN input gives no answer.
Fast fair tie ranking and repeatable real random sampling.

losses.loss: Infinite input to mean, min, max or rank no longer gives None.
losses.mitigation: the release note lists each case; a one-line math.is_inf check restores the alarm.

whyNot.reason: Native rules overflow needlessly, hide NaN, and make kde_random not random.
Current Jet rules turn overflowing sums into NaN, refuse useful infinities and rank long lists slowly.

recommendation.tradeoff: Native-only results change to the documented answers. Jet results change only where Jet was wrong or refused: overflowing sums, infinite input to mean, min, max and rank, and rank speed.

decisions.situation: Core's statistics functions, such as average (mean), total (sum), ranking and minimum, exist twice today. One copy is written in Jet; the other is Rust code used when programs run natively, and the two give different answers. For example, the average of 1e308 and 1e308 is 1e308 in the Jet copy but infinity in the native copy, so a result changes with how the program is run. That breaks trust for anyone analysing data, and it breaks Jet's rule that every way of running a program gives the same answer. You are deciding which single set of rules every execution level follows. We recommend the careful Jet rules, improved so overflowing totals come out right, infinities work where the math allows, and ties rank quickly.

decisions.title: Detect hidden control characters in text
decisions.gist: Should Core ask whether text contains any control character, whether all of it is control characters, or both?
decisions.lesson: Control characters are invisible codes such as newline and tab. Validating a name means refusing it if any control character hides inside. Asking whether every character is a control character is a different question. Every option uses Unicode's fixed control list and gives empty text a clear answer.
decisions.explainer:
Unicode gives every character a category. The control category, called Cc, is a short fixed list: the codes 0 to 31 and 127 to 159. Newline (10), tab (9) and carriage return (13) are in it. Lookalikes such as the zero-width joiner, the line separator U+2028 and the paragraph separator U+2029 belong to other categories, so they are not controls here.

Two questions sound alike. "Has a control" is true if at least one character is a control: "ann" plus a newline has one. "Is control" is true only if every character is a control: "ann" plus a newline is not. An identity check, which decides whether a name is acceptable, needs the first question.

Jet already names its whole-string checks with is_: text.is_whitespace("  ") asks whether every character is whitespace. Option A adds the first has_ function, meaning "at least one". That gives readers a simple rule: is_ means all, has_ means any.

Empty text has no characters, so it contains no control: has_control("") is false. is_control("") would also be false, like is_alphabetic, is_numeric and is_whitespace.
decisions.story: Ana builds a tool that registers capture names. A user submits "ann" with a newline at the end. Ana wants that name refused, even though almost every character is an ordinary letter.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-04. No public control-character check exists in Core/text. Core/text/text.jet:888 has a private is_control used for grapheme boundaries. It excludes tab, newline and carriage return, so it does not match Unicode's Cc list.

Core/text/text.jet:68-71 public scalars() builds one String per character, and the private decode_scalars at 353-357 builds a list. The native Rust classifier at crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/Text.rs:386 tests Cc through the generated general-category table.

D-TEXTUNICODE1=A places Unicode classification in core.text, so the new function lives there, not in core.text.parse. The existing whole-string checks is_alphabetic, is_numeric and is_whitespace (text.jet:119-147) mean all characters and return false for empty text. The proposed calls were not run.

options.name: has_control: true if any character is a control
options.detail:
Add `text.has_control(value)`. It answers true as soon as it finds one control character, and false otherwise. Empty text gives false. Ana's check is one line: refuse the name if `text.has_control(name)` is true.

It never builds a String per character. The whole control list is bytes 0 to 31, byte 127, and the two-byte forms C2 80 to C2 9F. So the function scans the raw bytes once and stops at the first match. It is plain Jet source, so every tier runs the same code.
options.technical:
core.text: pub fn has_control(value: String) -> Bool Never!. True iff some scalar has General_Category Cc in Unicode 17.0.0, which is U+0000..U+001F and U+007F..U+009F.

Implementation: one pass over value.bytes(). A byte below 0x20 or equal to 0x7F matches. Byte 0xC2 followed by 0x80..0x9F matches. Valid UTF-8 guarantees 0xC2 is a lead byte here, so no other sequence can match. It stops at the first match and creates no per-scalar String or list.

Tests compare it with the generated Unicode 17 Cc table for every scalar. The private text.jet:888 helper is renamed is_grapheme_control with unchanged behavior, so the two meanings never share a name.

options.name: is_control only: true if every character is a control
options.detail:
Add `text.is_control(value)`, following the existing is_ family. It is true only when the text is not empty and every character is a control. "ann" plus a newline gives false, because a, n and n are letters.

Ana's check cannot use it directly. She must walk the name one character at a time with `text.scalars`, which builds a small String for each character, and test each one.
options.technical: core.text: pub fn is_control(value: String) -> Bool Never!. True iff value is nonempty and every scalar is Cc in Unicode 17.0.0. Same byte rule, tests and rename as A. Ana's identity check loops text.scalars(name), which allocates one String per scalar (text.jet:68-71).

options.name: Both functions
options.detail:
Add both `has_control` and `is_control`, sharing one byte rule. Ana uses has_control, and is_control is there for whole-string classification.

No program in the repository needs is_control today. It is extra surface to document and test with no current user.
options.technical: Both signatures exactly as in A and B, one shared private byte classifier, the same tests and the same rename.
options.code:
use core.text as text
fn accepted(name: String) -> Bool Never! { !text.has_control(name) }
print(accepted("ann"))      // true
print(accepted("ann\n"))    // false
print(accepted(""))         // true
print(text.is_control("\t")) // true: every character is a control

comparisons.note: Rust char.is_control uses the Unicode Cc category; callers write any() for the contains question.

recommendation.why: Ana's check needs the "contains any" question, and A answers it in one call with one byte scan. The name follows a clear rule: is_ means all, has_ means any.
gains: Ana's check is one call that builds nothing per character.
Clear naming: is_ means all characters, has_ means any.
The same plain Jet code runs on every tier.

whyNot.reason: Ana's check needs "contains any", so B makes her write a loop that builds a String per character.
is_control has no current user; it can join later under the same naming rule without changing has_control.

recommendation.tradeoff: One small function covers the real need; the every-character question waits until someone needs it.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Check empty text, ann, ann plus newline, tab, CR, U+0000, U+001F, U+007F, U+0080, U+009F, U+00A0, U+2028, U+2029 and U+200D. Compare has_control with the generated Unicode 17 Cc table for every scalar.

Show that no per-character String or list is created. Confirm the renamed private grapheme helper behaves exactly as before.

surface.gist: Should Core ask whether text contains any control character, whether all of it is, or both?
surface.lesson: Control characters are invisible codes such as newline and tab. Validating a name means refusing it if any control character hides inside. Asking whether every character is a control character is a different question. Every option uses Unicode's fixed control list and gives empty text a clear answer.

current.note: Core has only a private helper, and it skips tab, newline and carriage return.

wild.note: Rust tests one character; the contains question uses any().

options.name: has_control: any character is a control
options.gist: One call answers whether a control character hides anywhere in the text.
gains: Ana's check is one call with one byte scan.
Clear rule: is_ means all, has_ means any.

proposed.code:
use core.text as text
fn accepted(name: String) -> Bool Never! { !text.has_control(name) }
print(accepted("ann"))      // true
print(accepted("ann\n"))    // false: ends with a newline
print(accepted(""))         // true

options.name: is_control only: every character is a control
options.gist: A whole-string check in the existing is_ style.
gains: Matches the existing is_ family exactly.
losses: Ana must loop, building one String per character.
Copying is_control alone wrongly accepts ann plus newline.

options.name: Both functions
options.gist: has_control for Ana, is_control for whole-string checks.
gains: Both questions have a direct answer.
losses: is_control has no current user to justify it.

proposed.code:
use core.text as text
fn accepted(name: String) -> Bool Never! { !text.has_control(name) }
print(accepted("ann\n"))    // false
print(text.is_control("\t")) // true

recommendation.why: Ana needs the contains-any question, and A answers it in one call with one byte scan and a clear name.
gains: One call, nothing built per character.
is_ means all, has_ means any.
Same plain Jet code on every tier.

whyNot.reason: B forces a per-character loop for the common check.
is_control has no user yet and can join later unchanged.

recommendation.tradeoff: One small function covers the real need without unused surface.

decisions.situation: Control characters are invisible codes inside text, such as newline, tab or the old terminal bell, rather than letters you can see. Jet has no public way to ask whether a string contains one. So a name like "ann" with a hidden newline at the end can pass a check and later break a log line, a file name or a terminal display. This matters most for programs that accept names or identifiers from users or files, and for reviewers who want hidden characters refused. You are deciding which question Core answers: does the text contain any control character, is every character a control character, or both. We recommend one function, text.has_control, that answers the "contains any" question by scanning the bytes once with no extra memory.

decisions.title: Make bad sign-extension widths impossible to pass by mistake
decisions.gist: How should sign_extend refuse widths outside 1 to 64: through the width's type, an error result, or caller checks?
decisions.lesson: Sign extension reads the low bits of a number as a signed value. Widths below 1 or above 64 make no sense. Today they crash the program in one tier and pass silently in another. Every option keeps all valid results identical; they differ only in where a bad width is caught.
decisions.explainer:
Computers store negative whole numbers in a pattern called two's complement. In an 8-bit field, the bit pattern for 255 means -1, and 128 means -128. Sign extension takes the low bits of a number and reads them that way. The width says how many low bits count: 8, 16, 32, or anything from 1 to 64.

Jet has range types. `Int(1..64)` is an Int that is always between 1 and 64. When you write a literal such as 8, the compiler checks it. When the number comes from a running program, `Int(1..64).from_int(raw)` converts it and can fail, so you handle the failure once, right there. This already works today, as Examples/features/types/range_types.jet shows.

Mina's parser reads each field's width from the file. Under option A she converts the width once, right after reading it, and turns a bad value into her own parse error. Every later call is safe without extra checks.
decisions.story: Mina writes a parser for a binary file format. Each field states its own bit width. A damaged file with width 0 must give an ordinary parse error, not crash her program.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-04. Core/encoding/binary.jet:132-138 declares sign_extend(n: Int, bits: Int) -> Int Never! and computes 1 << (bits - 1) before any check. Recorded evidence in Docs/research/evidence-2026-09-29/3275-base-encodings-fixed-buffer.md:30 shows sign_extend(1, 0) stopping with E3010 Invalid shift count.

crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/EncodingBase.rs:313-319 is a separate 64-bit copy that returns the input unchanged for widths outside 1..64. The JIT symbol calls it (crates/jet-jit/src/Encoding.rs:924-926). So tiers disagree on bad widths.

Internal callers in binary.jet:349-365 pass only the literal widths 8, 16, 32 and 64. Inline range types and their diagnostics exist today. E0135 rejects an out-of-range literal (tests/ui/inline_range_out_of_bounds.stderr). E0136 requires the fallible form for a runtime value (tests/ui/inline_range_runtime_needs_try.stderr). The proposed calls were not run.

options.name: The width's type only allows 1 to 64
options.detail:
Change the parameter to `bits: Int(1..64)`. A call with a literal width, like `sign_extend(255, 8)`, compiles exactly as today. A literal like 0 or 65 is a compile error, so the mistake never reaches a user. The function itself can no longer fail, so it keeps returning a plain Int.

A width read from a file starts as a plain Int. Mina converts it once with `Int(1..64).from_int(raw)` and handles failure there, usually by returning her own parse error. If she forgets and passes the plain Int, the compiler rejects the call, because a plain Int is not an Int(1..64). This decision adds a fix line to that error that suggests the conversion; that suggestion is new and is checked before the change lands.
options.technical:
pub fn sign_extend(n: Int, bits: Int(1..64)) -> Int Never!. For width w, v is n masked to its low w bits. The result is v - 2^w when bit w-1 of v is set, otherwise v. n is an exact Int of any size or sign; negative n is masked the same way.

Width 64 uses an all-ones mask computed directly, never 1 << 64. It maps 2^63 to -2^63 and 2^64-1 to -1. Width 1 maps even values to 0 and odd values to -1. Width 8 maps 128 to -128, 127 to 127 and -129 to 127.

One implementation serves every tier. The EncodingBase.rs copy follows the same exact-Int law and loses its invalid-width branch. Internal unpack callers are unchanged. Update the registry signature rows (CorePlatformSignatures.jet:395, fixed_sigs.rs and core_calls) and the core-library reference table. The function has no stop path, so it is allowed under -[!Panic]>.

Diagnostics. A literal outside 1..64 is E0135, the existing inline-range error. A plain Int argument is rejected as a type mismatch, because Int is not Int(1..64). Proposed, not current: that error's fix line suggests `Int(1..64).from_int(raw)?`. An unhandled from_int call is the existing E0136 (tests/ui/inline_range_runtime_needs_try.stderr).

options.name: Return a BinaryError for a bad width
options.detail:
Change the result to `Int BinaryError!`. A width outside 1..64 returns `BinaryError.Range` before any arithmetic.

Every caller must now handle a possible error, even when the width is a fixed literal like 8 that can never be wrong. The internal unpack code and example programs gain error handling that never fires. A wrong literal width is still found only when the program runs.
options.technical: pub fn sign_extend(n: Int, bits: Int) -> Int BinaryError!. bits < 1 or bits > 64 returns Err(BinaryError.Range) before shifting. Same valid-width law and single implementation as A.
options.code:
use core.encoding.binary as binary
print(binary.sign_extend(255, 8) ?? 0)   // -1; the ?? never fires for 8
print(binary.sign_extend(127, 8) ?? 0)   // 127
print(binary.sign_extend(1, 0) ?? 0)     // 0: Range is found only at run time

#Error
enum ParseError { BadWidth }             // Mina's own error type

fn field(raw: Int, width_from_file: Int) -> Int ParseError! {
    binary.sign_extend(raw, width_from_file) ?? return Err(ParseError.BadWidth)
}

options.name: Callers check the width; a bad width stops the program
options.detail:
Keep `-> Int Never!`. A width outside 1..64 stops the program with a clear message, the same in every tier.

Mina must remember to check the width herself before every call. If she forgets once, a damaged file stops her parser.
options.technical: pub fn sign_extend(n: Int, bits: Int) -> Int Never!. It checks 1..64 first and stops with E3010 otherwise. Same valid-width law; the Rust silent pass-through is removed.

comparisons.note: Rust often moves a range check into a type, such as NonZeroU32, so later code cannot misuse the value.
Without a type, Rust checked shifts let callers refuse a bad width before the arithmetic.

recommendation.why: A catches wrong literal widths while compiling and makes file-read widths pass one check where they enter. Valid calls stay exactly as short as today.
gains: Fixed widths like 8 need no change and no error handling.
Wrong literal widths are caught while compiling, not in production.
Widths from files are checked once, where untrusted data enters.

whyNot.reason: B makes every fixed-width call handle an error that cannot happen, and still finds wrong literals only at run time.
C relies on every caller remembering a check; one forgotten check lets a damaged file stop the program.

recommendation.tradeoff: The width's type does the checking, so valid code stays short and bad widths cannot slip through.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Check every width 1..64 against a two's-complement reference, with negative inputs, -129, 2^63 and 2^64-1. Assert literal widths 0 and 65 give E0135. Assert a plain Int width is rejected and the error's fix line suggests Int(1..64).from_int(raw)?, and an unhandled from_int gives E0136.

Assert Int(1..64).from_int fails for 0, 65 and -1. Migrate every signature row and tier caller, and prove the Rust pass-through branch is gone.

surface.gist: How should sign_extend refuse widths outside 1 to 64: by the width's type, an error result, or caller checks?
surface.lesson: Sign extension reads the low bits of a number as a signed value. Widths below 1 or above 64 make no sense. Today they crash the program in one tier and pass silently in another. Every option keeps all valid results identical; they differ only in where a bad width is caught.

current.note: The Jet code shifts before any check, so width 0 crashes; a Rust copy returns the input unchanged.

wild.note: Rust moves the range check into a type, then uses the value freely.

options.name: The width's type only allows 1 to 64
options.gist: Literal widths are checked while compiling; file widths are checked once on entry.
gains: Fixed-width calls stay exactly as they are today.
Wrong literal widths fail at compile time.

options.name: Return a BinaryError for a bad width
options.gist: A bad width returns BinaryError.Range at run time.
gains: A bad width becomes an ordinary error, never a crash.
losses: Every fixed-width call handles an error that cannot happen.
Wrong literal widths are found only at run time.

options.name: Callers check; a bad width stops the program
options.gist: Keep a plain Int result; callers guard every call themselves.
gains: No signature change for any caller.
losses: One forgotten check lets a damaged file stop the program.

recommendation.why: A catches wrong literal widths while compiling and checks file widths once where they enter. Valid calls stay as short as today.
gains: Fixed widths need no change or error handling.
Wrong literals fail at compile time.
Untrusted widths are checked once, on entry.

whyNot.reason: B adds never-firing error handling and finds wrong literals only at run time.
C depends on every caller remembering a check.

recommendation.tradeoff: The width's type does the checking, so valid code stays short and bad widths cannot slip through.

decisions.situation: Sign extension turns the low bits of a number into a signed value; for example, in an 8-bit field the pattern 255 means -1. Today binary.sign_extend crashes the program when the width is 0 or above 64, while a separate Rust copy silently returns the input unchanged. So a parser that reads the width from a damaged file can be stopped cold, and different tiers give different answers. This matters to anyone decoding binary file or network formats, and to reviewers who want bad input to become an ordinary error. You are deciding where a bad width is caught: by the width's type, by an error result, or by checks in every caller. We recommend typing the width as Int(1..64), so literal widths are checked while compiling and a width read from a file is checked once, where it enters.

decisions.title: Hand optional work to a background queue without waiting for queue space
decisions.gist: What should Jet add so a program can hand optional work to a background queue without waiting for queue space?
decisions.lesson: Optional work, like saving history, must never block the command the user is waiting for. A bounded queue holds a fixed number of jobs. When it is full, the program needs an immediate answer and its job back. Jet already has tasks, bounded channels and crash reporting; the question is how little to add.
decisions.explainer:
A task is a piece of work that runs alongside the rest of the program. A channel is a pipe between tasks: one end sends values, the other end receives them in order. `channel<T>(capacity: 8)` makes a pipe that holds at most 8 waiting values.

Today `send` on a full channel waits until there is room. That is right for most work, because nothing is lost. For optional work it is wrong: a slow disk would freeze the user's command. The program needs a send that never waits and says "full" instead.

Ownership matters. `^job` moves the job into the call, so the caller no longer has it. If the queue refuses, the job must come back, so the caller can drop it on purpose or note that it was skipped. Nothing should vanish silently.

A panic is a crash inside one task. In Jet, when you join a child task, its panic comes back as the value `TaskFailure.Panicked(reason)` instead of ending the program. So a worker can run each job as a small child task and keep going after one job crashes.
decisions.story: Mina's command saves an optional history record after it finishes, using a queue of 8. If the disk is slow or one save crashes, her command must still return at once, and later saves must still run.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-04. Source/ReceiptStore.rs:44-71 is the Rust model: a sync_channel of capacity 8 and one thread named jet-optional-history with catch_unwind around each job. ReceiptStore.rs:1927-1930 offers jobs with try_send and handles Full and Disconnected.

Docs/spec/spec.md:2125-2159 defines the builtin channel<T>(capacity: N) with FIFO order, and send waits when full. Examples/features/concurrency/channel_outcomes.jet:52-64 records that send after close, or after the receiver is dropped, returns normally and drops the value silently. Receiver already has try_receive(), but no try_send exists in Compiler/ or the spec.

spec.md:2207-2267 and Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:2542-2678 define task f(), task.detach(), and join() -> T !TaskFailure. A joined child panic becomes Panicked(reason) without ending the process (Examples/features/concurrency/task_panic.jet). Core/tasks/tasks.jet:27-85 TaskState is a plain value record, not a worker. Notice wording, the capacity of 8 and notice dedup stay CLI policy.

options.name: Add try_send; build the worker from existing parts
options.detail:
Add one method to the existing channel sender: `jobs.try_send(^job)`. It never waits for queue space. If the queue has room, the job is queued. If the queue is full or closed, the job comes back inside the error, so you decide what to do with it.

The worker is ordinary Jet: a task that loops over the receiving end. It runs each job as a small child task and joins it, so a crash in one job comes back as `Panicked` and the loop moves on. When the sender closes, the loop finishes the queued jobs in order and ends.

At shutdown you choose. Joining the worker waits for jobs already accepted, so none is lost. Detaching it lets the command return at once, and jobs still queued when the process exits are not saved.

Beginners copy one short pattern, shipped as Examples/features/concurrency/background_queue.jet and shown in the channel docs. Experts use the same pieces directly. Nothing else is added: no worker type and no second crash-catching tool.
options.technical:
Sender<T>.try_send(^value: T) -> Unit SendRefused<T>! with SendRefused<T> = Full(T) | Closed(T). It never parks and needs no Time.Wait effect. A refusal returns the identical value, never a copy. Payloads must be sendable (E1102).

Each try_send takes effect at one atomic point in the channel's order. At that point Closed wins: if the channel is closed or its receiver is gone, the result is Closed(value), even when the queue is also full. Otherwise, if the queue holds capacity values, the result is Full(value). Otherwise the value is accepted.

Capacity counts queued values only; a job being handled has already left the queue. Every accepted value, including one accepted just before close, keeps FIFO order and is drained. On channel<T>() with no buffer, try_send succeeds only by handing the value to a receiver already waiting in receive(). Otherwise it returns Full(value), as Go's select default and Rust's zero-size sync_channel do.

The worker pattern uses only task, loop value in receiver, a per-job task with join() -> T !TaskFailure, sender.close(), and join or task.detach(). After close, join() waits for the accepted jobs. A detached worker runs while the process lives and stops at process exit, so jobs still queued then are not saved. The job function's effects are checked as for any task.

Single-thread targets run the worker as a cooperative task on the same scheduler; there is no hidden inline fallback. try_send still returns without running any job. A queued job runs only when the foreground reaches a wait point. A native blocking file call inside a running job holds the one thread until it returns, as it would under every option.

options.name: A Worker type in core.tasks
options.detail:
Add `tasks.worker(capacity, handle, on_failure)`, which returns a Worker handle with `try_send`, `close` and `join`. It hides the loop and the per-job child task, so starting one is shorter.

But it is a second way to run background work next to `task` and channels. It brings its own lifecycle rules, failure callback and documentation, and it still needs the same try_send inside. Programs that outgrow it must be rewritten with tasks and channels.
options.technical: tasks.worker<T>(capacity: Int, handle: fn(^T) -> Unit, on_failure: fn(TaskFailure) -> Unit) -> Worker<T>. Worker.try_send(^T) -> Unit SendRefused<T>!, close(&self) and join(^self) -> Unit TaskFailure!. Same FIFO, close and ownership laws as A.

options.name: No new API: a detached task does each blocking send
options.detail:
Use only today's tools. For each optional job, start a small task that does the ordinary waiting `send`, and detach it. The command never waits, because the waiting happens inside the extra task.

But nothing limits how many of those tasks pile up. If the disk stalls, every new job adds one more parked task holding its data, so memory grows without limit. The program also never learns that history was skipped.
options.technical: No new surface. Each enqueue spawns task { sender.send(^job) } on a second sender made with ~jobs and calls task.detach(). Parked senders are unbounded; a send after close still drops silently.

comparisons.note: SyncSender.try_send never blocks and hands the rejected job back as Full or Disconnected.
Go spells a non-waiting send as a select with a default branch.

recommendation.why: A fills the one real gap, a send that never waits, and reuses tasks, loops and crash reports Jet already has. No second way to run background work appears.
gains: Enqueueing never waits for queue space; a full queue answers at once.
A refused job comes back to the caller; nothing vanishes silently.
One new method; tasks, loops and crash reports are reused.

losses.loss: On a single-thread target, a slow file write that is already running holds the only thread until it finishes.
losses.mitigation: This is physical and the same under every option. try_send still returns at once, and a queued job runs only when the foreground reaches a wait point. Jobs stay small, one record each, so each hold is one write.

whyNot.reason: A worker type is a second way to run background work beside task and channels, with its own rules to learn.
Detached senders pile up without limit when the disk stalls, and skipped work is never reported.

recommendation.tradeoff: One small method fills the only real gap; everything else is Jet that programmers already know.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Exercise capacity 8 in FIFO order, an immediate Full refusal and a Closed refusal after close, each returning the identical value. Check that Closed wins over Full on a full, closed channel, that a value accepted just before close is drained, and that an unbuffered channel accepts only into a waiting receiver. Assert try_send never parks, even while the worker is blocked on a slow job.

Show a crashing job reports Panicked and later jobs still run. Show join after close waits for accepted jobs, and a detached worker lets the command return at once. On a single-thread target, show try_send runs no job and queued jobs run at the next wait point. Prove queued and refused values drop exactly once on every target, and that the shipped example matches the spec text.

When it is full, the program needs an immediate answer and its job back. Jet already has tasks, bounded channels and crash reporting; the question is how little to add.

decisions.situation: Some work is optional, like saving a history record after a command finishes, and should happen in the background without slowing the user down. Jet already has tasks and bounded channels, but sending on a full channel waits for space, and sending after close silently drops the value. So a program that queues optional history behind a slow disk either freezes the user's command or loses records without a word. This matters for the Jet command-line tools now being ported to Jet, and for any app with logs, caches or uploads. You are deciding what Jet adds so a program can offer work to a queue and get an immediate yes or no. We recommend one new method, try_send on the existing channel sender, and building the worker from tasks and loops Jet already has. One limit is physical: on a target with a single thread, a slow write that is already running still holds that thread until it finishes.

decisions.title: Byte values in the shared DataTree
decisions.gist: Should the shared DataTree keep raw bytes as their own kind, and how should text formats write them?
decisions.lesson: A byte string and a list of small numbers can print the same but mean different things. Today the public tree cannot hold bytes, so generic CBOR reading fails. The choice is whether to add a Bytes kind, and whether text formats write it as numbers or refuse it.
decisions.explainer:
DataTree is a value that describes data without knowing your record type. Each value carries its kind: null, true/false, whole number, decimal number, text, list or object. Think of a labelled box: two boxes can hold the same things, but their labels still differ.

A byte is a small number from 0 to 255. Jet writes the type of a list of bytes as [U8]. A byte string is one value made of bytes, such as a photo or a hash. A list of numbers is a different kind of value, even when the numbers match.

CBOR is a compact binary format. It marks every value with a type code. The first byte 0x42 (66 in decimal) means "byte string of length 2". So the three bytes 0x42 0x01 0x02 mean "the bytes 1 and 2". An empty byte string is the single byte 0x40; a one-byte string holding 7 is 0x41 0x07.

A codec reads or writes one format. A round trip writes a value and reads it back. It is exact when the value and its kind both survive. Typed decoding means you tell Jet the type you expect, for example json.decode<[U8]>(text). Then Jet can rebuild bytes from numbers, because the type says what they are.

In the examples, :: gives a value a name. ?? panic("{err}") stops the program and shows the error if a call fails. print shows a value. Comments after // describe the intended output; none of these programs was run.
decisions.story: Sam keeps a folder of CBOR test files. His tool reads each file into the shared tree, compares it with the expected value, and writes a JSON report. The first file holding a byte string stops the whole tool.
decisions.detail:
## What the code does today

The Jet-visible DataTree has seven kinds: Null, Bool, Int, Float, Text, Array and Object (Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/CoreEnumRows.jet:74). The runtime's own tree already has Bytes (crates/jet-foundation/src/DataTree.rs:19). The public event reader already has DataEvent.Bytes (CoreEnumRows.jet:77).

Core CBOR refuses byte strings with Unsupported (Core/encoding/cbor.jet:169-170). The typed codec already turns a [U8] value into a Bytes tree, so CBOR can write a real byte string (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/EncodingTraits.rs:135-149). Typed [U8] decoding already accepts either a Bytes tree or a list of numbers (EncodingTraits.rs:466-471).

One runtime JSON renderer writes Bytes as a number list (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/JetStd/JSONDataTree.rs:39-42). Another one panics on Bytes (crates/jet-foundation/src/EncodingJson.rs:407). Today's public text encoders cannot fail: json.to_string, json.to_string_pretty, jsonl.to_string, toml.to_string and xml.to_string all return String Never!. cbor.to_bytes returns [U8] Never!.

## Same program in every option

Each option runs Sam's step on the same three input bytes 0x42 0x01 0x02. It reads them as a tree, writes CBOR back, writes JSON, and reads the JSON back as bytes. Only the result differs. None of the programs was run; the comments state the intended result under each proposal.

## Related choices that stay separate

This ballot does not change the runtime's Number and TypedText helpers (DataTree.rs:14-17). They hold exact text while typed decoding runs. It also does not change duplicate-key or object-order rules.

options.name: Add Bytes; text formats write a number list
options.detail:
Add a Bytes kind to the public tree. CBOR reads and writes byte strings exactly. Every text format writes Bytes as the plain list of numbers 0 to 255, the same way the runtime already does. Text parsing never guesses bytes; typed decoding into [U8] rebuilds them. No existing function signature changes.

Beginner: reading binary data just works, and JSON output looks like [1,2]. Expert: use CBOR for an exact untyped round trip, or name the [U8] type when reading text.
options.technical:
Public enum: DataTree gains Bytes([U8]). Its order is Null, Bool, Int, Float, Text, Bytes, Array, Object, matching the runtime tree in DataTree.rs:9-22 minus the two internal helpers. Bytes owns its list under the same ownership and copy rules as Text and Array. There is no second buffer type.

Equality is exact. Bytes([1,2]) equals Bytes([1,2]) and never equals Array([Int(1), Int(2)]). Test comparison keeps the kind. No text rendering is used to decide equality.

CBOR: major type 2 decodes to Bytes, including empty, all 256 byte values and bytes that are not valid UTF-8. The declared length is checked against EncodingLimits.max_item_bytes before any allocation, exactly like text strings (cbor.jet:173-175). A truncated string returns Truncated at its path. to_bytes and to_bytes_canonical write major type 2. Their signatures stay [U8] Never!.

Text formats: every text writer shares one rendering rule for Bytes, applied in place while it walks the tree. On reaching Bytes(b), the writer reads b by borrow and writes each byte as a decimal number straight into its output. The text is exactly what the equal Array of Int would produce, compact or pretty. No Array, copied list or second tree is built, so a large byte value costs only its output text. The runtime JSON renderer already writes Bytes without a tree copy (JSONDataTree.rs:39-42).

The rule covers json.to_string, to_string_pretty, dumps, dump, canonical, jsonl.to_string, toml.to_string, xml.to_string and xml.to_bytes. Their signatures stay: String Never!, [U8] Never!, and String EncodingError! for json.canonical, which gains no new error. The panicking Foundation JSON path (EncodingJson.rs:407) is cut over to the same rule. The JSON renderers then agree on every tier. No base64, hex or text guessing is added.

Parsing: json.parse, toml.parse, yaml.parse and xml.parse never produce Bytes. A number list stays Array(Int), so the Bytes kind does not survive a text round trip. Typed decoding of [U8], such as json.decode<[U8]>("[1,2]"), yields the bytes 1 and 2. A number outside 0 to 255 returns a FieldError at its path. That reuses the existing typed rule.

Events: DataEvent.Bytes already exists. A tree built from events maps it to Bytes, and writing a tree emits it, so the reader and the tree finally agree.

Migration: every Core match over DataTree gains a Bytes arm in the same change. A match with an else arm compiles unchanged. A user match that lists every kind gets the existing missing-arm compile error naming .Bytes at its line. There is no safe automatic default, so that author chooses the arm, such as .Bytes(b) -> handle b as [U8].
options.code:
use core.encoding.cbor as cbor
use core.encoding.json as json
// 0x42 means "byte string, length 2"; then the bytes 1 and 2
input :: [U8]{0x42, 0x01, 0x02}
value :: cbor.parse(input) ?? panic("{err}")
print(value)                    // a Bytes value holding 1 and 2
print(cbor.to_bytes(value))     // the same three bytes: 0x42 0x01 0x02
text :: json.to_string(value)
print(text)                     // [1,2]  (JSON has no byte type)
print(json.parse(text) ?? panic("{err}") == value)  // false: untyped JSON gives numbers
again :: json.decode<[U8]>(text) ?? panic("{err}")
print(again)                    // the bytes 1 and 2 again: the type says so

options.name: Keep bytes out of the public tree
options.detail:
Keep the seven-kind public tree. Generic CBOR reading keeps refusing byte strings with Unsupported at their path. Programs that need bytes must decode into a typed record or a [U8] value instead.

The runtime keeps its private Bytes kind for typed CBOR, so the Jet-visible tree and the runtime tree keep two different kind lists. Sam's tool must skip or fail on every byte-string file.
options.technical:
No public enum change. cbor.parse keeps returning Unsupported for major type 2 (cbor.jet:169-170). The typed path keeps using the runtime-only Bytes kind (EncodingTraits.rs:141-146), so typed [U8] fields still encode as CBOR byte strings.

The panicking Foundation JSON path must still be cut over, because typed values can reach it. Test tools must report a byte-string file as an explicit refusal, never as a pass. The public tree and DataEvent keep disagreeing: events can report Bytes, but a tree cannot hold them.

options.name: Add Bytes; text formats refuse it
options.detail:
Add the same Bytes kind and exact CBOR support as A. But every text encoder refuses Bytes with an Unsupported error instead of writing numbers. That makes the loss impossible to miss, but it changes seven public text-encoder signatures from "cannot fail" to "can fail".

Every existing caller of those encoders must add error handling, even for trees that never contain bytes.
options.technical:
Same enum, equality, CBOR, event and typed-decoding rules as A. Text encoders check the whole tree before writing anything. The first Bytes value returns EncodingError.Unsupported with its exact path, and no partial text is returned.

Signature changes: json.to_string, json.to_string_pretty, json.dumps, jsonl.to_string, toml.to_string and xml.to_string change from String Never! to String EncodingError!; xml.to_bytes changes from [U8] Never! to [U8] EncodingError!. Every caller migrates. The runtime JSONDataTree.rs renderer must also start refusing instead of writing numbers.

comparisons.note: CBOR has a separate type code for byte strings, so a CBOR library can read and re-write them exactly. JSON has no such type; libraries that write bytes to JSON must pick a convention.

recommendation.why: Bytes become an ordinary tree kind, CBOR stays exact, and text formats keep the number list the runtime already writes. Nothing that works today changes signature.
gains: Generic CBOR reads and writes byte strings exactly.
No encoder signature changes; existing callers keep compiling.
Public tree, runtime tree and event reader finally agree.

losses.loss: Untyped JSON reads a byte list back as an Array of numbers, so the Bytes kind is lost in a text round trip.
losses.mitigation: JSON has no byte type, so no text rule can keep the kind without guessing; this limit is physical and flagged in the summary. json.decode<[U8]> or a typed [U8] field restores the bytes exactly, and CBOR keeps the kind with no type named.

losses.loss: A user match that lists every tree kind needs one Bytes arm, and its author must choose what bytes mean there.
losses.mitigation: Core's own matches are migrated in the same change, and matches with an else arm need no change. For the rest, the existing compile error names .Bytes and the exact line, and the author adds one arm, for example .Bytes(b) -> handle b as [U8].

whyNot.reason: B keeps generic CBOR failing on byte strings and keeps two different tree kind lists inside Jet.
C makes seven text encoders fallible, so every caller adds error handling even when no bytes exist.

recommendation.tradeoff: A accepts JSON's own limit, softened by typed decoding, instead of refusing bytes or changing every text encoder.

decisions.checkInstructions:
CBOR round trip: empty, one byte, all 256 values, invalid UTF-8, a length at max_item_bytes and one above, and a truncated string. Check Bytes never equals Array(Int) in equality and test comparison.

Text writers: json.to_string, to_string_pretty, dumps, dump, canonical, jsonl.to_string, toml.to_string, xml.to_string and xml.to_bytes. Each writes Bytes as the number list on every tier. Cover a Bytes value nested inside arrays and objects, and one at max_item_bytes. Show that peak memory tracks the output text, with no Array copy built. The Foundation JSON panic is gone.

Parsing never yields Bytes. json.decode<[U8]> accepts [0,255] and rejects 256 and -1 at their paths. Events and trees agree on Bytes in both directions.
