decisions.situation: Jet has one shared data tree, called DataTree, that every file format reads into and writes out of, like a universal box for JSON, TOML, XML and the binary format CBOR. The public tree has no slot for raw bytes. So reading the CBOR value "the bytes 1 and 2" fails with an Unsupported error, although Jet's own runtime tree and its event reader already have a Bytes kind. This bites anyone who handles binary data without a fixed record type, such as test tools that compare CBOR files or converters from CBOR to JSON. You are deciding whether the public tree gains a Bytes kind, and what text formats do with it. We recommend adding Bytes, keeping CBOR exact, and writing bytes as a plain list of numbers in text formats, which is what the runtime already does, so no function signature changes. One limit cannot be removed: JSON has no byte type, so untyped JSON reads that list back as numbers; asking for the [U8] type restores the bytes exactly.

decisions.title: Keep the field order of parsed data objects
decisions.gist: Should parsed data objects keep the order their fields arrive in, while ordinary Maps stay sorted?
decisions.lesson: A DataTree is Jet's box for any parsed data. Its objects keep named fields in an ordinary Map, and Maps sort their keys. So a file read and written back can come out reordered. The fix must keep order all the way from reading to writing. Ordinary Maps should not change, and code that builds objects should keep working.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A DataTree is the value Jet makes when it reads JSON, TOML, YAML or CBOR: numbers, text, lists and objects. An object is a group of named fields, such as {"name": "Ana"}. A Map is Jet's ordinary key-to-value table, and it always lists keys in sorted order. Parsing means reading text into a value. Writing, also called encoding, turns the value back into text.

Today the runtime already stores each object as an ordered list of name and value pairs. But the Jet code that parses files first collects the fields in a Map. The Map sorts them, so the order is gone before the list is made. The JSON writer's own comment says it keeps insertion order, but the order was lost earlier.

Option A changes only what an object holds: it becomes that same ordered pair list. A literal such as DataTree.Object(["b": x, "a": y]) keeps the written order, as an earlier decision already promised. Passing a Map still works and hands over the Map's sorted order. Parsers switch to the pair list. Ordinary Maps do not change at all.

Option B makes every Map in the language remember insertion order instead. Option C keeps objects sorted and changes the writers' promise and the reference test files to match.

All three options run the same program: parse {"b":1,"a":2}, then write it back. In the code, :: names a value, and ?? panic("...") stops the program with that message if parsing fails.
decisions.story: Ana reads a small JSON settings file, changes nothing and writes it back. She expects the fields in the order she wrote them. Her cache Maps elsewhere in the program should stay sorted, as they are today.
decisions.detail:
Code facts. crates/jet-foundation/src/DataTree.rs:1-21 stores Object as an ordered Vec<(String, DataTree)> and says parsers enforce duplicate policy instead of collapsing through a map. crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerCoreLib/core_literals.rs:22-29 types a source Object payload as a Map but lets compiler-generated encoders pass the ordered pair list. crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core.rs:2680-2681 backs Map with a sorted BTreeMap.

Core/encoding/json.jet:540-566 and toml.jet:33-44 collect object fields in Maps. json.jet:96 promises insertion order, and json.jet:630-645 assumes a Map keeps it. The native compiler recovers written order only when it can trace the keys written into one Map inside one function (crates/jet-jit/src/jit/functions_compile.rs:13862-13927 and 14059-14072).

Ratified context. Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:3899-3907 (D-SERDE13/14/15) says hand-built objects use the key-value literal, insertion-ordered, and does not accept the pair-list form. D-DATATREE-ERGO1=A (syntax-decisions.md:3916-3922) added equal_unordered, which ignores object field order. Proposed examples are not executed.

options.name: Objects keep arrival order; Maps stay sorted
options.detail:
An object remembers its fields in the order they arrive. Reading {"b":1,"a":2} and writing it back gives {"b":1,"a":2}. Ordinary Maps keep sorting, exactly as today.

You build objects the same ways as today. A literal keeps the order you wrote. A Map you pass in hands over its sorted order. To build an object in a loop and keep arrival order, push name and value pairs onto a list and pass the list. A compiler warning suggests this when you fill a Map and then turn it into an object.

Looking up a field works as today with .field(name). Writers that must sort, such as canonical JSON, still sort.

Because order now counts, == treats {"b":1,"a":2} and {"a":2,"b":1} as different. To keep old code's answers, jet fix rewrites each existing == or != between data values to equal_unordered, which compares by content and is already in the language.
options.technical:
Payload: DataTree.Object holds the existing ordered list [(key: String, value: DataTree)]. That is the shape compiler-generated encoders already pass (core_literals.rs:22-24) and the runtime already stores (DataTree.rs:21). No new collection type, wrapper or hidden index is added.

Construction: a key-value literal in Object position builds the pair list in written order, keeping D-SERDE14. A [String: DataTree] Map value is accepted and contributes its sorted iteration order. A pair list contributes list order. This amends the D-SERDE13/14/15 record only by accepting the pair list for programmatic building. The native compiler's key-tracing recovery is deleted, so every execution level follows this one rule.

Lint: when a Map filled by add calls in the same function is passed to DataTree.Object, a warning suggests the pair list, with a machine-applicable rewrite. Loop building looks like: fields := [(key: String, value: DataTree)]{} then &fields.push((key: k, value: v)) then DataTree.Object(fields).

Lookup: .field(name) scans the pairs, as the runtime already does. Parsers check duplicates with a temporary key set that is freed when the object closes. A 100,000-key object therefore parses in n log n time, not n squared.

Duplicates: strict JSON, TOML including inline tables, YAML and text-key CBOR reject a repeated name before building the object, with their existing Syntax errors. json.parse_allow_duplicates keeps the later value at the first name's position; its event reader still reports every occurrence. YAML merge keys keep their existing codec rule; no new merge support is added.

INI: Core/encoding/ini.jet is its own ordered sections codec, where a repeated key keeps the last value in its first place. A port that projects INI into a DataTree passes pairs in that order. With inherited sections, parent a=1,b=2 then child b=3,c=4 projects a,b,c with values 1,3,4. Interpolation changes values, never positions.

Transforms: a merge keeps left positions, replaces colliding values in place and appends right-only fields in right order. Filtering keeps survivor order. Renaming applies the codec's duplicate rule before publishing. Canonical writers (json.canonical, canonical CBOR) sort a borrowed view and never change the object.

Equality: == compares objects field by field in order, which is what the runtime's derived equality already does. equal_unordered (D-DATATREE-ERGO1) ignores field order and is the documented way to compare documents by content.

Equality migration: today parsed objects arrive sorted, so == on them ignores arrival order in practice. jet fix rewrites every direct a == b and a != b whose operands are statically DataTree to a.equal_unordered(b) and its negation, keeping today's answers. Equality reached through generic code cannot be rewritten at that site. Examples are assert_eq, list contains and a derived == on a record holding a DataTree; jet fix lists each such use for review.

options.name: Every Map keeps insertion order
options.detail: Every Map in Jet, not only data objects, would remember the order keys were added. The parsed file round-trips. But every program that loops over any Map would see a different order than today. Code that relies on sorted keys would have to sort them itself.
options.technical: Change Map globally to insertion order: replacing a value keeps the key's first position, removal deletes it and reinsertion appends. Key equality rules stay; traversal no longer follows Comparable order. Migrate every Map iterator, formatter, snapshot, sorted-key algorithm and runtime adapter, and preserve the whole INI arrival-order chain. Beginners get insertion order everywhere; experts sort keys explicitly for ordered traversal and canonical output. This explicitly amends the sorted-Map contract in D-MAP-KEY1.

decisions.title: Canonical Unicode lower, upper and title predicates
decisions.gist: Which rules should Jet use to decide whether text is lowercase, uppercase or title case?
decisions.lesson: Jet's is_lower, is_upper and is_title give different answers on different execution paths today. A titlecase letter such as ǅ is neither lower nor upper. Every option uses one pinned Unicode version everywhere. They differ in how a title word is found, and in odd cases like AB, They're and A1b.
decisions.explainer:
Words first. A scalar is one Unicode character code. A cased letter has a case: lowercase like a, uppercase like A, or titlecase like ǅ. ǅ is one character standing for the two letters D and ž, written capital-then-small. A case property labels a character. A case mapping converts it, like a to A.

Option A uses the labels. is_lower means: at least one cased letter, and every cased letter is labelled Lowercase. is_upper is the same with Uppercase. Digits, spaces and Chinese characters have no case and are skipped. So ǅ is neither lower nor upper, and 界 alone is false for all three.

For is_title, A splits text into words with Unicode's standard word rules, which Jet already ships. In each word, the first cased letter must be uppercase or titlecase, and the rest lowercase. An apostrophe or a digit between letters stays inside the word, so They're and A1b are titles. A space or hyphen starts a new word.

A also makes title() use the same words. So title("they're") is "They're", where today's compiled title() gives "They'Re". title()'s output passes is_title whenever every letter has both a capital and a small form, which covers ordinary alphabets.

A few letters have no capital form at all: ª (the raised a in Spanish 1ª) and ᵃ (a raised phonetic a). title() leaves them alone, because Unicode gives them no capital, so is_title("ª") stays false. Jet does not invent capitals for them. An accented letter such as é gives the same answer whether it is stored as one character or as e plus a separate accent mark, because the mark stays inside its word.

Option B keeps the compiled path's rules: a letter counts as lowercase when uppercasing changes it, which makes ǅ both. Its title check accepts AB. Option C copies Python: any character without case, including an apostrophe or digit, starts a new word, so They're fails.

Edge cases under A. Empty text and digits-only text are false for all three. Mr. Smith is a title, because the space starts a word. Mr.Smith is not, because Unicode keeps a period between letters inside one word, as in e.g. or 3.14. ª and ᵃ are lowercase but never a title.

Reading the code: use core.text.parse as text lets the code call text.is_title. loop value in [...] runs once per string. The printed tuple shows the three answers as true or false.
decisions.story: Mina validates product labels such as AB, ǅabc, They're and 界. Her tests run in the interpreter and her service runs compiled; both must give the same answers.
decisions.inWild:
// https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str.istitle
print("AB".istitle())     # False
print("ǅ".islower(), "ǅ".isupper(), "ǅ".istitle())
# False False True
decisions.detail:
Current code. Core/text/parse.jet:488-505 tests ASCII byte ranges for is_lower and is_upper. Lines 509-527 test is_title with case mappings and reject uncased letters. crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/Text.rs:944-957 treats a cased letter as lower when uppercasing changes it, so ǅ counts as both.

Text.rs:1649-1667 checks titles with the Rust toolchain's own tables, not Jet's pinned data. Text.rs:317-336 title() starts words after any non-alphanumeric character. Card #4475 records the exact current native answers, including the corrected ABC abc row.

Data. Tools/agent/gen-unicode-tables.mjs already pins Unicode 17.0.0 inputs by checksum, including DerivedCoreProperties.txt and WordBreakProperty.txt. Text.rs:342 notes the shipped standard word segmentation. Examples are proposed, not run.

options.name: Unicode properties and Unicode words
options.detail:
is_lower and is_upper read Unicode's Lowercase and Uppercase labels for cased letters. is_title and title() both use Unicode's standard word boundaries. Every execution path reads one generated table.

Beginner: the answers match what a reader expects, including They're and ǅabc. Expert: the exact properties and word rule are listed below. title() and is_title agree on every letter that has capital and small forms; the rare exceptions, such as ª, are derived from the Unicode data and pinned by tests.
options.technical:
Data: the generator emits UNICODE_LOWERCASE and UNICODE_UPPERCASE from DerivedCoreProperties, so Other_Lowercase and Other_Uppercase are included. Titlecase is General_Category Lt from UnicodeData. UNICODE_CASED and the word-break tables already exist. Source, evaluator, comptime, JIT, AOT and Web all call these; no path uses toolchain case functions.

is_lower(s) is true when s has a Cased scalar and every Cased scalar is Lowercase. is_upper is the same with Uppercase. Lt scalars are neither. U+00AA is lower because it carries Other_Lowercase.

Words come from Unicode text segmentation (UAX #29). is_title(s) is true when s has a Cased scalar and, in every word, the first Cased scalar is Uppercase or Lt and every later one is Lowercase. Words with no Cased scalar are ignored. No normalization is applied; combining marks stay in their word by WB4. The storage-form promise covers precomposed versus decomposed accented letters, which the shared vector tests; no general canonical-equivalence guarantee is made.

title(s) title-maps the first Cased scalar of each word and lowercase-maps the rest, using the standard full SpecialCasing mappings unchanged. Final_Sigma works as today, and no replacement letters are invented.

The guarantee is narrowed to what those mappings allow. is_title(title(s)) holds when s has a Cased scalar and two conditions hold. Each word-leading Cased scalar title-maps to text whose first Cased scalar is Uppercase or Lt. Every other Cased scalar lowercase-maps to Lowercase scalars.

The generator derives both exception sets from the pinned data. One holds Cased scalars with no Uppercase or Lt title form, such as U+00AA and the modifier letter U+1D43. The other holds Cased scalars with no Lowercase form, such as U+1D400. It emits them as test vectors and checks every other Cased scalar against the rule.

A future Unicode version needs owner ratification and one regenerated cutover. One shared vector covers every input above, plus empty, digits, Other_Lowercase (U+00AA, U+1D43 as title inputs and outputs), precomposed and decomposed accents, ZWJ, Mr. Smith and Mr.Smith, at every dispatch point.

options.name: Keep the compiled path's rules
options.detail:
Adopt the compiled path's mapping-based tests everywhere, on the pinned Unicode table. A cased letter is lower when uppercasing changes it, and upper when lowercasing changes it.

Beginner: learn the quirks, since AB counts as a title and ǅ as both cases. Expert: use separate property checks when you need real Unicode classification.
options.technical: is_lower(s): a Cased scalar exists and every Cased scalar c has upper(c) != c. is_upper mirrors it with lower. is_title runs the current Text.rs state machine on pinned Uppercase, Lowercase and Alphabetic tables. Because it leaves toolchain tables, a few answers can still shift. title() keeps its current word rule.

options.name: Python's rules
options.detail:
Use the same Lowercase and Uppercase labels as A. is_title follows Python: any character without case, including an apostrophe, digit or combining accent, starts a new word.

Beginner: answers match Python, including Python's They'Re quirk. Expert: decomposed accents can change the answer.
options.technical: is_lower and is_upper equal A. is_title: after the start or an uncased scalar, the next Cased scalar must be Uppercase or Lt; after a Cased scalar it must be Lowercase. Every uncased scalar resets, Case_Ignorable marks included. title() uses the same reset rule.

comparisons.note: Python documents case predicates using cased Unicode characters.
comparisons.code:
// https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str.istitle
print("AB".istitle())     # False
print("ǅ".islower(), "ǅ".isupper(), "ǅ".istitle())
# False False True

recommendation.why: Use Unicode's own case properties and word boundaries, the same ones title() uses. Every execution path then gives one answer that matches what readers expect.
gains: One answer on every execution path, from one Unicode table.
is_title agrees with title(), so They're counts as a title.
é gives the same answer stored as one character or two.

losses.loss: Some current answers change: title("they're") becomes "They're" instead of "They'Re", and the source path's English-only checks start recognising letters such as é.
losses.mitigation: One cutover updates every recorded test and doc, and the release notes list each changed answer. Every option changes some answers, because today's paths already disagree.

losses.loss: Letters with no capital form, such as ª and ᵃ, can never make a title.
losses.mitigation: Unicode defines no capital for them, so no rule could. is_title honestly says false, and the shared vector pins these cases.

whyNot.reason: B keeps quirks: AB is a title and ǅ is both lower and upper. Its title() output fails its own is_title.
C copies Python's known word-splitting quirk, so They're and A1b fail, and stored accents change answers.

recommendation.tradeoff: A follows the Unicode standard rather than Python's simpler splitting, and keeps title() and is_title in agreement.

decisions.checkInstructions:

In the generator, derive the two exception sets (no Uppercase/Lt title form; no Lowercase form) and check is_title(title(c)) for every other Cased scalar. Migrate docs and the exact callsite assertions that recorded the old answers, including title("they're").

decisions.situation: Jet has three yes-or-no text checks: is_lower, is_upper and is_title, which asks whether every word starts with a capital letter. Today they give different answers depending on how a program runs. The source version only understands English letters, and the compiled version calls AB a title and calls the letter ǅ both lowercase and uppercase. A program that sorts or validates names can therefore behave differently in testing and in production, which surprises beginners and breaks the runtime port's parity tests. You are deciding which single rule all execution paths follow. We recommend Unicode's case properties and standard word boundaries, shared with title(), so They're is a title and title()'s output passes is_title. One limit cannot be designed away: a few rare letters, such as ª, have no capital form in Unicode, so no rule can turn them into a title.

decisions.title: Machine-sized numbers at the C boundary, and target size facts
decisions.gist: Should Jet add a machine-sized number type, or keep Int everywhere and check sizes only where C needs them?
decisions.lesson: C's size_t is 32 or 64 bits wide, depending on the target machine. Jet's Int has no fixed width. The choice is where that difference is handled: a new general number type, a check inside each C call, or a small checked carrier the compiler enforces at the C edge.
decisions.explainer:
A bit is a 0 or 1; a byte is 8 bits. Unsigned means a number is never negative. The target is the machine a program is built for, which may differ from the machine that compiles it.

Int is Jet's ordinary whole number. It is exact: it never wraps around or silently loses digits, and it can be negative. Small values are stored in one 64-bit slot on every target; very large ones use more memory automatically.

size_t is C's unsigned size type. It is 4 bytes wide on 32-bit targets, with a maximum of 4294967295. It is 8 bytes wide on 64-bit targets, with a maximum of 18446744073709551615. A C allocator is a function that reserves a requested number of bytes.

The boundary between Jet and C is called the ABI: the agreed widths and positions of values passed to C. A carrier is a small wrapper type whose only job is to move one checked value across that boundary.

In the examples, :: names a value. #Unsafe("reason") marks code the compiler cannot prove safe; the reason is a written promise checked by reviewers, not by the compiler. ?? { ... } runs the block when the call fails, with err holding the failure. ^p hands p over so it cannot be used again. Comments describe intended results; none of these programs was run.
decisions.story: Mina ports a C library and Jet's SQL parser. She reserves scratch memory for count times 8 bytes, and she runs a query with a large LIMIT. Both must behave the same when she builds for a 32-bit target from her 64-bit laptop.
decisions.detail:
## What the code does today

Jet's SQL parser reads LIMIT with Rust's usize (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/SqlQuery.rs:681-684). It reads GROUP BY and ORDER BY column numbers the same way (SqlQuery.rs:615, 648), and checks GROUP BY numbers against the SELECT list (SqlQuery.rs:387-405). So the accepted range depends on the target. The limit only truncates the in-memory result list (SqlQuery.rs:1037-1038, 1073-1074).

The compiler records pointer size per target (Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Target/Layout.jet:226-227). It guesses from the target name's prefix and defaults unknown names to 8 bytes. That guess is not safe to publish as a fact.

Jet has fixed-width U8 to U64 and I8 to I64 types, and Int (BuiltinStatics.jet:209-222). Conversions are destination-owned: U64.from_int(n) returns U64 String! when the value may not fit (BuiltinStatics.jet:224-272). Core's existing native wrappers take Int, for example mem.from_addr(addr: Int) and sys.umask(mask: Int). checked(a op b) accepts only one +, -, * or /, and returns an optional value (crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerInfer/calls/direct_calls.rs:581-620).

## Common to every option: SQL is the same on every target

SQL LIMIT and column numbers stop depending on the machine. LIMIT accepts any exact nonnegative Int, so every value a 64-bit build accepts today, up to 18446744073709551615, keeps working, and larger ones work too. Only the effective row count is capped. A limit at or above the number of result rows returns every row, which is all any limit that large can mean. Negative or malformed text is the existing LIMIT error. LIMIT 4294967296 now works on 32-bit and 64-bit builds alike.

A column number must be between 1 and the number of items in the SELECT list, which is the result's column count, not the table's. So SELECT name FROM person ORDER BY 3 is refused even if person has three fields. The existing rules that GROUP BY may not point at * or at an aggregate stay. Zero stays refused.

## Common to every option: two exact target facts

Add $build.pointer_bytes, an Int that is 4 or 8, and $build.usize_max, the Int 2^(8 × pointer_bytes) − 1. They fold at compile time from the selected target, like the existing $build.os. They never describe the compiling machine.

The prefix guess with an 8-byte default is replaced by a table of supported targets. An unknown target, or one whose C ABI width differs from its architecture's usual width, fails target selection with a diagnostic before any fact exists. This ballot adds no new OS, architecture or byte-order facts.

## Same program in every option

Each option reserves count × 8 bytes of scratch memory, frees it, and reports a refused size without stopping the program. With count 2 it reserves and frees 16 bytes on any target. With count 4294967295 on a 32-bit target the size does not fit size_t. Every option then prints a refusal and returns, and no memory is touched.

options.name: Int everywhere; a checked CSize only at the C edge
options.detail:
Your code keeps using Int for every size. Core functions that call C, such as the raw allocator, also take Int. Inside Core, the C side of each call takes core.mem.CSize, a small carrier that can only be made by a range check. So the check happens exactly once per call, and Core cannot forget it: the code would not compile.

A size that does not fit size_t is refused as the call's ordinary failure, before any C code runs. Beginners see only Int. Experts writing native code see one tiny type with two functions.
options.technical:
core.mem.CSize is opaque. Its layout is the selected target's size_t: 4 bytes with alignment 4, or 8 bytes with alignment 8.

CSize.from_int(value: Int) -> CSize String! returns a CSize when 0 ≤ value ≤ $build.usize_max. Otherwise it returns the same String error that U64.from_int uses for a value that does not fit. Int.from_csize(size: CSize) -> Int is exact and cannot fail. That follows the existing destination-owned from_<source> rule.

CSize has equality and nothing else. It has no arithmetic, ordering, literals, text parsing or codec. It cannot be stored in a public data format. Arithmetic always happens in Int, and the result is converted once at the edge.

Native provider declarations use CSize for every size_t parameter and result. A value read back from C, such as a returned length, becomes Int through Int.from_csize. So no raw machine word ever reaches user code.

The proposed raw allocator is mem.alloc_raw(size: Int, align: Int) -> mem.Ptr<U8> AllocError!. Its body converts size and align through CSize.from_int. A failed conversion returns AllocError before any C call, because a size that size_t cannot hold can never be allocated. Alignment rules stay with the existing raw-pointer owner, D-RAWPTR2.

Cost: Int's carrier is one 64-bit slot, JetInt(u64), on every target, including 32-bit ones (crates/jet-foundation/src/Numeric.rs:3099-3100). Values up to 2^62 − 1 stay inline in that slot. That slot is separate from the selected target's pointer and size_t width, which only CSize uses. Larger sizes use Int's big-number path, are above every real address space, and the allocator refuses them.

options.name: A general USize number type
options.detail:
Add USize, a new built-in unsigned whole-number type as wide as the target's size_t. You convert Int to USize once, then do arithmetic in USize. Its range, layout and generic code depend on the target.

The C side takes USize directly. Beginners meet a second whole-number type whose largest value changes with the build target. Default USize arithmetic stops the program on overflow, so recoverable code must use checked(...).
options.technical:
USize joins the unsigned fixed-width family with target-selected width. USize.from_int(Int) -> USize String! and Int.from_usize(USize) -> Int follow the destination-owned rule. USize{literal} must fit the selected target at compile time.

Unannotated literals stay Int. Mixing USize with Int or another width needs an explicit conversion, except shift counts. A shift count may be any integer type, as today; a count that is negative or at least the width stops with the existing overflow error.

Arithmetic +, -, *, / and % returns USize and stops with the existing located overflow error on overflow or division by zero. checked(a op b) works unchanged: one +, -, * or /, returning an optional USize. Remainder, shifts and nested expressions are not covered by checked. Wrapping and saturating forms stay explicit opt-ins.

Codecs: USize writes its exact value. Typed decoding checks the receiving target's maximum. A value that does not fit becomes an ordinary FieldError at its path, inside the existing [FieldError] result, so several bad fields are all reported. A 64-bit writer's 4294967296 therefore fails to decode on a 32-bit reader. Portable data formats must use U32, U64 or Int.

Cost: the parser, type checker, constant folding, generics, layout, hashing and every codec gain a target-dependent type. Generic code compiled for USize must be built separately per target width.

options.name: Int everywhere; each C call checks by convention
options.detail:
Your code is exactly the same as in A. The difference is inside Core: the C side of each call takes a plain Int. Every native call must remember to check the range itself before encoding the value as size_t.

There is one fewer type. But a forgotten check compiles, and on a 32-bit target it would silently drop the high bits of a large size. Reviews and tests, not the compiler, must catch that.
options.technical:
No CSize type. Native provider declarations take Int for size_t parameters. Each provider checks 0 ≤ value ≤ $build.usize_max before encoding, using a shared helper by convention.

User-facing behavior is identical to A: same signatures, same AllocError on a size that does not fit, same SQL rules. A user who calls two raw functions with the same unchanged size pays the cheap range check twice, as in A.

The only difference from A is enforcement. A provider that omits the check is a silent truncation bug, found only by review or a 32-bit test.

comparisons.note: Rust's usize is a full number type whose width follows the target. The same text parses on a 64-bit target and fails on a 32-bit one.

recommendation.why: Everyday code keeps one exact Int. The C edge gets a compiler-enforced check, so a size can never be silently cut on a 32-bit target. No new general number type is needed.
gains: Users keep one whole-number type, Int, on every target.
The compiler forces the size check at every C call.
SQL limits and column numbers mean the same everywhere.

whyNot.reason: B adds a target-dependent number type to every user, generic and codec, although only the C edge needs it.
C behaves like A for users, but a forgotten check inside Core compiles and silently cuts sizes.

recommendation.tradeoff: A spends one tiny internal type to make the C-edge check impossible to forget, and keeps every other number exact.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Run the same scratch program on selected 32-bit and 64-bit targets, compiled from a 64-bit host: count 0, 2, the largest fitting count, one above it, and a negative count. Each refusal must print and return, not stop, and must happen before any C call.

SQL: LIMIT 0, 4294967296, 2^63, 18446744073709551615, 2^64, -1 and malformed text give identical results on both widths. Every nonnegative limit at or above the row count returns all rows. Column numbers 0, 1, the SELECT-list length, one above it, * and an aggregate follow the stated rules on both widths. A three-field table with a one-item SELECT refuses ORDER BY 3.

Facts: $build.pointer_bytes and $build.usize_max match each supported target. An unknown target and an architecture with a different ABI width both fail target selection. A Core native call whose size_t parameter is not CSize must fail to compile.

surface.gist: Should Jet add a machine-sized number type, or keep Int and check sizes only where C needs them?
surface.lesson: C's size_t is 32 or 64 bits wide, depending on the target machine. Jet's Int has no fixed width. Choose who handles that gap: a new number type, a check each C call must remember, or a carrier the compiler checks.

current.note: SQL LIMIT borrows Rust's machine-sized usize, so its range depends on the target.

wild.note: Rust's usize is a full number type whose width follows the target.

options.name: Int; checked CSize at C edge
options.gist: Sizes stay Int; Core's C calls take a carrier made only by a range check.
gains: One whole-number type for users.
The compiler forces every C-edge size check.

options.name: General USize type
options.gist: A new number type as wide as the target's size_t.
gains: Native-width arithmetic on sizes.
losses: A second whole-number type whose range changes per target.
Every generic and codec must handle it.
Default overflow stops; recovery needs checked(...).

options.name: Int; each C call checks
options.gist: Same user code as A, but Core's C calls take plain Int.
gains: One fewer type, even inside Core.
losses: A forgotten check compiles and silently cuts sizes.

recommendation.why: Everyday code keeps one exact Int. The compiler forces the size check at the C edge, so sizes are never silently cut. No new general number type.
gains: One whole-number type, Int, everywhere.
The compiler forces every C-edge size check.
SQL means the same on every target.

whyNot.reason: B puts a target-dependent type in front of every user, although only the C edge needs it.
C looks the same to users, but a forgotten check compiles and silently cuts sizes.

recommendation.tradeoff: One tiny internal type makes the C-edge check impossible to forget; every other number stays exact.

decisions.situation: C code measures memory with a number called size_t, which is 32 bits wide on some machines and 64 bits on others, depending on the machine the program is built for. Jet's ordinary whole number, Int, has no fixed width, so Jet needs one safe place where an Int becomes a size_t. Today that conversion is missing, and the runtime's SQL parser borrows Rust's machine-sized usize, so a query with LIMIT 4294967296 works on a 64-bit build and fails on a 32-bit one. This matters to experts porting C libraries and to anyone whose program must mean the same thing on every target. You are deciding whether Jet gets a general machine-sized number type, or keeps Int everywhere and checks size_t only at the C edge. We recommend keeping Int everywhere, checking a size once inside Core's C calls with a small CSize carrier, and making SQL limits the same on every target.

designAway.loss: Experts convert exact values at C boundaries (prior CSize draft)
attempts: Core native wrappers take Int and convert internally, as existing Core wrappers already do.
designAway.outcome: Removed: user code never sees CSize.

designAway.loss: CSize arithmetic needs a to_int round trip
attempts: Arithmetic always happens in Int; conversion happens once inside the C call.
designAway.outcome: Removed: there is nothing to round-trip in user code.

designAway.loss: CSize text parsing grammar undefined
attempts: Drop CSize.parse; parse with the existing Int.parse and pass Int.
designAway.outcome: Removed: one decimal grammar.

designAway.loss: Exact Int big-number cost near 2^64
attempts: Values up to 2^62 - 1 stay inline in Int's 64-bit carrier slot on every target; larger sizes exceed every real address space and are refused.
designAway.outcome: Negligible.

designAway.loss: SQL results differ by target
attempts: LIMIT accepts any exact nonnegative Int and caps only the effective row count; ordinals bounded by the SELECT list.
designAway.outcome: Removed for every option.

designAway.loss: Guessed pointer width
attempts: Supported-target table; unknown targets fail selection.
designAway.outcome: Removed.

decisions.title: Export Jet components against an existing WIT world
decisions.gist: How should a Jet sandbox package follow an existing WIT contract, such as Zed's extension world?
decisions.lesson: Zed loads extensions only through its own fixed WIT contract. Jet sandboxes today invent their WIT from Jet code, so they cannot follow Zed's. Both options name the existing world, check every type and generate the glue code. They differ in how Jet functions are paired with WIT functions.
decisions.explainer:
Words first. WebAssembly is a portable program format. A component is a WebAssembly program plus standard typed entry points. WIT is the text file that lists those entry points. A world is one named list: the functions a host offers the plugin (imports) and the functions the plugin must offer the host (exports).

The host and plugin do not share memory. Glue code copies text, lists and records across the boundary; this is called lifting and lowering. After a call, a cleanup step frees temporary copies. A resource is a host object, like Zed's worktree. A borrow lends it for one call only; an own hands it over for good.

Pinned means a fixed, checked version of a file that never changes behind your back. Zed's WIT files come pinned inside a dependency package, never fetched from the network during a build.

Option A adds one field, world:, to the sandbox target. Jet then pairs each WIT export with the public Jet function of the matching name, using a fixed spelling rule: language-server-command becomes language_server_command. Option B adds a second file that pairs every WIT function with a Jet function, one row each.

Zed's world has 19 exports, but most extensions need one or two. Under A, the zed_sdk package offers a default for each, just as the Rust SDK does. One pub use line re-exports the defaults you want, and jet fix writes it. Under B, each default still needs its own table row.

Reading the code: pub fn makes a function visible to the host. -> zed.process.Command String! means it returns a Command, or fails with a text message. That maps to WIT result<command, string>. Ok(...) is success. Zed's trust setting still decides whether the command may run; this ballot does not change it.
decisions.story: Sam ports Jet's Zed extension from Rust to Jet. Zed must still receive exactly the command jet self lsp with an empty environment, and no Rust code may remain.
decisions.detail:
Current code. Tools/editors/zed/wasm-src/src/lib.rs:7-28 implements the Rust extension and keeps the literal command. Sandbox packages use the target sandbox { entry, name, export } (crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Package/Blocks.rs:975-1058). Their WIT is generated from public functions (Docs/spec/spec.md:3992; D-PLUGIN-EXPORT1=A).

The real contract is zed_extension_api 0.7.0, wit/since_v0.6.0/extension.wit. It is package zed:extension, world extension, with 19 exports and a world-level worktree resource. language-server-command takes a string and borrow<worktree>, and returns result<command, string>. command comes from interface process: command, args and env-vars.

Ratified context: D-PLUGIN1=A (declared needs plus a lent Authority), D-DEP-WASM1=A (Wasmtime Component Model) and D-ONCE-SANDBOX1=A (target name sandbox). Examples are proposed, not run; no component was built or loaded.

options.name: Name the world; pair by name
options.detail:
Add world: "namespace:package/world" to the sandbox target. Jet reads that pinned world, generates typed Jet modules for its types, and pairs each export with the entry module's public function of the matching name. It checks every type, then generates the glue code.

Beginner: write the functions you need, and let jet fix add the one pub use line for defaults. Expert: rename by writing a one-line pub wrapper with the WIT name, and read the generated binding listing.

A missing, extra or wrongly typed function is a compile error naming the WIT function and the exact Jet signature expected.
options.technical:
Manifest: sandbox { entry: "...", world: "ns:pkg/world" }. world and export are mutually exclusive. The WIT package is found in this package's wit/ folder or in a pinned dependency's wit/ folder, never on the network. Two providers of one WIT package name is an error.

Names: functions, fields and parameters become snake_case; types become PascalCase under Jet's acronym rule; interfaces become modules under wit.<namespace>.<package>. Enum and variant cases become PascalCase selectors. A WIT name that is a Jet keyword gets a trailing underscore. A tuple<A, B> becomes a Jet tuple with members item0, item1.

Collisions: WIT names cannot contain underscores, so the keyword rule never collides. Two WIT names in one scope can still differ only by letter case, such as http-get and HTTP-get. If they map to the same Jet spelling, the world is rejected with E1260. The message names both WIT names and the shared Jet spelling, such as http_get. Zed's world has no such pair.

Types: u8 to u64 become U8 to U64, s8 to s64 become I8 to I64, f32 is F32 and f64 is F64, string is String. list<T> is [T], option<T> is T? and result<T, E> is T E!. Records become Jet structs. Variants and enums become Jet enums, with payloads for variant cases. borrow<R> becomes a read parameter of type R that cannot escape the call, and own<R> becomes ^R.

Flags: a WIT flags type becomes a generated Jet struct with one Bool field per label, in WIT order, all false by default. So the empty set is all false, and a combined set has several fields true. Equality and ordinary struct update are its operations. Lowering writes only declared bits. Lifting reads the declared bits and ignores undeclared ones, following the Canonical ABI's flag unpacking. A flags type beyond the pinned toolchain's label limit is E1260.

Exports: the entry module's public functions, including pub use re-exports, must equal the world's exports. This amends D-PLUGIN-EXPORT1 for world packages. E1260 names any WIT shape the pinned toolchain cannot lower. The diagnostic for a missing export prints the expected signature and offers the pub use defaults line.

Glue: generated lift and lower code checks lengths, alignment, UTF-8 and enum or variant tags. Cleanup runs exactly once after each call. A guest stop traps at the boundary and never unwinds into the host. Resource handles share one host table.

Imports: each WIT import is checked against authority.needs and the lent Authority (D-PLUGIN1=A) before linking. The zed_sdk package also declares Zed's 6-byte zed:api-version custom section, which the build copies into the component.
options.code:
// package.jet
name: "jet_zed"
version: "0.1.0"
deps: { zed_sdk: ./zed_sdk }   // Jet port of zed_extension_api 0.7.0; ships its pinned WIT files
packages: { jet_zed: sandbox { entry: "extension", world: "zed:extension/extension" } }

// extension.jet (the entry module)
use wit.zed.extension as zed   // Jet types generated from the pinned WIT files

// Zed calls this to learn how to start the language server.
// worktree is a read-only loan (WIT borrow) and cannot be kept after the call.
pub fn language_server_command(language_server_id: String, worktree: zed.Worktree)
    -> zed.process.Command String! {
    Ok(zed.process.Command{command: "jet", args: [String]{"self", "lsp"}, env: []})
}

// The other 18 exports Zed's world requires, using the SDK defaults (jet fix writes this list).
pub use zed_sdk.defaults.[
    init_extension,
    language_server_initialization_options,
    language_server_workspace_configuration,
    language_server_additional_initialization_options,
    language_server_additional_workspace_configuration,
    labels_for_completions,
    labels_for_symbols,
    complete_slash_command_argument,
    run_slash_command,
    context_server_command,
    context_server_configuration,
    suggest_docs_packages,
    index_docs,
    get_dap_binary,
    dap_request_kind,
    dap_config_to_scenario,
    dap_locator_create_scenario,
    run_dap_locator,
]
// Zed calls language-server-command and receives command=jet, args=[self, lsp], env=[]

options.name: Name the world; pair with a written table
options.detail:
Same world: field, generated types and glue as A. Add bindings: naming a module that fills in a generated, typed table with one field for every WIT export. Each field holds the Jet function that serves that export. The compiler checks that every field is filled and every function type matches.

Beginner: copy a supplied table and keep it in step with the world. Expert: any Jet name can serve any WIT function without a wrapper. Each default still needs its own field.
options.technical:
Manifest: sandbox { entry, world, bindings: "module" }. For each world, Jet generates a struct type, here wit.zed.extension.Exports. It has one field per WIT export, named by A's name rule. Each field's type is the exact Jet function type of that export, such as language_server_command: fn(String, Worktree) -> process.Command String!.

The bindings module must declare pub BINDINGS :: Exports{...}, a compile-time constant struct literal. Ordinary struct checking applies: a missing field, an unknown field and a function of the wrong type are each compile errors. Each error names the WIT export and the expected Jet signature. Field values must name functions directly, so the binding is fixed at compile time. Glue, imports, flags, names and resources match A.
options.code:
// package.jet
name: "jet_zed"
version: "0.1.0"
deps: { zed_sdk: ./zed_sdk }   // Jet port of zed_extension_api 0.7.0; ships its pinned WIT files
packages: { jet_zed: sandbox { entry: "extension", world: "zed:extension/extension", bindings: "wit_map" } }

// extension.jet (the entry module)
use wit.zed.extension as zed   // Jet types generated from the pinned WIT files

// Zed calls this to learn how to start the language server.
// worktree is a read-only loan (WIT borrow) and cannot be kept after the call.
pub fn language_server_command(language_server_id: String, worktree: zed.Worktree)
    -> zed.process.Command String! {
    Ok(zed.process.Command{command: "jet", args: [String]{"self", "lsp"}, env: []})
}

// wit_map.jet: one typed field for every one of the 19 WIT exports, checked against the world
use wit.zed.extension as zed
use zed_sdk.defaults as d
pub BINDINGS :: zed.Exports{
    language_server_command: extension.language_server_command,
    init_extension: d.init_extension,
    language_server_initialization_options: d.language_server_initialization_options,
    language_server_workspace_configuration: d.language_server_workspace_configuration,
    language_server_additional_initialization_options: d.language_server_additional_initialization_options,
    language_server_additional_workspace_configuration: d.language_server_additional_workspace_configuration,
    labels_for_completions: d.labels_for_completions,
    labels_for_symbols: d.labels_for_symbols,
    complete_slash_command_argument: d.complete_slash_command_argument,
    run_slash_command: d.run_slash_command,
    context_server_command: d.context_server_command,
    context_server_configuration: d.context_server_configuration,
    suggest_docs_packages: d.suggest_docs_packages,
    index_docs: d.index_docs,
    get_dap_binary: d.get_dap_binary,
    dap_request_kind: d.dap_request_kind,
    dap_config_to_scenario: d.dap_config_to_scenario,
    dap_locator_create_scenario: d.dap_locator_create_scenario,
    run_dap_locator: d.run_dap_locator,
}

comparisons.note: WIT bindings generate checked component adapters from a world.

recommendation.why: Matching by name needs no extra table. Generated glue keeps memory safe, defaults remove boilerplate, and every mismatch is a clear compile error.
gains: Write only the functions you need; defaults cover the rest.
Mismatches are compile errors that name the exact expected function.
Generated glue handles text, lists, cleanup and resources safely.

whyNot.reason: A hand-written row for every WIT function adds upkeep without adding safety; renames already work through a one-line wrapper.

recommendation.tradeoff: A pairs functions by a fixed naming rule; a one-line wrapper covers any rename, so nothing is lost.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Build the Jet Zed extension against the pinned 0.6.0 world, load it in real Zed, and check that it starts jet self lsp with an empty environment. Check missing, extra and mistyped exports, keyword and acronym names, and the defaults line from jet fix. Check that a world with http-get and HTTP-get is E1260 naming both and http_get.

Round-trip strings, lists, options, results, resources and flags: empty, one label, all labels, and a lifted value with an undeclared bit. Prove borrow escape refusal, cleanup exactly once, trap containment, Authority denial before linking and the api-version section.

Both options name the existing world, check every type and generate the glue code. They differ in how Jet functions are paired with WIT functions.

current.note: The extension is Rust; Jet sandboxes cannot follow a WIT contract written elsewhere.

wild.note: wit-bindgen generates checked glue from an existing world.

options.name: Name the world; pair by name
options.gist: Name the world; matching public functions are paired, checked and glued.
gains: Write only the functions you need; defaults cover the rest.
Mismatches are compile errors that name the exact expected function.
Generated glue handles text, lists, cleanup and resources safely.

options.gist: Name the world; a hand-written typed table pairs every function.
gains: Any Jet name can serve a WIT function directly.
losses: A table field is needed for every WIT function.

recommendation.why: Matching by name needs no extra table. Generated glue keeps memory safe, defaults remove boilerplate, and every mismatch is a clear compile error.
gains: Write only the functions you need; defaults cover the rest.

recommendation.tradeoff: A pairs functions by a fixed naming rule; a one-line wrapper covers any rename, so nothing is lost.

decisions.situation: Zed, the code editor, loads extensions as WebAssembly components: small sandboxed programs that offer an exact list of typed functions written in a WIT file. Jet can already build sandboxed components, but it invents their WIT from the Jet code, so it cannot follow a contract someone else wrote, like Zed's. That is why Jet's own Zed extension is still Rust code that returns the command jet self lsp. This matters to anyone writing plugins for existing hosts in Jet, and to the goal of porting all Rust to Jet. You are deciding how a Jet sandbox package declares an existing WIT world and how its functions are paired with it. We recommend naming the world in the package file and pairing functions by name automatically. Types are checked, glue code is generated, and one line supplies defaults for functions you do not need.

decisions.title: Typed low-level tools for the Jet runtime, and who may use them
decisions.gist: Should Jet approve these low-level runtime tools, and should only Jet's own code, any package, or approved packages use them?
decisions.lesson: Rewriting Jet's runtime in Jet needs unsafe low-level tools: atomic words, empty-start slots, C callbacks and foreign ownership. Safe code never uses them. You approve each tool group, then choose who may import them: bundled code only, any package, or bundled code plus packages you admit by exact version.
decisions.explainer:
The runtime is the engine under every Jet program. It shares data between tasks, calls C and talks to the operating system. Today it is written in Rust. Porting it to Jet needs tools ordinary Jet code never sees.

An atomic word is a 4- or 8-byte value that tasks can change without ever seeing half an update. An ordering says what else becomes visible with that change. Relaxed promises only the word itself. Release publishes earlier writes; Acquire sees what a Release published. AcqRel does both, and SeqCst also puts all such operations in one agreed order.

An owner must free storage. A loan borrows it for a while without owning it, and a guard keeps a loan valid. An uninitialized slot is storage that starts empty and is filled exactly once. Finalization runs an owner's cleanup after its last user is gone.

C is the language most system libraries use. Its ABI is the agreed layout of values passed between languages. A callback is a function handed to C to call later. A panic is a crash-stop; unwinding is cleaning up stack frames during one.

#Unsafe("reason") marks code the compiler cannot prove safe. The reason is a written promise checked by reviewers. A provider is a package that implements one of these low-level services. In the examples, :: names a value, U64{0} is an unsigned 64-bit zero, and none of the code was run.
decisions.story: Priya ports Jet's runtime and its peer launcher from Rust into Jet. She must publish shared values between tasks, pass borrowed data to C, receive C callbacks, and stop safely without leaking anything.
decisions.detail:
## What this vote decides

Two things. First, which tool groups are approved; each group has a stable ID below. Second, who may import the approved tools; that is the A, B or C choice. The recommendation approves every group. To decline a group, name its ID in the ratification comment, for example "A, decline NATIVE-CALLBACK". A declined group stays blocked, and so does the work listed under it.

## Tool groups

NATIVE-ATOMIC: inline 64-bit and 32-bit atomic words. Declining blocks the runtime atomic port and signal flags.

NATIVE-STORAGE: Cell<T> with guarded loans, Uninit<T> fill-once slots, and typed place, take and drop over D-RAWPTR2 storage. Declining blocks the portable collector's storage port.

NATIVE-ABI: borrowed byte extents, opaque C handles, C layouts with real unions, and unaligned fixed-width loads. Declining blocks C calls, OS imports and Arrow import.

NATIVE-EXACT: an owned word holding Jet's exact Int across atomics. Requires NATIVE-ATOMIC. Declining blocks exact-Int atomics.

NATIVE-CALLBACK: C callback export and invoke, once-callbacks, host-panic capture and signal handlers. Requires NATIVE-ABI. Declining blocks C exports and signal handling.

NATIVE-LIFECYCLE: erased owners with checked downcast, final owners with one release, and weak handles. Declining blocks native-owned runtime values and finalizers.

NATIVE-TASKLOCAL: task-local guards that restore earlier state. Declining blocks task-local runtime state.

NATIVE-OS: the peer launcher's operating-system rows. Requires NATIVE-ABI and NATIVE-CALLBACK. Declining blocks the peer launcher.

NATIVE-ARROW: claimed import of Arrow C data. Requires NATIVE-ABI and NATIVE-LIFECYCLE. Declining blocks Arrow C import (D-COLUMNAR-BOUNDARY1=A).

## Related decisions recorded separately

These are separate owner votes, home card #4494 unless noted. Nothing here approves them. D-SIMD-NATIVE1 covers vector intrinsics, CPU feature dispatch, black_box and fence. D-ARRAY-INIT1 covers non-allocating [T#N] repeat and from_fn (home #4500). D-FLOAT-BITS1 and D-CHAR-SCALAR1 are standalone primitive ballots.

## Prerequisites

D-RAWPTR2=A owns raw allocation, pointers, casts and windows. D-UNSAFE-DEPS1=A owns which dependencies may use #Unsafe. D-USIZE-TARGET1 owns the size_t carrier and target pointer facts. The pending D-UNSAFE-EFFECT outcome decides how #Unsafe propagates through signatures; every declaration below adopts it unchanged. #4378 owns lossless native paths and #4409 owns InvalidData.

## What the code does today

The runtime's atomics are Rust: crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/Atomic.rs:325-337 loads with SeqCst, swaps and drops the old owned bits. C exports catch any unwind and exit through the runtime report boundary with code 101 (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/CAbi.rs:20-46).

Native owned values are Rust Arc<dyn Any + Send + Sync> with identity and downcast (crates/jet-foundation/src/MIR.rs:3954-3979). The peer launcher is Rust (Tools/ci/compiled-workload-peer-launcher.rs). Arrow C import rejects a missing base release callback (crates/jet-foundation/src/ArrowData.rs:896-902). It keeps a pointer claimed until its callback returns (ArrowData.rs:991-1016), and it keeps the provider library alive (ArrowData.rs:408-410).

## Same program in every option

Each option runs Priya's sample: it publishes 1 into an atomic word, reads back the old 0, fills a slot with "ready" once, and borrows it without copying. It prints nothing. A, B and C differ only in which packages may compile it.

options.name: Private by default; outside providers admitted by the owner
options.detail:
The tools live in core.mem.native. Jet's own bundled runtime and platform code may import them. An outside package may import them only after the owner admits that exact version, by name and content hash, in the compiler's single provider registry. Every other package gets a compile error.

An application that depends on an admitted provider still lists it in policy.unsafe_deps, as today. Admitted providers are rebuilt with every Jet change, so private tools can still change. When a private tool changes, Jet ships the provider's migration in the same change, and the new version's entry lands in the same Jet release.

The small ongoing cost: each new provider version needs a quick owner check of what changed since the last admitted version. Beginners never see these tools. Experts can ship a real outside provider once it is reviewed.
options.technical:
Admission: the compiler has one provider registry, embedded in its own source. An entry names either a bundled source unit or an outside package plus the exact content hash from its lock file. A package name, path, manifest field or dependency alone cannot grant access. Only an owner-ratified registry entry does.

Versions: admission is per version. A changed provider version has a new hash, so it needs a new entry, and the owner reviews only the diff from the last admitted hash. An unadmitted import of core.mem.native gets a front-end error: private native tools are only available to admitted providers. The error names the registry, the owner-admission route and any admitted replacement hash.

Consent: an application using an admitted provider must still list it in policy.unsafe_deps (D-UNSAFE-DEPS1=A). The lock pins the provider's #Unsafe gates. So admission and per-application consent stay two existing steps, not one new mechanism.

Compatibility: admitted outside providers are part of Jet's own build and test suite. A change to a private tool carries a migration patch for every admitted provider, built and tested in that same Jet change. The provider author publishes the patched version, and its hash entry lands in the same Jet release. There is no public stability promise.

Old locks: each Jet release lists the provider hashes that compile against its private tools. An application whose lock pins an older hash keeps building on the Jet release that admitted it. On a newer Jet it gets the front-end error naming the admitted replacement, so updating the lock is the fix.

Prototyping: a provider author prototypes in a local Jet checkout, where the registry is ordinary editable source. Publishing needs the owner's entry.

Revocation: removing an entry makes the next build of that provider fail with the same front-end error, naming the revoked hash and any replacement. Applications see that error, not undefined behavior. A revocation lands in a Jet release like any other fix.

The operations, signatures, effects, target rules and acceptance are identical in A, B and C. They are listed in the shared contract below. InitError and ExtentError are new error types owned by this module; their exact cases are listed below.

Shared contract, NATIVE-ATOMIC. AtomicWord64.new(U64) -> AtomicWord64 and AtomicWord32.new(U32) -> AtomicWord32 are inline. They are 8 bytes with alignment 8, and 4 bytes with alignment 4. They never box, lock or call the public Atomic.

Each word has load(&self, LoadOrder) -> word, store(&self, word, StoreOrder), swap(&self, word, Order) -> word and fetch_add_relaxed(&self, word) -> word. It also has compare_exchange(&self, expected, desired, success: Order, failure: LoadOrder) -> {exchanged: Bool, observed: word}. compare_exchange_weak has the same signature and may fail spuriously.

Orders are typed per operation, so an invalid order can never be written or computed. LoadOrder is Relaxed, Acquire or SeqCst. StoreOrder is Relaxed, Release or SeqCst. Order is Relaxed, Acquire, Release, AcqRel or SeqCst. A failure order may be any LoadOrder, independent of the success order, as in C++17 and Rust 1.64.

So .Release passed to load is a compile-time type error naming LoadOrder. A dynamic order is already a LoadOrder or StoreOrder value, so there is no runtime check, error or stop. Each of the three types is identical in A, B and C.

Signed I64 and I32 views are equal-width bit casts. U64 to U32 keeps the low 32 bits explicitly. Exact Int is never used as scratch for bits.

NATIVE-STORAGE. Cell<T>.new(^T) -> Cell<T> stores T inline. borrow(&guard) -> @T gives a shared loan, and borrow_mut(&exclusive_guard) -> &T an exclusive one. A loan cannot escape its guard, and a guard cannot be destroyed while a loan lives.

Uninit<T> has three states: Empty, Filled and Taken. new() -> Uninit<T> starts Empty. write_once(&self, ^T) -> Unit InitError! moves Empty to Filled. On Filled it returns .AlreadyFilled, and on Taken it returns .Taken; either way the passed value is dropped once, never leaked.

borrow_initialized(&self) -> @T InitError! lends the value when Filled, and returns .Empty or .Taken otherwise. take(&self) -> T InitError! moves Filled to Taken and returns the value, with the same errors otherwise. A slot is never refilled after take, so fill-once holds for its whole life.

A write_once or take while a loan from borrow_initialized is live is refused at compile time, by the same loan rule Cell uses. Dropping a Filled slot destroys T once; dropping an Empty or Taken slot does nothing. InitError has exactly three cases: .Empty, .AlreadyFilled and .Taken.

Typed place, take and drop reuse D-RAWPTR2 allocation, with checked size and alignment through D-USIZE-TARGET1's carrier. Zero-size allocation uses one byte. A failed allocation keeps every earlier owner intact.

NATIVE-ABI. ByteExtent.from_raw(pointer: *U8, length: Int, owner: @Owner) -> ByteExtent ExtentError! needs a nonnegative length; otherwise it returns .NegativeLength. Null is allowed only for length 0; otherwise it returns .NullPointer. The foreign provider promises the real capacity, because a raw pointer cannot reveal it.

ByteExtent.bytes(&self) -> @[U8] borrows without copying. load_u16, load_u32 and load_u64, plus the signed I16, I32 and I64 forms, take (&self, offset: Int, order: ByteOrder) and return the fixed-width value or ExtentError. ByteOrder is .Little, .Big or .Native, the selected target's order.

A negative offset, or an offset + width beyond the length, returns .OutOfBounds before any byte is read. The sum is checked without overflow. ExtentError has exactly three cases: .NegativeLength, .NullPointer and .OutOfBounds.

Opaque String and cursor handles are one target-sized word, never a Rust layout. Calls borrow handles, except drop and builder finish, which consume them. UTF-8 extents keep their String owner alive without copying.

C layouts admit nested pointers, fixed arrays and real untagged unions with selected-target size and alignment. For example, IO_STATUS_BLOCK is 8 bytes with alignment 4 on Win32, and 16 bytes with alignment 8 on Win64. errno and GetLastError are read immediately after the call, before any cleanup or other native call.

NATIVE-EXACT. ExactWord is the one owned word holding Jet's exact Int. It has borrow(&self) -> @Int, retain(&self) -> ExactWord, consume(^self) -> Int and from_int(^Int) -> ExactWord. to_i64(&self) -> I64 String! uses the existing checked-conversion error. clone_from_atomic(&AtomicWord64) -> ExactWord holds a hazard, reloads and retries if the word changed. Equality keeps its guard through the comparison, which defeats ABA reuse.

NATIVE-CALLBACK. Callbacks crossing C are fn(...) -> T Never!: they cannot return a failure. A panic inside one is caught at the boundary, reported once, and exits the process with code 101. It never unwinds into generated frames.

OnceCallback consumes its closure and code owner exactly once on every path. catch_host_panic and resume_host_panic keep panic payload ownership. SignalCallback<I32> is a nullable C function pointer, so null is SIG_DFL and full-width -1 is SIG_ERR.

A signal handler may only Release-store an AtomicWord32. It may not allocate, lock, format, panic or enter the runtime. Pre-exec callbacks obey the same rules after fork.

NATIVE-LIFECYCLE. ErasedOwner.new<T>(^T) keeps one allocation identity, and same(&a, &b) compares it. downcast_ref<T>(&self) -> @T? lends. downcast<T>(^self) -> T ErasedOwner! returns the original owner unchanged on a mismatch. try_take<T> also needs a unique owner with no active loan.

FinalOwner.new<T>(^T, release: fn(^T) -> Unit Never!) runs release once, after the last strong alias. Finalization is marked before release runs, so a weak upgrade during release fails. A weak upgrade never revives finalized storage.

NATIVE-TASKLOCAL. TaskLocalGuard.push(^state) installs state for this task and restores the earlier state once on normal return, failure or caught panic. Nested guards restore in reverse order. No loan outlives the guard.

A terminal no-unwind exit does not pretend to run stack cleanup. Condition waiting keeps using the existing SharedGuard.wait.

NATIVE-OS. Peer-launcher rows include borrowed SockFprog for prctl, variadic prctl with C default promotions, process-group spawn with checked pre-exec setup, raw wait status and create-new status files. They also include lossless native paths, Windows AppContainer and the environment lock. A failed isolation setup refuses to launch rather than weakening isolation.

Argument and environment text keeps raw bytes or real UTF-16, including lone surrogates. Clocks keep full machine-word precision before checked Int conversion. Rows are selected per OS, C library, architecture and ABI, so Linux glibc rows never apply to musl or Darwin.

NATIVE-ARROW. Import requires nonnull top-level schema and array release callbacks. A null one means already released, so it is refused with the Ownership error before anything is read. The consumer calls only the two top-level callbacks, once each. It never calls child or dictionary callbacks; the producer's top-level callback releases those.

Each claimed pointer is Live or Finalizing in one process-wide registry. Under its lock, Live changes to Finalizing, and the lock is released before foreign code runs. The entry is erased only after the callback returns, so a re-entrant import of the same pointer is refused. A failed import rolls back its claims the same way.

An imported Arrow owner is task-local, not Send or Sync, by default. Moving it to another task needs an explicit producer guarantee of thread safety. The provider library's owner is kept alive until after the last release callback returns. A poisoned registry lock is repaired only after re-checking the registry under the exclusive guard; otherwise it stays poisoned.

Arrow text: format is required UTF-8 C text, and name is optional UTF-8 C text. Metadata is length-prefixed bytes read with checked lengths, never a C string. The fixed-width loads above read Arrow buffers with ByteOrder.Native.

Targets. Each declaration states its own target need, and only code that names it is checked. AtomicWord64 needs lock-free 64-bit atomics; AtomicWord32 needs 32-bit ones. C callbacks and exports are native-only, never Wasm. OS rows apply only under the matching $build.os. A program that never names an unavailable tool compiles normally. Nothing ever falls back to a lock.

options.name: Public audited tools for any package
options.detail:
The same tools are public as core.mem.raw. Any package may import them inside #Unsafe. Applications still approve such dependencies through policy.unsafe_deps.

Outside experts need no admission. But every tool's exact signature and ownership rule becomes a public promise. Changing one later breaks outside code that Jet cannot migrate for its authors.
options.technical:
Same groups, signatures, effects, target rules and acceptance as the shared contract in A, under core.mem.raw. There is no provider registry for these tools. Every package can import them, and applications gate them with policy.unsafe_deps (D-UNSAFE-DEPS1=A).

A change to any exported layout, ordering rule or ownership rule is a breaking public change. It needs a full public cutover and a migration path for outside code.

options.name: Private to Jet's bundled code only
options.detail:
The same tools live in core.mem.native, and only Jet's own bundled runtime and platform code may import them. No outside package can ever qualify, even after review.

The tools stay fully changeable. But an expert who needs a new low-level provider, such as a GPU or database driver, must get it merged into Jet itself.
options.technical: Same groups, signatures, effects, target rules and acceptance as the shared contract in A. The provider registry lists only bundled source units. An outside package importing core.mem.native gets the front-end error, and no registry entry can name an outside package.

comparisons.note: Rust offers the same kinds of tools publicly, inside unsafe code, and documents each ordering and ownership rule as a public promise.

recommendation.why: A keeps the tools private, so Jet can still change them, yet lets reviewed outside providers use them. Ordinary packages stay locked out, and applications still consent through unsafe_deps. Approve every group.
gains: Ordinary packages cannot reach runtime internals.
Reviewed outside providers can still ship.
No public stability promise, so the tools can evolve.

losses.loss: Each new version of an outside provider needs an owner-admitted registry entry, and private-tool changes require a coordinated provider release.
losses.mitigation: The owner reviews only the diff from the last admitted hash. Jet ships each provider's migration patch in the same change, and the new entry lands in the same release. Old locks keep building on the Jet that admitted them, and newer Jet names the replacement hash.

whyNot.reason: B turns every internal layout and ownership rule into a public promise that outside code depends on.
C forces every low-level provider into Jet itself, even after a successful review.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds an owner check per outside provider version, a diff review that is itself the safety control, plus release coordination Jet performs, instead of a public promise or a closed door.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Build a requirement matrix that maps every group ID and every declaration to its tests. Each row lists static refusal tests, runtime positive, control and restored tests, targets and the suite path. The gate stays open until every row has a receipt. A facade-only proof closes nothing.

Admission: an unadmitted package fails; an admitted package at the pinned hash compiles; a changed hash fails; a removed entry fails with the revoked hash named. An old lock builds on its admitting Jet release and, on a newer one, fails naming the replacement hash. An application without unsafe_deps fails.

Atomics: every valid ordering per operation, full-word compare and signed views. Every invalid order, literal or dynamic, is a compile-time type error. A failure order stronger than success is accepted. Storage: loan-escape refusal, every Uninit transition, each InitError case, write or take during a live loan refused, and drop in each state. Extents: each ExtentError case, including offset overflow.

Callbacks and lifecycle: panic in a callback exits 101 without unwinding, finalizer re-entry, weak upgrade during release, and task-local restore on every path.

Arrow: a null base callback is refused, and child callbacks are never called. A re-entrant import of a Finalizing pointer is refused, and so is a default cross-task move. Also test provider unload while an alias exists, metadata with zero bytes and non-UTF-8 bytes, offset overflow and undersized extents.

Targets: AtomicWord32-only code on a 32-bit target, a C export on Wasm, and a Windows row on Linux. Unrelated code still compiles. Run the original runtime tests and the 24 peer-launcher tests, Windows rows on a real Windows host.

decisions.situation: Jet's runtime, the hidden engine under every program that shares memory between tasks, calls C and talks to the operating system, is still written in Rust. To rewrite it in Jet, its authors need low-level tools that safe Jet deliberately lacks, such as atomic memory words, slots that start empty, raw C callbacks and ownership of foreign data. Without them the port stalls; for example, the peer launcher that runs isolated child processes cannot be written in Jet at all. Ordinary programmers never touch these tools, but their mistakes would corrupt memory, so who may use them matters to everyone's safety. You are deciding which tool groups to approve and who may import them: only Jet's own bundled code, any package, or bundled code plus outside packages you approve one by one. We recommend approving every group, private by default, with owner-admitted outside providers pinned to an exact reviewed version.
