decisions.title: Exact F32 floating-point bit casts
decisions.situation: An F32 is a 32-bit number with a fractional part, like 1.5. Inside the computer it is stored as 32 on/off bits, and the same 32 bits read as a whole number make a U32 word. Some programs must copy those bits exactly. A file loader that reads a saved number and writes it back must not change one bit, even for a special "not a number" (NaN) marker that carries hidden extra bits. Jet already has bit helpers for its 64-bit Float in the math module, math.to_bits and math.from_bits, but nothing for F32. You decide how the F32 pair is spelled. We recommend two math-module functions, math.f32_to_bits and math.f32_from_bits, beside the Float pair, so all bit casts share one home and Jet's naming rule.
decisions.gist: Should exact F32 bit casts be math-module functions beside the Float pair, or methods on the F32 type?
decisions.lesson: A bit cast reads a number's 32 stored bits as a whole-number word, or the reverse, without doing any math. A adds math.f32_to_bits and math.f32_from_bits next to the existing Float pair. B puts F32.from_bits(word) and value.bits() on the type. C uses value.to_bits(), which Jet's conversion rule forbids. All three keep every bit, including NaN markers.
decisions.explainer:
Plain words first. A bit is a 0 or 1. F32 is a 32-bit fractional number type. U32 is a 32-bit unsigned whole number, from 0 to 4294967295. U32{...} writes one directly, and 0x... is hexadecimal (base 16) notation. A bit cast keeps all 32 bits and only changes how you read them.

An ordinary example: F32 1.0 is stored as the bits 0x3F800000, which read as a U32 are 1065353216. That is not the number 1, because a bit cast is not a numeric conversion. The numeric conversion U32.from_f32 already exists and turns 1.0 into 1.

Special patterns. NaN means "not a number": a marker with spare bits that some programs use to carry a small code. 0x7FC00001 is a NaN carrying code 1. 0x80000000 is negative zero, which equals zero in math but has a different sign bit. A bit cast keeps both exactly.

What does not change. Arithmetic on a NaN may change its spare bits, as on every chip. Only copying, storing, passing and these two casts promise the exact bits. Byte order (which byte is written first in a file) stays a separate choice, made by codec calls such as write_f32_le.

From a plain Int. Turn it into a U32 first with the existing checked U32.from_int. -1 or anything above 4294967295 fails there, before any bit cast.

Syntax notes: :: names a fixed value, and Never! means the call cannot fail.
decisions.story: Mina's compiler loads a saved image file that contains an F32 NaN marker with extra bits 1. She must write the same 32 bits back unchanged, so the saved file stays byte-for-byte identical.
decisions.detail:
Code facts checked. Core/math/math.jet:184-185 already has math.to_bits(n: Float) -> Int and math.from_bits(bits: Int) -> Float for the 64-bit Float. Math functions already accept F32, for example math.sqrt(F32{9.0}) in Examples/features/lowlevel/sized_floats.jet. BuiltinStatics.jet:209-221 lists F32 as its own 32-bit kind, separate from Float/F64. It lists U32.from_f32 at :235 as the existing numeric conversion.

D-SHAPE-CONVERT1=A (syntax-decisions.md:903-914, spec.md:108-109) says typed conversion is Target.from_source(value). It also says source-owned to_* conversions are not Jet syntax. That rules out value.to_bits() as written in the earlier draft. U32.from_int is the checked Int bridge (Examples/features/ports/murmur3_x86_32/run.jet:35).

Scope. This ballot is F32 only. Exact 64-bit runtime leaves float_policy_to_bits(Float) -> U64 and float_policy_from_bits(U64) -> Float exist on the port-runtime worktree. They are in Core/math/runtime/kernel_float_policy.jet:18-19, and native registration is held under #4467. This vote adds no second 64-bit engine and changes no Float, binary or CBOR path.

Exact law for the chosen pair. Every one of the 2^32 F32 patterns is valid input. That includes both zeros, both infinities, subnormals (tiny numbers near zero) and every quiet or signaling NaN sign and payload. Signaling NaN means one whose spare bits ask the chip to raise an alarm. Quieting means the chip clears that alarm bit.

from_bits then to_bits returns the identical word with no arithmetic and no quieting. Sema, constant evaluation, the evaluator, JIT, AOT and Web keep the F32 carrier. They never widen it to 64 bits, never round-trip through host text, and never use a scratch Int. F32 compiler-image and native consumers migrate to the chosen pair. Standalone card #4494 owns this capability.

options.name: Math-module functions beside the Float pair
options.detail: Add math.f32_to_bits(value: F32) -> U32 Never! and math.f32_from_bits(word: U32) -> F32 Never!. They sit next to the existing math.to_bits and math.from_bits for Float, so every bit cast in Jet lives in one module with one naming pattern. They are plain functions, so there is no receiver question and no source-owned to_* method. Both are pure: no memory allocation, no effects, and no possible failure. Beginners never need them; experts write one short call.
options.code:
use core.math as math

fn payload() -> U32 Never! {
    marker :: math.f32_from_bits(U32{0x7FC00001}) // NaN carrying code 1
    return math.f32_to_bits(marker)               // same 32 bits back
}
print(payload())                                 // 2143289345 (0x7FC00001), unchanged
print(math.f32_to_bits(F32{1.0}))                // 1065353216 (0x3F800000), not 1
print(math.f32_to_bits(math.f32_from_bits(U32{0x80000000}))) // 2147483648: negative zero kept
word :: U32.from_int(-1) ?? U32{0}               // -1 is not a U32: check fails, fallback 0
print(math.f32_to_bits(math.f32_from_bits(word))) // 0

options.name: Representation pair on the F32 type
options.detail: Add F32.from_bits(word: U32) -> F32 Never! and value.bits() -> U32 Never!, read from a plain value. This mirrors String.from_bytes(bytes) and text.bytes(). The calls are short and the width is in the type name. The cost is a second home for bit casts. Float keeps math.to_bits and math.from_bits in the math module, while F32 would use methods, unless a later vote moves Float too.
options.code:
use core.math as math

fn payload() -> U32 Never! {
    marker :: F32.from_bits(U32{0x7FC00001}) // NaN carrying code 1
    return marker.bits()                     // same 32 bits back
}
print(payload())                            // 2143289345 (0x7FC00001), unchanged
print(F32{1.0}.bits())                      // 1065353216 (0x3F800000), not 1
print(F32.from_bits(U32{0x80000000}).bits()) // 2147483648: negative zero kept
word :: U32.from_int(-1) ?? U32{0}          // -1 is not a U32: check fails, fallback 0
print(F32.from_bits(word).bits())           // 0
print(math.to_bits(Float{1.0}))             // Float still uses the math module

options.name: Rust-style from_bits and to_bits methods
options.detail: Add F32.from_bits(word: U32) and value.to_bits() -> U32, copying Rust. This is familiar to Rust users. But value.to_bits() is a source-owned to_* conversion, which the ratified D-SHAPE-CONVERT1 rule says is not Jet syntax. Choosing C means amending that rule for one type, and it still leaves Float's math.to_bits as a second spelling.
options.code:
fn payload() -> U32 Never! {
    marker :: F32.from_bits(U32{0x7FC00001}) // NaN carrying code 1
    return marker.to_bits()                  // needs a D-SHAPE-CONVERT1 exception
}
print(payload())                            // 2143289345 (0x7FC00001), unchanged
print(F32{1.0}.to_bits())                   // 1065353216 (0x3F800000), not 1
print(F32.from_bits(U32{0x80000000}).to_bits()) // 2147483648: negative zero kept
word :: U32.from_int(-1) ?? U32{0}          // -1 is not a U32: check fails, fallback 0
print(F32.from_bits(word).to_bits())        // 0

comparisons.note: Rust has exact width-matched bit methods. They do not convert numerically, and Rust documents that arithmetic may change NaN bits.

recommendation.why: A puts the F32 pair beside the Float pair that already exists, so Jet has one home and one spelling pattern for bit casts. It also follows the ratified conversion rule with no exception.
gains: All bit casts live in core.math with one naming pattern.
No source-owned to_* method and no receiver question.
Pure, allocation-free, and exact for all 2^32 patterns, including NaN codes and negative zero.

whyNot.reason: B reads nicely, but it gives bit casts a second home: F32 methods beside Float's math functions.
C needs an exception to the ratified rule against source-owned to_* conversions, and it also splits bit casts across two homes.

recommendation.tradeoff: A's calls are a few letters longer than a method. use core.math as math keeps each call to one short name, the same way Float bit casts are already written.

gains: One home and one pattern for bit casts.
No rule exception and no receiver question.
Pure, allocation-free and exact for every pattern.

whyNot.reason: B splits bit casts between F32 methods and Float's math functions.
C needs an exception to the to_* conversion rule and also splits bit casts.

decisions.title: Checked Unicode scalar construction and streaming
decisions.situation: Every character in Unicode text has an official number, called its scalar: a is 97 and the smiling face 🙂 is 128578. Jet's Char type holds one character, but today nothing turns a number into a Char or back, so file-format readers cannot refuse invalid numbers such as 55296. Separately, loop c in text.chars() first builds a full list of characters, wasting memory when only the first few are needed. You decide how the conversions are spelled and whether scanning needs a new cursor type. We recommend Char.from_u32 and U32.from_char, following Jet's existing conversion rule. We also recommend that the compiler stream eligible chars() loops one character at a time, once a measurement shows it is faster, so nobody learns a new API. One cost remains and is flagged for your approval: a scan that pauses between calls rereads from the start each time or keeps today's list.
decisions.gist: Should Char-number conversion follow the standard from_ naming, with chars() loops streamed by the compiler, or use new cursor and helper APIs?
decisions.lesson: A Unicode scalar is the official number of one character, such as 97 for a. A adds Char.from_u32 and U32.from_char, and makes the compiler stream eligible chars() loops without building a list. B adds the same conversions plus a hand-held cursor type that can pause and resume. C puts conversions and the cursor in core.text helper functions. All three refuse invalid numbers.
decisions.explainer:
Plain words first. A scalar is the official Unicode number of one character. Valid scalars are 0 to 1114111 (hex 0x10FFFF). The exception is the reserved block 55296 to 57343 (hex 0xD800 to 0xDFFF), called surrogates, which are never characters on their own. UTF-8 is the rule Jet uses to store each character as 1 to 4 bytes.

A scalar is not always one visible letter. The text "é" is the letter e followed by a combining accent mark, so it shows as é but holds two scalars. "é".len() is 2. Joining marks into visible letters stays in the opt-in core.text.unicode module.

Syntax legend. U32 is a 32-bit unsigned whole number, and U32{128578} writes one directly. Char? means maybe a Char: Val(c) when there is one, None when not. x ?? return None means: if x is missing, stop here and give back None. :: names a fixed value and := names a changeable one. &cursor.next() marks a call that moves the cursor forward.

Streaming. Today loop c in text.chars() builds a list of every character, then walks it. Under A, when the list is used only by that loop, the compiler decodes characters straight from the text instead. The output is identical. Nothing is allocated per character, and an early return or break stops the decoding.

This ships only after a paired measurement shows it beats today's list. If the loop body reassigns text, or the list is kept or passed on, the compiler builds the list as today. Nothing is ever refused. A program that wants an owned list still writes list :: text.chars().

Pausing. Some readers take one character now and the next one in a later call. A has no cursor that remembers its place between calls. Such a reader either loops from the start again each time, which allocates nothing, or keeps the full list. B and C add a cursor that remembers its place.
decisions.story: Rae writes a file-format reader. She reads the first character's number from a field, and she must refuse the number 55296 because it is not a valid character. She wants this to work without learning a new cursor type.
decisions.detail:
Code facts checked. BuiltinMethods.jet:210 declares String.chars() -> [Char] (TBuiltinOp.Chars). S41 (syntax-decisions.md:1378-1380) makes s.len() count scalars and keeps graphemes in core.text.unicode. No Char-number conversion exists in the builtin method or static registries. No String method decodes one character at a byte position, so no existing API resumes a scan without a list.

D-SHAPE-CONVERT1=A (syntax-decisions.md:903-914) spells typed conversion Target.from_source(value), with the source type's snake-case name as suffix. It bans source-owned to_* conversions. BuiltinStatics.jet:224-239 lists that pattern for numbers, such as from_u32. So Char.from_u32 and U32.from_char are the rule-following names. The earlier draft's Char.from_scalar and c.scalar() were not.

Receivers follow D-MEM1 (Examples/features/effects/method_receivers.jet): plain self reads, &self writes. A cursor's next is a write (Examples/features/collections/held_cursor.jet). The earlier draft's &self on read-only calls was wrong.

AGENTS.md:165-168 requires any surface added for performance to beat the plain spelling in a paired two-program cell before ratification. A adds no performance surface. The chars() streaming is an internal lowering with identical results, and it ships only if it measurably beats today's list-building on the same scan. This ballot claims no measured win. Card #4494 owns the capability.

Pause-and-resume cost, exact. Under A, a reader that takes characters one call at a time and restarts the streamed loop decodes k characters on call k. Reading the first n characters that way costs n(n+1)/2 decodes and no allocation: 10 characters cost 55 decodes. Keeping text.chars() instead decodes and stores the whole text once. B's cursor decodes one character per call and stores only a position.

options.name: Standard conversions and compiler-streamed chars() loops
options.detail:
Add Char.from_u32(value: U32) -> Char?. It returns Val for every valid scalar, including 0 and noncharacters, and None for surrogates and anything above 1114111. Add U32.from_char(c: Char) -> U32, which never fails. Both follow Jet's existing destination-owned conversion rule, the same pattern as U32.from_int. Int callers convert with U32.from_int first.

No new streaming API. The compiler lowers loop c in text.chars() to read characters directly from the text when the list has no other use. It shares the one UTF-8 decoder that chars() already uses. Results never change, so beginners and experts write the same loop they write today.

The lowering ships only after the paired measurement wins. Loops that reassign the source, or lists that are kept or passed on, still build the list.

Pausing between calls has no cursor in A. The reader below restarts its streamed loop on each call, so call k decodes k characters and nothing is allocated. For a short prefix this is small: the first 10 characters cost 55 decodes in total. A reader that walks a long text across many calls keeps the list from text.chars() instead.
options.technical:
Char.from_u32: U32 -> Char? Never!, accepting 0..=0x10FFFF minus 0xD800..=0xDFFF. U32.from_char: Char -> U32 Never!, exact and allocation-free. Both are registered as BUILTIN_NUMERIC_SOURCES-style destination statics. There is no truncation, no replacement character, and no normalization, case mapping or grapheme segmentation.

Lowering: a for-loop whose iterable is a String.chars() call is fused into an in-place UTF-8 scan with a byte offset. The call result must not escape, and the loop body must not reassign or move the source binding. Otherwise the existing list is materialized. There is one decoder for the fused and materialized paths. The fused path ships only after a paired same-input cell shows it strictly beats materialization in time and allocations.

No resumable iterator is added. A restarted fused scan to scalar index k is O(k) time and O(1) space; resuming via text.chars() is O(n) time and space up front.
options.code:
// Read the first and then the second character, in two separate calls.
fn scalar_at(text: String, at: Int) -> U32? {
    n := 0
    loop c in text.chars() {            // streamed: no list, stops early
        if n == at -> return Val(U32.from_char(c))
        n += 1
    }
    return None                         // text is too short
}
text :: "🙂a and a long tail"
print(scalar_at(text, 0))             // Val(128578): decodes 1 character
print(scalar_at(text, 1))             // Val(97): starts again, decodes 2
print(scalar_at("", 0))               // None: empty text
print(Char.from_u32(U32{128578}))     // Val('🙂')
print(Char.from_u32(U32{55296}))      // None: 55296 (0xD800) is a reserved surrogate
print(Char.from_u32(U32{1114112}))    // None: above the largest scalar, 1114111
print("é".len())                   // 2: e plus a combining accent, shown as é

options.name: Standard conversions plus a hand-held cursor
options.detail:
Same conversions and the same loop streaming as A. Also add text.char_iter(), a cursor that reads the original text in place and hands out one character per &cursor.next(). Each call decodes one character and stores only a position, so pausing between calls costs nothing extra.

While the cursor is still in use, the source text cannot be reassigned, because the cursor is reading it. Copying a cursor copies its position, not the text. Under AGENTS.md this is a surface added for performance, so it is ratified only if it beats plain chars() in a measured pair. Otherwise it is dropped.
options.technical: String.char_iter(self) -> CharIterator Never! holds a read loan of the UTF-8 bytes and a byte offset. CharIterator implements Iterator with Item = Char and next(&self) -> Char? Never!. Each call advances 1 to 4 bytes. Moving, dropping or reassigning the source while the loan is live is refused. chars() collects the same iterator, so there is one decoder.
options.code:
// Read the first and then the second character, in two separate calls.
text :: "🙂a and a long tail"
cursor := text.char_iter()                   // reads text in place, no list
first :: (&cursor.next()) ?? panic("empty")  // decodes 1 character
print(U32.from_char(first))                  // 128578
second :: (&cursor.next()) ?? panic("short") // decodes 1 more
print(U32.from_char(second))                 // 97
empty := "".char_iter()
print(&empty.next())                         // None: empty text
print(Char.from_u32(U32{128578}))            // Val('🙂')
print(Char.from_u32(U32{55296}))             // None: reserved surrogate
print(Char.from_u32(U32{1114112}))           // None: above 1114111
// other := "hi"; c := other.char_iter(); other = "new" // refused while c is in use

options.name: Named text-module helpers
options.detail: Put everything in core.text: char_from_scalar(U32) -> Char?, char_scalar(Char) -> U32 and char_iter(String) -> CharIterator. The validation and cursor rules match B, including one decode per call when pausing. Helper names do not follow the destination-owned conversion rule. Every number conversion would look different from U32.from_int and the other numeric conversions.
options.technical: core.text.char_from_scalar: U32 -> Char? Never!; core.text.char_scalar: Char -> U32 Never!; core.text.char_iter: String -> CharIterator Never!, with the same loan and next(&self) contract as B. The same performance gate applies to char_iter.
options.code:
// Read the first and then the second character, in two separate calls.
text :: "🙂a and a long tail"
cursor := core.text.char_iter(text)          // reads text in place, no list
first :: (&cursor.next()) ?? panic("empty")  // decodes 1 character
print(core.text.char_scalar(first))          // 128578
second :: (&cursor.next()) ?? panic("short") // decodes 1 more
print(core.text.char_scalar(second))         // 97
empty := core.text.char_iter("")
print(&empty.next())                         // None: empty text
print(core.text.char_from_scalar(U32{128578}))  // Val('🙂')
print(core.text.char_from_scalar(U32{55296}))   // None: reserved surrogate
print(core.text.char_from_scalar(U32{1114112})) // None: above 1114111

comparisons.note: Rust checks scalars when building a char, and its chars() reads a string one character at a time without building a list.

recommendation.why: A uses the conversion names Jet already uses for numbers. It gets streaming from the loop everyone already writes, so there is nothing new to learn and nothing to borrow by hand. Its one cost, pausing between calls, is flagged below for approval.
gains: Checked conversions that follow the existing Target.from_source rule.
Eligible loop-only chars() scans stream once the measured gate passes; other uses build the list as today.
No new cursor type, no borrowing rules for users, and no performance surface to gate.

losses.loss: A scan that pauses between calls has no cursor. It restarts its loop on each call, so call k decodes k characters, or it keeps the full list in memory. B's cursor decodes one character per call.
losses.mitigation: The restart path allocates nothing and is small for prefixes: the first 10 characters cost 55 decodes. Whole-text scans stay one streamed loop. This cost is flagged for owner approval; choosing B removes it at the price of a cursor type.

whyNot.reason: B adds a cursor type that users must learn. It blocks reassigning the text while the cursor is in use, and it is ratified only if it wins a measured race. Its real advantage is cheap pause-and-resume.
C has the same cursor costs as B. It also names conversions differently from every other Jet conversion.

recommendation.tradeoff: A pause-and-resume reader restarts its streamed loop, decoding k characters on call k with no allocation, or keeps the full text.chars() list. B's cursor avoids that cost but adds a type and a borrowing rule.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: BallotRevBeginner3. Skill: rli5. The reader followed the smile and surrogate results but lacked the syntax, surrogates, a combining-mark case and the borrowing cost. The revision adds a legend, empty and a🙂 outputs, a valid build, an upper-bound refusal and an e-plus-accent example, and removes user-facing borrowing from the recommendation.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: undisclosed. Adversarial model family: undisclosed. Fresh agent: BallotRevAdversary3, then BallotRevFinalE. Reviews found wrong receivers, unteachable edge cases, overpromised streaming and a hidden pause-and-resume cost. The recommendation follows D-SHAPE-CONVERT1, gates streaming on measurement, and shows the pause cost in one shared two-call program for owner approval.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Test Char.from_u32 at 0, 0xD7FF, 0xD800, 0xDFFF, 0xE000, 0x10FFFF, 0x110000 and the U32 maximum. Include noncharacters and supplementary planes, and check U32.from_char round trips.

Check that fused chars() loops print the same as list-building ones, including early return, break, empty text, a kept list and a body that reassigns the source. Run the paired same-input scan cell for time and allocations before shipping the fused lowering.

Run the two-call scalar_at program and confirm it allocates nothing and decodes 1 then 2 characters. Keep the existing codec, escape_debug and scalar_at tests.

decisions.title: Checked native SIMD implementation tools
decisions.situation: SIMD means one processor instruction works on several numbers at once; newer chips add such instructions in groups, such as AVX. Jet's runtime, the engine under every program, is being rewritten from Rust into Jet. It must use those instructions only on chips that have them, because an older chip without AVX would crash. Today's Rust runtime, built for chips without AVX, checks the chip on every lane operation and falls back to plain loops. Jet code names instructions only through hand-written assembly. You decide what tools the Jet runtime gets; you asked that beginners get safe, automatic speed while experts keep exact control. We recommend the tools Jet already approved for everyone: a #Multiversion function is built once per chip level, and the best copy is picked once at start. Beginners write plain loops or lane values (groups of numbers) and change nothing. Experts opt in to exact widths, named instructions, assembly and a build error when a loop stops vectorizing.
decisions.gist: Should runtime SIMD use the approved per-chip-level copies, raw permits, or no CPU checks, with automatic beginner speed and expert control?
decisions.lesson: Beginners keep writing plain loops and lane values and get the same answers under every option. A builds the runtime's fast paths with #Multiversion, the tool Jet already approved for everyone, so the chip is checked once at start. Experts opt in to named instructions with those same tools. B gives runtime authors permits (proof the chip was checked) and unsafe blocks (code the compiler cannot check). C adds nothing, so only builds made for a newer chip go fast.
decisions.explainer:
Plain words first. A processor (CPU) is the chip that runs the program; a core is one of its processing units. A CPU feature such as SSE, AVX or AVX2 is a group of extra instructions that some chips have and others lack. A CPU level bundles features: x86_64 is every 64-bit x86 chip, x86_64_v2 adds SSE3 through SSE4.2, and x86_64_v3 adds AVX, AVX2 and FMA (fused multiply-add). A register is a tiny storage slot inside the CPU.

To vectorize a loop means the compiler rewrites it to use SIMD instructions, so each step handles several numbers. Core is Jet's standard library; the runtime is the part of it every program runs on.

A lane value holds several numbers that one instruction processes together. Lanes<F64, 4> holds exactly four F64 numbers. Lanes<F64> holds as many as the widest register of the chip level the code is built for. These names come from the ratified lane decision and replace today's F64x4 spelling. Bit-identical means every bit of the answer matches, including the sign of zero and very small (subnormal) numbers.

NaN ("not a number") results, such as 0.0 / 0.0, are NaN on every path. Which NaN bit pattern comes out is not promised, exactly as for ordinary Float math in Jet today. Comparisons treat every NaN alike, so compare answers always match. math.to_bits can show the pattern, so printed bits of a computed NaN may differ between chips and tiers.

Jet runs code in several ways, called tiers: compile-time evaluation, an interpreter, a JIT for quick development runs, and full native builds. A portable build targets the oldest chip level, so it runs on every chip.

The beginner path. Plain loops and Core collection operations vectorize automatically for the chip level the build targets. In a default x86_64 build that means 128-bit SSE2 instructions, because Jet never copies unmarked code per chip on its own. Core's own hot kernels, such as list sums, can be marked #Multiversion inside the runtime once a measurement justifies it. Then they use AVX2 on chips that have it, even in a portable build. The beginner writes no marker.

Same answers for beginners. Plain loops and Core operations give the same bits for every non-NaN result on every chip, tier and build. Lane values use the build level's registers. So Lanes<T> code that adds across chunks can change in its last bits between builds for different chip levels; Lanes<T, N> pins the width.

The expert path, each step opt-in. Lanes<F32, 8> pins an exact width. #Multiversion on a function builds one copy per chip level. Inside it, prep if $build.cpu.has(.AVX2), an if decided while building each copy, selects named instructions from core.arch, the typed instruction module. jet build --cpu and --features build the whole program for a newer chip. #FFI(asm), hand-written assembly, reaches instructions core.arch lacks; it needs an #Unsafe block, code the compiler cannot check. #Scalar, already ratified, keeps a function from vectorizing.

New in this vote, each declinable by name. #Vectorized (group VEC-LOCK) on a function turns a loop that stays scalar into a build error naming the loop and the reason. JET_CPU_MAX (group CPU-CAP), a setting in the program's environment, caps the chip level chosen at start, for tests and for machines whose cores differ. Decline one by name, as in "A, decline VEC-LOCK".

A also lists each loop's vectorize verdict in jet inspect choices, applying D-AUTOPIN1=A's rule that every automatic choice can be seen. Without VEC-LOCK the verdict stays visible, but nothing fails the build. Without CPU-CAP, mixed-core machines lose that safeguard and the per-level tests need a real chip of each level.

Why once at start. A copy is chosen when the program starts, not on every call, so a four-number add inside a copy is one plain instruction with no check. Each call from unmarked code into a marked function is one indirect call, so Core marks whole loops, not single lane operations. The operating system may still move a running program to another core. So, as today, every core must have the same features.

Mainstream systems give every core one feature set: Arm Linux reports only features all cores share, and hybrid x86 chips give every core the same instructions. Virtual machines that move between hosts rely on the hypervisor showing one feature set, as today. JET_CPU_MAX covers rare machines whose cores differ.

Build targets. With no flags, Jet builds for the target's baseline chip level. A program built with --cpu or --features for a newer chip checks the chip at start. On an older chip it stops with a clear message instead of crashing. Copies depend only on the listed levels and the target, never on the build machine, so a cross build from any host gives the same program. Today's release builds still pass target-cpu=native, so card #4192 must land first.

The web. WebAssembly cannot check the chip at start, so a marked function has one web copy. Whether it uses WebAssembly's 128-bit SIMD depends on the web target, which this vote does not change. Browsers have no environment settings, so JET_CPU_MAX does not apply there.
decisions.story: Priya ports the runtime's lane math from Rust to Jet. It must use AVX on chips that have it, stay correct on chips that do not, and never request new memory. Kai, an expert user, needs one AVX2 shuffle, an instruction that reorders lanes, by name and wants his build to fail if a hot loop stops vectorizing.
decisions.detail:
Code facts checked. D-SIMD1/D-SIMD2 and D-SIMD3=B (syntax-decisions.md:3235-3255) ratify lane types, scalar-order reductions, #Scalar and raw intrinsics behind #Unsafe. D-LANES1=A (card #4167) replaces the twenty named lanes with Lanes<T, N> and the native Lanes<T>. D-FRED1=A fixes one eight-way pairwise Float reduction order on every run mode.

Ratified CPU law. D-CPU-DISPATCH1=A (card #4168) adds #Multiversion(levels), prep if $build.cpu.has(...) and typed core.arch intrinsics generated from vendor tables. One start-up probe in the Prelude binds the best copy. Its copies must give identical bits, and the interpreter and JIT run the baseline copy. Per-CPU copies must compose with D-ACCEL1=A's measured acceleration, not add a second selection mechanism. Automatic cloning of unmarked code was its rejected option D and stays rejected here.

Composition. Under A, a copy fixes only the instruction level. D-ACCEL1's measured gate still decides threads and column copies inside it, so the two never choose the same thing.

Build flags. D-FFI-ASM-CPU1=B makes the target baseline the default and adds --cpu and --features. D-CPU-DISPATCH1 treats that, not D-SIMD3's host-CPU default (syntax-decisions.md:3246-3248), as the law for unmarked code. Card #4192 removes the target-cpu=native flag that Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Host.jet:141 still passes. A depends on it: until it lands, even the baseline copy could use the build machine's instructions.

Other law. #FFI(asm) needs an enclosing #Unsafe (Docs/spec/safety.md:50, Docs/spec/spec.md:2460-2461). D-AUTOPIN1=A says every automatic choice can be seen and locked, but its listed examples do not yet include vectorization.

The Rust runtime. crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/SimdLanes.rs checks features per call with is_x86_feature_detected, a cached flag read (:1063-1192). It does so only in builds without AVX (:1722-1727); AVX builds, including today's target-cpu=native release builds, use AVX directly. Its feature-gated kernels are at :814-1057, and its portable math uses ordinary Rust operators (:75-88). It stores F64x4 as a 256-bit __m256d only when the build target has AVX (:1389-1399, :1213). Its #Scalar barrier uses black_box plus a compiler-only SeqCst fence (:9-17).

What changed after owner question q0z7el6v. The earlier A added a fixed list of per-call self-checking kernels in core.mem.native.simd. That was a second way to pick instructions beside #Multiversion, against I8, and it gave experts no named instructions. The new A drops that module and builds the runtime from the ratified tools. B is a variant of the run-time feature blocks D-CPU-DISPATCH1 rejected as its option B.

NaN bits today. Rust documents that arithmetic NaN results may have any sign and payload, which can differ between targets and between compile-time and run-time evaluation (https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.f32.html#nan-bit-patterns). IEEE 754 does not fix one NaN payload either. Jet has no canonical arithmetic NaN rule; its canonical NaN is a CBOR encoding rule (syntax-decisions.md:4155). Jet shows those bits through math.to_bits (Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md:1753). So no option can promise identical NaN bits without a new rule.

Interaction with D-RT-NATIVE-CAP1=A (card #4494). That vote left vector intrinsics, CPU dispatch, black_box and fence to this ballot. Under A none of them joins the private core.mem.native surface. Dispatch and intrinsics are public ratified tools, and black_box and fence stay inside the compiler. Under B they would live in core.mem.native.simd, open to bundled code and owner-admitted providers.

Scope. This ballot chooses the runtime's SIMD tools plus two new, declinable spellings. The #Vectorized lock is group VEC-LOCK; it also makes #Vectorized with the ratified #Scalar an error. The JET_CPU_MAX cap is group CPU-CAP. Intrinsic names such as x86.mm256_permute4x64_pd are illustrative; D-CPU-DISPATCH1's vendor tables set the spelling. No measured speed win is claimed. AGENTS.md's paired performance cells still apply before any speed claim.

New law in this vote. Five points are new rules, not readings of earlier votes. First, inside a #Multiversion function, Lanes<T> has the widest listed level's width in every copy. On a target the list does not name, such as Arm or the web, the function has one copy and Lanes<T> keeps D-LANES1's native width.

Second, typed core.arch intrinsics that only take and return lane values are checked by the copy's level and need no #Unsafe. D-SIMD1/D-SIMD2 keep raw intrinsics behind #Unsafe. D-CPU-DISPATCH1's example calls a typed one without #Unsafe but states no rule. Third, compile-time evaluation runs the baseline copy, as D-CPU-DISPATCH1 already requires of the interpreter and JIT.

Fourth, this vote narrows D-CPU-DISPATCH1's identical-bits rule, which states no NaN exception, to every non-NaN result. NaN sign and payload stay unspecified, as for scalar Float. Fifth, jet inspect choices lists each loop's vectorize verdict, naming vectorization in D-AUTOPIN1=A's law.

options.name: One approved tool: per-chip-level copies, with opt-in expert control
options.detail:
Jet's runtime writes its fast paths with the same tools users get, so there is one way to use newer chips. A hot runtime kernel is an ordinary Jet function marked #Multiversion(x86_64, x86_64_v2, x86_64_v3). The compiler builds one copy per CPU level. At start, the program checks the chip once and binds the best copy. The baseline copy is the fallback, written once.

Kernels written with plain loops or lane math need no permit, no #Unsafe block and no separate fallback. Inside each copy the compiler keeps lane values in that level's registers, so a four-number add is one AVX instruction in the v3 copy. A kernel that names an instruction through prep if writes the other branch itself, as reverse4 below does. The forced-level tests check that both branches give the same bits.

Beginners write nothing new. Plain loops and Core collection operations still vectorize automatically for the build's chip level, which is 128-bit SSE2 in a default x86_64 build. Lanes<T> uses the widest register of that level. Core's measured hot kernels, such as list sums, use the best listed chip level the running chip has, even in a portable build.

Experts opt in, one explicit step at a time. Lanes<F32, 8> pins a width. #Multiversion with prep if $build.cpu.has(.AVX2) names typed core.arch instructions per chip level. jet build --cpu=znver4 --features=+avx2 targets one chip for the whole program. #FFI(asm) inside #Unsafe reaches anything else, and the already-ratified #Scalar keeps code scalar.

Two spellings are new in this vote, each declinable by its group name. #Vectorized (VEC-LOCK) makes a loop that stays scalar a build error naming the loop and the reason. JET_CPU_MAX=x86_64_v2 (CPU-CAP) caps the copy chosen at start, for tests and for machines whose cores differ.
options.technical:
Dispatch. A hot runtime kernel is an ordinary Jet function marked #Multiversion under D-CPU-DISPATCH1=A. The Prelude start-up probe reads the OS-enabled features once and binds each marked function to its best copy. Calls from inside a copy to other marked functions stay at that level and are direct. A call from unmarked code is one indirect call that cannot be inlined, so Core marks whole loops. Unmarked code uses the build's chip level and never checks the chip.

Build independence. Copies depend only on the listed levels and the target, never on the build host, so cross builds match host builds. A depends on card #4192: while release builds pass target-cpu=native, even the baseline copy could use the build machine's instructions.

Registers. Inside a copy, lane values lower to that level's registers. Lanes<F64, 4> is one 256-bit register in the x86_64_v3 copy and two 128-bit registers below it. Inside a #Multiversion function, Lanes<T> has the widest listed level's width in every copy, and narrower copies use several registers (rule fixed by this vote). Lane permutations use AVX2 instructions only in copies whose level has AVX2.

Other targets. On a target the list does not name, such as Arm or WebAssembly, the function has one copy and Lanes<T> keeps D-LANES1's native width. WebAssembly has no start-up chip check.

Result law, shared by every copy and every tier, including compile-time evaluation. Every non-NaN result of a basic operation (add, subtract, multiply, divide, square root, conversion) is the correctly rounded IEEE 754 result. Rounding is to nearest-even with subnormals preserved, so bits match. Other math functions use one Jet algorithm in every copy, never a vendor vector math library.

NaN. Results are NaN exactly when the baseline copy's result is NaN. NaN sign and payload are unspecified, as for scalar Float, so math.to_bits may show different NaN bits between copies, tiers and architectures. This vote narrows D-CPU-DISPATCH1's identical-bits rule to that. Negation flips only the sign bit, so it is bit-exact.

Copies use no FMA, no approximate reciprocal or square-root instructions and no reordering unless the function's effect row admits non-reproducible results (D-CPU-DISPATCH1). That covers typed core.arch intrinsics too; approximate instructions give different bits on Intel and AMD chips. Reductions use D-FRED1's fixed order.

The interpreter, JIT and compile-time evaluation run the baseline copy (I9). A cross build evaluates compile-time code by the target's rules, not the host chip's. Debug and release builds follow the same law, so optimization changes speed, never non-NaN bits. The guarantee assumes Jet's default floating-point environment: round to nearest, no flush-to-zero or denormals-are-zero.

Expert instructions (rule fixed by this vote). Typed core.arch intrinsics that only take and return lane values are checked by the copy's level and need no #Unsafe; one used outside a matching copy is a build error. Intrinsics that read or write through raw addresses, and every #FFI(asm) body, stay behind #Unsafe (D-SIMD1/D-SIMD2, D-SIMD3=B). Intrinsic names in examples are illustrative; D-CPU-DISPATCH1 generates them from vendor tables. Kernels never allocate. The #Scalar barrier stays a compiler-internal operation, and no core.mem.native.simd module exists.

#Vectorized (group VEC-LOCK, new) on a function or method extends D-AUTOPIN1=A to vectorization. Every loop in its own body, not in callees, must vectorize at each chip level it is built for. Otherwise the build fails with a registered diagnostic naming the loop, the level and the blocking fact. #Vectorized and #Scalar on one function is a build error.

The verdict comes from the sema vectorization proof shared by every tier (Docs/audits/tier-parity-architecture-2026-09-03.md:139), so jet check, jet run and jet build give the same diagnostic. The interpreter and JIT may still run a proven loop scalar, with the same bits. Optimized native builds must emit the vector form or fail with that diagnostic. A loop needing instructions the baseline lacks fails at the baseline level.

JET_CPU_MAX (group CPU-CAP, new) is read once by the start-up probe, which runs on every tier. Its value is a level name such as x86_64_v2. It can only lower the copy chosen, never raise it. An unknown name stops the program at start on every tier with a registered diagnostic. The forced-level test matrix uses the same setting.

It never lowers code built with --cpu or --features, which still needs those features on every core. The interpreter and JIT always run the baseline copy, so there it only checks the name. Browsers have no environment, so it does not apply on the web. It joins the table in Docs/spec/reference/environment.md beside JET_SCHEDULER_THREADS.

Static path. Builds made with --cpu or --features check the chip before main and stop with a registered diagnostic when a required feature is missing (D-FFI-ASM-CPU1=B). Unsupported architectures run the baseline copy, and importing core.arch never rejects unrelated code.

options.name: Expert permits, raw instructions and a register type
options.detail:
Give runtime authors the raw pieces instead. with_feature(.AVX, enhanced, fallback) checks the chip and hands a permit to the enhanced function. Raw instructions need that permit and an #Unsafe block. A NativeF64x4 register type is usable only while the permit is live. Authors write the fallback themselves, and each author must keep it matching the fast path, including for NaN results.

This is the most flexible option for runtime authors. Only the guarded function is duplicated, and with_feature can wrap a whole kernel, so its cached flag read runs once per kernel call. It adds a permit lifetime that must never cross a pause or escape. It also needs a separate permit for each feature, such as AVX2 for some lane shuffles, and an unsafe block at every raw instruction.

It relies on the same same-features-on-every-core assumption as A. It is also a variant of the run-time feature blocks that D-CPU-DISPATCH1 rejected as its option B. Users would keep #Multiversion while the runtime used permits, so Jet would have two ways to use newer instructions.
options.technical:
with_feature<T, E>(feature, enhanced: fn(FeaturePermit) -[E]> T, fallback: fn() -[E]> T) -[Env, E]> T. Raw intrinsics are #Unsafe fn requiring the matching permit. NativeF64x4 offers from_array, splat, to_array, lane, lane_const<I>, add, sub, mul, div, sqrt and neg. It also offers mul_lane_scale<I> and gather_lane<I>, each tied to an AVX or AVX2 permit.

opaque_value<T>(^T) -> T and compiler_fence_seqcst() are exposed for #Scalar. Permits must be non-storable, non-escaping and invalid across suspension. NaN payloads, the floating-point environment and the uniform-feature requirement are as in A, but each author upholds the result law by hand. The module lives in core.mem.native.simd under D-RT-NATIVE-CAP1=A admission: bundled code and owner-admitted providers only.

options.name: No runtime CPU checks; compiler auto-vectorizing only
options.detail:
Add nothing. The runtime writes plain loops, and the compiler may turn them into fast instructions only when the build targets a chip known to have them. A program built for a portable target never uses AVX in Core, even on a chip that has it. That is a speed regression from today's Rust runtime, which checks at run time. With no run-time check, Core needs no same-features-on-every-core assumption. NaN bit patterns are unspecified here too.

C also has no start-up check in Core, the smallest binaries, and one instruction set per binary to test.
options.technical: No core.mem.native.simd module, and Core marks nothing #Multiversion. Unmarked code uses the build's chip level (D-FFI-ASM-CPU1=B), and --cpu builds keep the start-up check from A. The #Scalar barrier stays compiler-internal. Per-call runtime dispatch from SimdLanes.rs:1063-1192 is dropped. Users may still mark their own functions #Multiversion, so user code could outrun Core. The result law and NaN rule from A apply.

comparisons.note: Vector<T> picks its width for the running machine when the JIT starts, and Vector128<T> and Vector256<T> pin exact widths. Avx2.IsSupported becomes a constant during JIT compilation, so unsupported branches vanish. This is the closest match to A's split between automatic defaults and opt-in named instructions.

Rust auto-vectorizes through LLVM with no in-language guarantee, and its portable std::simd is still unstable. Experts pair #[target_feature] functions with is_x86_feature_detected!. Calling such a function from code without the feature needs unsafe, because the compiler does not check the guard. Its arithmetic NaN bit patterns are documented as unspecified.

@Vector(n, T) is a built-in vector type, and std.simd.suggestVectorLength picks a width for the build target at compile time. CPU features come from -mcpu for the whole build. Zig has no built-in run-time dispatch.
SIMD[dtype, width] is the one vector type, and simd_width_of returns the width for the compile target. Width and target queries resolve at compile time.
comparisons.code:
# Mojo 1.1.0: https://mojolang.org/docs/std/sys/info/simd_width_of/
from std.sys.info import simd_width_of
comptime W = simd_width_of[DType.float32]()          # lanes for the compile target
var v = SIMD[DType.float32, W](1.0)                   # splat
var q = SIMD[DType.float32, 4](1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0)    # exact width

comparisons.note: Go's compiler does not auto-vectorize ordinary loops, and the language has no portable vector type. Go 1.26 added an experimental, amd64-only simd/archsimd package behind GOEXPERIMENT=simd. A portable package is only planned.
Both compile one function per CPU target and choose a copy once at start. That is the model #Multiversion follows.

recommendation.why: A gives beginners automatic, safe speed and gives experts exact control by opt-in, through one approved mechanism. The runtime uses the same #Multiversion copies as everyone, so nothing new is private and the chip is checked once, not on every call.
gains: Beginners write no marker or unsafe code: plain loops, lane values and Core operations vectorize automatically.
Experts opt in to exact widths, named instructions per chip level, whole-build CPU flags, audited assembly and a must-vectorize build error.
Identical bits for every non-NaN result on every chip and every tier.
One way to pick instructions, shared by users and the runtime.

losses.loss: Checking once at start assumes every core the process may run on has the same features. On a machine that breaks this, a copy chosen on one core could run on another.
losses.mitigation: Mainstream systems give every core one feature set: Arm Linux reports only shared features, and hybrid x86 chips give all cores the same instructions. Today's Rust runtime makes the same assumption. On a nonuniform machine, JET_CPU_MAX caps the chosen copy to a level every core has.

losses.loss: Chips with AVX but no AVX2, sold mainly from 2011 to 2014, run the x86_64_v2 copy with 128-bit registers, where today's Rust runtime uses AVX.
losses.mitigation: Answers are identical and the code is still vectorized. An AVX-only level can be added to a kernel's list later if a paired performance cell shows it matters.

losses.loss: The SIMD port waits for #Multiversion, core.arch and Lanes (cards #4168, #4167), which are ratified but not built. It also waits for card #4192, because target-cpu=native would leak the build machine's instructions into the baseline copy.
losses.mitigation: The Rust runtime keeps today's per-call checks until they land, so nothing regresses. No stopgap mechanism is built that would later need removal.

losses.loss: Marked functions are compiled once per chip level, so binaries grow.
losses.mitigation: Only marked hot kernels pay, and each marked Core kernel needs a paired performance cell showing a gain first.

losses.loss: Each call from unmarked code into a marked function is one indirect call that cannot be inlined. Single lane operations no longer jump to an AVX kernel per call; they use the build level inline.
losses.mitigation: Core marks whole loops, not single lane operations, and calls between marked functions at one level are direct. The paired performance cells decide each marked kernel; no speed is claimed before them.

losses.loss: This vote narrows D-CPU-DISPATCH1's identical-bits rule to non-NaN results, so math.to_bits can show different NaN bits between copies, tiers and architectures.
losses.mitigation: NaN-ness, compares and sign-bit operations still match exactly. Rust, today's backend, documents the same freedom for scalar Float. A canonical arithmetic NaN rule would need its own vote.

whyNot.reason: B duplicates #Multiversion with permits, unsafe blocks and hand-written fallbacks, a second way to use new instructions. It is a variant of the run-time feature blocks D-CPU-DISPATCH1 rejected, and it keeps A's core assumption.
C needs no new tools, but portable builds lose the fast paths today's Rust runtime provides. Core would also trail user code marked #Multiversion.

recommendation.tradeoff: A waits for ratified tools that are not built yet and for card #4192. It adds two small spellings, #Vectorized and JET_CPU_MAX, each declinable by name. Like today's runtime, it assumes the same features on every allowed core. It narrows identical bits to non-NaN results; no option promises NaN bit patterns. Under every option, a beginner's own loops in a default x86_64 build vectorize with SSE2 only. Every option needs a forced-level test matrix on real chips.

hybrid.synthesis: A takes C's default, plain code that the compiler vectorizes with no run-time checks in unmarked code. It takes B's goal, expert access to named instructions, but reaches it through ratified #Multiversion and core.arch instead of permits.

harvest.use: Typed core.arch intrinsics inside #Multiversion copies, checked by chip level, with #FFI(asm) behind #Unsafe for the rest.

harvest.aspect: No run-time checks in ordinary code.
harvest.use: Unmarked code is built for the target chip level and never checks the chip; only marked kernels get copies.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: SimdReview. Skill: rli5. The beginner pass tested the complete ballot with explain, predict, modify and derive tasks, and all four succeeded from the page after fixes. It fixed untaught terms (vectorize, Core, tier, portable build, prep if, core.arch, #Unsafe, CPU core, shuffle, permits) and named both decline groups and their effects.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: undisclosed. Adversarial model family: claude. Fresh agent: SimdAdversary. It rechecked every cited line and outcome, all accurate, relabeled four rules as new law, admitted reverse4's hand-written fallback and gave B and C their real gains. It disclosed to_bits NaN drift, SSE2 user loops, Lanes<T> width drift, indirect calls and #4192, and added web, Arm, cross-build, debug, hybrid-core and approximate-intrinsic cases.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Run every marked Core kernel and every example under JET_CPU_MAX set to x86_64, x86_64_v2 and x86_64_v3 on real hardware, and with no cap. Run the same matrix in compile-time evaluation, the interpreter and the JIT, which run the baseline copy. Compare bits with the baseline copy for every non-NaN result, including signed zero, infinities, subnormal inputs and outputs, and exact I64 compares.

For NaN cases, check NaN-ness and compare answers only. Cover two NaNs with different payloads, signaling NaNs, 0/0 and infinity minus infinity, and sign-bit negation of NaN, which must be bit-exact.

Check that Lanes<T> inside a #Multiversion function has the widest listed width in every copy and gives identical sums. Check that the AVX2 lane-permute intrinsic (illustratively x86.mm256_permute4x64_pd) is a build error outside an AVX2 copy and needs no #Unsafe inside one. Check that reverse4 prints [4.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.0] under every cap.

Check #Vectorized: decay fails with the named reason under jet check, jet run and jet build; a vectorizable loop passes; #Vectorized with #Scalar is refused. Check an unknown JET_CPU_MAX value stops at start on every tier, and that the cap never raises the chosen copy.

Build with --cpu=znver4 --features=+avx2, run on a chip without AVX2, and expect the start-up diagnostic, not a crash. Run on an AVX-only chip and expect the v2 copy. Check the #Scalar barrier and zero allocations. Rerun the full SimdLanes tests and the required paired performance cells before any speed claim.

Edge cases. Repeat the bit matrix in debug and release builds. After card #4192, build the same program for x86_64 on an x86_64_v4 host and on an Arm host; the binaries' copies and the non-NaN outputs must match. Check that JET_CPU_MAX does not lower a --cpu build, and that a web build runs one copy and ignores JET_CPU_MAX.

Check that FMA and approximate reciprocal or square-root intrinsics are refused in a copy whose effect row does not admit non-reproducible results. Check that optimized native builds emit vector code for each loop #Vectorized accepts.

surface.situation: SIMD means one processor instruction works on several numbers at once; newer chips add such instructions in groups, such as AVX. Jet's runtime, the engine under every program, is being rewritten from Rust into Jet. It must use those instructions only on chips that have them, because an older chip without AVX would crash. Today's Rust runtime, built for chips without AVX, checks the chip on every lane operation and falls back to plain loops. Jet code names instructions only through hand-written assembly. You decide what tools the Jet runtime gets; you asked that beginners get safe, automatic speed while experts keep exact control. We recommend the tools Jet already approved for everyone: a #Multiversion function is built once per chip level, and the best copy is picked once at start. Beginners write plain loops or lane values (groups of numbers) and change nothing. Experts opt in to exact widths, named instructions, assembly and a build error when a loop stops vectorizing.
surface.gist: Should runtime SIMD use the approved per-chip-level copies, raw permits, or no CPU checks, with automatic beginner speed and expert control?
surface.lesson: Beginners write plain loops and lane values under every option. A builds runtime fast paths with #Multiversion, approved for everyone: one copy per chip level, best copy picked at start. Experts opt in to exact widths, named instructions, assembly and a must-vectorize check. B gives runtime authors permits and unsafe blocks. C adds nothing; only newer-chip builds go fast.

current.note: Built without AVX, today's Rust runtime checks the chip on every call, then runs an AVX kernel or a plain loop.

wild.note: C# picks the Vector<T> width per machine; experts opt in to named instructions behind IsSupported.
wild.code:
int lanes = Vector<float>.Count;          // width chosen per machine
if (Avx2.IsSupported) {                   // constant once the JIT compiles
    var r = Avx2.Permute4x64(v, 0x1B);    // named instruction, opt-in
}

decisions.title: Where checked SQL gets its database map
decisions.situation: A database map, called a schema, lists tables and columns. Today Jet keeps query data separate but can miss a wrong column name until deployment. Beginners need early errors, while experts need to respect tables managed by other teams. You choose where checked queries get their map. We recommend source declarations for tables Jet owns and reviewed saved maps for outside tables. Each new connection must read the live map before use; pooling and warm-up move this cost away from requests. Later outside administrator changes remain outside that one-time guarantee.
decisions.gist: Should SQL use source declarations, saved database maps, or a per-table mix?
decisions.lesson: A combines owned source and outside snapshots. B uses snapshots for both. C checks instruction kinds without a map. D describes both tables in source, but only owned tables receive generated migrations. All four read the same Ada/team row and migrate only person.
decisions.explainer:
A snapshot is a saved map, not a copy of rows. A catalog is the database's own live map. Owned means Jet may propose changes to that table; described does not necessarily mean owned. A migration is a reviewed sequence of database changes. A fingerprint is a digest of map facts, not data or passwords. Admission is the connection-start comparison. Drift means the live facts changed. Nullable means a value may be absent. A database function may do hidden work.

:: names a value. -[DB.Read]> lists possible read work, not permission. [String:DBValue]? is an optional row map: Val(row) or None. DBError! is an ordinary database error. SQL.Query is the proposed read label; SQL.Schema is the separate proposed table-change label. New commands/APIs below are proposals, not executed results. Existing row extraction remains fallible.
decisions.story: Mina owns person(id,name,team_id). Another team owns team(id,name). Seed person(7,Ada,3) and team(3,Blue), both visible. Her request joins them and gets Ada/Blue. Her separately reviewed migration adds nullable email only to person; it must never change team.
decisions.inWild:
sqlx::query!("SELECT p.name, t.name FROM person p JOIN team t ON p.team_id=t.id WHERE p.id=?", 7i64);
// cargo sqlx prepare; commit .sqlx; cargo sqlx prepare --check
decisions.detail:
This vote chooses map sources, not the independent CLASS/AUTHORITY/GUARD/RAW votes. Its labelled examples require CLASS=A; DB.Schema examples require AUTHORITY=A. Otherwise the same query/migration uses current SQL and current read/write/migration gates. No Unsafe-effect choice is required just to compile checked SQL. Raw construction follows whichever separate raw/effect votes win.

For A/B/D, compile table/column/expression/binding/nullability facts against one normalized dialect model. Source declarations and snapshots feed that same checker. Duplicate object descriptions fail. Query result decoding stays fallible. Database wire count bounds do not depend on the host's size_t, the machine-sized unsigned integer. A wrong name such as naem fails compilation; C reports it only during execution.

Fixture saved-map format is version1 {dialect:"SQLite",objects:[...]}. Each table entry has name,owner,columns,primary_key. Column entries have name,type,nullable. External team is {name:"team",owner:"External",columns:[{name:"id",type:"INTEGER",nullable:false},{name:"name",type:"TEXT",nullable:false}],primary_key:["id"]}. Owned person has id INTEGER/name TEXT/team_id INTEGER, all non-null, and primary key id. Full dialect facts include constraints/defaults/indexes/generated fields and reachable routine effects. No rows, URLs, credentials or tenant data are saved.

Each physical connection compares the combined map before first use. Reusing that admitted connection adds no repeat admission read. Reconnect, checked migration, explicit snapshot/source identity change or registered routine change invalidates its admission. No cross-connection cached success substitutes for inspection. Denied catalog access or mismatch returns DBError before requests; repair by approved inspection permission or reviewed migration/snapshot refresh, then reconnect. Never silently pull production facts.

Admission proves only that moment's facts. Database-enforced read/write/schema permissions remain binding during execution. Effect-changing administration outside those permissions is outside the guarantee, not merely a promised future DBError: it may succeed with changed behavior. Deployment must prevent such changes during traffic or coordinate them with draining/re-admission. Registered external functions remain expert-reviewed contracts. Unknown reachable effects fail closed, even on Dynamic/raw paths; broad grants and reasons cannot supply missing proof.

A supported late catalog/type fact can be resolved by the checked runtime constructor on the actual connection. An arbitrary unknown writing function cannot. decisions.title: One expert gate for unchecked SQL
decisions.situation: An unchecked database instruction is text an expert supplies without the usual text check. Today Jet asks for an expert reason for library-defined checked text, but built-in SQL can skip that gate. That makes a dangerous path harder for reviewers to find. You decide whether both paths must have the same visible reason. We recommend one guarded constructor, with ordinary checked text unchanged. Unknown hidden database work still needs proof before execution; a reason is not that proof.
decisions.gist: Should every unchecked SQL constructor require an expert reason?
decisions.lesson: A closes the built-in permission gap without adding steps to checked SQL. B retains the gap. Creating an instruction does not execute it. Database access stays checked when the instruction runs.
decisions.explainer:
A checked constructor tests text. SQL.Query.from(text) is the proposed checked path for text arriving later. A raw constructor skips that test. #Unsafe("reason") records an expert promise for code inside its braces, not a database grant. An audit report lists reasons and functions reaching them. Dynamic means the exact instruction kind is not proved yet.

:: names a value. SQL{...} binds inserted data separately from command text. -[DB]> lists possible database work, not permission. [String:DBValue]? is an optional row: Val(row) or None. DBError! is a normal database error. Construction does no DB work. Execution needs the conservative possible DB effects and matching held permissions.
decisions.story: Mina receives text reading Ada from person(7,Ada). Her helper returns that instruction; a scoped call executes it under normal database permissions.
decisions.inWild:

// Dynamic: sqlx::query(text).bind(7i64).
decisions.detail:
One unchecked constructor: SQL.raw(text:String,omit_where:Bool=false)->SQL.Dynamic Never!, inside lexical #Unsafe(reason). This permission rule applies under every Unsafe-effect choice. Creation records raw/Unsafe facts but does no DB work. Checked literals and .from keep their own existing permissions. Built-in and library CheckedText raw constructors share the gate and source/package/reason audit facts.

With CLASS=A, raw returns the single Dynamic carrier. With GUARD=A, omit_where sets its sealed intent_all_rows bit; execution checks authority.db.omit_where on every call. No source setter mutates this bit. Without CLASS=A, return the current SQL carrier with guarded creation; labels are not silently approved. Without GUARD=A, omit_where is not exposed. Without AUTHORITY=A, use current DB.Read/DB.Write ceilings and migration authority, not an unapproved DB.Schema.

Runtime checking can resolve supported catalog facts unavailable during compilation. It cannot prove arbitrary hidden routine effects from a reason or broad grant. Unknown reachable effects refuse execution before work, with the missing fact identified. Recovery: deploy a reviewed routine with supported effect metadata, or replace it with supported SQL. Otherwise use an independently reviewed database interface, not a pretend-safe raw bypass. Raw never bypasses class checks, migration restrictions or row policy.

CheckerInfer/calls/method_calls.rs:1223-1272 and CheckerItems.rs:680-717 ground the built-in/library gate difference. TypedText.rs:6-8 wraps raw text without database execution. decisions.title: SQL statement kinds and checked sinks
decisions.situation: A database instruction can read rows, change rows, or change a table. Today a helper can return table-drop text without a checked kind label, so the receiving method cannot reject it by type. Beginners need early mistakes caught, while experts review indirect calls. You decide whether the label travels with the value. We recommend inferred labels and checked methods, plus checked constructors for text arriving later. Hidden work still refuses when neither compile-time nor runtime checking can prove it.
decisions.gist: Should checked database instruction labels travel with returned or stored values?
decisions.lesson: A keeps Query, Mutation or Schema attached to each instruction, even after return or storage. B keeps the current text-and-bindings value. Existing runtime migration permissions remain in both. Unknown text uses a checked runtime constructor; unchecked text keeps visible expert obligations.
decisions.explainer:
Query reads rows; Mutation changes rows; Schema changes tables. A DBScope is a live connection with permissions and rules limiting visible rows. A sink is the method receiving an instruction. A carrier is the instruction plus its checked facts. A dialect is the database grammar. Triggers and stored routines do hidden database work; a UDF is a database function. A CTE is a named inner query and may write.

:: names a value. -[DB.Read]> lists work, not permission. [String:DBValue]? is Val(row) or None; DBError! is a normal database error. The seed is person(7,Ada),(8,Bo), all visible. Reading id8 gets Bo; id9 gives None. Deleting id7 with RETURNING gets Ada, then None. A function returning only SQL.Mutation may erase compile-time result refinement; its sealed Rows/Count field still receives a runtime pre-execution check. Only statically known wrong result kinds promise compile refusal.

Reviewed routine facts feed the single dialect model. Exact proposed entry: {name:"lookup",identity:"sha256:<body-or-library-digest>",effects:["Read"],dependencies:[]}. The approved provider verifies actual identity on the connection. Missing/mismatched facts refuse execution. This is an expert effect contract, not proof of arbitrary code. A reason or extra grant cannot replace facts. Supported late catalog facts can be rechecked; unknown hidden work needs replacement or reviewed supported metadata.

Without AUTHORITY=A, preserve existing Read/Write and migration gates, not DB.Schema. Without GUARD=A, intent_all_rows stays false with no omission-grant rule. Without RAW=A, no new raw gate is imposed. CLASS chooses no schema source. These outcomes are proposed, not exercised.
decisions.story: Mina maintains a person table. She reads Ada, deletes one person, and changes the table through migrations. She wants mistakes caught before deployment without giving every request permission to drop tables.

// cargo sqlx prepare; commit .sqlx; CI: cargo sqlx prepare --check
decisions.detail:
Proposed checked constructors are SQL.Query{literal}, SQL.Mutation{literal}, SQL.Schema{literal}; SQL{literal} infers the label. Explicit head mismatch is a compile diagnostic. Each head has from(text:String)->that exact class TextError! through the same parser. Query.from rejects known reachable writes. The constructor itself does not access the DB or grant permission. Connection-specific unknown dependencies are verified before execution, never guessed safe.

Query is a read-only SELECT. INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, writing CTEs and RETURNING writes are Mutation. Any reachable table-change operation promotes the value to Schema, which only migration accepts. Transaction-control text BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK/SAVEPOINT is rejected everywhere; existing typed scope controls stay the one transaction mechanism. Exactly one statement is fully parsed, not classified by its first word.

The sealed core.db.SQL record has class, dialect_id, template:String, bindings:[DBValue], effect_bits, result_kind:Rows|Count, provider_identity, schema_identity and optional audit:{site,reason,package_digest}. intent_all_rows:Bool defaults false and represents permission to omit WHERE, not permission to affect a provably broad row set. Version1 wire uses these exact fields/tags. Source cannot mutate or forge the record.

All untrusted storage/Web decoding reruns the one checker on text, binding types, class/effects/result shape, intent and current provider/schema identities. Missing/stale/mismatched evidence returns decode/classification error; a Query tag on DROP never becomes a sealed Query merely because its tag is known.

query_one(scope,Query|Mutation|Dynamic)->[String:DBValue]? DBError! and query_all(...)->[[String:DBValue]] DBError! accept only verified Rows statements. Mutation rows require Write, Query rows Read, plus every verified transitive effect. execute(scope,Mutation|Dynamic)->Int DBError! accepts Count or discards returned rows only when explicitly choosing count execution. migrate(scope,name:String,steps:[Schema|Dynamic])->Int DBError! remains the Schema route. Wrong known class/result kind fails compilation; Dynamic reanalysis refuses incompatible sinks before execution. No row-loss restriction is introduced for DELETE...RETURNING.

Example: scope.query_one(SQL.Mutation{"DELETE FROM person WHERE id=7 RETURNING name"}) returns Val({name:"Ada"}) with DB.Write on the two-row seed. A second call returns None. scope.execute of that Mutation returns affected count1 on the original seed. db.decode<T:Decode> still reports [FieldError]!; row_text remains a fallible dynamic extraction. No arbitrary requested Jet result-struct proof is claimed.

CLASS-only mode without SAFETY schema input checks explicit SQL structure and approved builtin routine effects offline. It may demand Query/Mutation from structure, but cannot certify hidden connection-specific work.

Every adapter's prepare/admission boundary must obtain complete reachable routine/trigger/view facts from its engine or enforce an equivalent engine authorizer for the claimed effect set before execution. Missing enforcement returns DBError, never a widened grant. Unknown UDF text needs declared routine facts or Dynamic. No startup schema fingerprint is required in this mode; per-statement runtime effect enforcement still is. Approved existing row-policy syntax restrictions stay in force and are not silently expanded by this parser.

Labels and evidence survive return/storage/coercion/transport. Dynamic text is conservatively reclassified and still cannot DROP through execute. Other SQL gate votes are independent. Current query_one optional cardinality is preserved; this vote approves travelling labels, checked runtime heads and row-returning mutation admission, not a cardinality change.

decisions.title: A distinct permission for database table changes
decisions.situation: Changing a database table is different from reading or editing its rows. Jet already checks reads and row writes separately on scoped calls, but its migration route has no distinct table-change work label. Reviewers cannot ask for that extra label before a helper drops a table. You decide whether table-changing work needs its own Schema label and permission. We recommend that one new check, with ordinary reads and row writes unchanged.
decisions.gist: Should table-changing migrations need a distinct DB.Schema effect and grant?
decisions.lesson: A adds Schema to the existing Write and waiting requirements for migrations. B keeps the existing migration-route checks without that separate label. Read/Write scope ceilings already exist and are not reapproved here. Broad wrapper labels are corrected to those existing meanings in either option.
decisions.explainer:
An effect lists a function's possible work; a held grant is deployment permission to do it. DB.Read reads data; DB.Write changes rows; DB.Schema changes tables. Time.Wait means waiting. A migration is a separately reviewed database-change entry. A DBScope is a connection with held grants and row rules. A ceiling limits permitted work; it does not grant it.

:: names a value. -[DB.Read]> lists read work; DBError! is a normal error. [String:DBValue]? is an optional row: Val(row) or None. Dynamic means the instruction's kind must be checked at execution. Checked Query.from validates late-arriving text before producing a read label. A row policy limits which users' records may be touched, regardless of the Schema grant. These examples are proposed results, not exercised or owner-approved.
decisions.story: Mina maintains a person table. She reads Ada, deletes one person, and changes the table through migrations. She wants mistakes caught before deployment without giving every request permission to drop tables.
decisions.inWild:
sqlx::query!("SELECT name FROM person WHERE id = ?", 7i64);
// cargo sqlx prepare; commit .sqlx; CI: cargo sqlx prepare --check
decisions.detail:
Current checked scoped calls already record DB.Read for query/query_one and DB.Write for execute, and reject hidden writes under a Read ceiling with E0740. Source: CheckerCoreLib/db_methods.rs:9-26,98-117; Syntax/effects_surface.rs:37-39. The broad Core/db/db.jet facade declarations are an implementation-contract reconciliation, not evidence that Read/Write were absent. Query_one currently returns an optional row; no cardinality cutover is approved.

This choice adds only DB.Schema for migration/table-change operations, retaining DB.Write and Time.Wait. A requires all three in the function row and held grants; B keeps existing DB.Write/Time.Wait and its current scoped migration-route authorization. Neither allows DROP through ordinary execute. Ordinary reads/writes and inferred scopes stay as approved, and row extraction should use its existing actual effects rather than acquiring new database work by boilerplate.

When D-SQL-CLASS1=A supplies verified statement effects, each sink requires their full transitive set in addition to the operation minimum. Query rows require DB.Read for Query, DB.Write for row-returning Mutation, and no Schema value is accepted by a non-migration sink. Known hidden read/write effects join the row/grants; reachable Schema promotes the class to Schema. If CLASS=B, A still assigns Schema to the existing typed db.migrate route; runtime migration policy remains its existing enforcement. This explicit combination needs no implied class approval.

Only unchecked unresolved Dynamic needs all DB leaves. Checked class-specific from(text) validates/narrows before use, allowing runtime reads with Read-only permission. Unknown hidden work fails closed before execution; #Unsafe grants neither database permission nor row access. The existing checked read/write labels are never broadened by this new Schema choice.

options.name: One checked rule
options.detail: Add DB.Schema at the migration route and any independently verified reachable table-change effect. Infer ordinary rows; explicit ceilings and grants must include Schema. Correct source wrappers to existing checked Read/Write laws, without reballoting them. A read-only application needs no new permission; a reviewed migration entry adds its one new label.

options.name: Keep the current rule
options.detail: Decline only the extra Schema label. Keep existing Read/Write ceilings, migration authority, waiting and row rules. Reconcile broad source wrappers with their actual checked scoped meanings in both options. The same read and named DROP migration work without the new Schema grant.

comparisons.note: SQLx checks queries, not Jet deployment authority. A checked query alone is never evidence that its caller holds read/write/table-change permissions. https://docs.rs/sqlx/0.8.6/sqlx/macro.query.html

// cargo sqlx prepare; commit .sqlx; CI: cargo sqlx prepare --check

gains: Ordinary Read/Write APIs stay unchanged; only deliberate table-changing entries add Schema.

whyNot.reason: Table-changing helpers have no separate work/grant label beyond existing migration authorization.

recommendation.tradeoff: The checker infers ordinary facts; deliberate exceptions remain visible and permission checked.
