decisions.title: A reminder when a row condition is missing
decisions.situation: A row condition says which database records a write should change. Jet keeps inserted data separate from command text, but a forgotten condition can still erase every person. Beginners and reviewers need a visible reminder before that write runs. You decide whether a missing condition requires explicit all-row intent. We recommend the reminder plus a clear planned-purge helper; it does not prove that a written condition is narrow.
decisions.gist: Should omitting WHERE require explicit intent and a permission to omit that condition?
decisions.lesson: A requires WHERE or an explicit all_rows marker and grant. B keeps writes without that reminder. WHERE true still touches every visible row, so row rules and review remain necessary. The class and permission labels need their separate votes.
decisions.explainer:
WHERE is the condition selecting rows. A predicate is that yes/no condition. Mutation changes rows; Schema changes tables. A migration is a separately reviewed table-change entry. A row policy limits which users' records the scope may touch; it is not disabled by all_rows. Nested writes are writes inside named inner SQL queries.

:: names a value; -[DB.Write]> lists write work, not a grant. DBError! is a normal database error. The examples start with person(7,Ada),(8,Bo), both visible. WHERE id=7 changes one row. A planned purge changes two when called on the original seed; do not run it after the narrow-delete example and expect two.
decisions.story: Mina maintains a person table. She reads Ada, deletes one person, and changes the table through migrations. She wants mistakes caught before deployment without giving every request permission to drop tables.
decisions.inWild:
sqlx::query!("SELECT name FROM person WHERE id = ?", 7i64);
// cargo sqlx prepare; commit .sqlx; CI: cargo sqlx prepare --check
decisions.detail:
D-SQL-CLASS1=A supplies checked labels. DB.Write already exists on scoped calls; the separate DB.Schema choice is not a prerequisite for this row-write reminder. Require a real WHERE clause on ordinary literal UPDATE/DELETE including nested writes. Quoted WHERE/comments do not count. WHERE true is accepted and can affect every visible row. This permission controls omission of a clause, not a provably broad row set or tenant access.

SQL.Mutation.all_rows{literal} sets sealed intent_all_rows=true. The receiving execution checks authority.db.omit_where=true plus existing DB.Write on every call, not just construction. Exact grant: package {authority:{holds:{allow:[DB.Write]},db:{omit_where:true}}}. Default omit_where is false. The teaching diagnostic offers two repairs: add the intended WHERE condition, or use the planned-purge spelling and its omission grant. No raw block is needed for a planned purge.

all_rows.from(text)->SQL.Mutation TextError! performs the same checked runtime analysis. The sole audited SQL.raw(text,omit_where:Bool=false) marks that same sealed bit only when requested; it still requires the same execution grant. Return/storage/Web transport retains the bit; untrusted decode reruns the checker, never accepts a forged field. No ordinary source setter mutates it. Raw construction bypasses neither row policy nor intent/authority checking.

Normal writes add no ceremony. An explicitly planned missing-condition write adds one confirmation and a per-entry grant. TRUNCATE remains Schema/migration-only. Existing row policy still limits users' rows; no syntax can prove an arbitrary condition touches few records. B keeps current review/runtime rules with no missing-clause reminder. CLASS=B leaves this typed spelling blocked rather than silently inventing another class mechanism.

options.name: One checked rule
options.detail: Use the one missing-condition reminder, marked-purge helper and exact grants in detail. Ordinary one-row writes need no marker. The teaching fix makes a planned broad write explicit without unchecked SQL; its grant is set once for that entry. WHERE true remains broad, and this honest limitation is visible in the lesson.

options.name: Keep the current rule
options.detail: Decline only the missing-condition reminder. Keep CLASS=A's travelling labels, existing DB.Write checks and ordinary row policy. A plain Mutation DELETE without WHERE needs no marker or omission grant under this option. It still affects only rows permitted by the receiving scope.

decisions.title: Keep expert work visible without changing safe callers
decisions.situation: An expert memory block lets someone do work the compiler cannot fully prove safe. Today Jet asks for a reason, but a function's work list, called its effect row, does not name Unsafe. Security reviewers still need to find a raw read hidden behind a safe helper. You decide whether expert work stays tracked inside its reviewed boundary, only in a report, or on every caller. We recommend compiler-inferred tracking discharged at the reviewed boundary, with no new annotation on safe callers. The expert reason remains a human promise, not a proof.
decisions.gist: Should reviewed boundaries contain Unsafe tracking, only report it, or pass it to callers?
decisions.lesson: A tracks expert work locally and discharges the label when the reviewed boundary executes it. B keeps the same permission and audit sites without an effect label. C passes the label to every caller. None proves an expert promise true.
decisions.story: Eli reads a live local cell through a raw pointer, an address of memory. His safe helper returns 7 to ordinary app code. Reviewers must still see the reason and operations behind the helper.
decisions.inWild:
fn sample() -> i32 { let cell = 7; let p = &raw const cell; unsafe { *p } }
fn app() -> i32 { sample() }
decisions.detail:
A/B/C preserve lexical permission, ownership, Close/defer cleanup and operation claims. The separate raw-SQL vote applies identically; this vote grants no constructor permission. Exit observation is independent. Owned raw handles may escape under existing ownership/type/caller duties; borrowed pointers never outlive owners. No new pointer taint replaces those rules.

Returning, storing or spawning a callback does not execute its body. Keep its future row, captures and unsafe-call bit. A parent gate cannot discharge delayed work. Pointer-containing structs and trait objects preserve ordinary owner/capture facts. Unknown dynamic targets are never safe evidence.

The compiler infers ordinary rows. Safe wrappers and callers need no new annotations. Proposed jet fix --unsafe-effects previews changes to obsolete explicit Unsafe signatures/effect queries, then makes one clean cutover; no compatibility alias. Expert-marked functions retain the caller-review requirement even if their bodies have gates. Neither removed labels nor reports prove reasons correct.

All options use one version1 audit {root,packages,sites,edges,unknown_edges,policy}. Site identity is package content digest+normalized module path+source byte span+operation kind. Sites include reason, operation claims and package policy. Deduplicate sites, keep distinct call edges, represent recursion as graph cycles. Package metadata carries row, unsafe-call bit, captures and site IDs; missing/incompatible required metadata fails policy checking.

Proposed jet audit --transitive --policy report lists sites and unknown_edges without failing on uncertainty. --policy forbid refuses reachable sites or unknown edges. Local unsafe:.Forbid prevents local gates but permits approved safe dependency calls. Reporting stays the default; strict transitive policy is an expert choice, not routine callback ceremony.

Illustrative output, not exercised: {root:"app",sites:[{id:"digest:module:span:read",reason:"cell remains live",operations:["address","read"]}],edges:[["app","sample"],["sample","digest:module:span:read"]],unknown_edges:[],policy:"report"}. An unresolved callback adds its call identity to unknown_edges. Review a known target/package to resolve it; never invent a target.

Grounding: Effects.jet has no Unsafe. Markers.jet declares reason/obligations. UnsafeObligations.rs validates then strips operation claims. Examples/features/memory/rawptr.jet teaches *cell/p.*. Examples/features/effects/effect_levers.jet uses callback bounds and -[via callback]>.

options.name: Infer tracking; contain local raw work
options.detail:
Add Unsafe to the existing solver. Locally executed raw operations and marked expert calls introduce Unsafe. Their reviewed boundary discharges only that known component; other effects remain. Unknown callback row E stays E. When known Unsafe is added beside E locally, remove only the added component. Never subtract a possibly inherited Unsafe from unknown E.

A #Unsafe-marked function publishes its ordinary body row plus Unsafe and retains its unsafe-call bit: entering that API itself needs caller review. The body's gate discharges implementation work, not its entry obligation. A wrapper calling it inside its own gate discharges the known entry component. An ungated call refuses even when its row permits Unsafe.

Branch/recursive inference joins possible work then discharges locally executed reviewed components. A callback with its own gate can have -[]> and fit a safe bound. Calling a known fn()-[Unsafe]> inside a gate discharges its known Unsafe; returning it as fn()-[]> refuses because it has not run. Other callback effects and unknown via-callback work remain. Reasons still need site metadata, exactly as in B/C.

options.name: Keep lexical checks; report raw routes
options.detail: No Unsafe effect. Keep the identical lexical permission, obligations and ownership rules. Generate the same version1 audit from existing raw-site facts. Safe callback ceilings remain as today; they cannot name Unsafe as a type-level label. No effect vocabulary or open-row tracking migration. This is a real complete design, not weaker pointer permission.

options.name: Pass Unsafe to all callers
options.detail: Add Unsafe but never contain it at a gate. The same program returns7 when sample/app both declare Unsafe. Declaring app -[]> is refused. Correct safe wrappers still require the label; container callers inherit it if their implementation uses raw memory. No hidden standard-library exemption. A gate authorizes only local permission; it is not a row handler here.

comparisons.note: The official book recommends safe abstractions around unsafe implementation and separately documents caller obligations for unsafe fn. This supports A's contained trust boundary; Rust does not supply the proposed Unsafe effect or exit-obligation solver. Read 2026-10-03: https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch20-01-unsafe-rust.html
comparisons.code:
fn sample() -> i32 { let cell = 7; let p = &raw const cell; unsafe { *p } }
fn app() -> i32 { sample() }

It burdens ordinary safe interfaces with implementation details instead of containing locally audited work.

recommendation.tradeoff: Shared site metadata is needed in every option. Inference and a previewing fix remove routine annotation work; human review and honest unknown edges remain.

decisions.title: Exit checks on audited memory blocks
decisions.situation: Jet lets experts fence off a small block of raw memory code, called an audited block and written #Unsafe("reason") followed by braces. Inside it they can take a value’s address and read through it, which ordinary Jet code cannot do. Today there is no way to say that a condition must still be true when that block finishes. An expert who wants that check must copy an assert in front of every exit by hand, and one forgotten early return goes unchecked. Jet already has the right tool for whole functions: #Post(condition, "message"), which is checked in every build unless a module explicitly opts out or a proof removes it. You decide whether audited blocks may carry that same #Post marker. We recommend yes: reuse #Post's spelling, rules and error, and check it whenever the block finishes normally, with no new keyword and no debug/release difference.
decisions.gist: Should audited memory blocks accept the existing #Post exit check that functions already use?
decisions.lesson: An audited block is a fenced-off piece of raw memory code. A tells experts to put the same #Post(condition, "message") marker they already put on functions above that block; Jet checks it every time the block finishes normally. B adds nothing, so experts copy assert lines by hand. C invents a new ensures keyword with its own rules. The check is about the program's own values; it never proves a raw memory read was safe.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A raw address (a pointer) is the memory location of a value. *cell takes cell's address; pointer.* reads the value stored there. An audited block, #Unsafe("reason") { ... }, is the only place raw addresses are allowed, and it must say why it is safe. The assert no_alias / assert valid_ptr, aligned lines are existing typed safety claims that the obligations: .Track setting asks for after each raw operation.

A contract is a promise the compiler checks for you. Today a function can carry #Pre(condition, "message"), checked when it starts, and #Post(condition, "message"), checked before it returns. Both are checked in every build, not only in debug builds. A failure stops the program with error E3005 and the message you wrote. A condition must be pure: it cannot print, write files or change anything.

Two exceptions already exist. A module may explicitly opt out of contract checks. A check that jet prove shows is always true is removed.

Option A lets the same #Post marker sit on the line above an audited block. Example: #Post(cell == 7, "cell must still be 7"). Jet checks it each time the block finishes normally: it falls off its end, or it leaves through return, break or continue.

A return statement is judged the same way the function's own #Post judges it. If the function declares an Option or Result answer, return None and return Err(...) are ordinary answers, so the check runs. If the function's failure is implicit (it declares Int but may still fail), return Err(...) is a failure exit. The check is skipped on failure exits, on a panic (a crash stop) and on cancellation. That first problem stays the reported problem, untouched.

The condition may use any name that is visible where the block starts, such as cell or a function parameter. Reading a value that the block moved away is refused at compile time, exactly as reading it after the block would be. Number values like Int are copied, so they never hit this rule. The block form has no result value, so the name result is refused there.
decisions.story: Eli reads a local number through a raw address inside an audited block. He wants the program to stop loudly if that number is not 7 when the block finishes, on every exit path, in every build, without learning a second contract system.
decisions.detail:
This ballot only decides an optional exit check for audited blocks. D-UNSAFE-EFFECT separately decides how audited blocks interact with effects. The existing per-operation safety claims (D-UNSAFE-OBLIG1) and the existing cleanup are unchanged.

Owned resources are already closed automatically, in reverse order of creation, by the existing cleanup code. That happens on every return and on every unwinding stop (error, panic or failed contract). A hard process abort skips cleanup, as it does today; this ballot does not change that. No new cleanup duty is added. An earlier draft proposed a Closed/Zeroized duty; it is removed because cleanup already guarantees it.

Code facts checked for this ballot. Function #Pre/#Post contracts are decision D-PREPOST1, shown in Examples/features/contracts/pre_post.jet. Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md lines 2833-2838 say they are checked in every build. The same lines make per-module strip an explicit opt-out and a proof a second erasure route.

Examples/features/contracts/carrier_binding.jet lines 10-31 show how a function #Post treats a returned failure today. A function that declares Option or Result checks #Post on both Val/Ok and None/Err. A function with an implicit failure carrier skips #Post on Err. contract_result_mode in crates/jet-codegen/src/TIR/lower/functions.rs picks between them (Direct versus ResultPayload/OptionPayload).

Contracts.jet keeps a declaration's #Post clauses in one contract scope around its body. Runtime failures go through jet_contract_fail in crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core.rs, which reports E3005 and unwinds, so ordinary cleanup still runs. Registry row E3005 says the check runs in every build. The obligations: .Track audited-block form exists in Examples/features/lowlevel/unsafe_obligations.jet. Block-sited markers already exist for user markers, for example marker Checked($sites: [.Block]). Block #Post itself is proposed, not current.

options.name: Reuse #Post on audited blocks
options.technical:
Grammar: one or more #Post(expr, "msg") markers may precede an #Unsafe(reason, ...) block statement. Each expr is type-checked as Bool under the existing D-PREPOST1 condition rules, including the purity rule. Lowering evaluates the clauses in source order on each normal completion edge of the block, before that edge leaves the block scope.

Normal edges are fall-through, break, continue and every return edge that the enclosing function's own #Post would check. A return edge (explicit return or one produced by ?) is classified by the enclosing function's existing TContractResultMode. In Direct mode every returned carrier, including Err and None, is normal. In ResultPayload/OptionPayload mode only the Ok/Val carrier is normal; Err/None is a failure edge, as in contract.return.carrier.test. Failure edges, panic, cancellation and contract-failure unwinding skip the clauses and keep their original completion unchanged.

On a return edge, block clauses (innermost block first) run before the function's #Post clauses. The first false clause calls the existing jet_contract_fail path with clause kind Post; later clauses do not run. The E3005 code, report, test-stop record and proof record are unchanged.

Names resolve in the scope at block entry. A read of a moved or destroyed place is the existing use-after-move error. The name result in a block #Post is refused; extend the E0144 wording to say result only exists in a function #Post. Proof erasure and the per-module strip opt-out are inherited unchanged. No new diagnostic code, build flag, profile fact or cleanup owner is introduced.
options.code:
use core.mem

fn sample(value: Int) -> Int {
    cell :: value                 // a fixed local number
    #Post(cell == 7, "cell must still be 7")
    #Unsafe("cell is live and its pointer stays local", obligations: .Track) {
        pointer :: *cell          // take cell's address
        assert no_alias
        observed :: pointer.*     // read the number through that address
        assert valid_ptr, aligned
        return observed           // #Post is checked on this exit
    }
}

print(sample(7)) // 7
print(sample(8)) // stops in every build: E3005 Post contract failed: cell must still be 7

options.name: No exit check; hand-written asserts
options.detail: Add nothing. An expert who wants the check writes assert(condition, "message") in front of every way out of the block. Today's tools already support this, and it adds nothing new to learn. The cost is that the expert must find and repeat every exit by hand. A later early return added without its assert is silently unchecked.
options.technical: No grammar or lowering change. Existing assert(expr, msg) panics on false. Coverage of exits is the author's responsibility; no compiler check tracks missing exit asserts.
options.code:
use core.mem

fn sample(value: Int) -> Int {
    cell :: value
    #Unsafe("cell is live and its pointer stays local", obligations: .Track) {
        pointer :: *cell
        assert no_alias
        observed :: pointer.*
        assert valid_ptr, aligned
        assert(cell == 7, "cell must still be 7") // repeat before every exit
        return observed
    }
}

print(sample(7)) // 7
print(sample(8)) // stops with the assert message, only because the assert was written here

options.name: New ensures keyword with its own rules
options.detail:
Add a new line, ensures condition, at the start of an audited block. Only a narrow kind of condition is allowed: plain comparisons of numbers, characters and true/false, with no arithmetic, indexing or function calls. Checking builds (dev, debug, ci) run it; ordinary release builds skip it unless a new --check-unsafe-exits flag is given.

A false check stops with a new error E3198, and it is also checked on error and panic exits. That means a false check replaces an existing error as the main reported problem; the original error is kept only as a cause.
options.technical: Adds ensures <total Bool expr> inside #Unsafe, new diagnostics E3198 (false) and E3199 (non-total expression), a new build fact unsafe_exit_checks included in cache identity, and --check-unsafe-exits. Evaluated on every completion that reaches cleanup frames; a false predicate becomes the primary fault with the pending completion attached as a structured cause.
options.code:
use core.mem

fn sample(value: Int) -> Int {
    cell :: value
    #Unsafe("cell is live and its pointer stays local", obligations: .Track) {
        ensures cell == 7
        pointer :: *cell
        assert no_alias
        observed :: pointer.*
        assert valid_ptr, aligned
        return observed
    }
}

print(sample(7)) // 7
print(sample(8)) // dev/debug/ci: stops with E3198; plain release without --check-unsafe-exits: 8

comparisons.note: Rust has no block exit check. Programmers hand-place debug_assert before exits, and those checks vanish from release builds.
comparisons.code:
// https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/macro.debug_assert.html
debug_assert!(cell == 7);

recommendation.why: A reuses the contract Jet already has, so there is one way to state an exit promise. It is checked in every build and never hides an existing error.
gains: One contract marker for functions and audited blocks, with the same rules and error.
Every normal exit is checked automatically, including early returns added later.
Same behavior in every build; real failures stay the reported problem.

whyNot.reason: B works today but makes the expert repeat the assert at every exit, and a forgotten exit is silently unchecked.
C creates a second contract system next to #Post. It behaves differently in release builds, and a false check can push a real error into second place.

recommendation.tradeoff: A's only cost is running the written comparison at each normal finish. That is a few instructions for small numbers, and a proof removes it entirely. Blocks without #Post pay nothing.

The recommendation now reuses #Post, defines returns by the function's own carrier mode, and states the opt-out, proof and hard-abort exceptions.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Before closure, add block #Post parsing, formatting and lowering. Run the 7/8 fixture in dev and release and expect the same E3005 stop. Cover fall-through, return, break and continue exits.

Cover carrier returns. return None in a declared Option function and return Err(...) in a declared Result function both run the block check, so 8 stops with E3005. return Err(...) and ? in an implicit-carrier function skip it, and the caller receives the original Err. Show that panic and cancellation exits keep their original report and skip the check. With both a block #Post and a function #Post, show that the block clause runs first and only the first false clause is reported.

Confirm existing cleanup runs exactly once on the E3005 stop. Refuse result in a block #Post, and refuse reading a moved value. Check that jet prove erases a proved block #Post. Confirm the per-module contract opt-out still applies.

A puts the #Post(condition, "message") marker functions already use above that block, checked every time it finishes normally. B adds nothing; experts hand-copy asserts. C invents a separate ensures keyword. The check covers program values only, never raw memory safety.

losses: The assert must be repeated before every exit.

options.name: New ensures keyword with its own rules

recommendation.why: A reuses the contract Jet already has. It is checked in every build, covers every normal exit and never hides an existing error.
gains: One contract system for functions and blocks.
No build-dependent behavior and no new flag.
Blocks without #Post pay nothing.

whyNot.reason: B makes experts repeat the assert at every exit, and a forgotten exit goes unchecked.
C duplicates #Post, changes behavior in release builds and can demote a real error.

surface.situation: Jet lets experts fence off a small block of raw memory code, called an audited block and written #Unsafe("reason") followed by braces. Inside it they can take a value’s address and read through it, which ordinary Jet code cannot do. Today there is no way to say that a condition must still be true when that block finishes. An expert who wants that check must copy an assert in front of every exit by hand, and one forgotten early return goes unchecked. Jet already has the right tool for whole functions: #Post(condition, "message"), which is checked in every build unless a module explicitly opts out or a proof removes it. You decide whether audited blocks may carry that same #Post marker. We recommend yes: reuse #Post's spelling, rules and error, and check it whenever the block finishes normally, with no new keyword and no debug/release difference.

decisions.title: Names for Jet's entry and exit checks
decisions.situation: A contract is a check written on a function: what must be true when it starts, and what must be true when it finishes. Jet spells them #Pre(cond, "msg") and #Post(cond, "msg"), and the exit checks just ratified for #Unsafe blocks reuse #Post. When ratifying that, the owner said post alone can read as after, an HTTP POST or a social-media post. You are deciding whether to keep Pre and Post or rename the pair everywhere. We recommend #Requires and #Ensures, the words Dafny, Eiffel and .NET use, because each reads as a plain sentence about the condition.
decisions.gist: Should Jet's entry and exit checks keep the names #Pre and #Post, or be renamed?
decisions.lesson: A contract is a written check. The entry check must be true when a function starts; the exit check must be true when it finishes, and can read result. Jet spells them #Pre and #Post, and #Unsafe blocks will reuse the exit check. Post can also mean an HTTP POST or a social-media post. A renames them #Requires and #Ensures. B uses #Expects and #Ensures. C keeps #Pre and #Post.
decisions.explainer:
Plain words first. A function is a named piece of code with inputs and a result. A condition is a true-or-false test, such as n > 0.

A contract is a condition the author writes on the function. The entry check must be true when the function starts; it is about the inputs. The exit check must be true when the function finishes; it may read result, the value being returned.

If a check is false, the program stops with error E3005 and the author's message. Checks run in every build unless a proof shows they always hold.

The word post has many everyday meanings. In programming it also names the HTTP POST request, which Jet's web code uses, as in mux.post("/order", ...).

Jet also has prep, which marks work done while building. #Pre and prep look alike but mean unrelated things.

On 2026-10-04 the owner ratified exit checks above #Unsafe blocks, reusing #Post, and asked about the word. This ballot picks the pair of names; the meaning of the checks does not change.
decisions.story: Sam reads a web handler: #Post(result.status() == 200, "must succeed") sits above fn handle_post(req: HTTPRequest). He first thinks the marker registers an HTTP POST route, not a check on the returned value.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-04. crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Markers.jet:36-38 registers marker Pre and marker Post (function and method sites, repeatable). D-PREPOST1 (Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:2833-2838) defines them: pure conditions, result inside the exit check, checked in every build. A failed entry check quotes the call site; a failed exit check points at the body. D-PREPOST1 was ratified on 2026-07-01 as @pre and @post, and D-CONTRACTCASE1 respelled them #Pre and #Post under the PascalCase law, D-CASING1.

D-UNSAFE-EXIT-OBLIGATIONS=A (ratified 2026-10-04) puts the exit check above #Unsafe blocks; Markers.jet does not accept that site yet. Its ratification comment: "dont love the term post on its own because it might refer to "after" or posting in the networking/http terms or a social media post, etc". That ballot rejected a separate ensures keyword with its own rules. Every option here renames the one existing marker instead.

Uses today: seven .jet files (Examples/features/contracts, tests/fixtures, tests/fuzz, tests/ui). About two dozen more files hold the spelling inside Rust tests (Source/ProveSolver.rs, tests/dev_parts/routine.rs), docs and generated site pages. The runtime stop prints the clause word. crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core.rs:1427-1442 passes "Pre" or "Post" into the E3005 report and the proof record, and proof reports name clauses such as add_fee.Post.

The meaning of the checks does not change in any option: purity, result, E3005, proof erasure, block placement and repeatability stay as ratified. Only the two words change, in one cutover with jet fix and no alias.

options.name: #Requires and #Ensures
options.detail:
The entry check becomes #Requires(cond, "msg") and the exit check becomes #Ensures(cond, "msg"), on functions, methods and #Unsafe blocks. Each reads as a sentence: this function requires n > 0, and ensures result >= 0.

Neither word has an HTTP or timing meaning, and neither looks like prep. Dafny, Eiffel, .NET Code Contracts and Rust's experimental contracts use these words. jet fix renames every use in one cutover.
options.technical: Markers.jet renames Pre and Post to Requires and Ensures with unchanged parameters, sites and repeatable flag. The parser, sema registration, diagnostics wording, formatter, grammars, syntax-decisions.md and Syntax.rs change together. The clause word in E3005 reports and proof records changes on every tier, including the JIT runtime host. The old names become a teaching error with the jet fix rewrite.
options.code:
#Requires(n > 0, "n must be positive")
#Ensures(result >= n, "never shrinks")
fn grow(n: Int) -> Int {
    return n * 2
}
print(grow(4))   // 8
print(grow(0))   // stops: E3005 n must be positive

options.name: #Expects and #Ensures
options.detail:
The entry check becomes #Expects and the exit check #Ensures, the names of the C++ Core Guidelines' Expects and Ensures checks.

Exit checks read as well as in A. Expects is softer: in everyday English an expectation can be disappointed without anything stopping, while the check does stop the program. Jet's tests already use .expect_fail for an expected stop (Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:1665), so expect would carry two meanings.
options.technical: Same cutover as A with Expects in place of Requires.
options.code:
#Expects(n > 0, "n must be positive")
#Ensures(result >= n, "never shrinks")
fn grow(n: Int) -> Int {
    return n * 2
}
print(grow(4))   // 8
print(grow(0))   // stops: E3005 n must be positive

options.name: Keep #Pre and #Post
options.detail:
Nothing changes. Pre and Post are short, and C++26 contracts and Ada 2012 use the same words, so experts from those languages recognise them.

The owner's concern stays: post reads as after, an HTTP POST or a social-media post, beside web code that calls mux.post. #Pre also stays one letter away from prep.
options.technical: No change. The block form keeps the #Post spelling ratified in D-UNSAFE-EXIT-OBLIGATIONS=A.
options.code:
#Pre(n > 0, "n must be positive")
#Post(result >= n, "never shrinks")
fn grow(n: Int) -> Int {
    return n * 2
}
print(grow(4))   // 8
print(grow(0))   // stops: E3005 n must be positive

options.name: #Precondition and #Postcondition
options.detail:
The entry check becomes #Precondition and the exit check #Postcondition. These are the textbook names, and they keep the pre and post that C++26 and Ada experts know. They answer the owner's words, post on its own: the whole word cannot mean an HTTP POST.

The costs: they are the longest names, 12 and 13 letters, on lines that also carry a condition and a message. They read as labels rather than sentences.
options.technical: Same cutover as A with Precondition and Postcondition.
options.code:

#Postcondition(result >= n, "never shrinks")

    return n * 2
}
print(grow(4))   // 8
print(grow(0))   // stops: E3005 n must be positive

recommendation.why: A replaces post, which the owner flagged as ambiguous, with words that read as plain sentences and have no web or timing meaning. It keeps every rule of the checks unchanged.
gains: No clash with HTTP POST, social posts or after.
Reads as a sentence: requires n > 0, ensures result >= n.
No look-alike of prep.

losses.loss: Every existing #Pre and #Post use must change, including docs, tests, diagnostics, E3005 text and proof record names.
losses.mitigation: jet fix renames the seven .jet files in one cutover. The two dozen Rust tests, docs and site pages are edited in the same change, before block exit checks are built.

decisions.title: Checked library rules for targets and database text
decisions.situation: The compiler is the program that turns Jet code into a runnable program for one kind of machine, called the target. Today every target, and the rules for checking SQL database text, live inside the compiler. So supporting a new board such as a RISC-V machine, or a stricter SQLite check, means waiting for a compiler release. You decide whether a library may supply those rules, once an expert names it and records a fingerprint of its exact contents. We recommend allowing both kinds, while ordinary programs keep the built-in rules and change nothing. Library SQL rules can only refuse more. One trust remains and is flagged: an admitted target library must translate the checked program faithfully, and pinning and shared tests reduce that trust without proving it.
decisions.gist: Should checked libraries supply machine targets and stricter SQL rules, or should either remain compiler-owned?
decisions.lesson: A target is the kind of machine a program is built for. A lets an expert add both a target library and a stricter SQL rules library. B allows target libraries only. C keeps both inside the compiler. D allows SQL rules libraries only. The beginner's program and its result are the same under every option; only the expert's package setup differs.
decisions.explainer:
Plain words first. The compiler translates Jet into machine instructions. A target is the machine those instructions are for, for example riscv64-unknown-linux-gnu. A backend is the part that writes the instructions. A dependency is a library your package uses. Its hash is a fingerprint of its exact contents: change one byte and the hash changes. The lock file already records that hash for every dependency.

SQL{"SELECT … {id}"} is checked database text. Jet already checks it while compiling, and every {hole} is sent to the database as a separate value, never pasted into the text. The compiler also decides whether a call reads or writes. For example, query_one counts as a DB.Read and execute counts as a DB.Write. A function marked -[DB.Read]> can therefore never hide a write.

Two kinds of job. Checking jobs decide facts about your program: types, ownership, read or write, hole binding. The compiler keeps all of them under every option. Translating jobs turn the checked program into machine instructions. A target library does a translating job.

A translator can be wrong. The compiler checks a library backend's output for shape, address fixups and declared features. It cannot check that every instruction means what your program said. So admitting a target library trusts its authors, just as using the compiler trusts the authors of the built-in x86-64 backend.

A SQL rules library is different. It only reads your query and the database's table list, called a schema, and may refuse. It never writes code and cannot allow anything the compiler refused.

Admitting a library. An expert names it once in the existing authority.trust block, with the capability it gives and its hash. If a later update changes the library, the build stops and shows both hashes. It names the line to update after review. Unchanged libraries need no action.

The flow in pictures:

```text
your SQL{"…"} ──► compiler checks ──► sqlite_rules (may only refuse) ──► one core.db.SQL value ──► database call
checked program ──► target library backend (trusted translator) ──► shape and feature checks ──► linker
```
decisions.story: Rae maintains a RISC-V board and a stricter SQLite checker. Her users already write SQL{"…"} queries and get Ada back. Rae wants to ship her two rule libraries without waiting for, or forking, the compiler, while her users' code stays exactly the same.
decisions.detail:
This vote decides where these rules may live. It does not set SQL policy or target meanings. D-SQL-SAFETY and its gates own the SQL value, class law and schema map. D-USIZE-TARGET1 owns the selected build facts. Unratified recommendations from those ballots are not treated as approval.

Code facts checked. CheckedText already exists: a library type implements check and encode_hole, and sema runs check at compile time. See Constructors.jet sema_expression_checked_text_literal and Examples/features/text/checked_text/types/module.jet lines 17-69. SQL is one such String-backed type, and SQL{"…"} turns holes into parameters (Examples/features/safety/checked_text_sql.jet). SQL.raw is the existing explicit unchecked escape (Examples/features/io/db.jet), and tainted input to it is refused with E0721.

The compiler's own core.db method table tags query_one with DB.Read and execute with DB.Write (Examples/features/io/db_read_footprint.jet, E0740). That example also shows the database setup used here: db.open_memory, db.policy, with_policy, db.migrate and execute.

The only machine-code backend is x86-64 (Compiler/JetBackend/Source/X64), tested by golden and fixture suites in Compiler/JetBackend/Tests. Package files already have deps, targets and authority blocks (Examples/embedded/battery/package.jet). Dependency hashes are lock-backed and enforced by E1204 (D-BOUND-PROV1).

CoreSourceParts.rs is a private owner and source table with no target predicate. No general target provider exists today; every provider interface here is a proposal.

options.name: Optional checked target and SQL rules libraries
options.detail:
Ordinary packages change nothing and use the compiler's built-in rules. Existing CheckedText types, such as a user's Pattern or Query type, keep their check and encode_hole code unchanged. An expert may admit a target library, a SQL rules library, or both. Each is named with its capability and hash in the existing authority.trust block. The build uses that library only when its rules are needed.

SQL rules. At most one SQL rules library per package. It checks every SQL{"…"} written in that package, after the built-in SQL check. Its admission names one schema file, such as schema.sql, holding the CREATE TABLE lines. The library may only refuse, for example a misspelled column.

It cannot mark SQL as read-only when the compiler sees a write, and it cannot paste a hole into the text. SQL.raw, the existing unchecked escape, is unchanged and not run through the rules.

Targets. A target library's output is checked for shape and for every feature it claims to support. Unsupported features stop the build before any machine code is written. Built-in targets never use a library backend.

Updates are safe by default: a changed library hash stops the build until the expert reviews it and copies the new hash. The proposed message reads: rv changed since you admitted it. It shows the old and new hash, then says: review the update, then set authority.trust.compiler.rv.hash to the new hash.

The one remaining trust. A target library is trusted to translate the checked program faithfully, as the built-in backend is. Admission requires it to pass the same backend fixture suites the built-in backend runs. That is evidence, not proof.
options.technical:
Admission: authority.trust.compiler maps a direct dependency to {gives: [.Target | .SQLRules], hash} plus, for .SQLRules, schema: a package-relative path. The hash must equal the lock's integrity hash, and a mismatch is a new registered teaching refusal. Transitive registrations, overlapping target IDs and a second .SQLRules entry are refused with one refusal naming both entries. A workspace policy may narrow admissions, never widen them. No provider gains application DB, FS, network or FFI authority.

Target discovery reads one data-only manifest before parsing target code. It lists the target ID, OS, architecture, ABI, pointer size, endianness and supported features. Only the selected target's files are loaded. The descriptor must match the manifest exactly.

TargetBackend.emit(CheckedMIRImage, TargetDescription, BackendOptions, CompilerBudget) -[]> NativeObject BackendFailure! is pure, bounded compile-time Jet. NativeObject holds sections, symbols, relocations, unwind and debug records. The compiler validates shape, bounds and relocation kinds. Any feature outside the manifest's declared set, such as TLS, atomics, varargs or an unwinding mode, is refused before emit.

The existing linker stays the link owner. Admission records a passing run of the shared backend fixture suites. Semantic preservation of CheckedMIRImage is trusted to the admitted provider; validation does not establish it.

SQL rules: the provider exports one impl SQLRules { fn analyze(query: SQLText, schema: SchemaFacts) -[]> SQLRuleError! }. It is not a CheckedText implementation and creates no new text type. Existing CheckedText check/encode_hole contracts and implementations are unchanged; no migration.

Selection is fixed per package: the package's single .SQLRules admission applies to SQL{"…"} literals in that package's own modules. Each dependency's literals use that dependency's own admission, or none. analyze runs after core SQL's own CheckedText check. SQLText is the literal with holes as parameter markers; SchemaFacts is the parsed schema file.

analyze may return Ok() or a refusal with message and span. Sema still computes hole binding, the read or write class from the core.db method table, effects and captures. Rules run only at compile time. The provider hash and schema-file hash enter the build facts and cache key, so either change rechecks every literal. SQL.raw is unchanged.

If D-SQL-SAFETY ratifies a source schema map, that map replaces the schema: file as the single schema input.

options.name: Target libraries; compiler SQL rules
options.detail: Target libraries work exactly as in A, with the same hash admission, feature checks and translation trust. SQL checking stays inside the compiler. A stricter SQLite rule, such as checking column names against the schema, waits for a compiler release. Until then a misspelled column is found only when the query runs. Existing CheckedText types keep working unchanged.
options.technical: Target admission, manifest discovery, TargetBackend.emit, refusal rules and the trusted-translation boundary are identical to A. No .SQLRules capability exists; core.db.SQL checking remains compiler-owned.

options.name: Compiler-owned target and SQL rules
options.detail: Nothing new is admitted. RISC-V support and stricter SQLite checks arrive only inside a reviewed compiler release. Until that release ships, the RISC-V build is refused as an unknown target, and a misspelled column is found only when the query runs. Existing CheckedText types keep working unchanged.
options.technical: No provider registration. Target support and core.db.SQL checking stay compiler-owned. Existing CheckedText libraries and the Jet backend sources are unchanged.

options.name: Compiler targets; SQL rules libraries
options.detail: SQL rules libraries work exactly as in A: one per package, with a named schema file, and they may only refuse more. Targets stay inside the compiler, so RISC-V waits for a compiler release. No outside library ever writes machine code, so there is no extra translation trust. Existing CheckedText types keep working unchanged.
options.technical: SQLRules admission, schema input, per-package selection and compile-time-only rules are identical to A. No .Target capability exists; target support stays compiler-owned.

comparisons.note: Mojo's documentation says standard types such as Int and String are ordinary library types, checked by a restricted compile-time evaluator. That is precedent for library rules. It does not show that Mojo adds whole new machine targets from libraries. Read 2026-10-03: https://mojolang.org/docs/manual/types/ and https://mojolang.org/docs/manual/metaprogramming/comptime-evaluation/

recommendation.why: A lets experts add targets and stricter SQL checks without a compiler release. Beginners change nothing, and the compiler keeps every checking decision. The one added trust, a library backend translating faithfully, applies only to experts who admit one.
gains: New boards and stricter SQL checks ship as ordinary, fingerprinted libraries.
SQL rules can only refuse more; read/write and hole binding stay compiler-owned.
Existing CheckedText types and ordinary packages change nothing.
A changed library stops the build until someone reviews it.

losses.loss: An admitted target library is trusted to translate the checked program faithfully. A wrong library backend could skip a check or compute a wrong answer, and no compile-time check catches that.
losses.mitigation: No checker can prove a new machine-code writer correct, so this trust is physical and flagged in the summary. Only an expert who admits a library for a board the compiler lacks takes it; built-in targets never use one. The reviewed version is pinned by hash, output shape and features are checked, and the shared backend fixture suites must pass.

whyNot.reason: B opens targets but keeps stricter SQL checks waiting for compiler releases, although SQL rules libraries can only refuse more.
C makes every new board and every SQL rule wait for a compiler release, even when nothing about the language changes.
D avoids trusting outside translators, but every new board waits for a compiler release. A limits that trust to experts who opt in for a board the compiler lacks.

recommendation.tradeoff: A adds one trust that the compiler cannot check: an admitted target library must translate faithfully. Hash pinning, review on change, shape and feature checks and the shared fixture suites reduce it but do not prove it. Only experts who admit a target library take it on.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: BallotRevBeginner3. Skill: rli5. The reader could not run any example and stumbled on compiler jargon, the renewal step and hidden residual trust. The revision defines every term, shows one complete package setup, shows the hash refusal, and states the shared machine-code limit.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: undisclosed. Adversarial model family: undisclosed. Fresh agent: BallotRevAdversary3, then BallotRevFinalE. Reviews found unrenewable admission, unspecified SQL checker selection, a hidden CheckedText migration and backend trust presented as compiler safety. The revision pins hashes, adds a refuse-only per-package SQLRules capability with a schema file, keeps CheckedText unchanged and flags backend translation trust.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Run the same people program under all four options with the exact package blocks. Build with the riscv64 command, run it on the board and expect Ada. Mark build results and run output separately. Change sqlite_rules to a new version and expect the hash refusal, then accept it by copying the new hash.

With sqlite_rules admitted, expect the nmae typo refused at build time citing schema.sql; without it, expect a run-time database error. Refuse a second .SQLRules entry. Show a dependency's literals use only that dependency's admission. Change schema.sql and expect every literal rechecked. Show SQL.raw is not run through the rules.

Show that a lying SQL rule cannot change the read or write class or paste a hole. A lying backend object must be refused for shape or for an undeclared feature. Prove that unselected target files are never parsed. Keep all existing backend, CheckedText and DB tests unchanged.

decisions.title: One meaning for text formatting
decisions.situation: Formatting turns values into text for people to read. Two implementations disagree on percentages, scientific numbers, records, sizes, rounding and padding, so the same request can print different text. That makes examples and saved output unreliable. The owner chose one set of outputs, combining useful behavior from both rather than selecting either implementation unchanged.
decisions.gist: Should every formatting call use the owner's chosen outputs instead of either conflicting implementation's full set?
decisions.lesson: Scientific notation writes a value as a short number times a power of ten. SI size units use powers of 1,000; binary units use 1,024. Padding adds a repeated fill to reach a width. Half away from zero sends an exact halfway value to the larger magnitude, including negative values.
decisions.explainer: Beginner path: call fmt and get the examples below on every execution path. Expert path: rely on exact rounding, exponent normalization, size units and fill behavior rather than choosing a runtime. Shared work: keep one source-owned implementation and migrate adapters, output expectations and documentation together. Unchanged functions stay unchanged. The row choices are independent; B and C show the two previous sets for comparison.
decisions.story: Sam saves a report and wants percentages, sizes and rounded numbers to look the same however the program runs.
decisions.detail:
Owner chat on 2026-10-05 selected the per-row outputs for card #4588. This ballot records those choices, not a new request to select an implementation wholesale. Evidence: $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/Idiom-Runtime/HANDOFF.md:56-74 compares Core/text/fmt.jet and the runtime port of Fmt.rs. That comparison is explicitly source reading, not execution. Its :41-44 describes adapter collapse and the then-live Rust route. $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/Idiom-Runtime2/HANDOFF.md:29-33 identifies the remaining adapter sweep.

The owner's result is mixed: grouped percent, short normalized sci, SI bytes and padding match the described Rust behavior. Decimal half-away rounding and removal of negative zero match the described Jet behavior. Pretty records combine Rust's space before the brace with Jet's commas; empty collections remain on one line. D-FMT-BYTES1 already ratified decimal fmt.bytes with a separate fmt.bytes_binary. The size row confirms that law; it does not reopen it or retire bytes_binary.

The prior pretty behaviors also differed on trailing text and empty collection forms. The owner did not choose a new trailing-text rule here. Those behaviors are not silently decided by this record. This ballot author exercised no formatting programs.

options.name: Use the chosen rows
options.detail: Use grouped percentages, short normalized exponents, spaced records with commas, one-line empties and SI sizes. Round decimal halfway values away from zero and suppress negative zero. Empty fill means space; centered fill restarts on each side.
options.technical:
One public meaning behind core.text.fmt, owned by Core/text/fmt.jet. Exact rows: percent(12345.6,0) = "1,234,560%". sci(1234.0,2) = "1.23e3"; sci(0.00123,2) = "1.23e-3"; sci(0.0,2) = "0.00e0". Normalize again after rounding: sci(9.999,2) = "1.00e1". Exponents have no redundant plus sign or leading zeroes.

pretty("P{x: 1, y: 2}") = "P {\n  x: 1,\n  y: 2\n}". Empty collections stay on one line, including "[]". bytes(1536) = "1.5 KB"; bytes(1000) = "1 KB"; SI base is 1000, not 1024. Preserve the separately ratified bytes_binary function.

decimal(0.125,2) = "0.13"; decimal(-0.125,2) = "-0.13"; decimal(-0.0001,2) = "0.00". Decimal rounding is half away from zero, not ties to even. The decimal/grouped rounding row uses that rule and suppresses negative zero. pad("ab",5,"") = "ab   ". pad_center("x",4,"ab") = "axab": the shorter left side gets one character and each side starts at a. All tiers use this same contract. No parallel legacy implementation remains.
options.code:
fmt.percent(12345.6, 0) // 1,234,560%
fmt.sci(9.999, 2) // 1.00e1
fmt.pretty("P{{x: 1, y: 2}}") // P {\n  x: 1,\n  y: 2\n}
fmt.bytes(1536) // 1.5 KB
fmt.decimal(0.125, 2) // 0.13
fmt.pad_center("x", 4, "ab") // axab

options.name: Keep the previous Jet rows
options.detail: Keep ungrouped percent, padded exponents, records without an opening space, expanded empties and truncated binary sizes. Decimal rounding already has the chosen behavior. Empty fill does nothing, and centered fill uses one continuous pattern.
options.technical:
Recorded source comparison, not a live-output claim. percent(12345.6,0) = "1234560%". sci(1234.0,2) = "1.23e+03"; sci(0.00123,2) = "1.23e-03"; sci(0.0,2) = "0.00e+00". sci(9.999,2) = "10.00e+00", without post-rounding normalization.

pretty record = "P{\n  x: 1,\n  y: 2\n}"; pretty("[]") = "[\n]". bytes(1536) = "1 KiB"; bytes(1000) = "1000 B"; bytes(25000000) = "23 MiB". This bytes alternative was offered but conflicts with the already-ratified decimal bytes contract. It is not a lawful reopening of that row.

decimal(0.125,2) = "0.13" and decimal(-0.0001,2) = "0.00". pad("ab",5,"") = "ab"; pad_center("x",4,"ab") = "axba". The independent rows explain what the owner rejected without implying that every B row lost.

decisions.title: How a chain of ?? fallbacks groups
decisions.situation: The ?? operator gives a fallback when a call fails, as in read() ?? "". A common job chains them: try the main service, then a backup, then a fixed answer. Today primary() ?? backup() ?? "none" is rejected, and the backup's failure escapes to the caller, because the chain groups from the left. You decide how a chain groups; we recommend grouping from the right, as C#, Swift, JavaScript and Kotlin do.
decisions.gist: Should a ?? b ?? c mean a ?? (b ?? c), so a chain of fallbacks ends at the last one?
decisions.lesson: ?? takes the value on its left, or, if that failed or is empty, the value on its right. In a chain, the grouping decides which fallback guards which. A groups from the right, so each fallback is tried in turn and the last one ends the chain. B keeps today's left grouping and teaches parentheses. C requires parentheses in every chain.
decisions.explainer:
Jet's ?? is the fallback operator. On its left is an optional or fallible value. If that value is present it is the result; otherwise the right side runs. The result must be the plain success type.

When several ?? appear in a row, the compiler must group them. Today it groups from the left: (primary ?? backup) ?? "unknown". The inner part produces a plain value while backup's own failure travels up to the caller. The outer ?? then sees a plain value and reports E0405, because ?? only works on a value that can fail.

Option A groups from the right: primary ?? (backup ?? "unknown"). The backup is guarded by the final text, and the main call is guarded by that result. This is how C#, Swift, JavaScript and Kotlin's ?: read the same chain. Parentheses still work when someone wants another grouping.

Option B keeps left grouping and turns the confusing report into a teaching error that shows the parentheses. Option C makes any chain of two or more ?? an error until it is parenthesized.
decisions.story: Kofi fetches the weather from a main service, falls back to a backup, and finally to the text "unknown". He writes primary(city) ?? backup(city) ?? "unknown". Jet rejects the last ?? and reports that his function can now fail, although every path has a fallback.
decisions.detail:
Current state: spec.md:826-830 defines ?? as the fallback for an optional or fallible value with precedence looser than && and ||, and E0405 when it does not produce the enclosing success type. Associativity is not written.

Probe (APICompLearn e09_fallback_fixed.jet, dev-05ea86f65): primary(c, p) ?? backup(c, b) ?? "both timed out" gives E0405 "?? only works on a fallible value, not String", plus E2402 at the callers. With explicit parentheses, f02_fallback_paren.jet prints the expected fallbacks.

Source: 10 Python anti-patterns (ts38mSIUPSg), where nested try/except fallback chains (primary API, then backup API) hide which failure is which (claim learning-compilers:AP1).

Proven approaches. C#'s ??, Swift's ??, PHP's ??, JavaScript's ?? and Kotlin's ?: are all right-associative, so a ?? b ?? c tries a, then b, then c. Swift declares its NilCoalescingPrecedence group with right associativity for exactly this reason.

Left grouping survives only where the operator returns the same loosely typed value on both sides, as Perl's // does. In a typed fallback that unwraps an optional or a failure, left grouping only checks when the middle operand cannot fail.

options.name: Group from the right
options.detail: a ?? b ?? c means a ?? (b ?? c). Each fallback is tried in turn, and the last one ends the chain. Explicit parentheses still override.
options.technical: The parser gives ?? right associativity at its existing precedence. Sema already handles each ?? on its own; the right operand of the outer ?? becomes the inner ?? expression. The rule is shared by every tier and the formatter.
options.code:
text :: primary(city) ?? backup(city) ?? "unknown"
// tries primary, then backup, then "unknown"

options.name: Keep left grouping, teach parentheses
options.detail: a ?? b ?? c keeps meaning (a ?? b) ?? c. When that fails E0405, a teaching error shows the right-grouped parentheses.
options.technical: Diagnostic change only. Every fallback chain needs parentheses.
options.code:
text :: primary(city) ?? (backup(city) ?? "unknown")
// without the parentheses: teaching error

options.name: Require parentheses in chains
options.detail: Two or more ?? in one expression are an error until parenthesized, either way. This removes any question of grouping by forcing it to be written.
options.technical: The parser treats ?? as non-associative, as Jet already does for a mixed && and || chain (E0082).
options.code:
text :: primary(city) ?? (backup(city) ?? "unknown")
// primary ?? backup ?? "x": error, add parentheses

comparisons.note: ?? is right-associative.
comparisons.code: string s = a ?? b ?? "x";   // a ?? (b ?? "x")

comparisons.note: ?? is declared right-associative so chains read left to right.
comparisons.code:
// precedencegroup NilCoalescingPrecedence { associativity: right }
let s = a ?? b ?? "x"

comparisons.note: The elvis operator ?: is right-associative.
comparisons.code: val s = a ?: b ?: "x"

recommendation.why: A makes the obvious chain mean what every reader expects and what C#, Swift, JavaScript and Kotlin already do. Left grouping only type-checks when the middle step cannot fail, so it never helps a real fallback chain.
recommendation.tradeoff: None in practice: no chain that checks today changes meaning.

Matches four mainstream languages.
