decisions.title: Which call marks are still required when the signature already says what happens
decisions.situation: Today a Jet call repeats what the called function's signature already says. If bump edits its parameter, the caller must write bump(&score). If archive takes its parameter, the caller must write archive(^title), even when title is never used again. The compiler already knows both facts, because leaving a mark out is an error whose fix names the exact mark. The ratified copy decision already says a last use moves with no mark, but calls have not caught up. This vote decides which call marks stay required, which the compiler supplies, and whether a call may add a copy. We recommend keeping & wherever a call edits a value, while a plain value moves at its last use without ^.
decisions.gist: Must a call still write & and ^ when the called function's signature already says the value is edited or taken?
decisions.lesson: A parameter written &T may change the caller's value, and a parameter written ^T takes the value away for good. Today the caller repeats that mark at the call: bump(&score) and archive(^title). The compiler can always work the marks out from the signature, so they are there for people reading the code. Writing ~x asks for an independent copy, and no option here changes that meaning.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. x := 1 makes a name you may change later, and x :: 1 makes one you may not. A receiver is the value before the dot, as in &tags.push("hot"). A name's last use is the last place it appears on every path through the function. A name used again on a later loop pass, or captured by a lambda, has no last use there.

Some values run cleanup when they are released, such as a file that closes or a lock that unlocks. Their types implement Close or #MustFinish, or hold such a value in a field. This ballot calls them values with cleanup.

Beginner path: you write & when a call changes one of your values, and the error tells you where if you forget. You never write ^ for a plain value you are finished with; Jet hands it over at its last use. You still write ^ to hand over a value with cleanup, so the moment it closes is in the text. You write ~ only when you want to keep using a value after giving it away.

Expert path: every edit is visible at the call in any viewer, including a code review page with no editor. A written & is always true, because & on a parameter that only reads becomes an error. Gray editor hints show where a move was inferred. In generic code, a take of a value of type T always writes ^, since T may have cleanup.

Shared by every option: the compiler checks exclusive edits and moves exactly as today. Marks never change the generated code, except that option D adds shared storage and copies.
decisions.story: Mia writes bump(score) and gets an error telling her to write bump(&score). She asks why Jet makes her type what it already knows. Her teammate Ravi reviews her pull request in a browser, with no editor and no hints. He wants to see which calls change his values and which calls take them away.
decisions.detail:
Owner question, 2026-10-06: are the call marks &x, ^x and ~x technically needed, since the signature says which arguments are edited and the compiler can infer last-use moves? Short answer: no call mark is needed by the compiler. Each missing mark is already an error whose fix names the exact mark, which shows the compiler knows. The marks are a promise to readers, and the vote is about which promises are worth their keystrokes.

Probes on the dev candidate dev-595e0dca3, jet check and jet run, 2026-10-06. bump(score) to an &Int parameter is E0202 with the fix &score. p.heal(2) on an &self method is E0224 with the fix &p. archive(title) to a ^String parameter is E0209 even when title is never used again. grow_both(&xs, &xs) is E0204. bump(&score) on a score made with :: is E0111.

Four more probes show where today's marks can mislead. show(&score) to a plain read parameter is accepted with no warning, so a written & can overstate. A lambda keep :: () -> archive(^title) called twice is accepted and prints vault twice, so ^ inside a lambda does not end title. pair(t, ^t), reading and taking one name in one call, passes sema and then crashes the compiler with an internal error.

The fourth probe is reviewer ReadA3's: a Session struct holding a Lock field, passed as hand_off(^held), never prints release db. The nested cleanup is lost today. The first two gaps are fixed inside option A, because A's promise to readers depends on them. The last two are defects for the ownership card under every option.

Ratified law. D-MEM1=A (2026-07-03) chose bare for read, & for write and ^ for take, both mirrored at call sites so that mutation and moves are always visible. D-CAP-RECEIVER1=D (2026-09-27) put the same marks on receivers, as in &buf.append("!"). D-COPY-DEFAULT1=A (2026-09-29) then said an unmarked last use moves in every position. The owner's comment on it: the compiler chooses if unmarked, and the programmer can write marks for exact control.

What D-COPY-DEFAULT1 leaves open at calls. It says an unmarked use that is not the last shares the value, which today means a copy at the share site. It also says a receiver take on a local read again later still needs ^. For an argument passed to a take parameter, the two sentences point different ways. Today's compiler follows neither: it demands ^ even at a last use (E0209).

So every option except B finishes the last-use half of D-COPY-DEFAULT1 for arguments. B narrows that decision back to today's behavior. A and C settle the open sentence the way the receiver rule does. A take of a name that is read again stays an error until the call writes ~ or the code is reordered. D settles it the other way, with an implicit share.

Why a call should differ from a binding. In ys := xs the new name ys shows that a second value now exists. In archive(note) nothing on the line shows that archive keeps its own copy of note; only the callee's signature says so. That is the reason A keeps a written ~ at calls while bindings share silently.

Drop timing. A value with cleanup is closed when its owner's scope ends. Probe: with hand_off(lock: Lock) the program prints got db, after call, release db. With hand_off(lock: ^Lock) and hand_off(^held) it prints got db, release db, after call. If a callee changes from read to take and the move is inferred, the release moves earlier with no edit at the call.

For a lock guard, that silently shortens the protected region. So A, C and E keep ^ required when a value with cleanup goes to a take parameter. That includes a struct that holds one in a field, and any value of a type parameter T, because a generic body cannot know. Plain memory has no visible cleanup, so moving its release changes cost only, never output. Mojo makes the opposite choice: values are destroyed right after their last use.

Refactor safety. If a callee changes a parameter from read to &, today every caller fails to build until it writes &. Under A and B that stays true. Under C and D, a caller holding a := name compiles unchanged and its value starts changing; a :: name still fails with E0111. Under E, the build fails only in packages that deny the lint.

The ^ side. If a callee changes from read to take, a caller passing a plain value at its last use compiles unchanged under A and now moves it. Nothing observable changes, because nobody reads the value again. A caller passing a value with cleanup fails to build until it writes ^, so the earlier release is always visible in the diff.

Performance. Marks never reach generated code. A, B, C and E lower every call the same way: plain pointers for edits and bitwise moves for takes, with no counter. Only D changes cost. A value reused after a take is shared, which today means a full copy at the call, and later a counter with a copy on first write. jet audit copies and !Mem.Copy can find or forbid those copies.

Edge cases, part one. Aliasing: grow_both(xs, xs) stays E0204 in every option, because both parameters are edits; without marks the error must name which parameters edit. One name in two slots of the same call, as in pair(t, t), has no last use in that call. Loops: a name declared outside a loop is never a last use inside it, which is E0121 today. Branches: a last use in one arm moves on that path only.

Edge cases, part two. Closures: a captured name is never a last use inside a lambda. Under A, a ^ on a capture moves it into the lambda, and calling that lambda a second time is an error. Fields: a take of a field, such as archive(^doc.title), keeps ^, as D-COPY-DEFAULT1 already says. Function values carry access in their type, so calls through them infer the same way.

Edge cases, part three. Method receivers: A and B keep &tags.push("hot"), while C, D and E allow tags.push("hot"). A window outside a call, such as edit :: &values[2..3], has no signature to read, so its & stays required in every option.

Opt-in spelling. D-CALLPOLICY2=C limits #Policy to call wrappers, so option E uses the lint wall from D-LINTPOLICY1=A instead. The precedent is auto_derive, which a package denies with policy: { lints: { deny: [auto_derive] } } in package.jet. The copy spelling follows the open D-COPY-WORD1, and every option works with ~x or x.copy().

Peers. Rust, Swift, C# and Hylo all require a mark when an argument is edited. Rust and Hylo move or consume at a last use with no mark, and a later use is an error, which is option A's rule. Swift does that only for noncopyable types; a copyable value that is used later is copied, like option D. Mojo and C++ copy unless the caller writes title^ or std::move(title).

On receivers, Rust, Swift, Mojo and C++ never mark an edit, while Hylo and Jet do. Hylo is the closest match to option A as a whole.

options.name: Edits stay marked; a last use moves without ^
options.detail:
A call that edits a named value still writes &, on arguments and on receivers alike. A plain named value passed to a ^ parameter at its last use moves with no mark, as bindings and receiver calls already do. A name that is read again still needs ~ for a copy, or a reorder, so a call never adds a copy by itself.

Writing ^ stays legal and is checked: a later use is an error. A value with cleanup keeps a required ^ at take parameters, so the moment it closes is always written. So does a field take, and a take of a value whose type is a type parameter.

Two fixes make the marks honest. A & on a parameter that only reads becomes an error, with a fix that removes it. A ^ on a captured name inside a lambda moves it into the lambda, and a second call of that lambda is an error.
options.technical:
This amends D-COPY-DEFAULT1=A at call arguments. The last-use move applies there; the implicit share does not, matching that decision's receiver rule. Sema already computes last use for bindings and taking receivers. E0209 narrows to names read again, and its fix offers ~x or a reorder.

A name in two argument slots of one call has no last use in that call. Values with cleanup are types that implement Close or #MustFinish or hold one by value; a type parameter counts as one. Lowering is unchanged: a move is a bitwise move with no counter.

jet fmt neither adds nor removes marks, and editor hints show inferred moves. E0202, E0224, E0204 and E0111 are unchanged. The spec section Ownership and borrowing, the E0209 text, and one new error for an & that does not edit change.

options.name: Keep every call mark, as today
options.detail: Every edit writes & and every hand-over of a named value writes ^, at its last use too. Leaving one out is an error with a one-key fix. A reader sees every change and every move in any viewer. This narrows D-COPY-DEFAULT1: arguments stay out of step with bindings and receiver calls, which already move at a last use with no mark.
options.technical: No change to the compiler. D-COPY-DEFAULT1=A's every-position wording is narrowed in the spec to bindings and receivers, matching what E0209 enforces today. A value with cleanup passed without ^ stays E0201, the error for a value that cannot be copied.

options.name: Edit and move marks become optional
options.detail: A call may leave out & and ^; the compiler reads the signature and edits or moves anyway. A written ^ is still checked, so it can never hide a later use. ~ stays required for a copy at a call, so a call still never adds one by itself. Editors show the inferred marks as gray hints, and jet fmt --explicit-marks writes them into the file. Values with cleanup keep a required ^, as in A.
options.technical: E0202 and E0224 retire as errors; sema records an inferred edit fact per call for hover, hints and the formatter flag, which mirrors the existing --explicit-copies flag. E0209 narrows as in A. E0204 and E0111 stay. Lowering is unchanged.

options.name: The compiler also chooses copies at calls
options.detail: No call needs a mark at all. A value used again after being passed to a ^ parameter is shared, as D-COPY-DEFAULT1's share rule reads for bindings. Today a share is a full copy at the call; later it becomes a counter and a copy on first write. A read argument that overlaps an edited argument gets its own copy. Two edits of one place stay an error, because no copy can make that mean anything.
options.technical: As C, plus E0209 retires: a name read again after a take lowers to the D-COPY-DEFAULT1 share. jet audit copies lists every added copy, and !Mem.Copy forbids them in a function. Values with cleanup cannot be copied, so they move at the last use with no mark and keep E0121 on a later use. ~ is never required at a call.

options.name: Optional marks, plus a lint a package can make required
options.detail: The same as C for most code. A new lint, unmarked_access, covers every call that edits or moves a named value without its mark. It is quiet unless a package denies it, like auto_derive, because it would otherwise fire on most calls. A package that wants today's rule denies it in package.jet. Then an unmarked edit or move fails the build, with a fix that adds the mark. Jet's own Core and compiler packages would opt in; the examples would not.
options.technical: As C, plus one stable lint name under D-LINTPOLICY1=A, with a Safe fix that inserts & or ^. No #Policy key is added, because D-CALLPOLICY2=C limits #Policy to call wrappers. jet inspect dossier records the deny like any other lint wall.

comparisons.note: Edited arguments need &mut, but method receivers borrow mutably with no mark. A named value moves with no mark, and a later use is error E0382. Copies are spelled .clone().

Hylo writes & wherever a value changes: inout arguments, += and mutating receivers. A sink parameter consumes its argument with no mark, and a later use is an error suggesting v.copy(). That is option A.
comparisons.code:
bump(&score)
&tags.append("hot")
let saved = archive(title)   // sink: consumed, no mark

comparisons.note: inout arguments need &, and mutating methods are unmarked. A consuming parameter (SE-0377) takes a value with no mark; if a copyable value is used later, Swift copies it, like option D. consume x (SE-0366) ends a name on purpose.
comparisons.code:
bump(&score)
tags.append("hot")
let saved = archive(title)   // copies if title is used later

comparisons.note: Every edited argument must say ref, and every out argument must say out, with no exception. Optional marks exist only on read-only parameters: in may be left out, and C# 12 warns when a ref readonly argument has no mark.
comparisons.code:
Bump(ref score);   // required
Show(in big);      // optional
Show(big);         // also fine

comparisons.note: mut arguments carry no call mark. A var parameter gets a copy unless the caller writes title^, and a type that cannot be copied is an error, which is close to option D. Values are destroyed as soon as possible after their last use, not at scope end.
comparisons.code:
bump(score)                 # mut parameter: no mark
var saved = archive(title^) # transfer; archive(title) copies

comparisons.note: A T& parameter is invisible at the call, so any call may change a variable. Moving a named value needs std::move, and copies are implicit. Google's C++ style guide long asked for pointer output parameters so the change showed as f(&x).
comparisons.code:
bump(score);                          // int& edit, unmarked
auto saved = archive(std::move(title));

recommendation.why: The compiler needs no call mark; the marks exist for readers. Readers most need to see which calls change a value, and Rust, Swift, C# and Hylo all keep that mark on arguments. A move at a last use is already unmarked in Jet bindings and receivers, so arguments should match.
gains: Every changed value stays visible at the call, in any viewer, and a written & is always true.
Arguments move at a last use like bindings and receivers.
No new copies, counters, lints or settings; generated code is unchanged.

losses.loss: Edits still need & on arguments and on receivers.
losses.mitigation: Forgetting it is an error whose fix writes the mark, and jet fix applies it. The receiver mark was ratified separately in D-CAP-RECEIVER1, and Hylo marks receivers too.

losses.loss: A move at a last use is not visible in plain text.
losses.mitigation: A later use is still an error, so an inferred move never changes output. Values with cleanup, field takes and generic takes keep a written ^, and hover shows every inferred move.

losses.loss: A name read again after a take needs ~, unlike a binding, which shares silently.
losses.mitigation: At a call nothing else shows that a second value exists, so the ~ is the only sign. The error offers ~ or a reorder.

whyNot.reason: B keeps a ^ at last uses that tells the reader nothing new, and narrows D-COPY-DEFAULT1 so arguments differ from bindings and receivers.
C hides edits from anyone reading without an editor, and a callee that starts editing silently changes callers' values.
D lets a call keep a silent copy of a value the caller still uses. At a binding the new name shows the copy; at a call nothing does, and today that copy is a full one.
E turns edit visibility into a per-package setting, so the same code reads differently from project to project and examples teach the hidden form.

recommendation.tradeoff: Keep the mark that tells readers something, and drop the one that only repeats what the compiler knows.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: ReadB3. Skill: rli5. Explain, predict and modify passed, and probes confirmed today's errors and the 42 2 draft vault draft output; derive failed because cleanup values, last use, := and :: were undefined outside the detail. The repair defines them in the explainer, adds A's unwritten-move loss to the surface, and states E's default.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: claude-opus. Adversarial model family: claude-opus. Fresh agent: ReadA3. The review showed D-COPY-DEFAULT1 already shares non-last uses, so A's no-copy rule amends it at calls; the cleanup rule missed wrappers, generics and fields, and Swift was miscited. The repair states the amendment, widens the cleanup rule, folds the & and lambda ^ fixes into A, defines one name in two slots, and files two crashes.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Drafted by BallotCallsite for the owner's call-mark question. Ran validate.mjs offline only; no Tower write. The change touches E0209, E0202 and E0224 and the ownership spec, so it uses the full two-reader profile.

Option mapping from the brief: brief A is B here, brief B is C, brief C is D, and brief D is E. Option A is the split the evidence supports, listed first because new ballots list the recommendation as A.

Owner acceptance for A, each a jet check or jet run probe. archive(title) at title's last use compiles and moves. bump(score) to an & parameter is still E0202. show(&score) to a read parameter is refused with a fix. A Session holding a Lock prints release db at the same point with an inferred move and with ^.

More acceptance for A. forward<T> with sink(x) is refused and asks for ^x. pair(t, t) and pair(t, ^t) give a defined error, not a crash. A lambda that moves a capture refuses a second call.

Defects for card #3645 under every option: a nested Close field is never released when its owner moves (ReadA3 probe c1), and pair(t, ^t) crashes the compiler (c4). After ratification, one cutover updates the spec, E0209 and examples, and jet fix removes ^ at argument last uses.

surface.gist: Must a call still write & and ^ when the signature already says the value is edited or taken?
surface.lesson: &T in a signature means a call may change your value, and ^T means it takes the value away. Today the call repeats the mark: bump(&score), archive(^title). The compiler can always work the marks out, so they are for readers. A last use is the final place a name appears. ~x still asks for a copy.

current.note: Today every edit and every hand-over is marked at the call, even at a last use.
current.code:
bump(&score)              // edits score
&tags.push("hot")         // edits tags
kept :: archive(~note)    // copy: note is used later
saved :: archive(^title)  // last use of title

wild.note: Both mark an edited argument and move at a last use with no mark. Hylo marks receiver edits too.
wild.code:
bump(&mut score);            // Rust
let saved = archive(title);  // Rust: moved, no mark
&tags.append("hot")          // Hylo: receiver edit marked
let saved = archive(title)   // Hylo: consumed, no mark

options.name: Mark edits; last use moves unmarked
options.gist: & stays at every edit; a plain value needs no ^ at its last use.
gains: Edits stay visible in any viewer.
Matches how bindings already move.
losses: & still required before the dot: &tags.push.
A move at a last use is not written.
Locks, files and generic values still write ^.

proposed.code:
bump(&score)
&tags.push("hot")
kept :: archive(~note)
saved :: archive(title)   // moves, no ^

options.name: Keep every mark
options.gist: Today's rule: every edit and every hand-over is written.
gains: Everything visible without tools.
losses: ^ repeats what a last use already says.
Arguments differ from bindings, which move unmarked.

proposed.code:

&tags.push("hot")
kept :: archive(~note)
saved :: archive(^title)

options.name: Marks optional
options.gist: The compiler reads the signature; editor hints show its choice.
gains: Least typing at every call.
losses: Edits invisible outside an editor.
A callee change can silently edit callers.

proposed.code:

tags.push("hot")
kept :: archive(~note)
saved :: archive(title)

options.name: Compiler picks copies too
options.gist: No marks; a reused value is shared, a full copy today.

losses: Silent copies at calls.
Edits invisible outside an editor.

tags.push("hot")

saved :: archive(title)

options.name: Optional, with a package switch
options.gist: Like C, but a package can make the marks required.
gains: Each team picks its own rule.
losses: Code reads differently per package.
The default still hides edits.

recommendation.why: The compiler needs no call mark. Readers most need to see which calls change a value, and most peers mark edited arguments. Jet already moves unmarked at a last use elsewhere.
gains: Visible, honest edits in any viewer.
One fewer mark in common code.
Generated code unchanged.

losses.loss: & stays at every edit.
losses.mitigation: The error writes the fix for you.

losses.loss: A move at a last use is not written.
losses.mitigation: A later use is still an error; locks and files keep ^.

whyNot.reason: Keeps a mark that adds nothing at a last use.
Hides edits from readers without an editor.
A call could copy silently; nothing on the line shows it.
Makes visibility a per-package setting.

attempts: Make & optional with editor hints (option C); rejected because review pages and plain diffs show no hints.
Require & only on arguments and drop it on receivers; not adopted here because D-CAP-RECEIVER1=D ratified one rule for both.

designAway.loss: An inferred move is not visible in plain text.

Keep ^ only where cleanup timing is visible: values with cleanup, wrappers holding them, fields and type parameters; kept.

decisions.title: Spelling copy and move as words: x.copy(), copy(x) or copy x
decisions.situation: You decided on 2026-10-06 that copies and moves become words. Jet moves a value at its last use with nothing written, and the ~x copy mark and ^x move mark go away. That frees the ~ and ^ symbols. You named two forms, x.copy() and copy(x), and the same pair for move. This vote picks one form for both words; the signature word for a take parameter defaults to move T unless you override it. We recommend the method form, x.copy() and x.move(), because Jet already ships .copy() on its collections and a method chains with no parentheses.
decisions.gist: Should a deliberate copy and an early move be written x.copy() and x.move(), copy(x) and move(x), or copy x and move x?
decisions.lesson: A copy is a second, independent value: changing one never changes the other. A move hands a value to a new owner, and the old name can no longer be used. Jet already moves a value at its last use, the final place a name appears. You write move only to end a name early, for example to release a lock at an exact line. You write copy only when you want a snapshot that stays the same while the original changes.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. x := 1 makes a name you may change later, and x :: 1 makes one you may not. &board.push(2) marks a call that changes board. A place is a name with optional fields and indexes after it, such as game.boards[0].cells. A take parameter is a parameter that keeps the value it is given. Today it is written name: ^T.

Some values run cleanup when they are released, such as a file that closes or a lock that unlocks. impl Lock.Close gives Lock a cleanup step, and move self means close takes the lock itself. Cleanup runs when the value's last owner finishes, which for a local is the end of its scope.

An early move. A move statement with nothing receiving it, such as held.move() on its own line, ends held there and runs its cleanup at that line. Without it, held would be released at the end of run, after everything else printed.

When a copy is required. before :: board makes a live view, not a value, so changing board while before is still used is error E0212, whose fix asks for a copy. A field or index read, such as game.boards[0].cells, already gives its own value, so a copy there is allowed but never required.

Beginner path: you rarely write either word. When Jet stops you with E0212, the fix adds the copy word. You write the move word when you want a value gone at a chosen line.

Expert path: a written move is checked. A later use of the name is an error, so an edit that adds a use cannot silently turn the move into a shared value. Under a policy that forbids hidden copies, a reviewer searches one word.

Shared by every option. The words behave the same in every option; only their look changes. Parameters that take a value say move in the signature by default: name: move T and move self. Every ~ and ^ in Jet's code is rewritten in one cutover.
decisions.story: Mia snapshots a game board before a move, so she can undo it. Later she wants a database lock released at an exact line, not at the end of the function. She looks for one obvious way to say make my own copy and one for give this up now, in a language where both are usually automatic.
decisions.detail:
Owner direction, 2026-10-06 04:15: copies move from the ~x mark to a word, x.copy() or copy(x). Moves become implicit at a last use, and an explicit early move is spelled x.move() or move(x). This frees the ~ and ^ symbols. This ballot asks which form. A keyword form, copy x and move x, is added because Swift chose it after trying the function form.

What the direction already settles. D-COPY-DEFAULT1=A (ratified 2026-09-29) made a last use move and a non-last use share; the first write then copies. The open D-CALLSITE-MARK1 (card #4706) asked whether calls still write ^. The owner has now answered its ^ half: no mark at a last use. Its & half, whether edits stay marked, is still that ballot's vote.

D-CALLSITE-MARK1's option A also kept a written move for values with cleanup at take parameters. If that rule survives, the written move uses the form chosen here. The open D-COPY-WORD1 (card #4620) asked x.copy() against ~x. The owner's direction answers it, so this ballot replaces it, and D-COPY-WORD1 should be closed as superseded.

Amended law. D-SHAPE-COPY1=A (~x) and the ^ call mark of D-MEM1 and D-CAP-RECEIVER1=D are amended. D-SIGIL-ALGEBRA1=B already voted to retire infix a ^ b (power) and a ~| b (exclusive or), though that is not built yet. After both cutovers neither symbol has any meaning left. D-SIGIL-FREED1 decides what, if anything, they mean next.

Every current use of ~ and ^, from the lexer and parser (crates/jet-lexer/src/Lexer/Scan.rs:715-726; crates/jet-parser/src/Parser/Expressions/binary_unary.rs:785-887). First, ~expr copies any value, a fresh one included: ~make() compiles. Second, ^place moves a name or field; before a method call it takes the receiver, as in ^buf.seal(). An index cannot move: ^xs[1] is E0225, the element stays in its list.

Third, f(^x) marks a take argument (calls.rs:171). Fourth, name: ^T and ^self declare take parameters (functions_params.rs:1086 and 1113). Fifth, task ^name { } moves one name into a task (primary.rs:978-987). Sixth, defer close(^res) is the only defer form, and it ends res at the defer line (control.rs:2446-2465). Infix ^, ^=, ~| and ~|= are retired by D-SIGIL-ALGEBRA1. No ~ or ^ appears in patterns or types.

Census, 2026-10-06, comments and strings stripped, every .jet file in Examples, Core, Compiler and Jetpack (script $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/BallotSigils/census.mjs, Jetpack counts from ReadSigilsA's rerun). Prefix ~ copies: 360, 968, 663 and 567, 2,558 in all. Take parameters: about 340 ^T and 71 ^self. There are also 23 defer close(^...) lines and 4 task ^name captures.

The built-in .copy() method already exists on lists, maps, sets, Bits, text and byte buffers (Collections.rs). It has 16 uses in Examples and 6 in Jetpack, such as xs.copy().equal(xs). D-COPY-WORD1's classifier found that most ~ sites copy a name that is never used again or only read again, so a move or a share would behave the same.

Probes on the dev candidate dev-595e0dca3, jet run, 2026-10-06 ($JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/BallotSigils/probes; reviewer probes in scratch/ReadB3 and scratch/ReadSigilsA). Today's spelling of the ballot program prints using db, release db, after release, 2 3 vault (p17). Without close(^held), release db prints last, at the end of run (p18). A bare statement ^held is E0003 today (q9).

More probes. Without the copy, before :: board then &board.push(2) is E0212 (p12). A field or index snapshot needs no copy: before :: game.boards[0].cells then a push prints 2 3 (ReadB3 m1). archive(game.titles[0]) also compiles while the field is still read (p14). ~xs.len() copies the length, not the list (p6).

Name probes. A user type may declare fn Player.move(&self, dx: Int), and a free fn move(p: &Player, dx: Int) compiles too; the program prints 6 (p4). A field named move is legal, and move := 1 is a legal local. fn Point.copy(self) and a field named copy are E0003, because copy is still a keyword (p3, q4). copy(xs) gives E0991, which teaches ~ (p5).

Name collisions in Jet's own code. No type in Examples, Core or Compiler declares a copy or move method, and no code calls .move(). Core has module functions files.move(from, to), files.copy(from, to) and math.copy (Core/files/files.jet:1119; CoreModuleExports.rs:355,399). The Compiler uses move as a loop variable in X64/Select.jet. Jet has no uniform call syntax (D-UFCS1 declined).

Form A, the method. x.copy() and x.move() are recognized in sema after name resolution. On a value, they are the copy and the hand-over; on a module, files.move(from, to) is still the module function. A user method named copy or move on a type is an error with a rename fix, such as step or walk. Renaming a published method is a breaking API change, flagged by the API snapshot check.

More on A. A field named move stays legal, and x.move without parentheses reads that field. A field named copy becomes legal, since copy stops being a keyword. x.copy() works on any value, fresh ones included; x.move() works on a name or field only, so xs[0].move() and make().move() are E0225.

Form B, the function. copy(x) and move(x) become reserved names in the prelude, the names every file sees, recognized the same way. A user's free fn move must be renamed, and use core.files.{copy} collides; methods named move stay legal. The built-in .copy() method retires, and jet fix rewrites its 22 uses to copy(x), so there is one spelling.

Swift on B. Swift's first SE-0366 draft used move(x) as a special function and dropped it. The authors said a function that accepts only certain expressions and does nothing at run time is unusual (se0366, Alternatives considered). SE-0377 also rejected a library copy function because it pollutes the global names.

Form C, the keyword. copy x and move x are contextual keywords, as Swift does and as Jet's own shared expr does (D-CONC-SHARE1). The word is an operator only when a name follows on the same line. So move(x), hero.move(2), files.move(a, b) and fn move(...) stay ordinary calls and names, and no user code is renamed.

More on C. The operand is a name followed by fields and, for copy, indexes, with no calls. So copy xs.len() is E0225 with a fix that writes (copy xs).len(), as Swift also limits the operand. A fresh value needs no keyword. The built-in .copy() method retires, and jet fix rewrites its 22 uses.

The parameter word. A type position cannot hold a method or call, so every option uses a word there. The default is move T and move self, so a signature and a call use the same word. Swift's SE-0366 authors liked a parameter word that matches the operator. The owner may override the word with a comment on this ballot.

Alternatives to move T, with precedent. take T is Jet's own term in error text, but Swift dropped take because it is confused with a call taking its arguments (SE-0377). consume T is Swift's choice. sink T is Hylo's, and owned T was Mojo's. Keeping ^T in signatures is possible too, but then ^ is not freed.

New rules, not only spelling. First, a move statement with nothing receiving it ends the name and runs its cleanup at that line, as close(^held) does today and Swift's consume x does. Second, a written move of a captured name inside a lambda moves it in when the lambda is made, so calling it twice is an error. Today such a lambda runs twice (ReadA3 probe p16).

More new rules. Third, a task or lambda never sees a last use of a name it captures, so an unwritten capture is shared, as today; writing the move word moves it in. task ^name { } retires. Fourth, defer close followed by the move word ends the name at the defer line, as today; defer close(res) with no word stays an error.

Formatter and migration. jet fmt prints only the chosen form and never adds or removes a word. After the cutover, ~ and ^ are teaching errors whose fix writes the chosen word, until D-SIGIL-FREED1 decides. One cutover runs jet fix over Examples, Core, Compiler, Jetpack and tests, rewriting every ~x, ^x, ^T and ^self one for one.

The second pass. jet fix then removes a written move at a proven last use of a whole local without cleanup, never a field take, a type parameter or a value with cleanup. It also removes a copy when no write reaches either side while both are live, since the share behaves the same. Lambdas that move a capture and run twice stop compiling, which is the intended fix.

Defects found during review, for cards under any option. A copy of a [[Int]] list, written ~xs or xs.copy(), still sees a later &xs[0].push(9), so inner lists are shared (ReadSigilsA q5). A struct with a [[Int]] field crashes jet run in its derived compare (p1c). Examples/ffi/workflows/external-package/app.jet reads image.width after defer close(^image) [INFERENCE: predicted E0121, not run].

options.name: Method form: x.copy() and x.move()
options.detail:
A copy is written x.copy() on any value, and an early move x.move() on a name or field. Both read left to right and chain like any method: board.copy().len(). Editor completion after the dot lists both with their documentation. The existing built-in .copy() on collections becomes the one copy spelling for every type.

The cost: copy and move become reserved method names on every type, so a user's fn Player.move must be renamed, and a published one breaks callers. Module functions such as files.move(from, to) stay, because they are resolved as module members.
options.technical: Sema recognizes the two method names after name resolution and produces Expr::Copy and Expr::Place(Take), so no runtime method exists. A user method declaration of either name gets a teaching error with a rename fix. x.move() on a fresh value or an index keeps E0225. A move statement with no receiver lowers to the move plus an immediate drop. Lowering is otherwise unchanged. Syntax.rs replaces SIGIL_COPY and SIGIL_MOVE with the two names and adds the contextual parameter word.

options.name: Function form: copy(x) and move(x)
options.detail:
A copy is written copy(x) and an early move move(x). The parentheses show exactly what is copied, and the words read like C++ std::move. Chaining wraps the call: copy(board).len(). The built-in .copy() method retires, so copy(x) is the one spelling.

The cost: copy and move become reserved prelude names, the names every file sees. A user's free fn move must be renamed, and use core.files.{copy} collides; methods named move, such as hero.move(2), stay legal.
options.technical: Sema recognizes the two reserved call names after name resolution and produces Expr::Copy and Expr::Place(Take); no function value exists, so neither can be passed as a value or shadowed. A user free function of either name gets a teaching error with a rename fix. jet fix rewrites the 22 built-in .copy() calls. Lowering is unchanged. Syntax.rs replaces the two sigils with the reserved call names and adds the contextual parameter word.

options.name: Keyword form: copy x and move x
options.detail:
A copy is written copy x and an early move move x, as Swift writes copy x and consume x. Both are contextual: the word is an operator only when a name follows on the same line. So fn move(...), move(x) and hero.move(2) stay ordinary names and calls, and no user code needs a rename. The parameter word move T reads the same as the operator.

The cost: the operand is a name with fields, or indexes for copy, and no calls, so chaining needs parentheses: (copy board).len(). The built-in .copy() method retires, so copy x is the one spelling.
options.technical: Two contextual keywords, recognized only before an identifier on the same line, like shared expr (D-CONC-SHARE1). copy becomes contextual instead of fully reserved, so fn Point.copy and a field named copy become legal. An operand with a call, such as copy xs.len(), is E0225 with a fix that writes (copy xs).len(). jet fix rewrites the 22 built-in .copy() calls. Lowering is unchanged.

comparisons.note: Copy is an ordinary method, a.copy(), used throughout its specification. A sink parameter consumes its argument at a last use with no mark. That is option A for copy.
comparisons.code:
fun current() -> Int { x.copy() }
let saved = archive(title)   // sink: consumed

comparisons.note: copy x (SE-0377) and consume x (SE-0366) are contextual keywords, operators only before a name; consume x alone ends x. SE-0366 first proposed move(x) as a special function and dropped it. That is option C.
std::move(x) is a library function, which is option B's shape. Copies are implicit, the opposite of Jet.
comparisons.code:
auto saved = board;
hand_off(std::move(lock));

comparisons.note: Moves are implicit, and a later use is an error. A copy is the method .clone(). An early end is the function drop(x).
comparisons.code:
let saved = board.clone();
drop(lock);   // released here

comparisons.note: A postfix x^ transfers ownership, the mark Jet is giving up (Mojo manual, Ownership).
comparisons.code: hand_off(lock^)

recommendation.why: A keeps the form you proposed and the .copy() Jet already ships, and it chains with no parentheses. C is close: it is shorter and reserves no user names, but it adds two contextual keywords to expressions and needs parentheses to chain. The method's one real cost, reserving move as a method name, hits no code in Jet's repository.
gains: Matches the owner's proposal and the built-in .copy() already used in examples.
Chains with no parentheses: board.copy().len().
Editor completion after a dot shows both words with their documentation.

losses.loss: move becomes a reserved method name on every type, so a game's fn Player.move must be renamed, and a published one breaks its callers.
losses.mitigation: The declaration error offers a rename such as step or walk, and the API snapshot check flags the break. No type in Examples, Core or Compiler declares move today.

losses.loss: x.move() looks like an ordinary method but is a compiler-checked hand-over that only accepts a name or field.
losses.mitigation: copy is reserved the same way today. Hover explains both, and xs[0].move() or make().move() keeps the E0225 message.

losses.loss: The method form is longer than the keyword form: held.move() against move held.
losses.mitigation: Both words are rare after the cutover, because its second pass removes moves and copies the compiler proves unneeded.

whyNot.reason: B reserves two free function names that look like real functions but cannot be passed as values. Swift tried move(x) and dropped it for that reason.
C is shorter and renames nothing, but it adds two contextual keywords to expressions, needs parentheses to chain, and retires the .copy() method examples already use.

recommendation.tradeoff: Reserve one more method name in exchange for the form you proposed, which chains and matches today's .copy().

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: ReadB3. Skill: rli5. A probe showed a field snapshot needs no copy and the written move sat at a last use; the repair snapshots a whole name and shows a real early release.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: claude-opus. Adversarial model family: claude-opus. Fresh agent: ReadSigilsA. It found C's stated surprise ruled out by C's own rule, the parameter word and release-now unstated and index moves wrong; the repair fixes each.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Drafted by BallotSigils for the owner's copy and move direction. Ran validate.mjs offline only; no Tower write. The change touches Syntax.rs, both parsers, the formatter and every example, so it uses the full two-reader profile. D-COPY-WORD1 (card #4620) asks the same copy question and should be closed as superseded when this is posted. D-CALLSITE-MARK1's options should be restated in words.

Owner acceptance for A, each a jet run probe. The A program prints using db, release db, after release, 2 3 vault, today's output for today's spelling (probes/p17). ~x and ^x are teaching errors whose fix writes .copy() and .move(). fn Player.move is refused with a rename fix, while files.move(from, to) and a field named move still work.

More acceptance. held.move() followed by a use of held is E0121. xs[0].move() and make().move() are E0225. A lambda that moves a capture refuses a second call. The parameter word is move T unless the owner overrides it.

After ratification, one cutover replaces SIGIL_COPY and SIGIL_MOVE in Syntax.rs, the lexer, both parsers, formatter, fix-its, docs and every example. It also deletes the stale ~T comment at core_surface.rs:371. jet fix rewrites one for one, then its second pass removes unneeded moves and copies. Proof: identical goldens before and after jet fix.

surface.gist: Should copy and early move be x.copy() and x.move(), copy(x) and move(x), or copy x and move x?
surface.lesson: A copy is an independent second value. A move hands a value over, and the old name is gone. Jet already moves at a last use with nothing written. You write move only to end a name early, such as releasing a lock now, and copy only for a snapshot.

current.note: Today a copy is ~, a move is ^, a take parameter is ^T, and releasing early needs close(^held).

decisions.title: How 130 Rust leaves with unusual scope labels enter the Rust-exit registry
decisions.situation: Jet is removing Rust from its toolchain, and every remaining Rust function that Core still calls must be listed in one checked registry with its removal condition. Agents recorded these functions in scratch notes, and 130 of them carry labels the registry cannot accept. Some notes disagree with each other, others say compiler primitive, seed-only or waiting on an owner decision. The registry accepts only two kinds, leaf and port. We recommend mapping all 130 onto those two kinds with one fixed rule, keeping each original label in the removal note.
decisions.gist: How should the 130 recorded Rust functions whose scope is neither leaf nor port enter the checked Rust-exit registry?
decisions.lesson: The registry has one row per Rust function that Core still calls. Each row says whether it is a leaf (raw host code that stays until a native replacement exists) or a port (code that will be rewritten in Jet), plus a removal condition. A check fails on any unlisted function. Scratch notes gave 130 functions other labels, so they cannot enter as written.
decisions.story: An agent removes a Rust helper for float powers and finds the registry check failing on 130 functions it never touched. The scratch notes call them compiler primitives, seed-only, or owner-gated, and 54 notes disagree between leaf and port. The agent cannot tell which label is right, so nothing gets admitted and the guard stays red for everyone.
decisions.inWild:
# Go's move off C kept one list of remaining C files, each with a reason,
# and deleted the list when the last file went (Go 1.5, 2015).
# Rust's src/tools/tidy keeps allowlists with one entry and reason per exception.
decisions.detail:
Source: card #4742 and the FixTooling h4742 research note (h4742-rust-leaves-missing.md, unmapped.tsv). Registry: Tools/agent/rust-leaves.tsv, checked by Tools/agent/rust-exit.mjs. Its parser admits only the scopes leaf and port (rust-exit.mjs:78).

The 130 SCOPE-UNRESOLVED ids, by recorded label. Conflicting rows: leaf / port 53 and port / leaf 1. Owner-gated: D-TRANSFORM-IDENTITY1 25, owner-gate 1, owner-gated native Float specialization 2. Compiler-owned primitives: compiler-seam 16, exact-Int primitive 7, leaf layout binding only 7, machine Float bitcast, projection, power and hypot 5, scalar-exact leaf 2. Also 5 compiler-owned projections and intrinsics in core.encoding. Seed-only: 6 (seed verification, native-seed carrier, dead seed glue, bootstrap).

Rule under A. A conflicting row becomes port when a Core.jet dispatcher exists, else leaf, the rule already used for unscoped rows. Every other row becomes leaf. Its removal condition starts with a fixed tag: intrinsic:, seed: or gated:<decision>, followed by the original label text.

Flag for Main: D-TRANSFORM-IDENTITY1 has no Tower record (tower decision show fails), so 25 gated rows cite a decision that does not exist yet.

Context: the check already fails at base for other reasons (520 unregistered dispatchers, 352 changed dispatchers, six areas over their line ceilings). This vote settles only these 130. The whole registry retires when the last Rust leaves.

options.name: Map all 130 onto leaf or port with one rule
options.detail: Conflicts resolve by the existing dispatcher rule. Compiler primitives, seed-only code and owner-gated rows become leaf rows whose removal note starts with a fixed tag and keeps the original label. No new registry kind is added, and every one of the 130 is checked from now on.
options.code:
# rust-leaves.tsv rows (7 columns, abridged)
core.math.decimal.small_float    ...  intrinsic: machine Float power primitive  ...  leaf
core.math.int_abs_seed           ...  seed: seed/verification only              ...  leaf
core.math.ScreenPoint.mixed.add  ...  gated:D-TRANSFORM-IDENTITY1 owner-gated ... ...  leaf
$ node Tools/agent/rust-exit.mjs --check   # these 130 now covered

options.name: Add new registry kinds
options.detail: The registry gains kinds such as intrinsic, seed and gated, and the checker learns them. Each kind is visible as a column value, not a note prefix. It adds parser rules and checks to a registry that is deleted at the Rust exit.
options.code:
core.math.decimal.small_float    ...  intrinsic
core.math.int_abs_seed           ...  seed
core.math.ScreenPoint.mixed.add  ...  gated

options.name: Admit only the 54 conflicting rows now
options.detail: Resolve the leaf-versus-port conflicts by the dispatcher rule and admit those 54. The other 76 stay out until their owner gates and compiler work settle. The guard keeps reporting them as unregistered.
options.code:
$ node Tools/agent/rust-exit.mjs --check
# core.math.decimal.small_float, core.math.int_abs_seed, ... stay unregistered
# 76 such ids remain

comparisons.note: Rust's tidy tool keeps plain allowlists: one entry per exception, with the reason in a comment beside it.
comparisons.code: src/tools/tidy/src/deps.rs: EXCEPTIONS

recommendation.why: Every one of the 130 becomes checked today, no original label is lost, and the short-lived registry gains no new rules.
recommendation.tradeoff: The scope column says leaf for compiler primitives; the removal tag carries the finer kind and is easy to search.

whyNot.reason: It grows the checker for a registry that is deleted when Rust leaves.
It leaves 76 functions unchecked and the guard red with no end date.

losses.loss: Finer kinds live in a note prefix, not a column.
losses.mitigation: Fixed tags (intrinsic:, seed:, gated:) make every kind searchable in one grep.

decisions.title: Honest effects on public jobs and CSV functions
decisions.situation: Jet function signatures say which outside resources a call may touch, such as files, the environment or a database. Several public jobs and CSV functions performed that work without declaring it, so the checker rejected them and their effect lists were corrected. Callers need those lists to know whether a function fits their own resource restrictions. You choose truthful declarations, moving the work into separate calls, or removing these public functions; we recommend retaining the corrected effects.
decisions.gist: Should public jobs and CSV functions declare the resources they actually touch?
decisions.lesson: An effect list states what a function can do outside its local calculation. The checker rejects hidden database, environment or file work. A lists the real effects, B moves the work into separate calls, and C removes the functions. Callers must obey whatever effects remain.
decisions.explainer: An effect declaration is a promise to callers, not permission to hide behavior in a helper. Correcting a declaration may require callers to update their own effect lists. A pure planning interface is a different public design.
decisions.story: Maya reads a job function's signature before using it in restricted code. She needs to know whether that call may access her files, environment or database.
decisions.detail: The source ballot identifies seven jobs functions and four CSV functions whose DB, Env or FS declarations were corrected. Extra Time.Wait entries had already been removed. The code below uses the existing core.encoding.csv.query interface to illustrate FS propagation; it is not a claim that every jobs function has the same effect list.

options.name: Keep the actual effects listed
options.detail: Retain database, environment and filesystem effects wherever the public function really uses them. Preserve the current operations and update callers to carry the required effects.
options.technical: Use each affected function's actual DB, Env and FS set; do not reintroduce unnecessary Time.Wait effects. Failures retain current T E! syntax.

options.name: Move outside work into separate calls
options.detail: Make public planning functions free of those resource effects. Return plans that callers explicitly execute through separate effectful functions, changing how jobs and CSV operations are used.
options.technical: Separate pure planning values from DB, Env or FS execution. Callers invoke the execution step deliberately.

options.name: Remove the affected public functions
options.detail: Make the seven jobs functions and four CSV functions private until a replacement design exists. Their public names disappear rather than gaining truthful effect declarations.
options.technical: Remove the affected public exports and migrate callers; do not leave compatibility aliases.
options.code:
// Affected jobs and CSV names are no longer public.
// Existing callers must migrate or stop using them.

recommendation.why: A tells callers the truth while keeping the existing operations instead of redesigning or removing them.
gains: Callers can see database, environment and filesystem access before making a call.

losses.loss: Affected callers must carry newly explicit resource effects.
losses.mitigation: List the affected callers and update each signature once to match the actual resource access.

whyNot.reason: B requires a new planning/execution API rather than correcting the declarations on today's operations.
C removes working public operations that existing callers may use.

recommendation.tradeoff: Carry honest resource effects through callers instead of hiding access, redesigning the API, or removing operations.

decisions.checkInstructions: Check the affected jobs and CSV signatures against their transitive DB, Env and FS work. Update the caller inventory and verify restrictive callers are rejected correctly. Confirm unnecessary Time.Wait entries remain removed.

surface.gist: Should public functions list the resources they really touch?
surface.lesson: Effects tell callers about outside work. Some jobs and CSV functions hid file, environment or database access and were rejected. A keeps corrected declarations, B separates planning from execution, and C removes the functions. Execution still needs honest effects in every option.

current.note: A CSV call cannot hide its file access.

wild.code: readFile :: FilePath -> IO String

options.gist: Keep operations and correct their resource declarations.
gains: Callers see real outside access.
losses: Caller effect lists may need updates.

options.name: Separate planning and execution
options.gist: Put outside work in an explicit execution call.
gains: Planning can remain free of resource access.
losses: Public operations and callers need redesign.

options.name: Remove public operations
options.gist: Make the affected functions private until redesigned.
gains: No misleading public declarations remain.
losses: Existing public callers lose those operations.

proposed.code: // Affected jobs and CSV functions become private.

recommendation.why: A preserves useful operations and makes their existing resource access visible.
gains: Honest signatures for callers.

losses.loss: Some caller signatures must change.
losses.mitigation: List affected callers and update their actual resource effects once.

whyNot.reason: B changes the API instead of correcting its current promise.
C removes useful public operations.

recommendation.tradeoff: Keep honest effects in caller signatures rather than hide work or remove functions.

decisions.title: A second owner for an open folder handle
decisions.situation: An open folder handle identifies a folder that the program has already checked, rather than looking up its name again. The package resolver needs to give a checker its own handle, but copying today's single-owner resource is rejected. Reopening the path could reach a different folder if the name changes, which breaks that checked identity. You choose handle duplication, borrowed access, or reopening; we recommend one duplication operation that preserves the open folder.
decisions.gist: Should Jet let a program duplicate an open folder handle?
decisions.lesson: A folder handle is an owned resource. Two independent owners need two handles to the same open folder, or one owner must lend access. Reopening a path is different: the name may now identify another folder. A duplicates, B borrows, and C reopens.
decisions.explainer: The important property is folder identity, not merely getting the same path string. A second handle preserves that identity without introducing a new pathname lookup or additional authority.
decisions.story: Bea's package resolver opens and checks a project folder, then gives it to a checker. She needs the checker to hold the same folder even if its name changes.
decisions.inWild:
# Python duplicates an existing descriptor without reopening its pathname.
# https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.dup
second_fd = os.dup(first_fd)
# POSIX dup creates a second descriptor for the same open file description.
# https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/dup.html
# Each descriptor can be closed independently.
decisions.detail: The source ballot's resolver currently attempts to copy its root folder handle. This vote chooses resource ownership, not the name of a path resolver. Directory.duplicate is proposed API, not claimed to exist in the current build.

options.name: Duplicate the held handle
options.detail: Add a fallible operation returning another owned handle to the same open folder. Require the existing filesystem permission and perform no pathname lookup.
options.technical: Proposed Directory.duplicate() uses FS and returns Directory IOError!. Reuse descriptor duplication and preserve independent close behavior.

options.name: Keep one owner and lend access
options.detail: Keep one owned handle and pass borrowed folder views through the resolver and checker APIs. Add no new Core operation, but redesign consumers so they do not retain independent owners.
options.technical: Package compose and member APIs receive borrowed Directory access instead of owned handles.

options.name: Reopen the folder by path
options.detail: Give each consumer a newly opened folder using its pathname. Avoid a duplication operation, but allow the pathname to resolve to a different folder between opens.
options.technical: Consumers call Directory.open(path) instead of duplicating the held descriptor.
options.code:
second :: Directory.open(root_path)
// A new pathname lookup may reach another folder.

recommendation.why: A preserves the already-checked folder and independent ownership with one small operation, without reopening a name or expanding authority.
gains: The resolver and checker retain the same checked folder independently.

losses.loss: Core gains one folder operation to maintain.
losses.mitigation: Reuse descriptor duplication and test independent closure plus preservation of the held folder when its path changes.

whyNot.reason: B preserves identity but requires a larger ownership redesign across package consumers.
C can reopen a different folder after a pathname change, losing the checked identity.

recommendation.tradeoff: Add one tested resource operation instead of changing consumer ownership or repeating a potentially different path lookup.

decisions.checkInstructions: Test duplicate handles close independently and still refer to the originally opened folder after its pathname changes. Confirm duplication has the existing FS authority requirement and propagates IOError failures.

surface.gist: Should a checked folder handle have a second independent owner?
surface.lesson: An open handle holds one specific folder. Copying it is rejected today. A duplicates the handle, B lends access from one owner, and C reopens the name. A name can change; a duplicate retains the checked folder.

current.note: Copying the owned folder resource is rejected.
current.code:
second :: root.copy()
// Rejected: folder handle has one owner.

wild.note: Descriptor duplication preserves the open resource; source is in the long form.
wild.code: second_fd = os.dup(first_fd)

options.name: Duplicate the handle
options.gist: Make another owner of the same open folder.
gains: Preserves checked folder identity.
Each owner closes its own handle.
losses: One new Core operation.

proposed.code:
// Proposed API:
second :: root.duplicate()

options.name: Lend access
options.gist: Keep one owner and pass borrowed views.
gains: No new Core operation.
No repeated pathname lookup.
losses: Package consumers need an ownership redesign.

proposed.code:
check_folder(&root)
// Checker borrows; resolver owns.

options.name: Reopen the name
options.gist: Open the folder path again for each consumer.
gains: Uses ordinary opening.
losses: The name may now identify another folder.

proposed.code: second :: Directory.open(root_path)

recommendation.why: A retains the checked folder without a new name lookup or a broad consumer redesign.
gains: Independent ownership of the same folder.

losses.loss: One more Core operation.
losses.mitigation: Reuse descriptor duplication and test independent close and identity preservation.

whyNot.reason: B changes ownership across the package APIs.
C can reopen a different folder and lose the checked identity.

recommendation.tradeoff: Add one operation to preserve identity and independent ownership.

decisions.title: Services, workflows and HTTP server on the native runtime
decisions.situation: Jet's service engine stores jobs durably, workflows track their progress, and the HTTP server handles web requests. These implementations still depend on Rust, so a native program using them fails during linking instead of serving requests or reporting delivery status. This blocks service authors even though the HTTP server can be ported separately from the larger job engine. You choose a complete port, continued exclusion, or HTTP first; we recommend restoring HTTP first while keeping the other gaps explicit.
decisions.gist: Should native Jet restore the HTTP server before the service and workflow engine?
decisions.lesson: An HTTP server handles web requests. Durable services and workflows also track jobs and stored progress. All are missing natively. A ports everything, B leaves everything unavailable, and C ports HTTP first. C still owes separate service, workflow and WebSocket ports.
decisions.explainer: The HTTP server does not require the complete durable service engine. A narrower port can restore web serving while leaving unavailable APIs honestly rejected. WebSocket remains outside that first HTTP slice.
decisions.story: Doris runs a web service that also checks background-job delivery. Her native build cannot serve requests today; she wants HTTP restored without confusing it with completed job support.
decisions.detail: The source ballot reports ServiceAuthority.rs at about 3,250 lines and services/workflow backing at about 7,300 lines. Nine runtime functions cover delivery queries, durable sends, retries, dead letters and workflow results. Service delivery providers were ported in 98f69b7ba. Relevant evidence is tests/services_runtime.rs and tests/cases/services_runtime/. These are source-ballot estimates, not measurements of a Jet port.

options.name: Port all families now
options.detail: Port service authority, the services tree, workflows, HTTP and WebSocket together. All public behavior returns natively after the complete port; the cutover waits for the larger effort.
options.technical: Preserve service signatures, replay, retention, file locks, channels and delivery state. Port HTTP routing, streaming parsing, response writing and WebSocket guards.

options.name: Keep all families unavailable
options.detail: Leave these families outside the native runtime pack. Programs using them fail with a missing-provider error. The cutover proceeds without them, matching the source ballot's current state.
options.technical: Nine service/workflow symbols remain unbound. HTTP routing and WebSocket remain Rust-only; E2104 reports missing providers.

options.name: Port the HTTP server first
options.detail: Port HTTP routing, request parsing, response writing and route caching first. Restore web serving while services, workflows and WebSocket remain unavailable pending their separate ports.
options.technical: Add native HTTP serve-once and dispatch support with route-cache validation and root control. Service/workflow symbols remain unbound; WebSocket is not included in this slice.

recommendation.why: C restores the HTTP server independently of the larger durable service engine, while keeping unfinished features visible.
gains: Native web serving returns before the full service engine is ported.

losses.loss: Services, workflows and WebSocket remain unavailable natively.
losses.mitigation: Retain explicit refusals, list the missing service symbols, and track the separate ports without claiming those features work.

whyNot.reason: A ties web serving to completion of the entire service and workflow engine.
B keeps HTTP unavailable even though its narrower port can restore web serving separately.

recommendation.tradeoff: Restore HTTP first while clearly excluding services, workflows and WebSocket until their own ports complete.

decisions.checkInstructions: Restore HTTP routing, route caching, streaming request parsing, root control and response-writing tests. Keep service and workflow exclusions explicit. Error timing follows D-NATIVE-GAPS1; this vote does not override that diagnostic decision.

surface.gist: Should native Jet restore HTTP before services and workflows?
surface.lesson: HTTP serves web requests. Services and workflows also store jobs and their progress. None works natively today. A ports all families, B leaves them unavailable, and C restores HTTP first. C does not restore WebSocket or durable jobs.

current.note: Native web serving fails during linking.
current.code:

decisions.title: Whether formal proof closeout must precede cutover
decisions.situation: Formal closeout combines the compiler's separate Lean proofs and checks the standing release qualification, rather than merely running native tests. That gate is currently reported as not met and deferred under the owner's directive, even when the native suites pass. A release can therefore claim those test results but cannot claim completed proof composition or the qualification it has not earned. You choose continued explicit deferral or requiring closeout before cutover; we recommend retaining deferral without hiding or weakening the recorded gap.
decisions.gist: Should cutover proceed with formal closeout explicitly not met, or wait for its completion?
decisions.lesson: Tests exercise examples; composed proofs support a stronger claim over the compiler. The formal gate is not met today. A keeps it visibly deferred while native suites gate cutover, and B requires it first. Neither choice may treat passing tests as completed proof composition.
decisions.explainer: The receipt must distinguish native test success from formal proof discharge. Deferral changes the cutover condition, not the truth of the unmet gate. Reporting the gap does not eliminate its assurance cost.
decisions.story: Doris prepares a release after native tests pass. She must tell users that formal composition remains uncompleted, rather than letting a green suite imply a proof claim it does not support.

# That is a precedent for precise proof scope, not evidence that Jet's gate passed.
# Lean checks theorem declarations against its kernel.
# https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/axioms_and_computation.html
decisions.detail: Directive #59 and Docs/spec/reference/jetpack-epoch5.md record NOT MET, deferred per owner #59. Commit 3d77da6f6 keeps formal closeout explicitly deferred outside the native cutover suite; there is no skip option. D-COMPILER-PROOF-TOOLS1=A pins Lean 4.29.1 via ce42a475a. The source ballot records the 07:00 goal as unmet on #4717 and attaches this vote there. Stage equivalence and suites do not discharge Lean or the standing safety-net qualification.

decisions.situation: The cutover deletes the Rust implementation. We recommend retiring the first three and keeping sandbox builds on an external rustc until Jet emits WASM natively.

decisions.title: Rust as a performance peer and test oracle after the cutover
decisions.situation: After the cutover, no part of the Jet compiler, runtime or user programs is written in Rust. The performance gate still races Jet against Rust programs, and some tests compare Jet's answers with Rust reference programs. You choose whether those Rust programs stay as outside measuring sticks. We recommend keeping Rust only on the measured side, exactly like the Go, C++ and Zig peers, and deleting the five Rust test files nothing runs anymore.
decisions.gist: May Rust stay as a measured peer and reference program outside the Jet product?
decisions.lesson: A peer is a program Jet is raced against; it never ships with Jet. A keeps Rust only where it is measured and deletes dead Rust tests. B removes every Rust peer. C also rewrites the peer launcher in Jet.
decisions.explainer: The performance gate names Rust with a 1.05 parity band and forbids dropping a peer. Removing Rust peers removes those required cells. Keeping them puts no Rust into the compiler, runtime or user programs. The Rust compiler and Cargo stay installed in the dev shell under every option, because two ratified features call them: user Rust libraries and sandbox plugin builds.
decisions.story: Sam runs the performance dashboard after the cutover. It still builds the Rust n-body peer with Cargo, and he needs to know whether that is allowed or a leftover to delete.
decisions.inWild:

# https://benchmarksgame-team.pages.debian.net/benchmarksgame/
rustc -C opt-level=3 nbody.rs
# Zig's own perf tracking compares against C built by an external compiler.
# https://github.com/ziglang/gotta-go-fast
decisions.detail:
Revised 2026-10-10 because the owner did not ratify the posted A. The posted A listed one loss: the dev shells still install rustc and cargo. That loss does not belong to this choice. The default shell keeps cargo and rustc under every option, because D-FFI-RUST1=A builds user Rust helpers with Cargo and D-RUST-EMIT1=A keeps sandbox plugin builds on an installed rustc. The posted C (a separate peer shell) therefore removed nothing and is replaced.

Inventory on the cutover-prep branch (git ls-files '*.rs', 171 files). Measured side, kept: Tools/gauntlet (25 peer programs) and Tools/perf (17 peers, including one Cargo crate). Also kept: Tools/agent-eval (15 peers and reference oracles), tests/compiled_workloads/adapters/peer (4 peers), and the peer launcher Tools/ci/compiled-workload-peer-launcher.rs.

Dead, deleted by A: Compiler/JetRuntime/Tests/thread-rust-fixture.rs and utf8-corpus.rs are retired. Their runners report UNCOVERED and never invoke rustc (owner #38/#59, Tower #4923). http-body-reference.rs, sentry-ledger-reference.rs and int-hazard-fixture.rs are referenced by no script; only the Tower board names them. The frozen JSON fixtures beside them are data and stay.

Not in scope and governed elsewhere: the RustBridge support crates (D-CUTOVER-HOMES1=A), FFI examples and tests that exercise user Rust libraries (D-FFI-RUST1=A), and the Zed extension (D-ZED-EXT1).

Why the launcher stays with the peers. Tools/ci/compiled-workload-runner.mjs wraps only peer commands in the launcher, inside runMeasured. Its run time is therefore part of every Rust, Go, C++ and Zig peer's measured time. Rewriting it changes every peer number at once and needs a new same-run equality proof, for no product gain. It is peer-side equipment, like the peers' own compilers.

Precedent: the Benchmarks Game builds each language with its own toolchain; Zig's gotta-go-fast compares against C built by an external compiler. Neither project ships the peer toolchains. AGENTS.md Strict performance gate: Jet must beat every matched peer; against Rust, 1.05 is parity; never drop a peer.

decisions.title: The Zed editor extension written in Rust
decisions.situation: Jet's plugin for the Zed editor colors Jet code and starts Jet's language server. Zed only loads plugins built to WebAssembly through its Rust kit, which Jet cannot target yet, so the plugin keeps a 28-line Rust file that just starts the server. You choose whether Zed support stays. We recommend keeping it as a prebuilt plugin that nobody must compile, and rewriting those lines in Jet once Jet can emit WebAssembly plugins.
decisions.gist: Should Zed support stay after the cutover, and in what form?
decisions.lesson: Zed plugins must be WebAssembly built from Rust today. Jet's plugin only starts the language server. A keeps it prebuilt and replaces the Rust once Jet can emit WebAssembly. B drops Zed support. C moves the plugin to its own repository.
decisions.explainer: An editor plugin runs inside the editor, not inside Jet. The compiled plugin file is committed, so installing it needs no Rust tools. Rebuilding is only needed when the 28 lines change, and the install script then fetches Rust on demand. The highlight rules, grammar and settings are plain data files.
decisions.story: Lee edits Jet code in Zed. The plugin starts the language server so Lee gets errors, completion and rename while typing, and Lee needs that to keep working after the cutover.
decisions.inWild:

# https://zed.dev/docs/extensions/developing-extensions

# The Gleam Zed extension is a Rust wrapper for a non-Rust language server.
# https://github.com/zed-extensions/gleam
decisions.detail:
Revised 2026-10-10 because the owner did not ratify the posted A. The posted A kept the plugin but left its Rust with no exit. The posted C (rewrite later) was the exit, offered as a rival instead of a stage. The new A joins them: keep Zed support now, with the same trigger the owner already ratified for sandbox plugin builds in D-RUST-EMIT1=A. Those stay on an installed rustc until Jet emits WebAssembly natively, and so does this shim.

Facts on cutover-prep. Tools/editors/zed holds extension.toml.in, languages/jet/*.scm highlight rules, a prebuilt grammars/jet.wasm, a prebuilt extension.wasm (203 KB), install.sh and wasm-src. wasm-src/src/lib.rs is 28 lines. It returns the literal command jet self lsp and nothing else; Zed's worktree-trust gate decides whether the process may start.

install.sh skips the WebAssembly build when extension.wasm exists. A forced rebuild uses rustup if present, else nix-shell -p rustup, so the Jet dev shell never needs Cargo for Zed. The VS Code extension is JavaScript and unaffected.

Cleanup A includes. README.md still tells contributors to run cargo build for jet, cites crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax.rs, and lists cargo test --test lsp. install.sh prints nix develop -c cargo build. These become the native jet build and native language-server checks.

Why the shim cannot leave today. Zed loads only WebAssembly components that implement its extension interface, and its only supported kit is the zed_extension_api Rust crate. Jet's plugin target lifts a rustc-built module into a component (D-DEP-WASM1=A), so it still needs rustc. A hand-written WebAssembly component would be unreadable and harder to audit than 28 lines of Rust.

Precedent: Zed's Gleam and Elixir extensions are Rust wrappers that start a non-Rust language server. They live in separate repositories because Zed's registry pulls them as git submodules; that is option C.

decisions.title: New homes for the non-Rust assets that lived under crates/
decisions.situation: Deleting crates/ would also delete non-Rust assets the native compiler and Jetpack still embed. The cutover branch moved them. The Prelude .jet and web runtime .js files went to Compiler/Prelude. Batteries, starter components and the jet-dev catalog went into Jetpack packages. Compiler-extension fixtures went to tests/fixtures. The FFI bridge runtimes and support crates went under RustBridge. You choose whether these homes stand. We recommend ratifying them as placed.
decisions.gist: Do the cutover's new directory homes for former crates/ assets stand?
decisions.lesson: Each moved asset now sits beside the package that embeds it. A ratifies the placement, B gives the Prelude its own top-level folder, and C nests each asset under its owning package's Source.
decisions.explainer: Embedded files must live inside the embedding package's source root. Placement changes only paths, not behavior. A later move is another full path cutover.
decisions.story: Mo looks for the diagnostics registry after the cutover. Today it is at Compiler/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet, and Mo needs that path to stay put.

decisions.detail: The Prelude .jet registries, DomRuntime.js and Core/*.js are in Compiler/Prelude/. Batteries are in Jetpack/Provider/Batteries/. Components and the jet-dev catalog are in Jetpack/Environment/. Compiler-extension fixtures are in tests/fixtures/compiler_extension/. FFI bridge runtimes and support crates are in RustBridge/Runtime and RustBridge/Support.
